Accompanied by the commentary composed by Ānandagiri and the Śāṅkara-bhāṣya composed by the venerable Śrī Śaṅkara Bhagavatpāda. Om! Salutations to the Supreme Self. Now begins the Commentary (Bhāṣya) composed by the venerable Śrī Śaṅkara Bhagavatpāda. Om! Salutations to the Supreme Self.
Salutation to that one whose nature is knowledge, from whom the entire world is born, into whom it likewise dissolves, and by whom it is sustained. || 1 ||
I perpetually bow down to those venerable teachers by whom all the Vedāntas were previously explained according to the authority of words, sentences, and means of valid cognition. || 2 ||
Now follows the commentary composed by Ānandagiri:
That which is non-different from light and bliss, which has been revealed by this very [Upaniṣad], and which is explained in the Brāhmaṇa—that shall be the invisible, fearless Brahman. (1)

Desiring to comment upon the *Taittirīyaka Upaniṣad*, which belongs to a specific branch of the *Yajurveda*, the venerable author of the commentary briefly demonstrates— under the guise of an obeisance— the subject matter of that text. This subject is the Brahman,

which is indicated in a general way for those of dull intellect by its "external" definition (*taṭasthalakṣaṇa*) as the cause of the origin and so forth of the world, and is specifically determined by its "essential" definition (*svarūpalakṣaṇa*) such as "truth," "knowledge," and so on.

Regarding the phrase "from which it was born": since the ablative case is common to both the sense of the efficient cause (*nimitta*) and the material cause (*upādāna*), neither type of causality is intended here. Because the dissolution of an effect is necessarily restricted to its own material cause, he specifies its nature as the material cause with the word "in which.
Since the term "from which" is commonly used for an efficient cause—such as merit (*dharma*) and so forth—it refers here to the status of being a non-common (specific) cause.
He said: "By which" refers to that which is of the nature of knowledge; this is an indication of its essential definition (*svarūpalakṣaṇa*). || 1 ||

In order to declare that devotion to the guru is an internal means for the attainment of knowledge, he pays homage to the gurus with the words "by whom" (yaiḥ). [He refers to those] who have explained [the texts] through the discernment of the words, the sentences, and the means of valid cognition such as inference. || 2 ||

In the preceding section, the obligatory rites (*nitya-karma*) were established for the purpose of destroying accumulated demerit (*durita*), and the optional rites (*kāmya-karma*) for those desiring specific fruits. Now, the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*) is introduced in order to eliminate the cause of the undertaking of ritual action.

Desire (*kāma*) must be the cause of ritual action, because it is that which impels one to act; for when desires are absent, there is no activity on the part of those whose desires have been fulfilled.

He indicates his intended purpose with the words "taittirīyaka," etc. One might object: since for one who has mastered the language, the recollection of word-meanings arises from the words themselves, and since the meaning of a sentence consists precisely in the connection (*saṃsarga*) of those word-meanings recalled by the words—and furthermore, since the purport of the Upaniṣads has already been determined by the author of the Sūtras—a separate undertaking of commentary would be useless. Anticipating this objection, he says: "vispaṣṭārtha" (for the sake of clarity), [meaning] for the sake of those of dull intellect who [cannot grasp it] on their own.

The meaning is: for the benefit of those who desire a specific and doubt-free knowledge of all the subjects contained within the Upaniṣads, since it is impossible to remember every single subject [otherwise]. || 3 ||

To dispel the doubt that—since the purpose of the Upaniṣads (liberation) could arise from ritual actions alone, and thus the meaning of the Upaniṣads would already be understood through an inquiry into karma—it is not appropriate to begin a separate commentary—the author states the subject matter of the *karmakāṇḍa*: "The obligatory [rites]," etc.
By using the term "dharma" in the aphorism, "Now, therefore, the inquiry into dharma" (*athāto dharmajijñāsā*), Jaimini has excluded the investigation of established entities (*siddhavastu*).

The meaning is that the Upanishads do not have their purpose exhausted by those [works]. And those ritual acts (karmāṇi) are for the purpose of destroying accumulated demerit; according to the scriptural text, "By dharma one drives away evil," they are also for the sake of the supreme good (niḥśreyasa). Not only are those acts which must necessarily be performed while living, as well as those optional ones (kāmyāni) for those seeking specific fruits, required; even those [optional acts] are not for the sake of the supreme good alone. [As it says: "One desiring heaven, one desiring cattle..."
Because there is no scriptural statement such as "one who desires liberation should do this," the meaning is that the fruit of ritual actions (karma) is indeed worldly existence (saṃsāra).

Having stated the subject matter of the *Karmakāṇḍa*, he now states the subject matter of the *Upaniṣads*, which was not previously investigated there. With the words "Now," etc., he explains that the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*) is commenced in this treatise for the purpose of removing the cause for the undertaking—that is, the performance—of rituals. Therefore, it uproots action along with its root.

The meaning is that the Upaniṣads do not have their purpose already realized [by other means], because they are opposed to the section on ritual action (*karmakāṇḍa*). One might object: "The cause for the performance of ritual action is the injunction (*niyoga*); since that is established by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), there is no contradiction with knowledge (*vidyā*). Anticipating this, he says: "The cause of ritual action... Only this much—that "this is the means for that"—is made known by the scripture. As for who acts toward what, that proceeds from desire alone.

The intention is that there is not even the possibility of an injunction being the motivator [in this case]. The positive concomitance (*anvaya*) has been stated as "when desire exists, there is activity.

He states the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) as "in the absence of desire, there is no activity. Regarding the word "authoritative" (*āpta*): the attainment of the desired object is remembered upon the cessation of desire. (4 ka. ṭa.)

Because one is established in one's own self, further activity is untenable. And when there is the desire for the Self, there is the attainment of all desires; for the Self is indeed Brahman, as the author will state that the knower of That attains the Supreme. Therefore, upon the cessation of ignorance, establishment in one's own self is the attainment of the Supreme. "He finds fearlessness and a firm foundation... this one consisting of bliss..."

This is because of such scriptural passages as, "He approaches the Self," and so forth. Since optional (*kāmya*) and prohibited (*pratiṣiddha*) actions are not undertaken, and since the results of those already begun are exhausted through experience, and since there is an absence of transgression (*pratyavāya*) due to the performance of obligatory (*nitya*) duties, liberation (*mokṣa*) consists simply in abiding in one's own Self without effort. Alternatively, [liberation] is the unsurpassed pleasure denoted by the word "heaven" (*svarga*).
If it is argued that because karma is the cause, liberation comes from karma alone, we say no; for karma is manifold. (1 M)

[This is] the cause. It is not knowledge (*vidyā*). Therefore, raising the objection as to how there can be an undertaking of knowledge for the sake of abandoning the cause that is karma, [the author] says: "And when there is the desire for the Self" (*ātmakāmatve ca*). Through the pleasure derived from an object of desire, there is merely a temporary cessation of desire, but not its eradication; for we observe that the longing for objects arises once again. Even the desire for the Self is unrestrained—[thinking] "The Self alone is the reality, nothing else exists beyond it."

Such a state occurs when there is a desire for the self (*ātmakāmatva*). For, not knowing the self—which is of the nature of non-dual bliss—one desires while perceiving external objects, due to the presence of longing and desire. Therefore, since desire is rooted in ignorance (*avidyā*) regarding the self, the knowledge of the self alone is the cause of its cessation; this is the meaning. Let it be that the knowledge of the self is opposed to desire; now, the knowledge of Brahman is introduced for the purpose of abandoning the causes of ritual action (*karman*).
To the question "How was this stated?", he replies: "The Self. The scriptural passage cited refers to the Supreme Self (paramātman) consisting of bliss.

Thus, having established that the commencement of the commentary on the Upanishads is justified—since its subject matter has not been covered by the ritual section (karmakāṇḍa) and since it aims at the unsurpassable goal of liberation (niḥśreyasa), which cannot be attained through rituals—the author now sets forth the intention of those who argue for the necessity of a new beginning: "Of the optional and the prohibited... and so forth.

The meaning is this: when there is the non-arising of a body for one who has reached the ultimate state, the abiding in one's own true nature (*svarūpa*) constitutes the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*); and since the non-arising of the body will be established simply through the absence of its causes, what is the purpose of undertaking the investigation into the means of knowledge? He states another view: "Or rather" (*athavā*). That very same thing which is the means for attaining heaven, such as the *Jyotiṣṭoma* sacrifice and others, is itself the means for liberation, because [liberation] is unsurpassed bliss; for the referent of the term "heaven" does not exist anywhere other than in liberation.

The meaning is that since suffering necessarily arises when there is a body, [suffering] will necessarily arise in future existence as well. [The author] refutes the view that [the cause of suffering] consists of the karma of a single lifetime by means of the words "No," and so forth.

Although a seeker of liberation (*mumukṣu*) might not initiate any action—whether desirable or forbidden—in the present body, nevertheless, because it is possible for many [karmas] to have been accumulated (*sañcita*), the absence of a cause [for future suffering] is unestablished (*asiddha*). For the most part, all [karmas] remain unmanifest.
Since the atoms, having come together, initiate a single body, and because [the body] is exhausted through the experience of all [the atoms], accumulated karma itself does not exist there.

"You are Brahman manifest before my eyes. I shall speak of you alone as Brahman manifest before the eyes.

For indeed, there exist various karmas performed over many previous births—both those whose fruits have already begun to ripen and those whose fruits have not yet begun—which possess contradictory results. Therefore, among these, those whose fruits have not yet begun are exhausted through experience within a single birth."

From this possibility follows the occurrence of the commencement of a body caused by residual karma, as well as the establishment of the existence of that residual karma. If it is argued that the obligatory rites (*nitya-karmāṇi*) are for the purpose of exhausting uncommenced desirable and undesirable fruits—based on hundreds of scriptural and traditional texts such as, "Those here whose conduct has been pleasant... by the remainder [of their works]"—it is not so; for [the consequence would be] non-performance [of those rites].

Because of the hearing [in scripture] of sin (pratyavāya). The word "sin" refers to that which is undesirable. Since it is accepted that obligatory rites (*nitya*) are for the purpose of avoiding the future suffering that constitutes sin—which arises from the non-performance of what is obligatory—they are not for the purpose of exhausting karma whose fruit has not yet begun. Even if they were indeed for the purpose of exhausting uncommenced karma...
Even so, the obligatory rites (*nitya-karmāṇi*) would destroy only impurity, not purity; for there is no contradiction [between them].

Indeed, no contradiction with the obligatory rites is possible on the grounds that action yielding desired results is pure by nature; for a contradiction is logical only between the pure and the impure. Furthermore, since desire—the cause of action—is not removed in the absence of knowledge, [the obligatory rites cannot remove it].
For one such as you, the destruction of all karma is possible. For desire belongs to one who does not know the Self, because its object is a fruit that is not the Self;
and desire for one's own Self is impossible, since it is eternally attained. Furthermore, it has been stated that the Self is itself the Supreme Brahman.

This was stated in order to dispel such doubt. Regarding the phrase "having contradictory results": since actions such as the Jyotiṣṭoma and the Brahmahatyā—which have heaven and hell as their respective fruits—cannot possibly be exhausted through experience within a single body, and because there is generally no evidence for this [body] being the manifestor of all [karmic residues], the meaning is that the persistence of a weaker [action] is possible when it is obstructed by a stronger one. This is merely a possibility; there is no authoritative proof for this here.

Anticipating this doubt, he says: "By the remainder of karma" (*karmaśeṣa*). The meaning is that by stating, "Having experienced their own respective karma after death, they then obtain birth through the remainder," it demonstrates the existence of a remainder of karma for those descending from heaven. Having granted the existence of accumulated karma (*saṃcita-karma*), he says: "By the performed [rites]" (*iṣṭa*) [to show] that there will be no commencement of another body. He says: "No" (*na*), to indicate that what follows contradicts the established conclusion (*siddhānta*).

He states that even if it is accepted that the performance of obligatory rites (*nitya*) and so forth by one desiring liberation (*mumukṣu*) is for the purpose of exhausting accumulated karma (*sañcita-karma*), the desired goal is still not achieved; thus he says, "Even if indeed... Furthermore, as for what was said—that one desiring liberation should avoid rites performed for specific desires (*kāmya*)—that too is difficult to accomplish in the absence of the power of discrimination (*viveka-bala*). For as long as fundamental ignorance (*mūla-ajñāna*) persists, the arising of desire is difficult to ward off; thus he says, "Nor [is there cessation] of the causes of action..."
[Objection: But surely desire is not rooted in ignorance, because desire is observed even among those who know the Self. To this, he says: "And with regard to one's own self," etc.

Anuvāka 1. Accompanied by the commentary of Śaṅkara and the sub-commentary composed by Ānandagiri:
"I shall speak the Ṛta; I shall speak the Satya.

Furthermore, the non-performance of obligatory duties (*nitya*) is a non-existence; therefore, it is impossible for there to be a transgression (*pratyavāya*) resulting from that. Consequently, the non-performance of obligatory duties is merely the defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) of the process of transgression being incurred due to previously accumulated sins.

Thus, in the phrase "not performing the prescribed duty" (*akurvan vihitaṃ karma*), the present participle suffix *-śatṛ* is not untenable. Otherwise, [if it were a mere absence], how could a positive entity arise from a non-entity?

For those who perceive "all this is the Self" according to reality, desire is impossible precisely because of the absence of objects; the activity toward eating and so forth is merely a semblance of desire, as there is no real attachment—this is the meaning. One should not suspect that even they possess a desire for the attainment of Brahman via the path beginning with light (arcirādi), as he says: "And by themselves... Furthermore, regarding what was said concerning the sin arising from the non-performance [of duties]—
Regarding the statement that the obligatory rites (*nitya*) are for the sake of liberation, he says: "And of the obligatory [rites]... Here, "obstruction" (*pratyavāya*) refers to future suffering.

The non-existence [of these rites] cannot be the cause of that [suffering], which is positive in nature; for the scripture states, "The sinner [is affected] by sin. The meaning is that suffering has its cause in the performance of prohibited acts.
"By failing to perform prescribed duties, by practicing what is censured,
and by becoming attached to the objects of the senses, a man meets with downfall."

Anticipating the objection that the suffix *śatṛ* (the present participle marker) implies that even the non-performance [of an act] constitutes a cause for sin (*pratyavāya*), he says: "Therefore, prior... and so forth. If the performance of obligatory and occasional rites had been carried out correctly, then there would have been a destruction of accumulated demerit (*durita*). However, because one has not performed what was enjoined, it is inferred by the learned (*śiṣṭas*) that sin will arise; just as in the case of doubt...

Regarding the example "the Vedic scholar" (*śrotriya*): the meaning is that because the suffix *śatṛ* is derived in another sense [as a present participle], one cannot understand its status as a cause for non-performance on the strength of that derivation. Now, since the suffix *śatṛ* is prescribed in both senses—namely, in the sense of a characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) and a cause (*hetu*) according to the rule *lakṣaṇahetvoḥ kriyāyāḥ*—why is it not understood here specifically as a cause? To this he replies: "In another way" (*anyathā*). [This refers to] a positive effect (*kārya*) which is itself of a positive nature...

The meaning is that if one asserts through the suffix *śatṛ* that non-existence (*abhāva*) is a cause—something already understood through perception and other means—there would be a contradiction with all valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
Now, you too accept that the non-performance [of a duty] is characterized by sin; and the Bhaṭṭas maintain that non-perception (*anupalambha*) is the cause for the cognition of non-existence.

It is accepted [by some]. Logicians also accept that the absence of an obstructer (*pratibandhakābhāva*) and the respective prior non-existences (*prāgabhāva*) are the determinants of their respective effects.

How then can it be said that only a positive entity (*bhāva*) is a cause? As it has been said: "Just as a positive entity is a cause, so too is a negative entity (*abhāva*) considered a cause of an effect.
To this we reply: We do not, for our part, accept that a negative entity is a cause by its own nature (*svarūpeṇa*). Rather, [we maintain that it is a cause] through the cognition of it (*tajjñāna*).

It is accepted that [the non-performance of a duty] makes known the transgression (*pratyavāya*); however, it is not accepted that it produces the transgression in its capacity as a cognition. For otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that a transgression arises even from the mere knowledge of the non-performance of a mandatory (*nitya*) rite. Furthermore, according to some followers of the Bhāṭṭa school, the apprehension of absence (*abhāva-pramiti*) arises from the non-perception of what is perceptible (*yogyānupalambha*) once it has been known; yet, if the cause of that apprehension were the destruction of the causal conditions (*hetu-dhvaṃsa*), then the apprehension of absence would result in being a form of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). According to the Logicians (*Tārkika*s) as well, the counter-positive...

Since it would entail the fallacy of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśrayatva*) if antecedent non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) were the cause, it lacks scriptural authority (*prāmāṇikatva*). This is because even antecedent non-existence must be known in its specific form.

As for the claim that liberation is indeed produced by action because unsurpassed bliss—which is denoted by the word "heaven"—is caused by action, that is not so, because liberation is eternal. For nothing that is eternal is ever brought into being. In the world, whatever is produced is impermanent; therefore, liberation is not produced by action.

If it is argued that there is the capacity for the constant commencement of actions accompanied by knowledge (*vidyā*), we say no, because of contradiction. It is contradictory to say that something is both eternal and commenced; for that which has perished does not arise again. If it is argued that liberation (*mokṣa*), though eternal like a negation-by-destruction (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*), is indeed commenced, we say no, because liberation is of the nature of a positive entity (*bhāvarūpa*). [A negation-by-destruction is not.]

The claim that "it begins" is merely a conceptual construction, because there is no specific distinction within non-existence itself. For non-existence is the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) of existence. Just as existence, though undifferentiated, is qualified by [particulars] such as pots and cloths, so too is non-existence. It is simply the indicator (*jñāpaka*) of the jar; for [one says], "Since this did not exist previously, it has now arisen. But it does not possess the status of a producer (*janakatva*).

If antecedent non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) were a cause by virtue of its being invariably prior, it would follow that the prior time itself would reside in itself. The meaning is that since there is an invariable concomitance (*vyāpti*) such that whatever effect is of the nature of an entity is impermanent, and since liberation is the cessation of unsurpassed fear, it would necessarily be impermanent because it is an entity.

This is said by accepting the premise that the non-existence resulting from destruction (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*) is an effect, and then explaining the concomitance as: "Whatever effect is distinct from the non-existence resulting from destruction is impermanent. However, in reality...

He states that even the status of being an effect (*kāryatva*) does not belong to destruction (*pradhvaṃsa*). He says: "In destruction... To begin with, destruction has a produced substratum (*janyāśrayatva*), but it does not have the status of being an effect. This is because [the Vaiśeṣikas] accept that being produced is a modification of an existing entity (*bhāvavikāra*). Nor does it possess the definition [of an effect] as the inherence (*samavāya*) of existence (*sattā*) in what was previously non-existent, for that is not accepted [by them]. Nor is there a connection with a subsequent time, because there is no relation with time. [This is so] because of the relationship between the delimiting factor and the delimited (*avacchedāvacchedakabhāva*).

Since [the relation of inherence] is rooted in *samavāya* (inherence) and is observed to be based on a different kind of relation, if the nature of the subsequent time were to consist in its being the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) of destruction, then its nature could not consist in being the delimiting factor of anything else. Therefore, because negation (*abhāva*) lacks any specific qualification, its status as an effect is merely a product of conceptual construction; this is the intended meaning. Furthermore, because the nature of negation consists solely in its specific variety of non-existence and because it is opposed to existence (*bhāva*), it is not of the nature of a positive entity.

He says that *dharma* arises: "as a positive entity" (*bhāva*). The state of being a cloth (*paṭabhāva*) and the state of being a jar (*ghaṭabhāva*), as well as existence and non-existence, are thus without distinction; they are conceptualized through their connection with action and qualities, just like substances and so forth. For non-existence does not coexist with qualifiers in the manner of a blue lotus (*utpala*) or similar things. If it possessed qualifiers, it would simply be an existent entity (*bhāva*). Because knowledge, action, and the agent are eternal, liberation—produced by the continuity of knowledge and action—is eternal.

If it is argued that [the self] is indeed the agent, we say no; for agency is of the nature of suffering, like the current of the Ganges. Furthermore, if agency were to cease, liberation would be interrupted. Therefore, liberation is abiding in one's own self upon the cessation of the causes of appropriation—namely ignorance, desire, and karma. Moreover, the self itself is Brahman; liberation is the cessation of ignorance through the realization of that.

Thus begins the *Brahmavidyopaniṣad*. "Upaniṣad" refers to knowledge (*vidyā*). It is called *upaniṣad* because it shatters or destroys the embryo of birth, old age, and so forth for those who practice it, or because it brings about the cessation [of suffering], or because it causes one to attain (*upanigam*) Brahman. Alternatively, it is so called because there is no higher good (*paraṃ śreyaḥ*) beyond it. Since the text has that as its purpose, the book itself is also called an *upaniṣad*.

May Mitra—the deity who presides over the day and the function of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), and whose face is auspicious—be gracious to us. Just as a single entity appears as if divided due to the distinctions of its limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) regarding existence and non-existence, so too does non-existence, being of a single uniform nature, appear as if divided by the distinctions of its limiting adjuncts through the cognition of negation. Furthermore, it is associated with the actions of "being born" and "perishing."

Due to its association with the quality of being designated (*khyāti*), an entity (*bhāva*) is conceptualized as if it were a substance; however, the meaning is that it is not possessed of distinctions in reality (*tattvataḥ*). For this reason as well, he states that it is not possessed of distinctions in reality, beginning with "na hi" (for not). Indeed, it is well known that a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) must be concomitant with the qualified (*viśeṣya*). Furthermore, there can be no coexistence of an absence (*abhāva*) with a counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) as its qualifier. If the destruction of a jar were eternal, it would follow that the jar itself is also eternal.

Because [absence] would contradict its own nature as an absence if it were to coexist with the pot, since it is accepted that existence and non-existence are opposed by their very nature of not abiding together. Therefore, the meaning is that the notion that "absence is qualified by its specific counter-positive and possesses properties such as being an effect" is merely an illusion. Having thus refuted the objection regarding permanence raised by the example of destruction (*pradhvaṃsa*), he now addresses the objection from another perspective.

By the passage beginning with "knowledge and action" (*vidyākarma*), it is stated that the agent of knowledge and action is eternal; however, it should not be asserted that because the means (*sādhana*) are continuous, the goal (*sādhya*) must also be continuous. For if agency were never to cease, there would follow the consequence of no liberation (*anirmokṣa*); yet if it were to cease, the continuity of the means would be absent, resulting in the destruction of liberation itself. The concluding summary is: "Therefore," because the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*) is difficult to attain without the knowledge of Brahman.

He states that the well-known usage of the word *upaniṣad* with respect to the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*) is also proof for the fact that this very knowledge is the means to the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*). He says: "The *upaniṣad*. The meaning is "from sharpening" or "from loosening. The sense is that when this knowledge serves as the instrumental cause, the supreme good—Brahman—becomes the *upaniṣad* of the individual soul (*jīva*), appearing as its own Self. Thus [he explains] the etymology of *upaniṣad*.

"Vistīrṇakrama" is the one who takes pride in his feet. Such are the deities of the internal self (*adhyātmadevatā*). "I declare. By both the indirect and the direct, it is indeed *vāyu* that is being designated. Since that object is also dependent upon you, I shall speak of it as you alone. Since even "truth"—which is accomplished through speech and body—is itself to be accomplished by depending on you, I shall speak of you alone as truth.
May that Brahman, who is the self of all and is named Vāyu, being praised by me, protect me, the seeker of knowledge, and [grant] the attainment of knowledge.

Now, therefore, because the primary aim is the knowledge of the meaning, the chapter on phonetics (*śīkṣādhyāya*) is commenced so that there may be no cessation of effort in the recitation of the text of the *Upaniṣad*. Phonetics (*śikṣā*) is that by which one is taught (*śikṣyate*); it is characterized by the correct pronunciation of syllables and so forth. Śi-...

Or, *śikṣā* refers to phonemes (*varṇa*) and so forth, because they are to be learned (*śikṣyante*). *Śīkṣā* is simply *śikṣā*. *Daivyam* means pertaining to the Veda (*chāndasam*). We shall explain—that is, we shall describe clearly and completely—the *śīkṣā* concerning the *ṛta*. This form [of the verb] is derived from the root *cakṣiṅ* (to speak) with the prefix *vyāṅ*, because the object is made manifest (*vyakta*). In that context, the phoneme (*varṇa*) is the letter *a*.

*Ādiḥ* refers to the beginning. *Svara* refers to the accents, such as the acute (*udātta*) and others. *Mātrā* refers to the durations, such as the short (*hrasva*) and others. *Bala* refers to a specific degree of articulatory effort (*prayatna*). *Sāma* refers to the evenness of pronunciation, that is, the utterance of phonemes with a medium velocity. *Santāna* means continuity; it signifies *saṃhitā*. For this is the subject matter to be studied. The chapter in which this instruction (*śikṣā*) occurs is called the *Śīkṣādhyāya*.

We shall explain the Upaniṣad of the *Sahitā*. It consists of five sections: concerning the worlds (*adhiloka*), concerning the luminaries (*adhijyautiṣa*), concerning knowledge (*adhividyā*), concerning progeny (*adhipraja*), and concerning the self (*adhyātma*). These are called the "Great *Sahitās*."
They say: Now, with respect to the worlds (*adhiloka*): the earth is the prior form;
the sky is the subsequent form; space is the junction. || 1 ||

"May that splendor and luster which is Brahmanic glory be mine together with [the teacher's]"—this is the benediction consisting of the disciple’s words. For such a request is appropriate for the disciple because he has not yet achieved his purpose; it is not appropriate for the teacher, because he has already achieved his purpose. Indeed, one is called a "teacher" (*ācārya*) precisely because he has achieved his purpose. Now, immediately following this, because the injunction characterized by study is exceedingly important...

Since an intellect cultivated by the *grantha* (the text) cannot be suddenly introduced to the domain of the knowledge of its meaning, we shall therefore explain only this very treatise—the *Upaniṣad* of the *Saṃhitā*, which is the philosophical vision concerning the *Saṃhitā*. This means [we shall explain it] within five topical sections (*adhikaraṇa*), which serve as the bases for the objects of knowledge. What are these?

He said: "With regard to the worlds" (*adhiloka*) means that vision which pertains to the worlds. Likewise, there are those pertaining to the luminaries (*adhijyotiṣam*), to the sacrificial rites (*adhividham*), to progeny (*adhiprajam*), and to the self (*adhyātmam*). These five subjects of the Upaniṣads are both "great" and "compilations" (*saṃhitā*); they are great because their subject matter consists of vast entities such as the worlds and so forth, and they are compilations because they deal with the *saṃhitā*.

Those who know the Vedas call them the "Great Compositions" (mahāsaṃhitā) and speak of them thus. Now, the vision regarding these [compositions] as they have been introduced is stated; the word "now" (atha) is used everywhere for the purpose of intending to explain the sequence of the visions. Earth is the prior form—the prior letter is the prior form. One should perform the visualization of earth upon the prior letter of the *saṃhitā*.

This is what has been stated. And likewise, the subsequent form is space (*ākāśa*), which is the intermediate world (*antarikṣaloka*). The "junction" (*sandhi*) is the middle, for in it the preceding and succeeding forms are joined together. || 1 ||

He states that the reason for the method of worshipping [the Lord] as the Protector (Bdopa) has been expressed by the word "therefore" (*ataḥ*). Regarding the phrase "since [it is] exceedingly" (*yato 'tyartham*): the locative case in *pañcasu* should be understood as functioning in the sense of the instrumental; furthermore, the word *adhikaraṇa* is a synonym for "object" (*viṣaya*). It has been stated that the other deities are limbs of this Brahman, whose nature consists of the vyāhṛtis *bhūr*, *bhuvaḥ*, *suvaḥ*, and *mahaḥ*. In that [locus]...

For that Brahman, when being meditated upon as characterized by attributes such as "consisting of mind" (*manomaya*), is not directly perceived like an *āmalaka* fruit in the palm of one's hand. Furthermore, the path for attaining the state of being the Self of all must be explained; thus, the section of the recitation (*anuvāka*) begins with the word "He" (*sa*).
This [word] "He," skipping over the intervening text, is connected with the phrase "this person" (*ayaṃ puruṣaḥ*). "This which is within... [and so forth].

In the heart, within the heart—that is, the "inner heart"—there is a mass of flesh shaped like a lotus, the abode of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*), containing many channels, hollow, with its stalk pointing upward and its opening downward; this is well-known and perceived when an animal is being dissected. Within that, there is this space (*ākāśa*), which is indeed well-known, like the space inside a water-pot. In that—
This is that Person (*puruṣa*). He is called "Person" because he dwells in the city (*puri*) of the body, or because he has filled (*pūrṇa*) the worlds beginning with the earth.

He is "consisting of mind" (*manomaya*); "mind" (*manas*) is consciousness (*vijñāna*). He is "consisting of that" because he is perceived through it, as it is the instrument of the act of knowing (*manute*). Or, "mind" is the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*)—he is "consisting of that" as its presiding deity, or characterized by its marks. He is immortal...

He states that no differentiating means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is found that is established as non-erroneous regarding this matter: "And because there is no enjoining [authority]" (*vidhāyakābhāvāt*). Worship by means of form is now described. Through the connection with the number five, there is the attainment of the *paṅkti* metre; from that, everything possesses the nature of the *pāṅka* (fivefold). And the sacrifice is fivefold. The *paṅkti* consists of five feet, according to the Vedic revelation: "The sacrifice is fivefold. Therefore, they conceive of everything—from the worlds to the Self—as being fivefold; they conceive that very thing as the sacrifice.
He fashions [the sacrifice]. By means of that imagined sacrifice, he attains Prajāpati, who consists of the fivefold (*pāṅka*).

To the question, "How is all this fivefold?", he says: earth, intermediate space, heaven, the quarters, and the intermediate quarters—this is the fivefold world (*loka-pāṅka*). Fire, wind, the sun, the moon, and the stars—these are the deities (*devatā-pāṅka*).

The pentad: water, herbs, trees, space, and the self—this is the pentad of elements (*bhūta-pāṅka*). The mention of "the self" refers to the Virāj, because it concerns the elements; this is intended as an illustration of the two pentads of elements, worlds, deities, and so forth, since both the pentads of worlds and deities have already been stated. Now, immediately following that, [the text describes] the pentad with respect to the self (*adhyātma*).

A triad is mentioned: the pentad of the vital airs beginning with prāṇa; the pentad of the sense organs beginning with the eye; and the pentad of the bodily constituents beginning with the skin. For all this internal [reality] consists of these, and the external is likewise a pentad.
Having thus analyzed and conceptualized it, the seer—the Veda, or some sage endowed with such vision—declared this, saying: "It is fivefold."

What does he say? "All this is fivefold; by means of the fivefold internal [world], through the commonality of number, one unites, encompasses, and fills the fivefold external [world]. It is perceived as having a single self—this is precisely what it means.
The meaning is that he who knows "all this is fivefold" becomes the very self of Prajāpati. || 1 ||
Thus ends the seventh section. || 7 ||

By such [statements] as these, in response to the inquiry as to how earth and the other elements possess the nature of the *pāṅkta* (fivefold), he says: "Because of the accomplishment of the metre called *paṅkti*.

He further states: "The number five," meaning that not only is the metre *paṅkti* accomplished through the connection with the number five, but the accomplishment of the nature of sacrifice (*yajña*) can also be effected; thus he says: "And sacrifice is *pāṅkta*. [The portion regarding] the wife—
The meaning is that sacrifice (*yajña*) is "fivefold" (*pāṅka*) because it is accomplished by means of five things: the sacrificer, his son, the divine, the human, and wealth.

Or, according to the maxim that "a vision [of something] bears fruit when directed toward its lower [manifestation]," one should understand the three internal fivefold sets by way of the external fivefold set;
with this intention, he says: "by way of oneness of self. Thus ends the seventh section.

Even though the syllable *Oṃ* is merely sound, when it is meditated upon through the vision of the higher and lower Brahman, it leads to the attainment of the higher and lower Brahman.
It becomes the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*). For that [syllable *om*] is the objective support (*ālambana*) for both the higher and the lower Brahman, just as a reflection is for Viṣṇu.
This is because of the Vedic revelation: "By this very abode, one follows after one or the other. "Om.
The word "iti" is intended to delimit its essential nature. One should hold in mind—that is, meditate upon—the fact that this syllable *om*, which is of the nature of sound, is Brahman.

"Om! All this is indeed pervaded by the letter 'A' in the form of sound," according to another Vedic text which says, "Just as with a bird. For that which is denoted is dependent upon the denoter; therefore, all this is said to be the letter 'A'. The subsequent passage is for the purpose of praising the syllable Om, because it is the object of meditation. "Om"—this is its imitation.

[The word] *mukaraṇam* [means] "I shall do" or "I shall go. Another person imitates this by saying "Oṃ," once it has been uttered. Thus, the syllable *oṃ* is an imitation (*anukṛti*). The particles *ha*, *sma*, and *vā* indicate well-known facts (*prasiddhi*). It is well known that the syllable *oṃ* is an imitation. Furthermore, they cause [the announcement] to be heard preceded by the words "Let it be heard! (*āśrāvaya*), according to each respective perception.
They proceed thus: "Om," say the chanters as they sing the *sāmans*;

"Om," says the *brahmā* as he gives the impulse (*prasauti*) and grants permission; with "Om," he causes the announcement (*āśrāvayati*) preceded by the command (*preṣa*); and "Om" [is said] for the *agnihotra*.

He knows. When told, "I shall sacrifice," he gives his assent simply by saying "Om. Preceded by a restatement of the conduct of a Brāhmaṇa, he introduces the subsequent section with the words "With the *vyāhṛtis* for himself," and so forth. For indeed, all the ritual acts of those who know the Veda proceed after uttering the syllable *Oṃ*; therefore, because [the rite] is embraced by faith, upon its omission—

The meaning is that since the Brahman taught by the Cow (Gopada) would not enter the intellect, meditation is prescribed by taking up that very [Oṃkāra]. Now, one might object: "Since Oṃkāra is a mere sound and is insentient, it lacks the cognition 'I have been meditated upon by this person'; how then can it be the bestower of results?
Anticipating this doubt, he says: "The Supreme and the Non-supreme," etc. Just as in the worship of an image and so forth, the Lord alone is the bestower of results in all cases.

[The word] *bhāvaḥ* [indicates the state]. To the question, "What is the similarity between the syllable *oṃ* and Brahman when Brahman is superimposed upon *oṃ*? he says: "*Omitīdam*" (This is *oṃ*). The mantra-recitation "I am the mover of the tree" (*ahaṃ vṳkṣasya rerivā*) is for the purpose of *svādhyāya* (private Vedic study). And *svādhyāya* leads to the arising of knowledge (*vidyā*), because of the context; for this entire section has knowledge as its purpose, and no other purpose is perceived. Furthermore, the arising of knowledge is possible for one whose being (*sattva*) has been purified by *svādhyāya*. "I am the mover of the tree... [and so forth].

I am the impeller, like the wind, of the tree of worldly existence which is characterized by destruction, acting as its inner controller (antaryāmin). My fame and renown are as lofty as the peak of a mountain. I am "ūrdhvapavitra," meaning that for me, the Self of all, the supreme Brahman—which is the upward-reaching cause, the purifier, and that which is revealed by knowledge—is my purifying essence; such am I, the "ūrdhva-."

"Purifying. "Like a prize-winner" means like one possessing a prize (*vāja*), that is, like Savitṛ who possesses food (*anna*). Just as it is well known from hundreds of Śrutis and Smṛtis that immortality—the pure reality of the Self—resides in Savitṛ, so too do I become my own immortal, beautiful, and pure reality of the Self. "Wealth" means riches, and "splendid" means radiant.

The knower of Brahman continues [in life] with the thought, "I am that very reality of the Self. Alternatively, the knowledge of Brahman is "resplendent" (*savarcas*) because it illuminates the reality of the Self. It is "wealth" (*draviṇa*) as it were, because it is the cause for the gateway to liberation. In this interpretation, the phrase "has been obtained by me" must be supplied. By this, the claim that knowledge and action combined initiate liberation is refuted. [Objection: Knowledge and action merely remove the causes that obstruct liberation. [Reply: No, because action is seen to have other fruits.

If it is argued that the fruit of action is seen to consist in origination, refinement, modification, and attainment, whereas liberation (mokṣa) is the opposite of such fruits like origination and is to be attained by means of a journey according to scriptural texts on going—such as "By the door of the sun" and "Going upwards from these two"—and thus liberation is something to be reached; [we reply: No, because [liberation] is omnipresent.

Because it is non-different from those who go [to it], because it is the cause of ether and the other elements, and because it is all-pervading, Brahman is omnipresent. Furthermore, since all individual conscious selves (*vijñānātman*) are not distinct from Brahman, liberation is not something to be attained [as a destination]. For that which is to be gone to must be a place different and separate from the goer. Indeed, that which is non-different from the goer cannot be reached by that very same goer; this is due to the principle of "non-difference from that" (*atadananyatva*).

And because of well-known [scriptural authority]: from hundreds of such Śrutis and Smṛtis as, "Having created that, He entered into that very thing," and "Know Me also as the Knower of the Field (Kṣetrajña). If it is argued that there is a contradiction with Śrutis concerning movement and sovereignty [of the soul], and if it should be thought:
"If the Self were unattainable, then the Śrutis regarding its going—whether it be in one way or another..."

If it is argued that there would be a contradiction with such scriptural passages as, "He who desires the world of the fathers [attains it] by means of women or vehicles," we say: no, because those passages have the *kāryabrahman* (the effected Brahman) as their subject matter. For, having rejected the combination [of knowledge and works] with respect to the *kāryabrahman*, the text extends the principle of equal combination [to other cases]. By this [it is meant]: [there is no contradiction] even when the defects of those who maintain [the doctrine of] non-eternality and so forth are attached.

This is the meaning. Regarding the phrase "of liberation": ignorance (*avidyā*), demerit (*adharma*), and so forth are the causes that obstruct liberation; knowledge (*vidyā*) and ritual action (*karman*) are the means that remove them, not the producers of its essential nature (*svarūpa*). Therefore, the abiding in the essential nature is eternal. Furthermore, it is well known that even a destruction (*pradhvaṃsa*) which is produced can be eternal—this is the meaning. Commentary: In that case, there is no requirement for auxiliary factors for knowledge. He says, "Not [the fruit] of action," because the fruit of action is something entirely different and well-known.

[The types of fruits of action are: production, as in the case of the sacrificial cake (*purōḍāśa*) and so forth; purification, as in the case of rice (*vrīhi*) and so forth; modification, as in the case of *soma*; and attainment, as in the case of the Veda. Because it is not an object [of cognition] and because it is not within the scope of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that apprehends a delimitation, even the definition is individually non-defective despite being optional.

The Taittirīya Upaniṣad:
[In the Brahmavallī,] that knowledge of Brahman which belongs to Brahman is like the light of the sun and like the heat of fire— the very nature of Brahman—

That very nature is distinct; it does not depend upon any other cause, because its nature is eternal. Furthermore, since all entities are inseparable from it in terms of space and time, and since it is the cause of time, space, and so forth, and because of its unsurpassed subtlety, there exists for it no other object—whether subtle, concealed, remote, or past—that remains unknown.

Therefore, that Brahman is omniscient, whether existing in the present or the future; and from the words of the Mantra: "Without hands or feet, He is swift and a grasper; He sees without eyes, He hears without ears. He knows the knowable, yet there is no knower of Him.
They call Him the foremost, the Great Person. For there is no knower of the Knower—

Furthermore, according to such scriptural passages as, "There is no destruction [of this], because of its indestructibility; for there is nothing second to it," and so forth, Brahman is established as eternally known even though its nature is knowledge. This is because it is non-different from the nature of the knower and because it does not depend on instruments or other causal conditions. Therefore, it is not the meaning of a verbal root (dhātvartha), since it is not of the nature of an action (akriyārūpatvāt).
For this very reason, Brahman is not the agent of knowledge; and for this same reason, it is not even denotable by the word "knowledge.

Nevertheless, it is indicated—though not directly expressed—by the word "knowledge," which refers to the attributes of the intellect (buddhi) and serves as its reflection. This is because Brahman is devoid of such categories as genus (jāti), which are the grounds for the application of words; and the same applies to the word "truth" (satya).

Since Brahman has a nature in which all distinctions have subsided, how can it be omniscient with respect to external existence and universals? To this he says: "And of all entities... For the establishment of an object consists precisely in its non-intervention from consciousness; and since everything is non-intervened by Brahman, whose nature is consciousness, Brahman is figuratively designated as omniscient. It is eternal...

He cites scriptural authority for the statement that knowledge exists in Brahman with the words, "And from the wording of the mantra. He states that objections such as "Brahman is non-eternal because it possesses knowledge, like worldly knowledge," are also refuted by the reasoning already set forth, with the words, "The essential nature of the knower. Worldly knowledge is non-eternal because it depends upon instruments and other factors; however, knowledge that is the very nature of the Self does not depend upon instruments and the like.

The sense is this: since [the self] exists even when all the functions of the organs have ceased in deep sleep—otherwise, the very establishment of deep sleep would be impossible, and there would be the undesirable consequence of the possibility of reflective awareness (parāmarśa)—therefore, in a matter to be understood through the purport of scripture, there is no room for inference based on general observation (sāmānyato dṛṣṭa). It is eternal...
The meaning is: "precisely because it is of the nature of the Self.
For this very reason—and because knowledge is eternal—it is not possible to attribute agency to Brahman even in that regard;

"And for this very reason" [is the phrase]. How then is the usage "Brahman is consciousness" (vijñānaṃ brahma) possible? To that he says: "Even so. "He who knows [Brahman] hidden in the secret cave, in the highest heaven..."

Brahman is indicated by the word "truth," but Brahman is not merely that which is denoted by the word "truth. In this way, words such as "truth" and so forth, existing in mutual proximity, act as mutual restrictors and restricted; they serve both to exclude [the world] from what is denoted by words like "truth" and to function as indicators (lakṣaṇa) of Brahman. Therefore, it is established.

"From which words turn back, together with the mind, not having attained it"—and [the passage] "in the unexpressed, the non-abode," thus the inexpressibility and the state of being beyond the meaning of a sentence of Brahman are established, as has been explained. He who knows—that is, understands—Brahman as it is hidden, situated in the cave (guhā); for the root *guh* means to conceal...

The term *guhā* (the cave) refers to the intellect (*buddhi*), because within it the categories of knowledge, the object of knowledge, and the knower are concealed. Alternatively, it is so called because within it the two goals of the person—enjoyment and liberation—are hidden. Within that supreme, most excellent void (*vyoman*), namely the unmanifest space known as the *avyākṛta*; for that indeed is the supreme void, in which, as it is said, "in this imperishable [space] all things are contained. Thus, it is the imperishable.

Because of the proximity of the *rasa* (the essence), the cave (*guhā*) is the unmanifest space (*avyākṛtākāśa*) itself, due to its grammatical coordination (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the term "in the void" (*vyomni*).

Particular instances of existence (*sattāviśeṣāḥ*) are excluded. Furthermore, this state of being both inclusive (*anuvṛtta*) and exclusive (*vyāvṛtta*) is not a real entity (*vastu*), because it is established through mutual dependence.
The meaning is that Brahman is characterized as that in which this state of exclusion and inclusion is imagined—that which is excluded from all else and yet non-contingent.

Having thus stated the meaning of each individual word, he states the meaning of the sentence: "When this is so, [the words] beginning with 'satya' (truth)," etc. Although the primary syntactical connection of the words "truth" and so forth is with Brahman, nevertheless—just as in the case of the terms *aruṇā* (red) and *ekahāyanī* (one-year-old)—through a secondary (pāṣṇika) connection, there arises a mutual relationship among them due to their proximity.
Having been thus applied, they become restrictors of the meaning. Because it is qualified by "knowledge," the word "truth" (satya) does not apply to an insentient cause.

Because it is qualified by "truth," the word "knowledge" (jñāna) does not apply to knowledge that is dependent upon an object. Because it is qualified by "knowledge," the word "infinite" (ananta) does not apply to anything other than the knower. Consequently, that which is denoted by words such as "truth" in common worldly usage must be something distinct from those things.

The meaning is that, conceiving [Brahman] as "Being," they characterize Brahman—the substratum of all worldly superimpositions—as being that very Being. To the question, "What follows from this?", he says: "Therefore, it is established. Because it is not accepted that [Brahman] is denotable by the power of denotation (*vācaka-śakti*), it is inexpressible (*avācya*);

and because it is admitted that only the one [Being] is the object of indication (*lakṣya*) through the exclusion of all undesirable attributes, it is distinct from sentence-meanings consisting of the commingling of qualities, the qualified, and so forth.
The meaning is that the perishability of Brahman is thus established.

"That which follows the effect of the intellect (buddhi)—namely, that which is called the unmanifested (avyākṛta) in the supreme space—is placed therein"; this is the analysis of the two locative cases.

This has been explained by way of grammatical coordination (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*). Why is it that the conventional meaning of the word "ether" (*vyoman*) as the elemental space (*bhūtākāśa*) is set aside and it is explained as referring to the undifferentiated (*avyākṛta*)? To this he says: "For that... Because the elemental ether is subordinate due to being an effect, whereas the undifferentiated ether can possess the qualification of "supremacy" due to being the cause; furthermore, because of its proximity to the Imperishable Brahman in other recensions and in the *Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa*—

The meaning is that the unmanifest (*avyākṛta*) is indicated by the word "space" (*vyoma*). Having thus explained [the passage] according to the opponent's intention, [he now states] his own [view]. "He attains all desires together with the wise Brahman.

Even there, all categories of objects are hidden because they exist as causes throughout the three periods of time and because they are exceedingly subtle; therefore, it is logical that the Brahman contained within that [heart] is indeed the supreme space (vyoman) of the heart, as it serves as a limb of higher knowledge.

Because the sky is intended here as a constituent part of the seat (*pāsanāṅga*), its supreme nature is established by another scriptural passage: "That which is the space outside a person, that which is the space within a person, and this space within the heart. In that space of the heart, there is the cave which is the intellect (*buddhi*). In that [cave]—

"Brahman is deposited [within]; it is perceived through that mode of functioning as something distinct. For otherwise, there could be no connection with specific place or time for Brahman, because of its omnipresence and its lack of attributes.
Having thus known Brahman, what does he do? He enjoys (*anute*), that is, he experiences, all things without exception.
The meaning is "enjoyments. Why not [enjoy them] successively, as we and others do, such as heaven and so forth? He says:

no; rather, simultaneously, at one and the same moment, they are mounted upon by a single perception—eternal like the light of the sun, inseparable from the nature of Brahman, which we have described as "Being, Consciousness, Infinite. This is what is being stated.
"Along with Brahman. The wise one, having become Brahman, enjoys all desires together with the very nature of Brahman itself;

he does not enjoy them through a transmigratory self that is a mere reflection—like the sun reflected in water—conditioned by limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), and which depends upon causes such as merit (*dharma*) and the like, or upon instruments such as the eyes and other organs. In this manner, [he enjoys] the desires in succession.

The world does not hear [them]. How then? The meaning is that he hears all desires simultaneously—desires that do not depend on causes such as merit (*dharma*) and so forth, nor on instruments such as the eyes and other organs—in the manner already described: by means of the omniscient, omnipresent, and universal Self, whose nature is the eternal Brahman-Atman. By the "wise one" (*vipaścitā*), meaning the intelligent and omniscient one; for that indeed...

He explains the meaning [of the word *prāya*]: "But it is indeed that which is in the heart" (*hārdam eva tu*). The interpretation is appropriate that Brahman is manifested as being deposited as the witness within the intellect (*buddhi*) in that cave which is the elemental space (*bhūtākāśa*) delimited by the heart. This is because, through the distinction of perceivers, Brahman attains immediacy (*āparokṣya*); otherwise, if it were said that Brahman resides in the undifferentiated principle (*avyākṛta*) or the category of *māyā* in its collective form (*samaṣṭi*), the consequence would be that Brahman remains remote (*pārokṣya*).

Knowledge that is mediated by distance (*pārokṣya*) does not remove the superimposition of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*), which is immediate (*aparokṣa*). Therefore, since it is intended that Brahman is directly perceived within one's own heart through its non-difference from the consciousness of the immediate witness (*aparokṣadraṣṭṛcaitanya*), the meaning is that the space of the heart (*hṛdayākāśa*) alone—being subordinate to the act of realization—is what is intended here.

"Vaipaścityam" means omniscience; thus, it was heard by Brahman, whose very nature is omniscience. The word "iti" marks the conclusion of the mantra.

The entire meaning has been indicated by the Brāhmaṇa passage, "The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme"; and that indicated meaning has been explained in brief by the Mantra. And so forth. In that context, it was stated at the beginning of the mantra, "Brahman is truth, knowledge, and infinite. How then is it truth, knowledge, and infinite? To this he says: for there are three kinds of infinity—spatial, temporal, and substantial.
For example, space is infinite spatially, for there is no spatial limitation of it.

It exists; however, space is not infinite in terms of time nor in terms of substance. Why? Because it is an effect. Brahman is not like space in having an end even in terms of time, because it is not an effect. For a thing that is an effect is delimited by time, and Brahman is not an effect. Therefore, it is infinite even in terms of time.
Thus, in reality. But how is there infinity in reality? Because everything is non-different from all else.

For a distinct entity becomes the "end" of another entity. Indeed, the cognition of one entity ceases when it encounters another entity. That from which a cognition is withdrawn is its end. For example, [the end of] "cowness"—
Because it turns back from non-horseness (*aśvatva*), the nature of "cowness" (*gotva*) is limited by non-horseness; thus, it is indeed finite.

And that limit is observed among distinct entities, but there is no such differentiation in Brahman. Therefore, Brahman is infinite even in terms of its reality (*vastutaḥ*). But how is it said that Brahman is non-different from all things? Because it is the cause of all things. For [Brahman is the source] of all things...

Brahman is the cause of time, space, and so forth. If it is argued that [Brahman] is in fact finite with respect to its effects, we say no; for the reality of the effect is unreal. Indeed, apart from the cause, there is no such thing as an "effect" that exists in reality, such that the cognition of the cause would cease. The modification is a mere verbal handle, a name—just as [the clay-pot is nothing but clay].

"‘What indeed?’—‘The Real alone. ‘The Existent alone is the Real,’ according to another Vedic text. Therefore, because it is the cause of ether and the rest, Brahman is infinite in terms of space. For ether is well known to be infinite in terms of space, and this [Brahman] is its cause; thus, the infinity of the Self in terms of space is established. Indeed, it is not non-pervasive..."

Therefore, nothing whatsoever is seen arising in the world that is all-pervading; hence, the infinity of the Self is unsurpassed spatially because it is not an effect, temporally because there is no other distinct entity, and substantially for the same reason;
thus, its truth is likewise unsurpassed.

The meaning is that the plural number is used figuratively because he experiences the joys of the forest (*vanavānandān*). By means of the words "all indeed" (*sarva eva*) and so forth, the author restates the preceding section in order to introduce the subsequent text; for by declaring [the Self] to be the cause of space and the other elements, the manifestation of its infinity (*anantya-prapañca*) is being established immediately thereafter.

In order to demonstrate the purport of the treatise, he restates a specific point among those previously mentioned with the words "And there... First, he states that the entity is finite in order to explain its actual infinity, using the passage beginning with "For it is divided... He then summarizes the infinity explained at length with the words "Therefore, it is established... Because space, which is unconditioned by spatial limits, is the cause [of the world], it is all-pervasive.

The meaning is that the soul’s unsurpassed infinity is established in three ways: spatial infinity because it has no parts; temporal infinity because it is unproduced, for if there were anything from which it could be excluded, that would not exist as a separate entity, since it is impossible for an effect to exist apart from its material cause; and substantial infinity as well. "Therefore" means that from this very unsurpassed infinity, its reality is also established, because only that which has an end—such as a snake imagined in a rope—is unreal.

The Taittirīya Upaniṣad:
From this very Self, indeed, space was produced;
from space, air; from air, fire; from fire, water; from water, [earth].
From the earth come plants; from plants comes food;
from food comes the person. This very person consists of the essence of food.
[Brahmavallī]

The word "therefore" (*tasmāt*) refers back to Brahman as formulated in the root aphorism (*mūlavākya*). By the phrase "from this" (*etasmāt*), it refers to that Brahman which was immediately characterized by the mantra-text and previously formulated by the Brāhmaṇa-text; and since it was just characterized as "Brahman is truth, knowledge, and infinite," [the meaning is: from this Brahman, from the Self, from the Self—

From that which is denoted by the word [Brahman]. For the Self is the essence of all this; "That is the Truth, That is the Self"—from such other scriptural passages, Brahman is the Self. From this Brahman, whose nature is the Self, space (ākāśa) was produced, brought forth. Space is characterized by the quality of sound and provides room for material objects. From that—

From ether, by means of its own quality of touch and the preceding causal quality of sound, air arises as possessing two qualities; the word "arisen" (saṃbhūta) is understood to carry over. And from air, by means of its own quality of form and the two preceding qualities, fire arises as possessing three qualities. From fire, by means of its own quality of taste and the three preceding qualities, water arises as possessing four qualities.

They were produced. From water, by means of its own quality of smell and the previous four qualities, earth was produced with five qualities. From earth, plants; from plants, food; and from food transformed into the form of semen, the person (*puruṣa*)—possessing the configuration of a head, hands, and so forth—was produced. Indeed, this very person consists of the essence of food (*annarasamaya*).
It is a modification of the essence of food (*annarasa-vikāra*). For the seed—the semen—is a concentrated luster gathered from all the limbs, conditioned by the form of a male;

therefore, whoever is born from it must likewise have that very form of a male. This is because, among all species, one observes a rule regarding the form of the progenitor in those being born. Even though all [beings] are modifications of the essence of food, Brahma—
Since the status of being a member of the lineage (*vaṃśyatva*) is common to both, why is only the person (*puruṣa*) mentioned? Because of his preeminence (*prādhānya*). But what is this preeminence?

It is the qualification for ritual action and knowledge (*karmajñānādhikāra*). For it is the person alone who, by virtue of being capable, having a desire [to act], and not being excluded, is qualified for ritual action and knowledge—being one who desires, is learned, and is competent. Indeed, the Self (*ātman*) is manifested more fully in the person.

Having thus stated the purport of the passage concerning creation, he analyzes the words, beginning with "Therefore" (*tasmāt*). Since the Supreme Self is the material cause (*upādāna*) everywhere up until the final effect, air was produced from the Supreme Self itself when it had assumed the state of ether; for this very reason, its quality persists in what follows. Furthermore, the use of the word "quality" (*guṇa*) is intended to imply dependence [of the quality] upon that [substance], through the conceptualization of difference, and not in the Vaiśeṣika sense.

It should be understood that [the text] speaks of "possessing sides" with the intention of referring to a distinction in principles (*tattva-bheda*), because there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for a real difference [between them]. He states the intended meaning of the mention of "person" (*puruṣa*) with the words "of all [beings] as well. Regarding the phrase "because of being capable," it has been stated that this refers to the possession of the capacity for the discrimination between injunctions and prohibitions; in that regard, he cites the corroboration of the *Aitareyaka* Śruti: "But in the person alone... [referring to] a human body and so forth, which possesses the caste (*jāti*) of Brahminhood and so on.

Of that [sacrificial horse], this indeed is the head; this is the right wing; this is the left wing; this is the body (ātman); this is the tail, the foundation. Regarding this, there is also this verse. Thus ends the first section. 1.

For that person here is intended to be led by means of knowledge to the innermost Brahman; and since his intellect, which has habitually identified with non-self external forms,

cannot suddenly be made to have the innermost inward Self as its object and become supportless without some specific point of reference, [the text proceeds] by means of the perceived body as the self—

Introducing [the subject] by means of a metaphorical conception, like the illustration of the moon on a tree branch, he says: "This indeed is its head. Thus it is said. The application [of these terms] to the wings and other parts is as follows: for one facing east, this right arm is the southern wing; this left arm is the northern wing; and this middle portion of the body is the *ātman* (self) of the limbs, according to the Vedic scripture: "For the *ātman* is the center of these limbs. This [part referred to by] "this" is the limb below the navel.

That tail is the foundation (*pratiṣṭhā*). It is called the foundation because one stands firm by means of it; it is like a tail due to the common characteristic of hanging downwards, just as the tail of a cow. By taking this as the primary model, the status of the subsequent sheaths, beginning with that consisting of breath (*prāṇamaya*), as being figurative forms is established, like a statue formed by molten copper poured into a mold. On this point, there is also this verse:
Regarding that very meaning spoken by the Brāhmaṇa, which reveals the self consisting of food (annamaya-ātman), there is this verse as a mantra.

The meaning is that the Self is manifest with excellence through the manifestation of the excellence of knowledge (*svarāmatiśayena prakaṭa ātmā jñānātiśayadarśanāt*). The meaning is that one desires to attain an imperishable fruit by means of complete (*matsrnyena*) practice of knowledge, action, and so forth. That discriminative knowledge (*vivekajñāna*) by which the preeminence of the Person (*puruṣa*) is intended—that—

He states that [the five sheaths] do not exist for dogs and the like with the words, "Now, for others. With the words beginning "For he," he explains the intended meaning of the presentation of the five sheaths. By the use of the terms "wings" and "tail," he demonstrates the conceptualization of the form of a bird (*suparṇa*). Subsequently, through that conceptualization, there occurs the removal of attachment to external objects within the self by means of the intellect (*buddhi*).

The injunction for meditative worship (*upāsana*) is not intended here for the purpose of stabilization. This is because the introductory and concluding sections are fully exhausted by establishing the identity of Brahman and the Self alone; furthermore, if the middle portion of the text were intended to enjoin meditation, it would result in a split in the sentence (*vākya-bheda*). Therefore, according to the maxim "Praise of a subsidiary is for the sake of another," just as the mention of results in the *prayāja* and other rites is merely an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), so too is the mention of results in the case of the "consisting of food" (*annamaya*) and the others.
Taittirīya Upaniṣad: From food indeed, O Bahvṛca, all creatures are born— whatever creatures exist upon the earth.
They have taken refuge in it; moreover, they live by means of food alone, and in the end, they even pass away into it. For food is the eldest of all beings;
therefore, it is called the "all-healing" (*sarva-auṣadha*). Indeed, all these [beings] enter into food.
Those who worship food as Brahman—food, indeed, is the eldest of beings;
therefore it is called the "all-healing" (*sarvauṣadha*). From food beings are born;
once born, they grow by means of food. It is eaten, and it eats.

"Beings. Therefore, it is called "food" (*anna*). From that food—having been transformed into the state of sapid juices and so forth—the word "or" (*vā*) serves to indicate a traditional recollection—that all creatures (*prajā*), both stationary and moving, are born. Whatever [creatures] there may be, undifferentiated, resting upon the earth, having taken recourse to the earth.

All those various beings are born from food alone; moreover, once born, they live by food alone—they maintain their vital breaths (prāṇas), which means they grow. Furthermore, they also go toward this very food; they enter into it. The word "api" (also) has the sense of "prati" (toward). The meaning is that they dissolve back into food. This occurs at the end, in the finality.

Upon the completion of growth, which is characterized by life—why is it food? Because it is the eldest, the first-born of all beings, living creatures; for food is the cause of the other elements, such as those consisting of food (annamaya) and so forth.
Therefore, all progeny originate from food, live by food, and dissolve into food. And because this is so—
All medicinal herbs are said to be food that pacifies the burning of the bodies of all living beings.

The fruit for one who knows food as Brahman is stated: they indeed obtain everything, the entire collection of food. Who? Those who meditate upon food as Brahman, as previously described. How [is it so]? "I am born of food, my self is food, I am non-decaying; therefore—"

"Food is Brahman. But why is it said that the meditation on food as the Self has the attainment of all food as its fruit? For food is the eldest (*jyeṣṭha*) among beings. Because it was produced prior to all beings, it is indeed the eldest; therefore, it is called "all-healing" (*sarvauṣadha*). Consequently, it is logical that for one who meditates on food as the Self, there is the attainment of all food. Food—
"Beings are born from this; once born, they grow by means of this"—this is repeated for the sake of a summary.

Now, the etymological definition of "food" (*anna*) is stated: because it is eaten and consumed by beings, and because it itself eats and consumes beings, it is called "food" (*anna*) due to its being consumed by beings and its being the consumer of beings. The word "iti" [marks the end of the definition].

This is for the purpose of completing the *Makōśa* [The Sheaths]. It should be understood that even though the hearing of the fruit [the result] is mentioned in relation to the selves beginning with the one consisting of food (*annamaya*) and ending with the one consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*), this is merely an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*). This is because the realization of the Self remains as the final goal, following the dissolution of each preceding notion through the stabilization of each successive notion. Thus ends the first and second sections. 1, 2.

"And because the elements themselves [are derived from it], therefore it is called food (anna). Thus ends the second section. [Page 54] Accompanied by the commentary of Śaṅkara along with the sub-commentary by Ānandagiri.
Different from this self consisting of the essence of food is another inner self consisting of breath; by that this [self] is filled. And that very one is of the form of a person.
Thus. Following his human form, he is of human form. Of him, the out-breath (*prāṇa*) is the head; the diffused breath (*vyāna*) is the right wing;
the downward breath (*apāna*) is the left wing; space is the body. Pṛ...
The earth is the tail, the support. Regarding this, there is also this verse.
Thus ends the second section.

Desiring to show, by means of knowledge, that the innermost Brahman is the inner self (*pratyagātman*), the scripture removes the five sheaths created by ignorance—just as one winnows the rice grains within them by removing the many layers of husks—starting with the passage: "From this very one, consisting of the essence of food," and so forth. From this aforementioned [self]...

Different from and distinct from the self consisting of the essence of food (*annarasamaya*) is another, inner, internal self—the *prāṇamaya* (consisting of vital breath). Like the physical body itself, this is falsely imagined as the Self. "Vital breath" (*prāṇa*) refers to air; that which consists of it is the *prāṇamaya*. This self consisting of the essence of food is filled by that *prāṇamaya* self, just as a leather bag is filled with air. That indeed is this...

The self consisting of breath (*prāṇamaya ātmā*) is indeed of the form of a person (*puruṣavidha*), that is, it has the shape of a person with a head, wings, and so forth. Is this due to itself? No; he says: "It is well known that the self consisting of the essence of food (*annarasamaya*) is of the form of a person. Following that form of the self consisting of the essence of food—its state of being a person—the self consisting of breath [is likewise]."

It is not by its own nature, but like an image cast from a mold. Thus, following the human form of each preceding one, each subsequent one becomes human-shaped; and each preceding one is filled by each subsequent one. But how does it have this human shape? It is said: of that *prāṇamaya* (consisting of breath), the breath itself is the head, and the breath is the...

Of that modification of air, *prāṇa*—which is a specific function emerging from the mouth and nose—is figuratively conceived as the head because of the scriptural statement. In all cases, the conception of the wings and so forth arises solely from the scriptural statement. *Vyāna*, which is the function of *vyāna*, is the right wing; *apāna* is the left wing; and space is the self (*ātman*), which is the... [ākāśa].
The sixth specific function is called "the self" (ātman). It is the "self" because, within the context of the functions of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), it stands in the middle;

thus, in relation to the other peripheral functions, it is the self. For it is well-known from the Vedic revelation that "the self is the center of these limbs," and this establishes the status of the central one as the self. "The earth is the tail, the support. [The word] "earth" refers to...

The earth-deity is the supporter of the internal vital breath (*prāṇa*), because it is the cause of its stability. For another scriptural passage states: "This very [earth] holds fast the downward-breath (*apāna*) of the person. Otherwise, due to the upward movement caused by the function of the upward-breath (*udāna*), or due to its weight, the body would either fly up or fall down. Therefore, the earth-deity is the tail, the foundation. Prā—
Regarding this self consisting of breath (*prāṇamaya*), there is this verse concerning that very subject—the self consisting of breath. Thus ends the second section. 2.
