Taittirīya Upaniṣad 52:
After the vital breath (prāṇa) the gods breathe, as do humans and animals.

For breath (*prāṇa*) is the life-force (*āyus*) of living beings; therefore, it is called "the whole life. Those who meditate upon breath as Brahman attain their entire life-span. [From the *Brahmavallī*]

"The gods breathe after the breath. The gods, Agni and the others, breathing after the breath—the self that is Vāyu, which possesses the power of the vitalizing function—become one with it and breathe; they perform the act of breathing and become possessed of activity through the action of breathing. Because this concerns the internal self (*adhyātma*), "gods" refers to the sense organs.

Or rather, they are called "men" because they breathe after the principal vital breath (*prāṇa*) and move according to it. Likewise, both humans and animals possess movement only through the activity of breathing. Therefore, living beings do not possess a self solely by means of the limited self consisting of food (*annamaya*); rather, they also [possess it] by means of that which is contained within it, namely the self consisting of vital breath (*prāṇamaya*).

By the very fact of possessing that which pervades all bodies, humans and other beings possess a self (*ātman*). In this way, all living beings possess a self by virtue of the [sheaths] beginning with the *manomaya*, which are composed of the elements starting with space (*ākāśa*), which are progressively subtler, each pervading the one preceding it, culminating in the *ānandamaya*, and which are produced by ignorance (*avidyā*). Likewise, they possess a self by virtue of their inherent nature [which is composed of] space and the other elements.

They possess a Self through that which is eternal, unchanging, all-pervading, characterized by truth, knowledge, and infinity, which transcends the five sheaths, and is the Self of all. For it is also implied by the sense of the matter that He alone is, in the ultimate sense, the Self of all.
As it was said, "The gods breathe after the vital breath (prāṇa)," he asks why that is so, and replies: "For the vital breath..."

Because the life—meaning the duration of existence—of living beings consists of breath; for according to another Vedic text, "As long as the breath dwells in this body, so long is there life. Therefore, it is "all-life" (*sarvāyuṣam*). "All-life" means the life of all; that which is indeed all-life is called "all-life. This is because death is universally recognized to occur upon the departure of the breath; for this is well known in the world.

The full span of life belongs to the vital breath (*prāṇa*). Therefore, those who, having stepped away from this external, unique self consisting of food (*annamaya*), meditate within upon the common self consisting of vital breath (*prāṇamaya*)— thinking, "I am the *prāṇa*, the self of all beings, because I am the cause of life"— they go to the full span of life in this world and do not depart [prematurely].
It has been explained through superficial observation that each subsequent sheath (*kośa*) is indeed the self (*ātman*) of each preceding sheath; however, that is incorrect.

For it would result in the word "self" being used in its primary sense [only for the innermost sheath], and it would contradict the use of the pronoun "this" (*etad*) which refers to the subject under discussion [the Supreme Self]. Therefore, the intended meaning is stated: here, by the word "self," it is the conscious self (*cidātman*), which is the substratum for the superimposition of all the sheaths, that is intended. Likewise, in the passage beginning with "svābhāvike"—

"No," [he says]. "By implication" means: because of the force of the word *ātman* (Self), and because it is logically untenable for that which is imagined to be the substratum. "From the uncommon" means: having departed from that which has a distinct nature, one should abandon the notion of "Self" there. "Common" means: common to all the senses; for it is observed that through eating and so forth performed by the vital breath (*prāṇa*), nourishment and other benefits accrue to all [the senses]. Of all beings...

Regarding the phrase "the Self": the construction is that this very element of consciousness (ciddhātu), which is the Self of the preceding [sheath] by way of the *sūtrātman*, is the Self of that [sheath] consisting of vital breath (*prāṇamaya*).
Just as there are many grains of husked rice, so too are the various fluids. [Page 56] Third Section. Accompanied by the commentary of Śaṅkara and the sub-commentary (Ṭīkā) composed by Ānandagiri.
"For the life-span of beings is not fixed; therefore it is called 'the whole life-span.
Of that [self], this very one is the embodied self (śārīra ātmā), which belongs to the former. Now, different from this one consisting of breath (prāṇamaya) is another, inner self."

It consists of mind; by that it is filled. This very one is indeed of the form of a person. Following its person-like form, he is of the form of a person. Of this [person], the Yajus is the head; the Ṛc is the right wing; the Sāman is the left wing.

The meaning is that they die by death before their lifespan has been reached. However, "a hundred years" is more appropriate as the full measure of life, because this is well-known from the Vedic revelation (*śruti*). What is the reason? For the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is indeed the life-span of living beings;
therefore, it is called the "full measure of life. Whosoever meditates upon Brahman as possessing a particular quality becomes a partaker of that very quality.

The repetition beginning with "For breath indeed" (*prāṇo hi*) is for the purpose of stating the cause for the attainment of the fruit of knowledge. Of that preceding one, the *annamaya*, this very one existing within the *annamaya* body is the embodied self (*śārīra ātmā*). Who is it? It is this one consisting of breath (*prāṇamaya*). The rest, beginning with "From him, verily, from this," has already been explained. Another inner self consists of mind (*manomaya*). "Mind" means—
The internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), consisting of volition and the like, is made of that; thus he is "mind-made" (*manomaya*), just as [the self] is "food-made" (*annamaya*).

This is the inner self of the one consisting of vital breath (*prāṇamaya*). Of this [self], the *Yajus* alone is the head. *Yajus* refers to a specific type of mantra characterized by an indefinite number of syllables, feet, and pauses; the word *yajus* denotes that class [of mantra], and its status as the head is as follows:

Because of its predominance. And its predominance arises from its direct contribution (*saṃnipatyopakāra*) to the sacrifice and other rites. For it is by means of the *yajus* that the oblation is offered, or else there is the scriptural injunction regarding the assignment of the head and other parts through the utterance of *svāhā* and so forth; this [assignment] applies everywhere. For the mind—whose nature consists of the volition toward those [objects], such as place, effort, resonance, accent, phoneme, word, and sentence—is their manifestation.

A mental modification (*vṛtti*) which, through the doors of the instruments such as the ear and so forth, is characterized by the convention of "Yajus" is called *yajus*. Likewise for *ṛc* and *sāman*. And thus, since mantras are modifications of the mind, it is the modification itself that is repeated; therefore, mental recitation (*mānasa-japa*) is logically established. Otherwise, because [the mantra] would not be an object [of the mind], the mantra could not be repeated.

By the word "Yajus," the external Yajurveda is meant. Anticipating the objection as to how that [external Veda] can be the head of this internal, mind-made [Veda], he says: "For by the mind... Although the word "Yajus" is conventionally established (*rūḍha*) for a collection of words, nevertheless...

The meaning is that because the Veda (*śruti*) is beyond suspicion, its authority establishes that the specific mental modification (*manovṛtti*) which is the object of the technical designation "Yajus"—consisting of the resolve that "these letters in this sequence are to be studied as the Yajurveda"—is what must be grasped. He also states the reasoning that supports the Veda: "And if it were so," etc., and "Otherwise," etc. [This refers to the argument that] if words were external substances like jars, then the mind—

The Taittirīya Upaniṣad: the trunk is the *raḥ* section; the self is the instruction (*ādeśa*); the tail is the Atharvāṅgirasaḥ [in the Brahmavallī].

Because [the mantra] is like a jar or other such objects, mental recitation (mānasa-japa) is not tenable. Furthermore, the repetition of the mantra is enjoined many times; if it is argued that the repetition of the mantra occurs through the repetition of the recollection of its constituent syllables, we say no, because the primary meaning is possible. In the case of the injunction, "He recites the first verse three times" and "the last verse three times," the repetition of the *ṛc* (verse) is heard. In that context...

If the *ṛc* were not the object [of the repetition], and if the repetition were performed by means of a mental recollection (*smṛti*) having that as its object, then the primary meaning— the repetition of the *ṛc* itself, as enjoined in the rule "he repeats the first verse thrice"— would be abandoned. Therefore,

the word *yajus* refers to the consciousness of the Self (*ātmacaitanya*), which is without beginning or end, delimited by the adjuncts of mental modifications (*manovṛtti-upādhi*) and established in those very mental modifications.

The self-knowledge that is expressed [in scripture] is the mantras; thus, the eternity of the Vedas is established. Otherwise, if they were objects [of perception], they would be non-eternal like form and other such things, which is not tenable. Furthermore, the Śruti states, "That in which all the Vedas become one is the Self within the mind," thereby declaring the oneness of the eternal Self.

If the *gāyatrī* and other mantras were eternal, [this] would be consistent. The meaning is that there could be no mental recitation (*mānasa-japa*), because it is impossible for the mind to have as its object that which exists in the supreme ether—the imperishable syllable (*akṣara*)—and because the mind lacks independence regarding external objects. For this reason as well, he states that the nature of mantras must be asserted as being mental modifications (*manovṛtti*). He says: "And the repetition of mantras. If words were external substances like pots and the like, [then...]

The repetition of the *mātṛkā*s is not possible in the same way as it is for jars and other objects; for it is action alone that is repeated, and since repetition would otherwise be impossible, it has been stated that they must be considered actions. In this regard, one might suspect that there is another way to account for it [by suggesting they are not actions]. To this, he says: "Regarding the syllables (*akṣara*). Since the *smṛti* is distinct from the mantras, a figurative sense of repetition would result [if they were not actions]; therefore, there is no other way to account for it. He clarifies this by saying: "Thrice."

By the words "the first," and so forth: when the *samidh* oblations are offered by the Adhvaryu, the Hotṛ recites the eighteen-verse hymn beginning with "ma vo vājā abhidyavaḥ. Among those verses, the meaning is that the repetition is prescribed by scripture, such that the Hotṛ should recite the first verse of the hymn and the final verse three times each. Having stated that mantras are modifications of the mind (*manovṛtti*), [the text proceeds] to [discuss] the modifications of the mind...

He states that [the mantras] have consciousness as their essence (*cidātmatā*) precisely because they are established as being always pervaded by consciousness. Regarding the phrase "therefore" (*tasmāt*): it has been stated that since mantras are mental modifications (*manovṛtti*), their manifestation (*āvirbhāva*) is not possible [in the ordinary sense]. He further states that their eternity is also possible through their being consciousness by way of a traditional lineage (*paraṃparayā*). Regarding the phrase "if this is so" (*evaṃ ceti*): it means while they possess the nature of consciousness (*caitanyarūpatve sati*). Regarding the phrase "otherwise" (*anyatheti*): if one does not accept that they have the nature of self-luminous consciousness, then like color and other [sensory objects], they would be [mere] objects of cognition.

Otherwise, even non-eternality would follow as a consequence. Since this logic would lead to the absurdity that the words of Kālidāsa and others are also eternal, this is merely a fallacious argument. One should not say, "Let it be non-eternal," for he says, "This is not tenable. The meaning is that because the eternity [of the Veda] has been declared by the scripture stating, "By the word, which is manifold and eternal" (*vācā virūpanityayā*), it is not logical for the Vedas to be non-eternal. The meaning is as follows: since the identity of the Self with the insentient [mind] through self-luminosity is impossible due to the contradiction between the insentient and the sentient, it is indicated that the nature of the Self is consciousness (cidātmatva) which pervades the mental modifications (manovṛtti). Furthermore, being present in the mind as the Witness (sākṣitayā), the Vedic verses (ṛcaḥ)—consisting of injunctions and prohibitions—abide in identity with the Imperishable (akṣara), which is like the supreme ether (parama-vyoman), Brahman. Thus they are established.

"From which words turn back, together with the mind, not having attained it," and so forth. Of that preceding one consisting of breath (*prāṇamaya*), this very one is the embodied self (*śārīra*). "Embodied" means existing within the body consisting of breath.
Who is he? It is this one consisting of mind (*manomaya*). "From that, indeed, from this one," and so forth, is as before. Another [self] within.

The Self consists of consciousness (*vijñānamaya*). It is internal to that which consists of mind (*manomaya*); this *manomaya* is said to be the Self of the Vedas. Consciousness (*vijñāna*) is the intellect whose object is the meaning of the Vedas, characterized by certainty; it is an attribute of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) defined by determination. That [Self] consists of such consciousness, being established through certainties of knowledge that take the form of valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*).

That Self consists of consciousness (*vijñānamaya*). For sacrifices and other rites are sustained by being preceded by the cognition that constitutes valid knowledge (*pramāṇa-vijñāna*). And the fact that it is the cause of sacrifices and so forth will be stated in the following verse. For in one who possesses the cognition of certainty, faith (*śraddhā*) arises first regarding the duties to be performed. Because it precedes all duties, it is like the head; it is the head. *Ṛta* is truth.

It is exactly as explained. *Yoga* means reasoning or application; *ātman* is like the self. The meaning is that the wording of the mantra (*ā-mantra-varṇa*) demonstrates oneness. The meaning is that it instructs by pointing out the specific details to be extended and the specific details to be performed, saying, "This is to be done in this manner. It is not possible for speech and mind to be the objects of their own speech and mind, because that would involve a contradiction of self-action (*svātmani vṛttivirodha*). And regarding that Brahman consisting of mind, [the text says] "upāsaka... etc. [and] "ṛg... etc.; it is praised; from it the *Ṛg* and other Vedas are born; it protects.

Faith is its head; righteousness is its right wing; truth is its left wing; meditation is its body; greatness is its tail, the foundation. On this point there is also this verse. Thus ends the fourth section. 4.

Consciousness performs the sacrifice; it also performs ritual acts. All the gods worship consciousness as the supreme Brahman. If one knows consciousness to be Brahman, and if one does not become negligent because of that, [one casts off] evils from the body.

In the Brahmavallī, for one who possesses the Self, who is disciplined, and who is concentrated, the factors such as faith and the rest become capable of realizing the truth as it is, like the limbs of a body; therefore, concentration (*samādhāna*)—which is yoga—is the essence of that which consists of consciousness (*vijñānamaya*). This is the Greatness.

The tail is the support. "Mahas" refers to the principle of Mahat (the Great), which is the first-born. This is based on another Vedic text: "The Great Yakṣa is the first-born. It is called the tail because it is the cause of support;

"Consisting of knowledge" (*jñānamaya*). "Another inner self consisting of bliss" (*ānandamaya*).

Because of the Vedic scripture. The internal nature of that which consists of consciousness (*vijñānamaya*) is thus established. Joy (*harṣa*) is that very thing; and that same joy, when intensified, is delight (*pramoda*). "He becomes non-existent indeed, if he knows Brahman as non-existent. But if he knows that Brahman exists, then they know him as existing. This is his [teaching].

Such is the embodied self (śārīra ātmā), which belongs to the former [the cosmic self]. Now, therefore, follow these further questions: If one knows—that is, if one understands—that Brahman is non-existent (*asat*) or equivalent to the non-existent, then he becomes like that which is non-existent, namely, one who has no connection with the purpose of man (*puruṣārtha*). Who is this person who has no connection with the purpose of man? It is he who knows—that is, perceives—that Brahman is non-existent (*asat*), meaning it does not exist. If [he should know this]...

If one knows that Brahman exists as the opposite of that—that which is the locus of all conceptual constructions, the seed of all activity, and in which all particularities have subsided—then why is there any doubt regarding its non-existence? We reply: because Brahman is beyond empirical discourse (*vyavahārātīta*). For it is only within the sphere of empirical discourse, which consists merely of verbal designations (*vācārambhaṇamātra*), that "existence" [is attributed].
When the intellect has been cultivated regarding that which is the opposite [of the phenomenal world]— that which transcends empirical discourse— it also realizes non-existence.

Just as it is well known that a jar or the like, being established as an object of empirical discourse, is "non-existent" when it is the opposite of that [empirical reality], so too, by analogy with that, there might arise the suspicion here that Brahman does not exist.

Therefore it is said: "If one knows that Brahman exists. What, then, would happen to one who knows that "It exists"? To this he says: the knowers of Brahman know this very person—who possesses the nature of the existent Brahman and has attained the Self that is ultimately real—as one who truly exists. Therefore, because of this knowledge of existence, he is to be understood by others as being like Brahman itself.

This is the meaning. Alternatively, he who thinks "Brahman does not exist" arrives at the non-existence of the entire path of the virtuous—characterized by the regulations of the social classes (*varṇa*) and stages of life (*āśrama*)—due to his lack of faith, because that [path] exists for the purpose of realizing Brahman. Therefore, such a nihilist (*nāstika*), being non-existent (*asan*), is called a "non-person" (*asat-puruṣa*) in the world.

One who knows that "Brahman exists" as being the opposite of that [non-existence] understands, through faith, the true path characterized by the established order of castes, stages of life, and so forth, which is the means for attaining that Brahman; therefore, the virtuous recognize him as a "good person" (sat) standing on the right path. For this reason, one should indeed regard Brahman as "existing."

The meaning of the sentence is "it is to be attained. Of that preceding self consisting of consciousness (*vijñānamaya*), this very one existing within the body consisting of consciousness is the embodied self (*śārīra ātmā*). Who is he? It is this one consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*).
Regarding him, there is no doubt as to his non-existence; however, because Brahman is devoid of all distinctions, there might be a suspicion of its non-existence—[but such is not the case here].

The doubt is justified. Since Brahman is thus the universal commonality for all, therefore—after this—the "subsequent questions" (*anupraśnāḥ*) are those questions of the listener, the disciple, which follow upon the teacher's statement. For Brahman is indeed common to both the knower and the ignorant, because it is the cause of ether and the rest; therefore, even for the ignorant...

Some maintain that this verse is an illuminator of the *ānandamaya* (the one consisting of bliss); in response to them, he says: "With reference to Him. The meaning is: because [Brahman] is perceived as possessing specific attributes (*saviśeṣatayā*). Furthermore, since Brahman is common to all, its state of being an object of worldly transaction (*vyavahāryatva*) would apply toward everyone, yet it is not so seen; therefore, from this too, the suspicion of non-existence arises. [This is stated] because [Brahman] is the cause of ether and the rest.
"Diti" means that it is distinguished by its being the cause of all living beings. By whose power was this other question obtained?
[End of] the Sixth Section (Khaṇḍa 6), together with the commentary by Ānandagiri and the Śāṅkara-bhāṣya.
Does anyone go to that world after departing from here without knowledge? Or does the wise person go to that world after departing?
There is a doubt regarding the attainment of Brahman. Or rather, does even one who lacks knowledge [go] to that world, the Supreme Self, after departing from here?

The word *cana* also has the sense of "even"; thus, the second question should also be understood as: "Does even one who is ignorant go to, or reach, [Brahman], or does he not go? Because of the plural number in the term *anupraśnāḥ* ("subsequent questions"), there are two further questions regarding the knower.
If even an ignorant person does not go to Brahman, which is the common cause, then for the knower as well, there would be no attainment of Brahman.
A doubt is raised; therefore, the question is asked regarding him: "Does the knower [attain]? Even though one who knows Brahman is a "knower," the question remains:

does he, having departed from here, attain that world? This being the case, when the substitution of *ay* and the elision of *ya* have been performed, there is a prolation (*pluti*) of the vowel *a* in the word *samaśnutā*; furthermore, the vowel *u* following it—namely, the *u* of *u iti*—is drawn down from below, as is the letter *t*.

Having joined the word *uta* from before with the word *uta* that precedes *āho*, he asks: "Or rather, does the wise man [attain it]? One question is: "Does the wise man attain that world? Another question is: "Or is it that even the wise man does not attain it, just as the ignorant man does not? Or perhaps there are only two [questions]: those concerning the wise and the ignorant.

As for the plural number [in "yau"], it is appropriate in view of the other questions that arise by implication. From the scriptural hearing, "If one knows Brahman as non-existent" and "If one knows Brahman as existent," a doubt arises as to whether it exists or not;
therefore, the first subsequent question—whether it exists or does not exist—is not already established. Because Brahman is impartial...

The second [question] is: "Does he go or does he not go? Even though Brahman is uniform, it is suspected that just as for the ignorant person, so too for the knower there might be no going. The third supplementary question is: "Does the knower partake of [Brahman], or does he not partake?
To provide answers to these, the subsequent text is commenced. Among those [questions], first, [the existence of Brahman] alone...
To this it is replied: As for that which was stated, "Brahman is Truth, Knowledge, Infinite," it must be explained how its nature as Truth is established;
therefore, this is said: its truthfulness is expressed by the very mention of its existence (*sattva*). For it has been stated that "only that which exists is Truth.
Therefore, truthfulness is expressed by the very mention of existence. How is this meaning understood?
These subsequent sentences of this text are indeed connected with this very meaning through the following of its words;
they declare that "That is Truth," beginning with the passage, "If this space were not bliss," and so forth.
In this regard, a doubt arises as to whether Brahman is non-existent. Why? Because whatever exists is perceived in its specific form, just as...

He says: "Brahman is non-existent. This is because of the force of the word "if" (*cet*), which implies the possibility of its existence; the meaning is that if existence is established for Brahman, its reality is thereby proven, since the negation of what exists is impossible. "In this sense" means that by establishing its existence, it is shown to have a real entity as its object.

Intending that the proof of Brahman’s existence is nothing other than the exclusion of non-existence (*asattva*), he raises the doubt regarding its non-existence with the words, "In that regard, [it is] not non-existent. By relying on the worldly pervasion (*vyāpti*) that "whatever is an effect is preceded by an existent," it is first established that there is an existent cause. Furthermore, because that cause is not limited by space and so forth—since it is the cause of space and so forth—it is designated by the term "Brahman."

[The opponent argues: "Like a jar or similar objects; that which does not exist is not perceived, as for example a hare's horn and so forth. Likewise, Brahman is not perceived. Therefore, because it is not apprehended through its specific characteristics, it does not exist. [Reply: That is not so, because Brahman is the cause of space and the rest. Brahman is not non-existent; why? Because all effects, such as space and the like, [proceed from it].

That which is born from Brahman is perceived; and whatever is born is seen in the world to have an existent cause, such as clay or a seed for effects like a jar or a sprout. Therefore, because it is the cause of space and the rest, Brahman exists. Furthermore, no effect is perceived in the world that is born from the non-existent; for if the effects such as name and form were from the non-existent—

Because it would lack self-nature (*nirātmakatva*), it could not be perceived; yet it is indeed perceived, therefore Brahman exists. If the effect were derived from the non-existent, then even when being grasped, it would be permeated by non-existence; but this is not the case, therefore Brahman exists. In this regard, another scriptural passage asks, "How could existence arise from non-existence? thus declaring the impossibility of existence arising from non-existence.

According to logic: therefore, it is reasonable that Brahman is indeed existent. Now, if it were a cause like clay, seeds, and so forth, it would be insentient; however, this is not so because it possesses the quality of desiring. For in the world, there is no insentient entity that desires. Indeed, we have stated that Brahman is omniscient; therefore, its status as a desirer is established. Because it is a desirer—

If it is argued that [Brahman] acts like those who have unfulfilled desires, we say no; for unlike others who, being under the sway of others, are impelled by defects such as desire due to their lack of independence, the desires of Brahman do not act as His instigators. How then? Since they are characterized by truth and knowledge, they are pure because they are identical with His own Self; therefore, Brahman is not impelled by them. Rather, He is the instigator of them.

The state of being expressible (*vācyatva*) is established. Since that [expressibility] is not perceived specifically, a doubt regarding its non-existence arises; this is excluded by its being a cause. However, existence is not proven from the fact of being a cause, because that would entail the fallacy of the unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*). This is the intended meaning. For this reason as well, one should entertain the doubt of non-existence regarding the material cause of the world; thus he says: "Nor of the non-existent," etc. "By logic" means: because no positive concomitance (*anvaya*) with the non-existent is observed.

The meaning is "by means of this reasoning. Having thus dispelled the doubt regarding non-existence, he proceeds to refute the doubt regarding insentience (*acetanatva*) against the proponent of the Māyāvāda as a corollary, beginning with the words "tadyadi" (if that...). Although in the Sāṃkhya system the capacity to desire is unestablished because the conscious principle (*cetana*) is immutable, nevertheless, by the force of worldly pervasion (*vyāpti*), he states that the doubt regarding insentience is removed on account of its being a desirer, saying "na hi" (for not).

Then, suspecting that by the force of worldly pervasion (*vyāpti*) alone, even the state of having unfulfilled desires would follow, he says, beginning with "because of being a desirer," and so forth. The meaning is that while living beings possess unfulfilled bliss because they are subject to another's control, that is not the case for Brahman. To the question, "Of what nature, then, are the desires of Brahman? he says, "characterized by true knowledge" (*satyajñānalakṣaṇā*). [The compound] *satyajñānalakṣaṇa*...

Those whose nature is such are so described. This is what is meant: Brahman, reflected in *māyā*, is indeed the cause of the world; it is the desirer through desires that are themselves transformations of *māyā*. And because those transformations are pervaded by consciousness (*cit*) that is not overwhelmed by ignorance (*avidyā*) and the like, they consist of truth and knowledge. Furthermore, due to its identity with Brahman, [the Self] is pure, being untouched by defects. Consequently, there is a distinction between these and the desires of the individual soul (*jīva*).
It is established (*siddham*). In that case, the desires of Brahman would lead even those who perform meritorious deeds to obtain undesirable results, because of his independence (*svātantrya*).

Sixth Section. With the commentary of Śaṅkara, accompanied by the sub-commentary of Ānandagiri: "Was there anyone who heard this? 3? He desired: 'May I become many.'"

Brahman [acts] in dependence upon the karma of living beings; therefore, Brahman possesses sovereignty over its desires. Consequently, Brahman is not one whose desires are unfulfilled, and because it does not depend on any other means of accomplishment. Furthermore, unlike others, whose desires depend on external causes such as merit (*dharma*) and so forth, and who depend on other means consisting of effects and instruments distinct from their own self; [Brahman’s desires are not thus dependent].

Brahman does not depend on external causes and the like; rather, [it depends on] nothing other than its own self. This is what he says: "He desired; He, the Self. From whom space was produced, He desired—He had a desire. How?
"May I be many, may I become abundant, may I come to be manifold. How could one who is single [be many], without [becoming] something other than himself?

It is said that there would be multiplicity upon entry; "I shall be born," "I shall arise. For this becoming many does not refer to a different object in the same way that the birth of a son [is distinct from the father]; rather, it refers to the manifestation of name and form which reside within the Self. When name and form, which were residing in the Self and unmanifested, become differentiated (*vyākriyete*), then those names and forms [become manifest as] the very nature of the Self.

By the very renunciation of its own name and form, Brahman—undivided in space and time—is differentiated in all states; that differentiation of name and form is Brahman’s becoming many. Otherwise, it is not possible for the partless Brahman to undergo either multiplicity or diminution, just as there can be no diminution or multiplicity of space.

The distinction is created by other objects; therefore, it is through them alone that the Self becomes manifold. For there exists no object other than the Self—whether non-self in nature, or distinguished by space and time, subtle, concealed, remote, past, present, or future—that is separate from it. Consequently, name and form in all their states have the Self as their essence, being nothing but Brahman itself.

Anticipating the objection that [desire] might arise from contact with a body and so forth, he says: "But of those... One should not suspect that Brahman possesses a body and so forth on the grounds that desire is unproven to be produced by connection with a body and so forth; thus he says: "And because it does not depend on other means. [Regarding] desire—

The meaning is that because the illusory power (*māyā*)—which possesses various forms—is non-different from Brahman, its transformations, namely the objects of desire, are also non-different from Brahman; therefore, there is no dependence upon causes such as the body. "By means of that alone" means by means of the transformation of *māyā*, which consists of the powers of name and form (*nāmarūpa*).

If it is accepted that *māyā*—consisting of the powers of name and form and being insentient in nature—is distinct [from Brahman], then like the *pradhāna*, it would exist separately, and thus the doctrine of non-duality (*advaita*) would be lost.

Anticipating this objection, he says: "Certainly not" (*na hi*). Does that which is distinct from the Self establish itself independently or through another? Not the first, because that would entail the loss of its insentience (*jāḍya*) and the loss of its distinctness. Not the second, because no relation with a means of valid cognition (*pramā*) can be established. For neither conjunction nor any other relation, nor the status of object and subject (*viṣaya-viṣayibhāva*), is possible between two things existing in different places and times, since one must seek a regulating cause (*niyāmaka*) for such a relation. Nor can the relation be the very nature (*svabhāva*) of the things themselves.

The point is this: since the two natures would be exhausted by their very relation, it would follow that the relata themselves do not exist; nor can a thing be related to itself, as that would result in the fallacy of self-dependence (*ātmāśraya*). Furthermore, if such an object does not exist and [the relation] functions merely as a conventional usage, it would follow that the usage is false, and thus one ultimately arrives at the doctrine of the indeterminable (*anirvacanīya-vāda*). This is because no entity distinct from the Self is possible.

Therefore, he says "ataḥ" (therefore), meaning that name and form are established only through identity with the Self. If so, [what of the objection that] Brahman is... [page 67] ...limited by its effects and causes?
[End of fragment].

"May I procreate," he thought; he performed austerity; he...

[From the *Brahmavallī*]
Brahman is not identical with those two; yet, since they do not exist at all apart from it, they are said to have Brahman as their essence.
Through those two limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), Brahman—which is that very Self—participates in all worldly transactions, such as the knower, the known, knowledge, words, and their meanings.
Being full of desire, He performed austerity (*tapas*). Here, "austerity" refers to knowledge. Of whom this knowledge...
Because of another scriptural passage stating "This [Brahman] is austerity," and because He has all His desires fulfilled, austerity is simply impossible for anyone else.

"He performed austerity" (tattapo'tapyata) means that He, as the Self, engaged in reflection concerning the creation of the world to be emanated and so forth. Having thus reflected and performed austerity, He [created] all this in accordance with the causes such as the karma of living beings.

He created—that is, he brought forth—the world as it is experienced by all living beings in all its states, according to their experience, in various forms, and across space and time. Having created this world—whatever this "whatever" may be, that is, the world without distinction—it is stated what he did next: he entered into that very world which he had created.

In this regard, the following must be considered: how did [the Creator] enter? Did he enter by that very same self through which he was the creator, or by another? What, first, is the logical position? Since the suffix *ktvā* is heard in the text, it is logical that he who was the creator entered by that very same self. But is this not improper? For if Brahman is the cause like clay, then because the effect is of the same nature as that [cause], [it would follow that the effect is already present].

For it is the cause itself that has transformed into the nature of the effect; therefore, one should not say that the world-appearance is unattached because it is as if the effect has not entered into it. To this he says: "Not Brahman. The meaning is: Brahman is not of that [world's] nature, because it is non-inert (ajaḍa), and because its establishment is possible even by setting that aside. If so, how then are those two of the nature of Brahman? To this he says: "Those two, that... [te tad].

The meaning is this: just as one who has awakened from a dream cannot maintain the experience of eating the sky, because that which was superimposed lacks any possibility of existence, so too name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), which are objects of experience, are said to have the nature of Brahman—the self of experience—and not with the intention of asserting their actual reality. He states that it is not only Brahman’s possession of manifold forms that is due to the limiting adjunct of *māyā*, but also its being the locus of all worldly transactions; thus he says, "by those two. This refers to the indeterminability (*anirvācyatā*) of the entry.

In order to demonstrate the purport of the statement regarding the entry of the individual soul (*jīva*) into its identity with Brahman through the act of illumination, he begins the inquiry with the words, "In this regard, this must be considered," and so forth. Upon reflection, the proponent of the final view (*siddhāntin*) asserts that the entry occurs for the purpose of creation, in accordance with the scriptural use of the suffix *-ktvā*. The opponent (*pūrvavādī*) objects: "But this is not tenable," because there is a contradiction between the sequence of the two actions—creation and entry—occurring at prior and subsequent times.

If [the cause] exists, the identity of the action would be understood through the hearing of the suffix *-ktvā*, but a subsequent time for the entry is not possible; the meaning is that at the very moment of creation, the material cause already exists in the form of the effect. He explains this very point with the words: "For the cause itself... Just as the entry of Devadatta is seen into a house or similar place where he has not previously entered, so too [an entry] after the emergence of the effect would be separate— [The sentence continues: ...from the effect. After the manifestation [of the world], the re-entry of a separate cause is untenable; for there is no entry of clay into a jar apart from its transformation into the jar. If it is argued that, just as clay enters into a jar in the form of powder, so too does the Self enter into the effects of name and form through another aspect, this is not so, according to other scriptural texts.

"...having entered by means of this living self (jīva-ātman). This is not tenable because Brahman is one. However, in the case of clay, since it is manifold and possesses parts, its entry into a jar as clay-powder is logical; for the clay-powder has regions where it has not yet entered. But this is not so for the Self, given its oneness and partlessness.

Furthermore, since there is no location that has not already been entered, how can entry be possible? Yet, entry is logical because it is stated in scripture: "He entered into that very [being]" (*tadevānuprāviśat*). If it is argued: "Let it then be possessed of parts; for, being possessed of parts, entry by the individual self (*jīvātman*) into the effects of name and form is just as logical as the entry of a hand into the mouth," we reply: No, because it is not empty (*aśūnya*).

Because there is no region devoid of self (ātman) apart from the locus of the effects of name and form, which have evolved into the nature of effects, into which the individual soul (jīvātman) could enter. Furthermore, if it were to enter the cause itself, it would lose its status as an individual soul, just as a jar loses its jar-nature upon entering the clay; and yet the scripture says, "He entered into that very [cause]."

It is not logical for the Śruti to enter into its own cause. If it is argued that it must become a different effect, [and that] "it entered into that very thing" means that the effect which is the individual self (jīvātman), having evolved into name and form, attains the state of yet another effect—this is not so, because of contradiction. For a jar does not attain the state of another jar; [this is known from] the scriptural texts on distinction (vyatireka).

Furthermore, because of the contradiction [with scripture]: the scriptural texts which describe the individual soul (*jīva*) as being distinct from the effects of name and form would be contradicted; moreover, liberation would be impossible if it were to attain that [state of Brahman], for one cannot attain that very thing from which one is being liberated. Indeed, a thief who is bound does not attain the state of his own shackles.

The meaning is that entry is not possible. Having set forth the view of a certain proponent of the Siddhānta (the final conclusion), the Pūrvapakṣin (the opponent) refutes it with the words "Just as a jar," and so forth. [The opponent asks: "If entry by the Creator or by anyone else is not possible, then how is entry to be explained?"

The proponent of a partial view (siddhāntyekadeśin) asks: "How so? He states that it should not be said that [the space] does not exist at all. He says: "And it is logical. He himself provides the reasoning: "It possesses parts indeed. The opponent (pūrvavādī) refutes this: "No, because it is not empty. For Brahman, when transformed into the form of an effect, its very effect—consisting of name and form—is the location; there is no other region apart from that. Ya-...

One should not suspect that the individual soul (*jīvātman*), as a specific effect, will enter into that very cause which has itself transformed into the form of the effect; thus he says: "If the cause alone... Having granted the entry of the specific effect for the sake of argument, a refutation was stated, but that is not possible because it contradicts scripture; thus he says: "That very same... By means of the word *tat*, which refers back to the cause, the effect is indicated.
The entry of another effect into that [place] is prescribed because there is no possibility of a location not already occupied; therefore, there is no contradiction with the Śruti.

Having thus set forth the view of a certain proponent of the Siddhānta, he refutes it with the words "kāryāntaram eva" (only another effect) and so forth. (Note: The fragment "jha. ru. vātmanā patra" appears to be a scribal or editorial mark.)

If it is argued that [the world] has evolved through the distinction between external and internal according to the *Brahmavallī*, and that the very same causal Brahman has evolved as the body-container (*śarīrāvāratvena*) and as the inner individual self (*jīvātman*) which is contained within it (*ādheyatvena*), [we reply: no,
for that which is external...

Because entry is logically possible. For that which is already situated within something cannot be said to have entered it; rather, entry would mean the entering of what was previously outside, as this is the observed meaning of the word "entry," as in the expression, "having built a house, he entered it.
If it is argued that the entry is like the reflection of the sun in water or other such reflections, we say no, because [the Self] is not limited.

And because it is incorporeal and formless. The arising of reflections such as that of the sun in water and the like—which are limited, corporeal, and possess a nature of clarity—would occur in one place upon another; but this is not the case for the Self, because it is immortal and is the cause of space and the rest, being all-pervading. [Therefore, there can be no reflection] in a substrate located at a distant place...

Furthermore, because there is no other interior space, entry is not logical, as in the case of a reflection. If that is so, then there is no entry at all, nor do we perceive any other doctrine; yet there is the Vedic revelation: "It entered into that very [being].
And scripture is the cause for the arising of knowledge regarding objects beyond the senses. Nor from this statement—

"Even for those who exert effort, consciousness arises. Well then, this sentence—'Having created that, He entered into it itself'—is useless and should therefore be rejected. No; because it has another purpose. Why this misplaced deliberation? There is another primary meaning intended by this sentence which must be recalled. [It concerns] Brahman—

"He attains the Supreme. "Brahman is Truth, Knowledge, and Infinite. "He who knows it as hidden in the cave [of the heart]"—this knowledge is both intended here and is the subject under discussion. Furthermore, for the purpose of following the true nature of Brahman, if one were to employ the word *tat* (That), which denotes the cause such as space (*ākāśa*), as a figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of the effect, then a figurative indication of something unintended would result; in that case, how...?

Another partial proponent of the established doctrine (*siddhāntaikadeśin*) says that the word [“water”] should be taken in its primary sense alone. [The author] says “external,” etc. He states that in this view, the primary meaning of the scriptural mention of “entering” would not be obtained, saying “not external,” etc. Having set forth the opinion of another Vedāntin, he refutes it with the words beginning “in water,” etc. Having thus rejected the partial proponent of the established doctrine, the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvavādī*) concludes: “Thus.”
[The opponent] says: "It is not so. [The author] replies: "No," for it has been stated that there is no entry for Brahman, and consequently, the entry of anything else is also impossible.
He further states that the entry of the other cannot even be postulated, citing the scriptural text: "He entered into that very thing" (*tadevānuprāviśat*).
That scripture speaks of the entry of the Creator; and since that scripture is our authority as Mīmāṃsakas, we cannot contradict it.

The sense is that the conceptualization of entry [into Brahman] is improper once [the Self] has been deposited [as the inner controller]. Then, fearing the objection that "one should simply state that Brahman itself enters by taking refuge in the scripture," he says: "And not... Therefore, he concludes that this sentence is indeed devoid of meaning, like the saying, "The blind man found the jewel. [He uses the word] "hanta" [to express irony]. It is devoid of meaning either because the object within the scope of the word's power (*śakti*) is impossible, or because the object within the scope of the intended meaning (*tātparya*) is impossible.

Not the first [alternative]. For just as the reflection of incorporeal things like space occurs in water even when it is not at a remote distance, so too, although Brahman is incorporeal, its state of being reflected in internal organs (*antaḥkaraṇa*) and the like after the time of creation is possible, since it is already reflected in indeterminable ignorance (*anirvācyāvidyā*). Thus he says: "No. Nor is the second [alternative], as he says: "Because it serves another purpose. This is clarified: for what purpose?

Having entered into that, the effect ending with the "consisting of food" (*annamaya*) has been demonstrated, and the pursuit of Brahman has begun. Therein, distinct from the self consisting of food is another inner self consisting of breath (*prāṇamaya*); within that is the one consisting of mind (*manomaya*), and within that is the one consisting of consciousness (*vijñānamaya*). This is the cave of consciousness—

That which was entered there is shown to be the specific Self consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*). Therefore, by means of attaining the characteristic mark (*liṅga*) of the one consisting of supreme bliss, the Self— which is the culmination of the increase of bliss— is to be known within this very cave as the "Brahman-tail," the foundation, the locus of all conceptual constructions, yet itself free from conceptual construction (*nirvikalpa*).
Its entry is thus conceived.
For Brahman is not perceived elsewhere, because, being devoid of attributes (*nirviśeṣatvāt*), it lacks any connection with attributes that could serve as a means of perception.

This has been seen: just as there is a specific relationship between Rāhu and the moon or the sun, so too the relationship between the cave of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) and the Self is the cause for the perception of Brahman. This is because of the proximity [of the Self] and because the internal organ is of the nature of luminosity.
And just as the perception of a jar or other objects is characterized by light, so too [the perception of Brahman] is characterized by the light of the cognition of the intellect (*buddhi*).
If there were no perception of the Self, then the statement "it is hidden in the cave which is the cause of perception" would remain merely a theoretical premise.

However, here it is further stated that "having created that, He entered into it," referring to the state of its functioning. Thus, this very cause of ether and the rest, having created the effect, has—as it were—entered into it; it is the seer and hearer within the cave of the intellect (*buddhi*).
It is perceived as having specific qualities, such as "the thinker" and "the knower. That very [perception] is its entry;

therefore, Brahman exists as its cause. Because it exists, it should be perceived as "it exists" through its effects by means of inference and so forth. Beyond this—immediately after entering the cave of the intellect—it is indeed the one consisting of bliss (ānandamaya) that is distinguished.

The meaning is this: since the gender of the qualified [Brahman] is seen to be inseparable from the gender of the substantive [the Self], and because the Self—whose nature is Brahman and which culminates in the increase of bliss—is to be realized within this very cave by means of that non-separation, the "entry" is described as being inexpressible (anirvācya), like the entry of the sun into water; such is the intended sense.

He says "na hi" (not indeed) because the perception of Brahman is possible only within the cave of the intellect (*buddhi*); therefore, entry into that very place is intended. Now, one might object: "How can Brahman, which cannot be perceived elsewhere, be perceived in the intellect? Anticipating this doubt, he says "viśeṣa" (particularity), meaning that it is possible due to a specific capacity of the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*). [The phrase] ending with "saṃnikarṣāt" (due to proximity) means precisely through the contact with the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) in the case of the body, a jar, and so forth.

The manifestation of consciousness does not occur by itself; rather, the meaning is that the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) manifests consciousness without any mediation, as established through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*). Just as a face is not reflected in an object like a jar which is non-luminous by nature, but is reflected in water and the like which are luminous by nature, so too, because the internal organ possesses the natural quality of clarity (*prasāda*), it receives [the reflection of consciousness].

In that regard, he states that Brahman is apprehended; and [he gives another reason] because it is of the nature of light (*avabhāsātmatva*). Furthermore, just as light is accepted—even though it shares the same quality of insentience (*jāḍya*)—as being capable of overcoming the veil characterized by darkness (*tamas*), so too, despite the same quality of insentience, the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) itself, when transformed into the form of a cognition (*pratyayākāra*), must be accepted as having the capacity to overcome the veil characterized by ignorance (*ajñāna*). Thus he says: "And just as... (*yathā ca*).

In the Brahmavallī:
"It became the manifest and the unmanifest, the defined and the undefined, the supported and the unsupported, consciousness and non-consciousness, the true and the untrue."
It became the Real (satyam). Whatever exists here is that; they call it "the Real.

Having entered [it], what was both "being" (sat)—the formed (mūrta)—and "non-being" (tyat)—the formless (amūrta)—became so. The formed and the formless, whose names and forms were yet undifferentiated, are differentiated by the Self abiding within them; and when undifferentiated, they are designated by the terms "formed" and "formless."
Since those [objects] were not distinct from him in terms of space and time, it is said that "He became those.

Furthermore, both the defined (*nirukta*) and the undefined (*anirukta*): the "defined" is that which has been extracted and specified as "this is that" by distinguishing it from homogeneous and heterogeneous classes through its particularities of space and time; the "undefined" is the opposite of that. The defined—

In the *Nirukta* as well, these are indeed qualifiers of the formed (*mūrta*) and the formless (*amūrta*). For example: "being" (*sat*) and "that which is" (*tyat*) correspond to the perceptible (*pratyakṣa*) and the imperceptible (*parokṣa*); likewise, "having a dwelling" (*nilayana*) and "not having a dwelling" (*anilayana*). "Having a dwelling" means a nest or a support, which is a property of the formed alone; "not having a dwelling" is its opposite, a property of the formless alone. Thus, "that which is," the unexpressed (*anirukta*), and that which has no dwelling are properties of the formless.

Even though they are of the nature of *dharmatā*, these [terms] refer only to the realm of the evolved (*vyākṛta*), because it is heard that they exist at all subsequent times. "That" (*tyad*) refers to the unmanifested (*anirukta*), such as the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and so forth; that itself is the non-abode (*anilayana*). Therefore, these qualifiers of the formless belong only to the realm of the evolved. "Consciousness" (*vijñāna*) is the sentient; "unconsciousness" (*avijñāna*) is that which is devoid of it, the insentient, such as stone and the like.

And "truth" here refers to the domain of conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) by virtue of its context, not to absolute truth (*paramārtha-satya*); for Brahman alone is the single absolute truth. Here, however, "truth" is used in a relative sense regarding the domain of conventional usage; water and the like are called "true" in comparison to falsehoods such as a mirage. And "falsehood" (*anṛta*) is the opposite of that. But what did all this become? Beyond that—
What, then, is that Brahman which is the ultimate reality? Because it has been introduced as "Brahman is truth, knowledge, and infinite," [it is that].

Since this entire collection of modifications—whether consisting of the formed (*mūrta*) or the formless (*amūrta*), beginning with truth and so forth—is without distinction, it became one Brahman alone, denoted by the word *sat* (Being). This is because there is no existence apart from it, due to the modification of name and form (*nāmarūpa*).

Therefore, they call that Brahman "Truth. Regarding the inquiry previously raised as to whether Brahman exists or does not exist, this has been stated in response: the Self desired, "May I become many. "In the beginning, this was indeed non-existent (asat). By "non-existent," the unmodified Brahman is meant, which is the opposite of the differentiated forms of name and form; it does not, however, mean absolute non-existence, for from non-existence, existence cannot be born.

Thus: "In the beginning," prior to creation, this world—which is differentiated by specific names and forms (*nāmarūpa*)—was indeed Brahman alone, denoted by the word "Non-being" (*asat*). From that Non-being, Being (*sat*) was born, having emerged with its specific names and forms clearly distinguished. What is that effect distinguished from it? It is not like a son [distinguished] from a father; rather, it is that very Non-being.

It made itself—that is, it made its very self—denotable by the word *bdat* (the Self). Because it is so, that Brahman alone is called "well-made" (*sukṛta*) and "self-made. It is well known in the world that Brahman is the self-agent, because it is the cause of all.
Or, because it made everything by itself through its entire essence, therefore it is that very same [Brahman] even in the form of merit (*puṇya*).

Brahman is declared to be the cause that is liberated [from all bonds]. Therefore, that Brahman exists because of the well-known status of merit. For this reason also, it exists.

Why? Because it is essence (*rasa*). From what is the well-known status of Brahman as essence established? To this he says: "That which is made is indeed essence. In the world, even those Brahmins who are devoid of external means for pleasure, who are free from effort and desire, [attain this]. Although the qualified [Brahman] is the object, the meaning is that the essential nature itself is the object. Thus ends the sixth section. ||6||

Indeed, Brahmins are seen to be entirely free from fear even when causes for fear exist; and that would be illogical if Brahman, which is the protection from fear, did not exist. Therefore, they—

Because fear is seen in those [who perceive duality], there exists that cause of fearlessness, which is Brahman. When does this practitioner become one who has attained fearlessness? The intention is that he becomes one who has attained fearlessness when he sees nothing else and does not conceive of any internal difference within himself. On the other hand, while in the state of ignorance, because this person is possessed of ignorance—

One perceives the object presented by ignorance as being like a second moon seen by one suffering from ophthalmia (*taimirika*), even while within this very Brahman which is the Self. Furthermore, "even a slight interval" (*aram api*) means that one creates a gap, a fissure, or a perception of difference. For it is the perception of difference itself that constitutes the creation of an interval;
the meaning is that one perceives even a slight distinction. Now, because of that perception of difference—

For one who perceives duality, fear does not arise from any other cause; therefore, for the ignorant person, the Self alone is the cause of fear for the Self. This is what he says: "That very Brahman is indeed the source of fear" for the ignorant one who perceives duality, who thinks, "The Lord is one, I am another; I am a transmigrating being. For such a one who possesses the vision of duality, it is that very Brahman, known as the Lord, who is the object of fear.

Fear arises for one who creates even a slight distinction, failing to perceive [reality] as a unity. Therefore, even though he is a knower, he is truly ignorant who does not see the single, undivided reality of the Self; because of the perception of a cause for annihilation, fear arises regarding that which is considered subject to annihilation. Since there is no cause for annihilation in that which is not subject to annihilation, when that cause for annihilation is absent—

If it were subject to annihilation, it would not be logical for there to be fear resulting from the perception of it; yet the entire world is seen to be possessed by fear. Therefore, from observing the fear of the world, it is understood that there must certainly exist a cause of fear—a cause of annihilation that is itself non-annihilable—on account of which the world fears. Regarding this matter as well, there is this verse: thus [it is said].

"Brahman is bliss. Now follows this inquiry, this deliberation, concerning that very bliss of Brahman.
What is to be inquired about regarding bliss? It is said: Is bliss produced by the connection between an object and a subject, like worldly bliss, or is it innate? Such is this inquiry into bliss.

Therein, worldly bliss (*laukika ānanda*) is the most excellent, being caused by the perfection of external and internal means. It is this very [bliss] that is pointed out for the purpose of following after the bliss of Brahman (*brahmānanda*). For, by means of this well-known bliss, the bliss accessible to a mind whose objects have been withdrawn can be followed after. Worldly bliss, too—

A mere fraction of that very bliss of Brahman, when its consciousness is obscured by ignorance (*avidyā*) and as that ignorance increases, becomes manifested in the world as the unstable, worldly [bliss]— perceived by Brahmā and others according to their respective cognitions and through the power of their connection with objects and means of action under the influence of karma; that very [bliss], along with ignorance, desire, and action—
Through progressive excellence, this bliss is perceived by learned Vedic scholars who are unaffected by desire, as they ascend through higher and higher levels— beginning with humans and Gandharvas—

The human *gandharvas* are those who, through excellence in ritual action and knowledge, have attained the state of a *gandharva*. There would be clarity of mind for the Gandharva; from that specific clarity, there is the manifestation of a specific excellence of happiness.

In this way, as one moves from each preceding stage to each succeeding stage, an increase in bliss a hundredfold becomes possible due to the specific nature of that clarity. However, the first mention of "not overcome by desire" refers to the enjoyment of objects within the human realm.

The *Ājānajā* gods are those born in divine stations due to the excellence of their *smārta* (tradition-based) actions.

The *Karmadevas* are those who, by means of purely Vedic rites such as the *agnihotra*, attain the state of gods. The "gods" (*devāḥ*) are the thirty-three *havirbhuj* (sacrificial-eaters). Indra is their lord; his preceptor is Bṛhaspati. Pra—
Brahmā is the Lord of Creatures, the Virāj, whose body is the three worlds; he is both the aggregate and the individual, pervading the entire sphere of transmigratory existence.

Where these various forms of bliss attain unity, where there is the Dharma caused by that, the knowledge concerning it, and the unsurpassed state of being unassailed by desire—that is this Hiraṇyagarbha, the Brahmā; of him, this...

Therefore, it is understood that these three are the means (*sādhana*). Among them, while being learned in the Vedas and being upright are constant requirements, the state of not being overcome by desire is what is elevated; thus, its status as the preeminent means is understood. Of that non-desire—

The meaning is that the bliss of Brahman, which is perceived through the excellence of its destruction [of suffering] and is directly perceptible to the learned Vedic scholar (*śrotriya*), attains its state of being the supreme goal and the aforementioned enemy-status from the word "good" (*sādhu*). [There are] thirty-three:
eight Vasus, eleven Rudras, twelve Ādityas, Indra, and Prajāpati. For this purpose, the Mīmāṃsā has been commenced.

The connection is as follows: the bliss of that Brahmā Hiraṇyagarbha, which is directly perceived by his worshiper, is but a "mātrā" (fraction) of that which is this supreme bliss (*paramānanda*), which is innate. To provide scriptural authority for the fact that the bliss of Hiraṇyagarbha is merely a fraction, he cites another Śruti passage:

"Of this very [bliss]," and so on. It is not only the bliss of Hiraṇyagarbha that is a fraction; rather, it includes everything previously mentioned, beginning with the universal sovereign (*sārvabhauma*) and so forth.

The construction is as follows: "That very [Brahman] whose measure, having become differentiated and attained manifoldness, has reached oneness in that Kaivalya (isolation)—which is the direct perception of the knower of Brahman who is free from desire and is unsurpassed bliss. By mentioning the direct perception of one who is free from desire, he refutes the notion that it is merely scriptural. The meaning is that this refers to the intention [of the text], and not to the intention of a relationship between object and subject (*viṣaya-viṣayibhāva*), because of the negation in such passages as "He makes a difference within the invisible, the bodiless" (*adṛśye'nātmye... antaram kurute*). By means of inquiry (*mīmāṃsā*), it has been determined that Brahman exists as unsurpassed bliss. Since it is stated that this [Brahman] is directly perceived by one whose desires have been destroyed, non-difference is established. Therefore, the identity of the individual soul with Brahman, which is unsurpassed bliss, is established; for it was introduced at the outset in the passage, "The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme," and has been demonstrated through this inquiry as "I am That.

"How does one who has gone to that state find fearlessness and a firm foundation?"—this is appropriate.

The subsequent questions concern the attainment and non-attainment of Brahman by the wise and the ignorant respectively; among these, the final question—whether the wise man attains or does not attain—is stated here for its resolution. Having departed from this world— this world being a collection of perceived and unperceived objects of desire— what happens to him from this world?

The meaning is that [the two] are brought together. He raises an objection in order to show that the mention of the sun (*āditya*)—which is intended as a designation for the divine adjunct (*adhidaivika-upādhi*)—is not what is primarily intended. The meaning is that, when there is a description of identity with the stationary [the Self], it is appropriate to mention the right eye. [Page 80] Eighth Section. Accompanied by the commentary of Śaṅkara and the sub-commentary (ṭīkā) composed by Ānandagiri:
Having departed from this world, one approaches this self consisting of food (annamaya).
Thus, he approaches this self consisting of breath; he approaches this self consisting of mind; he approaches this self consisting of consciousness.

Having departed and returned, having become indifferent, he approaches this aforementioned self consisting of food (*annamaya*); that is to say, he does not perceive the collection of objects as distinct from the physical body consisting of food, but perceives everything that has become gross as the self consisting of food. Then, [he approaches] this inner one, the self consisting of vital breath (*prāṇamaya*).

[He reaches] that which is undivided and situated within the Self consisting of all food. Then he approaches this Self consisting of mind, the Self consisting of consciousness, and the Self consisting of bliss. Then he finds fearless support in that which is invisible, incorporeal, undefined, and without abode. Regarding this, it must be considered: who is this one who knows thus, and how does he transition? Is it the higher...?

Is the agent of this transition other than the Self, or is it distinct from it, or is it that very Self? What follows from this? If it were other, there would be a contradiction with the Śruti: "Having created that, He entered into that very thing";
"He is one, another am I"; "He does not know"; "One only, without a second"; "That thou art. Now, if it were that very [Self]...

The statement that "one approaches the Self consisting of bliss" is untenable because it involves a contradiction between the object and the agent [of the same action]. Furthermore, it would follow either that the Supreme [Self] itself is subject to transmigratory existence (*saṃsāritva*) or that the Supreme does not exist at all. If the fault incurred in both cases cannot be avoided, then this inquiry is useless. However, if no fault arises in one of the two positions, or if there is a third, non-defective position, then that alone is the [correct] teaching.

The thought that it is "for one's own sake" is indeed useless; this is true, for the fault incurred in determining that [it is not for another] cannot be avoided. However, if one of the three positions were determined to be faultless, the inquiry would be useless; but since that has not been determined, this inquiry is indeed purposeful, as it aims at such determination. It is truly purposeful.
[This is] reflection (*cintā*), because it serves the purpose of ascertaining the meaning of the treatise. You reflect, yet you will not reach a definitive conclusion;

For that attainment of one's own Self which is taught by means of the knowledge of Brahman (brahmavidyā) has as its purpose the removal of the non-Self—which is a specific entity such as food and so forth, produced by ignorance (avidyā), and superimposed as the Self. How is it understood that this is its purpose? From the fact that only knowledge is taught; and the observed effect of knowledge is the cessation of ignorance, and that is what is intended here.

If it is argued that knowledge alone is taught as the means for attaining the Self, just like the instruction on the knowledge of the path, then [we reply]: the teaching of knowledge alone as the means is not a valid reason for [the Self] being identical [to the body]. Why? Because we observe the instruction on the knowledge of the path even when reaching another location. If it is objected that one does not go to the village itself [but to a place beyond it], we say no, because of the difference in nature (*vaidharmya*).

For in that context, a cognition whose object is a village is not taught; rather, only that cognition whose object is the path for attaining it is taught. It is not so here, where a cognition having as its object some other means apart from the cognition of Brahman is taught. The cognition of Brahman, depending upon the aforementioned means such as ritual action (*karman*), is taught as the means for attaining the supreme goal.
If it is argued that [liberation] is something to be attained, no; for this has already been refuted by the statement, "Because liberation is eternal," and so forth.

Furthermore, scripture shows that he who resides in the effect has that very Self as his essence, in the passage: "Having created that, He entered into that very thing. Moreover, because the state of being established in fearlessness is logically consistent: for if the possessor of knowledge perceives nothing other than his own Self, then there is fearlessness.

"One finds a firm foundation" (pratiṣṭhāṃ vindate) would be [said] because of the absence of another, a different source of fear; for if that other were produced by ignorance (avidyā), its unreality could be established through knowledge (vidyā). If it is argued that you are not perceived by the blind Mirika, even though he possesses sight—on the grounds that "he is not perceived thus"—we say no, because there is no perception of either when they are in a state of meditative absorption (*samāhita*). If it is argued that the lack of perception in deep sleep is like being distracted by something else, we say no, because there is a total lack of perception [of anything]. If it is argued that since other things are perceived during waking and dreaming, those states must therefore exist, we say no, because waking and dreaming are produced by ignorance (*avidyā*).

The apprehension of something other [than the Self] during waking and dreaming is produced by ignorance (*avidyā*), because it does not exist when ignorance is absent. If it is argued that the non-apprehension [of anything] in deep sleep is also produced by ignorance, we say no, because it is natural. For the true nature (*tattva*) of a substance is its changelessness, since it is independent of anything else; modification is not its true nature, because it depends on another. Indeed, the reality of a thing does not depend upon causal factors (*kāraka*).

Reality (*tattva*) is the specific nature of that which exists; and a specific nature dependent upon causal factors is a modification (*vikriyā*). [Objection: "But this is not so for the waking and dreaming states. [Response: It is not so. Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of even the silver in a mother-of-pearl shell being real. Thus he says: "Not ignorance. Therefore, the statement regarding the bondage of the forest—that the individual soul (jīva), having become Brahman which is the Self of all in deep sleep, does not perceive anything distinct from itself precisely because of its non-existence—is incorrect; this is the meaning. What is the sense of the claim that even an existing thing is not apprehended due to the power of ignorance? Does it mean that the prior absence of apprehension arises, or is it the superimposition of non-manifestation, or rather the persistence of the unmodified essential nature in the form of non-apprehension? Not the first, because the antecedent non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) is admitted to be beginningless. It is not the third, as he says: "not because of its being natural (*svābhāvikatvāt*)."

[The word] *diti* [means]: the state of abiding in one's own essential nature (*svarūpa*) is not an effect of knowledge, because it is non-adventitious (*anāgantuka*). [It is] "unchanging" (*avikriya*).

This is the distinction. For that which is the nature of something, independent of anything else, is its true reality (*tattva*); that which depends on another is not its true reality, because it ceases to exist when that other is absent. Therefore, since it is inherent (*svābhāvika*), there is no distinction in deep sleep as there is in the waking and dreaming states. However, for those who hold that the Lord is other than the Self and that the effect is other [than the cause], there is no cessation of fear.

Since fear must have another cause, it is impossible for that which already exists [the Self] to undergo destruction, nor can that which does not exist come into being as a Self. If it is argued that another entity, dependent on something else, is the cause of fear, we say no, because that other entity is subject to the same logic.
Whatever other cause of fear there might be—whether eternal or non-eternal—it would likewise depend on factors such as demerit (*adharma*) and so forth.

For such a person as well, since there is no destruction of the self (*ātman*), fear does not cease; or, if there were destruction of the self, there would be the mutual transformation of existence and non-existence, resulting in a total lack of confidence in everything. However, in the view of oneness (*ekatva*), there is no fault, because transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*) along with its causes is imagined through ignorance (*avidyā*). For the second moon seen by one with cataracts—
There is neither gain nor loss. If it is argued that knowledge and ignorance are attributes of that [Self], we say no, because they are perceived directly.
Discrimination and non-discrimination are perceived directly like color and other qualities; they reside within the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*).
For color, being directly perceptible, does not have the seer as its attribute. And ignorance is [known] by its own direct experience—

The fool thinks, "I am burning; my consciousness is undiscriminating. Likewise, the distinction from ignorance (*avidyā*) is experienced. The meaning is that [consciousness] is established without depending on its own nature, which is characterized by the absence of modification. The modifications such as grasping are not inherent, because they depend on something else, like the redness of a crystal. That which was stated—that it is unchanging because it is established without dependence—is now clarified.

He explains: "For [the word] *yat*... Having thus established in his own view that fearlessness is possible for the knower because there is no Lord—distinct from the existence of consciousness—that could serve as a cause of fear, he states its impossibility in the dualistic position: "Of those who... If something other than Being (*sat*) remains in its own nature or has perished, let there be no destruction [of fear], because that would involve contradiction and infinite regress. Well then, if fear arises from non-existence (*asat*) itself, the attainment of fearlessness will occur.

Anticipating this objection, he says: "And not of that which is non-existent. It is not by the mere existence of a separate Lord that He is a cause of fear; rather, [the Lord is so] in dependence upon the merit, demerit, and so forth performed by living beings.

Anticipating the objection that for one who is liberated there will be fearlessness because of the absence of those [causes], it must not be said by the Sāṃkhya: for even demerit and the like are "existent" according to him, since he does not admit their absolute non-existence. This is also the case in the systems of the Naiyāyikas and others, where [only] that which exists...

He says, "Not even that," because the absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) of an effect is difficult to ascertain; therefore, even by that [definition], [non-existence] cannot be expressed. Furthermore, if existence were to fall into non-existence, then what confidence could there be regarding dharma and so forth even in the Self? Therefore, he says, "Of the existent and the non-existent," meaning that in the view of anyone, a reversal of nature—that is, the transition of everything into non-existence—is not possible. He concludes his own position with the word "one."

Regarding the phrase "in your own view": by asserting that fear imagined through ignorance (*avidyā*) is removed by knowledge (*vidyā*), one implies that knowledge and ignorance are accepted as attributes of the Self (*ātman*). Consequently, one raises the objection that the production and destruction of these attributes would entail the Self's susceptibility to modification (*vikāritva*) and impermanence (*anityatva*). To this, [the author] replies: "Of knowledge and ignorance. Since it is possible for imagined knowledge and ignorance to serve as the causes of fear and fearlessness within the Self, there is no evidence [for their being actual attributes of the Self].

On the contrary, since it is an object of cognition, one can infer that it lacks selfhood, just like color and other such qualities; thus he says: "Not so, because it is perceptible.
