Therefore, knowledge (*vidyā*) and ignorance (*avidyā*), as well as name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), belong only to the side of name-and-form; they are not attributes of the Self. This is because of another scriptural passage: "That which is the bringer-forth of name-and-form, that within which they are, that is Brahman. Furthermore, those two, name-and-form, are merely conceptualized—like day and night in the sun—and do not exist in an ultimate sense, [for] in this non-duality, [one attains] this one consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*).

If it is argued that the self cannot be both the object and the agent [of the action] because it "approaches itself" (*upasaṃkrāmati*), we say no; for this "approaching" consists merely of consciousness (*vijñānamātratva*).

Here, an approaching like that of a leech or similar creatures is not being taught; rather, the meaning of the scriptural statement regarding "approaching" is merely consciousness. But is it not the case that a primary, literal approaching is heard in the text, as it says "he approaches"?

If it is argued that [the self] does [migrate], we say no, because this is not observed in the case of the *annamaya* (the physical body). For, as one approaches the *annamaya*, no migration—whether like a leech from this external world or otherwise—is observed. Nor is there a migration of the self through the return of the *manomaya* (mental sheath) or the *vijñānamaya* (intellectual sheath) after they have gone outside. If it is argued that [migration occurs] within one's own self... [no,] because it is within oneself.

Because it would contradict the action [described] in the context that "one approaches another consisting of food," there would be a contradiction if one who consists of mind or one who consists of consciousness were to approach only their own self. Likewise, the transition of the one consisting of bliss (ānandamaya) into the Self is not tenable. Therefore, "transition" does not mean reaching [another], nor does it refer to the [stages] beginning with the one consisting of food.

By the method of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*), it follows that [the transition] has no other agent; rather, it has as its agent one distinct from the selves beginning with the "consisting of food" (*annamaya*) and ending with the "consisting of bliss" (*ānandamaya*).

Furthermore, the transition is established as being mere knowledge (*jñānamātra*). And since it is mere knowledge, it belongs to the Inner Controller who, residing within the "consisting of bliss," created all this—from space down to the "consisting of food"—and having entered therein, is connected with the cave of the heart.

The delusion of selfhood regarding non-self entities such as the body made of food (*annamaya*) and so forth, which arises through the process of transmigration, is but the reflection of the element of consciousness (*cid-dhātu*). This consciousness, though deluded by the attributes of its own limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), is conventionally designated as both "the deluded one" and "the one who possesses right vision," yet in reality, it does not possess either knowledge (*vidyā*) or ignorance (*avidyā*). Thus he says: "And those again... By the logic already stated, one who possesses the knowledge of Brahman is non-different from Brahman.

It is said: therein, he refutes the statement of others by means of the passage beginning with "abheda etam" (non-difference, this...). The meaning is that the one consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*) is not the Supreme Self, nor is there an entry or transition into it; rather, what is intended here is the transcending or sublation of that which was grasped through delusion as the self—the *ānandamaya*—by means of the knowledge of the identity of Brahman, which is beyond all objects. Or else, [as in the case of] a bird in its nest...

The meaning is "as in the case of entering. Although a literal transition (*saṃkramaṇa*) is not possible in the case of that which consists of food (*annamaya*), nevertheless, it is observed that when the mind (*manas*) and the intellect (*buddhi*) are engaged with external objects, their turning away from those and abiding in their own essential nature (*svarūpa*) constitutes a transition; likewise, he says that for one who is suffering, abiding in the essential nature of that which consists of bliss (*ānandamaya*) will be the transition. [He says] "of that which consists of mind" (*manomayasya*). Abiding in the essential nature...
He says "No," because [the soul] is not adventitious and because it would contradict the context; therefore, that is not the primary transition (*saṃkramaṇa*).

Or, if the transition were merely knowledge, what would be the result? To this he says: "And if it were merely knowledge. Since the primary sense is impossible, it is indeed logical to accept a secondary meaning; therefore, through the realization of the true nature of the substratum, there is simply the sublation of that which was previously superimposed.

Ninth Section.
He who knows the bliss of Brahman fears nothing from anywhere. This, indeed, does not afflict him: "Why did I not perform what is good? [or, "Why have I done evil?"]

"What evil have I done? He who knows thus protects these two selves; for he indeed protects both these selves. By the method described, he does not fear anything from any cause, because of the absence of such a cause. For it is not...

Therefore, there exists no other distinct entity apart from the Knower from which he might fear; for it has been said: "When one perceives even a slight difference through ignorance, then fear arises for him. Since the effect of ignorance—which is the cause of fear—is destroyed for the Knower, like the second moon seen by one suffering from ophthalmia, he does not fear from anything.
This is appropriate. Furthermore, the mantra cited refers to the "mind-made" (manomaya) self because the mind is the means for the realization of Brahman.

In that context, having superimposed the nature of Brahman upon it for the sake of its praise, only fear in general was prohibited by the words "he fears nothing at any time. Here, however, in the context of non-duality, the phrase "he does not fear from anything whatsoever" prohibits the very cause of fear.
It is said: "Is it not the case that there is a cause for fear, namely, the non-performance of good and the performance of evil? It is not so. How is this stated?

[The text says: "This one who is such as has been described"—the words *ha vāva* serve to emphasize—does not burn, does not agitate, and does not cause distress. But how is it that the non-performance of good and the performance of evil do not [burn]?

It is said: "Dependent upon" means that at the approach of the time of death, one experiences remorse, thinking, "Why? Why did I not perform good, auspicious deeds? Likewise, out of fear of the suffering of falling into hell, one experiences remorse, thinking, "Why? Why did I perform forbidden, sinful deeds?"
These two—the performance of good and the performance of evil—do not afflict him in the same way that they afflict the ignorant man.

Why, then, do they not afflict the knower? It is said: he who knows this protects himself—that is, he pleases or strengthens himself—by regarding both these causes of affliction, the good and the evil, as the Supreme Self.

The meaning is that he sees. For since both merit and demerit are thus [perceived], this wise one, having rendered these two—merit and demerit—void of their own specific forms by means of the very form of the Self, truly protects the Self.

Intending to show that what is called "excess" (*tiriktam*)—which consists of the specific forms of names and which serves as the cause of benefit and harm—is not a real entity because it is non-existent due to its difference from the Light (Consciousness) and because it does not manifest, he says: "by its own specific form. It was the Self alone that, through ignorance, was perceived in the form of the good and the evil; but now, those very things which were my causes of benefit and harm are seen to be the Self alone.

By means of knowledge, he indeed delights his own self through the imitation of fear; for when merit and demerit are being produced according to the worldly view, the wise man both rejoices and does not grieve. Thus it is said: "He truly protects. This is the ninth section. || 9 ||

Section Six.
Now, having withdrawn from the narrative, the Śruti itself declares through its own words the matter concluded by the narrative:
"This very [knowledge] was known by Bhṛgu (bhārgavī) and was taught by Varuṇa (vāruṇī)."

This knowledge is established and fully perfected in the supreme sky, in the cave of the space of the heart, within non-dual supreme bliss; it has proceeded forth from the self consisting of food (annamaya) and so on. Whoever else, by this very means of austerity and by this same sequence, enters therein and knows Brahman as bliss—he too, by virtue of being established in that knowledge, [becomes that very Self].

The meaning is that one remains established in bliss, the supreme Brahman, and becomes Brahman itself. Furthermore, the visible fruit of this is stated: he becomes "possessed of food" (*annavān*), meaning food exists for him. If [the state of] being possessed of food were merely by virtue of existence, there would be no distinction in the knowledge [of all beings], as everyone is possessed of food simply by existing. Thus, one who eats food is a "consumer of food" (*annāda*). He is radiant...

The meaning is that he becomes fire. He becomes great. To the question "By what [does his] greatness [consist]?", it is said: he becomes great through progeny, such as sons; through cattle, such as cows and horses; through *brahmavarcasa*, which is splendor caused by tranquility, self-control, knowledge, and so forth; and through fame, which is renown caused by the practice of auspicious deeds. Thus ends the sixth [section].
Section Six.

The meaning is as follows: having reflected that even this [Brahman] does not possess a complete definition because it is itself an effect, and having independently determined its cause, he realized that Brahman—qualified by *māyā* and denoted by the word "Bliss" (*ānanda*)—is that which is sought by all.

Then, realizing that it is impossible for one qualified entity to be the self of another qualified entity, he understood that Brahman is pure bliss (*viśuddhānanda*), characterized merely by its status as the cause.

Anticipating the objection, "How can the qualification 'abundance' (prabhūtatva), which was not explicitly heard [in the text], be inserted? he replies: "By its mere existence" (sattāmātreṇa). The meaning is this: if "mere existence" were intended here, then even a dog or a pig would possess food—since their bodily maintenance is necessarily implied by food—and thus no specific excellence of the fruit of knowledge would have been stated; therefore, by the force of that [context], the qualification "abundance" is inserted. And this is the visible fruit for the knower of Brahman.

1. *ja* and *ru*: seeking disrespect; *a*: not seeking disrespect. 2. *ka*, *kha*, *ga*, *ca*: in all verbal forms (*sarvākhyāteṣu*); *ja*:
in verbal forms denoting existence (*sattvākhyāteṣu*).

He who knows thus. This is the Upaniṣad. Thus ends the tenth section. || 10 ||

"Bhṛgu said to him: 'That from which they enter—that you must seek to understand; that is Brahman. [Bhṛgu] understood: 'The thirteenth is food, breath, mind, and discernment. [He understood: 'Twelve by twelve is bliss.
This is the tenfold food. One should not revile it. Breath is the body, and food is water; one should not despise it. Light is food; it is abundant."
One should fashion eleven [bricks] on the earth and eleven in the sky; no one [should place them] in the sixty-first region—thus says Bhṛgu. He who knows this [attains] fifteen [years of life].
May he protect us both; may he nourish us both; may we perform heroic deeds together.
May we both study with vigor; may we not harbor mutual hatred. Om, peace, peace, peace. Hariḥ Om.
Thus ends the Bhṛgu-vallī.
Thus ends the Taittirīya Upaniṣad in its entirety.
By means of form: *suvar-jyotiḥ* (of golden light), *suvar-ādityaḥ* (the sun of heaven); the syllable *nakāra* is used in the sense of comparison.

The meaning is that our light—our radiance—is like the sun, shining forth once and for all (*sakṛdvibhātam*). Thus, one who is peaceful and self-controlled [should study] this Upaniṣad concerning the knowledge of the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) as prescribed in the two *vallīs*; one should study this aforementioned Upaniṣad.
Being devoted, patient, and composed, and having undertaken great austerity like Bhṛgu—he who knows thus, for him this fruit is as described above. Thus ends the tenth section. || 10 ||

Thus ends the third chapter in the Commentary on the Taittirīya Upaniṣad, composed by the venerable Śaṅkara Bhagavat, disciple of the venerable Govinda Bhagavatpūjyapāda, the illustrious wandering ascetic teacher (Paramahaṃsa Parivrājaka Ācārya). And this Commentary on the Taittirīya Upaniṣad is completed.
*Oṃ tat sat*.

Thus it has been explained. "I overcome" means "I withdraw [into myself]"; the meaning is that through the knowledge of the identity with the Lord (*īśvara*), the ego-sense is sublated, and therefore there is no cause for fear—this is the sense. The particle *na* is used in the sense of "like. Thus ends the tenth section. || 10 ||
For those desiring a clear understanding of the meaning, this commentary (*ṭippaṇa*) has been composed upon Śaṅkara’s firm *Bhāṣya* on the *Taittirīyaka*.
Thus ends the third chapter of the Commentary on the Taittirīya Upaniṣad, composed by Śrī Bhagavadānandajñāna, disciple of the venerable Śrī Śuddhānanda, the holy Paramahaṃsa Parivrājaka Ācārya. 3.
And this commentary on the Taittirīya Upaniṣad is completed. Oṃ tat sat.
The *Taittirīyopaniṣaddīpikā* composed by Śaṅkarānanda:
Now I shall expound the commentary on all the passages as determined by the words of Śaṅkara and Viśvarūpa.
The *Kṛṣṇayajus*, marked by the name of the *tittiri* bird, is exceedingly meaningful for the purpose of purifying the meaning of words. || 1 ||

Various rituals characterized by "eternity" and other such qualities have been previously described; seeing that the highest good (*niḥśreyasa*) is not attained through them, the Veda, beginning the *Upaniṣad* for the sake of knowledge of Brahman, observes that even great beings encounter obstacles created by the gods regarding the knowledge of Brahman.
With the intention that this [following mantra] should be recited for the pacification of those obstacles by one seeking the science of Brahman, it is first recited:

Thus: *śam* means happiness. May *mitra*—the deity presiding over the function of *prāṇa* (out-breath) and the day—grant us (*naḥ*) *śam*, happiness; and may *varuṇa*—the deity presiding over the function of *apāna* (in-breath) and the night—grant us *śam*, happiness. The word *naḥ* (us) is to be supplied [with each]. *Śam naḥ* has already been explained. May it be (*bhavatu*); may it come to pass (*bhūyāt*). This word is to be connected with every instance of the word *śam*. *Aryaman* is the deity of the eye, the solar orb...
The deity presiding over the *lāsya* [dance] is the one; "śam naḥ" has been explained. Indra is the deity presiding over the strength of the arms;

Bṛhaspati is the deity presiding over speech and the intellect. "Śam naḥ" is to be supplied as a refrain. "Śam naḥ" has been explained. Viṣṇu is the deity presiding over the feet; his qualification is "Urukrama," meaning he whose stride is wide.

He whose stride is vast is *urukrama*, meaning he who pervades all. Alternatively, this word may be independent: *urukrama* refers to Virāj, the deity presiding over all food (*anna*). The phrase "may there be peace for us" (*śaṃ naḥ*) is to be supplied [to each].
Having thus prayed to the deities presiding over the gross and subtle [levels], one now [prays] to those presiding over the powers of unmanifest knowledge and action (*jñāna-kriyā-śakti*).
He pays homage to the proud deity (*māninī devatā*). "Homage" (*namaḥ*) means an act of salutation. To Brahmā, who possesses the conceit (*abhimānin*) of the unmanifest (*avyākṛta*);

because that [unmanifest] has not yet produced its effects and is thus incapable of action, he again pays homage to the one who possesses the conceit of the effect (*kāryābhimānin*), who is non-different from it.
"Homage" (*namaḥ*) means an act of salutation. To you, O Vāyu—O you whose primary power is action, O possessor of the powers of knowledge and action!

Now, one might object: "One should offer salutation only to that which is to be explained, and I am not that which is to be explained. To this he replies: You alone are the one who identifies with the powers of knowledge and action, and nothing else. Brahman—free from the limitations of space, time, and substance—is directly perceived by the scripture as being self-luminous, or as the witness of the intellect and other faculties, and as identifying with the unmanifested [Māyā].

"You are form; you exist. [The student asks: "If I am Brahman, then what of you? To this he replies: "I shall declare that you yourself—who are directly perceived as the effect, yet are the self-luminous cause characterized by the conceit of being the agent—are indeed Brahman. Thus, having understood through the teacher the identity between the consciousness conceiving itself as the effect and the consciousness conceiving itself as the cause, [the student realizes]: "I am Brahman."

"I shall speak," that is, "I shall declare. [Objection: Is this not being said by you to me in a figurative sense? To this he says: "The Truth (*ṛtam*)," meaning I shall speak and declare that which is non-figurative. [Objection: Even when you speak of the non-figurative, such a thing has never occurred. To this he says: "The Real (*satyam*). All this is this Self alone; it is one only, without a second.
1. Kha. ga. *kṛtsnam* | 2. Kha. *ṇoktam* | [page 103] Composed by Śaṅkarānanda.
In the chapter on training (*śikṣādhyāya*),

the identity understood from such scriptural teachings as "There is no diversity here whatsoever," "That thou art" (*tat tvam asi*), and "I am Brahman" (*ahaṃ brahmāsmi*) constitutes the uncontradicted nature of reality; like the night for an owl, this nectar is not mine alone, but is established by all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

The meaning is "whose nature is unimpeded. Since I shall speak—that is, I shall tell—therefore, may you, who are presenting me as the form of Brahman, protect me; may you, whose limiting adjuncts are the effect and the cause, preserve me.

One might object: "Let there be no affliction by internal and other sufferings for you, whose speech, body, and mind are serene, as well as for your disciple; however, let the opposite be true for the Guru, since [the invocation] lacks intent regarding the Guru. Anticipating this doubt, he himself offers a prayer even concerning the Guru: because knowledge cannot be obtained by a disciple without a Guru, therefore, [he prays for the welfare of] the speaker... or [the listener].

The meaning is: "May [He] protect—that is, preserve—the teacher, the one who expounds the Vidyā. Having read the two *tat* words following the word "therefore" (*tasmāt*), both those *śrauta* *tat* words may also be explained as referring to Brahman. Alternatively, the two sentences devoid of the word *tat* are recited in reverse order from the beginning for the sake of showing reverence toward the protection of the teacher and the Self: "May He protect me; may He protect the speaker."

This has been explained. Even though the teacher is indeed Brahman through the realization of Brahman, and the disciple is likewise endowed with the fourfold qualifications and is himself vigilant, nevertheless, because of the presence of many extremely subtle transgressions caused by destiny (*daiva*), there may arise internal, external, and celestial sufferings for the disciple, which would obstruct the production of the knowledge of Brahman.
Then, for the purpose of destroying the threefold suffering, he recites the word "peace" three times: *śāntiḥ śāntiḥ śāntiḥ*.
May the threefold suffering of speech, mind, and the other senses come to rest—for me, who am qualified for the knowledge of Brahman; such is the meaning.

Although from this point onward one should have begun with "The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme," nevertheless, since there is no realization of the Self for one who is excessively extroverted, certain meditations (*upāsanās*) are first described to entice such a person toward introversion by means of their fruits. [Objection: If this is so, then one should have begun instead with "Now, therefore, concerning the Saṃhitā" and so forth, rather than this.

"Śīkṣām," and so forth. True; nevertheless, because the primary purpose of the Upaniṣads is the knowledge of their meaning, one might suspect that the meaning could be understood through recitation in any manner whatsoever. To dispel this doubt, "Śīkṣām" and so forth are recited first. There is no other utility [for them] than this: that in this very word, "śikṣām," the letter *ś* occurs.

When merely the phonemes (*mātra*) are uttered, there is no comprehension of the meaning, nor is there the Vedic purity of recitation. Furthermore, in the Veda, a word or sentence lacking its respective phonemes, accents, and so forth, does not convey an acceptable meaning; on the contrary, it results in the destruction of the perceived meaning.

Since even those various Upaniṣads possess the status of Veda, the knowledge of meaning arises from the utterance of words and so forth as established by the order of recitation within their respective branches (*śākhā*), endowed with their specific phonemes, accents, and other features.

For the sake of this purpose—that which is to be done—the reading is *śīkṣām* according to Vedic grammatical usage. By means of this, the phonemes (*varṇa*) and so forth are taught; or, the phonemes and so forth themselves are the teaching (*śikṣā*). We shall explain that *śikṣā*. We shall describe it clearly and comprehensively in various ways. The phoneme (*varṇa*) begins with the letter *a*; the accent (*svara*) begins with the acute (*udātta*); the measure (*mātrā*) is... [and so on].

The *svādi* [group of consonants] is [produced] by means of strength (*bala*), the location of the breath (*prāṇa-sthāna*), and effort (*prayatna*). *Sāman* arises from equality (*samatā*) [of these factors], as well as from the wonder (*adbhuta*) of [the articulation being] delayed (*vilambita*), excessive (*atyadhika*), or deficient (*atinyūna*)—[regarding] the chewing (*khadana*). 1 (kha) [Page 104] 2. [Variant reading: *divi*.
The first Anuvāka: [From the *Taittirīyopaniṣaddīpikā*].
The meaning is that recitation in a uniform manner, avoiding the nasalization (*nāsikya*) and so forth, is "non-affliction," like the carrying away of a tiger's cub. *Santānaḥ*—this...

The meaning is that the *saṃhitā* consists of words or sentences in a fixed sequence. The word "iti" indicates completion. The *śīkṣādhyāya*—so called because it is taught (*ukta*) in the *Śikṣā*, or because the *śikṣā* is studied (*adhīyate*) and understood (*avagamyate*) by means of it—is thus concluded. || 1 ||

Now, following the maxim of the lamp on the threshold (*dehalīpradīpanyāya*), the Veda—in the form of a disciple—performs a common auspicious invocation for both what has been said and what is yet to be said, for the purpose of instructing the disciple. "Together" (*saha*) means with both of us, teacher and disciple. "Fame" (*yaśaḥ*):

the sense is that there may be glory arising from teaching and studying, such that "this one is the disciple of this teacher" and "this one is the teacher of this disciple. This is the remainder [of the sentence].

And regarding the phrase *kṣyamāṇe ca*: "May we both [attain] it" has been explained together [with the previous]. *Brahmavarcasam*—*brahman* here refers to the caste of the Brāhmaṇa; its splendor is *brahmavarcasam*. The meaning is: "May we two, intent upon the performance of our respective stages of life (*āśrama*), become long-lived.
Now, after the exposition of the chapter on phonetics (*śīkṣādhyāya*), even for those who have performed auspicious rites, there is no turning inward [of the mind].
For this reason, the arising of the knowledge of Brahman occurs without [other means]. Of the *saṃhitā*, which consists of words and sentences in a fixed sequence;

the *upaniṣad*—because it brings one near (*upa*) to the desired goal and, by loosening and destroying what is undesired (*niṣad*), causes its destruction—the intellect whose object is that is the *upaniṣad*; that we shall explain. It has been explained in the five [books].

In the five topics (*adhikaraṇa*), which are the bases (*ādhāra*). He states the topics: *adhilokam* means with reference to the world; *adhijyotiṣam* means with reference to light—*adhijyotiḥ* itself is *adhijyautiṣam*; *adhividya* means with reference to knowledge; *adhiprajam* means with reference to progeny, the lineage consisting of sons and so forth. 1.

"Internally" means with reference to the self, that is, the body. "Those beginning with 'adhiloka'" refers to them. "Great conjunctions" (*mahāsaṃhitāḥ*) means those great conjunctions which are considered within the word-conjunctions (*pada-saṃhitā*) and sentence-conjunctions (*vākya-saṃhitā*). "In this manner" (*iti*): thus do those who know the *saṃhitā* explain, that is, they relate them fully and completely.

Now, immediately after explaining those [meditations] as the Great Compositions (*mahā-saṃhitā*), the meditation "with reference to the worlds" (*adhiloka*) has been explained. The statement, "We shall explain the secret doctrine (*upaniṣad*) of the Composition," applies here to all four subsequent sections that are about to be taught. Earth is well known as the world *bhūḥ*. "The prior form" (*pūrva-rūpa*) means the form or essential nature of the preceding letter; one should perform the visualization of Earth upon the preceding letter.

The meaning is as follows: "Heaven" refers to the heavenly world (*svargaloka*); it is the form of the subsequent syllable, meaning that one should perform the visualization of the heavenly world upon the subsequent syllable. "Space" refers to the intermediate space (*antarikṣaloka*); it is the "junction" (*saṃdhi*)—so called because heaven and earth are joined together within it—the middle point between the preceding and subsequent syllables; the meaning is that one should perform the visualization of the intermediate space in the interval between them. "Wind" refers to the vital breath of the world...

"Existing within the belly of the three worlds, *sandhāna* means that by which the preceding and succeeding forms are joined; the meaning is 'connection. The sense is that one should perform the visualization of Air (*vāyu*) upon the connection between the preceding and succeeding phonemes. For example, in the mantra *iṣetva*, that letter *e* which is above the letter *ṣ* is of the nature of Earth (*pṛthivī*), and that letter *t* which is above it is of the nature of Sky (*dyu*)."

The word "of the phonemes" (*varṇānām*) is to be understood as the ellipsis. Just as a tigress carries her cubs from one place to another by holding them in her mouth without causing injury through the impact of her teeth or the like, so too the pronunciation of phonemes without causing any strain to the articulatory positions (*sthāna*) and so forth is what is grasped by the term "smoothness" (*sāma*). This is the intended meaning. The word "dehalī" refers to the area near the door of a house. A lamp placed there illuminates both the interior space of the doorway and the courtyard situated outside it.
The meaning is that this auspiciousness (*maṅgala*) should be understood as common to both what has been stated and what is yet to be stated.
According to Śaṅkarānanda’s commentary on the Śikṣādhyāya:
the middle region between those two letters consists of the nature of space (*ākāśātman*); in that region, the *saṃhitā* occurs by reason of the conjunction of the two.

One should meditate on that other letter *ta* which is brought forth by the *bhāṃ* sound as being of the nature of air (*vāyu*). This same principle should be applied to the four subsequent limbs of worship as well. The word "iti" signifies the conclusion of the present Upaniṣad. He now states the Upaniṣad under discussion: "With respect to the worlds" (*adhiloka*) has already been explained.
Now, he states that even this tetrad follows immediately after the preceding meditation with respect to itself:
fire is *abhri* (the lightning-strike); the sun is the lunar orb; water is *nīra*; lightning itself is *vaidyuta*, having its origin in light;

the teacher is the preceptor (*guru*); the student is the disciple (*antevāsī*); knowledge is that which is being spoken by the teacher; and instruction is the discourse between the teacher and the disciple.

Utterance with excellence. Of knowledge (*vidyā*). The mother is the progenitress; the father is the progenitor. Offspring (*prajā*) refers to sons and so forth. Procreation (*prajana*) is the production of offspring. The lower jaw (*adharā hanu*) extends from the lower lip to the chin-bone. The upper jaw (*uttarā hanu*) extends from the upper lip to the root of the nose. Speech (*vāk*) is the faculty located in the palate and other regions, capable of uttering phonemes. The tongue.
This is well-known. In the other four sets of recitations (*paryāya*) as well, with the exception of the final word, the identical text is to be explained as before.
The word "iti" signifies the conclusion of the *Mahāsaṃhitā*. These *Mahāsaṃhitās* beginning with *adhiloka* have been explained.
Now he states the fruit for all five: "He who," referring to the qualified person, [who studies] these [recitations] in the aforementioned manner...

The *Mahāsaṃhitā*, beginning with the worlds, has been explained; it is described as being variously and completely manifest. "One who knows" (*veda*) means one who understands or should worship. It is joined (*sandhīyate*), that is, connected. [It is joined] with progeny (*prajā*), characterized by sons and so forth; with cattle (*paśu*), such as cows and so forth;
with spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*), the splendor appropriate to the Brahmin caste; and with food and the like (*annādya*), where "food" (*anna*) is that which is to be eaten.

The meaning is: by means of rice, barley, and so forth; by means of *suvarga*, that is, heaven; and by means of the world, that is, the fruit of action consisting of progeny and the like—he becomes endowed with these. || 2 ||

Now, since no one of dull intellect is able to understand Brahman without the generation of intelligence (*medhā*), [the text] states the mantras for recitation that produce intelligence for one who desires it. That which is well-known as the *Oṃ* syllable is the bull—the most excellent—of the meters (*chandasaḥ*), such as the *Gāyatrī* and others among the divisions of the *Ṛgveda* and so forth; it is "all-formed" (*viśvarūpaḥ*), meaning it possesses all forms, like the auspicious Śaṅkara upon the leaves of every tree.

The meaning is that he is established in this world (*jagati*). "From the *chandas*" means from the aforementioned *ṛk* verses and so forth. "Superior" (*adhi*) because he pervades everything. "From the immortal" (*amṛtāt*) means from the Self (*ātman*) which is self-luminous. "He came into being" (*sambabhūva*) means he brought about his manifestation.
By accepting the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with "from the *chandas*" and "from the immortal," it is explained as: "he exists perfectly as one who is superior."

That which is born of the immortal; that which is the essence of the *chandas* (Vedic meters). "Mā"—me—"Indraḥ": Indra, because he is the designator (*vācaka*) of the Supreme Self (*paramātman*). May he "spṛṇotu"—may he protect, may he gladden me; the meaning is, "may he make me endowed with *medhā* (intellectual power and retentive memory).
He states the blessing (*āśis*) which is the fruit resulting from the attainment of *medhā*: "Of the immortal"—of that Brahman which is its source—"I am that. I am that.

[May it be] through identity. O God, O God! May I become the sustainer—that is, the supporter—by virtue of being the illuminator of the self, which is self-luminous. Since even the attainment of intelligence is impossible without bodily health and so forth, he therefore prays for that as well. "The body" (śarīram) refers to the gross, perishable frame. "Of me," the qualified seeker. "Vicarṣaṇam" [refers to] the discerning [mind].

The *Taittirīyopaniṣaddīpikā*: "Vicakṣaṇam" means free from disease. The word "bhūyāt" (may it be) is to be supplied here through ellipsis with the subject "the person," as will be stated later.

"Jihvā" is that which serves as the substratum for the organ of speech. "Me" refers to me, the qualified seeker. Regarding the "sweetness" (*madhutvam*) of the tongue: [it is so called because] it is most sweet.

She who possesses the quality of speaking what is pleasant, beneficial, and true—which is the abode of the Vedas—is *madhumatī*. She who is exceedingly *madhumatī* is *madhumattamā*. With my two ears, that is, with my two organs of hearing, I have heard much (*bhūri*) and widely (*viśruvam*). The meaning is that there is no [ordinary] hearing for the sake of direct personal realization (*ātmasākṣātkāra*).

Now he speaks of the absolute proximity of the syllable *oṃ* to Brahman. It is the sheath (*kośa*) of Brahman—of that which is characterized by truth, knowledge, and so forth—a specific covering that exists pervasively, like the sheath of a sword. Just as a sheath is filled with a sword, so too is the *praṇava* (the syllable *oṃ*) filled with Brahman. You are such [a sheath]. Even though it is of this nature, for those whose vision is obscured by ignorance—
He says that it cannot be attained [by ordinary means]: "by *medhā*, by the worldly faculty of retaining what has been heard; it is 'covered' (*pihita*), i.e., obscured.

Since you possess such qualities, therefore protect—meaning, guard for me, who am the qualified seeker—all this that has come within the range of my hearing through scripture, such as 'I am Brahman' (*ahaṃ brahmāsmi*) and so forth. [This is for the sake of] the direct realization of the Self.
The meaning is: "Perform [the recitation] until the conclusion of the fruit of the letter *takāra*.

Having thus described the recitation of mantras preceded by reflection on their meaning for those who possess intelligence, [the author notes that] even for an intelligent person who is outward-looking and devoid of prosperity (*śrī*), there is no inclination toward the inward-facing [Self]. Therefore, for one desiring prosperity, [he teaches] the mantras that bestow prosperity, beginning with the *praṇava*.
He states the indicative marks (*liṅga*) along with the *pādaka* [of the verse]: "Bringing" (*āvahantī*) means conveying from all sides; "spreading" (*vitanvānā*) means extending in various ways;

"making" (*kurvāṇā*) means performing; "for a long time" (*cīram*) means for many periods. If there is a word-break as *acīram*, it should be explained as "quickly. "Of herself" (*ātmanaḥ*) means of her own; the ellipsis is "the abiding of her glory" (*śriyaḥ avasthānam*). "Garments" (*vāsāṃsi*).

Clothes; these belong to me, who am a petitioner for them. Cows are well known. The word "and" (*ca*) serves to include unmentioned items such as horses and so forth. Food and drink: that which is eaten is food (*anna*), and that which is drunk is drink (*pāna*); food and drink together are *annapāne*. The second "and" (*ca*) serves to include the previously mentioned clothes, cows, food, and drink. From this day forward, forever, until the direct realization of the Self—

"Always making her own dwelling, always carrying out and extending [her duties] such as providing clothing and so forth in my house—[she] should make it her own place. This is how the passage should be explained, having supplied the ellipsis.

Now, one might ask: "Since I am the giver of *medhā* (intellect), how can I be the giver of *śrī* (prosperity)? To this he says: "Therefore" (*tataḥ*). The sense is this: because I am the giver of *medhā*, therefore this state of *śrī* can be given even by ordinary people such as kings and others. However, *medhā* cannot be given by anyone other than you, the treasury of Brahmā. Therefore, [I am the giver] of Brahmā, who is the giver of that which is exceedingly difficult to obtain, such as *medhā*.

How great is the effort of the treasury of the syllable *Oṃ* for the purpose of bestowing prosperity (*śrī*)? For me, who desires prosperity—bring (*āvaha*), that is, cause to arrive, that very prosperity which, dwelling long in my house, procures food, drink, clothing, and so forth, and which spreads it abroad. [Bring it] "lomaśām," meaning possessing hair such as the wool of goats and sheep; that is to say, abounding in the consciousness of the *maṇḍala*. With cattle...
"Vāśvādibhiḥ" means together with [the deities] beginning with Vāśva. "Svāhā" means: "May my speech, denoted by the word *svāhā*, bring forth prosperity (*śrī*).
That which it says is "svāva svāhā. From the observation of the word "svāhā," it is understood that this mantra—and those to be mentioned later—has the purpose of an oblation (*homa*).
[Page 107]
In the *Śikṣādhyāya* composed by Śaṅkarānanda,

the sacrificial materials (*homadravyāṇi*) are to be understood from their respective *gṛhya-sūtras*; these include milk, clarified butter, *bilva* fruits, and so forth, each according to its own mantra and proper place.
Or [the deity is] the essence of the *praṇava*. As for the deities such as Agni and so forth, they are to be understood according to their respective application.

"Ā mā māṃ śrīkāmaṃ yantu" means "let them come"—that is, let them come here—to me, who am desirous of prosperity. The *brahmacārins* are young students seeking study, residing in all directions. *Svāhā* has already been explained. By the *brahmacārin*—

He states the purpose for not approaching [the fire]: here, by the word *dharma*, fame (*yaśas*) is indicated; [thus he says] "may I be famous" (*yaśasvī*) among people (*jane*), that is, in the world (*loke*). *Svāhā* has already been explained. He states the purpose here as well:

"more excellent" (*śreyān*) means praised to a superlative degree; "from one more wealthy" (*vasyasaḥ*) means from one who possesses greater wealth (*vasyo’ntarāt*). And here, "wealth" (*vasu*) refers to divine [fortune].
May I obtain wealth; may I become [that]. *Svāhā* is explained [as before]. He states the purpose therein as well:

"Into you, who are the treasury of Brahman—into you, the syllable *A*, O *Bhaga*, the abode of complete virtue, knowledge, dispassion, sovereignty, fame, and glory—O *Oṃkāra*, the treasury of Brahman, O *Bhaga*, address to Him—I shall enter. *Bhaga* is the vocative of that [syllable]. O *Bhaga*, I shall enter.
"I shall effect entry. Svāhā" is explained.

Now, if you have entered me, then you are distinct from me, like a fish that has entered the ocean is distinct from the ocean; and if that were so, there would be no human goal (puruṣārtha) for you, just as there is none for the ocean. To this, he says: "He [is] by me..."
"You, who have become the treasury of Brahman, are the syllable Om. O Bhaga, do not [separate] me—your worshipper—from identity;

enter me, Svāhā! Grant me entry. The meaning is: 'May there be an unqualified identity between us. The rest has been explained. [Objection: But you possess the attributes of transmigratory existence, such as being the agent and the enjoyer; how can you be non-different from me, the Lord?"

Therefore, he says: "In that Lord, who is non-different from me, the *oṃkāra*—in that which has a thousand branches. It has a thousand branches; that is, it is one whose branches consist of words and meanings, being the nature of the manifestation (*vivarta*) of sound and sense, and whose branches are infinite.
"O Bhaga," [the word] *bhaga* is connected with *nemṛjinā*. "I am in reality non-different from you, yet now [I am] through ignorance—"

The lay follower (upāsaka) has his eyes bound with cloth. [He says: "In you, the syllable Om, which is Brahman devoid of word and meaning, I cleanse myself through the realization 'I am Brahman'—that is, I immerse myself with the knowledge that agency and so forth, produced by ignorance, do not exist in reality. This is the meaning. *Svāhā* is explained as before.

Thus, having stated that the arrival of celibate students (*brahmacārin*) is a cause for liberation through traditional succession, he now further specifies that very point by means of two examples and another mantra. "Yathā" means in whatever manner. "Āpaḥ" refers to streams of water.
"Pravatā" means falling from a high place and flowing toward a low place; in the alternative where *pravatā* is taken as an instrumental, it means "by means of that which possesses a downward slope."

"By way of the path" is how it should be explained. "They go" means they proceed toward a lower region. Since an obstruction of waters by means of dams and the like is observed, he states another illustration: "As in the illustration," the months—Caitra and the others, consisting of two fortnights—go toward the year, which "wears away the days" (*aharjara*) because it causes the days to decay by absorbing them into its own belly; the word "they go" is understood to carry over. Thus...

In the case of the illustrative application (*dārṣṭāntika*), "me" refers to Śrīkāma; "brahmacāriṇaḥ chātrāḥ" refers to the student celibates. "O Creator" (*dhātaḥ*)—addressing him as "O Creator" because, being the source of all, he possesses the nature of a creator (*dhātṛ*).
"Let them come" (*āyantu*); "from all sides" means from all directions. "Svāhā" has already been explained. (Note:
*yogyam* is found in manuscript *ga*).

Now, if this is so, what is the relationship between "I" and "you," since [the Self] is of the nature of that very [consciousness]? To this he says: *prativeśaḥ*.

A *prativeśa* is a house situated near one's own house; in the same way, [the Self] is extremely proximate to the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of the individual soul (*jīva*) by virtue of its nature as consciousness.

Because you are the Reality, you are the *praṇava* (Om), the conscious Self, and the neighbor [of all]. Therefore, *pra bhāhi*—shine forth, illuminate yourself for me, your worshipper. *Pra padyasva*—enter into me; the meaning is: "Come to my own nature through the realization of the direct knowledge that 'I am Brahman'. Here, there are eight mantras ending with *svāhā*.

With all these eleven mantras, there is merely recitation; however, with the three ending in *svāhā*, for the purpose of the fire-oblation (*homa*), one should perform the oblation by reciting them with the addition of *svāhā*. It should be understood that the silent recitation (*japa*) is to be performed exactly as they are written in the text. ||3||

Previously, the thousand-branched nature of the syllable *oṃ* was described; now that its principal branches have been established, the preeminence of the *vyāhṛtis*—namely *bhūḥ*, *bhuvaḥ*, and *svaḥ*—within this expansion [of the syllable] is shown. Therefore, these *vyāhṛtis* reside in the heart. He describes the meditation upon them, which has self-sovereignty (*svārājya*) as its fruit: *bhūḥ* is the world of earth (*bhūrloka*); the expansion situated therein is denoted by the word *bhūḥ*. *Bhuvaḥ* is the intermediate world (*antarikṣaloka*).
The manifestation residing therein is called *bhuvaḥ*. Heaven (*svarga*) is *suvaḥ*; the manifestation residing therein is called *suvaḥ*.

In this manner—indeed, as they are being remembered—these three, which have just been mentioned, numbering three and consisting of the three Vedas, are the *vyāhṛtis*, so called because they variously and completely bestow (*vṛ*) upon the qualified seeker the desired [results].

The *vyāhṛtis* are so called because they carry away—that is, destroy—on all sides various things that are undesirable for the qualified person (*adhikārī*). Of those three, namely *bhūr*, *bhuvaḥ*, and *suvar*, the word *api* (also) and *ha* (indeed) are connected with the verb *pravedayate* (he proclaimed). This fourth [syllable], which completes the number four and will be mentioned hereafter, was proclaimed by Māhācamasya—he who is both great (*mahān*) and a *camasa*.

And Mahācamasa was perfected through many sacrifices characterized by those [qualities]; his descendant is Māhācamasya. "He made known" (pravedayate) means he announced with excellence, having understood and spoken; thus say the knowers of the tradition that the recollection of the seer is for the purpose of worship.
He states that [recollection]: "Great" (mahaḥ) refers to self-luminous splendor. "In this manner" (iti) refers to this way. Who is there in the act of making known?

To explain this excellence, he says: "That is the Great" (*tan mahas*). The meaning is that one should direct this vision toward that Brahman, which is devoid of delimitation by space, time, or substance. That which was called "Brahman" is the well-known Self (*ātman*) to be described hereafter—the primary substratum of the notion of "I" (*asmat-pratyaya*); the other [elements] are subordinate members. The other deities, such as Earth and the rest, are subordinate to the *vyāhṛtis*.
The meaning is that one should perform the meditation as follows: "I am the great Brahman-form; the deities of the *vyāhṛtis*, beginning with *bhūḥ*, are my limbs.
Now, having raised the doubt as to which deity resides in the words *bhūḥ* and so forth, he states the meaning of the *vyāhṛtis*: "*Bhūḥ* is the first..."
"mā" is a prohibitive particle; "iti" is for the purpose of quotation; "vai" is for the purpose of recollection. This manifest world is the *bhūr-loka*.
"Bhuvaḥ" refers to the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*). "Svaḥ" refers to yonder world. The intermediate space is the world situated between heaven and earth.
"Asau" refers to that invisible world, the heavenly realm (*svarga-loka*). "Bhuvaḥ svaḥ" is a synonym for the *vyāhṛti*s.

In the phrase "yad vai api," the two words *iti* are for the purpose of imitation (*anukaraṇa*). *Mahaḥ* is the fourth *vyāhṛti*. The word *iti* is for the purpose of imitation. Āditya is the vital breath of the universe, the presiding deity of the lunar orb; [one should meditate upon] Āditya as having the nature of the great *vyāhṛti*.

Śaṅkarānanda’s commentary establishes the greatness of one who is studying the *Śikṣādhyāya*. "By the sun indeed" means by the sun alone. "All" means the entirety.
The worlds are *bhūḥ* and so forth. They are magnified—that is, they are honored and become capable of all worldly transactions.
Now, he states that the *vyāhṛtis* have the nature of light and wind: "Bhūḥ" is indeed fire;
"bhuvaḥ" is wind; "suvaḥ" is the sun; "mahaḥ" is the moon. Indeed, by means of the moon, all lights...

"Three are magnified. Fire, wind, sun, and moon are well-known. All luminaries other than these—such as the stars and so forth—are included. Since fire and the others are contained within the scope of the word "all," they possess the nature of deities;
thus, it is not contradictory that the moon is magnified by its enjoyment [of them]. And as for wind, it is the essence of light...

Because it is the cause of the syllable *kṣā*, its recitation together with the triad of lights is not contradictory. The rest should be explained in the same manner as before throughout the four subsequent sections.

Now he states that the *vyāhṛtis* consist of the expansion of sound: "Bhūḥ" is indeed the *ṛcs*; "Bhuvaḥ" is the *sāmans*; "Suvaḥ" is the *yajus*; "Mahaḥ" is the *brahman*. Indeed, by means of the *brahman*, all the Vedas are magnified.
The *ṛcs* are verses whose syllables are bound into feet according to their meaning. The *sāmans* are those same *ṛcs* when they possess melody. Ya—

The prose passages (gadya) have their metrical forms (*chandas*) not intended to be expressed. In this regard, the reason for the Sāman being second and the Yajus being third must be accepted as based on scriptural injunction (*vācanika*).

Alternatively, because the Gandharvas dwell in the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*), singing (*gīti*) is predominant there; by analogy with that, the Sāman is second. Furthermore, because heaven is to be accomplished through ritual action (*karman*) established in the Yajus, [the Yajus is third].
And because of its connection with that ritual action, the *yajus* possesses the quality of being third. The syllable *oṃ* is Brahman, because it is the sheath (*kośa*) of Brahman;
by means of it alone, all the *ṛc*s and other Vedas are seen to be worshipped. The remainder of the passage in the four subsequent sections is to be explained as before.
Now, he states the functional nature of the *vyāhṛtis*: "Bhūḥ" is indeed the *prāṇa*; "Bhuvaḥ" is the *apāna*; "Su—"

*Var* is the vyāna; *maha* is food. Indeed, by means of food all the vital breaths (*prāṇas*) are magnified (*mahīyante*). Prāṇa has the function of exhalation; apāna has the function of inhalation; vyāna, situated at the junction of prāṇa and apāna, is the cause of vigorous action. *Anna* is that which is to be eaten. By "food," the vital breaths and the senses such as sight have been mentioned. The remainder of the passage is to be explained in the same manner as the preceding four sections.

The passage beginning with "This world" (*ayaṃ loka*) and so forth has been stated because there is no discrepancy in the wording across the four sets of fourfold enumerations (*vyāhati*). Therein, by the first set of fourfold enumerations, the world—consisting of form (*rūpa*), name (*nāma*), and action (*karman*)—is divided threefold;

and it is stated that the Sun (*āditya*) is the cause of form, name, and action when they are undivided. [It is further stated] of form, which is devoid of name and action, [that it is divided] threefold...

By the second [section], it was stated that the moon is the cause of food (*bhakta*). By the third, it was stated that the *praṇava* is the cause of name, which is devoid of form and action and is divided threefold. By the fourth, it was stated that food (*anna*) is the cause of action, which is devoid of form and name and is divided threefold. By this, the fact that these three pervade all things is established. This is now, in brief—

He said: "Those [are] well-known; indeed, they are what is remembered; these are the previously mentioned ones. There are four Vyāhṛtis: *bhūr*, *bhuvaḥ*, *suvar*, and *mahaḥ*—thus numbering four. Fourfold: this world, fire, breath, and speech—this is the fourfold Vyāhṛti *bhūḥ*. The intermediate space, wind, the Sāman, and the out-breath (*apāna*)—this is the fourfold Vyāhṛti *bhuvaḥ*."
1. The nature of sound. 2. (ga) And by that, the fourth section [ends]. [Page 110] 4.
The Taittirīya Upaniṣad Dīpikā:
"That world, the sun, the Yajus formulas, and the Vyāna breath—this is the fourfold *suvar* vyāhṛti.
The sun, the moon, Brahman, and food—this is the fourfold *mahas* vyāhṛti. Thus there are four [groups] of four.

The *kārās*. This is what he says: "Four by four"—the four beginning with *bhūḥ* are four in number; furthermore, each one of these, such as this world (*ayaṃ lokaḥ*) and so forth, is also fourfold due to its internal subdivisions. These *vyāttayas* have been explained.
It has been stated that each one of them is of four kinds; thus, the meditator who knows the *bhūḥ* and the others as having their fixed modes—

The meaning is that one should not worship [them] excessively. He knows—that is, understands and worships—each of these four individually and according to the rule, as being the limbs of the Self (*ātman*). "Brahman" is described as the Great Pervader (*mahāvyāptṛ*), devoid of the limitations of space, time, and substance. To the question, "What is the benefit when Brahman is known?", he says: "All..."
To this Great One—the meditator who contemplates, "I am Brahman; I am the Āditya, the Moon, and Brahman; food has become my limbs;

and the three worlds beginning with Bhūḥ are my vital breaths"—the gods, Agni and others, who have become his limbs, as well as speech and the rest, bring and present as an offering (*bali*) their desired forms, tastes, and so forth, just as subjects bring tribute to a sovereign king. They bring these and cause them to reach him.
They go. || 4 ||
Now, one might ask: "Where and how is the Great Brahman-Self worshipped? By what door does it depart from worship?

And having departed, in what form and staying where does it receive the offering from Devadatta? Anticipating this doubt, he demonstrates all of this. That [Self] is the transcendent; that which is well-known is this very one, the immanent. It is within the heart—that is, within the lotus-shaped organ of the heart.

In the center of a piece of flesh that is turned downward with its stalk pointing upward, having five apertures and surrounded on all sides by vessels like the filaments of a *kadamba* flower, there is space as an opening. In that space is this very person (*puruṣa*), directly perceptible, self-luminous, consisting of the Great Expansion (*mahāvyāpti*), and lying within the city (*puriśaya*). He is the form of the perfectly full Brahman, the mind—
*Mayaḥ* means one whose mind is preeminent; *amṛtaḥ* means devoid of death; *hiraṇmayaḥ* means the sun-like one, which signifies the omniscient one.
Thus, the answers to the questions "Where? and "How is he to be worshipped? have been given.
Now, he states the answer to the question: "By what door does he go forth?"—namely, *antareṇa tāluke*, meaning between the two palates.

The left and right portions situated above the root of the tongue at the interior of the mouth are called the *tāluka*, as is well known in the Yoga scriptures. This [palate] is perceptible through the touch of the tip of the tongue by one skilled in the practice of *pralambikā* (the hanging-tongue technique), or it is perceptible to the eye when facing another person. It hangs down like the udder of a young cow. It hangs down (*avalambate*).

It forms a knot; the meaning is that it remains hanging down. That [channel] is the "Indra-yoni" (the womb of Indra), situated between the two palates in the middle of the breast, which is the source of Indra—the Self consisting of bliss—and the locus of perception. Furthermore, the Indra-yoni is the cause of exit for the attainment of the *kārya-brahman* (the effected Brahman). In which region—that well-known place—is this? It is the hair-limit (*keśānta*), the root...

Starting from the *dhana* (the forehead), the region above it measuring ten finger-breadths is the *keśānta*. "Keśānta" means the end (*anta*)—that is, the cause of destruction—of "keśā," which are Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara (denoted by the syllables *ka*, *aśva*, and *īśa*). The *keśānta* is the human [state], meaning pure consciousness (*bodha*). It manifests (*vivartate*) without abandoning its nature as consciousness, appearing as the three unreal bodies (*dehatraya*) in their various forms.

It transforms into the form of the presiding deity and so forth, as well as their respective ego-sense (*abhimāna*). Alternatively, "the end of the hair" (*keśānām antaḥ*) means that there is no [further] existence; it refers to the root. Having pierced through—that is, having opened—the skull-bone (*śīrṣakapāle*), meaning the two fragments of the head (*mūrdhan*); the remainder of the sentence is "the channel (*nāḍī*) which has emerged. Those who are this breast...
It hangs down as if [from the head], situated in the middle of that where the hairline curves; the ellipsis is that it is established there.
The logical justification for this is the syntactical connection: "having pushed aside the two skull-hemispheres, she who has emerged is the 'Indra-yoni' (the womb of Indra).
By means of this [path], one goes toward the effect-Brahman (*kārya-brahman*); such is the meaning. By this, the path for the journey is stated.

Now, it is said that [the Self], abiding in those various modes of pervasion which consist of its own respective manifestations, grasps Devadatta and, being devoid of internal limitation (*adhyātmapariccheda*), exercises sovereign rule (*svārājya*). [The text says] "Bhūḥ. The meaning of "pervasion" (*vyāpti*) has already been stated. The word "iti" is for the purpose of imitating the act of pervading. In Agni, who consists of the first mode of pervasion—*prati-*...

It stands; it attains stability. This phrase is to be applied to the three subsequent sections that are about to be described. *Bhuvaḥ* has been explained as the second manifestation (*vyāhṛti*) in the form of Vāyu. *Suvaḥ* has been explained as the third manifestation in the form of Āditya. *Mahaḥ* has been explained as the [manifestation] in the effect-Brahman (*kārya-brahma*). Brahma—

When there is purity of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), it leads to the arising of the knowledge of Brahman, or [leads] to the Supreme Brahman. Here, although one ought to say "the Great" (*mahaḥ*) and "in the moon" (*candramasi*) according to the common reading, nevertheless—in order to demonstrate that [Brahman] pervades the entire collection of both the limbs of meditation (*upāsya-aṅga*) and the objects of meditation (*aṅgin*)—[the author], adopting a non-literal mode of expression (*anāsthā-vāda*), sets aside the moon and accepts "the Great" (*mahaḥ*) as Brahman, or "that Brahman" (*tad brahma*) as Brahman; thus, "the Great" (*mahaḥ*).

Thus he says "in Brahman. He speaks in order to dispel the doubt that the attainment of the attributeless Brahman (*nirguṇa-brahma*) occurs merely through the meditation on the *vyāhṛtis*. "He attains" means he reaches. "Sovereignty" (*svārājya*): one who shines or blazes by himself is a *svarāj*; the state of being such is *svārājya*.

[He attains] sovereignty. [Objection: Is not the attainment of Brahman alone also of this very nature? To this he says: "He attains" (*āpnoti*), meaning he reaches. "The Lord of Mind" (*manaspati*) means the protector of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), which is indicated by the word "mind" and possesses the powers of knowledge and action.

The meaning is that he is Hiraṇyagarbha, due to the conceit of having his own limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*). Having reached him, [he attains] the mastery over the instruments of action and knowledge...
He says that he becomes the lord of these: "the lord of speech" (*vākpati*). "Speech" is an indicative term for the entire class of organs of action (*karmendriya*).

"Lord of speech" means the master of speech. "Lord of sight" and "lord of hearing" are clear. The mention of sight and hearing is for the purpose of indicating the skin, the sense of smell, and the sense of taste.
"Lord of discernment" (*vijñānapati*): discernment is the intellect (*buddhi*); its lord is the "lord of discernment. Discernment—[the passage continues].

This is intended as an illustration of everything other than the "indeterminate" (avyākṛta). Having now stated all that was required, he begins to speak briefly for Prācīnayogya about that which was previously mentioned as the object of meditation in the passage beginning with "The Great Brahman, in that [space] is this Person," and which is the subordinate element to be attained by those who have realized Brahman.

The Śruti, appearing in the form of a father, speaks for the sake of the meditation of his own son. This [meditation] is the principal element in this practice of meditating upon the vyāhṛtis. "From that" means from that cause it comes to be; the word "it has been said" is to be understood as the ellipsis. "Having space as its body" (ākāśaśarīram) means that whose body is like the unmanifested space (avyākṛta); that is Brahman—thus it is "that Brahman."

Fifth Anuvāka [Page 112]:
Taittirīyopaniṣad-dīpikā.

That which is said to be non-different from the Great Utterances (*mahāvyāhṛti*), devoid of the limitations of space, time, and substance; whose self is Truth—that is, a self devoid of [dualistic] cognition and whose nature is consciousness-bliss (*cidānanda*); that which delights in the vital breaths (*prāṇa*)... [is the Truth].

"Delighting in the vital breaths" (*prāṇārāmam*) means it is established in all living beings. He dispels the suspicion that it might be indifferent or external by saying "delight of the mind" (*manaānandam*);

that is, its bliss consists of the mind. Then, fearing it might be subject to suffering, he says "abounding in peace" (*śāntisamṛddham*); peace is the cessation of suffering, and it is "abounding" in that sense, meaning it is perfected and devoid of all suffering.

[Objection: Granted that [Time] is the most excellent; nevertheless, because of its non-difference from all things, even death belongs to this very [Time]. To this, he says: "Amṛtam" means devoid of death. Since, through non-difference from it, the death of even another ceases, how could there be death for this Time? This is the meaning. Thus, O Prācīnayogya, if one is unable to understand in this manner that "I am That," [then one should look] among the ancients...

*Prācīnayogya* means one who is fit for the ancient [teachings] such as those of Kāśyapa and others; that is to say, he is superior to all. *Prācīnayogya* is his address. "Upāsva" (meditate upon) refers to the form of the great mystical utterances (*mahāvyāhṛti*), namely: "I am this, and the other aforementioned mystical utterances are my limbs"; or else it refers to the form well-known in another Vedic branch, beginning with "consisting of mind, having breath as its body," and so forth.

The meaning is: "Meditate upon [the Self] apart from the meditation on the *vyāhṛtis*, through a continuous flow of homogeneous mental impressions devoid of heterogeneous impressions, and thus directly realize the aforementioned attributes. Alternatively, this may be explained by raising the doubt: "What is the human goal (*puruṣārtha*) in attaining Hiraṇyagarbha?
Consequently, immediately after attaining Hiraṇyagarbha, for one in whom knowledge of Brahman has arisen, this Brahman about to be described— [Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly.]
In this view, beginning with the words "In this case," the speech of Pitṛ Prācīnayogya is to be understood. || 5 ||

Having described the meditation on the four *vyāhṛtis*, [the text] now speaks of the fivefold meditation (*pāṅka-upāsanā*), which results in the attainment of Virāj—the self consisting of the five elements—by adopting the number five that follows immediately thereafter: "The earth, the intermediate space, the sky, the quarters, and the intermediate quarters.
The five objects beginning with the earth are clear. The three worlds, the four cardinal directions, and the intermediate directions... [are the components].

The group of five beginning with *yyā* constitutes the pentad of the world-guardians (*lokapāṅka*). Fire, wind, the sun, the moon, and the stars—these five entities, fire and the rest, are manifest. This is the pentad of deities (*devatāpāṅga*). Water refers to liquid substances; herbs refer to rice and the like;
trees refer to those that bear fruit without flowers, such as the *aśvattha* and others; space refers to the elemental ether (*bhūtākāśa*); and the self (*ātman*).

The physical body is the *adhidaiva* (pertaining to the deities) and so forth. The word "iti" marks the conclusion. That which is spoken with reference to the elements (*bhūta*), such as earth and the rest, is the *adhibhūta*. In this world, even the gods are considered to be modifications of the elements; thus, accepting them as being of the nature of the elements, they are included under the category of *adhibhūta*.
This is the summary.

Now, immediately after the explanation of the fivefold division with respect to the objective world (*adhibhūta*), that which is fivefold with respect to the self (*adhyātma*)—referring to this gross body—is stated;

this is the sense of the remaining portion of the sentence. *Prāṇa* is the function of exhalation, having hunger and thirst as its domain. *Vyāna* resides at the junction of *prāṇa* and *apāna*, being the cause of vigorous actions. *Apāna* is the function of inhalation, being the cause of the discharge of feces, urine, and so forth. *Udāna*—

It is situated like a wedge in all our joints; when it moves, it causes hiccups and other ailments, and the instability of the prāṇa, apāna, and the rest leads to the binding of all vital breaths, moving upward as the cause of death. The *samāna* wind is so called because it carries what has been eaten and drunk equally from head to foot according to its function. These five winds, beginning with *prāṇa*, constitute the wind-system (*vāyu-pāda*).

The eye is the sense organ that apprehends form; the ear is the sense organ that apprehends sound; the mind is the cause of common cognition; speech is the vocal organ, the cause of articulation; the skin is the sense organ that causes the perception of touch. These five, beginning with the eye, constitute the pentad of sense organs (*indriya-pāṅka*). The skin is the tactile organ (*tvagindriya*).

The substratum (adhiṣṭhāna) is established as pervading [the body] from the feet to the head. Flesh is the intermediate transformation of food; it is soft yet has become solidified. "Strāvas" refers to the vessels (dhamanīs); because the singular is used for the genus, it means the channels (nāḍīs).
Bone is well known as the white substance that serves as the rafters, pillars, and so forth of the house of the body. Marrow is [located] between the blood and the flesh—

The form of the bone situated in a cool place during the intermediate state of warmth is contained within the marrow. This pentad beginning with skin and ending with marrow constitutes the fivefold set of elements (*dhātupaṅka*). The meaning is that this has been stated by referring to—that is, having taken as the subject—the fivefold set beginning with earth and ending with marrow. The *ṛṣi* is either the Veda or one who perceives the meaning of the Veda; he "spoke" means he uttered it. The term *pāṅka* refers to that which consists of five syllables.

The word *pāṅkta* refers to the form of the *paṅkti* meter. It is well-known (*vai*) by virtue of the number five. This entire world, beginning with earth, is all of it—without exception—sustained (*spṛṇoti*, i.e., gratifies) by that which is *pāṅkta*, that is, by that which is characterized by the number five. The meaning is that everything, including the nourished and the nourisher, is *pāṅkta*. Since this whole universe is *pāṅkta*, therefore it is by means of the *pāṅkta* alone [that it is sustained].

The phrase "he unites with the fivefold" (*pāṅktaṃ spṛṇoti*) is to be supplied. In this manner, for one who knows himself as the fivefold Viśva—this entire universe being fivefold and non-different from all—and who knows his own self as the fivefold, the attainment of the fruit of such a Virāj is established by implication; thus the Śruti has declared. || 6 ||

Because of the commonality of the number five, it has been stated that "all this is fivefold" (*pāṅka*); by that, Brahman, which is the self of all, resides in the heart, and the syllable *oṃ* was previously described as being the sheath (*kośa*) of that Brahman. Now, in order to establish its status as that sheath, he speaks again of the meditation on the syllable *oṃ*. *Oṃ* is the designator of Brahman. Thus [ends] the reference to the syllable *oṃ*.

The meaning is "for the sake of meditation. *Brahman* is that which is to be expressed (*vācya*). Because of the identity between the signifier and the signified, one should perform the visualization of the signified within the signifier;

the meaning is that it is like [visualizing] Viṣṇu in a Śālagrāma stone. Now, if there were actual similarity between the syllable *oṃ* and Brahman, then performing that visualization upon the *oṃ* would be appropriate; otherwise, it would be merely like the maxim of the blind man and the cow's tail.

Therefore, he says: *Om* has already been explained. "All this" refers to the entirety of cause and effect and so forth, which is accessible through various means of cognition. The meaning is that this entire expansion of sound (*śabdaprapañca*) is pervaded by the syllable *Oṃ*; thus, there is nothing here that requires further proof. Even though there may be disagreement regarding the identity (*tādātmya*) of word and meaning, there is no dispute concerning their relationship as signifier and signified.

There is no dispute regarding non-existence. If something is invariably concomitant with another, it is the effect of that [other]. For example, there is a similarity between smoke and fire as cause and effect, and likewise between two pieces of clay. Therefore, because the syllable *oṃ* and the Self are entirely non-different, they possess similarity;
thus, for the purpose of meditating upon the *oṃ*, the *oṃ* is praised as the cause of both worldly and Vedic activity.

"Om" has been explained. This is the designation of the syllable *oṃ*. Regarding imitation—[such as] "go," "drink," "read," and so forth—

The word *anu* refers to the acceptance of a command by a servant or similar person; *om*-making is its imitation. *Ha* indeed; *kila* is used for what is well-known; *vai* for what is being remembered; *api* is used as an additive. The meaning is that the syllable *oṃ* is not only the cause for worldly transactions, but also for Vedic ones. *Śrāvaya*: "Make the gods hear the mantra for the purpose of offering the oblation."
When it has been stated in this manner regarding the Vedic ritual, the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) cause the deities to hear from all sides;
that is, they cause them to listen. *Om* has already been explained. The *Sāmans* are the *Ṛks* accompanied by song.
They sing them during the sacrificial rite and recite them elsewhere as well. *Oṃ* has already been explained. *Śoṃ*: *Śam* means "face"; that very thing is...

*Śauṃ* is for the purpose of imitation. *Śastrāṇi* refers to specific *ṛc* verses designated by the term *śastra*. They recite (*śaṃsanti*) them during the sacrificial rite and elsewhere. *Oṃ* has already been explained. The *adhvaryu*, the priest of the *Yajus* formulas, performs the *pratigara* (response). *Gara* is simply the prescribed activity of speech, mind, and body; that which is connected with it is the *prati-* [gar].

*Gara* is an action; with respect to that, the meaning is "in the object" (*karmaṇi*), [as in] "in the two objects. He utters (*gṛṇāti*) sound; he performs the *pratigara*, which is a specific *yajus*. He recites (*pratigṛṇāti*). In this view, the ellipsis is "having uttered 'Om'. "Om" has been explained. The *brahmā* is a specific type of officiating priest (*ṛtvij*). He impels (*prasauti*), that is, he gives permission. "Om" has been explained.

When it is said, "One performs the *agnihotra*," the one standing nearby [the teacher] gives permission for the *agnihotra*—whether as a regular (*nitya*) or optional (*kāmya*) rite—by means of the word "perform" (*juhudhi*), granting the authorization. "Om" has already been explained. A Brāhmaṇa who is about to study—that is, intending to engage in the act of speaking with excellence for the purpose of recitation—says (or speaks).

He states the reason for [the word] "Oṃ" being at the beginning: *brahma* means the Veda; *upāpnavāni* means "I have obtained" by way of proximity characterized by mastery (*svādhīnatva*). This is with this intention. Now, one might ask: "Is it merely an intention? Anticipating this doubt, he says "no": one indeed obtains the Veda itself as *brahma*; one indeed obtains it through the proximity of mastery, not merely by intention.

[The word] "only" (mātram). Here, the fruit—namely, the attainment of the state of being the Self of all through the arising of the knowledge of Brahman—should be understood even though it is not explicitly stated. Alternatively, the statement beginning with "Omiti brāhmaṇaḥ" (The Brahmin [is] Om) expresses the fruit. In this view, the "Brahmin" is a renunciant (saṃnyāsī) endowed with the fourfold qualifications. He is about to declare pre-eminently [the truths]: "That thou art" (tattvam asi) and "I am Brahman" (ahaṃ brahmāsmi).
Intending to state such a collection of statements as these, [the author] declares that Brahman is characterized by truth, knowledge, and so forth. (7)

Now, one might object: "Even so, what should be done by one who lacks inward-turning through these meditations (*upāsana*) yet possesses the desire for liberation (*mumukṣā*)? Anticipating this doubt, he says that such a person must perform ritual action (*karman*) itself. "Truth" (*ṛtam*) refers to knowledge regarding action as prescribed by the scriptures. The word "and" (*ca*) serves to include both self-study (*svādhyāya*) and teaching (*pravacana*). And self-study and teaching—[are likewise to be performed].

Meditation (*dhyāna*), study (*adhyayana*), exposition (*pravacana*), or teaching (*adhyāpana*) constitutes the sacrifice to Brahman (*brahmayajña*). The word "and" (*ca*) serves to indicate the conjunction of these two with what has been previously mentioned.

Truth (*satya*) refers either to action performed through mind and body, or to truthful speech. Austerity (*tapas*) consists of practices such as the *kṛcchra* and *cāndrāyaṇa* penances, or abiding in one's own duty (*svadharma*). Self-restraint (*dama*) is the control of the external senses; tranquility (*śama*) is the pacification of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*). A—

There are three or five duties (*dharma*). The *agnihotra* is the obligatory Śrauta rite characterized by the morning and evening oblations.

*Atithis* are Brāhmaṇas and others whose family and lineage are unknown, who have come to the house for the sake of food and so forth even outside of specific lunar days such as the new moon; or they are those associated with the Soma sacrifice denoted by the word "guest. *Mānuṣa* refers to sons and other [dependents].

At marriages and other such occasions, there should be appropriate worship of relatives and others. *Prajā* refers to offspring, such as sons and so forth. *Prajana* means procreation; the meaning is approaching one's wife during her fertile period (*ṛtu*). *Prajāti* is the production of grandsons and further descendants. A son who is suitable and beloved by his mother is a boon for the daughter; the meaning is that in this same way, the accomplishment of [the welfare of] grandsons, granddaughters, and so on, must be ensured. In this regard—

The phrase "should be accomplished" (saṃpādanīyam) at the beginning [of each section] is to be supplied—following the singular, dual, and plural endings—in all twelve sections. Furthermore, the reading of both "study" (svādhyāya) and "teaching" (pravacana) everywhere is intended to demonstrate extreme respect for them. The remainder of the text, which has the same reading across the eleven sections, is to be explained according to the pattern of the individual sections.
Now he presents the opinions of the sages on this point. "It is true," so it was said; thus [it is].

*Satyavacas* means one who speaks the truth, or it is his name. *Rāthītari* means one belonging to the Rathītara lineage. "He considers what is to be performed"—although this will be stated later, it should be supplied here as appropriate. *Tapas* means austerity itself. *Taponityaḥ* means one who is constantly devoted to austerity.

"Constantly engaged" means one who is constant in austerity (*taponitya*), or it may be a proper name. "Pauruśiṣṭi" refers to the descendant of Puruśiṣṭa; *puruśiṣṭa* means one who has been repeatedly instructed (*śiṣṭa*) many times (*puru*) by his mother, father, and teacher.

Having stated the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), he states the established conclusion (*siddhānta*). "The study and teaching of the Veda" (*svādhyāyapravacane*) has already been explained. Thus it is not so.

"Truth or austerity is something else"—thus [it is said]. Nāka by name; he is a Maudgalya. *Mudgala* is so called because he causes (*galati*) joy (*mudaṃ*), which consists of the determination of the meaning of the scriptures, to flow forth (*sravati*); his descendant is a Maudgalya.
He establishes that this position is the final conclusion (*siddhānta*): "That is the practice of Vedic study and teaching; for it is austerity. Because of this, it is austerity.

This [term] has been stated as an *upalakṣaṇa* (an indicative mark) for the *satya* (truthfulness) as well; therefore, the remainder [of the meaning] is that this alone is superior. The repetition is for the sake of showing respect for this position. For that indeed has been explained as austerity (*tapas*). Now, one might object: since the obligation to study is established as being contingent upon the *brāhmaṇya-jāti* (the Brahmin caste), the performance of the vow (*vrata*)— [The text continues: ...is already established by that very [obligation]. To this we reply: No, because it is not so. For even if the obligation to study is established by the *jāti*, the performance of the vow is not necessarily established by that alone. Why? Because there is no fixed rule (*niyama*) regarding the duration of the vow. If it were so, then the vow would have to be performed throughout life. But that is not the case, for it is seen that the vow is abandoned when the teacher departs. Therefore, the vow is not necessarily established by the mere fact of being a Brahmin. Consequently, the statement "one should perform the vow" is made for the purpose of establishing its necessity. Furthermore, the word "vow" (*vrata*) is used here in the sense of "that which must be performed" (*kartavya*), and not in the sense of "that which is observed" (*anuṣṭheya*). This is because the vow is something to be undertaken (*upādāna*) at the beginning, whereas the act of observing (*anuṣṭhāna*) occurs subsequently. Thus, the vow is indeed established as something to be performed. And since it is established as such, the subsequent mention of the vow is intended to indicate its specific nature. Therefore, the meaning is: "One should undertake the vow. It is for this reason that the vow is mentioned again.
