Or [it might be argued that] teaching is compulsory. But because it is compulsory, its object—the study of one's own Veda (*svādhyāya*)—would also have to be compulsory; therefore, it is taught as something to be accomplished through the two words "study" (*svādhyāya*) and "recitation" (*pravacana*). Yet even this cannot be performed, because of being occupied with many other duties.
A mandatory injunction (*vidhi*) does not enjoin what is impossible to perform. Therefore, [the conclusion is that] "study and recitation alone"—whatever this may mean—[is what is enjoined].

Anticipating this very doubt, he says [in verse 8], intending to convey that "this mantra alone should be recited constantly; as for the others, they should be recited according to one's capacity," since there is no impossibility in doing so much.

"I am the performer of constant Vedic study (*svādhyāya*). Of the 'tree'—meaning the gross and subtle bodies which are distinct from the presiding deities and so forth, characterized by roots above and branches below—I am the *rerivā*, the impeller. My 'fame' (*kīrti*) consists of the merit and glory attained here and hereafter through the performance of duties appropriate to my own caste and stage of life (*varṇāśrama*) and through knowledge. My 'back' (*pṛṣṭha*) is exceedingly elevated."
The peak is the object of the vision of the two worlds; just as it is for a mountain, so it is for Meru. May this [vision] belong to me—whether it be a sacrifice or that which is suitable.
The Ninth Anuvāka [page 116] of the Taittirīyopaniṣaddīpikā.
15. This is the remainder [of the verse]. "Ūrdhvapavitra" means that for me—the aggregate consisting of the body and so forth—Brahman is the supreme, purifying cause;
thus, "I am Ūrdhvapavitra. The meaning is that even the tree is indeed myself. Like a "vājinī," where *vāja* is the food of the gods, [the red horse]... [rohitā-]

Since this form is well-known to people such as ourselves, Savitṛ is "Vājī" (the possessor of speed/energy). In Him, I am "Svamṛtam"—well-nourished by immortality—possessing forms such as the ruddy one (rohitādi), or possessing the nature of bliss itself. "Draviṇam" means wealth, such as gold and so forth;
here it refers to the nature of bliss itself. "Savarcasam": *varcas* is splendor, which is the direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) of Brahman; that which exists together with that is "savarcasam."

"Rcaḥ": *Savarcas* indeed means "possessing splendor. *Sumedhāḥ*: one whose intellect (*medhā*) is excellent—that is, one who possesses the capacity for retaining such scriptural teachings as "That thou art" (*tat tvam asi*) and "I am Brahman" (*ahaṃ brahmāsmi*)—is *sumedhāḥ*. *Amṛtokṣitaḥ*: sprinkled or moistened by the nectar of the Guru’s glance;
or, *amṛtaḥ* meaning "free from death," and *akṣitaḥ* meaning "devoid of other modifications. Thus, even in the absence of supplying the ellipsis "may this be mine," [the sense is complete].
"Knowledge of what is conducive to one's well-being" (*sātmyajñāna*) and "fame" (*kīrti*) should also be explained as "I am [this]. The *Śruti* says:

"In this manner," for one who is steadfast in his own duty (*svadharman*) and endowed with the vision of the seers (*ārṣadarśana*), there is the state of being "triśaṅku"—one whose "shafts" (*śaṅku*), consisting of suffering, are threefold: pertaining to the self (*ādhyātmika*), to external beings (*ādhibhautika*), and to the divine (*ādhidaivika*). For such a person, who is intensely tormented by the miseries of *saṃsāra*, there arises supreme detachment (*paramavairāgya*).

The meaning is "of one who has attained," or [the name] Triśaṅku. *Vedānuvacanam* refers to the realization (*veda*) that "I am the impeller of the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*), my glory is such, and the cycle of existence is through ignorance; but in reality, I am of the nature of the blissful Self, possessing the direct realization of Brahman by the falling glance of the Guru. Following (*anu*) that is the subsequent statement (*vacanam*), beginning with "I am of the tree" and ending with "sprinkled with immortality."
Up to this point is the recitation of the Vedas. || 9 ||

Truth and the other [virtues] are to be practiced by one desiring liberation who is inwardly oriented. Anticipating the doubt—whether these are to be practiced only when there is the desire for liberation and not otherwise—it is said that from the commencement of initiation until the direct realization of Brahman, or until death at the cremation ground, actions appropriate to one’s own caste and stage of life must be performed; for this purpose, one departs from the teacher’s house.

With the intention that "this is to be taught by the teacher to the *brahmacārin*," he says: "the Veda"—meaning either one of the [Vedas] beginning with the *Ṛgveda*, or merely his own specific *śākhā*. The singular number is used out of respect. Having taught two, three, or four [Vedas], along with their auxiliary sciences (*aṅga*) and secondary sciences (*upavidyā*), and having spoken of that at the time of initiation (*upanayana*), the teacher, having initiated the pupil, is the speaker of the Veda together with its ritual manuals (*kalpa*) and secret doctrines (*rahasya*).

He instructs the disciple—one who does not abandon him even as a shadow follows its object, who performs his studies at his call, and who is endowed with such characteristics of a disciple. He issues the instruction, which is the word of the Veda; the meaning is that he should perform the instruction.
Speak the truth—that which is perceived according to valid means of knowledge—and speech that is both beneficial and pleasant. [Speak] dharma... your own...

Perform the duties prescribed for your stage of life (*āśrama*); practice them. Do not be negligent regarding *svādhyāya*, that is, the daily study of the Vedas. Having brought to the teacher his desired and pleasing wealth—such as cattle and other property—as payment for all the knowledge [received]; and having taken a suitable wife, do not sever the thread of progeny—the lineage of sons, grandsons, and so forth.
"Do not cut off"— do not cause an interruption; the meaning is that for the sake of sons, grandsons, and so forth, one should undertake efforts for both visible and invisible purposes.

The duty of truthfulness and the other virtues has been stated; their performance, as well as that of others, is required. Among these very duties, at certain times, there is the knowledge of the Self of all. [Page 117] 1. Ga. omits "ve". 2. Ga. omits "namuktvā". 3. Kha. Ga. read "yāt | mā".
Composed by Śaṅkarānanda [in the Śīkṣādhyāya]
In order to ward off the notion that [the practice] might be abandoned, he says: "One must not be negligent regarding the Truth (satya) already taught; negligence must not be committed.

The meaning is that one must practice that very same thing without interruption. "One must not be negligent regarding the Dharma (dharma) already taught" has been explained. "One must not be negligent regarding the wholesome (kuśala), beneficial action (karma)—that is, the eightfold purpose"—this has been explained.

Regarding that: "For prosperity"—that is, through the sovereignty of prosperity—"one must not be negligent," as has already been explained. "By means of private study and recitation"—that is, by means of the constant study of one's own Veda and the non-forgetting of what has been studied, for the purpose of teaching others regarding matters seen in this world—"one must not be negligent," as has already been explained. Even though, by the very statement "Do not be negligent regarding your private study," negligence toward private study [is already prohibited]...

Even though that [result] has been attained, for the purpose of showing that great effort must be made toward the study of one's own Veda (*svādhyāya*) more than toward all other duties, he says "svādhyāya" once again.

Regarding the rites for the gods and the ancestors: the rite for the gods (*devakārya*) consists of the *darśapūrṇamāsa* and other sacrifices; the rite for the ancestors (*pitṛkārya*) consists of the *piṇḍapitṛyajña* and other offerings.

Alternatively, the rite for the gods refers to the *vṛddhiśrāddha* and others, while the rite for the ancestors refers to the *mṛtaśrāddha* and others; one must not neglect these two—this has been explained. Be one for whom the mother is a god (*mātṛdeva*); that is, one whose mother is his deity. [Be one for whom the father...]

May you become one for whom the father is a deity; that is, may you become one who regards the father as a god (*pitṛdeva*). May you become one for whom the teacher is a deity; that is, may you become one who regards the teacher as a god (*ācāryadeva*). May you become one for whom the guest is a deity; that is, may you become one who regards the guest as a god (*atithideva*).
By attending to your mother, father, teacher, and guests as if they were your chosen deities, and by acting according to their instructions, [you shall attain your goal].
The meaning is: through action, mind, or speech, perform only that activity which is desired [by the Lord], and do not perform any undesired activity even out of negligence.
Now, one might object: "Whatever was done by the ancients must be done; for instance, Jāmadagnya killed his own mother."

"Śunaḥśepa abandoned his own father; Yājñavalkya [abandoned] his teacher; Gautama approached Indra as a guest; Brahmā went unto his own daughter; Indra slew the three-headed Brāhmaṇa; the Kṣatriya Baladeva drank wine;
Soma abducted the wife of his guru—and so forth. Following the conduct of such great ones, I too shall perform [these acts]. To this, he says:

The meaning is that those actions which are well-known, blameless, and faultless—performed even by the great and free from censure in either scripture or the world—should be performed, whether they be worldly or Vedic. Such blameless acts have been practiced even by the great; for example, Jāmadagnya carried out his father’s command, as did Śunaḥśepa.

Yājñavalkya did not forget Viśvāmitra’s kindness; having attained the Sun through austerity, he received the Śukla-yajus; Gautama did not harbor anger even toward Indra, who was his wife’s paramour, even to the point of risking his own life;
Brahmā made a great effort for the sake of producing a son; and Indra [performed penance] for the sake of the well-being of the three worlds, despite being censured.

Even Balarāma, who is Śeṣa, accepted a body formed of semen and blood for the sake of the work of the gods and Brahmins; Soma brought great fame to his preceptor; such deeds as these must be emulated and performed by you.

[Objection: "But surely, I shall carry out such acts as obeying the father's word because they were performed by the great ones, and likewise [the killing of] the mother and so forth. To this, he says: "No," which has the sense of prohibition. The ellipsis to be supplied is: "other acts, such as the killing of the mother and so forth, are not to be practiced. [Note: 1. *ga* reads *darśādyānna*; 2. *kha* reads *smṛtiha*.]
The tenth Anuvāka.
The Taittirīya Upaniṣad Dīpikā.

"In that case, I shall not perform those blameworthy actions committed by others; however, I shall perform all those Vedic rites practiced by my venerable teachers, you, such as: 'One offers the Agnihotra,' 'One should not exclude anyone [from the sacrifice],' and so forth."

To the thought "May I be [thus]," he says: those well-practiced deeds established by our teachers or by the Vedas, which are being performed by us—such as "one should offer the *agnihotra* sacrifice" and so forth—as spoken of in the Vedas, or which are beautiful because they bring about the welfare of both worlds; these are called "well-practiced deeds."
These are to be attended to by you as a disciple and must be performed continuously.

He states that those practices which are censured by the teachers, whether they be established by tradition or mentioned in the Vedas, are not to be performed. The phrase "not others" implies that [practices] such as approaching the wives of others are not to be attended to. This applies to whoever they may be, whether relatives or non-relatives.

[This is] for you. "Whosoever" means those who are superior—that is, more highly praised—than we, [that is,] than us, [and] than your teachers; and who are they? To this he says: "Brāhmaṇas," meaning those who are characterized by the caste of Brāhmaṇahood. Of those aforementioned Brāhmaṇas, by you, our disciple, through the act of honoring indicated by the offering of a seat (*āsana*), [he should be honored]. Pra-...

One should offer relief—such as by providing a seat and so forth—to those who have come to one’s own home, thereby removing their fatigue; or else, when they are seated upon a seat in an assembly, that is to say, one should not even offer them relief, much less engage in conversation and the like. Rather, one should simply remain intent on receiving what they say. With faith...

With a nihilistic mindset (*nāstikyabuddhyā*). When there is excellence of place, time, and recipient, one should give—according to one's means—cows, land, gold, food, drink, and so forth, as is appropriate; it must be given. He says that it should not be otherwise: with lack of faith (*aśraddhayā*) or a nihilistic mindset, that which is not to be given (*adeya*) should not be given. With prosperity (*śriyā*), that is, with wealth and power, that which is to be given should be given. With shame (*hiyā*), that is, with modesty, that which is to be given should be given.

"Out of fear" means out of dread. "Should be given" means it ought to be bestowed. "By way of friendship" means through the practice of benevolence and so forth. "Should be given" means it ought to be bestowed. The intended meaning is that gifts made for the sake of prosperity and such things should be given preceded by a mind of faith, and not with a mind of atheism or lack of conviction.

Now, immediately after this great instruction: if, on the other hand, some doubt regarding action should arise in you, your disciple—who is performing the duties prescribed by me—whether it be doubt concerning actions such as the *agnihotra* or the *saṃdhyāvandana*, whether they be those mentioned in the *Śruti* or the *Smṛti*, such as: "One should offer the oblation when the sun has risen; one should offer the oblation before the sun has risen; [the *sāvitrī*] has the female deity..."

From such statements as "or the deity Puruṣa," there arises *vicikitsā*, which means doubt. The word *vā* (or) signifies an alternative (*viparyaya*), or it may mean doubt itself. Alternatively, *vṛtta-vicikitsā* refers to doubt regarding conduct (*vṛtta*), that is, the traditional behavior handed down through family lineage;
for example, the doubt some have regarding the marriage of a maternal uncle’s daughter, or the consumption of meat.
[The view that] "for some [the duration of the world] is a moment and so forth, but for others it is not," and so on—here the word *vā* signifies the opposite.

The meaning is that when doubt arises regarding Vedic or worldly action, there may be a contrary engagement due to the conceit of being wise. That might be so; however, those who are well-known as being free from passion and hatred, and who follow the scriptures accordingly—in that regard:
In that region where you reside; [there] are Brahmins, those who are encompassed by the caste of Brahminhood,
and who are reflective.

[Śikṣāvallī, Chapter 1] *Sammarsa* is the determination of the meaning of the scriptures through freedom from passion, hatred, and longing; those who possess this constantly are...

"Sammarśinaḥ" means those who are disciplined, devoted to the practice of rituals, and habitually engaged in the performance of obligatory and occasional rites. "Āyuktāḥ" means not prompted by others; that is, they are free from fear of others regarding both the verbal explanation and the practical application of the meaning of the scriptures. "Alūkṣāḥ" means non-harsh; that is, they are devoid of the intent to cause harm through speech that is piercing to the ear. They are "dharmakāmāḥ" (desirous of dharma).

Those for whom *dharma* alone is the object of desire (*kāma*)—that is, their longing—are "those who desire dharma" (*dharmakāmāḥ*). They would be; they should be. In what manner? In whatever way those Brāhmaṇas, distinguished by the aforementioned qualifications, conduct themselves—that is, perform their duties (*vṛtti*) or act—in that very manner you too should conduct yourself in that same rite or duty.

"Vartethāḥ" means "conduct yourself," that is, act accordingly or follow that [instruction]. "Atha" means "or else. "Teṣu" refers to those who have been "abhyākhyāteṣu"—that is, those who have been associated by someone with a fault that is being doubted. The rest has already been explained. This [section], beginning with "Speak the truth" and ending with "so should you conduct yourself among them," constitutes the *ādeśa*, the injunction regarding what ought to be done.

It is characterized by truth and so forth. By the narration of that, this collection of sentences—the instruction—is in the form of the words of a father and others. This aforementioned series of sentences is the realization of the secret of the Vedas, the Upaniṣads. This is the set of statements already mentioned. It is an injunction, having the nature of a command from kings; for it is ordained that by failing to carry out its meaning, one encounters great suffering.

The meaning is: because it is being enjoined, because it is spoken of with affection, because it is the essence of the Vedas, and because suffering results from its non-performance. Since this is so, therefore—*tat* (therefore)—in this manner, *satyādikam* (truth and the rest), which has been described in the aforementioned way, *upāsitavyam* (should be practiced); that is, it must be performed constantly and without interruption, either until the realization of Brahman or until death. This alone, and nothing else, is to be performed; for this very purpose, he says again: "In this way... (*evam uva*).

It is exactly so. The word "ca" (and) has the sense of a conjunction for inclusion. And having understood this—from truthful speech and so forth, up to behaving toward those who have been falsely accused—it is to be *upāsya*, meaning it is to be worshipped, that is to say, it must be performed constantly. || 10 ||

In order to instruct the disciples that peace (*śānti*) should be recited at the beginning and conclusion of study and exposition, and also for the sake of pacifying the obstacles to the knowledge (*vidyā*) about to be taught at the end of the section, the author recites that same *śānti* again with an additional *anuvāka*, having slightly altered certain words, while demonstrating its fruit: "May Mitra be auspicious to us... (*śaṃ no mitraḥ*).

May Varuṇa be auspicious; may Aryaman be auspicious to us; may Indra and Bṛhaspati be auspicious to us; may Viṣṇu of the wide stride be auspicious to us. Homage to Brahman! Homage to you, O Vāyu! You alone are the perceptible Brahman. To you alone, the perceptible Brahman, have I spoken. I have spoken the *ṛta*; I have spoken the truth. May that protect me; may that protect the speaker.

He has protected me; he has protected the speaker. Om! Peace! Peace! Peace! The specific difference lies in the substitution of the word *avādiṣam* ("I have spoken") in place of *vadiṣyāmi* ("I shall speak"), and *āvīt* ("he has protected") in place of *avatvit* ("may he protect"). The remainder, from the word *śam* up to *śāntiḥ*, is identical in reading and identical in meaning. *Avādiṣam* means "I have spoken. *Āvīt* means "he has protected."
Thus ends the first chapter in the *Taittirīyopaniṣaddīpikā*, the work of the venerable Śaṅkarānanda Bhagavat, disciple of the venerable Paramahaṃsa Parivrājaka Ācārya Nityānanda Pūjyapāda. || 1 ||
This Śīkṣāvallī is completed. 1. Ga. reads *ṣoktavā*. 2. Kha. reads *jñāmivājñā*; Ga. reads *evamukta*.

Om. Desiring to expound that knowledge of Brahman for the sake of which the preceding chapter proceeded, he recites the peace-mantra (*śānti*) once more by way of another method, so as to inspire the utmost reverence for it: "May [Brahman] protect us both together with [its] means of knowledge."

May Jha protect us. "Saha" has been explained [in the previous verse]. May he nourish us—that is, may he sustain us—by means of the knowledge of the fruit. "Saha," meaning together, refers to that excellence of power (*vīrya*), which is the splendor of knowledge characterized by liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*). "Karavāvahai" means let us two perform. "Tejasvi" means most powerful. "Nau" means of us two. "Adhītam" means understood from the mouth of the Guru. "Astu" means may it be so. Alternatively, may we two become radiant.

This is the remainder [of the sentence]. Or, it may be explained as "may the two of us be radiant. The remainder is: "May what has been studied be radiant. What more need be said? "Let us not hate" means let us not harbor hatred toward living beings or toward one another. *Oṃ śāntiḥ śāntiḥ śāntiḥ*—this has been explained.

Now, for the sake of establishing the engagement of the qualified seeker, the author states by means of a *sūtra* the fruit of the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*) indicated at the beginning of the preceding chapter:

"The knower of Brahman (*brahmavit*)—one who possesses the direct realization of Brahman—attains liberation (*mokṣa*); he attains it as if it were an ornament already upon his neck. [He attains] the Supreme Brahman, which is the partless, single essence, through the state of being devoid of ignorance (*avidyā*) and its latent impressions (*saṃskāra*), [realizing] 'I am That'."

The meaning is that having realized the Self, one becomes that very [Self]. That [state] occurs there, in Brahman, upon the supreme attainment of the knower of Brahman. This [verse], which will be spoken as a mantra, has been "uttered" (abhyuktā)—that is, declared—by the Person of the Veda (*vedapuruṣa*), as it illuminates all matters from every side. It is "Truth," distinct from the nature of untruth and negation. If so, [what is its] state?

Since form (rūpa) is insentient (jaḍa), he says: "Knowledge is distinct from the insentient. If it is a particular kind of existence that is distinct from both non-existence and [ordinary] existence, then objects such as jars would also be so; therefore, he says: "Infinite" (ananta), meaning devoid of limitations regarding space, time, or substance. If only this much were stated, it might be non-existence; therefore, in order to exclude that, he says: "It..."

Regarding the word "that" (*tyam*): when it is said that [Brahman] is "Truth" (*satya*) and "Infinite" (*ananta*), it might be thought to be insentient (*jaḍa*) as well; to exclude that possibility, he says it is "Knowledge" (*jñāna*).

Although, when it is said that Knowledge is infinite, there is no further function for the term "Truth"—since Knowledge is by nature distinct from the non-existent (*asat*)—nevertheless, the proponents of universal non-existence (*sarvāsadvādin*) maintain that even Knowledge is non-existent. To refute their position, he says it is "Truth."

The meaning is this: even by one who accepts the non-existence of everything, existence itself must necessarily be accepted; otherwise, even existence would be untenable. For reasons such as their mutual independence, it is existence alone that must be accepted, not non-existence. Furthermore, the distinction from the insentient belongs only to the Self, which is self-luminous bliss, [arising] from ignorance—

If it is argued that when there is dullness (*jāḍya*) regarding the Self, [the realization] arises from seeing that suffering is not the Self—[and thus] "knowledge" (*jñāna*) may simply be defined as such, making the inclusion of the term "endless" (*ananta*) redundant—it should not be so thought. This is because both the modification (*vṛtti*) of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) and ignorance (*avidyā*) are also designated by the word "knowledge.
[Note: 1. *ka*: by the sūtra concerning the distinctions of qualification for the preceding sections; 2. *kha*: "I am the Great One"].
Composed by Śaṅkarānanda.
In the Brahmavallī,

because the word "ananta" (infinite) is employed for the purpose of removing the notion that this knowledge is something limited, these three words constitute the definition of the essential nature (*svarūpalakṣaṇa*) with the meaning of an indivisible single essence (*akhaṇḍaikarasa*), just like the expression "the moon is the most excellent light."

Now he states the word for the object to be defined (*lakṣya*): Brahman is that which fulfills the meaning of the definition; it is the meaning of the verbal root *bṛh*, being "the Great" (*abhyadhika*).

And this greatness is not possible without its being distinct from the unreal, the insentient, and the finite. Therefore, the qualified seeker who knows—knows as placed or deposited in the cave (of the heart)—that which is real, consciousness, and infinite. [It is] hidden in the cave of the intellect, beyond the divine and the elemental...

[This occurs] when [the Self] is established through internal differentiation. And where does that occur? To this he says: "In the supreme," meaning more excellent than the elemental ether (*bhūtākāśa*).

"In the sky" (*vyoman*) means in the unmanifest (*avyākṛta*), which is the cause of the intellect (*buddhi*) and the locus of the activity of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), which is an effect of ignorance (*avidyā*). It is precisely there that Brahman, characterized as described above, becomes manifest; the meaning is that every qualified seeker realizes, "I am That. He is the knower of Brahman. In the marvelous...

He attains them through identity (*tādātmyena*). "All desires" means all objects of longing; "simultaneously" means at once, without succession—this is the meaning. In what form does he attain all desires simultaneously? To this he says: "By Brahman," that is, in the form of identity with Brahman. And what is the nature of Brahman? To this he says: "The All-knowing" (*vipaścitā*), which is self-luminous.
"By means of the single form of the knowledge of the 'Mān' [Mantra]. The word "iti" marks the conclusion of the mantra.

Having stated the essential definition (*svarūpa-lakṣaṇa*) of Brahman, and now keeping in mind its extrinsic definition (*taṭastha-lakṣaṇa*)—namely, being the source of the birth and so forth of the universe—the author, intending to explain in detail the aphorism (*sūtra*) which was briefly expounded by means of the mantra, [proceeds] with the unity of the referents of the terms *tat* and *tvam*:

It does not state that the Self is the cause of the world. Therefore, from this Brahman—characterized by existence, consciousness, and infinity; from this well-known Self which is remembered as the Self; from this Self who is the seer of the intellect, self-luminous, and the objective basis for the conventional usage of the word and concept "I"; [from this] arises space (ākāśa), which is well-known as having sound as its quality.

Space (*ākāśa*). "Arisen" (*sambhūta*) means produced. This term follows [the preceding] through the end of the masculine gender, according to its grammatical gender and number. From the aforementioned space arises wind (*vāyu*), which possesses the qualities of sound and touch and is characterized by movement. From the aforementioned wind arises fire (*agni*), the element of light, which possesses the qualities of sound, touch, and form. From the aforementioned fire arise waters (*āpaḥ*), which possess the qualities of sound, touch, form, and taste, and are liquid.
These are the essential elements. From the non-dual [Self], as previously described, arise earth—characterized by the qualities of sound, touch, form, taste, and smell—and solid ground.

From the aforementioned earth arise plants, which end with the ripening of their fruit. From the aforementioned plants arises food, known as that which is fit for consumption. From the aforementioned food arises the person, the gross body denoted by the word "puruṣa."
Now, having thus accepted the Puruṣa, and desiring to describe the nature of the Self as transcending the five sheaths (kośas), he first speaks of those sheaths.

That Puruṣa has been described; "vai" means well-known; he is directly perceived as possessing hands, feet, and so forth. "Puruṣa" has already been explained. "Consisting of the essence of food" (annarasamaya): the essence of food—that which is being consumed—is its vital sap, the refined substance consisting of semen and blood.

Its modification, consisting of the essence of food (*annarasamaya*), is of a distinct form. Of that bird-like Person: this very well-known [part] is the head; *śiras* means the skull. This is the right arm; "right" means situated on the right side. *Pakṣa* means a wing. This is the left arm; "left" means situated on the left side. *Pakṣa* means a wing. This, beginning from the throat—
The hip-region is the location. The self is the internal consciousness. This refers to the pair of feet situated below the hip-region. The tail is the [lower] part. 1. From the body.
"Nātpuru".
[Page 122] First Anuvāka | Taittirīyopaniṣaddīpikā (The Commentary on the Taittirīya Upaniṣad)

The justification for the tail being the "swing" (jhūla) is as follows: "Pratiṣṭhā" means that in which one stands; thus, it signifies a support. Even though we have not observed birds using their tails as a support, they do so by virtue of the force of the statement [that the tail is] the "pratiṣṭhā."
It is to be understood. Furthermore, even when that meaning has been stated regarding the bird, this verse—the mantra about to be spoken—becomes clear. || 1 ||
From food—that which is well-known as edible—beings, that is, living creatures, are born;

all of them whatsoever, meaning those born from sweat, from eggs, from a womb, and from sprouts. They are supported by the earth—the ground existing both within and outside the cosmic egg. Furthermore, being born of food, they exist through food alone, that is, through what is eaten while being consumed.

They live, meaning they sustain their vital breaths. Now, "after"—that is, immediately after the exhaustion of the karma that constitutes life—this food, even in the form of fire, earth, dogs, insects, and so forth, "goes," meaning they go into the food and dissolve within it; this refers to the end, at the conclusion. Thus, there is no contradiction with direct perception either, because the dissolution [of the self] into food is not stated to occur while the body still exists. And food is fourfold—

It is to be consumed as the cause for the production, maintenance, and dissolution of the bodies of all classes of living beings. For indeed, it is the "oldest," meaning the most preeminent and ancient cause, of the fourfold types of living beings.
Therefore, from that [cause], it is called the "universal medicine," meaning the remedy for hunger, thirst, and disease for every class of living being; this is what is stated and declared.

Now, in order to turn [the seeker] toward the knowledge of the Self by enticing him with a reward—following the context of praising the cause [of that knowledge] for one who, like a bird, has been tormented by the hunter of Time (Death)—he describes the meditation on food (*anna*) as a means: "All" means everything; "indeed" (*vai*) indicates what is well-known; "those" refers to those who will be mentioned; "food" (*anna*) means that which is to be eaten; "they obtain" means they attain; "who" refers to the practitioners; "food" means that which is to be eaten.

The meaning is that Brahman is superior to everything by virtue of the knowledge of Brahman. "They meditate" means they realize [it] through a continuous flow of cognition in a uniform manner. Previously, it was stated for the purpose of showing that food is the cause of all beings; now, in order to establish the possibility of meditation on it as being identical with Brahman, he recites [the following] again to demonstrate its possession of attributes equal to those of Brahman: "For food is [the source] of beings..."

It is the eldest; therefore, it is called the panacea for all things. Just as Brahman, being understood as the eldest among all beings, is called the medicine for the disease of worldly existence (*bhava-roga*), so too, because food is the eldest among all beings, it is called the panacea for all things. The meaning of the words has already been explained.
Furthermore, just as all beings are born from Brahman and abide in Brahman, so too [all beings arise] from food, which is that which is to be eaten.
The elements are of four kinds, beginning with those born from eggs; they are "born," meaning they arise; they are "already born," meaning they have arisen.

They "grow," meaning they attain increase, by means of "food," that which is edible. Therefore, because of its equality with Brahman, the intention is that meditation on this [body] as being identical with Brahman is appropriate.
Now he explains the meaning of the word *anna* (food). It is eaten (*adyate*), that is, it is consumed; "by beings" is the ellipsis. And it eats (*atti*)—it consumes as well.
The particle *ca* (and) serves to combine both the etymological derivations of *anna* as object (*karman*) and agent (*kartṛ*). "Beings" refers to those born from eggs and so forth.
Therefore, because it is eaten and because it eats beings, for that reason it is *anna*; it is called and designated by the word *anna*. Thus [ends the section].

This marks the conclusion of the first chapter (*kośa*). Therefore, from that which has been stated; indeed, from this well-known, perceptible [entity], namely the gross body composed of the essence of food (*annarasamaya*), which is a transformation of the essence of food—there exists another, distinct, internal, and inner [self].
[Note: The numbers 1 and 2 refer to variant readings in manuscripts *kha*: 1. *vanaka*; 2. *śvavikī*.]
kha.

Composed by Śaṅkarānanda.
[The Brahmavaśyā]

The Self is that which is denoted by the word "Self. It consists of breath (*prāṇamaya*), meaning it is a modification of breath. By that [consisting of breath], this visible gross body is filled—that is, completely pervaded. That is well-known; indeed, it is what is being recollected. This witness-consciousness, perceived directly, consists of breath.
It is truly of the form of a person, having the very shape of a person, like molten copper poured into a mold.
"Just as it is, so indeed [is he], and not otherwise.

Then, fearing that both [the statements]—"Is the person like another person? and "He is like that very same one"—might be independent [of each other], he says "no": "After that former one's state of being a person—that is, his likeness to a person—this [latter one]..."

Therefore, it is "the northern" [side]. "Human-shaped" means resembling a human being, but not independent; the sense is that, as before, it is easy to apply this same conceptualization here as well. Of that *prāṇamaya* (consisting of breath): *prāṇa* itself—the vital function (*vṛtti*) that effects exhalation—is the head, and nothing else. *Vyāna* is the right wing; *apāna* is the left wing.

Space is the self; earth is the tail, the foundation. Regarding this, there is also this verse. Vyāna and apāna have been explained in the preceding section. Ākāśa is the *samāna* residing in space. Earth is the *udāna* residing in earth, which, having become the stake for all vital breaths (*prāṇas*), moves upward. For by means of this, all the vital breaths are supported when their respective functions are withdrawn.

[The opponent replies: No; because of the context concerning air (*vāyu*), the words "ether" (*ākāśa*) and "earth" (*pṛthivī*) have been interpreted in some way as referring to the *samāna* and *udāna* breaths.

Alternatively, let these two words retain their primary meanings. In that case, the scriptural statement "there is no space for the sheaths" must be explained accordingly. The rest has already been explained. || 2 ||

The *prāṇa* is the primary vital breath (*mukhyaprāṇa*). The "gods" are the senses such as sight and so forth, as well as fire and the other elements. "After" (*anu*) means following after the *prāṇa*. They "breathe" (*prāṇanti*), that is, they move and act. "Humans" (*manuṣya*) are human beings; "animals" (*paśu*) are cows and the like. The word "and" (*ca*) is intended to include all embodied beings. These are the well-known meanings. The *prāṇa* is the primary vital breath. "For" (*hi*) means because it is the life-force (*āyuḥ*), the cause of living, for all beings, including those born from eggs and so forth.

By this, the doctrine that the body and the senses are the self is refuted. Therefore, "from whence life comes" means from that [source]. "Sarvāyuṣam" means indeed the whole of life; it is thus spoken and described. Now, as with the worship of mantras, he states the fruit of the worship of Prāṇa and the worship of Prāṇa itself. "All" means the entirety. "Those" refers to those who will be mentioned later. "Āyuḥ" is the cause of living, consisting of a lifespan of one hundred years.
They go; they proceed—those who worship *prāṇa* as Brahman. *Prāṇa* refers to the principal breath (*mukhyaprāṇa*). The rest has been explained.

The repetition is stated again in order to express that, like food, *prāṇa* also possesses equality with Brahman. For *prāṇa* is the life-span (*āyus*) of all beings; therefore, it is called "all-encompassing life" (*sarvāyuṣa*). This has been explained. Just as Brahman possesses the quality of being all-encompassing life, so too does *prāṇa*.
The word *iti* signifies "thus. The word *iti* marks the conclusion of the sheath of vital breath (*prāṇakośa*).

"Of that, this very one is the embodied self (*śārīra ātmā*), which is the same as that of the preceding [sheath]. Although the word *iti* ought to have been placed immediately after this, since the sheath of vital breath has not yet been concluded here, there is nonetheless a doubt because this sentence exceeds the scope of the sheath consisting of food (*annamaya*).

Because of this progressive sequence, the word "iti" is placed earlier in the text. Alternatively, since the order of meaning is more powerful than the order of recitation, the connection should be understood as occurring immediately after that [section], even though it is recited here [earlier]. Now, one might object: the *prāṇamaya* is not different from the preceding *puruṣa*, because it is included within it, just like the hands, feet, and so forth; to this, he says: "of that," namely, of the *annamaya*.

This very one just mentioned is the *prāṇamaya* (consisting of vital breath) itself. It is *śārīra*, meaning existing within the body. It is the *ātman* because it is the cause of all worldly activity. That which consists of vital breath is the *ātman*. Of the preceding—that is, of that which precedes the *prāṇamaya*. Of that preceding one.

The grammatical connection is: "That which consists of breath (prāṇamaya) is indeed this very self within the body (śārīra ātmā). This is the intended meaning: breath does not fall within the category of the gross body; for if it did, then [the breath] exiting through the nostrils would likewise be visible to the eye. "Therefore, different from this one consisting of breath is another inner self consisting of mind (manomaya); by that, this [self] is filled."

This very one is indeed in the form of a person. Following his personhood, he is in the form of a person. Of him, the *Yajus* is the head; the *Ṛk* is the right wing; the *Sāman* is the left wing; the *Ādeśa* (Instruction) is the trunk; and the *Atharvāṅgirases* are the tail, the foundation. Regarding this, there is also this verse concerning what was described as consisting of breath (*prāṇamaya*): [it is] consisting of mind (*manomaya*).

It is a modification of the mind. Its *yajus* is the mental activity directed toward the *yajus*; its *ṛc* is the mental activity directed toward the *ṛc*; its *sāman* is the mental activity directed toward the *sāman*. Its *ādeśa* (instruction) is the *brāhmaṇa* concerning the *yajus*, *ṛc*, and *sāman*; its mental activity is directed toward that. Its *atharvāṅgirasaḥ* are the mantras and *brāhmaṇas* seen by Atharvan and Aṅgiras; its mental activity is directed toward those. Its—

The reading is the same as before. Having spoken of the *prāṇamaya* (consisting of breath) in the place where the *annamaya* (consisting of food) was discussed, and the *manomaya* (consisting of mind) in the place where the *prāṇamaya* was discussed, it is to be explained as previously. || 3 ||

For here, the predominance of the four Vedas as the activity of the mind-made (manomaya) is stated. And since the Vedas, by virtue of illuminating Brahman, are not distinct from Brahman, [the text] praises the mind-made one by describing Brahman—which is non-different from the Vedas—as the cause of the entire world and specifically of the mind; for it says, "He made that mind," and thus Brahman is of a nature inaccessible even to the mind. Since He—

From Brahman— the cause of the entire universe and specifically of the mind, whose nature is truth, knowledge, and bliss— speech (vāk), consisting of the Yajus, Ṛk, Sāman, Atharva-Āṅgirasa, and other forms, turns back. Having resolved,
"We shall speak of Brahman," they set out but, failing to find entry into that Brahman, they say "no," like courtesans at the gates of a king's palace.

Having turned back from that which has been reached, they become frustrated in their resolve. For turning back is observed both upon reaching and upon not reaching what was intended. Thus, raising the doubt as to what they reach before turning back, he says "no"; the grammatical connection is: "without reaching," meaning "without obtaining, bliss. Now, [one might object]: even for those things beyond the reach of speech, such as the jasmine, *campaka*, and *ketakī* flowers—

To show that the understanding of the various categories beginning with sound occurs through the mind, he says: "by the mind" (*manasā*), which possesses the fivefold functions such as the *yajus* and so forth;
"together" (*saha*) means simultaneously; "bliss" (*ānanda*) refers to the bliss of Hiraṇyagarbha, which is even more excellent than that, an infinite bliss;
[this is] of Brahman, whose characteristics are truth, knowledge, and so forth. This genitive case is to be explained like the expression "the body of a stone statue" (*śilāputrakasya śarīram*).

The "knower" (vidvān) is one who possesses direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*). Having had ignorance removed through direct realization, he does not fear—that is, he does not undergo fear—because of the absence of a second [entity]. "At any time" (*kadācana*) means at any moment whatsoever. Since such a Brahman is his cause, the sense is that he is far superior to the one consisting of mind (*manomaya*). The word "iti" marks the end of the mantra, or alternatively, the end of the sheath consisting of mind (*manomaya-kośa*), as before.

It must be stated that this precludes the doubt that the mind is merely a portion of the vital breath (*prāṇa*). "Of that, this indeed is the embodied self (*śārīra ātmā*), which belongs to the former"—that is, of the former, the one consisting of vital breath (*prāṇamaya*); this very well-known one consisting of mind (*manomaya*) is the embodied self.
Composed by Śaṅkarānanda.
In the *Brahmavallī*, the sequence of the text has been explained and the meaning of the words has been clarified. By this, the status of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) as the Self has been refuted.
Therefore, from this very one consisting of mind (*manomaya*), there is another inner Self consisting of consciousness (*vijñānamaya*). By that, this [self] is filled. He, indeed...

This [self] is indeed of the form of a person. Following its form as a person, it is itself of the form of a person. Faith is its head; truth is its right wing; reality is its left wing; meditation is its trunk; and greatness is its tail, the support. Regarding this, there is also this verse: [following from what was said about the self consisting of mind], the self consisting of consciousness (*vijñānamaya*) is a modification of the intellect (*buddhi*).

*Śraddhā* is the mental function characterized by faith and conviction. *Ṛta* is the mental function directed toward the subject matter of the scriptures. *Satya* is the function directed toward that same subject matter when it is being carried out through speech and physical action. *Yoga* is the function free from doubt and error regarding the subject matter of the scriptures. Through this [function], the mind is indeed [directed] toward the performance of sacrifices and other rites.

The radiant reality of the intellect (*buddhi-tattva*), known as the first-born *mahat*, is situated in the sphere of the vital-breath (*prāṇamaya*); the mind (*manas*) is situated in the sphere of the mental (*manomaya*); and the consciousness (*vijñāna*) is situated in the sphere of the conscious (*vijñānamaya*). Having recited these, the remainder should be explained as before, following the same textual reading. || 4 ||

Consciousness is the intellect (*buddhi*). It extends—that is, it expands—the sacrifice, such as the *darśa* and others; the ritual acts, both Vedic, such as the *agnihotra*, the twilight prayers (*saṃdhyāvandana*), and so forth, and worldly ones, such as agriculture, trade, and so forth. It extends them.

He causes them to cross over. Moreover, it is for the sake of increase through the expansion of sacrifice. Regarding "knowledge" (*vijñāna*), it refers to the intellect (*buddhi*) arising from the expansion of ritual action and so forth. The "gods" (*devāḥ*) are speech and the others, as well as Agni and the others. "All" (*sarve*) means without exception. "Brahman" is characterized by truth, knowledge, and so on. "Eldest" (*jyeṣṭha*) means preeminently ancient; the meaning is that it is the cause. The "eldest" status of both knowledge and Brahman is their equality with respect to those two.
It should be understood that this was stated for the purpose of meditating on identity (*tādātmya*). "They meditate" means they perform meditation through identity with Brahman.
"Vijñāna" (consciousness) as Brahman has already been explained. "If" (*cet*) means even one who is distinct from the Veda knows—that is, meditates—this is the meaning.
"Therefore," from that meditation on Brahman as consciousness; "if" (*cet*) he does not become negligent—that is, he does not fall into negligence, nor does he become outward-facing.

The meaning is "he becomes. In the body—that is, in the gross body—he leaves behind, that is, abandons, all—that is, every single—evil deeds (*pāpman*), which are the causes obstructing the attainment of Hiraṇyagarbha, as well as all desires—that is, objects of longing. He partakes of, that is, fully attains, identity with Hiraṇyagarbha. The word "iti" marks either the end of the mantra or the end of the section on the *vijñānamaya* sheath, as before.

This indeed is the embodied self (śārīra ātmā) of that [preceding one]; it is the same as that of the former. The syntactical connection is: "Of that former one consisting of mind, this very one consisting of consciousness is the embodied self. The meaning of the words has been explained. By this, the status of the mind as the Self is refuted. "From this, therefore, from the one consisting of consciousness, there is another inner self, the blissful..."

That [bliss] by which this [world] is filled—that indeed is this very one, who is of the form of a person (*puruṣavidha*). Following his own personal form, he is of the form of a person. His joy (*priya*) is the head; his delight (*moda*) is the right wing; his bliss (*ānanda*) is the trunk (*ātman*); Brahman is the tail, the support. Regarding this, there is also this verse: "From that which consists of consciousness... [as previously described].

*t* | *Ānandamaya* means a modification (*vikāra*) of bliss; that is to say, bliss characterized by limiting adjuncts (*sopādhika*). *Priyam* is the pleasure arising from seeing a son or others; *modaḥ* is the pleasure arising from conversing with, sitting together with, and so forth, a son or others;

*pramodaḥ* is the pleasure arising from the fact that even sons and others who are seated together remain obedient to one's will; [and] the sight, acquisition, and enjoyment of a desired object— Please provide the text you would like me to translate. I am ready to assist you.

The *Taittirīyopaniṣaddīpikā*:
"And [the terms] *priya*, *moda*, and *pramoda* mean joy, delight, and extreme delight; *ānanda* is the general category of happiness that underlies *priya*, *moda*, and *pramoda*."

The mouth is Brahman, the unsurpassed bliss upon a fraction of which Brahmā and the other gods depend for their existence— just as the limbs of the body depend on the feet, the various vital breaths (*prāṇa*) depend on *udāna* within the earth, and all three Vedas, consisting of mantras and *brāhmaṇas*,
depend on the *Atharvāṅgirasas* as the means for accomplishing observed rites; and just as the various forms of intellect depend on the first-born intellect of Hiraṇyagarbha.

And likewise, the commonalities and particularities of pleasure are established in Brahman—the support of all—which is of the nature of unsurpassed bliss and consists of truth, knowledge, and so forth. The gross body, which is divided into the internal (adhyātma), elemental (adhibhūta), and divine (adhidaiva) aspects, constitutes the first sheath (*kośa*) of Brahman. [The second sheath is] the subtle body, which is the effect of ignorance (*ajñāna*) and possesses the powers of action and knowledge.

The fourfold sheaths (*kośa*) consist of that which is divided into four parts along with its cause. Even a subtle division considers the gross body’s entire empirical activity to be caused by the vital breath (*prāṇa*); thus, the vital breath—which is the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*) and constitutes the essence of the gross body—is the second sheath. Furthermore, because the vital breath is led here and there by the mind, as if by a child...

[This is] like the power of a young bull. Then, the third sheath is the power of cognition (*jñāna-śakti*) which is of an indeterminate nature, consisting of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), and called "mind" (*manas*). Since the mind, being of an indeterminate nature, is dependent upon determination, the fourth sheath is the intellect (*buddhi*), which is of a determinate nature and consists of the mind. Furthermore, since the intellect is dependent upon its objects during the three states [of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep], it is the cause and effect—

The fifth sheath (kośa) is the face delimited by the cowherd (gopādhyavacchinna). Therein also are *priya*, *moda*, and *pramoda*; wakefulness, dream, and deep sleep; and bliss (*ānanda*). Beyond this, because there is an absence of both the effects consisting of the elements and their derivatives, as well as their cause, Brahman—which is neither effect nor cause—is the substratum of all and the efficient cause for the manifestation of the five sheaths.

The meaning is that the Śruti has indicated this by the first Sūtra and explained it by means of the Mantra, as she has spoken. Having read "consisting of consciousness" (vijñānamaya) in the place where "consisting of mind" (manomaya) occurs, and "consisting of bliss" (ānandamaya) in the place where "consisting of consciousness" occurs, the remainder of the text—with its identical reading—should be explained as before. || 5 ||
Considering that because Ānanda and Brahman are non-different, the designation of Brahman is itself the designation of Ānanda, he reads [the text].
"Asat" means non-existent, unknown, or overwhelmed by people; this refers to what is about to be described. It is clear.
"Asat" means non-existent, equivalent to the horn of a donkey. Brahman is the tail—the cause—of that which consists of bliss (ānandamaya).

"By this," meaning by the aforementioned mode of non-existence; "veda" means he knows. "If" (cet) means: having stated the lack of purpose arising from the knowledge of non-existence, he now states the purpose arising from the knowledge of existence. "It exists" (asti), meaning it is found, as the cause of all and as the self of all—this refers to Brahman, the Supreme.
"By this," meaning by the aforementioned mode of existence; "if" (cet) means: if he knows; [he knows] that which is existent (santaṃ), meaning present, through speech.

The meaning is that he is to be honored with both mind and body. "This one" refers to the knower of the existence of Brahman. "Therefore," meaning because of that knowledge of the existence of Brahman, "they know him"—the word "all people" is to be supplied as the subject. The particle *iti* is used as before, either to mark the end of the mantra or to mark the conclusion of the section on the *ānandamaya*. "His very self, embodied, is that which belongs to the preceding [self]."

Of that former one, the one consisting of consciousness (vijñānamaya), this very one consisting of bliss (ānandamaya) is declared to be the embodied self (śārīra ātman); such is the meaning of these two terms.

Composed by Śaṅkarānanda.
[In the *Brahmavallī*, following the explanation of the fruit of knowing the existence or non-existence of Brahman, which is the substratum of the five sheaths: Therefore...

Since Brahman is the Self of all, and because it is therefore possible to form both the notions of "it exists" and "it does not exist," there follow further questions. These are inquiries made by those who, harboring doubts regarding the existence or non-existence of Brahman, and the attainment or non-attainment of Brahman by its knower, seek clarification; they consist of verbal compositions concerning subtle matters. The word "are recited" is to be understood as the ellipsis.

Moreover, even one who is ignorant—that is, one possessing doubt or erroneous knowledge regarding Brahman—regards that which is the cause consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*) and the tail, as a reality that is undetermined by its actual nature through the alternatives of existence or non-existence. It is "the world" (*loka*), because it is perceived by those who know it as self-luminous. "Having departed" (*pretya*) means having come to the next world, that is, having abandoned the body.

*Kaścana* means "anyone whatsoever. *Gacchati* means "goes" or "attains. The protracted vowel (*pluti*) is for the sake of deliberation. *Āho* introduces an alternative view. *Vidvān* means one who possesses knowledge free from doubt and error regarding Brahman. *Amuṃ lokam pretya* has been explained [previously]. *Kaścit* means "anyone whatsoever. *Samatām*—he attains or pervades equality. The protracted vowel is for the sake of deliberation. *U* is an emphatic particle. The sense is this: if there exists that...

If Brahman is characterized by such qualities as being beyond the reach of cognition and so forth, then it must be attainable even by the ignorant; for a thing does not undergo change of nature through ignorance, doubt, or error. If it is the self of all, then if the ignorant person does not attain it, the knower likewise would not attain it, due to the absence of any regulating factor. Alternatively, if it does not exist, then it cannot be attained even by the knower; for a human horn and the like [are never attained].

Regarding this doubt: even one who possesses knowledge free from error is capable of attaining it; yet, if that which is devoid of all particularities is attained by this [ignorant] person but not attained by the knower, we see no restrictive principle [to account for this]. By this, an objection has been raised against the meaning of the verse previously cited.

Let the attainment of the middle state by the learned and the ignorant rest for now. Regarding the non-existence of Brahman’s ignorance—which was sought to be established [by the opponent]—the author, refuting it by means of some further specific distinction while reiterating the previously stated fact of its being the cause of the world, establishes the boundary of the position that it does exist. That [Brahman], which was declared to be Brahman through both the Sūtras and the Mantras, [is thus reaffirmed].
It is well known that [the Self] is the cause and the support (puccha) of that which consists of bliss; how then could it be said that "this does not exist"? Now, one might object:
we have observed that conscious beings possess some degree of agency, and since this [agency] exists, we place our faith in its existence.
To this, he says: "He desired" (akāmayata), meaning He formed a desire. He states the object of that desire: "May I be many, may I be manifold. Manifold—

He also states the means for [bringing about] existence: "May I be born," that is, "May I arise. Having formed this desire in such a manner, the one possessed of desire (*sakāmī*) performed austerity (*tapas*), which is reflection (*paryālocana*) in the form of "this [should be done] by this [means] in this way," and so forth. He performed austerity regarding the object to be created.

That seeker of desire was an ascetic (*tāpasa*). Austerity has been described. Having performed austerity—that is, having directed his attention toward the aforementioned object—he first [produced] the effect, the cause, and so forth.

The meaning is: having determined [the goal], he created—this entire multitude of effects (*kāryajāta*) consisting of the primary elements (*bhūta*) and their derivatives (*bhautika*), and comprising both the sentient and the insentient. "All" means everything without exception. He states the meaning of the word "all":
"whatever this is"—that is, whatever is well-known and cognizable through such notions as "it exists" or "it does not exist," whatever it may be—that effect...

It has arisen; it is that which was created or produced. That very thing—meaning that which was created by itself. This restrictive particle *eva* functions according to the maxim of the lamp on the threshold (*dehalī-pradīpa-nyāya*)—[as applied here to both sides of the context].

Sixth Anuvāka.
