And this [word "he"] is connected with the phrase "entered by means of this. Although he did not actually enter following the creation of the object to be represented (*anukārya*), nevertheless, because he is present in all states like space, he indeed performed an entry. The meaning is that he became the object of the verbal cognition expressed by the word "entered.
Subsequently, having entered—that is, having made an entry—into the created effect; is he merely a bystander, like a stage-manager?

Having created [the world], he entered into it and remained there. Anticipating the objection that the means for his own becoming manifold—expressed as "May I be born"—is thus seen to be contrary [to reality], he says "No. That which is *sat* (being) consists of fire, water, and earth; and that which is *tyat* (that) consists of air and ether. The two particles (*ca*) conjoin the cognitions of those [elements]. It "became" (*abhavat*). This action is clear.

The term *pada* is connected to all four of the following categories as well: the defined (*nirukta*) and the undefined (*anirukta*). That which is stated exhaustively is "defined," such as: "a jar is that which has the shape of a broad base and belly," and so forth. Its opposite is "undefined," such as:
the various distinctions among the fragrances of *jāti*, *campaka*, and *ketakī* flowers, and so forth. The two *ca*s (and-s) are as before. And the abode (*nilayana*)—
And drinking, as well as having a support and being without support—the two "and"s (*ca*) are as before. And consciousness (*vijñāna*), and non-consciousness (*avijñāna*).

Consciousness consists of memory, doubt, error, certainty, and so forth; or it is their cause, or pure consciousness (*cinmātra*). Non-consciousness is the opposite of that. The two "and"s are as before. And truth, and falsehood—given that they have the nature of existence, how could someone, somewhere...?

That which is free from sublation by anything whatsoever is the real (*satya*); or, it is that which is free from sublation from the perspective of empirical usage (*vyavahāra*). That which is the opposite of this is the unreal (*anṛta*). The two *ca*-particles are as before. The meaning is that the entire aggregate of causes and effects, as well as Brahman, is the object of the notions "it exists" and "it does not exist," and that [aggregate] was indeed Brahman.
Now, one might object: from the statement "He became everything, being the cause of all," it is understood only that he became everything; however, it is not understood that "that is not unreal."

To this he says: "It is true that Brahman is of the nature of existence (bhāvarūpa), devoid of all sublation; it 'became'—that is, the aforementioned forms and so forth became. If the non-existent (asat) were the self of all, then all this would be perceived by everyone through all cognitions as non-existent, like a human horn or the son of a barren woman. Therefore, the non-existent is not the self of all, but rather the existent alone. This is because of [the fact of] perception.
The meaning is that even such activities as living would become impossible during exhalation.

Anticipating the objection that perhaps only these tenfold things—beginning with "Being" (sat)—and the cognitions thereof were real, he says "no. "Whatever this is"—meaning all of it, whether mentioned or unmentioned, and whatever is being imagined—the entire totality of it. That...

Even the "residue" (khila), being perceived as superimposed upon Brahman, is known to be non-different from the Real (satya). That which is "Real" is so called because it is fit for conventional usage (vyavahāra) by virtue of its being both formal (mūrta) and formless (amūrta). The division into the formal and the formless pertains solely to the five elements. Fire, water, and earth are formal; air and ether are formless. This same distinction between the formal and the formless applies to both cause and effect.

It should be understood in this way: the entire phenomenal world (*prapañca*), consisting of the elements and their derivatives, is "embodied" (*mūrta*) because it is gross; it is "unembodied" (*amūrta*) because of its causal nature, or else because it is not perceived due to the opposite of that [grossness]. Thus, in this manner, the knowers of Brahman (*brahmavid*) declare. In that regard, even concerning Brahman—which is devoid of all effects—the word "that" (*tat*) is used for the purpose of reinforcing the logical argument.

This is the reasoning for the truth of Brahman and the unreality of everything else: Is that which is real apart from Brahman eternal or non-eternal? If it were eternal, it would be an effect; and if it were an effect, it would be unreal—even against the will of one who does not desire it. [Notes: 1. kha. 'pisa'; 2. kha. 'bādhāra'; 3. kha. 'tīmūtīdi'; 4. ka. ga. evaṃ te.]
"to prā'!
Composed by Śaṅkarānanda.
[In the Brahmavallī, it is like the chewing of one's own tongue by oneself; even though there is eternity, there is non-omnipresence, and even though there is omnipresence—]

Even if there were a difference [between them], that same fault would remain. Therefore, Brahman alone is real, and nothing else. Because it is superimposed upon Brahman, [the world] is fit for the designation "real" (satya). Just as silver superimposed upon "this-ness" (idantā) is fit for the designation "this" (idaṃ).
This verse has been explained. || 6 ||
Indeed, that which is unreal is superimposed upon the Real; it is fit to be designated by the word "Real" because, consisting of name, form, and action, it is the object of a grosser intellect.

Devoid of that [unreal], the Brahman well-known from the scriptures or among the wise—which is characterized by reality, knowledge, and so forth, and is devoid of name, form, and activity—is the cause of the world.
While it should be said that "the Real is indeed [the cause]," the delusion of unreality regarding that which is devoid of name, form, and activity—

In order to explain how [the world] arises from that which is non-existent (*asat*), he says "or *asat*. This universe is to be understood through various conditions. "Before" means prior to the origin of the universe; it "was," meaning it existed. The meaning is that Brahman, variegated by ignorance (*avidyā*), was indeed the cause of the world, but not the collection of effects. "From that" means from the cause denoted by the word *asat*. "Vai" (indeed) indicates what is well-known. "Sat" refers to the word *sat*.

The subject matter is clearly defined by name, form, and action. It was born; it came into being. That cause of the world is variegated by ignorance (*avidyā*). Ignorance is its very self, which is of the nature of consciousness and bliss (*cidānanda*). The Self (*ātman*) itself is both the substratum and the object of ignorance.
It made itself manifold; it created itself in many ways. Therefore, because of making itself manifold from itself, from that [Self] which is the substratum of ignorance—

The nature of the Self is bliss, which is the result of one's own good deeds (*sukṛta*). This use of the suffix *su-* is in its own sense [of excellence]. By "one's own" (*sva*), it means that which was performed by oneself; thus, "well-done" (*sukṛta*) refers to that very thing done by oneself, which is spoken of and described by the gods as merit (*puṇya*) in an indirect manner. The word "iti" marks the end of the mantra. Now, an objection may be raised: since the inquiry began with "The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme," what is that Brahman? In response to this doubt, [it is said] beginning with "Truth" (*satya*)...

Having stated its definition and its essential nature, and having introduced the five sheaths (*pañcakośa*) in connection with the statement that it is the cause of space and the rest for the purpose of realizing that [nature], and having explained how benefit and harm result from the knowledge or lack thereof regarding the existence or non-existence of Brahman— the substratum of the fifth sheath—
when questions arose, this [passage] beginning with "He desired" was set forth for the sake of providing a definitive resolution.

Let it be said that everything up to the word ‘sukṛtam’ has been stated. Even so, the attainment of Brahman as the cause of all does not constitute the human goal (puruṣārtha), because only the attainment of bliss constitutes such a goal; therefore, he says: That which is well-known as the cause of the world—‘vai’ indicates it is being recalled—that is Brahman. It is ‘sukṛtam’, having made its own nature itself the object and the agent through the relationship of action and agent in relation to ignorance (avidyā). It is ‘rasaḥ’, the fluidity of bliss.

The meaning is: "self-luminous bliss. The word *vai* indicates that [this bliss] is well-known either as the nature of worldly pleasure, as the most beloved of all things, or as that which is being remembered; it is the *rasa* (essence) that will exist in liberation (*mokṣa*), though for living beings at present it remains merely beyond perception (*parokṣa*). *Rasa* is the very nature of the Self, consisting of bliss and non-different from one's own meritorious deeds (*sukṛta*). This is because of the two verses beginning with "Having obtained the *rasa*" (*rasaṃ labdhvā*), according to the principle of the linked chain (*śṛṅkhalānyāya*).

It is not connected with anything else, but with rasa alone. This is the qualified seeker (adhikārī). Having obtained—that is, having attained it—indeed, and not otherwise, he becomes blissful; that is, his essential nature becomes clearly manifest as the Self whose nature is bliss. Therefore, the meaning is that the attainment of Brahman is the supreme human goal (puruṣārtha).

Now, an objection is raised: "You state that bliss (*ānanda*) belongs to Brahman, which is the very self (*ātman*) of the well-performed action (*sukṛta*), yet the perception [of it] is contrary [to this]. Anticipating this, he states the impossibility of any other explanation (*anyathānupapatti*) as a response to that. [The text reads: "Who [could deny it] if the self were not bliss? (1) ... (variant readings noted). Even so, that...
[Page 130] Seventh Anuvāka. 7.
The Taittirīyopaniṣaddīpikā:
[He is] distinct from the self consisting of bliss (*ānandātman*). The particle *hi* signifies a reason. Indeed, what else indeed could perform the function of exhalation?

One should act. "Who" has been explained [previously]. One should breathe—that is, one should perform the activity of breathing. "If" (yat) means: if this self-luminous one; "ākāśa" means all-pervading like space, or that which is denoted by the word "ākāśa"; the meaning is that it is devoid of limitations of place, time, and substance. Regarding the interpretation where "ākāśe" is in the locative case, [it refers] in the space within the heart (hārdākāśe).
It should be explained as "intermingled with knowledge. Bliss (*ānanda*) is the self whose nature is bliss, characterized by being the object of supreme love.

It would not exist; it would not come to be. This is the meaning: all worldly and Vedic activities, as well as even the maintenance of life, proceed from the desire for the Self. If the Self were suffering or an instrument of suffering, then [the world] would be like a scorpion or its sting.

Otherwise, it would have to be abandoned like suffering itself. Or, if it were merely a means to suffering, things such as a wife, which are dear for the sake of the self, would not be so. Therefore, its nature as happiness remains. Since non-existence is a non-entity, it is contrary to experience to claim that the self consists in the absence of suffering. Furthermore, even pleasure, when it arises and is experienced, is seen to be dear because it serves the purpose of the self; it is not [dear] by its own...

By its very nature; otherwise, even that which resides in a diamond or similar object would be dear. Therefore, the Self, which is eternally self-luminous bliss, must be accepted as the object of supreme love. And this status of being the object of supreme love is inferred from the fact that all worldly and Vedic activities of life are inexplicable unless they are for the sake of that [Self]. If the Self were not blissful, no [activity] whatsoever—

[The objection is: "There would be [purposeful] activity. Now, if this [Self] is of the nature of bliss (*ānanda*), for what purpose does the world take up means for the sake of that bliss? To this, he says:
"This space, whose self is bliss, although self-luminous, is veiled by beginningless ignorance;
because it is established in the form of the relationship between means and ends, etc., therefore..."—this is the ellipsis. Thus...
It is connected with the word.

This very [Self] is both the means and the goal; in reality, it consists of degrees of the manifestation of the bliss of the Self, arising from the removal of degrees of ignorance through the varying degrees of the means for knowing the true nature of the Self. In the state of ignorance, it causes one to experience bliss.

It brings bliss to the entire world, from the smallest insect and moth up to Brahmā, from its manifestation from the source until the direct realization of liberation (*mokṣa*). The underlying sense is that once the Self, which is bliss, has been directly realized, there is no longer [the duality of] the goal and the means. Since even before that realization, the goal and the means were in reality of the nature of that [Self], it is not contradictory that it alone is the giver of happiness.
The meaning is as follows. Now, one might ask: "Once the existence of the Self is established, when and how does the knower alone attain [Brahman]?
To this, he says: *yadā* (when), at which time; for (*hi*), because it is stated that the cause which regulates the knower’s attainment of Brahman is indeed [the absence of ignorance].
The sense is that, by virtue of having realized Brahman directly, ignorance has been removed. Thus, like Pārthasārathi, [the word] *eva* (alone) functions here as a term denoting time.

It is connected with both the word denoting "the knower" and the word denoting "attainment," and not at any other time. He is indeed the knower and none other. In this true essence (rasa) which is devoid of difference from the Self—[an essence] that is invisible, being beyond the range of external and internal sensory cognition; that is "without a body" (anātmya), meaning that which has no body (ātmya)—that is, the threefold physical frame.
Now, one might object: "Are not objects such as a human horn seen to be beyond the scope of all knowledge, bodiless, and yet still within the range of speech?

To this he replies: "In the unutterable" (*anirukte*), meaning devoid of verbal expression; that is to say, beyond the range of words. One might further object: "Even that which is beyond the range of words [is perceived through] 1) various gestures or 2) various forms of identity."
Composed by Śaṅkarānanda.

In the *Brahmavallī*, the category of reality with its substratum is observed—as for instance, through the connection of ignorance (*avidyā*) with both the existent and the non-existent, and its being beyond the scope of the senses; therefore, he says: "In the non-abode" means that which is devoid of an abode, i.e., a substratum. Now, one might object: at the time of primordial dissolution (*prākṛta-pralaya*), everyone indeed finds their foundation in that very place.

To this he says: "Fearlessness" means that the latent impressions (*saṃskāras*) residing in *prakṛti* are fear itself, because *prakṛti* is terrifying due to being the cause of *saṃsāra*; therefore, that which is devoid of these is "fearless. It should be explained as "fearlessness according to reality. "He finds a firm foundation" means he attains a state of standing firmly through identity (*tādātmya*), characterized by the absence of adverse latent impressions, in the sense of "I am this."

Thus, at that time, having attained a firm foundation in this [Self], the wise one has reached fearlessness. Fear is ignorance (*avidyā*) along with its latent impressions (*saṃskāra*), which take the form of duality; he has reached—that is, attained—the manifestation of his own true nature as the Self, which is bliss, self-luminous, and devoid of that [duality], which is fearlessness.
This is clear. The meaning is that he becomes liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*) at all times.
Now, one might object: "Whether learned or unlearned, everyone is indeed established in Brahman, because it is the substratum of all;
therefore, even an unlearned person who has departed would attain Brahman. To this, he says:
"When"—at which time—"hi" (indeed) indicates the reason; because although the unlearned person is established in Brahman, [he does not realize] "I am Brahman," [the Brahman...].
He does not proceed [toward realization]. Like one born blind standing over a treasure, as described before;

he is well-known to be one who is doubting, deluded, and ignorant. In this Brahman, which is non-different from his own self (*svātmābhinna*), he nevertheless clearly creates even a slight (*aram*) distinction (*antaram*). Then, at that time, that [distinction] belongs to him.

For one who is in doubt, for one who stands in error, and for the ignorant, there is fear. This fear—born of ignorance (*avidyā*), its effects, and its latent impressions (*saṃskāra*)—is divided into the distinctions of the internal (*adhyātma*), the elemental (*adhibhūta*), and the divine (*adhidaiva*). It is the cause of unbearable suffering in speech, mind, and body, such as birth and so forth.

Brahman itself becomes the form of the aforementioned fear through doubt, error, and ignorance, just as a garland appears in the form of a snake and other things. Now, [one might ask]: "Is it not that..."
"Let it be so," [Durmukha said]. However, for one who is learned and authorized in scriptural action, there is the attainment of Brahman just as for a knower of Brahman;
therefore, he says: "But that has been stated. Brahman is of the nature of fear. The word "but" (*tu*) is for the purpose of removing doubt.
There is no equality between the ignorant person authorized in scriptural action and the knower of Brahman, precisely because they are contradictory due to their differing and non-differing growths.

That alone, and nothing else. "Fear" has been explained. "Of the knower"—that is, of one who knows ritual action (*karman*) and knowledge (*vidyā*). "Not reflecting"—meaning devoid of the reflection [of non-duality] such as "I am Brahman. This indeed is the difference between the knower of ritual action and the knower of Brahman. "Therein"—that is, in Brahman which, though not known as the Self, is terrifying. "This verse occurs"—this has been explained. The reasoning indicated by the word "even" (*api*) is as follows:

This is the summary: even nectar, or one's mother, father, kinsmen, and so forth—though they are not of a contrary nature—are perceived by oneself as contrary because of one's own desire for them; thus, even while not acting to one's detriment, they are seen as causing one's own harm, just like Brahman. (7)

Out of fear, out of dread—of this Brahman, due to ignorance of it as one's own Self—the wind blows; out of fear, out of dread, the sun rises, goes to its rising. "Of this"—thus it is supplied from the previous context. Out of fear of this—

This has been explained. The ellipsis is that Agni, as well as Vahni, performs acts such as burning; and Indra, though the lord of the three worlds, protects the three worlds—the first *ca* (and) serves to include all other great beings whose activities have not been mentioned.
The Eighth Anuvāka of the Taittirīyopaniṣaddīpikā.
The first [word] has the sense of accumulation; the second, "out of fear of Him," has the sense of connection. Death is that which causes the destruction of both the stationary and the moving.
It runs—that is, it proceeds toward all—in order to bring about the non-existence of all. The fifth is that which completes the number five, [the word] "out of fear."

The word "therefore" (*smāt*) is to be supplied as an ellipsis. The particle *iti* marks the conclusion of the verse. Now, an objection may be raised: the questions concerning Brahman have been explained; however, when the possibility was raised that the attainment of Brahman might not be a human goal (*apuruṣārtha*), the nature of Brahman as bliss (*ānanda*) was stated incidentally. One might then suspect that this bliss is either an absence of suffering or a positive state that is subject to degrees of excellence, and therefore not a true human goal. Anticipating this, he says: "That [bliss] is well-known. (*sā prasiddhā*).

This [inquiry] which is about to be described is the *mīmāṃsā*—the revered investigation by the knowers of Brahman—of *ānanda*, which is bliss in its positive nature. It has as its result the exclusion of [bliss] from being a non-entity, by virtue of its excellence;
and it has as its result the exclusion of [Brahman-bliss] from not being a human goal (*apuruṣārtha*), by virtue of its superiority to everything else. This is clear.
"Youth" (*yuvan*) refers to middle age, beginning from sixteen years until the appearance of graying hair, provided there is no impairment;

the meaning is that one possesses this youthfulness with the power of the sense faculties (*indriya-śakti*) undiminished. Since deformity of the body or the sense faculties might naturally occur even in youth—whether due to disease or other causes—he says "a handsome youth" (*sādhu yuvā*) in order to preclude that.

He is of a form equal to Kandarpa (the god of love) and endowed with youth; yet, lest such a person be a fool, he says [he must be] an *adhyāpaka*—meaning one who has studied the Vedas along with their limbs (*aṅga*) and sub-limbs (*upāṅga*), and is thus all-knowing. Even such a person, if he were merely one who fills his own belly or is excessively dull-witted, would obstruct that [teaching] in this system (*tantra*). Furthermore, he must be the most excellent (*āśiṣṭhaḥ*)—that is, one who is preeminently a benedictor and preeminently swift in action.

Furthermore, since [the mind] might be extremely feeble and thus exist merely as a living entity, he says: "Most firm" (*dṛḍhiṣṭhaḥ*), meaning exceedingly firm, with body, speech, and mind unaltered. Even such a person might be devoid of strength; therefore, he says: "Most powerful" (*baliṣṭhaḥ*), meaning endowed with excellence of strength.
Even one who has become thus might be devoid of wealth; therefore, he says: "Of him [who possesses] the aforementioned qualifications..."

Of the one remaining: this earth—the ground which is the girdle of the world encircled by the seven continents and oceans—is entirely full of wealth, that is, of cattle, gold, and so forth, which produce both seen and unseen happiness. This would be the case for a universal monarch (*cakravartin*) endowed with all auspicious marks; he is the one born as a universal monarch endowed with all marks.
"Ānanda" means bliss. "One" (ekaḥ) means that which is encompassed by the number one. "Human" (mānuṣaḥ) means existing among humans.

"Bliss" (ānandaḥ) is of the nature of existence, having happiness as its essence; the meaning is that there is no happiness for humans beyond this. "Those" (te) refers to those well-known [human beings]. "A hundred" (śatam) means a hundredfold, as explained regarding human blisses. The word "but" (tu), however, indicates a distinction.

He is known as "the invisible" (*parokṣa*). "One" (*eka*) means he is characterized by the number one. "Human *gandharvas*" (*manuṣya-gandharvāṇām*) refers to those who, being human, have attained the state of a *gandharva* in another birth; they are inhabitants of the intermediate region (*antarikṣa-loka*).

They possess power consisting of wealth and so forth; bliss (*ānanda*) is of the nature of happiness. For us *cakravartins*, who are distinguished by the aforementioned qualities, the supreme happiness of human *gandharvas* is a hundredfold the happiness [of those others]—this is the meaning. Here, the state of being "sinless" (*avṛjina*) for one who is a *śrotriya* (one who has studied the Vedas) is established by the context and thus is not explicitly mentioned. Furthermore, the quality of being a *śrotriya* is [attained through] the *cakra*...
And this is the same for one who dwells [in that state]. The word "ca" (and) is for the purpose of including the bliss of the human *gandharva*s.

He states the cause for attaining the bliss of the human *gandharva*s: "of one who is not overcome by desire"—that is to say, of one who is free from longing for the happiness of a universal monarch (*cakravartin*) characterized by the aforementioned qualities;
for he who is free from longing for something does not fall [into the power of] that thing.
Composed by Śaṅkarānanda.

Since the fruit becomes a hundredfold at each subsequent attainment up to that of Brahman, for this very reason, the phrase "of one learned in the Vedas and untouched by desire" was not recited in the first section.

A hundredfold the joys of the human *gandharvas* are equal to a single joy of the divine *gandharvas*, and of a learned one who is not overcome by desire. A hundredfold the joys of the divine *gandharvas* are equal to a single joy of the ancestors who dwell in the long-lasting world (*ciraloka*), and of a learned one who is not overcome by desire. These...

A hundredfold the joys of the Pitṛs who dwell in the world of the ancestors are equal to one joy of the gods by birth (*ājānajā devāḥ*), and also of a learned man (*śrotriya*) who is not overcome by desire. A hundredfold the joys of those gods by birth are equal to one joy of the gods by action (*karmadevāḥ*), who reach the state of gods through their ritual works— and also of a learned man [who is not overcome by desire].
And [the bliss] of one who is learned in the Vedas and is not overcome by desire. A hundredfold the joys of the gods who are deities by action (*karmadeva*) is equal to one joy of the gods.

And [the bliss] of one who is learned in the Vedas and is not overcome by desire. A hundredfold the joys of the gods is equal to one joy of Indra. And [the bliss] of one who is learned in the Vedas and is not overcome by desire. A hundredfold the joys of Indra is equal to one joy of Bṛhaspati...

And [the bliss] of one who is learned in the Vedas and untouched by desire. A hundredfold the blisses of Bṛhaspati are equal to one bliss of Prajāpati—and of one who is learned in the Vedas and untouched by desire. A hundredfold the blisses of Prajāpati are equal to one bliss of Brahman—and of one who is learned in the Vedas and untouched by desire.

"Of the gods and Gandharvas": those who are both gods and Gandharvas are "devagandharvas"; the meaning is that this refers to those whose karma has become the cause for obtaining bodies as Gandharvas lasting until the end of the kalpa. "Of the Pitṛs": this is a qualification of the Pitṛs; "ciralokalokānām" means those whose worlds—specifically the fruits of their karma—are long-lasting (cirāt dīrghasthāyinaḥ), and whose worlds and abodes are thus "ciraloka."
"Kalokāḥ" means those who endure for many kalpas. "Ājānajānām" refers to those born at the beginning of a kalpa;
they are called *ājānajāḥ* because they are born in the world of the gods (*ājāna*), and this is an adjective qualifying them. He states the substantive:
"of the gods," meaning those whose nature is luminosity, specifically the *karmadevas*. This the Śruti itself will explain later, as before.

Having stated the remainder [of the compound], he states the qualified object (*viśeṣya*). "Of the gods" (*devānām*) means of those who are superior to the *ājāneyas* and whose nature is luminosity. He explains this as "of the ritual-gods" (*karmadevānām*). Those who are well-known as performers of sacrifice; by means of ritual action, beginning with the *agnihotra* and ending with the *aśvamedha*;
they "go to" (*apiyanti*) the gods, whose nature is luminosity—the meaning is that they attain the state of being gods.

Of the thirty-three gods, such as Agni and the others who consume the oblation; of Indra, Śakra, the lord of the three worlds; of Bṛhaspati, the preceptor of the gods; of Prajāpati, Virāj; and of Brahmā, Hiraṇyagarbha—in these nine sequences, there is for the most part an identical recitation. Having explained the preceding [terms] in each case as referring to those who begin with them, one should appropriately apply the *gandha*— [Note: The provided source text appears to be incomplete.]

This should be connected with the words beginning with "heaven" (*svarga*). The meaning of the intended purport is that, by virtue of being free from the impact of desire (*akāmahatatva*) regarding each preceding object, the bliss of Hiraṇyagarbha is as great as his bliss is; thus, there is unsurpassed dispassion (*vairāgya*).
Since the bliss of Brahman, which is superior to that of Hiraṇyagarbha, is beyond the reach of speech and mind, the bliss of Hiraṇyagarbha itself is [described as] the ocean of the bliss of Brahman.

Having spoken merely by way of illustration, like a drop from the ocean, the Śruti has ceased; beyond this is the self-luminous bliss.
The intention of the Śruti is that "I am indeed not the means of knowledge.

By this, the bliss of Brahman is described as being positive in nature and unsurpassed. Nevertheless, one might ask whether that [bliss] belongs to Hiraṇyagarbha or to one situated within limiting adjuncts such as the body, rather than having the form of ourselves; therefore, he says: "That is the supreme..."

*Kṣaḥ* is the bliss superior to Hiraṇyagarbha; it is that which, though well-known, is self-luminous. It is described as the "tail of Brahman" within the *puruṣa*—the one denoted by the word *puruṣa* consisting of the five sheaths (*pañcakośa*). And although it is well-known, it is imperceptible (*parokṣa*) to people like us, yet perceptible (*pratyakṣa*) to the wise. [The syllable] *Ā* refers to Āditya...
In this solar orb, the two *ca* (and) particles found in the two sentences declare that the Puruṣa and the Āditya are merely a matter of verbal designation (*vācārambhaṇam*).

That [Self], existing in both the Āditya and the Puruṣa, is one and devoid of difference. Although the attainment of Brahman by the knower has been stated with the words beginning with "When," etc., nevertheless, it was not explicitly said, "You are That. For that purpose, having incidentally declared their identity, he speaks again of that attainment: "He—"
The qualified person (*adhikārī*) is anyone at all who, knowing the bliss of Brahman as non-different from the Person in the sun and the Person here [in the body], having departed (*pretya*)—

meaning having come forth completely from this perceptible world consisting of seen and unseen means and fruits, and being devoid of desire for this [world] like one who is dead— [realizes] this aforementioned self composed of food (*annamaya*), which is a modification of food and which reaches objects through the doors of the senses.

He approaches; that is, he correctly understands through close proximity that even this [self], which is composed of food and differentiated by internal, elemental, and divine distinctions, is in reality superimposed as "I am indeed this. He approaches this self composed of breath (*prāṇamaya*);
he approaches this self composed of mind (*manomaya*); he approaches this self composed of consciousness (*vijñānamaya*). This—
"He attains the Self consisting of bliss. This is clear. The four sections [of the text] are to be explained in the same manner as those concerning the "consisting of food" (*annamaya*).

The meaning is that through the knowledge of being the Self of all, one attains Brahman, which is Bliss. That too—[attainment occurs] when it is realized: "I am He," in that Brahman who is the essence, the tail, the substratum of the five sheaths; who transcends all bliss; and who is devoid of distinctions such as the divine (*adhidaiva*) and so forth.
The word "api" (also/even) implies that whatever is one's own self, from that one does not fear. Furthermore, there is nothing here other than Brahman;
since this person has Brahman as his self, it is logically established that he has no fear from anything whatsoever. This verse has been explained. || 8 ||

"From whence words turn back, together with the mind, failing to reach it—he who knows that bliss of Brahman fears nothing from anywhere. "From anywhere" means from anything whatsoever. The remainder of the text is identical in its reading and should be explained as in the section concerning the "consisting of mind" (*manomaya*), with this distinction: previously, it was explained as "from whence [it arises] as the cause of the mind," because of the context of the section on the "consisting of mind."

Now, since there is no cause for limitation, this should be explained as "from the Self that is the cause of all, which is Bliss. [Objection: But there are thousands of meritorious worldly beings who are free from fear; therefore, he says: "This" (etam)—meaning this well-known knower of Brahman—"verily" (vāva eva)—does not torment; that is to say, it does not cause distress, nor does it cause him to suffer. This refers to mental conviction (*mānasapratyaya*).
This is the ellipsis (*śeṣaḥ*). He indicates with a gesture where [the thought arises]: "In this deliberation born of grief for my elders and others, am I one whose power is diminished?
"Good" (*sādhu*) means auspicious or meritorious action (*puṇya-karma*); "I did not perform" (*nākaravam*) means I did not do it. "Ah, what misery! (*āḥ kaṣṭam*)—this is the ellipsis. What—?
1. Even so, it is reality.
Composed by Śaṅkarānanda.
[The *Brahmavallī* has been explained. "Sin" (*pāpa*) refers to an action censured by the Vedas and other authorities. *Akaravam* means "I have done. *Āḥ*—alas!—what misery!]

"Tiśeṣaḥ" (the remainder) indicates the meaning of the gesture (*abhinaya*). By this manner, even for those wandering in *saṃsāra* who are free from fear, there is still dread of merit and demerit; the intention is that [this state] is not touched by them.
Now, one might suspect: "In that case, is he then a materialist (*lokāyatika*)? Anticipating this, he says "no": "He is the qualified person (*adhikārī*), he who..."

This is well-known. Thus, the wise one is one who possesses the knowledge: "I alone am unsurpassed consciousness-bliss; there is no other entity whatsoever apart from me. These two—merit and demerit—he "protects" (spṛṇute), meaning he pleases the Self whose nature is bliss. The meaning is that he realizes: "I alone am these good and evil deeds. From that...

He says that he is not equal to a materialist (*lokāyatika*). For both merit and demerit—because this wise man indeed [knows] these two—he "satisfies himself" (*spṛṇute*), as has been explained. Since he is the Self of all, the meaning is that he experiences the distress born from the performance or non-performance of meritorious and sinful acts, but not through atheism like a materialist. He says this very thing: "He who thus..."

One who is qualified according to the Vedic tradition knows the non-dual Self, whose nature is bliss, as one's own self. The syntactical connection is: "He who knows thus—he indeed protects both these selves. The remainder [of the meaning] is that he is therefore distinct from the materialist (Lokāyatika). The word *iti* marks the end of the *Ānandavallī*, or it serves to indicate the imitation of the aforementioned knowledge of the Self. [This concludes] the *Upaniṣad*.

The *upaniṣad* is that which brings one very close to the Cause— which is the support of all, whose sole nature is unsurpassed bliss, which is undivided and free from all phenomenal proliferation— by means of the realization "I am That," and having thereby loosened the bonds of "I" and "mine," it causes one to settle (*sādayati*) and destroy ignorance along with its body and its latent impressions; thus, it is the term for that which expounds the knowledge of Brahman.
Or the Upaniṣad is the book itself. || 9 ||

Thus ends the second chapter, named the *Brahmavallī*, in the *Taittirīyopaniṣaddīpikā* composed by the venerable Śaṅkarānanda Bhagavat, disciple of the venerable Paramahaṃsa Parivrājaka Ācārya Ānandātman.

Thus has been declared the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*). Furthermore, the means for the realization of Brahman are the five sheaths (*pañcakośa*), beginning with the one consisting of food (*annamaya*). If, due to some obstruction, one is unable to realize them in that manner, then [the following] are intended to remove the cause of that obstruction.

Regarding austerity (*tapas*) and the rest: this chapter (*vallī*) is commenced for the purpose of enjoining the contemplation (*dṛṣṭi*) of Brahman upon austerity as its cause, and incidentally, for the sake of other forms of meditation (*upāsanā*). In this regard, the narrative (*ākhyāyikā*) is intended to demonstrate that the instruction of a teacher and so forth are auxiliary members (*aṅga*) of the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*), and to glorify that knowledge.
Bhṛgu by name—*vai* signifies what is well-known—was the son of Varuṇa, hence *Vāruṇi*. [He approached] Varuṇa, the one named Varuṇa.

He approached his father, the progenitor of Bhṛgu, in the manner prescribed by the scriptures for the sake of knowledge; having approached, he said this: "Teach me—perform the study. The meaning is this: "Do you remember Brahman? Then tell it to me. "O Venerable One" (*bhagavan*); "Venerable One" (*bhagavan*) means O worshipful one. By the phrase "Brahman is that which is exceedingly great, the cause of the birth and so forth of the world," [he refers to] Ma... [Note: The source text appears to be truncated here].
He approached in a line. Immediately thereafter, his father spoke this which is about to be described to that Bhṛgu. He spoke it preeminently.

"Food" is that which is eaten and by which the body—distinguished by internal and other divisions—is sustained. "Vital breath" (prāṇa) is the wind existing within the body, the eater itself, which is the power of action. Now he describes the instruments of experience, consisting of the powers of knowledge and action.

The eye is the cause for the apprehension of form; the ear is the cause for the perception of sound. This is an illustration [that includes] the skin, the tongue, and the nose. The mind (*manas*) is the internal organ common to all the instruments (*karaṇa*), possessing the power of cognition (*jñānaśakti*). Speech is the cause for that which is to be spoken.
This is an illustration [that includes] the hands, feet, anus, and genitals. In this manner.

This is the meaning: I shall describe that entire phenomenal world—consisting of the object of enjoyment, the enjoyer, and the means of enjoyment—as well as its definition as Brahman. As long as one does not possess self-knowledge regarding this, let the one who considers himself a scholar perform meditation on Brahman here and there. By that meditation, his sins being exhausted, he is able to realize Brahman, but no other.

Thus it is said. With that intention, the Śruti says: "To him"—to him who had been instructed regarding the phenomenal world—"Varuṇa indeed spoke," as is well known. "From whom"—from the single cause which is both the efficient and material cause—"these"—well-known—"beings"—comprehensible through various means of cognition, such as ether and the rest, as well as those born from sweat and so forth—"are born"—they arise—by which cause of life they are produced. Jā... [the text continues].

These [beings], having arisen, exist; they live, meaning they maintain their state characterized by the retention of life-force (*prāṇa*). They proceed—that is, they go—toward that place of dissolution, which is like clay for a jar; they depart, meaning they abandon their respective functions and natures.
They enter completely, meaning they effect a thorough penetration from all sides. That is the aforementioned world of birth.

It is the cause of persistence and destruction. "Desire to know specifically"—the meaning is: form the desire to know, "I am that," and understand it. Now, [an objection]: "I asked about Brahman, yet you are speaking of something else. To this he says: "That which has the aforementioned characteristics. The meaning is that Brahman is that which is denoted by the word "Brahman" and nothing else. The particle *iti* marks the conclusion of the father's speech.

Having heard his father’s words, that Bhṛgu performed *tapas*—that is, he engaged in reflection regarding which among the [four] mentioned, beginning with food, was characterized by the defining marks [of being the source of the world]. Alternatively, *tapas* may mean abiding in one's own duty (*svadharma*) or performing penances such as the *Kṛcchra* and *Cāndrāyaṇa*.
In this latter view, for one whose internal organ is purified by *tapas*, the unification of the mind and the senses arises.
Thus it should be explained: that ascetic was Bhṛgu; having performed—that is, accomplished—*tapas* of the aforementioned nature, he became exceedingly great.
Composed by Śaṅkarānanda.
[In the Bhṛguvallī,
that which is Brahman as the object of the intellect— Brahman itself, characterized by the definition of Brahman and denoted by the word "Brahman"— is indicated by this syllable *m*.]
By means of that, he understood; that is, he comprehended it with particular clarity. || 1 ||
The scripture declares the manner of that cognition: "From food, indeed; for from this very food—and not from anything else—verily, these beings are born; having been born, they live by it."
"Entering food, they merge into it. This has been explained; the only difference is that the word "food" (*anna*) stands in place of the word "place" (*pada*).

In this manner, having understood—that is, having realized—that food is of the nature of Brahman, and having observed through direct perception and reasoning the destruction of food, his heart was filled with doubt due to the two characteristics of food and Brahman. Once again, he [approached] Varuṇa...

He approached his father [saying], "Teach me Brahman, O Venerable One. To him he said: [the meaning of] "explained" has already been stated. The grammatical connection is that he indeed approached Varuṇa, his father. By means of austerity—as previously explained—and by means of self-knowledge as the method, you should desire to know Brahman; that is, achieve the realization of Brahman through thorough reflection.

Now he praises [the subject] by way of the view of the goal (*upeyadṛṣṭi*). By the phrase "Brahman is austerity, austerity is to be drunk as Brahman," it is effectively stated that one who seeks the knowledge of Brahman must accomplish the means, such as the discrimination between eternal and non-eternal entities. If one is unable to accomplish those, one should apply the view of Brahman to that [austerity]. Otherwise, [the following] which is to be stated here...
Furthermore, the designation "Brahman is austerity" in three different contexts would be redundant: "He performed austerity; having performed austerity... (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.6).

"He understood: 'Breath is Brahman. For indeed, from breath alone these beings are born; by breath, once born, they live; into breath they enter at their death and merge. Having understood this, he again approached his father Varuṇa, saying: "Teach me, venerable sir, Brahman. He said to him: "Discern Brahman through austerity."
"Know that austerity is Brahman. He practiced austerity. Having practiced austerity, he [realized it]. || 3 ||

"He understood: 'The mind is Brahman. For indeed, from the mind alone these beings are born; having been born, they live by the mind; into the mind they enter at death and merge. Having realized this, he again approached his father Varuṇa, saying, "Teach me, venerable sir, Brahman. He said to him: "Discern Brahman through austerity."
"Know that austerity is Brahman. He practiced austerity. Having practiced austerity, he [attained it]. 4.

"Consciousness is Brahman," he understood. "For indeed, from consciousness alone these beings are born; by consciousness, once born, they live; into consciousness they enter at death. Having understood this, he again approached his father Varuṇa, saying, "Teach me Brahman, O Venerable One. He said to him, "By austerity..."
"Desire to know Brahman. Austerity is Brahman. He practiced austerity. Having practiced austerity, he [perceived it]. || 5 ||
"Ānanda is Brahman," so he understood. "For indeed, from Ānanda alone these beings are born; by Ānanda, once born, they live; into Ānanda they enter at death.
1. kha. [This is] the investigation with the [textual] divisions.
The Sixth Anuvāka of the Taittirīya Upaniṣad-dīpikā. [Page 138]

Just as perishability is a defect in the case of food, so too is insentience a defect in the state of being Brahman; likewise, the nature of determination is a defect in the vital breath (*prāṇa*), and the state of being an experiencer of pleasure and pain is a defect in consciousness (*vijñāna*). Although the eye, the ear, and—

It has been taught as "mind" and "speech," but not as "cognition"; nevertheless, because the powers of action—speech and the rest—and the powers of cognition—the eye and the rest—share the same security and destiny as *prāṇa* and *manas*, their distinct cognition was not mentioned separately. Furthermore, since even the mind is dependent upon cognition (*vijñāna*), it is designated by means of [the term] "mind."

Knowledge (*jñāna*) has also been mentioned by implication from the context; therefore, its perception, the observation of defects, and the return to the father are not contradictory. Vital breath (*prāṇa*), mind (*manas*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*) are the causes of the *prāṇamaya*, *manomaya*, and *vijñānamaya* sheaths, while bliss (*ānanda*) is the cause of the *ānandamaya*. And its "tail" is the primary referent of the word "Brahman. Therefore, immediately after perceiving this—

The absence of returning to the father is indicated by the passage beginning with "He performed austerity" and ending with "thus. The four sections concerning breath (*prāṇa*), mind (*manas*), consciousness (*vijñāna*), and bliss (*ānanda*) are to be explained here in the same manner as the preceding section, as their textual readings are identical.

Now, the Śruti speaks of the matter established by the narrative for the purpose of praising this knowledge. That [knowledge] is well-known; it is now being described. It is *bhārgavī*, meaning that which was realized by Bhṛgu; it is *vāruṇī*, meaning that which was proclaimed by Varuṇa. This is *vidyā*, the knowledge of Brahman. It is established in the supreme, most excellent *vyoman*—the sky, the Self consisting of bliss. It is firmly established there.

The meaning is that they have reached their station and are fully established in the Self consisting of bliss (*ānandātman*). Now, he states the fruit described in the knowledge of the Self consisting of bliss: "He who"—the qualified seeker—"thus" [knows]—that within these, bliss is more internal than vital breath (*prāṇa*), mind (*manas*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*)—"I am this," i.e., he knows it, meaning he realizes it through direct perception.

Thus, the possessor of knowledge, being devoid of the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of ignorance, abides in Brahman alone. One who is unable to realize it in this manner should instead cultivate the vision of Brahman within the five sheaths (*kośa*), beginning with food. Through the purification of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), such a person likewise abides either in this body or in another body.

By the phrase "he who knows thus," since it is possible to enjoin the perception of Brahman even in food and other such things, [the text] states another visible fruit for the sake of such enticement: "He becomes possessed of food"—that is, always endowed with food; "an eater of food"—meaning one who consumes food, that is, free from disease; this is clear. "He becomes great"—that is, superior; this is clear. How so? Through progeny—through sons...

By means of offspring; by means of livestock such as cows and the like; and by means of *brahmavarcasa*, which is the splendor appropriate to the Brahmin caste. It is not only thus, but moreover, he is "great," meaning superior. How so? By means of fame and glory. The first [term], *mahat*, expresses the excellence of his knowledge; the second, however, [expresses the excellence] of his progeny and so forth, up to his fame. || 6 ||

Now he states the vow for this worshiper of food as Brahman: one should not revile food—that is, one should not perform censure of it. This non-reviling of food is the vow, the observance of the vow. Having previously established—as a matter of fact—that food and the eater of food are to be meditated upon in their natural state, he now states the opposite: "The vital breath (prāṇa) indeed is [the eater], having five functions. A—

The body that is to be nourished by food is the gross physical frame. It is "food-eating" because it consumes food, owing to its dependence upon food. It is said to be "in the vital breath" (prāṇa) which has five functions. It is "established," meaning it has attained its support, insofar as its existence is dependent upon that [breath].
(Note: Regarding the variants, *kha* reads *atha caivaṃ* and *gha* reads *athavaivaṃ*.)
Composed by Śaṅkarānanda.

[In this *Bhṛguvallī*, he now states the reverse order: "The vital breath (*prāṇa*) is established in the body. This is clear. As it has been said: "This body is of the nature of the vital breath; the food to be eaten is manifest as both the body and the vital breath. It is established in this body and in this vital breath."]

Just as a house is established upon bamboo, grass, and so forth, and bamboo, grass, and so forth are established within the house—this is well known—so too is it for any and every lay follower (*upāsaka*). "He who knows that this food is established in food becomes firmly established; he becomes possessed of food, an eater of food; he becomes great through offspring, cattle, and the splendor of sacred knowledge (*brahmavarcasa*); he becomes great in fame. This food is established in food.
"Veda" means he knows; it should be understood that he would know. This has been explained. || 7 ||

Food has been mentioned. One should not reject food being given, nor should one cast away what is already in the vessel; this observance characterized by the non-rejection of food is the "wearing of the vow" (*vrata-dhāraṇa*). Although it must now be stated that [the remaining elements are] mind (*manas*) and consciousness (*vijñāna*), nevertheless, because those two as well are effects of the primary elements (*bhūta-kārya*), they are subsumed under the term "vital breath" (*prāṇa*), which refers to the element of air (*vāyu-bhūta*).

With the word "tyāna" (food), he introduces the connection between the elements and their material derivatives: "Water, indeed, is food; light is the eater of food. Light is established in water; water is established in light. Thus, this food is established in food. He who knows this food as established in food becomes firmly established; he becomes possessed of food, an eater of food."

He becomes great; he becomes great in offspring, in cattle, and in the splendor of sacred knowledge (*brahmavarcasa*). He becomes great in fame. Water consists of the quality of fluidity and possesses four qualities. Light consists of the quality of illumination and possesses three qualities. The remainder should be explained as having the same reading as the synonyms for *prāṇa* and *śarīra*. || 8 ||

Food has been described as being manifold. One should clearly perform [the rites] by means of the methods prescribed in the scriptures, such as officiating at sacrifices and so forth; that constitutes the "much-doing" (bahukaraṇa) in this context. "Vrata" refers to the observance of vows. "The earth is food; space is the eater of food.
Space is established upon the earth; the earth is established upon space. Thus, this food is established upon food."

He who knows this food as established in speech becomes established; he becomes possessed of food and an eater of food; he becomes great in offspring, cattle, and the splendor of sacred knowledge (*brahmavarcasa*); he becomes great in fame. Earth is solid and has five qualities; space is porous by nature and has sound as its quality. The remainder of the text is to be explained through the same reading as the section on water and light. 9.

One should not reject—nor turn away from anyone, from a *caṇḍāla* down to a *brāhmaṇa* and so forth—who has arrived for the sake of lodging (*vasati*), thinking, "I shall stay in your house for tonight. This non-rejection of those who have arrived for the sake of lodging is the vow (*vrata*), that is, the observance of the vow. Thus, these forms of service constitute a sacrificial session (*satra*).

Because they yield the same fruit, it is understood that these [meditations] serve the purpose of providing options for one's desire; thus, one who desires the stated fruit should perform any one of the meditations mentioned here. Furthermore, the intended meaning is that by describing the mutual relationship of assistance between the five elements and their elemental derivatives, the culmination in universal non-duality (*sarvādvaite*) is demonstrated.

Now, the giving of food with faith is the cause for the arising of the knowledge of Brahman. Likewise, since it is impossible to perform [these duties] without food, there would be no non-rejection [of guests] even when one has a dwelling, were it not for food. Indeed, those with full bellies are never seen coming to the houses of householders uninvited for the sake of lodging; rather, they come only when afflicted by hunger. Therefore, the provision of food—
1 kha. *raṃ* pratyakṣaṃ prā | 2 kha. *ropa* | [page 140] Tenth Anuvāka 10]

The Taittirīyopaniṣaddīpikā [39] states that even a seeker of liberation (mumukṣu) dwelling in the householder stage of life (gṛhasthāśrama) must exert great effort for the sake of attaining knowledge; therefore, he says: "Therefore, ya—"

Therefore, for a householder, the accomplishment of the goals of human life (*puruṣārtha*) is not possible without food. Consequently, by whatever means—by any method or manner, meaning by any one of the [means] such as officiating at sacrifices (*yājana*) and so forth—one should obtain or acquire abundant food, such as that belonging to Brahmā and others. Although this was already stated by the phrase "one should make food abundant," it is nevertheless mentioned here because it is designated as a specific observance (*vrata*).

He speaks again in order to show that this is an independent rule for human purpose (*puruṣārtha*), rather than being a restrictive injunction (*niyamavidhi*) that is merely a subsidiary part of the fire-worship (*dupāsanāṅga*), thereby dispelling such a notion. Now, one might object: "Food should be prepared solely for one's own consumption and not for giving to another, as there is no authoritative evidence (*pramāṇa*) for the latter.
To this he says: "It has been prepared; it is ready" (*arādhi saṃsiddham*). "For him"—for the guest who has arrived at the house.

"Food is that which is to be eaten"—in this manner, the wise householders declare [this] with respect to their own wives and others. By this, the common consensus of householders is stated as the authority regarding the giving of food.

Now, regarding the food being given, it is said that the perfection of place, time, recipient, faith, and hospitality is an essential factor; for this reason, he states that "as it is given, so is the fruit. This is indeed well known. When food is given with the mouth—that is, in the primary place, at the primary time, to the primary recipient, and with a primary disposition consisting of faith, prostration, hospitality, and so forth—then [the result is as follows]. In the primary [recipient], the food...

*Madanīyam* means prepared, fully cooked, or given. If, then, at the mouth—in the primary place, at the primary time, by the primary mode, for the primary one—for this giver of food—food that is not edible (*anamadanīyam*) is prepared and becomes fully cooked. "This indeed is the *śrāddha* food in the middle; [it is offered] in the middle for him."

Food: it is prepared. Indeed, this food is prepared at the end; thus, food is prepared for him at the end. "In the middle" means in the middle region, at the middle time, and in the middle vessel, by means of a middling mode of life, as something moderate. "At the end" means in the final region, at the final time, and in the final vessel, by means of a lowly mode of life consisting of contempt and the like.

"Abundant. The rest has been explained in both previous instances. The meaning is that in whatever place, at whatever time, for a person of such caste and stage of life (*varṇāśramin*) with such conduct, and at whatever age, whatever food or other gift was given—even by the giver—it becomes for that person of such caste and stage of life with such conduct, at that same place and time, and at that same age, such food or other thing in abundance.
Now, he states that the supreme fruit which belongs to giving characterized by the aforementioned qualities belongs equally to the knowledge of that giving:
"He who knows the fruit of the gift of food—in the manner thus described—worships the highest fruit of the gift of food;
he too, primarily, obtains food. This is the sense. Therefore, food should be given from one's own mouth.

The meaning of the context is as follows: Having thus described the meditations on food, vital breath (*prāṇa*), mind, and consciousness—both in their effects and in some of their causes—he now describes the meditations on Brahman as bliss. "Security" (*kṣema*) means the protection of what has been acquired.
In this manner, one should meditate upon speech—that is, the organ of speech—as being my own form of Brahman. That meditation...
The intended meaning is that the fruit is of a secure nature (*kṣemarūpa*). Here, since no verb of action is seen, the word "one should meditate" (*upāsīta*) is to be supplied.
Furthermore, when no specific fruit is mentioned, it should be understood everywhere that the fruit corresponds to the qualities [of the meditation].
1. Kha. *gṛhasa* | 2. Kha. *so brāhmaṇāḥ* | 3. Kha. *hasthān prati pramā°* | 4. Kha. *thitam* | 5. Kha. *mukhyaṃ mukhyāyāsmā annadātre 'nna* | 6. Kha. *vāk kṣematra*. [page 141]

Yogakṣema: *yoga* is the attainment of what has not yet been attained, while *kṣema* is the preservation of what has already been attained. Bliss (*ānanda*) consisting of both these aspects is *yogakṣema*. In this manner, it is evident in the case of the *prāṇa* and *apāna* breaths. Action (*karman*), which consists of activity, is *brahman*. In this manner, it is evident in the case of the two hands. Movement (*gati*) is the activity of going.

"Brahman is in the form of the anus"—in this manner, clearly, [it refers to] the feet. "Brahman is liberation"—in this manner, [it refers to] the anus, that is, the organ of excretion. This marks the conclusion of the internal (ādhyātmika) meditations.
One should know the human—meaning pertaining to humans—perfectly known meditations (*samājñāḥ*, i.e., *upāsanāḥ*). The word "should know" is to be supplied as the ellipsis.

Now, immediately following the description of the worship of humans, [I shall describe] the divine—that is, those pertaining to the gods—the word "samājñāḥ" (names/designations) is to be supplied, as is the verb "kathayāmi" (I shall tell). "Tṛptiḥ" (satisfaction) refers to the contentment born from consuming and drinking the Brahman. In this manner, when rain—that is, when the streams of water have emerged from the interior of the clouds as hailstones—[there arises] strength, even for those who have become one with Brahman.

In this manner, *satva* is the cause of overcoming. In this manner, within lightning—that is, in its momentary radiance—Brahman is in the form of glory and fame (*yaśas*). In this manner, among cattle and other animals, Brahman is in the form of light (*jyotis*), that is, illumination. In this manner, among the stars—that is, the constellations (*nakṣatra*)—Brahman is procreation (*prajāti*), having the nature of generation.

"Amṛta" refers to sexual intercourse in the form of seeing, embracing, and so forth with the beloved of Brahman; "kṣudra" (trivial) refers to the pleasure arising from the cessation of the act of sexual intercourse; and "ānanda" (bliss) is the pleasure resulting from the fruit of having a son—in this manner. Regarding "upastha," it refers to the generative organ.
In this manner, "brahma" is the entirety of everything, including the elements beginning with space, as well as speech and body. In this manner [it is taught].

In the ether—whether in the elemental ether (*bhūtākāśa*) or the undifferentiated (*avyākṛta*)—that is Brahman. It is the "foundation" (*pratiṣṭhā*), meaning that in it the entire collection of effects and causes is established; thus, it means the support of all. In this manner, one should meditate—that is, one should perform meditation. Regarding that, he states the result: "One becomes possessed of a foundation," meaning one becomes possessed of a support. This is clear. "One should meditate upon it as 'the Great' (*tanmahaḥ*)."
"Sīta" means "he becomes great. *Mahān* refers to the splendor (*tejas*) whose form is the Great Utterance (*mahāvyāhṛti*), or it means "greater than all.
The rest has been explained. "One should meditate upon that as Mind (*manas*). "He becomes possessed of honor (*mānavān*). The mind consists of resolve (*saṃkalpa*) and conceptualization (*vikalpa*).
*Māna* means self-conceit (*abhimāna*) or reflection (*manana*); he is "possessed of that. In the sense of self-conceit, the meaning is "one whose self-conceit is unbroken."

The rest has been explained. One should meditate upon that as "Namas" (Salutation). "Namas" possesses the quality of bowing; the rest has been explained. Regarding this, he states the fruit: they are bowed to, that is, they become submissive or attain [their desires]. To this one who meditates upon the Brahman as "Namas"—to the meditator—[come] "desires," meaning objects of longing such as sons and so forth. One should meditate upon that as Brahman. He becomes possessed of Brahman. Brahman...

Or, *parivṛḍha* means having the form of the Vedas; one who possesses that is "possessed of Brahman" (*brahmavān*). In the sense of being sovereign (*parivṛḍha*), the meaning is that he himself becomes sovereign.

The rest has been explained. That is Brahman. Of Brahman—the unattached and indifferent—there is the "complete dying away" (*parimara*). The lightning, rain, the moon, the sun, fire, the rays, and the wind are the "complete dying away"; the space (*ākāśa*) which generates them is also the "complete dying away."

*Parimara*. Alternatively, *parimara* is time (*kāla*), which is the destroyer of all; and because it is connected with Brahman, it is space (*ākāśa*). Or rather, it is time itself as characterized by the quality of *parimara*. "In the act of withdrawing everything"—in this manner, one should worship, that is, perform meditation. "Around him," meaning on all sides of the worshipper, those who hate him perish—that is, they are destroyed.
1. "That in which there is no fire" (atyagniḥ).
[Page 142] The tenth Anuvāka. 10.
The Taittirīyopaniṣaddīpikā:
Those who harbor hatred—whether they be internal enemies such as desire and the like, external adversaries, or those born of one's own mother’s co-wife. Of oneself...

Whether they be dear ones who, due to wickedness or ignorance, act as enemies; or those who are well-known as unpleasant, burning the ears, eyes, and mind; or one's own kinsmen (*bhrātṛvya*), adversaries, and haters—even those thinking, "This person is our enemy," or "We must do what is harmful to him"—whether they be worshippers (*upāsaka*) or the object of worship, these [enemies] are in me.
The meaning is that by forming the resolve "debt" (*riṇa*)—that is, thinking "all these [beings] shall perish"—even toward those who have done no harm, they all meet their destruction.

Having thus described the meditations upon Brahman as bliss (*ānanda*), the text now, finding an eligible seeker whose mind is steady, speaks of the Self consisting of bliss (*ānandātman*) as previously explained, free from distinctions such as the divine (*adhidaiva*) and so forth: "He who is this in the person (*puruṣa*), and he who is that in the sun... (*sa yaścāyaṃ puruṣe | yaścāsāvādi-*).

They [are the five sheaths]. He is one. He who knows thus, having departed from this world, having approached this self consisting of food (*annamaya*), having approached this self consisting of vital breath (*prāṇamaya*), having approached this self consisting of mind (*manomaya*), having approached this self consisting of consciousness (*vijñānamaya*), having approached this self consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*)—this has been explained.

In the previous verse, however, there is this distinction: because liberation after death (*videhakaivalya*) was previously mentioned, the suffix *lyap* was applied to the five sheaths (*pañcakośa*). Now, however, because liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*) is being described, the suffix *laṭ* is applied to those very same [sheaths].

These worlds, beginning with the earth (*bhūr*), which are the fruits of karma; being one whose food is at will (*kāmānnī*)—meaning he possesses food to eat according to his desire—and one who takes form at will (*kāmarūpī*)—meaning he possesses a form according to his desire—he wanders along. Following after the direct realization of the Self (*ātmasākṣātkāra*), he moves correctly through and roams these worlds with a human body.
Nor by one who lacks authority. This which is about to be described is for the sake of favoring the world. *Sāma* is speech that establishes equanimity.

Having observed living beings pierced by the thorns of *saṃsāra*, his mind being deeply overcome with compassion, he sings—uttering exceedingly high-pitched sounds—and remains, staying while having taken up a body according to the analogy of a burnt cloth. Therefore:

"Come together, O people! Do not fall upon the thorns of saṃsāra"—such is the intention of the compassionate Mother, as expressed in the Śruti. "Hā 3 vuhā 3 vu-hā 3 vu!"—with these three utterances, she awakens those residing in the three worlds. "Aho! Aho! Aho!"—the protracted vowel (*pluti*) in all three words signifies wonder. "I am the Self of Bliss, unattached and indifferent..."

[This occurs] through beginningless, indefinable ignorance (*avidyā*). "Food" (*anna*) means that which is to be eaten, that which is to be enjoyed; this is addressed to those residing in the world of earth (*bhūrloka*). "I am food"—this has already been explained. The two statements [regarding] "I am food" and "I am the eater of food" (*annāda*) are addressed to those residing in the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*) and the heavenly world (*svarloka*).
"I" has already been explained. "Eater of food" (*annāda*): one who eats food is an eater of food, the enjoyer. This is addressed to those residing in the world of earth: "I am the eater of food."
This has been explained. [The phrase] "to those situated in these two worlds, the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*) and heaven" refers to the inhabitants of the two upper worlds.
Now, he speaks as before to those situated in the three worlds, declaring that the quality of being the author of fame (*kīrti*) also belongs to himself alone:
"I am the maker of *śloka*, I am the maker of *śloka*, I am the maker of *śloka*. *Śloka* means fame; one who makes that is a *śloka-kṛt*.

The word *kṛt* [is used]; the rest has been explained. Having previously declared his own status as the creator of the verse concerning the eater and the food (*annānnāda*) through three statements and an invocation, he now declares his nature as both cause and effect with respect to the three worlds by way of division: "I am the Self of Bliss; I exist as the first-born (*prathamaja*), meaning Hiraṇyagarbha. Of the Truth (*ṛta*)... [the rest of the passage].

The meaning is that he is the first creator of that reality which consists of both the manifest (mūrta) and the unmanifest (amūrta). Regarding the word "ṛtā," the prolation (*pluti*) is used for the sake of expressing wonder.
Just as a certain cloth, even when burnt, does not abandon its own form for some period of time, so too [is the nature of knowledge].

The meaning is that one whose karma has been burnt away by the destruction of latent impressions (vāsanā) remains singing, overcome with compassion, even while maintaining a body that has already perished. 2 ka.ga. *napravaṇaḥ* | a | 3 ka. *maja i* | [page 143]
Composed by Śaṅkarānanda.

Now, [an objection is raised]: "Are not the gods well-known as existing prior to *saṃsāra*? To this he says: "Pūrva" means first. From the gods—meaning from Agni and the others who constitute the limbs of Virāj—from the immortal (*amṛta*), that is, from the Veda which has the nature of being deathless (*amaraṇadharmin*). "Nābhāyi" means from the navel; the meaning is "from the secret core (*rahasya*) of the Veda. Here too, the protracted vowel (*pluti*) in the syllable "nā" is for the purpose of expressing wonder: [he is] one devoid of cause and effect.

He who is the giver of food—or of the Self—according to such statements as "I am the witness, indifferent, the womb of the Vedas," or "That thou art," and so forth, to those afflicted by hunger or tormented by the heat of saṃsāra; he who gives or bestows upon me that food which is of the nature of bliss—that giver has been described. Thus.

Thus performing the gift; in this way, by means of this gift. *Ā* is used three times; *vāḥ* means "protection" (*avatīti*). The letter *a* has the sense of wonder (*āścarya*). [The meaning is: "Even though I am entirely non-different [from the object], he protects me.
Now, one might ask: "If nothing is being given, how can you be said to have given? To this he says: *aham* (I) and *anam* (the food) have already been explained.

[Objection: "Surely, by the giving of food, there may be merit for oneself born from protecting you; however, let the donor who has no desire for that [merit] not give you, the food, or himself to another. Let him eat the food himself as he pleases—what harm is there to him? To this, he says: "Without giving me, the food that is to be eaten, or the Self in the form of that [food], to one who is not eating..."

"Devouring. [The root] *ad* means "I devour," as in "the devourer of food. The elision of the vowel *a* is for the sake of expressing wonder (*āścarya*). [It implies: "I devour even all beings in this manner.
Now, one might object: "Just as you devour this, so too will another devour you, just as a frog devours a small creature. [The text continues: "That..."
Because the world is pervaded by various powers, elements, and beings—such as serpents, crocodiles, and so forth—the attainment of these is not the goal of human endeavor (puruṣārtha).

Therefore, he says: "I am the Self of Bliss. The "universe" (viśvam) refers to the entire world; for beings arise within it, it is called "bhuvanam," which is simply "bhavanam" (the place of arising). This consists of ignorance, its effects, and the collection of their latent impressions (saṃskāras), existing in the form of cause and effect.

The meaning is as follows: "I have overcome" means I have surpassed; by means of my own nature of bliss, which is devoid of the limitations of space, time, and substance, and which is the object of the final mental modification (*caramavṛtti-sākṣātkāra*), I completely subdue all this through that causal form of the Self.
Therefore, there is no devourer of mine, but rather I alone am the devourer of all. Consequently, the attainment of Me is not a non-purpose (*apuruṣārtha*).
This is the meaning.

Now, one might ask: "If there is no difference from all others, what is his excellence? To this he says: "Suvarṇaḥ" means golden, having a color identical to that of the sun; "suvarṇajyotiḥ" means light, that is, radiance—I am the self-luminous nature of bliss.

The meaning is that there is a preeminence in me. Now the Śruti says: "He who," meaning the qualified seeker, "knows" (veda)—that is, realizes through direct perception—the Self which is bliss in the manner described above. The intention is that he too attains the fruit mentioned in the passage beginning with "he obtains these worlds. "Thus the Upaniṣad": this has been explained in the previous Vallī.

Thus ends the third chapter, named the Bhṛgu-vallī, in the Taittirīyopaniṣad-dīpikā, the work of the venerable Śaṅkarānanda Bhagavat, disciple of the venerable Paramahaṃsa Parivrājaka Ācārya Ānandātman, whose feet are worthy of worship. 3.
And this *Taittirīyopaniṣaddīpikā* is completed. 1. Kha. *ātmasvarū* | 2. Kha. *stvayyati* | 3. Kha. *ha suvarṇasta* | 4. Kha. *vyasyati*. [Page 144]

Having explained this Purva and Uttara Mīmāṃsā very concisely,
the compassionate Sāyaṇācārya is now prepared to declare the meaning of the Vedas.
The section on ritual action (karmakāṇḍa), ending with the Pitṛmedha, has been clearly explained through logical principles;
now, for the sake of realizing Brahman, I shall expound the Upaniṣads through reasoned arguments.
For here, the word "Upaniṣad" has as its sole domain the knowledge of Brahman, because the meaning of the constituent parts of that word is possible only in relation to knowledge. (6)
The prefix *upa* denotes proximity; that [proximity] culminates in the "facing toward" (the Self).
This is because proximity, as a gradation, finds its ultimate rest in the perception of one's own Self.
The meaning of the six categories will be found to be threefold within the Vidyā;
this has been clearly stated by the venerable Sureśvarācārya.
Having led this self toward Brahman, which is by its very nature free from duality, it destroys ignorance along with its products; therefore, it is called *upaniṣad*.

Having destroyed one's own ignorance, which is the root of all misfortune, it leads [the self] through its inwardness to the Supreme, which is free from all distinctions; therefore, it is called *upaniṣad*.
Since knowledge brings about the destruction of all causes of worldly involvement by cutting off their very root, it is therefore considered the Upaniṣad. || 11 ||
Because it is the cause of the aforementioned knowledge, the text also receives the name "Upaniṣad" due to its non-difference from that [knowledge], just as a plough is called "life. (12)

In this regard, the fourfold [set] is proclaimed for the purpose of removing such inquiries as: "What is the subject matter? What is the fruit? What is the connection? Who is the qualified person? (13).
In the Chapter on Training (*Śikṣādhyāya*),

it is stated that "an object of study is that which cannot be obtained elsewhere" is indeed the definition of an object (*viṣaya*). Since [the subjects of] the specialized application of medicinal herbs,
the determination of sounds, and so forth, are obtainable through Āyurveda, Jyotiḥśāstra, Vyākaraṇa, and the like, they fall within the scope of those respective sciences.

It has been stated. Here too, non-duality (*advaita*) is that which cannot be obtained through any other means. Indeed, the reality of the Self (*ātmatattva*), which is non-duality, is not obtained by any means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) other than the Vedāntas. Furthermore, it is recited in another portion [of the Veda]: "One who does not know the Veda does not comprehend that Great One. Just as by this scriptural passage (*śruti*) a means of knowledge other than the Veda is negated, so too in another scriptural passage—
It is not being denied that there is a portion of the Veda other than the Upaniṣads. Thus the Vājasaneyins declare:

"I ask you about that person who is known through the Upaniṣads" (*taṃ tv aupaniṣadaṃ puruṣaṃ pṛcchāmi*). One who is understood in the Upaniṣads alone is "known through the Upaniṣads. However, he who thinks that [the Self] is accessible through another means of knowledge should be asked: "Is it by perception, or by inference, or else—?"

Regarding the phrase "by means of perception" (*pratyakṣa*): even in the first case, is it by external perception or by mental perception? In that regard, the Talavakāras record the negation of external perception: "The eye does not go there. The Taittirīyas, Kaṭhas, and Śvetāśvataras record the reasoning for this: "Its form does not stand within the range of sight; it is not [seen] by the eye."

"Someone sees him"—in this regard, for the sake of seeing (*saṃdṛśe*) correctly, the form of this Supreme Self, characterized by blue, yellow, short, and so forth, does not exist; it is not present. Therefore, no creature whatsoever existing in the world, from Brahmā down to a blade of grass, perceives this Supreme Self with the eye. That the eye has color-form as its sole object is common knowledge to all people. [This is the view of] the outsiders (*tairthika*).
For there is no contradiction here between the learned and the common folk.

Just as there is no visibility for that which lacks form, so too there is no objectivity for the ears and other senses for that which lacks sound and the rest; thus it is taught in the Kaṭha Upaniṣad: "That which is without sound, without touch, without form, undecaying, likewise without taste, eternal, and without smell. Therefore, it is not an external perception.
This is the self. It must be stated what kind of mental perception (*mānasapratyakṣa*) this is:
is it of the form "My self is Bhadrasena," or of the form "I am a human, a Brahmin, a student of sacred knowledge (*brahmacārī*)," or else [is it] "This body is mine;
I am the master of the body, the knower by means of the sense organs such as the eyes, and the agent of actions such as speaking by means of the sense organs such as speech"?

Is it of the nature: "I am the agent by means of the mind, the enjoyer of pleasure and pain, and the one who goes to heaven or hell through merit and demerit"? Or is it of the nature: "I am Brahman alone, which is Truth, Knowledge, and Infinite, non-dual"? It cannot be the first, because that refers to a secondary self (*gauṇātmā*) and lacks the scope of the primary reality of the Self (*mukhyātmatattva*). For the Self is indeed threefold: the secondary self...

There is the false self (*mithyātman*) and the primary self (*mukhyātman*); it is just as there are three kinds of lions. For example: seeing the difference between the lion and Devadatta, yet perceiving the presence of qualities such as cruelty and valor belonging to the lion in Devadatta, one designates him as "this is a lion"—this is a figurative lion (*gauṇasiṃha*). Having seen a deer running in the thick darkness of a forest... [the text continues].

Having ascertained "this is a lion," one fears; this is a false lion (*mithyāsiṃha*). Having seen the king of beasts situated in the midst of broad daylight during the day, one recognizes him as "this is a lion"; this is the primary lion (*mukhya siṃha*). Thus... [kha. ga. ...ti vi; ka. kha. blue, yellow, short, long, etc.; ka ṅa. ...cāryevaṃ].
