Here, King Bhadrasena, perceiving his own distinction [from others] and observing his own qualities—such as the protection of wealth and so forth—in him, applies the notion "my self is Bhadrasena"; therefore, this is the secondary (gauṇa) self. Nor is it the second...

Third: [the notion] "I am a human being" and so forth, because such cognitions have the body as their object and thus have a false self as their domain. The great genus called "humanity" consists in the identity with the form of bipedality and so on. The intermediate genus called "Brahminhood" is to be understood as that which arises from specific parents. The stage of the student (*brahmacārin*) is to be known through sacramental rites (*saṃskāra*) such as the initiation (*upanayana*).

These, such as "you" and "I," are attributes of the gross body. Furthermore, that the gross body is not the Self is undisputed among all non-Cārvāka outsiders (tairthika). Therefore, because there is no perception of the existing distinction between the Self and the body, the cognition "I am a human being" has a false self as its object. And this [cognition] regarding the body as the false self—
This will be elaborated upon in the introduction to the *prāṇamaya-kośa*. Nor is the third [alternative] tenable, because that too has the subtle body (*liṅgadeha*) as its object.
For instance, the relationship of owner and owned is perceived in the form "this body is mine.
In that context, the body is the "owned" (*sva*) and the self is the "owner" (*svāmī*); the connection between the two is caused by karma. And karma is characterized by merit and demerit.
Because names are manifold, it assumes various high and low bodies in succession according to them. With this very intention, the Blessed One said:

"Just as a person, casting off worn-out garments, takes up others that are new, so the embodied self, casting off worn-out bodies, enters into other new ones. And the cause of that assumption of bodies is *karma*.

The Śvetāśvataras declare its nature as the efficient cause (*nimittatva*): "He who is associated with the qualities (*guṇa*), who is the agent of actions for the sake of their fruit—he alone is the enjoyer of that which has been done. He, whose form is the universe, consisting of the three qualities, the lord of vital breaths, wanders about according to his own deeds.
That individual self (*jīvātman*) who is associated with the qualities of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas* is "associated with the qualities" (*guṇānvaya*). [The word] *phala*...

Its nature consists of pleasure and pain, and its causes are actions in the form of merit and demerit; he is the agent of these two. Furthermore, he is the experiencer only of the action he himself has performed, and not of any other. Because the actions performed are manifold, he assumes many bodies in accordance with them, and thus he is "multiform" (*viśvarūpa*). Due to the influence of the three qualities (*guṇas*), he goes along the three paths; [the first is] *sattva*...

When the quality of *sattva* predominates, one practices the eight-limbed yoga (*aṣṭāṅgayoga*) beginning with restraints (*yama*) and observances (*niyama*), worships the Brahman with attributes (*saguṇabrahma*), and reaches the world of Brahmā (*brahmaloka*) by the northern path (*uttaramārga*) starting with light (*arcis*). When the quality of *rajas* predominates, one performs optional rites (*kāmyakarman*) such as the Jyotiṣṭoma and reaches the lunar world known as heaven (*svarga*) by the southern path (*dakṣiṇamārga*) starting with smoke (*dhūma*). [When] the quality of *tamas*...
When there is an abundance of merit, yet having committed major or minor sins, one reaches the world of hell by way of the third path.

In this manner, the individual self (*jīvātman*), the lord of the vital breaths, wanders through the three paths according to its own actions. Furthermore, the true nature (*svarūpa*) of that living being is declared in that very same [scripture]: "He is the size of a thumb, his form like the sun, consisting of volition and ego..."

"He who is endowed with taste; by means of the quality of the intellect and the quality of the self, he is seen to be as small as the tip of an awl, though he is indeed inferior. Because it is situated in the middle of the heart-lotus, which is the size of a thumb, the individual soul (jīva) is also said to be thumb-sized. Its residence in the heart is to be understood from another scriptural passage: "For this Self is in the heart. And humans, including even unlearned women—
Sometimes, indicating themselves as "I am this very person" by gesturing with their hand toward the region of the heart, they reveal [themselves] as being without a protector.

In the *Śikṣādhyāya*, they touch [the body] but not the head, back, feet, or other parts; therefore, because the individual soul (*jīva*) moves through various bodies such as those of elephants and mosquitoes,
even though it possesses contraction and expansion, its size is figuratively described as being the measure of a thumb, based on the size of the heart.

It is said: And that [Self] is like the sun. Just as the sun does not require any external light, such as a lamp, in addition to its own orb for the purpose of illuminating that orb, so too the individual soul (jīva), by virtue of its consciousness, does not require any other means for the realization of its own self. Now, one might object: even if there is no dependence on the eyes and other sense organs, there is still dependence upon the mind. "I am this... [and so forth].

This is because linguistic usage, such as the words "happy" or "suffering," is preceded by mental reflection (*dhyāna*). For the scripture states, "Whatever one reflects upon with the mind, that one speaks with speech"; and since the authors of the treatises have proclaimed that the employment of words is preceded by the speaker's intention.
Let it be granted, then, that linguistic usage is preceded by reflection; yet that reflection must concern an object already previously perceived.

The mind proceeds solely for the purpose of employing a suitable word; for it is impossible to determine beforehand that such a word is suitable when the object has not yet been perceived. This being the case, the mind, having engaged with insentient objects such as a jar, first brings the object to light, and subsequently contemplates the appropriate word. Thereafter, the person speaks. [This occurs] within the conscious self.
Since [the Self] shines forth by itself alone, meditation is required only for the restriction of specific words, not for its manifestation.

Otherwise, in moments devoid of the activity of meditation—such as deep sleep, fainting, and death—the distinction from those states caused by the experience of one's own Self would not exist; yet people perceive a very great distinction. Therefore, in worldly transaction, the individual soul...
Because it is self-luminous, its nature is like that of the sun. Intending this very point, the Vājasaneyins recite:
"O friend, by what means could one know the knower? And that *jīva* (individual soul) functions as endowed with volition (*saṃkalpa*) and egoism (*ahaṃkāra*).
Even though [objects] such as houses and fields are not ultimately real due to defects such as being accomplished through effort and being perishable, [it functions] for the time being...
Upon seeing the appearance of objects such as a house, the conceptualization that "this house and so forth is excellent" is *saṃkalpa* (volition).

And the conceit that "I am the owner of this house and so forth" is *ahaṃkāra* (egoism). The modification (*vṛtti*) of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) in the form of "this" is directed outward, while the modification in the form of "I" is directed inward; thus, there are only two modifications. Nevertheless, the object of the modification "this" is manifold.

Furthermore, due to the repeated recurrence of the activity of the "I-maker" (*ahaṃvṛtti*) at different times, worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*) proceeds uninterruptedly. And that agent of transaction is said to consist of both consciousness (*cit*) and the non-conscious (*acit*). As it is said: "By the quality of the intellect (*buddhi*) and by the quality of the self (*ātman*), [the self] is the size of the tip of an awl. The quality of the intellect consists of the forms of dissolution (*laya*) and emergence (*udaya*); the "I-maker" dissolves during sleep and emerges again upon awakening.

Furthermore, self-luminosity is a quality (*guṇa*) of the Self, and this has been described by means of the analogy of the sun. It is endowed with these two qualities. It is "the size of the tip of an awl" (*ārāgramātra*): just as an awl (*ārā*) is a fine iron needle placed at the tip of a staff for goading oxen during the time of plowing, and its tip is extremely minute, so too is this [Self] exceedingly subtle; otherwise, it would not pass through the openings of the channels (*nāḍī*).

Because its movement is obstructed and impossible [to perceive otherwise], this individual self (*jīvātman*) is "inferior" (*avara*), that is, lower than the Supreme Self (*paramātman*). It too is "seen" by living beings through the eye, just as form is perceived; it is experienced through the notion of "I" (*ahaṃpratyaya*). Even though it is self-luminous, it is said to be "experienced" by means of rendering it suitable for verbal expression. This, then, is the mental perceptibility (*mānasapratyakṣatva*) of the individual self. Ya—

Even though the author of the treatise has indeed made a distinction such as "insentient" or "possessing both natures," nevertheless, the essential nature of the individual soul (*jīva*) alone is what is accepted by all.

Even the notion "I" is indeed experienced. Furthermore, the gender (jāti) of that living being (jīva), such as femininity and so forth, is not inherent; rather, it is—

This [distinction] is caused by the limiting adjunct (upādhi) of the gross body. This too is declared in that very same [text]: "He is neither female, nor male, nor is he neuter; whatever body he assumes, with that he is joined. The meaning is that he is designated by the name of each respective [body]. Furthermore, the true nature of this agent-self (kartṛ-ātman) is clearly declared even in the Maitrāyaṇī [Upaniṣad].

Indeed, there exists another, inferior one called the *bhūtātman* (the elemental self), which—overpowered by the fruits of white and black actions—attains good and evil wombs, or wanders about, overcome by pairs of opposites, toward either a downward or upward course. This is distinct from that Supreme Self who was previously described in the passage beginning with "He is indeed pure, purified," and so forth. It is inferior to Him.

That which is inferior is called the *bhūtātman* (the elemental self). The five subtle elements undergo transformation into the form of the *liṅgadeha* (subtle body), just as iron is transformed when placed in fire. The conscious self (*cidātman*) enters into this *liṅgadeha*; therefore, this *liṅgadeha* is called the *bhūtātman*. And it is completely enveloped by the fruits of meritorious and sinful actions in the form of pleasure and pain, both white and black.

Pride leads one to attain a noble birth, such as that of a Brāhmaṇa, or a low birth, such as that of a Śūdra; likewise, it leads to a downward course, the lowest state of existence in hell, or an upward course, the highest state in the form of heaven. Being tormented by the pairs of opposites—such as cold and heat, honor and dishonor—and being born again and again while dying, he wanders through transmigratory existence.

[Objection: Mati [says]: Since that *bhūtātman* (the elemental self) has the subtle body (*liṅgadeha*) as its primary constituent, and since—just like the gross body—it is a false self, the attainment of the primary Self does not occur even through this mental perception [of the form] "I am the agent and the enjoyer. The falsity of the agent-self, which consists of consciousness (*vijñānamaya*), will be elaborated upon in the introduction to the sheath consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya-kośa*). [Objection: But [one says], "My Self..."

If it is argued that the primary attainment of the Self should not occur through the notions "I am Bhadrasena," or "I am a human being," or "I am the agent and enjoyer," but rather that the primary attainment of the Self occurs through the mental perception "I am Brahman"—let this be the fourth position—then it must be asked in response: what is intended here by the word "Brahman"? Is it the qualified (saguṇa) Brahman, or the unqualified (nirguṇa) Brahman?

Regarding the statement "Brahman": even if it possesses attributes (*saguṇa*), is the initial cognition "this is Brahman" a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) regarding Brahman, or is it produced by the practice of meditation? In the first case, since that [cognition] is produced by scripture (*śāstra*), it is not included within perception (*pratyakṣa*). If something were considered perception merely by virtue of being a mental cognition (*mānasa-pratyaya*), then it would follow that dharma and so forth would also be perceptible. In the second case, [there is the example of] the direct perception of a deceased son...
Because it is produced by mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*), it possesses no validity (*prāmāṇya*). For this very reason, the authors of the *Vārttika* say:

"Whatever fruit might arise from mental cultivation, and whatever fruit might arise from ritual action—that should not be considered [valid], just like [the pleasure] resulting from union with a courtesan. However, as for the direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) of the attributeless Brahman, that is a mental perception (*mānasapratyakṣa*).

Even though it is a form of knowledge (*kṣatva*), because it is preceded by the sacred scriptures (*śāstra*), its inclusion is strictly within *āgama* (scriptural authority). Therefore, the attainment of Brahman as the Self is not through perception (*pratyakṣa*), nor is its attainment possible through inference (*anumāna*), due to the absence of both a logical reason (*hetu*) and an illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*). For this very reason, it is stated in the *Amṛtabindu Upaniṣad*: "It is free from conceptual construction (*nirvikalpa*), infinite, and devoid of reason and example. This is because it is devoid of attributes (*nirdharmaka*).

In that regard, a logical reason (*hetu*) is possible; however, because [the subject] is non-dual (*advitīya*), there can be no illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*). But surely the author of the *Bhāṣya* accepted inference (*anumāna*) in the *Janmādi-sūtra*, given the existence of Vedāntic statements declaring the world's origin and so forth as having a cause?
[Note: Variants exist for the readings *virūpa*, *nyoro*, and *nyo'para* or *nyo'paro'va*.]
Composed by Vidyāraṇya.

In the *Śikṣādhyāya*, even inference (*anumāna*)—provided it does not contradict the Vedānta texts—is not precluded as a means of valid knowledge for the sake of strengthening the grasp of that meaning;
for this very reason, reasoning (*tarka*) is accepted, as the scripture states: "It is to be heard and it is to be reflected upon" (*śrotavyo mantavyaḥ*). This is not a fault.

The intention of the Bhāṣya is that while the Vedānta passages alone are the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) regarding Brahman, inference may also be employed for the sake of stabilizing the human intellect. In that regard, inference proceeds by depending upon superimposed reasons (*hetu*) and examples (*dṛṣṭānta*). If it is argued, "Let the establishment of Brahman (*brahmasiddhi*) also be accomplished by that [inference] alone," we say no; because its specific nature (*viśeṣa*) cannot be established. [For instance, one might argue: "The earth and so forth have an agent (*sakartṛka*), because they are effects (*kāryatva*)."...

Even if the existence of a mere Lord (Īśvara) were established by the inference "like the desired [sacrificial result]," the specific characteristics of being real, consciousness, infinite, and non-dual would not be established. Therefore, Brahman cannot be attained through inference either. Furthermore, even regarding scripture (Āgama), since the ritual section (Karmakāṇḍa) culminates solely in the cognition of the relationship between means and ends, there is not even the slightest suspicion of attaining Brahman therein. Now, as for the attainment of Brahman—

The authors of the *Vedāntakārikās* have stated thus: "When the nature of Brahman is established as that which is cognizable through all means of knowledge (*pratyaya*), the dissolution of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) is demonstrated by means of the Word (*śabda*). And this is logical; for Brahman is of the nature of Being, Consciousness, and Bliss (*saccidānanda*). Since existence (*sattva*), measurability (*māna*), and bliss (*ānanda*) are clearly evident in all things being cognized by the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*), Brahman is [the substrate] of all cognition.

It is so. Brahman is indeed known through all cognitive means along with its phenomenal expansion (*saprapañca*). The eyes and other senses do not perceive the pure reality by abandoning objects such as form, taste, and smell; otherwise, all people would be liberated without depending on teachers or scriptures. However, the human goal (*puruṣārtha*) arises only from the knowledge of Brahman as devoid of phenomenal expansion (*niṣprapañca*); yet, [the former] serves as a gateway to that realization.

In various places within the scriptures, Brahman is presented with full elaboration (*saprapañcam*). Furthermore, the knowledge of that Brahman—which is devoid of elaboration (*niṣprapañca*) and constitutes the supreme human goal—is produced by the scripture alone. This too has been stated by them: "It is not an object for other means of knowledge because its nature is one in which all elaborations have dissolved; thus it is held to have the Veda alone as its basis. Therefore, the reality of the non-dual Self, which is Brahman—

When the *śayyas* (the latent impressions) are severed, because there is an absence of any cause to obstruct the fruit of knowledge, all previously performed actions consisting of merit and demerit— which are the causes for future births— are also exhausted. Just as for a householder the three debts related to the gods, sages, and ancestors, and worldly disputes concerning houses, fields, and so forth, cease upon entering the state of renunciation (*pārivrājya*).
They cease in that same way. And this is logical: for actions reside in the agent-self (*kartṛātman*).

As long as that agent-self remains unified with the conscious self (*cidātman*), let the actions touch the conscious self; but once the connection with the agent-self has been removed through discrimination (*viveka*), how indeed could they touch the conscious self? And this was stated by the Blessed One:

It has been clearly stated: "The locus, as well as the agent, the various instruments, the diverse and distinct activities, and destiny as the fifth—these five are the causes of whatever action a person undertakes through body, speech, and mind, whether it be righteous or its opposite. This being so, he who perceives the Self alone as the agent..."

Because his intellect has been corrupted, that person of evil mind does not perceive [the truth]. The substratum is the gross body (*sthūla-deha*). Likewise, the agent is the subtle body (*liṅga-deha*), which is endowed with the reflection of consciousness. The instruments are the eyes and other organs, which constitute the limbs of the subtle body. Activity consists of various movements, such as seeing, hearing, going, and so forth, which are the effects of the vital breaths (*prāṇa-vāyu*). The impeller of the senses is the deity, such as the Sun and others.
The divine is that which has such a form. The five causes—beginning with the body—are the substrata for merit and demerit, which are accomplished through the body and so forth;

the conscious self (cidātman), however, is not. This being so, by those who are weary [of the world] without knowing the true nature of the self, agency is superimposed upon it. He whose state is free from egoism, whose intellect is not tainted—even having slain these worlds, he does not kill.

He is not bound. It is only with reference to the subtle body (*liṅgadeha*) alone that the knower of reality employs the conventional expression "I am the doer."

Thus, no stain exists upon the intellect (*buddhi*). When the suspicion of rebirth caused by actions performed through the subtle body (*liṅgadeha*) is removed, doubt and error cease to exist; therefore, his intellect is not stained. Or else: "Even though my task is accomplished, I shall continue to act according to the path prescribed by the scriptures out of a desire to favor the world; what loss is there for me? For this yogin who has accomplished his purpose, bliss alone constantly manifests in the mind. And it is declared thus: "He is indeed essence (*rasa*); for this [world] is nothing but essence."

"Having attained [It], he becomes blissful. That Supreme Self is indeed *rasa*, whose very nature is supreme bliss.
Having attained—that is, having directly realized—that Supreme Self, who is *rasa* by nature, this yogi becomes blissful within his own mind;
he becomes endowed with the joy born of knowledge (*vidyā*). Regarding the statement "he leaves behind joy and sorrow," the object [of that realization] is as follows:

Joy born of worldly enjoyment is forbidden, but not that which is born of knowledge (*vidyā*). And the Śruti made clear that joy born of knowledge by means of an illustrative example: "Moving through these worlds, eating what he desires and assuming whatever form he desires, he sits singing this Sāman: *Hāvu hāvu hāvu! "I am the eater of food; I am the eater of food. I am the maker of fame; I am the maker of fame," and so forth. Among all living beings, from Brahmā down to those with animal forms such as cows and buffaloes, whatever food is eaten by whichever being, the knower of Brahman eats that very food through that [being's] mouth, because he regards all bodies as his own. Thus it has been said in the *Upadeśa*—

"Along with the bones: 'All living beings, from Brahmā down to the immovable [plants], are known as my city; how could defects such as desire, anger, and the like arise in me from anything else? You; likewise, there is the wandering through all the worlds. In the word *sānni*, the syllable *ho* undergoes a modification of its phonemes for the purpose of singing, resulting in the production of the word *hā3vu*. The word *aho* expresses the marvel consisting in the attainment of the state of being the Self of all, merely by realizing one's identity with Brahman, which was previously limited to a single body. The repetition three times is for the sake of emphasis. The subsequent [text] speaks only of this very state of being the Self of all.

It is illustrated by this: whatever food there is—consisting of transformations of rice, barley, wheat, and so forth—and whoever is the eater of that food—whether in the form of a Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, or another who is a consumer—as well as whoever is the composer of verses, such as a poet or playwright, all that is indeed myself alone. This is because everything has the nature of pure consciousness (*jñāna-sat-mātra*), and because modifications of name and form are merely a matter of verbal designation (*vācārambhaṇamātra*). In this...
In this matter, repeated practice is for the purpose of removing doubt. This very bliss born of knowledge is also illustrated in the *Tṛptidīpa*:

"Being satisfied by the sense of having accomplished all that was to be done, and being satisfied again because he has attained what was to be attained, he thus reflects incessantly within his own mind:
'I am blessed, I am blessed; I know my own Self directly and eternally. I am blessed...'"

I am that very Brahman-bliss; it shines clearly before me. Blessed am I, blessed am I; today I do not behold worldly suffering. Blessed am I, blessed am I; my own ignorance has fled away somewhere. Blessed am I, blessed am I; there is nothing further for me to do. Blessed am I, blessed am I; everything to be attained has been fully realized today.

Truly! Blessed am I, blessed am I; may there be no comparison for my satisfaction in this world. Blessed am I, blessed am I; blessed, blessed, again and again blessed! Oh, what merit! Oh, what merit! It has borne fruit, it has borne fruit firmly!
Oh, by the attainment of this merit, oh, we are truly fortunate! Oh, the scripture! Oh, the scripture! Oh, the Guru! Oh, the Guru!

"Aha! Knowledge, aha! Knowledge! Aha! Bliss, aha! Bliss! Thus is the succession of fruits set forth. The first fruit is the manifestation of the Self, whose nature is the Supreme Brahman, which is the Self of all. Following that, there is the unraveling of the knot of ignorance, the breaking of the knot of the heart, the cutting away of doubt, the destruction of karma, the abandonment of joy and sorrow, and the dissolution of desire.

[In the chapter on training] "Sporting in the Self alone, delighting in the Self alone as one's activity, the state of having accomplished all that was to be done, and blissfulness"— this is the supreme fruit.
"Parā" (the higher). The answer to the questions "What is the subject matter? and "What is the fruit? has already been stated.

Now, the answer to the question "What is the relationship? is being given. The relationship between the section on knowledge (*jñānakāṇḍa*) and the section on ritual action (*karmakāṇḍa*) is characterized by the relation of the end and the means (*sādhyasādhanabhāva*). Knowledge is the end to be accomplished; ritual actions, however, [serve as the means] either by way of purifying (*saṃskārakatva*) or...
Or rather, the means for the accomplishment of knowledge are through the production of [right] inclination (*adṛṣṭa*). Thus, it is recorded as being a purificatory rite (*saṃskāraka*):

"He who possesses these forty purificatory rites attains union with and residence in the same world as Brahman. These are: conception (*garbhādhāna*), the rite for a male child (*puṃsavana*), the parting of the hair (*sīmanta*), the birth ceremony (*jātakarma*), the naming ceremony (*nāmakaraṇa*), the first feeding of solid food (*annaprāśana*), the tonsure (*caula*), the initiation (*upanayana*), the four Vedic vows (*vedavrata*), and the ceremonial bath (*snāna*).

Union with a partner in dharma, the five great sacrifices (*pañca-mahāyajña*), the seven *pākayajñas*, the seven *haviryajñas*, and the seven *soma-yajñas*—by these forty rites, a person’s mind is refined and attains fitness for knowledge (*jñāna-yogyatā*). Furthermore, the Vājasaneyins record that these serve as the cause for the desire to know (*vividiṣā*): "This very [Self] one seeks to know through the recitation of the Vedas... (*Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad* 4.4.22).

"They desire to know [Brahman] through sacrifice, through charity, through austerity, and through fasting. Regarding the two positions concerning the purificatory rite (*saṃskāra*) of the desire to know (*vividiṣā*), a distinction between them is shown in the *Vārtikasāra*: "Once the desire to know has arisen, it must necessarily bring about its own fruit by completing all the required means, just as hunger and the like do. Furthermore, the purification of the mind (*cittasaṃskṛti*) destroys the evil that acts as an obstacle."

The means for awakening, however, must be accomplished with effort. When one, impelled by the scriptures concerning caste, stage of life (*varṇāśrama*), and so forth, performs whatever action while perceiving fear in its non-performance, that is called "purificatory" (*saṃskāraka*) karma. When impelled by the injunction "That very [Self]... (*tam etam...*) with a desire for awakening, that which one offers to the Inner Controller (*antaryāmin*) becomes the cause of the desire to know (*vividipā*). Through such action, [one attains] the world of the ancestors (*pitṛloka*)...

Thus, it is said that the fruit of obligatory rites (*nityakarman*) is the attainment of the world; nevertheless, through these [rites], there arises even a desire for knowledge, because of the scriptural injunctions regarding them. In obligatory rites, purity (*śuddhi*) is primary; therefore, even the experience of results (*bhoga*) does not constitute an obstacle. Out of regard for the purification of the intellect, seekers perceive worldly enjoyment as fragile. Even in the case of optional rites (*kāmyakarman*), if one desires liberation, one should dedicate the fruit to the Lord. This was proclaimed by the Blessed One.

"For the cessation of the bondage of karma: 'Whatever you do, whatever you eat, whatever you offer in sacrifice, whatever you give, and whatever austerity you practice, O son of Kuntī—perform that as an offering unto Me. Thus you shall be liberated from the bonds of action consisting of good and evil fruits. Your right is to action alone, never to its fruits' (Gītā 3.19–18). Therefore, obligatory duties are to be performed as offerings unto the Lord."

Even the optional rites (*kāmya-karma*) generate a desire for knowledge (*vedanecchā*). Although such a desire arises once the beauty of knowledge has been understood through the statements of the Śruti, nevertheless, a lack of relish (*aruci*) toward that knowledge is produced by ritual actions (*karmans*). Just as for a man who loves milk but is afflicted by a bile disease (*pitta-roga*), even though there is a desire for milk, there is no relish in his mouth. That [lack of relish]—
How much more so when, through the application of medicinal herbs, the bile is pacified? Likewise, [it arises] by virtue of being the means for the complete eradication of suffering.

For one who has heard that the knowledge of Brahman is the cause for attaining the bliss of supreme delight, even though the desire to know it exists, no inclination toward the means of knowledge—such as hearing and so forth—arises due to the obstruction of sin. Thus it is stated in the Purāṇa: "The sacrifice of knowledge does not please men possessed of great sins; on the contrary, the sacrifice of knowledge appears as something to be loathed."

Regarding the phrase "from oneself": when that great sin which obstructs knowledge has been destroyed by actions dedicated to the Supreme Lord, an inclination toward hearing [the scriptures] and so forth arises. This very inclination is what is expressed here by the term *vividiṣā* (the desire to know). Thus, through a traditional sequence, ritual actions attain the status of being means to knowledge. And that sequence is shown in the *Vārtikasāra*:

Karmas assist toward the liberation of the Self by way of [producing] clarity; they do not do so directly like the knowledge of the Self, because they are not opposed to ignorance. For the eradication of ignorance, nothing other than knowledge is required. For the arising of knowledge, however, nothing else is required except tranquility (*śama*) and the like. For the arising of tranquility and the like, nothing else is required except the purity of the intellect (*buddhi*). The intellect—

Furthermore, for purification, nothing other than the obligatory and occasional rites (*nityādi-karman*) is desired; thus, by way of tradition, action alone is employed for the sake of realization. Therefore, action is the means (*sādhana*) and the realization of Brahman as the Self is the goal (*sādhya*). Such is the connection between the sections on ritual action (*karma-kāṇḍa*) and knowledge (*vijñāna-kāṇḍa*). No evidence whatsoever is observed for a connection other than this. In this regard, the aforementioned [connection]— [End of provided text]

Unable to endure this bondage, opponents arise in many ways. Among them, some describe liberation as being independent of the knowledge of Brahman; others declare that release results from the combination of knowledge and action (*jñāna-karma-samuccaya*); and still others, while accepting that knowledge alone is the cause of liberation, [propose it] either through the analogy of a flight of stairs or by the dissolution of desire (*kāma-pravilāpana*).

Or some maintain that the ritual section (*karmakāṇḍa*) has utility through its connection with [the knowledge of Brahman]. In this regard, the view of those who assert independence from knowledge is shown in the *Vārtikasāra*: "Because that which is prohibited has been cast aside, one does not go to a downward state such as hell; and because of the constant performance [of obligatory rites], demerit shall not touch him. Since there is no future birth, may well-being be attained free from obstacles."

"The karma that initiates the body is exhausted through experience; therefore, liberation is established for the inner self even without the realization of the one Self. A refutation of this position is also stated in that very same work: "Even for those who are extremely vigilant, since subtle transgressions are observed, what person, however skillful, could completely avoid prohibited and optional acts? One desiring liberation [must avoid] both sinful and optional acts."

The injunction "one should avoid" does not exist anywhere in the Veda by which that [avoidance] could be established. This avoidance of optional rites (*kāmya*) and the like is merely a fabrication of one's own imagination. Therefore, rebirth follows from both the prohibited and the optional. If it is argued that the fruit of the obligatory (*nitya*) rite is the desired destruction of accumulated demerit (*durita*), even so, there is no destruction of the merit (*puṇya*) derived from optional rites.

Regarding the destruction [of sin]: if a minor offense (*upapātaka*) is to be destroyed by the performance of obligatory rites (*nityakarman*), how can there be the destruction of acts such as killing, which cause infinite bodies? Even through obligatory rites, heaven is attained, just as in the case of the *agnihotra* performed for a specific desire (*kāmya*). This was stated by Āpastamba by means of the illustration of the mango tree: when a mango tree is planted for the sake of fruit, shade and fragrance are obtained as well.

In due season, one may likewise ascend to heaven by following the conduct prescribed for one's caste and stage of life (*varṇāśrama*). However, since numerous prohibited acts, as well as optional (*kāmya*) and obligatory (*nitya*) rites performed in previous births and in this life, remain [unexpiated], how can there be well-being for the self therein? If you say that the destruction of karma occurs through the realization of the oneness of the Self (*aikātmya-bodha*), then liberation would indeed be free from obstacles for you, just as it is for me; it is not otherwise.

In the chapter on training (*śikṣādhyāya*), Vidyāraṇya states:
"Others consider that in liberation there is a combination of knowledge and action (*jñānakarmasamuccaya*), which is threefold according to the relationship of primary and subordinate."

Combination (samuccaya) is as follows: for some, knowledge is primary; for others, action holds primacy; and according to the view of yet others, both are established as equal in importance. Combination occurs when two things that exist in the same place at the same time are non-contradictory and share a single result;
however, such combination does not apply to knowledge and action, because they stand in a relationship of sublation and sublated, like a lion and a jackal.

There is no coexistence of these two, as they do not abide in the same locus; because their natures consist of the goal to be accomplished (*sādhya*) and the means (*sārthaka*), they cannot exist at the same time.

Furthermore, the contradiction between these two in terms of their nature as cause, essence, and effect is manifest: superimposition (*adhyāsa*) is the cause of actions, while valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is the cause of awakening. That which has the form of action is not illuminating; rather, that which has the form of consciousness (*bodha*) is the illuminator. Birth is the future effect of action.

The cessation of that [bondage] arises from awakening; therefore, the combination [of both paths] is difficult to attain. How, then, can liberation occur through that alone? Just as one ascends to the roof of a palace by following a flight of stairs, some reach the state of knowledge after a long time through the sequence of all ritual actions. Beginning with the twilight prayers (*saṃdhyā-vandana*), by means of rites performed in due order, one attains the status of a knower at the conclusion of a thousand-year sacrificial session (*sahasravarṣa-satra*). Just so...

The instruction regarding the journey to a village situated on the road to a city is understood to be subsidiary to the instruction for reaching that city. Likewise, why does the discourse on the attainment of heaven and other realms by one standing on the path to liberation not become subsidiary to the instruction for liberation?

Or rather, the mention of heaven and so forth is for the purpose of enticing [the seeker] toward liberation, just as the singing of the virtues of villages situated on the road serves to reach the city.

[Objection: This being the case, all injunctions (*vidhi*) are for the purpose of qualifying one for the knowledge of the Self (*ātmajñāna*), acting as auxiliaries through the very means that have been observed.
[Reply: Do not say so. Just as for men traveling to a village, the intermediate stages constitute a remainder (*śeṣatā*) because they are part of the path;

how could heaven (*svarga*) and the like be a remainder when they are themselves the human goal (*puruṣārtha*)? That which serves as an inducement in human speech is appropriate there, but in the Vedas, it is not so.
Because of this absence, there can be no intention [to act]. Or rather, that alone is the intended meaning (*tātparya*) where one is led after being enticed;

therefore, the intention of the injunction (*vidhi*) is directed toward heaven itself, not toward liberation. And the visible means [of the prohibition] is the prevention of engagement through passion and the like. If that is the case, let it be so for prohibitions (*niṣedha*); however, injunctions do not restrain passion.

These [sacrifices] have passion as their cause; on the contrary, they increase passion by bestowing enjoyments. Since life is short, the performance of all [these] rituals is not possible. Therefore, the analogy of the flight of stairs is a fabrication of those with dull intellects. Others, however, say that one whose mind is corrupted by desire is unable to perceive that supreme non-duality because all desires remain unfulfilled. By means of rituals...

Through various meditations on Virāj and other deities, the wise man, having enjoyed the fruits up to the state of Virāj, attains identity with that very [Brahman]. By the enjoyment of all pleasures, through the path of the dissolution of all desires, even all actions become conducive to liberation. Although the bliss of Brahman is considered present here, it is not made an object of the mind; thus, it does not provoke a longing for the perceived worldly pleasures.

[The injunctions] belonging to the *karmakāṇḍa* are sufficient even to weaken desire; however, a person whose desire has been dissolved is then qualified for the *jñānakāṇḍa*. Do not say so, for the destruction of desire does not occur through its pursuit even in hundreds of years;
rather, from indulgence in it, there is only an increase, while cessation comes from seeing its defects. Desire is never satiated by the enjoyment of desired objects.

It is not pacified; like fire fed with oblations, it increases all the more. Because of the failure to perceive qualities or the perception of defects, one’s desires may diminish; therefore, for the sake of the complete cessation of all afflictions, one should take refuge in the knowledge of the Self. One should certainly not dissolve the ritual injunctions, even if they possess defects. A lustful person should never engage in the knowledge of the Self, or else he should recoil from that knowledge which devours all human enjoyments. And so it is said in the *Rāgigītā*:

But this is the statement: "O Gautama, he would rather become a jackal in the empty Vṛndāvana than ever accept a liberation devoid of the object [of divine service]. As for what was said—that one might be liberated after enjoying rewards up to the level of Virāṭ—that may indeed apply to gradual liberation (kramamukti), but not to immediate liberation (sadyo-vimocana). The realm of Prajāpati is not the fixed gateway to liberation."

This would be so; for no distinction whatsoever of reality is observed among limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*). There is no distinction in space (*ākāśa*) despite the limiting adjuncts such as jars, troughs, and the like—even when these are differentiated by distance, proximity, or whether they are imagined or unimagined.
Therefore, the reality does not differ in Prajāpati or in a worm. This is also known from reasoning and from scripture. And that which...

"Whoever," indeed, from such [a state] awakened among the gods—whosoever he may be, he alone became that; no others, says the Śruti which wards off partiality. And another Śruti says: "The one God in all beings. Therefore, due to the diversity of limiting adjuncts (upādhi), the reality of the Self (ātmatattva) is not differentiated. One who desires immediate liberation...

Desire dissolves through the perception of defects; therefore, the purport of the *karmakāṇḍa* is not its dissolution. However, others—certain [scholars] who understand profound logic—maintain that the dissolution of some form of duality is understood in the Veda in certain places. Indeed, the dissolution of the notion of the body as the self is found in the phrase "one who desires heaven" (*svargakāma*). Here, one who possesses a body and so forth is the qualified agent (*adhikārī*) with respect to the enjoyment of heaven.

Dissolution occurs directly in the prohibitions of activities arising from passion and the like; dissolution in injunctions also occurs through the assignment of those [activities] to other tasks. Even in the world, there is either the direct warding off from an undesired path or the instruction of an alternative path; let it be understood that the same applies in the Veda as well. Thus, by way of the dissolution of activities arising from causes such as passion, the Self—

"All injunctions exist for the purpose of [leading to] the authority of knowledge; let it not be so. Is the dissolution of distinctions among injunctions due to a desire for results, or is it postulated because of the purport [of the texts], or because [knowledge] is the cause of self-realization? First, it is not the former, because not all ritual injunctions require any further result beyond that which is understood from their own respective sentences. [End of fragment]

Furthermore, the injunctions would apply only to the performance of ritual action, for without such performance, heaven, cattle, and other rewards would be impossible. If the scripture’s purport were elsewhere, the fruit [of action] would be accidental. If it were for the sake of the fruit, there could be no dissolution [of the world], nor both [dissolution and fruit], due to the fault of splitting the sentence (*vākya-bheda*). Even if the purport regarding heaven is heard in the scripture, if dissolution is postulated by implication, that is not so; for [the existence of] the body and so forth is established by direct scriptural statement.

Because [the object] is established through dissolution: for when an elephant is directly perceived, there is indeed no inference of its footprints. Likewise, statements such as "not coarse" (asthūla) directly effect the negation of the body and so forth. Furthermore, the realization of the Self does not arise anywhere from the dissolution of the body; for such realization is possible even when there is no dissolution, and it is not observed during deep sleep when dissolution occurs. This realization is logically established only when the teacher, the scriptures, and so forth have not dissolved.

If consciousness [were established] merely by dissolution, then who could prevent it during deep sleep? Even when the appearance of a snake has dissolved, this rope is not seen in the darkness; on the contrary, this illusory snake dissolves through the observation of the rope. Now, if you say that the cause of differentiation is destroyed by the destruction of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*), do not say so; for the cause is never destroyed by the destruction of its effect. What is this cause? It is ignorance (*avidyā*).

In the Chapter on Training (Śikṣādhyāya), there may be an object [of negation] through the awakening to reality; however, because ignorance is destroyed therein, the dissolution of the phenomenal world (prapañca) is fruitless. If this phenomenal world were real, it could not be dissolved by anyone. Otherwise, by what means could the reality of one's own self (svātmatattva) be dissolved?

It is warded off. Furthermore, the dissolution of the whole cannot be brought about by births; however, a fragment dissolves of its own accord and not through scripture. Moreover, that which is yet to be is not to be destroyed, and that which has already come into being ceases of its own accord.
But the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) existing in the present perishes of its own accord because it is an effect. Furthermore, by means of non-duality alone is there the abandonment of all evil.

Therefore, once the human goal is fully accomplished, the futility of knowledge would follow. Consequently, since the human goal is established through the destruction of ignorance by means of the knowledge of the true nature of the oneness of the Self, the postulation of its dissolution [upon death] is purposeless. Furthermore, it is an established principle that all injunctions (vidhis) teach that something is a means to what is desired, whereas prohibitions (niṣedhas) teach that something is a means to what is undesired. Therefore, [it is not the case that... (Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly with "tasmātkā-". The translation reflects the available portion.)
In the *Malaya*, which is the path of the steps leading to the dissolution of duality, a connection between the two sections (*kāṇḍa*)—whether by way of conjunction or collection—is not appropriate.

Therefore, by process of elimination, the relationship previously described as that between the goal (*sādhya*) and the means (*sādhana*) is to be understood here as the connection between the two sections known as Knowledge (*jñāna*) and Action (*karman*).
Thus, the answers to these three questions—"What is the subject matter? What is the fruit? And what is the connection?"—have been stated.
Now, the answer to the question "Who is qualified? is stated. Here, this is considered:
Is the qualification for the Upaniṣads for one who desires to perform [ritual action], or for one who desires to know? First, it is argued that it is for the one who desires to perform. Why?
Because the Vedāntas have as their purport [the performance of] action. The disputed Vedāntas have as their purport action because they are a portion of the Veda, like the Karmakāṇḍa.

[Objection: But surely, since the *karmakāṇḍa* (the ritual section) is also a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*), its function must be merely that of making something known (*bodhakatva*), not that of causing action (*kārakatva*). For we observe that even among many who are well-versed in the *karmakāṇḍa*, there is no engagement in rituals. [Reply: This is not a fault. Just as the force of a river’s current or a powerful wind [acts], so too, even in the absence of a direct injunction (*codanā*), the command of a king or similar authority produces the cognition "this must be done by me," thereby instigating action.

Because it is that which initiates action; for this very reason, the authors of the *Bhāṣya* stated in the first Sūtra: "For that injunction (*codanā*) which is the definition of Dharma, while enjoining a person toward its own object, brings about his understanding. Thus, the non-engagement of many people is possible due to obstacles such as lack of faith, poverty, and so forth. Therefore, [the Vedāntas] are like the *Karmakāṇḍa*...

Since even in the case of *siddhārtha* (an existent fact) there is no finality [in mere knowledge], the qualification for this [Vedānta] belongs only to one who is intent on action (*cikīrṣu*). Therefore, the qualification for the *Upaniṣads* belongs only to one who desires to practice the cessation of the mind (*cittanirodha*) or discriminative discernment (*prasaṃkhyāna*), and not to one who merely desires to know (*jijñāsu*) their own duty (*svadharma*). This being the position reached, it is here replied: why should the Vedāntas be said to have as their purport only that which is to be accomplished (*kāryaparatva*)?

Is it because there is no linguistic acquisition (*vyutpatti*) regarding an established fact (*siddhārtha*), or because even if such acquisition exists, there is no purpose for it, or else because an object of knowledge distinct from a task to be accomplished (*kārya*) is impossible? It is not the first [alternative], because just as there is linguistic acquisition regarding tasks in the common usage of elders in a sentence such as "Bring the cow," so too is linguistic acquisition observed regarding an established fact in a sentence such as "A son has been born to you."

And on this point, many former teachers have exerted themselves. Nor is the second [alternative] possible; for, having begun with the manifestation of the reality of Brahman as the Self, there has been an extensive exposition of a series of purposes culminating in the fulfillment of all duties and the manifestation of bliss.

Nor is the third [alternative] possible; because the conscious Self is that very object of knowledge (*meyatva*). For this very reason it has been said: "There is no absence of the object of knowledge..."
There is doubt regarding the conscious self (*cidātman*), which is the witness of all activities; for if that were denied, it would follow that the entire world would fall into blindness.
[Page 162]
Introduction: The Taittirīyopaniṣaddīpikā, [19] The introduction to the Taittirīyopaniṣaddīpikā.

Nor does the entire *karmakāṇḍa* (section on ritual action) have as its sole purpose an injunction to act (*kāryaparatva*). This is because in prohibitions such as "A Brahmin must not be killed," there is nothing at all to be performed. Likewise, one should cite examples where even the *arthavādas* (explanatory passages) and other such texts have their purport in established facts (*siddhārtha*), such as the bodily form of the deities. And this has been elaborated upon in the *Devatādhikaraṇa* (the section concerning the deities). A—

Since the Vedāntas do not have as their primary purport an action to be performed (*kārya*), one who desires to act has no qualification (*adhikāra*) for them. Thus, when the view that the Vedāntas have as their purport an action to be performed has been refuted, the proponents of contradiction (*virodhavādinaḥ*) again raise an objection: "The conscious self (*cidātmā*) is not to be made known by the Vedāntas, because it is established through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*). [This is so] because in the states of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep, which are mutually distinct, the consciousness..."
There, the persisting self (ātman) is experienced. It is observed in cases such as genus and individual that the persisting is distinct from the excluded;

for example, Brahminhood is observed among the individuals Viśvāmitra, Kaṭha, and Kauṇḍinya. Therefore, by means of positive and negative concomitance alone, the conscious self is established. Intending this very point, it is stated in the Vārtikasāra: "By another means of knowledge..."

In this matter, words do not exert their power for success; therefore, a person is enjoined by the Śruti to restrain the latent impressions (*vāsanās*). For if the latent impressions are not restrained, they persist at the time of death, and a future birth—brought about by the final thought-moment—would become unavoidable. Whatever state one remembers while casting off the body at the end, that very state one attains, O son of Kuntī, for one's being is always shaped by that state.

Therefore, those latent impressions (*vāsanā*) consisting of the objects of the non-Self, known as waking, dreaming, and deep sleep, must all be restrained; for one fears rebirth from these. One should cultivate the singular contemplation of one's own Self, uninterrupted by the cognitions of the non-Self.
By that, the latent impressions which are the causes of birth are restrained. "One should worship one's own Self"—this is the direct injunction heard in the Śruti.

In order to establish its status as a constituent part [of the means], the conscious Self (cidātman) is restated in the Śruti: "As long as the single-cognition of the Self remains continuous with its own nature, one should perform meditation; thereby, the latent impressions (vāsanās) are destroyed. Once the impressions are exhausted, let the states of waking and so forth be conceptualized through another's perspective; however, for the Knower, by his own perspective, he sees nothing other than his own Self."

Thus, the perfected one (siddha) does not perceive the perishable body, whether it be stationary or moving, because he has realized his own true nature (*svarūpa*). Like a man blinded by the intoxication of wine who regards a garment as something specially adorned, [the body] has come to him by fate or departs by the power of fate. Therefore, all the Vedāntas indeed enjoin a person toward the path of self-contemplation (*ātma-upāsana*) for the purpose of restraining the various latent impressions (*vāsanā*).

Alternatively, those seeking liberation are enjoined to restrain the mind; for when that [mind] is restrained, all latent impressions (*vāsanā*) are indeed restrained. "The mind must be restrained until it reaches its dissolution within the heart"—thus the Śruti ordains the restraint of the mind for the sake of liberation. The *Pātañjala Yogaśāstra* culminates in the restraint of the mind. The activity of the mind—

The cessation of [mental] activity is liberation. Since the Self’s connection with misfortune has as its sole cause the latent impressions (*vāsanā*), liberation occurs through their suppression alone—whether there be other means or not. Because its nature is self-luminous, the Self shines by itself when the latent impressions of the mind have been suppressed, even without depending on any other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Thus, it is precisely through the medium of its effects that the light [of the Self is realized].

"Like my own statement: 'The validity of the Vedāntas is not held to be like that of the senses regarding an existing entity'—thus do the dull-witted explain, being solely enamored of the meaning of *niyoga* (injunction). This which was stated here is not correct, because *niyoga* is unnecessary;
since the desired object is accomplished through worldly means of knowledge alone, tell me, O wise one, what purpose is served by a Vedic *niyoga*?"

[In the chapter on training, regarding the mind: "If the mind and its latent impressions (vāsanās) exist, let there be misfortune in the waking state; if they are absent, as in deep sleep and so forth, let there be no misfortune."

It is not seen at all. Through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), cessation (*nirodha*) is recognized as the means for warding off misfortune; what unprecedented thing is then being enjoined? You have stated that meditation (*upāsanā*) and the restraint of the mind (*citta-nirodha*) are to be enjoined; I accept both of them exactly as such, as causes for enlightenment. The intellect, engaged in worldly transactions, [turns away] from meditation—*a-*...

Being inward-turned, it attains the capacity for self-investigation; for one of gross intellect cannot perceive the Self, which is devoid of sound, touch, and the rest. Therefore, the cessation of the intellect must be prescribed for the sake of subtlety. "This Self, hidden in all beings, does not shine forth; but it is seen by a subtle intellect through [the practice of] yoga"—such is the word of the Śruti. [The realization of] Brahman as the Self—

The fact that [the cessation of] latent impressions (*vāsanā*) and the intellect (*dhī*) are causes of enlightenment is not established by any other means of knowledge; therefore, let there be an injunction regarding these two. Through the cessation of the intellect dependent on meditation, the qualification for knowledge would be accomplished. Once qualification is established, the Vedāntas subsequently bring about the realization of the Self. Therefore, one who desires to effect the cessation of latent impressions or the cessation of the intellect has no qualification for the Vedānta.

What could that reality possibly be? Since the intent here is the cessation of the mind and its latent impressions (*vāsanā*), some have declared that the purport of the scripture lies in an injunction for realization. Thus, an injunction for realization is heard in the form, "The Self is to be seen.
Upon the inquiry, "Who is this Self?", it is described as "All is the Self. Sentences such as "Truth, Knowledge," etc., and "That thou art," etc., [serve this purpose].

Furthermore, [they] indeed present Brahman as one’s own self by way of being a supplement to an injunction (*vidhiśeṣatayā*). Thus they maintain that there is an injunction even with respect to a reality that is not connected to an injunction, due to the force of their attachment to injunctions. Regarding such people, this is said here: "Tell me, is oneness itself the object of the injunction, or is it the vision thereof? It cannot be the former, because it is eternally established and thus independent of any human effort."

[This is] not so. For vision is produced by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), not by performance. A form is seen with the eye; it is never seen through performance. Indeed, in the *Samanvaya-sūtra*, this was clearly refuted by the former teachers because, in the case of a contradiction with injunction (*vidhi-bādha*), human activity has no scope for entry. Therefore, the statement "it is to be seen" (*draṣṭavya*) is indeed an injunction regarding realization (*pratipatti-vidhi*). [It is] outwardly directed...

Alternatively, [the purpose of the Vedāntas] may be the exclusion of the world (khaṭvā-vyāvṛtti) or the desire for that which is to be enjoined. Knowledge of the Self produced by Vedic sentences does not touch upon an injunction;

rather, like sensory perception, it is established in an already existing fact. This being the case, the Vedāntas awaken one to the reality of Brahman—which is non-worldly, which has destroyed all duality, and which is immutable—the true nature of the principle of oneness.

What proof is there beyond words that are so capable of illumination? When the injunction for verbal knowledge has thus been refuted in the Vedāntas, other self-styled scholars have here proposed another method:

"There is indeed another means of realization characterized by reflection (*manana*) and meditation (*dhyāna*), which is prescribed along with its own means, even without an injunction for comprehension."

When the means such as tranquility (*śama*) and self-restraint (*dama*) are continuously present, meditation (*dhyāna*), which consists of contemplation without distraction, becomes easy to perform. Through the scripture—which takes the form of intermediate and great sentences (*avāntara-mahāvākya*)—and which brings about the awakening to the sword [of knowledge], a person first realizes that Brahman is one's own Self (*brahmātmatā*). Even when the reality (*tattva*) has been reached through the scripture, because its indirectness (*pārokṣya*) has not yet been removed, there arises the direct realization of it.

By this very [process], *prasaṃkhyāna* (contemplative enumeration) is enjoined. For *prasaṃkhyāna* is indeed repetition; however, in this context, it consists of both word and reasoning. Because it takes the form of mental reflection (*manana*), it is capable of bringing about direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*). Just as hearing (*śravaṇa*) is a means for verbal knowledge, so too is this [contemplation] effective because it results in the accomplishment of the two-fold goal.
[Notes: 1. *siddhitvā* | 2. *gahoto'tha* | 3. *gha. pritaḥ* | 4. *ṅa. haret* | 5. *ṅa. tū* | 6. *śabda* | 7. *ga. sidvyava* |
[Page 164] Introduction: The Taittirīyopaniṣaddīpikā.

And regarding experience: 'Reflection and meditative absorption (nididhyāsana)—having understood this very [Self], the wise knower of reality should cultivate wisdom'—by such passages, *prasaṃkhyāna* is enjoined for the sake of experience. Thus, when the purport is on absolute unity (*aikātmya*)."

Even though it is desired by the Śāstra, some maintain that [repetition] is for the sake of the effect (*kārya*); however, this is not at all tenable. Is repetition for the manifestation of the Self, or for its immediate intuition (*aparokṣya*), or for the removal of an obstruction, or for the fruit produced by the means of knowledge (*māna*), or for the removal of the doubt regarding the loss of the state of being a knower, or for the liberation of one who is already liberated? In every case, your effort is entirely for the sake of an injunction (*vidhi*).

It is fruitless; for since the triad beginning with the knower (pramātṛ) shines forth as possessing the very form of pure consciousness, and since it was previously unmanifest, what does it require upon its manifestation? The ego (ahaṃkāra) would be the knower, the expansion [of consciousness] is called the means of knowledge (māna), and the jar and so forth would be the object of knowledge (prameya)—this triad shines as clothed in consciousness. Even the body and such, though remote, appear as if directly perceived through His light. Vi-...

For him, there would be an immediate intuition (*aparokṣya*) of that [Self], just as of the Self itself, for which there is no other cause. Ignorance, too, is the creator of the separation from all objects of knowledge (*prameya*); by what could that which shines forth as unobstructed be obstructed? That which is established by its own majesty alone destroys darkness; such is the cognition born of the scriptures (*śāstra-dhī*). What other fruit produced by a means of valid knowledge (*māna*) could there be that might arise from an injunction (*vidhi*)? [This applies] to the knower and so forth...
Even when there is elision [of ignorance], that which remains as the witness of the elision is the unelided consciousness; how then can its elision be suspected?

Since the self is by nature liberated, its state of bondage arises only from ignorance. Once ignorance is destroyed through knowledge, what further requirement could there be for liberation? If it is argued that because the truth is known through the scriptures only in an indirect manner and is not yet directly experienced, therefore "contemplative realization" (*prasaṃkhyāna*) must be required—

That is not tenable. Is this mediacy (*pārokṣya*) due to the nature of the object of knowledge, or due to the nature of the word? In the first case, would it be the Brahmanhood that is mediated there, or the Selfhood? For the Śruti states, "That which is immediate and direct—that is Brahman," thereby declaring the primary immediacy of Brahman; how then can mediacy be suspected? Furthermore, the mediacy of the Self therein has already been refuted.

It has been explained: Sound itself is indifferent regarding the states of being indirect (*parokṣa*) or direct (*aparokṣa*). It makes known that which is separated by space and so forth through indirectness;

otherwise, it makes it known through directness, as in the case of "You are the tenth. However, for the reality of the one Self (*aikātmya-vastu*), there is not even the slightest separation by space, time, or substance; how then could there be a cognition of indirectness in that regard?

Because the reality known as the singular Self is obstructed only by the veil of ignorance (*tamas*), what need is there for meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*) regarding that which is neither to be accomplished nor to be attained?

If you argue that "one should act after having understood" according to the scriptural injunction, and thus meditative cultivation must be performed—let it be so. Nevertheless, there is no room here for your position whatsoever.

This scriptural instruction is not for the purpose of establishing the experience itself; rather, having understood that experience as being produced by the sentence, it enjoins one-pointedness toward that [experience] for the sake of withdrawing the mind from external objects. The intended utility here is described by the remainder of the passage: "One should not meditate on many words, for that is a weariness of speech. What is the use of saying more?
"Among the Vedāntas, which culminate in pure realization, only one who desires to know (bubhutsu) has the qualification; therefore, no one who merely desires to act (cikīrṣu) has it.

Thus have the subject matter, purpose, relationship, and qualified person of the Upaniṣads been defined. According to the principle that "the Veda produces valid knowledge for the qualified person," this Upaniṣad generates valid knowledge regarding the reality of Brahman as the Self for one who desires to know.
Thus. Nor should one dispute the authority of the Upaniṣads, for their authority is accepted as being self-evident.

[In the chapter on Training, regarding the lack of authority: "And because there is no cause for it. Is the lack of authority due to its being fruitless through ignorance, or due to its being sublated, or else due to its being a mere restatement? Not the first; for [the Upanishads contain] intermediate statements such as 'Brahman is truth, knowledge, and infinite,' and 'This self..."

This is because Brahman is apprehended even by the mere hearing of the great sentences (*mahāvākya*). Now, one might ask: are the meanings of the two words "Ātman" and "Brahman" worldly or non-worldly? Not the first, for that would entail the Veda being a mere restatement (*anuvādaka*) of what is already known. In the second case, there would be a lack of comprehension due to the impossibility of grasping the relationship [between word and meaning]. If it is argued that the relationship is grasped because the referents of the words are worldly...

Because the meaning of a sentence (*vākyārtha*) lacks worldly status, it cannot be considered a mere restatement (*anuvādaka*). With this very point in mind, it was determined in the *Dharmamīmāṃsā* that "a word whose capacity is understood from common worldly usage serves as an authority even in the Veda. That is incorrect, because the meaning of a sentence is difficult to define. Is the sentence-meaning a mere relation (*saṃsarga*), or is it a qualified entity (*viśiṣṭa*), or is it an indivisible, unitary essence (*akhaṇḍaikarasa*)? Regarding these, [according to the theory of] *abhihitānvaya*—

The Bhaṭṭas are the proponents of the theory that the meaning of a sentence is the relation (*saṃsarga*) between the word-meanings denoted by the individual words. However, the Prābhākaras, who maintain the theory of the expression of the related (*anvitābhidhāna*), hold that the meaning of a sentence is the *niyoga* (injunction) qualified by what is other than the [mere] capable [word-meanings]. Likewise, in this case as well, if the meaning of the sentence were either the relation between the self and Brahman, or Brahman qualified by the self, your own established tenet (*apasiddhānta*) would result.

Because the object of your preference—an indivisible, single-flavored reality—is unestablished. If it is argued that the meaning of a sentence must indeed be an indivisible, single-flavored reality, we say no, because there is a lack of any supporting example (*dṛṣṭānta*). Even if some kind of example were somehow available, there would be an absence of human purpose (*puruṣārtha*) due to the lack of anything to be abandoned or acquired. Furthermore, for the sake of establishing the indivisibility and single flavor [of reality], if the world is held to be false, then the Veda too would be false.

[Otherwise] there would be invalidity [of your own position]. To this it is replied: For you, in order to state the opponent's view as something to be refuted, the sentence "the reality is an indivisible, uniform essence" (*akhaṇḍaikarasaṃ vastu*) is employed; that very sentence must be accepted as the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*).

Indeed, in that case, neither a syntactical relation (*saṃsarga*) nor a qualified entity (*viśiṣṭa*) constitutes the meaning of the sentence; for if that were so, it would follow that [the reality] is not something to be perceived.

Indeed, neither of those two [theories] is refuted by you, because they are accepted as being your own views. Therefore, the statement that "the reality is of the nature of an indivisible essence (*akhaṇḍaikarasa*) through restatement" provides one illustrative example. The ancient teachers also describe it thus: "The sentence consisting of 'Being, Consciousness,' and so forth, has as its purport an indivisible object (*akhaṇḍārtha*), because it is a defining sentence (*lakṣaṇavākya*), like the sentence 'The moon is the most excellent light. Pra...

By the word *kṛṣṭa* (ploughed), the light of the stars is excluded; by the word *prakāśa* (light), clouds and the like are excluded. Thus, by this sentence, the intended moon—the mere meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*), an undivided whole—is conveyed. Similarly, a sentence such as *tat tvam asi* ("That thou art") has as its purport an undivided meaning, because it is a coordinate construction (*samānādhikaraṇa*) while having as its referent a substance that is neither cause nor effect.

This is like the sentence "This is Devadatta. Because it conveys the identity of the individual Devadatta as characterized by these current space-time coordinates in contrast to those mutually contradictory [past] space-time coordinates, it possesses the quality of having an indivisible meaning (*akhaṇḍārthatva*). Furthermore, the indivisible meaning of the sentence is established in the *Vārtikasāra*, because the word "Self" (*ātman*) is applied to the well-known Self. Indeed...

The worldly [meaning]—even the meaning of "Brahman" is well-known as something great through common usage. Thus, when the word-meaning is fully understood from the word by means of worldly measurement, who can prevent the supersensuous sentence-meaning from being derived from the Vedic sentence? Just as you yourself have explained even non-worldly meanings—such as the categories of *apūrva*, the deity, and heaven—from the sentence by means of worldly measurement after having first taught them.

Just as the meaning of heaven and so forth is understood by virtue of the statement being in accordance with reality (*yathārthavāda*), so too the meaning of Brahman is understood through the intermediate sentence (*avāntaravākya*). [Notes: 1. *kha* reads *avagamyate*;
2. *ga* reads *phalāt*; 3. *va* reads *bhāṣāḥ*; 4. *ka*, *kha*, and *ṅa* read *kaparama*.
