The *praṇava* is the support (*ālambana*). For this very reason, it is recited in the Kaṭha Upaniṣad with reference to the syllable *oṃ*: "This support is the best; this support is the supreme. Such a *praṇava* is covered—that is, pervaded—by *medhā*, the power of retention. O Supreme Lord, who is signified by such a *praṇava*, [grant] my hearing through my two ears.

Protect the secret meaning of the Vedas that has been understood by warding off defects such as forgetfulness. The mantra for recitation has been declared for the attainment of health and other benefits; now, the mantras for the purpose of *homa* (fire sacrifice) for the attainment of food, drink, clothing, and so forth, are being stated.
Among them, he first states the mantra beginning with "āvahanti. O Supreme Lord, denoted by the syllable *praṇava*, [that] Śrī who was described—
O Sustainer, bring prosperity for my sake from every direction and accomplish it entirely. What kind [of prosperity]? That is stated as follows:
bringing all those garments, cows, and food and drink for the purpose of my enjoyment from every direction and accomplishing them;
likewise, spreading—that is, extending and increasing—all that has been accomplished, and increasing what has been increased. That...

For me, who am a seeker of knowledge, may she—who has long been making [me] remain so that I do not perish—bring that very Śrī (Prosperity) such as this. Furthermore, of what kind is she? [She is one] by means of whom... [Note:
The text contains manuscript variants indicated by "ka. ṅa. myo'dhi", "gha hetuṃ ma", and "ka ca ṅa. hetuṃ ma"].
The Fourth Anuvāka. 4.
The Taittirīyopaniṣaddīpikā:
Because it exists together with such animals as hairy goats, sheep, horses, and so forth, it is manifold—
[The mantra] is joined with the *dhāra* [mantra]. "May this oblation of clarified butter and other materials be offered (*svāhā*) to the Lord who bestows such prosperity.

Now, for the sake of establishing the tradition of knowledge for one endowed with the prosperity consisting of abundance in clothing, food, drink, and so forth, he states five mantras for the *homa* intended to gather disciples: "May they come" (*ā mā yantu*), etc. For the student (*brahmacārin*) practicing Vedic learning...

"Let the disciples come to me"—that is, let them reach me, the teacher who is the propagator of the tradition. The word *vi-* denotes variety; the variety among the religious students (*brahmacārins*) consists in their various desires, such as the desire for cattle and other worldly goods, the desire for the heavenly world, the desire for the world of Brahmā, and the desire for liberation. The prefix *pra-* denotes excellence; in the acquisition of knowledge, excellence is the preeminence of one's discernment.

By the indeclinable *dam*, self-restraint (*dānti*) is denoted. Here, self-restraint is the cessation from the activities of the external senses, which are like the play of a child. By the term *śam*, tranquility (*śānti*) is denoted. Tranquility is the state of being free from mental defects such as anger and the like. The four mantras beginning with *vimāyantu* are mentioned because they belong to other Vedic branches (*śākhāntara*).
It is not recited in all regions. He now states two mantras that bestow fame, which arises from the continuity of the tradition: "May I have glory among the people.

O Supreme Lord, by Your grace, may I have glory among all people; may I become famous as "this one is a teacher. "Vasu" means wealth; one who possesses abundant wealth is "vasumān," and one who possesses it in excess is "vasīyān."

"I shall become even more excellent—that is, more praiseworthy—than such as you. He then recites three mantras that establish the causes for renown and excellence: "O Blessed One (*bhaga*)," and so forth. The word *bhaga* denotes the six qualities beginning with sovereignty (*aiśvarya*). As it is remembered in the tradition: "Sovereignty, complete virtue, fame, fortune, knowledge, and dispassion—these six are designated as *bhaga*."
By that [attribute], the possessor of it is indicated. O Blessed One, Supreme Lord, I enter into You—that Blessed One—so as to be one with You;
having entered into You, I shall worship You at all times. May You, who are such, also enter me;
having entered me, please favor me with Your grace. Into You, who possess a thousandfold variety of forms, I place myself.

"I purify" means I cleanse thoroughly; the meaning is that devotion to you alone is the cause of the highest good (*śreyaḥ*). He speaks a mantra that brings about many disciples, preceded by an illustration: "Just as the waters... Just as in the world the waters come swiftly by way of a slope—that is, by a path leading toward a lower region—and just as the months, such as Caitra, Vaiśākha, and so forth...

All [the days] reach the year that wears away by days. That year in which the three hundred and sixty days have become worn out and are included within it is this "day-wearing" (aharjara) year. Indeed, no month whatsoever ever exceeds the year. O Creator, Ordainer of the entire world, all these students of sacred knowledge (brahmacārins), according to the analogy of the months—

"Without overstepping me, let them come to me from every region with haste, according to the manner of water. Having stated the *homamantra*, he now states the *upasthānamantra*: "Thou art a neighbor (*prativeśa*). A house that serves as a place for removing fatigue is called a "neighbor. O Creator (*dhātṛ*), thou art my neighbor; therefore, illumine me, make me manifest.

Make me renowned as a teacher of the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*). For that purpose, take refuge in me; that is to say, grant me your grace. Thus [ends the section] in the work composed by the venerable Sāyaṇācārya, for the sake of Mādhava Vidyāraṇya, the sustainer of the empire of the illustrious Bukkaṇa. In the fourth [chapter], the mantras for the attainment of intelligence (*medhā*) and other qualities were taught. Now, the meditation (*upāsana*) upon Brahman is described in the fifth and sixth [chapters].

Even there, the division is such that the meditation on the deities of the limbs (*aṅgadevatā*) occurs in the fifth, while in the sixth, it concerns the Brahman who possesses those limbs (*aṅgin*). He shows the three *vyāhṛtis* as symbols (*pratīka*) for the meditation on the deities of the limbs: "Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ, Svaḥ. Bhūḥ—
The first is *bhuvaḥ*, the second is *suvaḥ*, and the third is *svaḥ*. These three in number are what is denoted by the term *vyāhṛti*.

They are called *vyāhṛtis* because they are the subject matter of utterance (*vyāharaṇa*); that is, they are mantras intended for recitation. Alternatively, they are *vyāhṛtis* because they are brought forth (*āhriyante*) or employed in various rites (*vividhe karmaṇi*). The word *vai* is used to indicate the well-known nature of their employment. A—
Regarding the placing of the *agnihotra* oblation and the placing of the *darśapūrṇamāsa* and *cāturmāsya* oblations, it is prescribed in the ritual application (*prayoga*) as follows:

"One should place the *agnihotra* with these *vyāhṛti*s," and "One performing the *darśapūrṇamāsa* and *cāturmāsya* sacrifices should place the oblations with these *vyāhṛti*s. Likewise, [it is prescribed] from the time of the fire-laying (*ādhāna*) onwards...

It is to be brought forth. Having shown the three *vyāhṛtis* well-known from the ritual section (*karmakāṇḍa*), he likewise shows another *vyāhṛti* as a representative symbol (*pratīka*) with the words "Of these" (*tāsām*). A sage for whom there is a large *camasa*—a specific vessel for drinking soma—is a "Great *Camasa*" (*mahācamasa*) sage. The greatness of the *camasa* is due to its being present at many soma sacrifices.
His offspring was the seer named Māhācamasya. He proclaimed this fourth *vyāhṛti*, "mahaḥ," which completes the number four, for those three *vyāhṛtis* beginning with *bhūḥ*;
that is, he taught it as the primary one for the purpose of meditation. The collection of particles "u ha sma" is used for the sake of indicating what is well-known. [The name of] the seer—
The inclusion of the word "great" (*maha*) is for the purpose of recollection during meditation. Regarding those four *vyāhṛtis*, he prescribes a specific view:

"That is Brahman. One should contemplate that which exists as the fourth *vyāhṛti*, "Great," as the reality that is Brahman. Precisely because it is Brahman, this very Self, whose form is the fourth *vyāhṛti*, resides within the body.

One should contemplate that the other deities of the *vyāhṛtis* are like the limbs, such as the hands and feet [of the body]. Alternatively, the fourth *vyāhṛti* is praised, because the word *mahaḥ* is derived from a verbal root meaning "to worship"; thus, it is appropriate to offer praise in the form of the venerable Brahman-reality. Just as the conscious Self (*ātman*) is superior in relation to the parts belonging to the body, so too...

In comparison with the other *vyāhṛtis*, the fourth *vyāhṛti*, "Mahaḥ," is superior. Having stated the *vyāhṛtis*, the text prescribes the visualization of them as the worlds: "Bhūḥ, indeed... Since all the worlds, being illumined by the sun, become venerable and fit for worldly activity, therefore the nature of the *vyāhṛti* "Mahaḥ" is that of the sun.
It has been stated. Now, he enjoins the visualization of specific deities within those very *vyāhṛtis*: "Bhūḥ" is indeed Agni.

For all the stellar lights situated around the lunar orb shine as objects of worship. Then, he enjoins the visualization of the Vedas within those very same [syllables]: "Bhūḥ" is indeed the *Ṛgveda*. [The syllable] contained in the three Vedas—
The *Ṛg* and other Vedas are without distinction; Brahman is the syllable *oṃ*, for by it all the Vedas are honored, as it is the beginning of the recitation of the Vedas.

Because it is preceded by the *praṇava* (the syllable Om), he now enjoins the meditation upon the vital breath (*prāṇa*): "The *bhūḥ* is indeed the vital breath. For by this food that has been eaten, the vital breaths are satisfied. He concludes the previously mentioned *vyāhṛtis*, which were associated with the meditations on the worlds and so forth, by saying:
"Those, indeed... Those *vyāhṛtis* beginning with *bhūḥ*—these four *vyāhṛtis* are the worlds, the deities, the Vedas, and the vital breaths.

They are divided into four types according to their perspectives. In that case, the single *vyāhṛti* "Bhūḥ" is fourfold: Earth, *Ṛgveda*, Fire, and Vital Breath (*prāṇa*). Thus, there are four *vyāhṛtis*. Likewise, since each of "Bhuvaḥ" and the others is also fourfold, they amount to sixteen. To include all of them, [the text mentions] the four—

"Four" is used distributively (*vīpsā*). He prescribes the meditation upon those *vyāhṛtis* with the words, "He who knows them. Whoever knows—that is, meditates upon—those *vyāhṛtis* as being endowed with the perspectives of the earth and so forth, for that meditator all the gods, Indra and the others, bring—that is, accomplish—an offering of worship (*bali*). Now, [one might object]: regarding the representative symbol (*pratīka*) consisting of the aforementioned *vyāhṛtis*—

For one who relies on a symbol (*pāsaka*), there is no attainment of the world of Brahman (*brahmaloka*). This is because the sūtra, "Bādarāyaṇa [holds that] he leads those who do not rely on symbols," determines that only those who meditate upon Brahman without symbols attain it. Consequently, since there is no attainment of Brahman, it is not logical for such a person to be worthy of worship by all the gods. This is not a fault, because that man who knows the *vyāhṛtis*—that man...
One meditates upon the Brahman as described in the *kṣyamāṇānuvāka*. Here, meditation on Brahman alone is primary; the meditation on the *vyāhṛtis* is secondary (*aṅga*).

Therefore, when the attainment of Brahman occurs, it is logical that one becomes worthy of worship by all the gods. Thus ends the [section] from the *Vedārthaprakāśa* composed by the venerable Sāyaṇācārya, under the supreme lord Mādhava Vidyāraṇya, the sustainer of the sovereignty of the illustrious Śrīkaṇṭha.

In the fifth [chapter], the meditation on the limbs was taught; in the sixth, however, the meditation on the "I" (aham) is taught. Therein, at the outset, he shows the nature of that which is to be meditated upon with the words, "He who is this... Within the center of the lotus of the heart, there exists an ether (*ākāśa*) the size of one's own thumb. By means of the two terms "he" (*sa*) and "this" (*eṣa*), which denote distance and proximity respectively, [the text refers to] that which is established in the Yoga-shastra as the separated [and the immediate].

Furthermore, that which is well-known from other scriptural passages is being described: in this very ether (ākāśa) exists the Person, the all-pervading Supreme Self (paramātman). Although He exists everywhere, nevertheless, for the sake of His perception and for the sake of meditation, the heart is taught as His location. For within the center of the lotus of the heart, the mind is restrained through meditative absorption (samādhi).
The mind is capable of directly realizing the Supreme Self, as another scriptural text states: "But it is seen by you through the intellect.
This capacity for direct realization is expressed by the word "this" (*ayam*), which denotes immediate perception.
Such a person, when meditated upon within the center of the heart, becomes gracious. For this very reason, in the Dahara and Śāṇḍilya Vidhyās—
It is taught as being in the heart. Within that heart, one should meditate upon the Person (*puruṣa*) who consists of mind (*manomaya*), whose primary essence is the mind.
For those desiring to know him realize that Person directly through the mind, and practitioners likewise contemplate him with the mind;
this is what is meant by "consisting of mind. "Immortality" means the absence of destruction. "Golden" means consisting of light, self-luminous.

This is the meaning. Having thus described the nature of the object of meditation (*upāsya-svarūpa*), [the text] shows the specific path for the meditator (*upāsaka*) with the words: "between the two palates" (*antareṇa tāluke*). This refers to the left and right portions situated inside the cavity of the mouth above the root of the tongue. 1. [In the directions... 2. *pra* (variant), *kha*, *dhye sa*.

In the chapter on training composed by Vidyāraṇya, it is asked: "What is meant by 'between the two palates'? It refers to that which is very small, like the teat of a young cow, located in the middle between the two palates."

A piece of flesh remains hanging down; the word *yat* is used to indicate that this piece of flesh is well-known in the *Yogaśāstra*. The word *etat* is used to indicate its perceptibility: it is perceived directly by touching the tongue when one has made the *lambikā-karaṇa*, and it is perceived by the eyes alone in the mouth of another. And that piece of flesh belongs to Indra, the Supreme...

The "womb" (*yonih*) is the place of the dog. According to the maxim of perceiving the moon at the tip of a branch, that piece of flesh indicates the channel known as *suṣumnā*, which is well-known in the Yoga scriptures and situated near it.

When the mind enters that channel and becomes one-pointed, it is capable of directly realizing the Supreme Self. With this very intention, the *Kṣurikopaniṣad*— [Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly; the translation reflects the portion available.]
It is said that there are one hundred and one channels (*nāḍī*); among them, the *suṣumnā* is remembered as the best.
The *suṣumnā*, which is stainless (*virajā*) and of the nature of Brahman, is merged into the Supreme. The *iḍā* stands on the left, while the *piṅgalā* stands on the right.
He who knows that supreme place between those two is a knower of the Vedas. Therefore, that channel is the abode of the Supreme Lord.

Moreover, it is also the "station" (*sthāna*) because it serves as the path for attaining immortality. That it is the path is also recorded by the Chandogas and the Kaṭhas: "There are a hundred and one channels of the heart; of these, one extends to the crown of the head. Moving upward through that, one attains immortality. This very Suṣumṇā channel is the womb (*yoni*) of Indra.

The *rasa* (vital essence), having cleared away [the obstructions] in the left and right skull-hemispheres and having pierced through them, abides specifically at that region of the head where the end—that is, the root—of the hair is located. Just as the "top" of the hair is called "end" because there is an absence of hair above it, so too the "root" is denoted by the word "end" because there is an absence of hair below it. Thus, one should meditate...
Having stated the exit-gate for the attainment of which fruit, he now demonstrates that fruit: "Bhūḥ, this is the earth," and so forth.

Through meditation on the three *vyāhṛtis*, one becomes established in Agni and the others; one attains that sovereignty which belongs to Agni, Vāyu, and Āditya. Through meditation on the fourth *vyāhṛti*, one becomes established in Brahman, who dwells in Satyaloka. [Of] Brahman...

He attains that sovereignty; this very point is elaborated upon by such statements as "self-rule" (*svārājya*). He himself becomes the king of the subordinate deities, beginning with Agni. It is stated that because of his kingship, all the gods bring him tribute.
Not only does he attain self-rule, but he also attains lordship over the minds of all living beings.

Having become the self of all living beings, one should perceive his sovereignty over all speech and so forth. The internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) is indeed one, yet it is designated by the two terms "mind" (*manas*) and "consciousness" (*vijñāna*) due to a distinction in its powers. By virtue of its instrumental power (*karaṇa-śakti*), it is called "mind"; however, by virtue of its agentive power (*kartṛ-śakti*), it is called "consciousness. Previously, this very [organ], residing solely within the body, was the sovereign of the mind, speech, and other faculties.

But now, through the power of knowledge (*vidyā*), having attained the state of possessing the Virāj as his adjunct— which is the self of all— he becomes the sovereign lord of the mind, speech, and other faculties residing within all bodies. Then, immediately after attaining the Virāj in its collective form, having produced the realization of the reality of Brahman, and with ignorance (*avidyā*) destroyed, he comes to possess this nature which is about to be described, beginning with the words "ākāśa" and so forth.

Its essential nature is now described: that Brahman whose body—its very form—is like space, being devoid of material form, is "space-bodied" (*ākāśaśarīra*). Alternatively, because space itself is Brahman, since it is the substratum for the conceptualization of the entire universe and is thus the self of all, [it is called space-bodied]. Or rather, [the term refers to] me.

The true nature of the Brahman: In the ether (ākāśa), both the foundational aspect (adhiṣṭhāna-bhāga), which consists of Being-Consciousness-Bliss (saccidānanda-rūpa), and the superimposed aspect (āropya-bhāga), which consists of name and form (nāmarūpa), are perceived. Among these, although name and form lack the status of Brahman due to their falsity, the foundational aspect [remains].

It is logical that Brahman possesses the nature of reality (*satyatva*). With this very intention in mind, it is called "the True Self" (*satyātman*). That Brahman whose self—its essential nature—is the Truth, which is uncontradicted and the substratum for the conceptualization of the entire world, is the "True-Self" (*satyātman*). Likewise, that Brahman in which there is the sport (*ārāma*) of the vital breath (*prāṇa*)—meaning its activity consisting of creation and so forth, which takes the form of play in every respect—is "that in which the vital breath finds its sport" (*prāṇārāma*). And the origin of the vital breath is as follows: [The text continues with the description of the origin of the *prāṇa* from the *ātman*. ...is born from the Self (*ātman*). This is stated in the following scriptural passage: "From this Self, the *prāṇa* was born first" (*tasmād vā etasmād ātmanaḥ prāṇo jāyata*). Furthermore, the term "sport" (*ārāma*) is used here to indicate the absence of any other purpose; it signifies that the activity of the *prāṇa* is for its own sake alone. Moreover, the word "Self" (*ātman*) is used here to denote the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), because it is the source of the individual self (*jīvātman*). This is because the individual self is not the cause of the *prāṇa*, whereas the Supreme Self is. This is understood from the scriptural statement: "From Him, indeed, comes the birth of the *prāṇa*" (*tasmād dhy evāsya prāṇa utpadyate*). Therefore, the meaning is that Brahman is the source of the *prāṇa*. Thus, it is established that Brahman is the True-Self, that in which the vital breath finds its sport, and that which is blissful. It is recorded in the *Āmnāya* (Veda) from the presence of Brahmā: "From this [Self] are born the vital breath (*prāṇa*), the mind (*manas*), and all the sense organs. he created the vital breath (*prāṇa*). Because it is the substratum for such play of the vital breath, it is called "delighting in the vital breath" (*prāṇārāma*). "It leads [one] there; for having obtained this very essence (rasa), one becomes blissful. Indeed, when Brahman—which is of the single essence of bliss—is realized, no distraction can ever arise for the mind submerged therein. This very tranquility is described in the Śvetāśvatara...

It is traditionally taught: "Having known Śiva, one attains ultimate peace. The Blessed One has also said: "The yogi of restrained mind, thus constantly yoking the self, attains the peace that culminates in Nirvāṇa and is established in Me. Therefore, Brahman is enriched by the peace residing in the mind; or rather, peace itself resides in Brahman.

Just as an illusion (māyā) is dispersed when it undergoes transformation into the form of the world, so Brahman is never transformed at any time, because of its immutably eternal nature. As the scriptures state: "The Self is unborn, great, and eternal," and so forth. Therefore, Brahman is enriched by peace established in itself. Likewise, this very Brahman is immortal, being devoid of death.

Death is the departure of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) from the body; this is understood from the traditional recollection of the verbal root *mṛ*, meaning "to abandon the vital breath. And that death occurs for the living being (*jīva*) who possesses the vital breath, but not for the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), who is devoid of vital breath. This must be considered: whether the meditation (*upāsanā*) in the fifth and sixth sections is different or indeed one and the same. For the moment, it is argued that it is different because of the difference in the objects of meditation and the difference in their results. In the fifth section, the object of meditation is the symbol (*pratīka*) consisting of the *vyāhṛtis* viewed as the worlds and so forth; whereas in the sixth, Brahman, characterized by qualities such as being composed of mind (*manomaya*), is the object of meditation. Thus [it appears].

[The opponent argues: There is a difference in characteristics. Therefore, since there is a difference in the meditations (*upāsana*), [the two are distinct]. To this we reply:
because the hearing of a single qualified person (*adhikārin*) occurs, the meditation is one and the same in both places. This was stated in the fifth [chapter]: "He who knows that... [and so on].

It is heard in scripture that only one who meditates on the *vyāhṛtis* as "Brahman" possesses the qualification for the meditation on Brahman. For instance, in the sixth [chapter], the fruit of the meditation on the *vyāhṛtis*—namely, "He becomes firmly established in the earth," and so forth—is taught together with it. Therefore, the meditation is indeed the same in both cases. As for the difference in the objects of meditation, that is also justified by the distinction between the subordinate (*aṅga*) and the principal (*aṅgin*). All this belongs to him.

The statement, "The gods bring the offering," will likewise be a result pertaining to a subsidiary element (*aṅgaphala*). In such cases as, "He whose ladle (*juhū*) is made of *parṇa*-wood hears no evil report," since the sacrifice cannot be accomplished without the *parṇa* substance, it serves the purpose of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*). Consequently, because there is no further expectation for a fruit, it is appropriate that the fruit mentioned is merely an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*). However, in this case, without the meditation on the *vyāhṛtis*—

Nor can it be argued that the meditation on the *vyāhṛtis* is taught merely for the sake of the fruit resulting from the perfection of the meditation on Brahman, and thus it is not an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*). Therefore, it is logical that they constitute a single meditation through the relationship of principal and subordinate parts. Furthermore, one should not suspect that by this same logic, the meditation on Brahman consisting of earth, intermediate space, and so forth—stated in the seventh section—is also identical with the preceding one; for [the case of] Śāṇḍilya, Dahara, and others...

Because, according to the principle [of systematic connection], they are separate meditations. That principle was considered in the third section (pāda) of the third chapter [of the Brahma-sūtras]: "Are the Śāṇḍilya, Dahara, and other meditations different, or are they not? Because of the excellence of meditating on the whole and because Brahman is one, there would be non-difference. However, because it is impossible to meditate on the whole and because Brahman is distinct through its attributes, the Dahara and others are different. Thus, they are distinct.

Because there is a distinct commencement [for each]. In the *Chāndogya*, the Dahara-vidyā, Śāṇḍilya-vidyā, Madhu-vidyā, and others are recited; likewise in other Vedic branches (*śākhā*). There, according to the principle of the preceding section (*adhikaraṇa*), since the meditation on the whole is superior and the object of knowledge (*vedya*)—Brahman—is one, it follows that all these constitute a single meditation (*vidyā*). To this, we reply: among the infinite...

Since it is impossible to perform the practice by unifying the various meditations (vidyās), one must understand that there is indeed a distinction between these meditations. Nor should one doubt the oneness of Brahman, the object of knowledge, because the systematic arrangement [of the texts] is justified by the difference in their attributes (guṇas). Furthermore, it is not impossible to determine the extent of each individual meditation, as this is established by the respective opening and concluding statements of each. Therefore—

There is a diversity among meditations (*dhyāna*). Thus, when there is a distinction between two forms of worship, only one should be practiced, not both. This too has been considered in that very [work]:

"In the case of 'I-grasps' (*ahaṃgraha*), is there no restriction, or is there a restriction of option? Since there is no restrictive factor, let it be understood as being according to one's desire (*yathākāmya*). However, because the direct realization of the Lord is accomplished through a single meditation alone—"

The futility of knowledge and distraction are the two factors that regulate conceptualization (*vikalpa*). There are two kinds of meditations (*upāsanā*): those involving identification (*ahaṃgraha*) and those consisting of symbols (*pratīka*). Since identification will be discussed in the fourth chapter regarding the meditations on the qualified Self (*saguṇātman*), those are called "identifications. Non-self objects that are consecrated by the vision of a deity and then meditated upon are called "symbols" (*pratīka*).

In that regard, among the "non-appropriations" (*agraha*), such as the meditations on Śāṇḍilya and others, one, two, or many meditations may be performed according to one's desire, because there is no restrictive rule for the option. Indeed, there is no reason for a restrictive rule of option such that only the meditation on Śāṇḍilya, or the meditation on the small space (*dahara*), or some other single one must be performed and not another. Therefore, [the practice is] according to one's desire.

This being the position reached, we reply: first, the "uselessness of others" (*anyānarthakya*) is one restrictive factor. For instance, the purpose of meditation (*upāsana*) is the direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) of the Lord; and if that is accomplished by means of a single meditation, then other meditations would be useless.
Furthermore, in the case of meditations, the direct realization is not produced by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); rather, it arises through uninterrupted contemplation (*bhāvanā*).

[It is] the conceit of identity with the object of meditation (*dhyeya*). And how could that conceit become firm for a person who, having performed one form of worship, abandons it and remains occupied elsewhere, resulting in distraction of the mind? Therefore, because futility and distraction act as restrictive factors, the option (*vikalpa*) is restricted. Just as in the case of the knowledge of the reality of Brahman (*brahmatattvavidyā*), so too in the meditation on Brahman (*brahmopāsana*), there is the "I-conception" (*ahaṃgraha*).

The syllable *Haḥ* should be employed. Regarding the knowledge of reality (*tattva-vidyā*), the grasping of the "I" (*ahaṃ-graha*) was considered in the first quarter of the fourth chapter [of the Brahma-sūtras]: "Is Brahman to be grasped by the knower as other than himself, or as his own self? One should know it as other, because of the contradiction between suffering and the sufferer. Since the contradiction is merely adventitious (*aupādhika*), it is therefore grasped precisely as one's own self; thus they grasp it through the Great Sayings (*mahāvākya*)."

They even cause their own disciples to grasp this: that the Brahman which is the subject matter of the scriptures must be apprehended by the living self (*jīva*) as something distinct from itself, because there is a contradiction between the state of being a sufferer and the state of being non-suffering for the *jīva* and *Brahman*, respectively. To this, we reply:

although the *jīva* is in reality of the very nature of *Brahman*, its experience of transmigratory states such as suffering is produced by the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*).

This has been explained in detail in the section on the ether (*viyat*) within the inquiry into the individual soul (*jīva*). Therefore, since there is no real contradiction, Brahman should be grasped precisely as the Self (*ātman*).

For this very reason, those who know reality grasp Brahman as the Self through such great sayings (*mahāvākya*) as "I am Brahman" (*ahaṃ brahmāsmi*) and "This Self is Brahman" (*ayam ātmā brahma*). Likewise, [the teacher] instructs his own disciples through great sayings such as "That thou art" (*tat tvam asi*).

Even the *pantya* [text] states this. Therefore, Brahman must be grasped precisely as the Self (*ātman*). This being the case, one should meditate thus: "I am the Supreme Self, consisting of mind, immortal, and golden. That the one consisting of mind is the Supreme Self was considered in the second quarter (*pāda*) of the first chapter by means of the example of the *Śāṇḍilya-vidyā*. This one consisting of mind is the embodied self (*śārīra*).

The Lord is indeed [the object of] the terms "breath" (prāṇa) and "mind" (mānasa); because He resides in the heart and is subtler than an atom, these terms apply to the individual soul (jīva), and thus the word "jīva" is used for Him. [This is so] because there is no distinction in the result [of meditation], as stated in Sūtra 3.3.58: "The option [is permissible] because the fruit is not different. Furthermore, [the Lord is the Self] because they approach Him as the Self and cause others to grasp Him as such, as stated in Sūtra 4.1.3: "But [He is] the Self, for they approach Him [as such] and cause [others] to grasp Him [as such]. And because of the teaching of what is well-known everywhere, as stated in Sūtra 1.2.1: "Because of the teaching of what is well-known everywhere."

In the *Śikṣādhyāya* composed by Vidyāraṇya:

"The Brahman residing in the syllable *kyam* requires [grammatical] suffixes such as the *taddhita*; the connection with the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and so forth is for the purpose of meditation, and the Brahman to be meditated upon is well-known from established usage."

In the third chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad, within the Śāṇḍilya-vidyā, this is recorded: "Consisting of mind (manomaya), having the vital breath as its body (prāṇaśarīra), and having light as its form (bhārūpa). Regarding this, a doubt arises as to whether it refers to the individual soul (jīva) or the Lord (īśa). The prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) is that it is the individual soul, because attributes such as the connection with the mind are easily applicable to the individual soul. The term "consisting of mind" (manomaya) signifies a modification of the mind; thus, there is a connection with the mind. Furthermore, [the text continues: "mā..."

The connection with *prāṇa* [in the phrase] "whose body is this" would not be appropriate for the Lord (*īśvara*), because of the prohibition: "For He is without *prāṇa*, without mind, pure. Likewise, what is heard in scripture—"This Self which is within the heart, subtler than a grain"—namely, its abiding in the heart and its subtlety, is in no way possible for that which is supportless and all-pervading.

When the conclusion is reached that [the person in the sun] is the individual soul (jīva), we reply: In the preceding sentence—"All this, indeed, is Brahman; as originating from, dissolving into, and breathing in That, one should meditate with calmness"—it is that very Brahman which is heard being mentioned that is required as the substantive (viśeṣya) by the two terms "consisting of mind" (manomaya) and "having vital breath for its body" (prāṇaśarīra), which are respectively a secondary derivative (taddhita) and a possessive compound (bahuvrīhi). This is the meaning of the sentence concerning calmness: [The final answer: It is Brahman. Why? Because of the context. For the preceding passage—"All this, indeed, is Brahman; as originating from, dissolving into, and breathing in That, one should meditate with calmness"—is intent upon enjoining calmness, and it is that Brahman which is heard therein that is required as the substantive by the two terms "consisting of mind" and "having vital breath for its body," which are respectively a secondary derivative and a possessive compound. This is the meaning of the sentence concerning calmness.

Since all this is Brahman—because it is born from That, dissolved into That, and breathes in That—therefore, because attachment, aversion, and the objects of the senses are impossible within Brahman, which is the Self of all, one should be tranquil at the time of meditation. Likewise, since Brahman is connected as the substantive in that sentence, the "consisting of mind" (*manomaya*) passage must also refer to Brahman. Nor is there [a contradiction] regarding the mind of Brahman...

The connection with the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) is untenable. For although it is untenable in the case of the unconditioned [Brahman], it is tenable in the case of the conditioned object of meditation, since that is for the purpose of contemplation. Therefore, that very Brahman which is well-known as the object of meditation in all the Vedāntas is what is to be meditated upon here as well. Indeed, nowhere in the Vedāntas is the individual soul (*jīva*) well-known as an object of meditation.

Therefore, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that it is Brahman alone. In this regard, just as the Brahman mentioned in the passage concerning tranquility (*śama*) is qualified by the attribute of being "consisting of mind" (*manomaya*), so too here, the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) denoted by the word *puruṣa*—which signifies the All-pervading—is qualified by the term *manomaya*. And the fact that [the word *puruṣa*] signifies the All-pervading has been demonstrated in the *Śreyomārga*: "The *puruṣa* is in the city (*puri*)."

[The opponent argues: "Is it because of lying in a city (*puri*), or because of being full (*pūrṇa*), or because of filling this [body] by means of that? If you say that in the case of 'lying in a city' (*puriśayana*), it might refer to the individual soul (*jīva*), we say no; for Brahman has been introduced as the subject in the passage, 'He who knows Him, he knows Brahman,' and because of the concluding statement, 'Brahman has space as its body. As for the word *hiraṇmaya* (golden), its reference to Brahman is as follows..."

This has been determined in the statement, "This golden person is seen within the sun. And that determination was stated in the first section (pāda) of the first chapter: "Is this golden one the self of a deity, or is it the Supreme Lord? Because of the mention of boundaries, support, and form, it is only the self of a deity and not the Lord; [for the Lord is characterized] by being the Self of all and by being free from all evils."

The Lord is considered [the object of meditation]. Limits and so forth, though residing in limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), may also belong to the Lord for the purpose of meditation. In the first chapter of the *Chāndogya Upaniṣad*, after describing the secondary objects of meditation related to the meditation on the *udgītha*, this is recorded in order to prescribe the primary object of meditation: "Now, that golden person who is seen within the sun."

The Supreme Self is the subject under discussion here, because its specific attributes are taught as being located within the heart. Although there is an absence of both merit and demerit being performed or yet to be performed due to their lack of eligibility for ritual action, nevertheless, because suffering produced by causes such as [encounters with] Asuras and the like does exist, the evil accumulated in other births—which serves as the cause of that suffering—indeed persists. [The practice continues] until completion, but not beyond that; birth [of the result] occurs from the final condition for the sake of its accomplishment. And since that [flow] is accomplished even in a short time, therefore—
When it is argued that repetition [of mental activity] occurs only as long as one desires and not until death, we reply:

the final cognition (*antya-pratyaya*) which causes the next birth is not easily obtained without repetition until death; for this very reason, the *Smṛti* says, "One is always permeated by that state. How then does the final cognition of one going to heaven through rites such as the *Jyotiṣṭoma* arise from karma?

We say it is because of the *apūrva* (the unseen potentiality). If it is argued that there is also an *apūrva* in the case of meditation (*upāsana*), we reply: certainly. However, by this much, the visible means characterized by uninterrupted repetition should not be abandoned. Otherwise, since everything such as pleasure and pain would be produced by an *apūrva*, the visible effort for the sake of eating and so forth would have to be abandoned. Therefore, because it is a visible means, [one should practice] until death—

The turning back [of the breath] must be performed. Regarding the specific distinction concerning the departure (*utkrānti*) of a practitioner endowed with such a practice, it was considered in the second quarter of the fourth chapter: "Is there no distinction, or is there a distinction, for the practitioner at the time of departure?

There is no distinction because of the statement regarding the heart as the point of illumination; however, there is a distinction because of the exit by another [channel]. He departs through the channel at the crown of the head alone."

Because of the reflection on the channels (*nāḍī*) and because of the power of the *vidyā*, there is a distinction due to the departure by another [route]. It has been stated that this departure of the worshipper is the same as the other departure up until the commencement of the path. Now, it must also be the same even at the commencement of the path, because of the scriptural hearing of equality regarding the illumination of the heart and so forth. For it is thus:

Regarding this very heart, it is heard in scripture: "The tip of it flashes forth; by that flash, this Self departs—either through the eye, or through the crown of the head, or through other parts of the body. This is the meaning: when, in the sequence beginning with "speech merges into mind," the subtle body (liṅgaśarīra) together with the individual soul (jīva) dissolves into the Supreme Self, leaving behind only its residual power.

When that occurs, the previous birth comes to an end. Then, for the sake of another birth, that *liṅga* manifests again in the heart. At that moment, there arises a certain radiance (*pradyota*) situated at the tip of the heart, which is well-known in the world as the "final cognition" (*antyapratyaya*), consisting of the contemplation of the state of the future birth to be reached; [the soul] is endowed with that.
"It departs through the channels"—this applies equally to all. Therefore, one might conclude that there is no distinction between the worshipper and the others.

To this we reply: the worshipper departs through the channel at the crown of the head (*mūrdhan*), while the others depart through the other channels. Why? Because the worshipper has meditated upon the channel at the crown of the head as part of the knowledge of the Brahman with attributes (*saguṇabrahmavidyā*).

And because of the human context; furthermore, this meaning is clearly understood from another scriptural passage: "There are a hundred and one channels of the heart; one of them extends to the crown of the head.

Moving upward through that, one attains immortality; the others serve for departing in various directions. The meaning is that while the other channels are employed for departing [from the body], they do not lead to the attainment of immortality.
Therefore, there is a distinction for the lay follower (*upāsaka*). From this [distinction], due to the specific departure by way of the channel at the crown of the head—[as stated in the Sūtra]:

"Then the flame of the heart blazes up; its door being illuminated, [the soul departs] by means of the hundred-and-first [channel], through the power of knowledge, through the application of recollection of the path which is a remnant of that [knowledge], and being favored by the one dwelling in the heart" (Brahmasūtra 4.2.17).

[The organs] have proceeded [into their respective objects]. That statement is recited in the *Kha* [Chāndogya Upaniṣad]: "Of this person, my dear, when he is departing, speech merges into the mind; the mind into breath; breath into fire; fire into the supreme deity. In that context, for the dying person, the ten sense organs—exemplified by speech—attain their essential nature in the mind.

There is no dissolution [of the mind]; rather, the mere cessation of its activity is what is meant by "non-dissolution"—this is the first consideration. And the second is that there is non-dissolution of the activity of that mind within the *prāṇa*. And the third is the dissolution of the activity of that *prāṇa* into its own self, the individual soul (*jīva*), as stated in the *Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad*: "At the time of death, all the *prāṇas* gather together into this Self."

Thus ends the third [section]. This departure (*utkrānti*), which consists in the dissolution of the functions [of the senses], extending up to the commencement of the path characterized by exiting through the channels (*nāḍī*), is exactly the same for these three—the practitioner engaged in merit and demerit (*dharma-adharma*), the meditator (*upāsaka*), and the knower of reality (*tattva-jñānin*)—and not different;
thus ends the fourth [section]. That individual self (*jīvātman*) in which the external senses, the mind, and the vital breaths dissolve through their functional activity...

The fifth [view] is that the individual soul (*jīvātman*), in which the light [of consciousness] has dissolved through its function (*vṛtti*) into the primary pentad of elements, that very pentad of elements dissolves—through its function alone—into the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) for a person who lacks knowledge of Brahman, but not by way of its own essential nature (*svarūpeṇa*). Thus, by these five investigations, the departure common to all has been examined. Here, the Supreme...

The completion of the previous birth occurred through the dissolution of this subtle body (liṅga-śarīra), which consists of the forms of the five elements, within the Self. Next, a specific detail regarding the departure through the cranial channel for the sake of the seeker's attainment of the world of Brahman was investigated;
that has been set forth here in the passage beginning with "between the two palates" and ending with "having pushed aside the two halves of the skull."

And this [departure] should be understood as an illustration of the path extending up to the attainment of the world of Brahman (*brahmaloka*). Regarding that path, six deliberations have been undertaken by citing passages from other Vedic branches. Among them, the Chandogas [cite]:
"Now, when he departs from this body, he ascends upwards by means of these very rays" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.6.5), [indicating] the solar path.

Regarding one who has departed [from the body], the scriptures declare a connection with the rays of the sun. On this point, the opponent raises the objection that although such a connection is possible for one who dies during the day, it is not possible for a practitioner who dies at night. To this, the reply is given:

even though the rays of the sun are not manifest at night, there is indeed attainment of the rays because the connection between the channels (*nāḍīs*) and the rays persists as long as the body exists.

The first investigation: Having raised the prima facie (pūrvapak�s) position that for a worshipper who dies during the southern course (*dakṣiṇāyana*), there is no fruit of knowledge because the northern path (*uttaramārga*)—consisting of the rays of the sun and so forth—is heard of [only] in relation to the northern course (*uttarāyaṇa*), it was stated [in the siddhānta] that there is indeed a fruit, because by the term "northern course" the deity presiding over it is intended. This is the second [investigation]. The Chandogya...

In the *Bṛhadāraṇyaka* and the *Chāndogya*, the path beginning with light (*arcir-ādi*) is taught in the knowledge of the five fires (*pañcāgni-vidyā*) through such passages as "they reach the light" (*te 'rciṣam abhisaṃbhavanti*). However, in another knowledge-text, the Vājasaneyins recite a path beginning with wind (*vāyv-ādi*), starting with "he reaches the wind" (*sa vāyum āgacchati*). Furthermore, in the *Paryaṅka-vidyā*, the Kauṣītakins [recite]: "He [traverses] this path of the gods" (*sa etaṃ devayānaṃ panthānam ā-*)...
The text recites that one goes from the world of fire to the world of Varuṇa and so forth;

therefore, having raised the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) that the northern path (*uttaramārga*) consists of various [stages], it is established that the connection of the worlds of Vāyu, Agni, and the others is possible as successive stages (*parva-viśeṣa*) within a single path. [Note:
*kha*, *la*, *va*, *ṅa* read "svātma"; *ga* reads "mala"].

In the *Śikṣādhyāya* composed by Vidyāraṇya, it was stated that there is only one path beginning with light (*arcir-ādi*). This is the third [path]; [now follows] that which was taught in the *Kauṣītaki*.

Having raised the doubt that it is impossible for the world of Vāyu to be situated along the path, its placement prior to the sun is stated in the *Bṛhadāraṇyaka*, because of the scriptural hearing that one reaches the sun and other worlds by means of the path granted by Vāyu; this is the fourth [stage]. Likewise, there is the placement of the worlds of Varuṇa, Indra, and Prajāpati—spoken of in the *Kauṣītaki*—along the path.

Anticipating the possibility that lightning and Varuṇa might be connected by way of rain, and on the grounds that the world of Varuṇa must therefore be situated above the world of lightning—at the end of the *asituntus*—it was stated that the worlds of Indra and Prajāpati are situated above the world of Varuṇa. This is the fifth [stage]. Regarding the path, concerning the *arcis* (flame) and other stages mentioned therein, the path...

Having thus refuted the status of being a land of enjoyment (*bhogabhūmi*), the state of being a *vaitānika* deity has been declared. This is the sixth [point]. Having raised the doubt as to whether this path, determined by these six investigations, is common to both the realization of the reality of Brahman (*brahmatattvāvabodha*) and the meditation upon Brahman (*brahmopāsanā*), it has been determined that this path belongs exclusively to the domain of meditation. Furthermore, even among meditations...
Having raised the doubt as to whether the path [is mentioned] only there [in the *Chāndogya*], it has been determined that the path is common to all meditations (*upāsana*).

By that path, the worshipper attains Brahman; for it is stated that the attainment of Brahman occurs by means of a person belonging to Manu who resides in the world of lightning, in the words: "That person belongs to Manu; he leads them to Brahman. In that context, it is indeed the Supreme Brahman that is attained.

Having raised the doubt that [the soul] might go [to the world of Brahmā], it was determined that since movement toward the Supreme Brahman is impossible, the worshiper of Brahmā can attain only the effected (kārya) Brahmā-world, which is a specific region of the universe. Likewise, having raised the doubt that even those who worship symbols (pratīka) might attain the world of the effected Brahmā, it was determined that this applies only to the worshipers of Brahmā and not to others. This [attainment] occurs by way of the path beginning with light (arcirādi-mārga).

This is elaborated by the scripture beginning with "The Brahmaloka is *pyo*; that very [world] is *bhūḥ*; he becomes established in Agni" and ending with "the Lord of Consciousness. In that state, when the attainment of the Brahmaloka has occurred, both the individual identification (*vyaṣṭy-abhimāna*) and the collective identification (*samaṣṭy-abhimāna*) are realized. Between these two, through the individual identification, one attains identity with the deities such as Agni, Vāyu, and Āditya, and [becomes established] in their [powers].

He becomes established in the various sovereign powers (*aiśvarya*). However, through the conceit of being the collective whole (*samaṣṭy-abhimāna*), having become the form of Brahmā who presides over the worlds beginning with the earth (*bhūrloka*), he attains his own kingdom. It is precisely for the sake of accomplishing such a state of being the form of Brahmā that the Kauṣītakins, in the Paryaṅka-vidyā, declare regarding the yogin going to the world of Brahmā: "Five hundred Apsarases run toward him, and a hundred..."

A hundred [attendants] with mirrors in their hands, a hundred with garlands in their hands, a hundred with collyrium in their hands, a hundred with garments in their hands, and a hundred with fruits in their hands adorn him with the adornment of Brahman. Adorned with the adornment of Brahman, he, knowing Brahman, attains Brahman itself. Thus, this very sovereignty characterized by the attainment of Brahman has been determined through four investigations after having been analyzed.

Having raised the doubt that yogins dwelling in the world of Brahmā (brahmaloka) must depend upon external means for the production of objects of enjoyment just like those dwelling in the human world, it was determined that mere volition (*saṃkalpa*) alone is the means for that. This is the first investigation.
Regarding that yogin who creates the entire range of objects of enjoyment by mere volition, [the question arises] concerning the locus of his enjoyment...

Having raised the doubt that the existence and non-existence of the body, as declared by two [conflicting] scriptural passages, are established according to the distinction between different types of persons, [the author states: for one and the same [person]...

It has been established that the existence or non-existence of a person's body is subject to his own will; this is the second [point]. When this yogi creates many bodies simultaneously by his own will, at that time, only one among those bodies is endowed with the individual soul (jīvātman).

Anticipating the objection that other bodies might be devoid of that [consciousness], it is determined that all those bodies are indeed accompanied by individual *jīvātman*s who follow the will of that one [yogin]. This is the third [type of creation]. Just as the creation of the objects of enjoyment for that yogin—the bodies and *jīvātman*s—occurs through mere volition (*saṃkalpa*), so too does the creation of the five great elements, beginning with space (*ākāśa*).

Anticipating the doubt that there might be a creation of the material world, such as the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*) and so forth, it has been determined that the agency of creating the world belongs solely to the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*), who is beginningless and eternally established, and not to the yogi. This is the fourth [point]. For the yogi who has attained self-sovereignty (*svārājya*) as determined by these four investigations, in this very world of Brahman (*brahmaloka*), [resides] the Nirguṇa Brahman—

When there is the direct realization of reality (*tattva-sākṣātkāra*), upon the conclusion of the world of Brahmā (*brahmaloka*), disembodied liberation (*videha-kaivalya*) occurs. This meaning is recorded in the scripture beginning with the words "from that" (*tataḥ*). Having this very point in mind, the venerable Vyāsa also formulated a sūtra:

"Upon the dissolution of the effect, [the soul departs] together with its presiding deity, because of the scriptural statement regarding what is beyond. This refers to the dissolution of the "effect," namely the world of Brahmā.

Because it is stated thus in both Śruti and Smṛti: "At the time of dissolution, after [the dissolution] has truly occurred, he attains the Supreme Brahman along with Brahmā, the four-faced Lord of that world. And: "Those whose purpose is well-ascertained through the wisdom of Vedānta, who are self-controlled through the yoga of renunciation, and whose being is purified—they, at the time of their final end in the world of Brahmā, are all liberated through the Supreme Immortality."

Thus says the Śruti. And the Smṛti states: "When the time of universal dissolution arrives, all those who have perfected their selves enter the supreme state at the end of the highest [Brahmā]. Thus it is established that for the worshiper of Brahman, there is gradual liberation (kramamukti) preceded by the attainment of the world of Brahman (brahmaloka). Thus ends [the section] composed by the venerable Sāyaṇācārya in the [Śrī-Bukkaṇa-Sāmrājya-...].
The sixth section in the Sāṃhitya Upaniṣad of the Yajur Āraṇyaka, within the *Vedārthaprakāśa* composed by the supreme lord Vidyāraṇya Mādhava, the upholder of the burden of the Vedas. || 6 ||

In the sixth section (anuvāka), the meditation on Brahman as characterized by qualities such as consisting of mind (*manomaya*) was taught. Since that Brahman lacks specific qualities perceivable by the eye and is therefore intended for those of the highest qualification, the meditation on Brahman endowed with qualities perceivable by the eye is now set forth for those of moderate qualification in the seventh section. Therein, first, the cosmic aspect (*ādhibhautika*)—
He demonstrates the triad of fivefold groups: "earth and the intermediate space," etc. This refers to the fivefold world beginning with earth;

the fivefold deities beginning with fire; and the fivefold substances beginning with water. Therein, by the word "Self" (*ātman*), the Virāṭ Puruṣa in his collective form is denoted. Thus, these three aforementioned pentads constitute the objective sphere (*adhibhūta*) grasped by the notion of "I."

"Adhibhūta" means that [the Self] exists depending upon the elements—earth and so forth—which are distinct from these aforementioned vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and others, and which are apprehended by the notion of "this" (*idaṃ-pratyaya*). The meaning is that the meditation having the elements as its object has been described.
To ensure that it is not confused with what is to be said next, he first sets forth a formal proposition and then shows the other three pentads after distinguishing them. A—

Regarding the term *athādhyātmam*: after the explanation of the three pentads concerning the external elements (*bhūta*), the remainder [of the meaning] is that the three pentads concerning the internal self (*ātman*) are now being stated. In this aggregate of the body, senses, and so forth, for one who is devoid of the refinement of the scriptures—[the following occurs] through the continuations [of the mantras]. [Note: The manuscript variants cited refer to specific textual readings.]
[Page 197] 54 Composed by Vidyāraṇya.

In the Chapter on Training (*Śikṣādhyāya*), the notion of "I" in a person is this self well-known in the world; the meditation that takes place with reference to it is *adhyātma*. There is only one wind residing within the body, which has five distinct functional modes (*vṛtti*) such as *prāṇa* and the rest. A—
This very point was aphorized by the venerable Vyāsa in his inquiry into the vital breath (*prāṇa*): "The fivefold function [of the breath] is designated as being like that of the mind.

Furthermore, the distinction of the locations of these functions has been illustrated by the ancients: "Prāṇa is in the heart; apāna is in the anus; samāna is situated in the navel; udāna is in the region of the throat; and vyāna is throughout the entire body. Such is this pentad of winds.
What [is it]? The five senses, beginning with the eye; the five elements, beginning with the skin; and by the word "sinews," fat is denoted.

By both of these—the triad of the five external elements (*adhibhūta*) and the triad of the five internal elements (*adhyātma*)—the entire world, which serves as the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of Brahman, is designated. This very nature of Brahman, characterized by the limiting adjuncts of the world, is to be meditated upon.

[This is] the conclusion. Now, by means of an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), it implies an injunction for meditation (*upāsti*). "Having meditated upon this" (*etad adhi vidhāya*): a seer (*ṛṣiḥ*), a certain sage who perceives the supersensible meaning of the scripture, having meditated upon this—namely, the earth, the intermediate space, and so forth—as its true nature (*svarūpa*), and having meditated upon it extensively until it reached direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*), [perceived] through his own experience that which is the self of all.

Having attained the form of Virāj, he declared to his disciples the reality established through his own direct experience. What did he say? That is now being stated: this entire perceived universe is the form of Virāj, characterized by the *pāṅkta* (fivefold) pattern associated with the *paṅkti* meter. By the word "vai" (indeed), its well-known nature is expressed; for this fivefold character of everything is well known. To illustrate: there are five syllables in a [line of] *paṅkti*...
By the scriptural mention of the *paṅkti* meter, there is the number five; likewise, the world (*jagat*) is also endowed with the number five.

This is because those who know the tradition have declared that all the five great elements in their quintuplicated form (*pañcīkṛta*) and their effects are called *virāj*. Such being the case, there exists between the world and the *paṅkti* meter a relationship characterized by similarity.

Because it exists [as such], it possesses the nature of the fivefold (*pāṅkta*). Likewise, the meditation on earth and the other elements is also fivefold, because it is endowed with sets of five. By means of that very fivefold meditation, the practitioner satisfies—that is, gladdens or attains—the fivefold Virāj-form. The meaning is that he reaches it. From this explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), the injunction is inferred: "One who desires to attain the fivefold Virāj should meditate in this manner. This being so...
And upon reaching the state of Virāj, gradual liberation (kramamukti) should be understood through the arising of the knowledge of reality (tattvajñāna), according to the principle previously stated.

Thus ends the seventh section (anuvāka) in the Sāhitya Upaniṣad of the Yajur Āraṇyaka, in the *Vedārthaprakāśa* composed by the venerable Sāyaṇācārya, under the patronage of the supreme lord Mādhava Vidyāraṇya, the sustainer of the empire of the illustrious Bukkaṇa.

In the seventh [section], the meditation on Brahman as conditioned by gross forms such as earth was taught for the dull-witted person of gross vision. In the preceding sixth section, the meditation on Brahman as conditioned by subtle forms such as mind was taught for the middling person of somewhat subtle vision. Now, in the eighth section, [the meditation] for the superior qualified person is [taught] regarding that which is designated by the *praṇava*, as propounded in the Vedānta.

That which is called the meditation on the Pure Brahman is now described; therein, the nature of the object of meditation is shown by the words "Om, etc. The syllable *oṃ* is the designator (*vācaka*) of the Supreme Self. Thus, the *Yoga-sūtra* spoken by Patañjali was already cited previously:
"Its designator is the *praṇava*" (*tasya vācakaḥ praṇavaḥ*). The word "iti" is for the purpose of excluding other meanings. By this very word "Om," [the meditation is performed].
That very Brahman which is to be established is the object of meditation here; for in this context, there is no adjunct such as the mind or an adjunct such as the earth.
[Page 198]

Or rather, it should be considered as follows: the meaning is that while uttering the syllable *oṃ*, which is the designator (*vācaka*), one should meditate upon Brahman, the designated (*vācya*).

He demonstrates the suitability of the syllable *oṃ* to be the designator of Brahman with the words, "Oṃ, this [is all]. Within this very syllable *oṃ*, this entire world—both in the form of sound (*śabda-rūpa*) and in the form of meaning (*artha-rūpa*)—is contained. This is because, according to such scriptural passages as "Just as by a conch-shell," sound is included within it.

The inclusion [of all things] within that [syllable] has been taught; furthermore, by such scriptural passages as "Speech is its thread," the inclusion of other objects within it by way of sound has also been taught. All of this was elaborated upon in the commentary on the word *viśvarūpa* in the passage, "He who is the bull of the Vedas.
This being so, since the *praṇava* consists of everything, its fitness to denote Brahman, who is the self of all, is possible.

He demonstrates the universal connection of the syllable *oṃ* by citing examples from certain Vedic practices: "The syllable *om* is an imitation of this. In sacrifices such as the Darśapūrṇamāsa, when the Adhvaryu priests—who perform the rites prescribed in the Yajurveda—utter the directive mantra "O Āgnīdhra, cause [the Hotṛ] to hear" (*āśrāvaya*), they then recite the mantra "Oṃ, cause [him] to hear" (*oṃ śrāvaya*).

For this very reason, Āpastamba has cited that mantra optionally with the vowel *ā* at the beginning, the vowel *o* at the beginning, and the syllable *oṃ* at the beginning: "āśrāvaya," "vi vo śrāvaya," and "śrāvaya. Among those options, the second—the one with the vowel *o* at the beginning—is cited here by the Śruti. The vowel *au* occurring in the mantra is for the purpose of address; [the meaning is] "O Ā..."

The meaning of the mantra is that one should announce the opportunity for the offering of oblations to the gods. In that mantra, this utterance of the syllable *oṃ* constitutes an imitation (*anukṛti*) of it; that is, the imitation, the emulating, the production of similarity, of the *o*-sound which forms the portion preceding the letter *m* in the *praṇava*—that very thing is this "om."

The phrase *tadanukṛti* (imitation thereof) [is used]. The three particles *pra*, *siddhi*, and *dyotana*—expressed by the formula *ha sma vai*—indicate that the similarity to the portion of the *praṇava* is well-known (*prasiddha*) in the case of the syllable *oṃ*. The word *api* serves to include the examples that are about to be mentioned.
Even the *adhvaryu*s cause the announcement (*āśrāvayanti*) by means of the syllable *oṃ*, which is indeed a portion of the *praṇava*. Likewise, the *sāman*-singers, the *udgātṛ*s as well, [do so].

The Bahvṛca Hotṛ priests also perform the chanting of the *sāman* preceded by the utterance of the *praṇava*. Furthermore, they recite the *śastras*—namely those called *niṣkevalya*, *prauga*, and so forth—precisely by uttering the *praṇava* and the word "oṃ śom.
For instance, when the Hotṛs request permission from the Adhvaryu to recite the *śastra*, they make this request with the following mantra:
"O Adhvaryu, *śoṃsāvaum*. In this [formula], the word *śom* is seen at the beginning and the *praṇava* (the syllable *om*) at the end.

With reference to this, it is traditionally taught: "With *oṃ śom*, they recite the *śastra*s. O Adhvaryu, the meaning of the mantra is a request for permission: "What recitation shall we, the Hotṛs, perform? This is when the Hotṛ recites the *śastra*s.
At that time, the Adhvaryu utters a sound toward the Hotṛ priest, the reciter, as an expression of encouragement;

this sound is called the *pratigara*. When he responds with that *pratigara*, uttering it, he employs the syllable "oṃ" [at the end]. Āpastamba has stated this very clearly: "While holding the *ṛtupātra*..."

By stating that "oṃ" is an imitation (*anukaraṇa*) of the letter *o* occurring previously, it is indicated—by means of the two principles that "a modified part is not different [from the original]" and "an imitation follows the form of its prototype"—that when [the particle] *u* follows it, the substitution of the single subsequent form (*pararūpa*) applies according to the rule *omāṅośca*.

[In the chapter on training,] he responds while standing in the *sadobila*; "prahvo vāḥ" and "sthā moda iva" are at the half-verses; "othāmoda iva"—

At the pauses [of the recitation], the *praṇava* (the syllable *om*) alone constitutes the end. When the first half of a single *ṛc* in the middle of the *śastra* has been completed, the Adhvaryu then employs this response (*pratigara*): "atha ā moda iva. By means of the syllable *oka*, the Hotṛ is addressed. The meaning is: "O Hotṛ, after the recitation of the half-verse (*ardharca*), a joy (*moda*) as it were has arisen for us. At the conclusion of the *ṛc*—

The *praṇava* (the syllable Om) should not be employed at the beginning of the *pratigara* response; rather, it exists for the purpose of signifying acceptance (*aṅgīkāra*). At the conclusion of the entire *śastra* recitation, the *praṇava* alone must be employed for the sake of signifying acceptance. Therefore, the *praṇava* follows along even into the *pratigara*. Furthermore, when the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*), namely the *brahmā*, who is knowledgeable in the ritual applications prescribed in the three Vedas, performs actions such as sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*)...

At that time, he impels his own officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), urging them with the syllable *oṃ* preceded by the sacred *praṇava*, saying "Oṃ, sprinkle! When the Adhvaryu priest draws the sacrificial substance— milk— from the vessel into the vessel called the *agnihotrahavaṇī* using the *sruva* ladle,
he then addresses the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) with the mantra beginning, "Oṃ, I shall draw up the oblation for the gods."

He requests permission; and that sacrificer grants the permission with the syllable *oṃ*. Thus the author of the Sūtras says: "He gives permission loudly, saying 'Recite this! Likewise, a Brāhmaṇa desiring to perform the *brahmayajña* employs the *praṇava* at the beginning of the sacred recitation named *brahmayajña*. And so it is traditionally taught in the section concerning the *brahmayajña*:

"Having placed the right and left hands together with the *pavitra* grass, he begins with 'Oṃ'. To "begin" means that he undertakes the *brahmayajña*. Thus, through these Vedic examples, the pervasion of the syllable *oṃ* has been explained in detail.
Now, under the guise of stating the fruit [of the practice], he deduces the rule for its meditative worship: "Brahman..."—that person who has attained Brahman...
"He who desires [something] should meditate upon Brahman as denoted by this word 'Om'"; through that meditation, he indeed attains Brahman. Now, the inquiry:

here it must be considered whether, in the statement "Om is Brahman," the perception of Brahman is enjoined with respect to the syllable *oṃ* as a mere symbol (*pratīka*), or whether the object of meditation, Brahman, is qualified by the word "Om."

"It is qualified by that. In this context, the syllable *om*—referring to it as "that which is *om* is Brahman"—is presented as the substratum for the imposition of the concept of Brahman (*brahmadṛṣṭi*). This being the case, the sequential presentation of the subject and the predicate is justified;
such is the prima facie view. To this we reply: here, the status of the *oṃkāra* as a qualifier must be understood according to the principle of the *udgītha*. That...

And this principle is demonstrated in the third pāda of the third chapter [of the Brahma-sūtras]: "Is it superimposition (adhyāsa), or sublation (bādha), or identity (aikya), or qualification (viśeṣyatā)? Here, regarding the syllable (akṣara), none of these is fixed, due to the absence of a specific reason. In the Vedas, the pervasive Oṃkāra is qualified by the Udgītha. In cases of superimposition and the rest, a result must be inferred; [otherwise] there would be a figurative indication (lakṣaṇā) of a proximate part."
"The syllable 'Om', this very one, one should meditate upon as the Udgītha"—thus the co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of the syllable and the Udgītha is heard in scripture.

Regarding this, there is a fourfold doubt. For instance, in the passage "One should meditate upon Name as Brahman," co-referentiality is heard for the purpose of superimposing the vision of Brahman upon the Name. Similarly, it is cited in cases of sublation (*bādha*) and so forth: "He who is a thief is a post."

Furthermore, since the superimposition of agency and so forth is based on the notion of "I" (*ahaṃpratyaya*), it is sublated by the realization of the Self as "not-I" (*anahaṃpratyaya*). In the ninth *anuvāka*, it was stated that the performance of *śrauta* and *smārta* rituals should be combined with the meditation on Brahman (*brahmopāsana*).

In connection with that, it was stated that the *brahmayajña* (the sacrifice of sacred knowledge) is the highest austerity (*tapas*). Now, for one who, though possessed of faith, is unable to perform the *brahmayajña* due to the absence of Vedic recitation caused by defects such as dullness of intellect, [the text provides] a mantra to be chanted (*japya*) for the attainment of the fruit of the *brahmayajña*.

The *Śamānuvāka* demonstrates this with the verse, "I am the tree" (*ahaṃ vṛkṣasya*). It is called "tree" (*vṛkṣa*) because it is cut down—that is, severed—by the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*). This transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*) has been clearly elucidated by a certain mantra in the context of the *Āruṇaketuka*: "He who knows the tree whose root is above and whose branches are below. Here, "above" means the Supreme Brahman, which is superior to the entire world; it is the "root," that is, the cause.

This tree of saṃsāra has its roots above; it has downward-branching limbs, namely the bodies of gods, humans, and animals, and is thus "downward-branching. This is also recorded in the Kaṭha Upaniṣad: "Rooted above and branching below is this eternal aśvattha.
It is called *aśvattha* because, due to its impermanence, it does not remain even until tomorrow (*śvas*). Its "eternality" (*sanātanatva*) refers to its beginninglessness.

This tree was also described by the Blessed One: "They call the imperishable Aśvattha tree that which has its roots above and its branches below; the Vedas are its leaves—he who knows it is a knower of the Veda. The remainder of the sense is: "May I, desiring liberation, become a cutter (rerivā) of this Aśvattha tree in the form of saṃsāra, using the weapon consisting of detachment from sense objects."
This word is derived from the verbal root *rī*, meaning "to injure. The Blessed One has declared that its cutting is performed by the weapon of dispassion (*vairāgya*):

"Having cut down this *aśvattha* tree with its deeply rooted roots by means of the firm weapon of non-attachment, one must then seek that Goal, having reached which they do not return again. When the tree of *saṃsāra* is thus cut down, my [teaching]—

It is like the ridge of Mount Ṛtīgir; just as the upper portion of a mountain is exceedingly lofty, so too my fame regarding liberation, being exceedingly exalted, spreads even into the worlds of the gods. Therefore, even the gods are not able to obstruct my human effort (*puruṣārtha*). And thus it is heard in scripture: "Neither the gods nor [the Asuras] were able to thwart him."
"He rules," [it is said]. "O Vājī, like my own immortality, I am one whose purifier is turned upward. Vāja is movement;
that which possesses it is the Sun (Āditya), for he always moves with speed. And thus it has been said:
"He who traverses two thousand yojanas, two hundred yojanas, and two more yojanas in half a moment—to him, salutation be! To him—

In the ripened sun, the Aditya, there exists excellent nectar (amṛta). For this very reason, in the Madhuvidyā, the Chandogas have recorded that the solar orb is of the nature of honey; they have taught that in its eastern and other quarters there are nectars of the colors red, white, and so forth, which consist of the fruits of actions proclaimed in the Ṛgveda and the other Vedas. "That which is the first nectar, upon that the Vasus subsist... [and so on].

By the words beginning with "they flow," the scriptures declare that those nectars are the sustenance for the Vasus and the other classes of gods. This very nectar situated within the solar orb is beautiful and exceedingly pure. Likewise, I too am "ūrdhvapavitra"—one whose purity is directed upwards, meaning my excellence and fragrance rise upward. (Note: Variant readings include *mārgeṣvṛ*).
