"In this chapter on training, I am one whose purity is such that I am purified from above; for me who am thus, may resplendent wealth (*draviṇa*) be accomplished. For wealth is of two kinds: human and divine. Among these, that which is visible to the eye, such as gold, silver, and so forth..."

The human is that which is heard with the ear; the divine is that which is understood in the Veda, such as the knowledge of Brahman and so forth. For this very reason, the Vājasaneyins prescribe the contemplation of the eye and the ear as human and divine wealth respectively in a certain meditation: "The eye is human wealth, for by the eye one finds it; the ear is divine, for by the ear one hears it."
Thus [it is said]. In this context, with reference to the "divine wealth" (*daivavitta*), it is qualified as "radiant" (*savarcasam*). "Radiance" (*varcas*) means strength;

because of its connection with that, the divine wealth—which is the knowledge of Brahman—is appropriately characterized by strength, since it brings about the cessation of the entire cycle of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*). May I, endowed here with this divine wealth in the form of the knowledge of Brahman—denoted by the word *draviṇa*—be possessed of excellent intelligence and sprinkled with immortality.

I am one whose intellect (*medhā*) is excellent—that is, I possess the power to comprehend both the texts and their meanings that expound the knowledge of Brahman; therefore, I am sprinkled (*ukṣita*), drenched with the nectar of the bliss of Brahman. Thus, the mantra beginning with "I [am] the tree" (*vṛkṣasya*) is the Vedic recitation (*vedānuvacana*)—the study of the Veda preceded by the teacher—according to the opinion of the sage named Triśaṅku.

The meaning of "subsequent speech" is the recitation of the Veda for the sake of the Brahma-sacrifice and as an austerity. Thus ends the tenth section in the Sāhitya Upaniṣad of the Yajurveda Āraṇyaka, within the *Vedārthaprakāśa* composed by the venerable Sāyaṇācārya, the minister of the empire of the illustrious Bukkaṇa and the spiritual preceptor of Mādhava Vidyāraṇyaparameśvara. 10.

In the tenth [section], the mantra to be recited as a substitute for the *brahmayajña* has been stated; thus, the *brahmayajña* becomes easy to perform even for one of dull intellect. Likewise, the combination (*samuccaya*) of the *śrauta* and *smārta* rites with the aforementioned meditation (*upāsanā*)—namely, "the *ṛta*, as well as study and teaching"—is firmly established as the cause of gradual liberation (*kramamukti*). Now, in the eleventh section, regarding mere ritual acts (*kevalakarman*)...
Intending that [the study of the Veda] is a cause for liberation by way of generating the desire to know (*vividiṣā*), he prescribes its instruction with the words, "Having recited the Veda...

The nature of the teacher is recorded by Manu: "That twice-born man who, having initiated a pupil, teaches him the Veda along with the ritual manuals (*kalpa*) and the secret portions (*rahasya*), him they call an *ācārya*. At the end, [he refers to] the previously mentioned *ācārya*...

One who always dwells in the proximity [of the teacher] is an *antevāsī* (resident pupil). For it is stated in the *Smṛti*: "He should dwell constantly with the teacher like a shadow, never abandoning him. To such a disciple, the teacher, having recited the Veda (*vedam anūcya*)—that is, after the initiation (*upanayana*) and subsequently having taught it—instructs him. He causes him to grasp the meaning that is to be practiced after the mastery of the text. By this, it is understood that [the instruction follows] once the study has been completed.

"One should not return from the teacher's house without having performed the inquiry into Dharma by means of the Veda. He shows the manner of this instruction in brief: "Truth," etc. By the word "truth" (*satya*), all those things well-known in the Smṛtis—such as non-violence, truthfulness, and non-stealing—are indicated. By the word "Dharma," the Agnihotra and other rites enjoined by the direct Śruti are meant.

[They] have been explained. Since Jaimini has aphorized that "Dharma is a purpose characterized by an injunction" (*codanā-lakṣaṇo 'rtho dharmaḥ*), the intended meaning of the two summary statements—that all Śrauta and Smārta rites must be performed—is as follows:

according to the maxim that "when a scriptural requirement has been fulfilled once, it is fulfilled," once the Śrauta and Smārta rites have been performed once, their subsequent abandonment is impossible; therefore, [there can be no] abandonment of them.

The text prohibits negligence regarding form (*rūpa*). Regarding the phrase "from one's own study" (*svādhyāyāt*): it refers to the Vedic study (*svādhyāya*) that has been acquired through formal recitation.

Do not commit forgetfulness or negligence; for according to the *Smṛti*, "the loss of what has been studied should be known as equal to the killing of a Brahmin. Having acquired wealth in the form of cattle, gold, clothing, and so forth—which is dear to the teacher—and having offered it to the Guru as a fee (*dakṣiṇā*), you should then perform the marriage ceremony. Do not cause the severance of the lineage (*tantu*) of progeny, consisting of sons, grandsons, and so forth.

Do not [neglect]. Regarding the truth (*satya*) and dharma (*dharma*) previously mentioned, negligence (*pramāda*) is the failure to practice them at times due to laziness; that too must not be committed. "Welfare" (*kuśala*) means security (*kṣema*); by that term, the action which is its cause is intended. And that is of two kinds: Vedic and worldly. For one who is chronically ill, or for one who might desire, "May I live the full span of life," therefore—

"One should perform this sacrifice," and so forth, refers to Vedic means that bestow longevity and health; "doubt" and so forth refer to worldly means. "Prosperity" (*bhūti*) means sovereignty; by this term, its cause is indicated. In that regard as well, "one desiring prosperity should sacrifice a white animal to Vāyu," and so forth, is Vedic; "accepting gifts" and so forth are worldly. In the absence of skill and prosperity, [the following applies]... *mu-* (incomplete).

Since the performance of rituals requiring three causal factors (*tri-hetuka-karma*) is impossible for those two [classes], their non-negligence (*apramāda*) must be enjoined. While negligence in the form of forgetting what has been studied was previously prevented, here negligence in the form of failing to perform the study of the Veda intended for teaching and the *brahmayajña* sacrifice is prevented. As for divine rites (*devakārya*), these include the worship of Vināyaka and the *anantavrata* and so forth, excluding those prescribed in the Purāṇas.

The ancestral rites (*pitṛkārya*) are performed annually and so forth. Now, with regard to one's mother and others, he prescribes worship by means of the conception of them as deities, having abandoned the conception of them as mere human beings: "Be one for whom the mother is a god" (*mātṛdevo bhava*). One who has a mother who is a deity to be worshipped—meaning a deity in the form of Rudra, Viṣṇu, Vināyaka, and so on—is a "mother-god" (*mātṛdeva*). The same applies to the subsequent [injunctions] as well. As it was said regarding *kuśa*...

"One must not be negligent regarding prosperity; one must not be negligent regarding well-being. In this regard, he points out a certain distinction with the words, "those which are blameless. Actions that cause security and sovereignty are of two kinds: blameless and blameworthy.
Among these, those previously cited—such as the sacrifice for long life (*āyuṣkāmeṣṭi*), receiving gifts, officiating at sacrifices, and so forth—are blameless.

These [virtuous deeds] are to be practiced; however, others such as malevolent rites (*ābhicāra*) and the like, although they may cause security by means of killing enemies, are not to be practiced because they are censured for leading to hell. Now, one might object: since the conduct of the learned (*śiṣṭācāra*) is authoritative just like the *Śruti* and *Smṛti*, all the actions performed by you, our teacher, ought to be practiced. To this, [the author] replies:
Furthermore, he shows the distinction therein with the words, "Those which are ours. Conduct is of two kinds: divine (*daiva*) and demoniac (*āsura*).

The Blessed One has declared both of them: "Fearlessness, purity of being, steadfastness in the yoga of knowledge, charity, self-restraint, sacrifice, study of the scriptures, austerity, uprightness, non-violence, truthfulness, freedom from anger, renunciation, tranquility... [ŚB 16.1.7]

Non-violence, compassion toward all beings, freedom from greed, gentleness, modesty, and steadiness; vigor, forgiveness, fortitude, purity, absence of malice, and lack of excessive pride—these, O Bhārata, belong to one born with divine fortune. Hypocrisy, arrogance, self-conceit, anger, harshness, and ignorance—these, O Pārtha, belong to one born with demoniac fortune.

"The divine endowment leads to liberation, while the demonic endowment leads to bondage"—thus it is said. In this regard, you should cultivate those virtuous practices belonging to us, such as fearlessness and so forth, which have been described by You; however, you must not cultivate hypocrisy and the like.
This principle is to be applied everywhere in the conduct of the cultured (śiṣṭa). For instance, Paraśurāma [Jāmadagnya], at the command of his father...
1 ga. It is characterized.
In the *Śikṣādhyāya* composed by Vidyāraṇya,
even regarding the passage stating that he killed his own mother, one must respect the noble conduct consisting in the fulfillment of his father’s command; however, not the killing of the mother—
Misconduct takes the form of killing; in this manner, other [examples] should also be cited. Now, he teaches a certain distinction regarding service to great persons (mahāpuruṣa):

"Whosoever among us... Those who are superior to us—meaning to you, our teachers—in terms of qualities such as age and learning, and who are steadfast in Dharma, their relief [is attained] through service such as offering seats and washing their feet. This is the hearing [of the Dharma].
"You must not show them disrespect; nor should you even breathe upon their seats.

What need is there to say that you must not engage in debate or the like out of a sense of self-importance or confidence? Therefore, you must simply accept the meaning as it is taught by him. Now, he teaches a certain distinction regarding giving.
Regarding the phrase "with faith": when wealth is given after having reflected upon it, then it must be given by you endowed with faith alone;
however, nothing at all should be given without faith, because a gift devoid of faith is of no use in either of the two worlds.
And so it has been said by the Blessed One: "Whatever is offered, given, or performed as austerity without faith—that [is fruitless]."

Thus it is said, O Pārtha: "Neither here nor having gone there is that [fruit]. This is the explanation under the interpretation of the word-break as *adeyam* (not to be given). Alternatively, the word-break is *deyam* (to be given). Just as one gives when endowed with faith, so too must one give even in the absence of faith; the very absence of the fruit of *sāttvika* giving is shown by the cited statement.

The fruit of giving characterized by passion (*rājasa*) and darkness (*tāmasa*) indeed exists; for this very reason, the Blessed One has declared a threefold classification of giving: "That gift which is given with the thought 'it ought to be given,' to one who does no service in return, at the right place and time, and to a worthy recipient—that gift is remembered as *sāttvika* (pure). But that which is given for the sake of a return favor, or again, aiming for a fruit, and which is given with reluctance—that is *rājasa* (passionate)."

"It is declared to be *tāmasa* (dark) when a gift is given at an improper place and time, to unworthy recipients, without respect, and with contempt. [This concludes the section on] the glory of wealth (*śrīvibhava*). *Hrī* is modesty; *bhī* is fear of the scriptures; *saṃvit* is the specific knowledge of place, time, and recipient.
By these words, the threefold gift mentioned previously is further elaborated. From the abundance of wealth comes *śrī*...

"I possess [wealth]. Just as male and female servants there might steal my property, so too might it be stolen by Brahmins"—thus despising [others], the gift one makes with prosperity as the motive is *tāmasa*. Or, "People equal to me give gifts; because of this gift, I feel great shame"—thus, with shame as the motive...

That which is given out of contempt as previously described is *rājasa*. That gift which is prescribed by the scriptures for the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) and others, given out of fear that "if I do not give it, I shall incur sin," is *sāttvika*.
In that regard, the four principal priests, headed by the *adhvaryu*, deserve complete sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*). [The others,] such as the *pratiprasthātṛ* and so forth—

He deserves half of that; the Neṣṭṛ and others deserve a third part; and the Unnetṛ and others deserve a fourth part—one endowed with such discerning knowledge (*viveka-jñāna*) should give as a *sāttvika* donor. Alternatively, all of this refers specifically to the domain of *sāttvika* giving. According to scriptural injunctions such as "one should not practice stinginess regarding wealth," one should give in accordance with one's means. [Regarding] a small gift—
Thinking, "By this, great shame will come upon my master," one possessed by such shame should give abundantly.

Having thus instructed on a matter to be performed that was previously unknown, he subsequently instructs on the means of reaching a decision regarding a matter to be performed that is doubtful. (1) [The] task.

Now, as for the phrase "if those": "action" refers to both *śrauta* action, such as the *agnihotra*, and *smārta* action, such as the *saṃdhyāvandana*. For one who has heard the two scriptural statements, "He offers when the sun has risen" and "He offers before the sun has risen," doubt may arise regarding the *śrauta* ritual.

Even regarding the Smārta [tradition], there is doubt due to two conflicting statements as to whether the deity of the Sandhyā is in male form or female form. Regarding *vṛtta*—the worldly conduct handed down through family lineage—even therein, doubt arises for one who observes contradictions such as marriage with the daughter of a maternal uncle or the eating of meat. At that time, in whichever country, at whichever time, and in whichever family one [is born]...

In those particular places, times, and families, you should conduct yourself in the same manner as the Brāhmaṇas who reside there—distinguished by such qualities as wisdom (*saṃmarśa*)—would conduct themselves regarding that doubtful matter. "Wise" (*saṃmarśin*) refers to those who are free from defects such as passion, hatred, and restlessness, and are skilled in determining the true meaning of the scriptures. [They are those who perform] the obligatory and occasional rites...

They are "engaged" (yuktāḥ) because they have personally set out toward the performance [of their duties]. Furthermore, they are "thoroughly engaged" (āyuktāḥ) because they are engaged from all sides; the meaning is that they are devoted in this way, thinking, "We shall perform [the rites] correctly and without deficiency. They are "not harsh" (alūkṣāḥ), being devoid of either harshness or stubborn resentment. They are "desirous of dharma" (dharmakāmāḥ), meaning they desire only dharma and not gain, honor, or the like. Thus, in this state of being free from doubt—

Having taught the means for determining legal matters (*dharmanirṇaya*), he next teaches the means for determining the exclusion from social intercourse (*avyavahāryatva*) regarding persons censured due to suspicion of grave sins (*pātaka*) and the like. "Now, concerning those who are falsely accused" (*athābhyākhyāteṣu*); this is to be explained as before. He concludes the aforementioned instruction: "This is the command" (*eṣa ādeśaḥ*). Beginning with "Speak the truth," one should conduct oneself toward them in that manner.

This entire collection of texts is *ādeśa*, which is the scriptural injunction (*śrauta-vidhi*). Just as a king commands his own servant, so too does the Vedic injunction command the performer. Because it stands in proximity to the *ādeśa*, the Smṛti injunction is called *upadeśa*. Since the Smṛtis are rooted in the Veda, they stand in proximity to it. [This applies to] that which is not directly perceived in the Śruti...

Even in the foundational *smṛtis*, the meaning of such statements as "speak the truth" is understood in this very same way. This utterance, "speak the truth," and so forth, is itself the *vedopaniṣad*—the secret of the Veda. Within the Veda, which consists of injunctions (*vidhi*), explanatory passages (*arthavāda*), and mantras, that which takes the form of an injunction is the essential portion. That which begins with "speak the truth" is this very instruction (*anuśāsana*), the command of the Lord. [Thus ends] the *Śruti-smṛti*...

Because it has been stated by the Lord, "These are my very commands," and because truthfulness and so forth—prescribed by the Śrauta and Smārta injunctions, the secret of the Vedas, and the form of the Lord’s command—must therefore be meditated upon and performed in the manner thus described.
The repetition, "It must be meditated upon in this way," is for the sake of emphasis. The term *uvaca* is a collection of indeclinables (*avyaya*).
This is for the purpose of retention. It must be practiced exactly in the manner described; it can never be abandoned.

Seeing such reverence for this [text], some describe liberation as being attained through ritual actions (*karma*) alone, while others maintain it is through the combination of knowledge and action (*jñāna-karma-samuccaya*). Both of these positions have already been refuted by us in the context of explaining the relationship between the earlier and later sections (*pūrva-uttara-kāṇḍa*) of the Vedas.

Although actions do not directly constitute the cause of liberation, their status as a cause is intended by way of generating the desire to know (*vividiṣā*); it is with this in mind that their instruction is recorded within the section on knowledge (*vidyā-prakaraṇa*). Whether liberation, the fruit of knowledge, is independent of action was deliberated upon in the fourth quarter of the third chapter: "Does the realization of the Self depend on action for its fruit, or not? Indeed, it does not depend [on it]."
And for this very reason, there is no dependence on fuel and the like. (Sūtra 3.4.5).

Composed by Vidyāraṇya [in the chapter on training]

Because dependence [of a principal act] upon its constituent parts is observed in the case of the *prayāja* offerings and so forth; and because independence is seen between knowledge and the lamp in the dispelling of ignorance and darkness, therefore here too, knowledge is independent of ritual action. [Thesis: The realization of the reality of Brahman under dispute requires ritual action as its own constituent part for the bestowing of its own fruit, because it is a principal act (*aṅgin*), like the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices which require the *prayāja* offerings and so forth.

Although in the first section (adhikaraṇa), by establishing that knowledge is an independent human goal, its status as a subordinate part (aṅga) of ritual action was refuted; nevertheless, its status as the principal part (aṅgin) was not refuted. Therefore, the reason [for our position] is not unestablished. Thus, when it is argued that realization depends upon ritual action, we reply: the subject under dispute, the knowledge of Brahman, does not depend on anything else for the removal of that which is to be removed by itself.

Because it is illuminating, like a lamp, and like the cognition of a jar. As for that which was stated regarding its being a subordinate factor (*aṅga*): what kind of subordinacy do you intend for action (*karman*) in that case? Is it subordinacy as an auxiliary that assists the result (*phalopakāryaṅgatva*), like the *prayāja* offerings and so forth, or is it subordinacy as an auxiliary that assists the essential nature (*svarūpopakāryaṅgatva*), like the husking (*avaghāta*) and so forth?
Not the first, because liberation would then be subject to impermanence due to being produced by action. In the second case, the probandum is lacking [in the example].

The illustration [is provided] because the *prayāja* offerings and so forth lack the status of being auxiliary factors that assist in the essential nature [of the sacrifice]. Therefore, once knowledge has arisen, it does not depend upon ritual actions for the bestowal of its own fruit. As for the dependence of knowledge upon action even for its own origination, that too has been considered in that very context: "Is this [knowledge] independent in its origination, or does it depend upon actions? Just as there is no dependence regarding the fruit, so too there is no dependence regarding its origination. [This concludes the section on] sacrifice.

The arising of knowledge depends on rites such as those for peace (*śānti*) and so forth, according to two scriptural passages. Just as a horse, though not required for a plough, is required for a chariot, so too *brahmavidyā* does not depend on ritual actions (*karman*) for its own fruit; yet, just as it does not depend on them for its fruit, it likewise does not depend on them for its own origination. Otherwise, the fallacy of the "half-old woman" (*ardhajaratīya*) would ensue—that it depends on them in some cases and does not depend on them in others. To this we reply: there is no such "half-old woman" inconsistency. *Note: The provided text appears to be a fragment from a commentary on the Vedānta Sūtras (likely Śaṅkara Bhāṣya on 3.4.26).*
This [objection] does not exist here, because by virtue of its inherent capacity (*yogyatā*), it is logical for the very same thing to be both required and not required for specific effects;

just as a horse, though not required for pulling a plow, is required for pulling a chariot, so it is in this case. Furthermore, there is no lack of evidence for the requirement of ritual action (*karman*) for the arising of knowledge (*vidyā*), as stated in the text: "Brahmins seek to know this very Self through the study of the Vedas and through sacrifice. (*tametam vedānuvacanena brāhmaṇā vividiṣanti yajñena*).

This is because it is understood that those forms of activity such as giving, austerity, and fasting are external means (*bahiraṅga-sādhana*) for the arising of knowledge by way of producing the desire to know (*vividiṣā*), whereas those forms of cessation such as tranquility, self-control, withdrawal, endurance, and concentration— expressed in the passage, "Having become tranquil,
self-controlled, withdrawn, patient, and concentrated, one sees the Self in the Self alone"— are [internal means] for the arising of knowledge.

Because they are enjoined as means (*sādhana*), it is understood that they are internal means; therefore, sacrifices and the like, as well as tranquility, self-control, and so forth, are required for the arising of knowledge (*vidyā*). Furthermore, the accomplishment of the stages of life (*āśrama*) by those very same causes of knowledge has been deliberated upon in that very [section]. [The question arises: Is there a double performance for the sake of knowledge and for the sake of the stage of life, or is it once? [This depends on] the distinction of purpose.

The application (*prayoga*) also differs. It is said that through the statement "for the sake of *śrāddha* there shall be satisfaction," and through the statement "likewise for the sake of knowledge there is the stage of life (*āśrama*"), there is a connection between the non-eternal and the eternal, as is held regarding the *khadira* wood. Those very rites such as sacrifices which are prescribed in the *vividiṣā* passage as causes for knowledge are the same as those prescribed in the earlier section (*pūrvakāṇḍa*) as duties of the stages of life (*āśramadharma*).

Since it might be argued that their performance [of duties] is due to a twofold purpose, we reply: just as when one eats for the sake of a *śrāddha* rite, satiety is accomplished as an inseparable consequence (*nāntarīyakatayā*), so too may the duties of the stages of life (*āśramadharma*) accomplished for the sake of knowledge (*vidyā*) be fulfilled. And it is not the case that knowledge requires everything;

for there is the scriptural statement regarding sacrifices and so forth, "And [knowledge] requires all [works], because of the scriptural mention of sacrifice etc., like the horse" (Sūtra 3.4.6), and also because the duties of the stages of life are enjoined [as auxiliaries to knowledge] (Sūtra 3.4.8).
1 ga. va. In the *kṣā* [section].

It should not be argued that there is a contradiction between the obligatory (*nitya*) and the non-obligatory (*anitya*) connection due to the desire-driven nature of the causal factors (*hetu*) and the obligatory nature of the duties of the stages of life (*āśramadharma*), because by the force of two scriptural statements, it is possible for a single action to possess two forms. Just as in the case of the *khādira*...

The sacrificial post (*yūpa*) is made of *rohitaka* wood; "one desiring vigor should make the post of *khadira* wood"—in this case, by these two statements, there is both the obligatory nature and the optional nature of a single thing. Likewise, for sacrifices and other rites that are of both kinds, there is performance only once. Furthermore, the fact that even the duties of those not belonging to a specific stage of life (*anāśramika-karman*) serve as a cause for knowledge was considered in that very same context: "There is no knowledge for one who does not belong to a stage of life."

Or rather, it does not exist at all; for there is an absence of the cause of knowledge, namely the state of belonging to an *āśrama* for the sake of purifying the intellect. [Objection: Everything exists indeed, because of the purification of the mind through *japa* and other practices related to the *āśramas*. For it is heard that the learning of Raikva and others was exceedingly pure even while they were in an *āśrama*. [Response: Having previously completed an *āśrama*, one who has not entered a subsequent *āśrama* for some reason is a *snātaka* who is without an *āśrama* (*anāśramī*). Vidhu...

It may be argued that for such a person (one who has left the order), the knowledge of reality is not possible because of the absence of an *āśrama* (stage of life) which is the cause for the purification of the intellect.

To this we reply: knowledge is indeed possible even for those who do not belong to an *āśrama*, because practices such as the silent recitation (*japa*) are causes for the purification of the intellect independently of an *āśrama*. This is supported by the Smṛti: "By recitation alone, a Brāhmaṇa attains perfection; there is no doubt in this matter. And it is also heard in the Śruti... [text continues].

In the science of cattle (*rgavidyā*), even one who is not in a stage of life (*anāśramin*) is qualified, as seen in the case of Raikva, who sought marriage. Likewise, Gārgī and others who were devoid of a stage of life may be cited as examples. Nor does this render the stages of life useless, for they serve as causes for an excellence of purity. Therefore, spiritual knowledge (*vijñāna*) is possible even for those outside the stages of life. Thus, in the work composed by the venerable Sāyaṇācārya...

In the *Vedārthaprakāśa* by the supreme lord Mādhava-Vidyāraṇya, the upholder of the imperial throne of the illustrious Bukkaṇa, this is the eleventh section (*anuvāka*) in the *Sāṃhitī Upaniṣad* of the *Yajurveda Āraṇyaka*. || 11 ||

In the eleventh chapter, the instruction of the teacher to the disciple has been stated. By that much, it was understood that there exist meditations (*upāsana*) and ritual acts (*karman*) which are external means for the knowledge of the reality of Brahman. Now, at the conclusion of the study of the text, the knowledge of its meaning, and the performance of those rites, [the author] shows in the twelfth chapter the peace-mantra (*śāntimantra*) to be recited: *śaṃ no mi-* [etc.].

Regarding the word *tra*: the meaning of the syllables is to be understood as being like the mantra recited at the beginning. At the time of the commencement, because Brahman had not yet been mentioned, it was recited as "I shall speak of Brahman" (*brahma vadiṣyāmi*). Likewise, because the removal of obstacles is something to be prayed for, it was recited as "may [it] protect" (*avatv iti*). But at the conclusion, since Brahman has already been mentioned and the host of obstacles has already been removed, [it is recited as] "it has protected" (*avā-*)...

It is read as *diṣṭamāvīt*. This further reference to the accomplished removal of obstacles is for the purpose of preventing ungratefulness (*kṛtaghnatva*). Otherwise, for a seeker of liberation who is unaware of the assistance rendered by deities such as Mitra and Varuṇa, the charge of ingratitude would follow, which is improper. For it is stated in the Smṛti: "An expiation is seen for the slayer of a Brahmin, but there is no expiation for the ungrateful."

Even when the performance of the means [of attainment] has been completed, the fruit might be obstructed by the fault of ingratitude (*kṛtaghnatva*). Lest that happen, the pacification of internal and other obstacles is accomplished; thus, the assistance rendered by the deity is recalled. "By illuminating the meaning of the Vedas and dispelling the darkness of the heart, may the Great Lord Vidyātīrtha bestow the four aims of human life. Thus [it is said].

In the commentary composed by the venerable Sāyaṇācārya, [entitled] *Mādhavīya-vedārthaprakāśa*, under the patronage of the supreme lord Mādhava Vidyāraṇya, who bore the burden of the empire of the illustrious Bukkaṇa—[this occurs] even within that [section], because it is seen there; Chapter 3, Section 4, Topic 9. I bow to that Great Lord Vidyātīrtha, whose very breath is the Vedas and who fashioned the entire universe from the Vedas. (1)
The means for the knowledge of Brahman has been clearly stated in the Sāhitya;
here, in the Vāruṇī Upaniṣad, this reality of Brahman is analyzed.

Therein, first, for the sake of establishing mutual harmony between the disciple and the preceptor, he recites the Jaapya mantra which brings about peace and prosperity for them: "Saha nāv avatu. Here, by the word "nau," both the disciple and the preceptor are meant.

In this life or in past lives, one whose desire to know (*vividiṣā*) has arisen through the performance of obligatory (*nitya*) and occasional (*naimittika*) rites prescribed in the *Karmakāṇḍa*, and who has become inward-turned and one-pointed in mind through the meditations (*upāsana*) taught in the *Sāṃhitya* and *Upaniṣad* sections,

examines the worthlessness of the worlds attained by means of optional rites (*kāmyakarman*) and the like; thereafter, becoming disillusioned, [he realizes] that liberation is not [attained] through ritual action.

Having thus resolved, the disciple intended here is one who approaches a teacher for the sake of attaining knowledge of the reality of Brahman, which is the cause of liberation. And the teacher intended is one who is learned (*śrotriya*), skilled in instructing due to his mastery of the meaning of the Vedas and scriptures, and established in Brahman (*brahmaniṣṭha*), being at no time devoid of outward-facing tendencies. Thus it is said in the Atharvaṇa:
The Kaṭhas recite: "Having examined the worlds acquired through karma, a brāhmaṇa should attain detachment; there is no 'unmade' [world] gained by mere action.
For the sake of realizing that, he should approach a teacher alone, with fuel in hand—one who is learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*) and established in Brahman.
And the Kaṭhas also recite: "A wonder is the speaker; skilled is its obtainer; a wonder is the knower; skilled is its expounder."

Regarding the phrase "thus instructed": although there is nothing further to be requested from the teacher because his purpose has been accomplished, the disciple, by means of this mantra, prays for the welfare of both of them. Whatever Brahman I shall come to know after the grace of the teacher, may that Brahman protect and preserve us both—both the teacher and the disciple—jointly; likewise, may it nourish and sustain us. Just as the teacher [is established]...

He instructs Rāma, and at the time of instruction, he requests protection such that I may grasp the matter as instructed, free from both non-comprehension and misconception. The simultaneity of both [instruction and protection] constitutes their coexistence in the act of safeguarding.
Observing how my ignorance is removed through the grasping of the instructed meaning, the Teacher—so that it may cease—[acts] as follows...

Just as one is satisfied by protection, so too is that which follows first requested. For the sake of accomplishing the stated purpose, let us both together, in our respective roles, exert our vigor—the capacity for our own purpose—within this knowledge;
and regarding that exertion of capacity, the means required is requested. That which has been studied belongs to us two, the teacher and the disciple.
May this collection of texts be radiant and illuminative of its own meaning. And may we two not harbor mutual hatred toward one another.

The meaning is that "hatred" on the part of the disciple is dissatisfaction [thinking], "The teacher has not explained it correctly," and likewise [hatred] on the part of the teacher is the failure to provide instruction; thus, liberation is not achieved. The meaning is "by means of action performed."

Thus ends the first section (anuvāka) in the Vāruṇī Upaniṣad of the Yajur Āraṇyaka, within the *Vedārthaprakāśa* composed by the venerable Sāyaṇācārya, under the patronage of the supreme lord Mādhava Vidyāraṇya, who sustained the imperial sovereignty of the illustrious Bukkaṇa. || 1 ||

In the first [section], for the purpose of averting obstacles likely to arise in the form of hatred and so forth, there is a recitation (*jaṃpya*) according to tradition. Here, the essence of the entire Upaniṣad is summarized as a *sūtra* at the beginning of the second *anuvāka*: "The knower of Brahman" (*brahmavit*).

Liberation through the knowledge of Brahman is the intended meaning of the entire Upaniṣad. The word "Brahman" (*brahma*) is derived from the verbal roots *bṛh* or *bṛhi*, meaning "to grow" or "to increase."

It denotes an object that possesses growth (*vṛddhi*), and here "growth" is intended in its absolute sense, because there is an absence of both context and qualifying words (*upapada*) that would cause restriction. However, if the subject under discussion were an object possessing only relative growth, or if some expressive qualifying word were employed, then a restriction would occur. But neither of these two conditions exists here; [the growth is] absolute.

The increase of meaning (*śayavṛddhi*) consists in the nature of being eternally pure, enlightened, and liberated, and so forth. With this very point in mind, it was stated by the venerable Bhagavatpāda in the *Śrīmacchārīrakamīmāṃsābhāṣya*: "There exists, indeed, Brahman, whose essential nature is eternally pure, enlightened, and liberated, and who is omniscient and omnipotent. For when the word 'Brahman' is etymologically derived, such meanings as eternal purity and the rest are understood from the root *bṛh*."

"Because of the pursuit of the meaning [of the word *brahman*]"—and this intention regarding the meaning will be clarified by the defining statement beginning with "Truth, Knowledge," and so forth. One who knows such Brahman—that is, one who realizes it directly through the mind—is a "knower of Brahman" (*brahmavid*). The Vājasaneyins record in their scripture: "It is to be seen by the mind alone; there is no diversity whatsoever here. And—
However, by means of the mind endowed with the senses such as the eyes, Brahman is apprehended precisely as qualified by name, form, and so forth, and not in its pure state.

Therefore, it is said that it is to be seen by the mind alone. [Objection: Even if there is independence from the eyes and other senses, there remains a dependence on Vedic statements, because Brahman is an object of knowledge established by scripture. [Reply: Certainly. For this very reason, it is said that it is to be "contemplated" (anudraṣṭavya).

It is said: the scripture that establishes Brahman is to be seen *anu*, meaning subsequently. Here, by the particle *eva* in the phrase "by the mind alone" (*manasaiva*), the external senses such as sight are excluded; whereas by the word *anu*, the scripture is accepted. Furthermore, one should not suspect that because it is accessible through scripture, there is a mediate (*parokṣa*) cognition—as is the case with merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*)—for the illustrative example here is dissimilar. [Brahman is] immediate (*aparokṣa*)...

For Brahman is indeed Being (*bhāva*), according to the scriptural text: "That which is Brahman is immediate and direct. There is a distinction, however, in that merit and demerit (*dharma-adharma*) are of a nature that is indirect (*parokṣa*). If it is argued that even though Brahman is intrinsically direct, it possesses indirectness [in its unmanifest state], this is true;
for this very reason, the Scripture, having indicated Brahman as the cause of the world, makes it known through subordinate statements such as "Being, Consciousness," and so forth.

Furthermore, in order to remove the delusion regarding its being beyond perception, [the scripture] makes known the identity of that Brahman with the inner self (*pratyagātman*) by means of the Great Sentence (*mahāvākya*).
Thus the Vājasaneyins recite: "He who knows thus, 'I am Brahman,' becomes this all.
Here too, intending precisely this identity with the inner self, it is said: "He who knows that which is hidden in the cave..."

By this statement, it is impossible even to suspect the delusion of "remoteness" (parokṣatva) regarding the inner self (pratyagātman). The meaning is that after hearing the scriptures which teach [Brahman] from children up to Brahmā, Brahman is to be seen by the mind alone.

The Self is directly perceived by all living beings through the mental perception of "I," as it is clearly and constantly employed in such a manner. Furthermore, objects such as jars, which are grasped by the eyes and other senses belonging to that inner Self (*pratyagātman*),
are called "immediate" (*aparokṣa*) because they are perceived without the mediation of inferential marks (*liṅga*) or other such means, even though they are not insentient.

How could even the slightest suspicion of remoteness (*parokṣatva*) be raised against that inner self (*pratyagātman*), which is free from the possibility of any obscuration, whose nature is consciousness (*cidrūpa*), self-luminous (*svaprakāśa*), and the illuminator of all? Its self-luminosity and its status as the illuminator of everything are declared in the Śruti: "Everything shines only after Him who shines; by His light all this is illumined."

"It shines"— this being so, it cannot be doubted that for the inner self (*pratyagātman*), who is in reality the illuminator of all and who appears through the mental modification (*pratyaya*) during the state of empirical transaction, there can be neither actual nor apparent remoteness (*parokṣatva*).
If it is argued that the Witness (*sākṣin*), being distinct from the five sheaths (*kośa*) beginning with the body, is remote, [the answer is] no, because of its...

Because it is by nature immediate (*aparokṣa*). When even that which is conjoined with inert things such as the body—which are capable of concealing [the Self]—is admitted to be immediate, then what need is there to say that that which is free from such conjunction is immediate?
Therefore, because of its identity with the immediate inner self (*pratyagātman*), Brahman, although accessible through scripture, is indeed immediately realized by the mind.
[Objection: But surely that which is apprehended by the mind cannot be Brahman at all. Thus the Talavakāras declare:

"That which one does not think with the mind, that by which they say the mind is thought—know that alone to be Brahman, and not this which people worship here. The meaning of this is as follows: that witness-consciousness (*sākṣicaitanya*) which every person seeks to comprehend by making it an object of the mind...

It is not capable [of perceiving itself]. However, that witness-consciousness by which that mind is illumined—this is what those well-versed in the secrets of the Vedas declare. O disciple, you should know that this very witness-consciousness is Brahman. But the practitioners of meditation (upāsakas), perceiving it as something distinct from themselves, see it in the form of an object of perception (*dṛśyatva*), like a jar or other things, as "this."
That which they worship as Brahman—the cause of the world established by their own [scriptural] tradition—is not this object of worship that constitutes primary Brahman.

Indeed, there can be no status as primary Brahman for that which is distinct from oneself, which is an object of perception, and which is qualified by limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*). If it is argued that what is made an object of the mind through concentration and directly realized is not Brahman, this is not a valid objection; for in this [state],...

In the Śruti, it is accepted that Brahman is an object of the mind; otherwise, how could it be said, "Know that very Brahman as yourself"? If it is argued that it is improper for the self-luminous witness (sākṣin) to be illumined by a manifestation produced by the mind—like a jar or other objects—then, in that case, let there be no "objectivity as the fruit" (phalavyāpyatva), but there will still be "objectivity as a mental modification" (vṛttivyāpyatva). And as for the witness...

When Brahman is pervaded by the mental modification (*vṛtti*) produced by the Great Sentence (*mahāvākya*), which manifests as "That [Brahman] is Thou," then through that very modification in the form of the knowledge of reality (*tattvavidyā*), the ignorance (*avidyā*) that causes the distinction between the inner self (*pratyak*) and Brahman is sublated. Furthermore, it is impossible for this modification to be a form of indirect knowledge (*parokṣajñāna*); for it is precisely the connection with the object that produces the specific form of the modification, just as in the case of the eye.

By the logic of *kaimutya* (the principle of "how much more so"), he establishes the absence of being beyond perception. The phrase "even those accompanied by the suspicion of an intervention" is the ellipsis to be supplied. The meaning is "in this manner. The word division is *aviṣayatvam* (non-objectivity). And thus, the sense is that the contradiction with the scriptural text, "That which the mind does not think," remains as it was.

The meaning is that there is no such contradiction, because that very scripture is intended only to establish the negation of being pervaded by the fruit [of cognition]. [The fruit] consists of a cognition produced by an operation conducive to knowledge.

Just as the mental modification (*vṛtti*) of the intellect, having assumed the form of a jar through its connection with the jar, is called "immediate cognition" (*aparokṣajñāna*) by people, so too, why should this [mental modification] not possess the nature of immediate cognition when it assumes the form of the Witness (*sākṣin*) through its connection with the Witness?

Nor should one suspect that the sentence is useless on the grounds that the modification already possesses that form simply through its connection with the object; for [the sentence is necessary to reveal] the cause of the world...

Since such an illusion of difference—the notion that Brahman, as characterized by [external] attributes, is distinct from the nature of the inner self—is sublated by the Great Sentence (*mahāvākya*), it follows that the mental modification (*vṛtti*) consisting of the identity of the inner self and Brahman arises precisely through its connection with the object by means of the negation of difference. Therefore, even the knowledge produced by the sentence is indeed immediate (*aparokṣa*). However, for one who is extroverted, whose mental modification—

It is not connected with a witness situated within [the heart], for from the very power of the words themselves, a mental modification (*vṛtti*) arises in the form of the identity of the inner self and Brahman. This knowledge is indirect (*parokṣa*), just like [knowledge] regarding dharma, adharma, heaven, or hell. For in this case, the absence of direct perception (*sākṣātkāra*) is not caused by a defect in the sentence; rather, it is caused by a defect in the person, characterized by being turned away [from the truth].

Just as, for example, when one facing east is unable to see a form situated to the west, the defect of the eye is not considered the cause [of that non-perception], so it is here. And when that person, whose mind is directed outward, brings about through meditation on Brahman— denoted by the term *nididhyāsana*— an inward-turned,
one-pointed modification of the intellect (*buddhi-vṛtti*) that is skilled in discerning subtle reality, then that modification of the intellect...

Connected with the inner self (pratyagātman), assuming its form and dispelling the delusion of difference through the grace of the [great] sentence, this is called the direct realization of Brahman (*brahmasākṣātkāra*). Prior to hearing the sentence, or subsequently through the meditation on the qualified Brahman (*saguṇabrahmopāsana*) or through profound reflection (*nididhyāsana*), for one who is turned inward, the witness-consciousness (*sākṣicaitanya*) is distinguished from the body and other such things by means of positive and negative concomitance (*anvayavyatireka*).

For the primary qualified seeker who has ascertained Brahmanhood through the intermediate statement by means of direct experience, the very realization of the identity of Brahman and the Self arises through the Great Sentence (*mahāvākya*), and not merely indirect knowledge (*parokṣajñāna*). With this in mind, it is stated in the *Vākyavṛtti*: "That which shines forth as the inner consciousness (*pratyagbodha*) is characterized by non-dual bliss; and that which is of the nature of non-dual bliss [is the Self]."

[The Self] has the single characteristic of inward consciousness (*pratyagbodha*). When there occurs such a realization of mutual identity (*tādātmya*), then indeed the non-Brahmanhood of the referent "Thou" (*tvamartha*) is excluded, and the remoteness (*pārokṣya*) of the referent "That" (*tadartha*) is likewise removed. If this is so, hear what follows from it: the inward consciousness remains as the singular form of complete bliss (*pūrṇānanda*). Now, [one might ask]: regarding the mutual identity of the inward [Self] and Brahman—

If identity (*tādātmya*) were accepted, the state of being an undivided single essence (*akhaṇḍaikarasatva*) would not be established; for even in the case of "the blue lotus" (*nīlam utpalam*), although there is identity, there is also the existence of a distinction between quality (*guṇa*) and substance (*dravya*). If it is argued that, likewise here, a distinction caused by "selfhood" (*ātmatva*) and "Brahmanhood" (*brahmatva*) would also follow, we say no. This is because of the disparity [between the two cases], as quality and substance are subject to mutual deviation (*vyabhicāra*). The quality of blueness (*nailya*) [is found] in clouds and so forth...

Furthermore, the term "lotus" (*utpala*) deviates [from its own referent] when it exists in a pond; and the substance "lotus" (*utpaladravya*), because it exists in both white and red lotuses, deviates from the quality of blueness (*nailyaguṇa*). Therefore, because there is a difference in meaning in those cases, they do not possess the nature of being indivisible (*akhaṇḍārthatva*). Here, however, since there is no mutual deviation between the Self (*ātman*) and Brahman, their identity of meaning establishes their indivisibility. And this was stated by Viśvarūpācārya—

This has been shown by the [sages]: "The nature of the Self is not other than Brahman, nor is the nature of Brahman other than the Self. The meaning is: "by means of the cessation of the delusion of identity and difference. [This is expressed] through such passages as "Truth, Knowledge... and so forth. The meaning is: "by means of the cessation of the delusion of difference. The third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) is used because it belongs to the class beginning with *prakṛti*. The meaning is "the state of being a blue lotus" (*utpalatva*). The meaning is also "the universal (genus) of the blue lotus" (*utpalajāti*).

This too has been shown by the Teachers: "The Self, though being this very Brahman, is tainted by remoteness due to delusion; and Brahman, though being that very Self, likewise perceived itself as having a second because of its state of duality. Furthermore, that very reality is called "Brahman" in its aspect as being accessible through scripture (*śāstra*), and it is called "Ātman" in its aspect as being directly perceived by the mind (*mānasapratyakṣa*). In this regard, because qualities such as being the cause of the world and omniscience—which are accessible through scripture—are indirect (*parokṣa*), there arises the delusion that Brahman itself is indirect. [Conversely,] because the body and so forth, which are perceived by mental perception in the form of the "I-notion" (*ahaṃpratyaya*), are not Brahman...

Even though the conscious self (*cidātman*) is the witness, there is the notion of its being non-Brahman. Because the two words [“Brahman” and “Self”] are employed to denote the distinction between those two—Brahman and the Self—when the object to be established is Brahman, which is indeed an indivisible single essence (*akhaṇḍaikarasa*) and consists of the immediate, inward-facing Self (*pratyagātman*), direct knowledge arises through the Great Sentence (*mahāvākya*).
A person endowed with such knowledge is what is intended here by the term "knower of Brahman" (*brahmavit*). Of such a person...

For it is heard that "attainment" (*prāpti*) consists in attaining the Supreme (*param*), because of its fitness for being attained by others. However, the word "Supreme" (*para*) implies otherness (*anyatva*), which is not possible here, since the Reality is non-dual. This is because it is prohibited by the scripture: "There is no diversity whatsoever here.
But if the word has the sense of "excellent," then Brahman alone must be denoted by the word "Supreme," since everything else is composed of *māyā*.

Because of its inferiority. That being the case, it is stated that the person who knows Brahman attains Brahman itself. The followers of the Atharva Veda, moreover, declare this quite explicitly: "He who indeed knows that supreme Brahman becomes Brahman itself. Now, an objection may be raised: in the expression "he attains the village," attainment is commonly understood as a conjunction with the village preceded by the act of going.

If it be argued that, just as a worshiper of Brahman with attributes (saguṇa-brahma) departs through the cranial channel (mūrdhanya-nāḍī), travels by the path beginning with light (arcir-ādi-mārga), and reaches the world of Brahman (brahma-loka), so too must the attainment of Brahman be described here [in the case of the knower of the attributeless], we say no. This is because both departure and travel are prohibited.
Departure is prohibited by the scriptural text, "His vital breaths (prāṇas) do not depart," and the prohibition of travel is recorded in the Smṛti.
"For the one who has become the self of all beings, seeing all beings correctly, even the gods are bewildered on his path as they seek his footsteps.

This is the meaning: he who knows Brahman has become the self of all living beings; he sees all living beings correctly as his own self. On his path, even the gods are bewildered. [Regarding] the northern and southern...

Those gods who exist as *ātivāhika* (conveying) beings upon the downward paths— all of them, while seeking the path of that seeker of the goal who is devoid of a path and is a knower of Brahman, do not see that path, even though they perceive the destination and the course of those worshippers traveling by the three paths, both those who perform sacrifices and public works (*iṣṭāpūrta*) and those sinners who do not perform such rites.

"They become deluded. Therefore, this [state] is figuratively designated as the attainment of Brahman. And scripture shows that dissolution: "His vital breaths do not depart; they are absorbed right here into Brahman alone.

The word "delusion" (*moha*) from the preceding passage also applies here. The meaning is: "of the two [souls] characterized by limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) imagined through delusion. The word "being" (*bhūta*) is to be supplied as the remainder of the sense.

Regarding the phrase "he attains [it] again" (*hy āpyeti*): even prior to awakening, being Brahman itself, one undergoes the delusion of being a *jīva* due to ignorance;

then, after awakening, just as Brahman exists through experience, so too does he himself "attain" it—that is, his own limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of *jīva*-hood dissolves and perishes. When someone who has been searching for a lost object is informed by another, he touches it with his hand and figuratively says, "Now this has been obtained. In the same way, the attainment of Brahman should be understood as figurative (*aupacārikī*). Indeed, those specific topics for investigation have already been cited. Nevertheless, because the section beginning with "the knower of Brahman" (*brahmavit*) and ending with "thus ends the Upaniṣad" is extremely profound, and because there are many matters to be investigated within it, those respective investigations are cited in close proximity to their corresponding passages for the sake of ease of understanding. As for that which pertains to a specific location...

It is well known that there are nine sections (*anuvākas*) beginning from "He who knows Brahman" (*sa brahmavid*). However, that [division] was devised for the sake of ease of recitation by those who do not grasp the full scope [of the text], and it does not follow the actual meaning. For they conclude each respective section in the middle of the statement "On this point, too, there is this verse" (*tad apy eṣa śloko bhavati*) and the recitation of that verse. And this is not correct. Why?

Because there is no completion of any particular meaning [within the individual sections], therefore, due to the lack of established division among teachers residing in other regions, this entire collection constitutes a single *anuvāka* (section). Intending exactly this, the commentator on the *Kāṇḍānukramaṇikā* cites the Vāruṇī Upaniṣad: "May He protect us both," "The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme," and "Bhṛgu, the son of Varuṇa... and so forth.
He declared that it consists of three utterances. In the Bhāradvāja-sūtra, this is cited as what should be whispered into the ear of one about to die:

"The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme" (*brahmavid āpnoti param*), and the two sections beginning with "Bhṛgu, the son of Varuṇa" (*bhṛguḥ ha vai vāruṇiḥ*). It is stated that the knower of Brahman whispers these into the right ear. From "The knower of Brahman" up to "Bhṛgu," the preceding text constitutes a single section (*anuvāka*).

Even for those who maintain that there are nine sections (*anuvākas*), there is the established consensus that it is a single creeper (*vallī*), since they designate it as the "Brahma-vallī. Furthermore, the venerable Commentators have also designated it as the "Ānanda-vallī. Therefore, like a creeper consisting of many stalks, this single section (*anuvāka*), though possessing various internal textual divisions, is indeed one. This being the case, the understanding—

To prevent confusion, it is appropriate to provide examples from Mīmāṃsā immediately following each respective statement. Here, the fact that the knowledge which is designated by the term "knowledge of Brahman" (brahmavid) is an independent cause for the human goal was deliberated upon in the fourth quarter of the third chapter [of the Pūrva-Mīmāṃsā Sūtras]. [The question was: "Is the realization of the Self a subsidiary part [of ritual action], or is it independent, since the Self... [and so on, regarding the transcendence of the body].

Without knowing the self, one should not perform rites; for the cognition of non-duality is not the cause of ritual action, rather it destroys such action. Conduct is for the sake of maintaining social order, whereas the knowledge of Brahman is independent. Without the knowledge that the self is distinct from the body, there would be no certainty regarding the soul’s transition to the next world, and thus no engagement in rites such as the Jyotiṣṭoma; therefore, [this knowledge] is the motivator for rituals.

When it is argued that the knowledge of the Self taught in the Upaniṣads is an auxiliary part of ritual action (*karma*), we reply: "The knowledge of the Self as distinct from the body has two purposes;
therefore, [it leads to liberation], according to the word [of scripture], so says Bādarāyaṇa" (Sūtra 3.4.1).

There are two kinds of knowledge regarding the self that goes to the other world: first, the knowledge of the individual self (*ātman*), and second, the knowledge of the reality of the self as Brahman (*brahmātmatattva*). Among these—

Even if the knowledge of the self as an agent were to induce activity, the knowledge of the reality of non-dual Brahman as the Self would not be an inducer of action; on the contrary, by negating action, its factors, and its fruits, it is indeed an inhibitor of activity. Now, one might object: "But even for those who know the truth, such as Janaka and others, conduct characterized by engagement in ritual action is observed. Certainly; this conduct is for the purpose of maintaining the world order (*lokasaṃgraha*). If [the knower of truth] were...

If actions must indeed be performed even for the sake of liberation, how then is the scriptural teaching regarding the futility of offspring and so forth to be understood? "What shall we do with offspring, we for whom this Self is this world? Thus, when the world that is the true nature of the Self has been directly realized, the futility of offspring—which serves as a means to attain worlds other than the Self—is declared in scripture. Likewise—
One should cite examples such as, "For what purpose shall we study? For what purpose shall we perform sacrifices?

Therefore, the knowledge of the reality of the Self (*ātmatattvajñāna*) is an independent means for achieving the goal of man (*puruṣārtha*), and not a subordinate part of ritual action (*karmāṅga*). Furthermore, the time for the arising of that knowledge has been considered in that very [context]: "In this very life, is knowledge restricted as being certain, or as being occasional? Ta-...

Sacrificial rites and the like, performed with the underlying intention (*abhisaṃdhi*) of seeking knowledge, are exhausted in producing the desire to know (*vividiṣā*). In the absence of an obstacle here, knowledge arises either in this very life or otherwise in another birth; this is established by such scriptural passages as "for the sake of hearing" (*śravaṇāya*) and from the case of Vāmadeva’s manifestation [of knowledge]. It is thus restricted that when hearing, reflection, and meditative absorption (*nididhyāsana*) are practiced, knowledge arises in this very birth; however, it is not restricted that it must arise in this life alone.

"Or in another birth" refers to an alternative regarding time. Why? Because for a person engaged in hearing [the scriptures] and so forth, the desire has as its object the arising of knowledge in this life. A person engages in these practices with the intention, "May knowledge arise for me right here. Furthermore, since sacrifices and other rites—which have unseen results (*adṛṣṭa*)—serve as means to that [knowledge], knowledge does not arise in another birth, just as [the fruit of] heaven [does not arise immediately].

Nor should it be suspected that [the result] arises in the next world, because sacrifices and the like have fulfilled their purpose even prior to the engagement in hearing and so forth by first producing the desire to know (*vividiṣā*). Therefore, when it is argued that the arising of knowledge is restricted to this life alone, we reply: Knowledge is possible in this very life provided there is no obstacle;

however, if an obstacle exists, then through the hearing and other practices performed here— [The text continues: ...knowledge arises. Consciousness arises within another birth; and various kinds of obstacles are heard of: "He who is not obtained for hearing even by many, whom many, though hearing, do not know—wonderful is the speaker, skilled is the one who has attained him; wonderful is the knower, well-instructed. Nor [is this attainment] through hearing and other practices performed in previous births.

It should not be argued that the arising of knowledge in another birth has never been observed before; for it is heard in scripture that knowledge arose even while Vāmadeva was still situated in the womb, according to the Śruti: "While lying in the womb, Vāmadeva spoke thus. Therefore, the arising of knowledge occurs either in this life or in another birth. "Size and measurement are not for the sake of worship, nor are distinctions and connections; they serve only to eliminate limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) through the negation of what is other, and nothing else.
Thus, that which has been established as Brahman by the negation of the perceptible—*neti neti* (not this, not this)—is therefore Brahman.

It must be admitted that there is nothing else. Why? Because of designations such as "bridge" and so forth. Now, it is taught that the Self is a bridge and a support, thus its nature as a bridge is taught. In this regard, just as in the world a bridge is a supporter of water that has both a near and a far shore, and one reaches the dry land after having crossed that bridge, so too is it with Brahman.
Because it sustains the world as its essence, Brahman must be something that is to be crossed over by means of some other entity.
Likewise, a measurement (*unmāna*) of Brahman is also heard in scripture: "Brahman has four feet," and "Brahman has sixteen parts.
Such measurement is observed only in things that have a second, such as cows and the like, but never in anything that is without a second. Similarly, [conjunction]...

The designation "being" (sat) is heard [in scripture]: "Then, my dear, he becomes united with Being. And that relationship is possible only if there exists something other than Being, namely the individual soul (san). Likewise, there is also the designation of a distinction between the seer and the seen in the passage: "Verily, the Self is to be seen. Therefore, when it is argued that there is no second Brahman, we reply: No.

To that extent, the primary sense of Brahman being a "bridge" (setu) is possible, for it would otherwise entail the absurdity of it being made of clay or wood. If one intends to speak of its being a "bridge" based on some general similarity to a bridge, then let only its quality of being a support (vidhārakatva) be intended; however, its having a second entity [as a counterpart] is not intended. This is because of the scriptural statement, "the bridge is the support. As for the measurement (unmāna), it is designated for the purpose of meditation (upāsti), since that is the context; but it is not...

For the sake of realizing the truth, the designation of difference is justified by depending on the emergence of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), just as the space within a jar and the space within a hut [are distinct].

Furthermore, the designation of relation is figuratively applied by depending on the destruction of the limiting adjunct, just as when a jar is broken, the space within the jar becomes one with the great space.

Therefore, since the reasons put forward to establish an entity separate from Brahman are otherwise explained (*anyathāsiddha*), [the conclusion remains that] "there is only one, without a second. Thus, [the Upanishad says] "other than..."

Because of the negation of praise, Brahman is indeed non-dual. Regarding the statement "he attains," it was said that this is not an attainment like reaching the world of Brahman (*brahmaloka*), because of the negation of departure (*utkrānti*).

This very negation was considered in the second quarter of the fourth chapter [of the Brahma-sūtras]: "Is the departure of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) from the individual soul (*jīva*) or from the body being prohibited? It is logical that the prohibition refers to the soul; otherwise, the body would remain alive."

It is traditionally held that when the body is like a heated stone, there is a dissolution of the vital breaths (*prāṇas*). Therefore, the body swells up; hence, [the breath] is prevented from leaving the body. For those who know the truth, it is stated that "his vital breaths do not depart"; thus, the departure of the *prāṇas* is negated.
The basis (*apādāna*) for this negation is the living self (*jīva*), and not the body. Otherwise, if there were no departure from the body...

When it is argued that this would entail the consequence of deathlessness, we reply: just as water poured onto a heated stone does not go elsewhere, nor is it seen there, but rather dissolves into its own nature, so too the vital breaths (*prāṇas*) of one who knows reality, though they do not depart from the body, do not remain in the body but dissolve. Therefore, the living being—
Because the forest is no longer present, there is the conventional usage "the body has died. And as long as [the vital breaths] have not departed, there is no such usage as "the body has died.
When the vital breaths that had not departed no longer abide in the body, the swelling of the body itself is the sign.
Now, rather than this much effort, let it be that the departure from the body occurs; however, the prohibition must have the living soul (*jīva*) as its point of reference.

[The opponent] says: "It will be explained in the *Brahmavalī*. [The author] replies: "Not so. Since it would be necessary for the soul to take up another body while the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) remain with the individual soul after departing from the body, liberation itself would not be possible. Therefore, the body alone is the point of departure (*apādāna*) for the negation of departure."

It is not the individual soul (*jīva*). It has been stated that by the word "attainment" (*prāpti*), the dissolution of the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of being a living soul is intended; that dissolution was also considered in that very context. As for whether speech and the other organs dissolve into their own respective causes or into the Supreme, the dissolution occurs into their own respective causes according to the Śruti statement, "The parts (*kalā*) have gone. However, because of the comparison with the merging of a river into the ocean, from the perspective of the enlightened one (*vidvaddṛṣṭyā*), the dissolution is into the Supreme.

"Others"—it has been stated that they have gone to a scripture devoted to other views, and so forth. For one who knows reality, the vital breaths (*prāṇas*), such as speech and the rest, while dissolving, dissolve into their respective individual causes, but not into the Supreme Self. This is because of the statement, "The fifteen parts (*kalās*) have reached their foundations (*pratiṣṭhā*)," which indicates that the vital breaths and the others, denoted by the word *kalā*, [dissolve] into what is denoted by the word *pratiṣṭhā*.

An objection is raised based on the scripture stating that for this person who has died, speech merges into fire, breath into wind, the eye into the sun, and so forth, which indicates the attainment of each respective cause. To this we reply: from the perspective of one who knows the reality, the merging occurs in the Supreme Self alone; this is determined by another scriptural passage: "As rivers flowing merge into the ocean and disappear."

"Having left behind name and form, even so the knower, liberated from name and form, attains the divine Person, higher than the high"—in this Śruti, the analogy of rivers merging into the ocean is presented. If the meaning that the dissolution occurs in the Supreme Self (the subject of the analogy) is not clear here, then it is understood clearly in another Śruti: "Just as these flowing rivers..."

"Just as the rivers, having reached the ocean, set and their names and forms are destroyed, and they are called simply 'the ocean'; even so, for this seer, these sixteen parts, having reached the Person, set and their names and forms are destroyed, and they are called simply 'the Person. They are destroyed—that is, they dissolve."
This Śruti refers to the vision of one who knows reality (*tattvavit*), whereas the scriptural statement "the constituent parts (*kalā*) have gone" refers to the perception of an external observer.

When the knower of reality is dying, people standing nearby, according to their own perspective, believe that his speech and other faculties have dissolved into fire and the other elements; therefore, there is no contradiction between the two Śrutis. Consequently, in the Supreme Self—

For those who know You, there is the dissolution of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*). Regarding the nature of liberation (*mukti*) that occurs upon the dissolution of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), this was considered in the fourth quarter (*pāda*) of that same chapter [of the *Brahma-sūtra*]: "Is the form of liberation something new like heaven, or is it ancient? It is new because of the statement regarding its production and because it is a fruit. But it is ancient because of the word 'own' (*sva*) in the passage 'in one's own form' (*svena rūpeṇa*); it is the manifestation—"

Manifestation and the fruit [of liberation] result from the destruction of ignorance. It is heard in scripture: "This serene being (saṃprasāda), having risen up from this body and having attained the supreme light, manifests in its own true form. This is the meaning of that passage:

it is called *saṃprasāda* because it becomes perfectly serene (*samyak prasīdati*) when the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) have subsided; and that *saṃprasāda* is the individual soul (*jīva*). Furthermore, [it refers to one who has abandoned] the identification with the three bodies...

Having abandoned [the body] and attained the Supreme Brahman, one remains in the form of liberation; however, in that state, this form of liberation is not pre-established for the individual soul (*jīva*), but is adventitious like heaven. Why? Because of the scriptural statement that it "is manifested" (*abhiniṣpadyate*), which indicates its nature as something produced. Regarding this, the Sūtra says: "Those [faculties] are merged in the Highest, for so the scripture declares" (Brahmasūtra 4.2.7). Furthermore: "The manifestation [of the self occurs] by its own [nature], because of the word 'own'" (Brahmasūtra 4.4.1).

When it is argued that [the Self] attains the form of liberation, we reply: because it is qualified by the word "own" in the phrase "he manifests in his own form," the form of liberation exists even previously. Furthermore, the word "own" here does not denote "belonging to oneself," for that would result in the uselessness of the qualification. Since whatever form one assumes in liberation is necessarily one's own, what is there to be excluded?
By that [word], it would be qualified. However, if the word *sva* (self) denotes the Self (*ātman*), its purpose is the exclusion of "one's own" (*svakīyatva*).

Furthermore, "manifestation" (*abhiniṣpatti*) does not mean origination, because origination is impossible for that which is already established. What then? Manifestation is the appearance of the state of being Brahman through the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*). This being so, there is no repetition between the two [phrases]: "having reached" (*upasaṃpadya*) and "manifests" (*abhiniṣpadyate*).
It should not be suspected that there is a contradiction; for by the word "attainment" (*saṃpatti*), the purification of the meaning of that term (*tatpadārtha*) is intended.

"Manifestation," however, is the comprehension of the meaning of the sentence. Nor is there a contradiction with its status as a fruit in the form of liberation if it were already established previously, because it is not previously established in its aspect as the nature of ceased ignorance. Therefore, it is indeed the ancient reality itself.

The nature of liberation. On this very point, others have reflected: "Is Brahman different from or non-different from the form of liberation? Because of the statement regarding the distinction between object and agent in the phrase 'having attained [Brahman] like light' (*sampadya jyotiḥ*), it appears different; yet because of the statement that he who has attained his perfected form is the 'Supreme Person' (*uttama-pumān*) and is therefore Brahman, it is non-different. The mention of difference is merely figurative. This was determined in the preceding section concerning the liberated one.

That essential nature must be distinct from the supreme Brahman. Why? Because of the designation of action and agent. In the passage, "This serene being (saṃprasāda), having reached the highest light," the individual soul (jīva), denoted by the word *saṃprasāda*, is taught as the agent in the act of reaching, while Brahman, expressed by the word *jyotis* (light), is the object. Therefore, [it follows that] for the liberated soul...

When it is argued that the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of Brahman is distinct [from the individual soul], we reply: the statement "having attained the light" (*jyotir upasaṃpadya*) was declared to concern the purification of the referent of the word *tat* (Brahman). Therefore, let there indeed be distinction at that time. However, the subsequent statement, "he manifests in his own form" (*svena rūpeṇābhiniṣpadyate*), establishes the nature of the liberated one as having reached the state of the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*). And that [nature] is not distinct from Brahman.

There is a distinction. For in the statement "He is the Supreme Person" (*sa uttamaḥ puruṣaḥ*), the pronoun *tat* refers back to the liberated nature whose form has been fully realized, and it declares that this very nature is of the essence of Brahman, which is denoted by the term "Supreme Person. Therefore, the liberated nature is non-different from Brahman. Furthermore, another point is considered: whether its qualified and unqualified states occur successively or simultaneously.

Because of their contradiction and because of the difference in time, there is a distinction between those two scriptural passages. Since a distinction is possible based on the difference between the perspectives of one who is liberated and one who is not liberated, simultaneity—which is non-contradictory—is [the conclusion], rather than a sequence that is not based on scripture. In the scriptures, Brahman, which constitutes the very nature of the liberated one, is presented in two ways: in some places as possessing attributes (*saviśeṣa*), and in others as devoid of attributes (*nirviśeṣa*). For instance: "Ya... [and so forth].

"The Self is free from evil, ageless, deathless, sorrowless, free from hunger and thirst, whose desires are true and whose resolves are true"— this is the scriptural statement regarding its possessing attributes. "Just as a mass of salt has no interior and no exterior,
but is entirely a single mass of taste, even so, my dear, this Self has no interior and no exterior, but is entirely a single mass of consciousness."

Regarding the scriptural statement on the absence of distinctions: these two states—having distinctions and being without distinctions—belong to Brahman in the state of liberation because it is seen as non-differentiated [Brahma-sūtra 4.4.4]. According to Jaimini, [the soul remains with distinctions] "on account of the mention [of distinctions] in the introductory passages and so forth" [Brahma-sūtra 4.4.5].
