[Objection: Two contradictory attributes cannot coexist simultaneously because they are mutually exclusive; therefore, both must be established as existing at different times.
To this we reply: Due to the difference in perceivers, the possession of attributes and the absence of attributes are both logically possible at one and the same time.

From the perspective of those who have attained liberation (*mukta-pratipatti*), there is indeed non-differentiation. However, from the perspective of those still bound (*baddha-pratipatti*), Brahman—the very nature of the liberated—appears as the cause of the world, characterized by attributes such as omniscience. For liberated persons never conceive of themselves as being endowed with qualities such as omniscience or the power of true resolve (*satya-saṃkalpatva*). This is because the cause for such a conception [does not exist].

Because primordial ignorance has been destroyed, bound souls—being possessed of ignorance—conceive Brahman, who is indeed without distinction, as being characterized by attributes such as omniscience. Therefore, since the establishment of different states occurs simultaneously due to the difference among perceivers, what is the use of this postulation of a difference in time? Consequently, both the state of having distinctions and the state of being without distinctions exist simultaneously.

Regarding liberation (*mukti*), another distinction is considered in the fourth quarter of the third chapter: "Is liberation accompanied by gradation or not? Because it is a fruit, like the world of Brahman; and like heaven, liberation indeed possesses gradation according to the difference between men.
[The reply is: "Brahman itself is liberation; Brahman is never heard of as having gradation. Therefore, liberation is uniform for gods and humans alike."

Or rather, it is as follows: the fruit known as the world of Brahman (*brahmaloka*) is fourfold, distinguished by *sālokya*, *sārūpya*, *sāmīpya*, and *sāṣṛṣṭi*. Among these, *sāṣṛṣṭi* is the possession of equal sovereignty with the Four-Faced One (Brahmā). Just as heaven is of many kinds according to the maxim that "the abundance of the fruit follows from the abundance of the action," so too liberation, because there is no difference in its status as a fruit, must also possess degrees of excellence.

To this we reply: what is called liberation (*mukti*) is simply one's own eternally established nature as Brahman; it will be explained that it is not some adventitious state like heaven. Furthermore, Brahman is heard of and determined to be of a single kind. Therefore, the liberation of whether it be the four-faced Brahmā or a human being is of exactly one kind. As for distinctions such as *sālokya* (residing in the same world) and so forth, because they are produced forms resulting from ritual worship, [they do not constitute the true nature of liberation].

By that very [means], there will be excellence; however, it is established that liberation (*mukti*) is not of such a nature. Knowledge and liberation, in the form of the means and the fruit, have been determined through the ten aforementioned investigations and indicated by the aphoristic statement (*sūtra*): "The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme.
Now, he cites a certain verse as a concise commentary on that aphorism.

Regarding the phrase "tadeṣā": *tat* means that, for the purpose of fully understanding the intention behind the meaning of the preceding sūtra; *eṣā* refers to this [verse] which is about to be spoken immediately hereafter and has been stated [or] recited on all sides. The meaning is that the entire intention of the sūtra is made perfectly clear within it.

Since the desire to know arises when one asks, "When it is said 'knower of Brahman,' what kind of Brahman is it?", its essential nature [is described] by the four words beginning with "satya" (truth).
[The seeker] is liberated. And those words, because they are in grammatical apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*), stand in the relation of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇa-viśeṣya*).

Just as there is a relationship of qualifier and qualified in the expression "the blue, large, fragrant lotus," so it is here. In that context, since Brahman is intended to be expressed as the primary object (*vadyatayā vivakṣitatvāt*), Brahman is the qualified, while the words "Real" (*satya*) and so forth [serve to distinguish it] from things contrary to their own respective meanings.

[They] exclude [others]. But surely there exist other lotuses contrary to the intended lotus, since it is observed that there is such as "the red lotus," "the small lotus," and "the slightly fragrant lotus. Therefore, the words "blue" and so forth serve to distinguish the intended lotus from those. Here, [one might think] "unreal Brahman," "insentient Brahman,"...

It is not the case that there are "Brahmans" in the plural sense of being diverse, for Brahman is indivisible. Just as that sun is one, so too is Brahman one; since there is nothing else to be excluded from it, qualifiers such as "Real" (*satya*) and so forth would be redundant. If this is argued, we say no. Because these function as qualifiers by way of defining characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), there exists something to be excluded. A qualifier merely excludes those things belonging to the same class (*sajātīya*).

A qualification (*viśeṣaṇa*) is that which differentiates [the subject] from everything other than itself, whereas a definition (*lakṣaṇa*) is a qualification in the form of a defining characteristic; such is the distinction between the two. This being so, words such as "real" (*satya*) will serve to differentiate [Brahman] from that which is unreal, insentient, and limited, which do not have the nature of Brahman. In the definition "space is that whose nature is to provide room," there is no homogenous [entity], such as another space, [to be excluded].

Just as heterogeneous material substances are excluded even when there is no [actual] thing to be excluded, so too let the unreal and other such things be excluded here. Since the words "real" (*satya*) and so forth are employed for the purpose of qualifying Brahman and are thus subservient to another,
they are connected with the word "Brahman" independently of one another— just as in the expressions "Brahman is real," "Brahman is knowledge," "Brahman is infinite," and "Brahman is [bliss]."

That form by which a thing is determined is called "real" (satya) if that form never deviates from it at any time; for example, the rope which serves as the substrate (adhiṣṭhāna) for everything. That which possesses deviation, however, is unreal (anṛta); for example, the snake perceived in the rope. Likewise, Brahman, which is the substrate of the entire universe, remains so even in liberation (mukti).

It is true that there is no deviation [from this rule]; however, because it is sublated by knowledge, the world is unreal due to its deviation from existence in liberation (*mokṣa*). For this very reason, the *Māṇḍūkya-śruti* demonstrates the falsity of the world, stating: "This duality is mere illusion (*māyāmātra*).
Furthermore, the Chandogas [the followers of the *Chāndogya Upaniṣad*] show, by way of illustration, the unreality of modifications such as a pot and the reality of their material cause, the clay.

They say: "The modification is a mere handle of speech, a name; 'clay' alone is the truth. One might suspect that Brahman must be insentient because it is real, like clay; anticipating this, it is said that it is "knowledge" (*jñāna*). The intention is that empirical reality (*vyāvahārika-satya*), however, is of the nature of consciousness (*acid-rūpa*). [One might further suspect] that Brahman must be limited because it is the referent of the word "knowledge," like the knowledge of a jar.

Anticipating this objection, it is stated that [the Self] is "infinite" (ananta). Based on the etymology "that by which a jar or other object is known (jñāyate) or manifested (sphoryate)," the word "knowledge" (jñāna) in common worldly usage refers to a specific modification of the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇavṛttiviśeṣa) that produces the relation between the jar and its manifestation.

Furthermore, that [modification] is material (bhautika), according to the Vedic scripture: "For the mind, my dear, consists of food" (annamayaṃ hi somya manaḥ). Therefore, it is logical regarding that knowledge...

[The term] *paricchinnatva* [means] being limited. Here, however, by the etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*) that "cognition" (*jñapti*) is "knowledge" (*jñāna*), it is said to be mere manifestation (*sphuraṇa*); because it lacks materiality (*bhautikatva*), it is infinite. "End" (*anta*) means limitation (*pariccheda*). And that is threefold: spatial, temporal, and substantial. In this regard, according to the scripture (*śruti*) stating, "It is all-pervading and eternal like space," [it exists] in all places and all times.

Due to the comprehension of its connection with action, there is no delimitation by space or time. For the Śruti declares: "This immortal Brahman alone is in front; Brahman is behind, to the south, and to the north; Brahman is spread out below and above—this entire universe is Brahman, the most excellent. Since this scripture teaches that Brahman is the self of all things, including the relation to all space and time, and since there is an absence of any entity distinct from Brahman, [there is no delimitation].

Nor is there any delimitation [of Brahman]. Thus, when that which is excluded from falsity, insentience, and delimitation by means of words such as "Real" (*satya*) and so forth is understood as Brahman, the meaning of the sentence is established. Now, an objection may be raised: since the words "Real" and so forth are intended merely to exclude what is other than that, and because the referent of the word "Brahman" lacks any worldly renown—unlike the referents of words such as "lotus"—the sentence would consequently result in referring to a mere void (*śūnya*).
Ka, Kha, Gha, Ṅa: "The characteristic is the form of *takara*. 2. Va: "That Brahman is after the cattle.

80. Composed by Vidyāraṇya [in the *Brahmavayā*]

If it is argued that [the term *brahman*] would be defeated—just like the meaning of the sentence: "Here comes the son of a barren woman, having bathed in the waters of a mirage, wearing a crest made of sky-flowers, and bearing a bow made of a hare’s horn"—we say no. This is because the meaning of the word *brahman* is well-established through its conformity with the meaning of the verbal root *bṛh* (to grow). Furthermore, the Blessed One has shown its establishment by another method as well: because it is the Self (*ātman*) of all. And [it is established] as *brahman*...
The existence [of Brahman] is well-established; for everyone indeed recognizes the existence of the Self (ātman). And since Brahman is the Self, its existence is established.

Furthermore, Brahman’s being the Self is established by such scriptural texts as, "This Self is Brahman. Therefore, since there is no sense of emptiness [in Brahman], it is logical that the words "Real" (satya) and so forth function both as qualifiers and as defining characteristics (lakṣaṇa). [Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly.]

Otherwise, what would be qualified, or what would be defined? Even though in reality there is no other Brahman, during the state of ignorance (avidyā), because of being conditioned by adjuncts (upādhi) that are unreal, inert, and limited, there exist three other Brahmans of the same class characterized by attributes such as unreality; therefore, the intended Brahman is distinguished from those [other] Brahmans by its quality of being real (satya).

It is qualified by words; however, in the case of a definition (*lakṣaṇa*), it is distinguished even from heterogeneous limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*). Just as the referent of the term "plurality" (*bhūman*) is defined by distinguishing it from the conventional usage of the triad of seer, seeing, and the seen, so it is here.
And thus the Chandogas declare: "Where one sees nothing else, hears nothing else, and understands nothing else."

Regarding the term "bhūmi" (the ground): that entity in which the "triplicity"—consisting of the notions such as "one sees another," and so forth—does not exist, is called "bhūmi. By this process of exclusion (*atad-vyāvṛtti*), the reality devoid of all conventional transactions (*sarva-vyavahāra*) is indicated. In the same way here as well, let that [reality] be indicated by words such as "satya" (truth) through the exclusion of falsity (*mithyātva*) and the like, thereby signifying that which is free from them. In this context, there is the state of being a mere qualifier (*kevala-viśeṣaṇatva*).

In this context, all three terms—*satya* (truth) and so forth—jointly establish the nature of Brahman by way of mutual restriction. To explain: the word *satya*, which denotes the absence of sublation, expresses a threefold truth. This threefoldness consists of the apparent (*prātibhāsika*), the empirical (*vyāvahārika*), and the ultimate (*pāramārthika*). [The first] refers to things such as silver in a mother-of-pearl shell, for as long as...

The appearance of the three worlds possesses "apparent reality" (*prātibhāsika-satyatva*) because it is not sublated [until waking]. The elements such as earth, as well as material objects such as bodies, possess "empirical reality" (*vyāvahārika-satyatva*) because they are not sublated within worldly transactional practice prior to the arising of the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*).
Brahman possesses "ultimate reality" (*pāramārthika-satyatva*) because it is not sublated even after the wisdom produced by the Vedānta has arisen. Ta...
The word "satya" (truth), though applicable to all three [levels of reality] without distinction, is restricted by the two words "jñāna" (knowledge) and "ananta" (infinite);

thus, it culminates in Brahman alone. For neither the empirical (vyāvahārika) nor the apparent (prātibhāsika) possesses the nature of consciousness (cid-rūpatva) or unlimitedness (aparicchinnatva). Furthermore, the word "jñāna," while applying both to the conscious reality and to knowledge in the form of the intellect (buddhi), [is here qualified by "satya"].

By means of the two words "ananta" (infinite) and "satya-jñāna" (true knowledge), [the term "Brahman"] is restricted to abide only in Brahman, whose nature is consciousness. Indeed, the modification of the intellect (*buddhi-vṛtti*) is not like Brahman—absolutely unsublated or devoid of the three kinds of limitation. And the word "ananta," while applying to space (*ākāśa*), which is devoid of spatial limitation, and to Brahman, which is devoid of all limitations, is restricted by the two words "satya" and "jñāna."
It abides in Brahman alone; for space has neither ultimate reality nor luminosity. [The word "vyāvartyate" means "is excluded.

Thus, these three terms—*satya* (truth) and the others—being mutually defined, establish Brahman as the immutable, non-dual reality whose nature is consciousness (*cid-rūpa*). As stated by the ancient teachers: "Immutability is truth; manifestation is called knowledge; and infinity as well as oneness—by these three, Brahman is thus understood. Among these, the word *ananta* (infinite) [excludes] the other...

Brahman is indeed qualified by way of exclusion alone. The words "Being" (satya) and "Knowledge" (jñāna), however, while presenting their own respective meanings—unchangingness and luminosity—attain the status of qualifiers by excluding, through implication, their opposites: falsity and insentience. As it has been stated by the authors of the Vārttika: "In that regard, the Infinite [is defined] precisely by the exclusion of finite things."

The qualifier [is established] through the mediation of the presentation of its own meaning, and the remaining two are qualifiers as well. First, the connection between the property (*dharma*) and the substratum (*dharmin*) is understood from the word; however, the exclusion (*apoha*) is known through another means of knowledge (*mānāntara*), and therefore it is considered non-verbal.
The impossibility of the coexistence of truth (*satyatva*) and knowledge (*jñānatva*) with falsity (*mithyātva*) and insentience (*jaḍatva*) constitutes that other means of knowledge.
Although the relationship between dharma and dharmin is not real, it nevertheless serves as a door to the awakening of Brahman;

for we observe that even through a reflection—which is itself illusory—there occurs the realization of the true original object, and because the sight of one’s beloved in a dream indicates the arrival of future fortune.
Thus, by means of these three qualifiers beginning with "satya," there is the awakening to the essential nature of Brahman, and from this [awakening], [the following] of Brahman...

The definition [of Brahman]: Alternatively, each one of those words individually, without depending on the others, is a definition of Brahman. When the false nature of ignorance and its effects is excluded by the word "satya" (truth), Brahman alone remains as the indivisible consciousness. Furthermore, even that attribute of truthfulness which serves as an indicator (*upalakṣaka*) of Brahman is itself merely false, because it is an effect of ignorance.

It is excluded by the very word "truth" (*satya*). Just as the powder of *kataka* fruit thrown into turbid water removes the previous turbidity and then subsides of its own accord, or as a medicinal mantra taken for the digestion of food digests itself as well, so it is here. And when the attribute of truth has been excluded, [the nature of] Brahman—
It should not be suspected that falsity (mithyātva) would follow as a consequence, because falsity has already been refuted at the very outset.

For once the impurity caused by the kataka powder has subsided, the previous turbidity does not return; nor does food become undigested again once the medicine has been digested. When both truth and falsity have been excluded, Brahman is devoid of attributes (nirdharmaka).
Thus it is characterized. Nor should it be suspected that such a thing does not exist at all, because it is untenable for it to be of the nature of the non-existent (*asat*).

The Chāndogyas declare its nature as being and as the Self; for, having introduced the existent reality with the words, "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone," they state, "That is the True, that is the Self. Therefore, that which is here intended by the word "True" (satya)—

It is understood that this very [Brahman] is both the form of existence (*sadrūpa*) and the form of the Self (*ātmarūpa*). For it is not possible for the existent to become non-existent, just as light cannot become darkness. Furthermore, the non-existence of the Self has already been refuted by citing the words of the Commentator (*bhāṣyakāra*).
Moreover, because Brahman is the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*) for the conceptualization of reality, falsity, and so forth, it cannot itself be unreal.

For effort (śrama) is not possible without a substratum (adhiṣṭhāna). Having this very point in mind, the Chāndogya [Upaniṣad] says: "Now some say..."—the meaning is "not making known" (*abodhayantau*). The meaning is "connection" (*saṃbandha*). "In the beginning, this was Being alone, one only, without a second. Having thus presented the opposing view—that "from non-being, being was born"—as the doctrine of others, [the Teacher] said: "But how indeed, my dear, could it be so? How could being be born from non-being?
Having thus refuted that position, he established his own position regarding Being: "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone, one only, without a second."

He concludes by way of the identity with Yama: "And this very position is logical. For if the non-existent were the material cause of the world, then the entire world would be perceived as permeated by non-existence—such that one would perceive 'the earth does not exist' and 'the waters do not exist. But it is not perceived in this way;
rather, everything is perceived as permeated by existence, such that one perceives 'the earth exists' and 'the waters exist. Therefore, the cause of the world [must be existent]."

Brahman is indeed of the nature of Being (*sat*). Just as in the *Chāndogya*, having taken for granted Brahman’s status as the cause, the merits and defects of the positions of "Being" and "Non-being" were set forth, so too here, having taken for granted Brahman’s nature as the inner self (*pratyagātman*), those two positions will be presented: "He becomes non-existent indeed, if he knows Brahman as non-existent; Brahman exists—"
"If one knows it thus, they know him as existing from that [knowledge]," so it is said. And the Kaṭhas also declare: "It must be perceived simply as 'it exists'.

Therefore, although Brahman is in reality devoid of the attribute of truth, it is nevertheless of the nature of existence (*sad-rūpa*) because it is the substratum for that conceptualization. For, according to the maxim that "when two things are mutually contradictory, there is no room for a third alternative," [truth and falsity...]

If it is argued that the absence of fear is illogical, do not say so; for its occurrence is possible, just as in the case of a neuter individual. Just as that individual is devoid of both femininity and masculinity—which are mutually contradictory—so too is this [Brahman]. If it is argued that such an individual is established by perception (*pratyakṣa*), then Brahman should likewise be established by scripture (*śruti*). For scripture [declares], "Brahman is Truth," and thus [it is] Truth...

If it is argued that by asserting "being denotable by words" (*vācyatva*), one accepts the attribute of reality (*satyatva*), we say no; for there is the scriptural prohibition of being denotable by words in the passage, "From which words turn back. As for the word "real" (*satya*), having been conventionally established in the world as denoting the attribute of empirical reality (*vyāvahārikasatyatva*), it functions by depending upon that superimposed empirical reality in Brahman, and [thereby negates] its opposite—namely, unreality (*asatyatva*).

By negating change (*thiyātva*), it defines the reality of Brahman as pure Being (*sanmātra*), devoid of the two attributes [of being and non-being]. Just as one might remove a thorn from the sole of the foot by means of another thorn and, having discarded both thorns, leaves only the bare foot remaining—so it is here. Therefore, the definition "Brahman is Truth" (*satyaṃ brahma*) is faultless. [Objection: But would it not follow that knowledge (*jñāna*) is an action (*kriyā*) in Brahman?

No; for if one follows the etymology "that by which something is known" (*jñāyate 'nena*), Brahman would be the instrument of the act of knowing, whereas if one follows the etymology based on the verbal root's meaning (*bhāvārtha*), it would be of the nature of an action. And both [alternatives] are untenable, since action is prohibited by the scriptural passage: "partless, actionless, and tranquil.
Therefore, if you say this definition is defective, do not say so; for the word "knowledge" (*jñāna*)—like the word "truth" (*satya*)—[is used in its conventional sense].

Because it possesses the characteristic [of being a verb]. However, the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) is the functioning of the intellect (*buddhi*). Thus it has been stated in the *Upadeśasāhasrī*: "The appearance of the Self (*ātmābhāsa*) is what is expressed by the verbal suffix (*tiṅ*), and the meaning of the verbal root is the activity of the intellect. Yet, through non-discrimination, both are said falsely to 'know. Through the reflection of consciousness (*caitanya*), cognition (*bodha*) arises pervaded [by it]; from the intellect, there is the manifestation of sound and so forth."

"The world is deluded by the enemy" (sastena momuhyate jagat). The word "knowledge" (*jñāna*), which is well-established for the intellect (*buddhi*) that possesses the reflection of consciousness and manifests objects such as sound and touch, is superimposed upon Brahman, whose attribute is the illumination of all that is visible.

The compound is "that which is conventional and has the nature of truth. The meaning is "it makes known. [Note: 1. ga. gha. read "iti tatpakṣam"; 2. ka. kha. ṅa. read "kalavya"; 3. ga. reads "yākāra"; 4. ga. reads "śasāha"; 5. ga. reads "pitaṃ sa" on page 226.]

Having employed that [intellect] for the purpose of warding off [ignorance], one thereby characterizes the reality of Brahman—which is the nature of the inner self (pratyagātman) and eternal consciousness—as being devoid even of that attribute. All of this has been clearly stated by the author of the Vārttika: "The intellect's function as a perceiver is figuratively attributed to its witness, because the intellect produces a mental modification (vṛtti) illuminated by the consciousness of the Self."

Embraced by those [mental modifications], all the fluctuations of the intellect (*dhīvṛtti*) arise like sparks from heated iron; indeed, they never arise devoid of consciousness (*cit*). Seeing that the cognitions produced by the intellect are permeated by pure consciousness (*caitanya*), the ignorant think, "Knowledge is being produced," whereas [the Self] is immutable (*kūṭastha*). Due to the absence of the intellect, the Seer is not limited as He was before; [so it is when] the intellect—

Even upon its arising, let it be experienced as likewise inactive; for "there is no loss of the seer's vision," and "just as a block of salt has no interior or exterior but is entirely a mass of flavor, even so, my dear, this Self has no interior or exterior but is entirely a mass of consciousness"—from such scriptural passages, there is the understanding that its essential nature is the single flavor of eternal consciousness. Such...

Since this very inactive Self is indicated by the word "knowledge," the definition "Brahman is knowledge" is likewise free from fault. Now, one might object: in the definition "Brahman is infinite," because of the negation of the threefold limitations, it would follow that Brahman is characterized by the absence of those [limitations]. Just as in the case of the negation "there is no jar on this ground," there is a characterization by the absence of the jar; [so too here].
If it is argued that, just as the earth's surface appears divided into parts, so too Brahman cannot be established as an indivisible single essence (*akhaṇḍaikarasatva*), we say: not so.

By negating the delimitation of the reality (*vastu-pariccheda*), one also negates the existence of anything real apart from Brahman; thus, having relied upon the very non-existence which is the effect of *māyā* to eliminate delimitation, one must—by the analogy of clearing-nut powder (*katakaraja*)—subsequently eliminate even that non-existence itself.
Thus, it is perceived as being of one essence with Being (*sat*). This being so, the restrictive emphasis in another Vedic text—"Being alone, my dear"—is justified.
Therefore, the definition that Brahman is infinite (*ananta*) is likewise faultless. With this in mind, the author of the *Vārttika* says:
"Because the Self is the source of time, space, and so forth, because it is the self of all, and because there is no other entity..."
The infinity of speech and the primary [senses] belongs to the Supreme Self; for there is no limitation by means of the imagined in that which is the unimagined reality.

And here, time and so forth are imagined, according to the scriptural teaching that they are "a mere beginning in speech" (*vācārambhaṇa*). By this very logic of "being real" (*satya*) and so on, Brahman is consciousness and bliss; herein this person becomes self-luminous. "That is full, this is full..."

The terms "bliss," "self-luminous," "full," and so forth, as stated in such scriptural passages as "This is that," should each be applied as defining characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*). For that purpose, qualities such as bliss and the rest are to be integrated here. Because the various misconceptions regarding Brahman—which are to be removed—are numerous, there is a multiplicity of defining characteristics. However, Brahman does not [become manifold] by this much.

There is indeed a multiplicity [of attributes]. Yet, it is established that the Nirguṇa Brahman alone is taught by all the defining characteristics (*lakṣaṇas*). The inclusion of bliss (*ānanda*) and other qualities was deliberated upon in the third quarter (*pāda*) of the third chapter [of the Brahma-sūtras]: "Are bliss and the rest not to be included, or are they to be included? They are not to be included, because these are fixed in their respective contexts, just like the 'leading' (*vāmanī*), the 'truthful desire' (*satyakāma*), and so forth. This is because these are being enjoined as...

The arrangement of the qualities of the [lower] deities shall be according to the specific injunctions; however, there is a synthesis of the fruits of realization across all recensional branches (*śākhā*).

"Bliss is Brahman," "Brahman is truth, knowledge, and infinite"—thus, qualities such as bliss and truth belong to the Supreme Brahman. (The meaning is that these belong to the *vyāvahārika* [empirical] Brahman). "Qualities such as bliss belong to the Principal [Brahman]. Sūtra 3.3.6.

These [qualities] are recited in the Vidyās; they are not to be combined with the higher knowledges (paravidyā) taught in the Aitareyaka and other texts, such as "Brahman is consciousness" (prajñānaṃ brahma), because a restriction is appropriate, just as in the case of the dwarf (vāmana) and other [attributes]. Attributes such as being a leader of desires and being an illuminator—expressed as "He indeed is the dwarf (vāmanī)" and "He indeed is the illuminator (bhāmanī)"—are recorded in the Upakośala-vidyā. Satya-...

In the Dahara-vidyā, qualities such as "desire" and "having true resolve" are recorded [in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad]. In that case, just as there is no mutual combination of these qualities, so too let there be a restriction (vyavasthā) regarding bliss and the other qualities. To this we reply: Your example is not valid. Since qualities such as "being a dwarf" (vāmanitva) are enjoined as objects of meditation, their restriction follows according to the specific injunction.
[The attributes] are appropriate. However, since bliss (*ānanda*) and the others have realization as their fruit, they are not [independently] enjoined.
Therefore, because there is no regulating injunction and because the fruit of realization is equal everywhere, bliss and the other qualities must be combined [in all meditations].
The fact that Brahman is devoid of distinctions was considered in that very same second chapter (*dvitīya-pāda*): "Is Brahman with form or without form?"... [text fragment] ...be?

Or rather, it is Śrīrūpa (the Form of Śrī) herself. Because of the existence of two types of scriptural statements, Brahman must be of a dual nature. However, that which is formless alone is what is to be propounded by the Vedāntas due to its being unprecedented (*apūrva*). As for the form, it is merely restated (*anūdyate*) for the purpose of meditation; thus, the state of possessing both [form and formlessness] is contradictory. On this point, scriptural passages such as "This Brahman has four quarters" establish Brahman as possessing form, while passages such as "Neither coarse nor fine" establish it as formless.

Therefore, when it is argued that Brahman is in reality possessed of both natures, we reply: that which is formless alone is what is propounded by the scripture, because it is not established by any other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). However, Brahman as endowed with attributes such as being the creator of the world can be understood through inference—namely, "the earth and so forth have a creator, because they are effects. For this very reason, [these attributes] are mentioned in the context of meditation (*upāsanā*), but they are not propounded as the primary purport (*tātparya*) of the teaching.

[Objection: It is not the case that both [properties] established by inference and scripture are real, because having form (*sarūpatva*) and being formless (*nīrūpatva*) are contradictory with respect to a single entity. Therefore, since having form—which is not the intended object [of the scripture]—is an error, Brahman is in reality indeed formless. This very Brahman, which is partless and of a single essence, is indicated by the statement "Brahman is truth, knowledge," and so forth. Brahman—

In the Ṛgvedic verse that serves as a commentary on the Sūtra "He attains the Supreme," the meaning of the word *brahman* is explained by the first quarter-verse; then, by the remaining three quarters beginning with "he who knows" (*yo veda*), both the act of knowing and the attainment of the Supreme are explained. Regarding the statement "the person who knows—that person attains [or pervades]": in response to the question "What does he know?", it is said: "In the cave, in the highest heaven... (*guhāyāṃ parame vyoman*).

Regarding the term "hidden" (*mannihita*): the "cave" (*guhā*) is the aggregate of the five sheaths (*kośa*) to be described hereafter, beginning with that consisting of food (*annamaya*) and ending with that consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*). Thus it is said elsewhere: "Within the body is the vital breath (*prāṇa*); within the vital breath is the mind (*manas*); beyond that is the agent (*kartṛ*), and beyond that is the enjoyer (*bhoktṛ*); this is the traditional succession of the cave. That which is the unmanifest cause (*avyākṛta*) of these five sheaths is this—

The supreme is called the void (*vyoman*). And that has been shown by those who know the tradition to be the unmanifest (*avyākṛta*). It is said that the ignorance of the Self, together with its appearance, which is the cause of the two bodies, is the unmanifest. Furthermore, scripture shows the state of this entire world as unmanifest prior to its origination: "In the beginning, indeed, this was unmanifest. This refers to the state of having entered into an indistinct condition.

Its own state is being indeterminate (*avyākṛtatva*). And that [state] is indeterminate because of its similarity to formlessness (*amūrtatva*); this is what is to be established in the *Akṣara-brāhmaṇa* of the Vājasaneyins. The meaning is that the Supreme [Self], possessing both characteristics (*ubhayaliṅga*), exists everywhere, not even in terms of location; this is what is to be understood. In the dialogue between Gārgī and Yājñavalkya, they record the word "ether" (*ākāśa*) in both the question and the answer. The question is: "In what, indeed, is ether woven like warp and woof? The answer is: "In this very Imperishable, O Gārgī, is ether woven like warp and woof."
Śvetaketu replied: "That supreme space (ākāśa) is so called because it is the cause of the five great elements—space, air, and the rest—as they are known in common worldly experience.

In that supreme space is deposited, that is, situated, Brahman. Although the world, consisting of the undifferentiated five elements and so forth, is superimposed upon Brahman—the imperishable substrate denoted by the word 'akṣara'—"

It is eternally established in that way; nevertheless, the intellect of one desiring to know, disregarding external objects such as form and taste, enters through the sequence beginning with the food-sheath (*annamaya*) up to the undifferentiated (*avyākṛta*), and directly realizes the reality of Brahman, which is devoid of phenomenal expansion (*niṣprapañca*). Therefore, with respect to the perspective of one desiring to know, it is metaphorically described as "established in the supreme ether" (*parame vyoman*). Or else, [it is said to be] in the cave within the supreme ether.

Because of the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the word "man" (*mān*), that which is indeed unmanifest (*avyākṛta*) is also designated by the word "cave" (*guhā*), since the entire world is hidden therein. Alternatively, that well-known space within the lotus of the heart (*hṛdayapuṇḍarīka*), which is measured by one's own thumb, is what is here called the "supreme ether" (*paramaṃ vyoma*). [It is that which is] the cause of the empirical usage of waking and the cause of the empirical usage of dreaming.

In comparison with the space within the body and the external space, it is logical that the space of the heart (*hṛdayākāśa*) is superior, as it serves as the locus for both deep sleep (*suṣupti*) and meditative absorption (*samādhi*), which are free from all suffering. The intellect (*buddhi*) situated in that space is the "cave" (*guhā*); within it, through the exhaustion and discernment [of worldly experience], one attains the enjoyment and liberation resulting from the cessation of the threefold transaction consisting of the knower, the known, and the act of knowing.

Because of its subtlety and hidden nature, Brahman is situated there as something to be apprehended by that intellect; for there indeed exists the inner Brahman. This has been clearly stated in the *Vārttika*: "The Brahman residing within the cave of the heart of the knower is not found as anything other than the inner self (*pratyak*); since it possesses the qualities of truth and so forth, the knower of it is the inner self itself. Even though it is one's own essential nature, [it is obscured] by desires—

Because it is enveloped by desire and the like, that [Brahman] is not perceived by those whose minds are directed outward; however, it is perceived by those whose minds are turned inward because they have overcome that veil.

This is incorrect. That Brahman, hidden within the intellect, is perceived by those whose intellects are turned toward the Self due to the removal of the afflictions of desire, ignorance, and so forth, but not by others whose intellects are directed outward. One whose intellect has properly turned away from things contrary to the goal of truth and the like—such is the nature of the intellect.

"Then, having entered within, one perceives the Self as Truth. If it is argued that, since Brahman and the individual soul (pratīca) are one, perception is untenable due to the absence of the triad of the object of knowledge, the knower, and the act of knowing, we say no; for such usages as "knowing," "attaining all desires," and "liberation" are merely figurative. This too has been stated: "Because there is no distinction from the knower, that Brahman is indeed not the most desired object [of desire]; [it is so called] because it is other than the knower..."

"And since that [knower] does not exist, how can it be said that 'one who knows'? The cognition that negates objects such as the unreal arises from ignorance regarding the reality characterized by Being and so forth. And in this way, one attains what was previously unattained simply through the destruction of ignorance. Likewise, one who has known knows; the liberated is liberated; that which was to cease has ceased—this I swear to you three times. Thus, like the knower...

Even though there is no distinction between knowledge and the object of knowledge, just as one realizes one's own state of being the tenth person through the sentence "You are the tenth," so too should one realize one's own Brahman-hood. However, as long as one's own Brahman-hood remains unawakened, one's status as an individual soul (jīvatva) does not cease merely by the awakening of Brahman. Therefore, it is precisely this individuality, hidden within the cave [of the heart], that must be known as Brahman.

[In the Brahmavallī: By this much, the "knowing" mentioned in the Sūtra has been explained. Through the words "he attains," etc., the attainment of the Supreme is explained. That person who knows Brahman attains—that is, simultaneously obtains—all desires, meaning all enjoyments belonging to all living beings.

The ignorant person, having sequentially assumed various bodies that are the fruits of his own karma, experiences various enjoyments through the form of the *jīva*— which is a reflection produced by limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) and dependent upon instruments such as the eyes, like the sun reflected in water. The wise one, however, experiences all enjoyments simultaneously through the conscious Brahman, whose nature is that of the omniscient Brahman.

Thus it has been said by the ancient teachers as well: "Having simultaneously realized all desires through a cognition devoid of succession, the knower of Brahman always perceives them; therefore, he is called omniscient. Two conscious entities are taught here: "Of these two, one eats the sweet fruit, while the other looks on without eating.

In this context, enjoyment—which pertains only to a single body—is obtained by the *jīva*, the enjoyer who is a reflection possessing limiting adjuncts (*sopādhika*). However, by the non-enjoying witness, which is the all-pervading Brahman-consciousness (*brahmacaitanya*) free from limiting adjuncts (*nirupādhika*), even the entirety [of experience] is attained.

The entire range of objects to be enjoyed is manifested. This is the common support for both the ignorant and the wise. If it is asked, "That being so, with what distinction in mind is this presented as the fruit for the wise," it is replied: Here, the wise man, having realized that my true nature is Brahman, which manifests all objects of enjoyment, is fully satisfied; the deluded person, however, is not so. This alone is the distinction intended.

The opponent objects: "Surely, by means of the Brahman-consciousness, the sufferings residing in bodies—just like the pleasures residing in them—must also be manifested. Consequently, through the awareness of those [sufferings], it would follow that even the Knower (the liberated one) would be subject to affliction. If this is argued, we say no; for the Witness, which is Brahman, is untainted by suffering. Thus the Kaṭhas recite: "Just as the sun, though the eye of the entire world, is not tainted..."
"Just as the one [sun] is not tainted by external defects visible to the eye, so the single inner self of all beings is not tainted by the suffering of the world, being external [to it].

If it is argued that Brahman is not tainted by happiness in the same way it is not tainted by suffering, let there be no taint of happiness; rather, happiness is the very nature of Brahman itself, as in such passages as "He understood bliss to be Brahman" and "Brahman is consciousness and bliss."

According to the scriptures: although bliss is the very nature of Brahman, when it is delimited by a mental modification (*cittavṛtti*), it is called "sensory bliss" (*viṣayānanda*). A person, impelled by desire toward desired objects, suffers from not obtaining them;
yet, at some point, through the power of merit, when an object is obtained and that desire ceases, there arises an inward-turned, sattvic [state].

One attains a certain state; and that mental modification (vṛtti) delimits the internal bliss of Brahman. This very delimited bliss of objects is what is intended by the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad when it says: "This is his supreme bliss;
all other beings subsist on a mere fraction of this very bliss. [Beginning with] Brahmā—

Existing within living beings at the ends of their physical frames, there are certain sensual pleasures that consist of mere fragments of the bliss of Brahman, delimited by sattvic mental states. These are what is intended here by the scriptural phrase "all desires" (*sarvān kāmān*).
They are called "desires" (*kāmāḥ*) because they are desired; indeed, it is only pleasures that are desired by living beings, not sufferings. It is among these very joys [that the term is used].

Having sublated the limitation imposed by the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) through knowledge, [one realizes] the reality that is the singular essence of bliss, free from such limitations, which is the very nature of Brahman.

Having understood through reflection that "what was to be done has been done" and "that which was to be attained has been attained," the knower of Brahman is always completely satisfied. Thus, in order to satisfy the inquiry as to what kind of Brahman, its knowledge, and its attainment are—within this Ṛgvedic verse beginning with "satyaṃ jñānam" (Truth, Knowledge), which serves as a commentary on the Sūtra—all three of these are now defined.
"Pitām" [is the vocative]. The word "iti" in the *Śrauta* [text] is intended to mark the conclusion of the *Ṛk*. For the Veda is twofold, distinguished as Mantra and Brāhmaṇa.

Even though a pot is produced by a potter as its instrumental cause (*nimittakāraṇa*), nevertheless, the potter possesses no excellence (*prakarṣa*) in its production. For the potter does not, like clay, persist throughout the entire duration of the effect, the pot.

Therefore, because of the excellence of its assistance toward the effect, primordial matter (*prakṛti*) is like the material cause (*upādāna*). Now, one might object: "But isn't the status of being the material cause (*prakṛtitva*) actually that of Māyā alone?"

But this is not the case with Brahman. Thus the Śvetāśvataras declare: "One should know Māyā as Prakṛti (primordial matter), and the Great Lord as the wielder of Māyā. This is not a fault, because Māyā, being the power (*śakti*) of Brahman, lacks independence. And what is seen? "His supreme power is indeed heard to be manifold; it consists of knowledge, strength, and action, and is inherent.

And, "Those who have attained the yoga of meditation beheld the divine power of the Self, concealed by its own qualities. Indeed, power never exists independently anywhere, transcending its own substratum. Therefore, that which belongs to Māyā, whose nature is power—its *prakṛti*...

That very [Self] is the causality (*prakṛtitva*) of Brahman, who possesses power (*śaktimat*). This Supreme Self, who is the Lord of Māyā (*māyin*) and Maheśvara, heard of elsewhere as being of the nature of *prakṛti*, is here indicated by the word "of the Self" (*ātmanaḥ*), ending in the ablative case. From that Lord of Māyā, the Supreme Self, ether (*ākāśa*) was produced—that is, originated. The Supreme Self alone [is the source] of ether, air, and—

The meaning is that it appears in the form of [the effect]. That material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*) which is clay produces a jar that is distinct from itself. The material cause which is milk transforms (*pariṇamate*) itself into the form of curds. The material cause which is a rope, together with ignorance (*ajñāna*), manifests (*vivartate*) in the form of a snake. In this regard, the Naiyāyikas and others [hold that] all [effects] follow the logic of the clay and the jar.

They say that the world, beginning with the earth, is originated by atoms (*māṇu*). The Sāṃkhyas, however, describe how *pradhāna*—which consists of the qualities of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*—transforms into the form of the world, such as the Great Principle (*mahat*) and the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*), according to the analogy of milk turning into curd. The Vedāntins, on the other hand, [describe it] according to the analogy of a rope and a snake, as the undivided, single-flavored ground upon which the imagination of the entire world is superimposed.

With the intention that Brahman alone, through the power of its own *māyā*, undergoes illusory transformation (*vivarta*) into the form of the world beginning with space, they establish the doctrine of creation. Among those three views, the theories of "commencement" (*ārambhavāda*) and "transformation" (*pariṇāmavāda*) have been refuted in the *Śārīrakamīmāṃsā*.

He spoke of the origin of the earth and other elements: when space, time, the directions, and the atoms have arisen from the Supreme Brahman, the root cause, and are established, then the subsequent creation beginning from that point, O Gautama—

Let it remain established in the manner described above. What is lost to us Vedāntins? Nor should one fear that the doctrine of Māyā is undermined by this much; for the visible world, including the systems of Gautama and others, has been produced solely by Māyā, which generates the diverse appearances of saṃsāra for all living beings from Brahmā down to a blade of grass.

If it is argued that by this very logic, the creation described by the Vedāntas must be an illusion, let it be so; for the Vedāntas are engaged precisely in making known the illusory nature of the entire creation. This is the effort [of this work]. Thus, in order to distinguish the Lord who is to be meditated upon, there are eleven principles that exist prior to the twenty-five principles mentioned by the Sāṃkhya.

In that regard, the difference appearing between the sound and touch [of fire] and the sounds and other qualities residing in space and air—though it exists—is indeed employed by *māyā* because it is a cause of wonder. As has been stated:

Water is produced from me. Sweetness is the specific quality of water; the attributes of the cause follow into it. Water exists, and it is wondrous in its nature due to its fluidity, which distinguishes it from other substances. In the currents of rivers where stones abound, a bubbling sound is heard. Its touch is cool, and its color is white. From such waters...

Earth has come into being; fragrance is its specific quality. Earth exists, and it is of a wondrous nature, distinguished from others by its solidity. And in that [earth], through the conjunction of material substances, a sound such as "kaṭakaṭa" is heard. Its touch is hard. Its color is of many kinds, such as blue, yellow, and so forth. Its taste is characterized by sweetness and the like.

All of this has been summarized in the *Pañcabhūtaviveka*: "Sound, touch, form, taste, and smell—these are the qualities of the elements. They [possess] one, two, three, four, and five qualities respectively in ether (*vyoman*) and the other elements. The echo is the sound of ether; in wind, there is the sound 'bī-sī'; in fire, there is the sound 'bhugubhu'; and its touch is neither hot nor cold; in fire, the touch is hot."
Light is its color; the sound of bubbles in water is its quality. Coldness is its touch, white is its form, and sweetness is said to be its taste.

On the earth, there is the sound of cracking; hardness is declared to be its touch. Blue and other colors are the forms of earth, while sweet, sour, and so forth are its tastes. Both fragrant and foul odors are its two qualities; thus have they been correctly distinguished. In this manner, [the qualities] of space and the rest—

The creation of the five elements ending with earth has been described. Plants, food, and the human being are composed of these elements; by the narration of their creation, the entire material creation—including mountains, rivers, oceans, and so forth—is implied. Although all bodies, such as those of animals, which are produced from sexual union, consist of food (*annamaya*), nevertheless, the human body is primary because it possesses the qualification for knowledge and action (*jñāna-karma*).
With this intention, the creation of the Person (puruṣasṛṣṭi) is mentioned here. And that preeminence is clearly perceived in the Aitareya [Āraṇyaka]:

"In the person alone is the Self more fully [manifested]; for he is most endowed with wisdom; he speaks what is known, he sees what is known, he knows the future, he knows the worlds and the non-worlds, and through the mortal he desires immortality—endowed thus, and then the others..."

Regarding these animals, hunger and thirst alone are their higher cognition; they do not speak what is known, they do not see what is known, they do not know the morrow, nor the worlds of light and darkness. This creation—beginning with space and ending with the Puruṣa, consisting of both the primary elements and their derivatives—is itself the material cause, thereby inducing the state of being a primordial nature (*prakṛti*) even within the Brahman that is its own substratum.

The specific nature of that Māyā is clearly taught in the *Uttaratāpanīya*: "Māyā is of the nature of darkness (tamas), contrary to experience; it is insentient, delusive in essence, infinite, and void. It is the eternal manifestor of this [world], which is its form;
though eternally ceased, it is perceived by the deluded as the Self itself, and it displays both the existence and non-existence of this [world] because of its established nature."
1. Ga. and Pa. also [read this]. 2. Ga. reads *rūpavā*. 3. Ga. reads *baḍamo*.
Vidyāraṇya composed [this commentary]. [In the Brahmavallī, it is stated:
"By virtue of being established and not being established, [the Self is] independent and dependent. The intended meaning of this Śruti has been elaborated upon in the Citradīpa.

And this *māyā* is of the nature of darkness (*tamas*), because of its description in the *Tāpanīya* [Upaniṣad]. The Śruti itself has declared that experience (*anubhūti*) is the proof for it; furthermore, the Śruti makes known that it is insentient (*jaḍa*) and delusive in nature. Because it is evident even to children and cowherds, the Śruti has stated its infinity. For the essential nature of non-conscious things such as jars and the like is indeed insentient; where [this occurs]...

"The intellect becomes dulled; that is delusion (moha)," so say the worldly people. Thus, this is experienced by everyone from the perspective of worldly experience (*laukika-dṛṣṭi*). From the perspective of reasoning (*yukti-dṛṣṭi*), however, it is indefinable, according to the Śruti: "There was neither non-existence nor existence" (*nāsadāsīnno sadāsīt*). It was not non-existent because it was manifest, nor was it existent because it was sublated. From the perspective of knowledge (*vidyā-dṛṣṭi*), it is heard to be void (*tuccha*), because it is eternally ceased.
Māyā is to be known as threefold—empty, indefinable, and real—by means of the three types of knowledge: scriptural, rational, and worldly.

It displays the existence and non-existence of this world through expansion and contraction, just like a painted cloth. For Māyā is indeed dependent, as it cannot be perceived without consciousness (citi).

Even as independent [power], it would be exactly so, since it effects a transformation in that which is unattached. It makes the immutable and unattached Self appear as the world; by means of the nature of the reflection of consciousness (cidābhāsa), it also fashions the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara). Without deviating from its immutable state, it produces the world and so forth. What wonder is there in Māyā, which accomplishes the impossible? Just as liquidity exists in water...
Fluidity, heat, and hardness exist in water, fire, and stone; likewise, the quality of being difficult to accomplish (durghaṭatva) is established in *māyā* by its own nature, not from anything else.

As long as the world does not know the wielder of *māyā*, it maintains a sense of wonder in its mind; but once it has approached [the truth] and attained tranquility, that wonder ceases. Indeed, objections arise against those who assert that the world is a real entity (*vastu*), but there is no objection to be raised against *māyā*.

It would be so because of the single nature of the objection. If there were an objection even to the objection, then I am objecting to your objection; therefore, that objection must be resolved, and it should not be further questioned. Since Māyā, whose sole body is wonder, takes the form of an objection, its resolution must be sought with effort by the wise. If you say that its very nature as Māyā must be determined—

Therefore, come to a decision! Let that characteristic of illusion well-known in the world be examined: that which cannot be defined, yet appears quite clearly—that people have designated as "illusion" (māyā) in the case of sorcery and the like. This world appears clearly, yet its definition is impossible; therefore, look upon the world as consisting of illusion, without partiality.
Then, when all the scholars began to investigate, ignorance appeared before them in certain respects:
"How are entities such as the body and the senses produced by *vīrya*?
Or, if it is asked how they are not consciousness (*caitanya*), what is their answer? If you say it is the very nature of *vīrya*, then how was that known by you?"

The positive and negative concomitances (anvaya-vyatireka) that are spoken of are rendered void of efficacy; "I do not know anything of this"—in the end, you alone are my refuge. For this very reason, the great ones proclaim its nature to be like a magical illusion (indrajāla). What else could be more like a magical illusion than this: that the semen, while remaining within the womb, perceives the positions of the hands and head, and successively produces various sprouts?
The meaning is that [the Self] perceives, eats, hears, smells, and likewise moves, though it is enveloped by various states such as childhood, youth, and old age;
for this is negated by the Vedic scripture stating, "In this, there is no diversity whatsoever.

thus he approaches. Let it be carefully examined and observed while the grains are being poured into the body; where are the grains, or where indeed—

Therefore, resolve that [the world] is *māyā*. Those logicians and others who harbor pride regarding etymological definitions have been well-trained in refutation and the like by means of [arguments involving] joy, sorrow, and so forth. Indeed, one should not apply logic to those entities which are inconceivable; for the world is of an inconceivable structure, even to the mind. It is of an inconceivable structure—
Determine that the seed-syllable *kt* is *māyā*. That very same single seed-syllable of *māyā* is experienced in the state of deep sleep (*suṣupti*).

He who is the Lord of Māyā (*māyī*), the Great Lord (*maheśvara*), as the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of *māyā*, is recorded by the Śvetāśvataras. They themselves declare his status as the creator: "From him, the Lord of Māyā creates this entire universe; and another [within him]..."
"By which [power] he is completely restrained. Regarding the purpose of creation, various opinions are recorded in the Māṇḍūkya branch:
"Others who contemplate creation believe it to be the production of manifold powers; by others, creation is conceptualized as being like a dream or an illusion;
creation is determined to be the mere will of the Lord; and some consider the birth of beings to proceed from Time."

Some consider it to be for the sake of time; others say it is for the sake of enjoyment, and still others say it is for the sake of sport. "This is the very nature of the Divine; what desire can there be for one whose desires are already fulfilled?"—this is one view. That which is the production, the arising of the world, is the manifestation of the Lord's power;
the Lord creates for the purpose of revealing that [power], according to this doctrine. Just as a dream occurs without prior deliberation...

The second view is that it arises from that [the Self] in a similar manner. The third view is that *māyā* is like a magical illusion (*indrajāla*) in the world; just as it takes the form of a wonder, it exists for the purpose of displaying such wonders. And just as when many kinds of food and drink are present, the desire of a particular person is the determining factor in what they take, so it is here as well.

The fourth view is as follows: just as the seasonal signs such as the emergence of flowers depend upon specific times, so it is with this [the fifth view]. The sixth view is as follows: just as agriculture, trade, and so forth are performed for the sake of one's own enjoyment, so it is with this. The seventh view is as follows: just as dice-games and the like are for the sake of sport, so it is with this. [And] just as the reality of Brahman...

The eighth view is that the essential nature (*svabhāva*) is the state of being of a single essence consisting of Truth-Consciousness-Bliss (*saccidānanda*); likewise, for that which is characterized by *māyā*, creation, maintenance, and dissolution are its inherent nature. Therefore, one who is free from desire need not postulate any specific purpose [for these acts]. This alone is the secret of the final doctrine (*siddhānta*). Now, one might ask: do not actions themselves produce the bodies of living beings in order to bestow their respective fruits?
If it is argued that [the fruit is given] by the Lord (Īśvara), we say no; for it has been deliberated in the second quarter of the third chapter that the Lord alone is the giver of the fruit.

[The question remains: Is it karma itself that gives the fruit, or is it the Lord propitiated by karma? [The conclusion is: Karma is the giver of the fruit through the intermediate medium of the *apūrva* (unseen potency). Because a fruit cannot be produced from an insentient thing, the fruit arises from the Lord who is worshipped according to the scriptures. [Thus, the fruit occurs] at a later time...

The hypothesis of *apūrva* (unseen potency) was previously proposed on the grounds that even for an action that perishes immediately after being performed, it is possible to yield a fruit occurring at a later time through the mediation of *apūrva*; thus, [the opponent] argued that postulating a Supreme Lord (*īśvara*) involves unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*). To this we reply: an insentient entity such as *apūrva* lacks the capacity to bestow specific fruits according to their respective degrees of intensity. In the world, [such a result is seen only from] service—...

*The fruit [arises] from this, because it is logical (phalamata upapatteḥ). A0 3, Pāda 2, Adhikaraṇa 8. 16. Ācāryāvalī. 2. Ka, Kha, Gha, Ṅa: in which [texts] "yo". 3. Ka, Kha, Ṅa: tadvattvam. 4. Kha: anukṣaṇavi. [Page 237]

Since it is not observed that direction (*dik*) or action (*kriyā*), which are insentient, [bring about results], one must therefore accept the attainment of the fruit from a Lord who has been worshipped, just as from a king who has been served. Nor is there any burden of conceptualization (*kalpanā-gaurava*), because the Lord is established by scripture and thus need not be conceptually constructed. For it is said: "He alone makes him perform good deeds whom He wishes to lead up from these worlds; and He alone makes him perform evil deeds... [whom He wishes to lead down].

The Śruti text, "He causes him whom He wishes to lead downward to act," declares that the Lord alone is the bestower of the fruits of dharma and adharma, as well as their instigator. Furthermore, if the existence of the Lord is established by valid means of knowledge, then for you, on the contrary, there would be the logical fault of complexity (gaurava) in postulating an unmentioned and unprecedented entity (apūrva). Therefore, the Lord, propitiated by actions, is the bestower of the fruit. Ta-...

The twofold causality of the Lord has been considered in the fourth quarter of the first chapter [of the Brahma-sūtras]: "Brahman must be both the efficient cause and the material cause because of His reflection; He is the efficient cause like a potter, and the material cause like clay and so forth. The state of being the material cause is also heard of in scripture regarding the Contemplator in the words 'May I be many'; and because all things are perceived through a single cognition, therefore Brahman is [both]."

[The section] concerning that which has fear as its nature: all scriptural passages establishing the world’s causality are the subject matter. In this regard, a doubt arises as to whether Brahman is merely the efficient cause (*nimitta-kāraṇa*) or also the material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*). On this point, the initial position is that it is only the efficient cause. Why? Because of the scriptural hearing of the reflection upon the objects of creation, as in "It thought" (*tadaikṣata*), and because reflection is [an activity].

When it is argued that [Brahman] is merely the efficient cause (*nimittakāraṇa*), we reply: from the passage, "It thought: 'May I be many, may I procreate,'" it is heard that the state of being many arises through the excellence of the very Seer's own manifestation. Therefore, He possesses the status of material cause (*upādānatva*) as well. Furthermore, by the passage beginning with, "By which, when heard, the unheard becomes heard," it is established that when the one Brahman is heard, the world, though unheard, becomes heard indeed.

It is explained as follows: this "knowledge of all through the knowledge of one" is easily established provided that Brahman is the material cause (upādāna) of everything, because in that case there is no effect apart from Brahman. However, if it were merely the efficient cause (nimitta), since all effects would exist as distinct from Brahman, how indeed could the knowledge of all through the knowledge of one be maintained? Therefore—

Brahman is the cause of both kinds [of effects]. The systematic harmony (*samanvaya*) of the Vedānta texts, which establishes its dual nature as cause, has been demonstrated therein by resolving contradictions with other scriptural passages. [Objection: Is this systematic harmony not tenable regarding the source of the world, or is it indeed tenable? It is not tenable, because of mutual contradictions among the Vedic statements. Even regarding disputes over the sequence of creation, that [contradiction] does not [apply here].

It is joined with *Svaṣṭṛ*. That which is unmanifest is called "non-existent" (*asat*); therefore, it is joined with the cause. This undertaking is begun to refute and then resolve that systematic harmony (*samanvaya*) of the Vedāntas concerning the cause of the world, which was established by the first three chapters (*pādas*). First, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is reached: this systematic harmony is not tenable. Why? Because of the Vedas... [text continues].
Because numerous contradictions are perceived among these [scriptures], and because the status of their authority itself is difficult to establish. To explain:

in the *Taittirīyaka*, it is heard that "From the Self, space was produced," whereby the Self is declared the creator of space and the other elements. In the *Chāndogya*, it is said, "It created fire," whereby It is the creator of fire and the others. In the *Aitareyaka*, it is stated, "He created these worlds."

With respect to the worlds, in the *Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad*: "From this [Brahman] is born the vital breath (*prāṇa*)," and so forth, with respect to the vital breath and the other elements. Not only [is Brahman the cause], but also primordial matter (*prakṛti*), because that would not contradict the initial proposition and the illustrative examples (Sūtra 1.4.23). Furthermore, [Brahman is the cause] because it is declared as the cause of ether and the other elements, just as it was previously designated (Sūtra 1.4.14).

The Taittirīyopaniṣaddīpikā, 95:
The contradiction exists not only by way of the effect, but also when the nature of the cause is presented: "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone."

In the *Chāndogya*, the cause is understood to have the nature of Being (*sat*), as in "In the beginning, this was Being alone. In the *Taittirīyaka*, however, it has the nature of non-being (*asat*), as in "In the beginning, this was indeed non-being. And in the *Aitareyaka*, it has the nature of the Self (*ātman*), as in "In the beginning, this was indeed the Self alone. Since there is thus a contradiction, the systematic harmony (*samanvaya*) [of the Vedānta texts] is not tenable—this being the position reached, we reply: Let it be so.

There is dispute regarding the created effects, such as space and the rest, and their sequence; however, the mention of space and the others is solely for the purpose of making known the second Brahman, which is not the primary subject of the text's purport. As for Brahman, the creator of the world, who is the actual object of the purport, there is no dispute whatsoever.
In some places, Brahman is expressed by the word "Being" (sat), while in other places, with the intention of conveying that He is the essential nature of all individual souls—

Because it is designated by the word "Self" (ātman). As for its designation by the word "non-existent" (asat), that refers to the unmanifest (avyākṛta) and does not intend absolute non-existence; for in another scriptural passage, "How could the existent be born from the non-existent?", the status of the non-existent as a cause is denied.
Therefore, since it is easy to establish a consistent unity of meaning, the concordance (samanvaya) with respect to the cause of the world is logical. In that very context, once again—

By refuting the scriptural status of causes such as atoms (*paramāṇu*), that very [Brahman] alone is established. Is the causality of atoms and the like also heard in scripture, or is it Brahman alone? From the examples of the banyan seed and so forth, that [causality] is heard of atoms and the like as well. However, the cognition of all things through a single cognition is not possible in the case of emptiness or atoms; whereas such [cognitions] would be possible in the case of Brahman. Therefore, Brahman alone is the cause.

The subject matter is the Vedānta. In this regard, there arises a doubt: is it the case that, as with Brahman, atoms, the void (*śūnya*), and so forth are also heard in scripture to be causes of the world in some instances; or rather, is the causality of Brahman alone established as the fixed rule everywhere?
[The opponent claims: The causality of atoms and the like is also heard in scripture. Why? Because [it is said]: "From the seed of the banyan tree here... and so on.

This is because of the hearing of an illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*). To explain: in the sixth chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad, while instructing Śvetaketu, Uddālaka cited seeds of the *vaṭa* tree containing great trees as examples in order to demonstrate that the gross universe is contained within the subtle reality.

Therefore, atoms similar to that [space] are heard of as the subject of comparison (*dārṣṭāntika*). Furthermore, regarding the void (*śūnya*), its status as the cause is heard directly in the scripture: "In the beginning, this was non-existent" (*asad vā idam agre āsīt*). And some poets speak of inherent nature (*svabhāva*) as the cause, while others likewise speak of time (*kāla*).

However, those two [theories] belong to the side of the time of becoming (*bhāva-kāla*). Therefore, when it is argued that even atoms and the like possess a causal status based on scripture (*śrauta*), we reply: the knowledge of all through the knowledge of one is not tenable according to the doctrines of the Śūnyavādins and others. This is because Brahman—which is unproduced by the void and so forth—is not known through the knowledge of the void and so forth. Furthermore, the analogy of the grain-seeds (*dhānā*) and the rest does not apply to Brahman, as it is beyond the senses.

This is established because [the cause] is subtle. The intention behind the word "non-existent" (asat) was explained in the fourth section (*adhikaraṇa*) as referring to the absence of name and form (*nāmarūpa*). As for the positions regarding intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and time (*kāla*), they were presented by the Scripture merely as prima facie views (*pūrvapakṣa*). Therefore, it is proven that Brahman alone, as declared by the Scripture, is the cause of the world, and not atoms or other such entities. Of this very systematic harmony (*samanvaya*)...
The contradictions with Smṛti and the contradictions with reasoning are resolved in the first quarter of the second chapter by thirteen topical sections (*adhikaraṇas*).
"By this, all [objections] have been explained—both those explicitly stated and those unstated" (Sūtra 2.1.6). [Note: Variant readings:
1. ga. ṅa. read *siddhāntasyai*].
In the Brahmavallī section composed by Vidyāraṇya,
the author of the compendium formulates the first topical section (*adhikaraṇa*) as follows: "Is there a restriction [of the Vedāntic teachings] by the Sāṃkhya Smṛti?"

Nor is there a conflict with the Veda in its systematic interpretation. Regarding Dharma, the Veda, which has scope, must be restricted by the Smṛtis of Manu and others, which have direct Śruti as their source; however, the rootless Smṛti of Kapila is sublated [by them], and therefore there is no restriction [of the Veda] by it.
In all the topics (adhikaraṇas) in this Pāda, the subject matter is the systematic interpretation (samanvaya) declared in the previous chapter. Among those, in this [topic]—
In this matter, there arises the doubt as to whether or not there is a restriction (abhisankoca) of the Vedic harmony by means of the Sāṃkhya Smṛti.
For the time being, it is argued that such a restriction exists. Why? Because the Sāṃkhya Smṛti is more powerful due to its lack of any other scope (anavakāśatva).
Indeed, the Sāṃkhya Smṛti is engaged solely for the purpose of determining the true nature of reality (vastu-tattva), and not for the sake of any duty (dharma) to be performed anywhere.

To establish this: if that [Smṛti] were to be sublated even with respect to that very subject matter, then it would have no scope at all. However, the Veda, while propounding both Dharma and Brahman, would still have scope regarding Dharma even if it were sublated with respect to the one Brahman.

Therefore, since the Smṛti has no scope [in that regard], it is logical that the Veda, which does have scope, should be restricted by it—this being the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa), we reply as follows.

It is not proper to restrict the authority of the Veda on the basis of the Sāṃkhya Smṛti. Why? Because it is sublated by the Smṛtis of Manu and others which maintain that Brahman is the cause [of the universe]. For the Smṛtis of Manu and others are more powerful, as they are rooted in the directly perceived Veda; the Smṛti of Kapila, however, is not so. Indeed, one finds no Veda whatsoever that serves as its root for the doctrine that Pradhāna is the cause.

We say: No, because it has already been determined that the Vedic sentences currently observed have Brahman as their ultimate purport. Therefore, it is not proper to restrict the authority of the Veda by means of the Sāṅkhya Smṛti. The author formulates the second section: Is there a restriction [of the Veda] by the Yoga Smṛti or not? For Yoga is indeed Vedic and is useful for the knowledge of reality; therefore, it is restricted by that [Smṛti].

Even in the case of Yoga, that [scripture] is not authoritative because it lacks *tātparya* (intentional focus on the ultimate truth). Therefore, there is no restriction [of its authority] regarding non-Vedic subjects such as *pradhāna* (primordial matter) and the like. The *yogasmṛti* is the Pātañjala Śāstra; the eight-limbed yoga (*aṣṭāṅgayoga*) taught therein is also found in the direct Veda, since yoga is elaborated upon in the *Śvetāśvatara* and other Upaniṣadic branches. Furthermore, this yoga is the [means of attaining] reality...

It is useful for knowledge; for it is heard in scripture that one-pointedness of mind, which is to be accomplished through yoga, is the cause of the direct realization of Brahman, as in the statement, "But by you, [Brahman] is seen through the intellect. Therefore, the Yoga-shastra is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). And that [Yoga-shastra] declares that the Pradhana alone is the cause of the world. Thus, the prima facie view being that the Veda is restricted by the Yoga-smṛti, we reply:

Although the *Yoga-smṛti* is authoritative because it possesses intent regarding the eightfold yoga (*aṣṭāṅga-yoga*), it is not an authority with respect to non-Vedic subjects such as the *Pradhāna*, because it lacks intent regarding them. For instance, having made the proposition "Now follows the instruction on Yoga" and having stated the definition of Yoga itself as "Yoga is the cessation of the fluctuations of the mind," [the author] elaborates upon that very [Yoga] throughout the entire treatise.
The intent regarding the word "month" (*māsa*) lies in its connection with that [time]. However, he did not propose *pradhāna* and the other categories as subjects to be established;

rather, while explaining the means such as the restraints (*yama*) and observances (*niyama*) in the second chapter (*pāda*), and while distinguishing between that which is to be abandoned, the cause of what is to be abandoned, the abandonment itself, and the cause of abandonment, he mentioned *pradhāna* and the rest incidentally as they are well-known in the Sāṃkhya tradition. Therefore, it is not the case that [he accepted them] therein.

If it is argued that there would be the undesirable consequence of leaving no room for the Vedic tradition (*smṛti*), [we reply] no, because that would lead to the fault of leaving no room for other traditions (*smṛti*). Sūtra 2.1.1.
By this, Yoga is also refuted. Sūtra 2.1.2.
