The Taittirīyopaniṣaddīpikā | 97.
The purport [is as follows]: Therefore, there is no restriction of the Veda by the Smṛti on Yoga. The third section [of the] Mīmāṃsā-sūtra...

Thus, [the objection] is either refuted by the reasoning known as "heterogeneity" (*vailakṣaṇya*) or it is not refuted. It is refuted because of the rule of similarity between the cause and the effect-entity. Even though similarity is observed in cases such as clay and a jar, heterogeneity with respect to its own cause is seen in the cases of the scorpion and hair; therefore, this fallacious reasoning (*tarkābhāsa*) is not a sublater. "The insentient world is not born from the sentient Brahman, because of its heterogeneity."

If something is dissimilar in its characteristics to another, it is not produced from that; for example, as in the case of a cow and a buffalo. Since this reasoning would refute the concordance [of cause and effect], we reply: the universal rule (vyāpti) that "whatever are cause and effect are similar in their characteristics" is seen to have exceptions in the cases of the scorpion and hair, because a conscious scorpion is produced from unconscious cow dung.

Furthermore, because insentient hair arises from a sentient person, dry logic that is independent of the Veda does not find a firm footing anywhere. As it has been said by the Teachers: "An object inferred with great effort by skillful inferents may be established in a completely different way by others who are more proficient. Therefore, because it is merely a fallacy...

An invalidating reason is not [present here]. He formulates the fourth section: "Is there sublation by the views of the atomists and others, or not? Since a cloth is seen to be produced from fewer threads, it is therefore sublated by these [theories]. Even the Smṛti accepted by the learned has been abandoned; how much more so a doctrine abandoned by the learned? There is no sublation by them, for in the theory of illusory transformation (vivarta), there is no rule of deficiency."

Granted that there may be no sublation [of our position] by the Smṛtis of Sāṃkhya and Yoga, nor by their respective reasonings; nevertheless, let the harmony [of our Vedāntic view] be sublated by the Smṛtis of Kaṇāda, Buddha, and others, as well as by their respective reasonings. For the supreme sage Kaṇāda recorded in his Smṛti that atoms are the cause of the world, and he set forth a reasoning to that effect: "The subject of dispute, the dyad..."
The world beginning with the letter *ka* is produced from something smaller than itself, because it is an effect-substance (*kāryadravya*), just as a cloth is produced from threads.

Furthermore, the Buddha was an incarnation of the Blessed Lord Viṣṇu; he remembered non-existence (*abhāva*) as the cause of the world and stated an inference favorable to that view: "The world under dispute is preceded by non-existence, because it is of the nature of an entity (*bhāvarūpa*), just as [the world] is in deep sleep."
"The world is a mere illusion of one's own sleep. Thus, when it is argued that these [Sāṃkhya] views are sublated by the more powerful doctrines of Kaṇāda and others, we reply:

When the Sāṃkhya and Yoga Smṛtis—which expound upon primordial matter (prakṛti), the individual soul (puruṣa), and so forth—were cited here and there by the crest-jewels of the Vedic tradition, the authors of the Purāṇas, as part of their respective contexts, yet were ultimately set aside due to their weakness regarding the question of the cause of the universe; at that time...

What more need be said regarding the weakness of the doctrines of Kaṇāda and others, which have been disregarded by all the learned? Indeed, in no instance within the Purāṇas such as the Brāhma or the Pādma is the process of the dyad (vyaṇuka) and so forth ever cited, even in passing; on the contrary, one frequently encounters reproach for those who honor, even in word alone, the rationalists and those of singular conduct, according to the injunction: "One should not honor, even with mere speech, the rationalists and those of singular conduct. As for that [which follows]...

The rule regarding the necessity of beginning with something smaller has been stated, but that does not apply to the theory of illusory manifestation (*vivartavāda*). This is because a delusion of a small blade of *dūrvā* grass can be produced by large trees standing on a distant mountain peak. Furthermore, as for the inference based on being preceded by non-existence (*abhāvapuraḥsaratva*), in that case too—[as stated in the Sūtra]: "Because this [world] is of a different nature [from Brahman], and its being so [is known] from Scripture" (Brahma-sūtra 2.1.4). By this, [the view of those who hold to] the non-acceptance by the learned (*śiṣṭāparigraha*) is also refuted.
They have also been explained [in the commentary on] Sūtra 2.1.4.

The example is deficient. This is because, since one must admit that the Self—which possesses the states—is of the nature of existence (*sad-rūpa*), the dream state is preceded by actual existence. Therefore, there is no sublation [of non-duality] by these views. [The author] formulates the fifth section:
"Is non-duality sublated or not, on account of the distinction between the enjoyer and the enjoyed? By means of perception and other valid cognitions..."

This distinction is sublated by another [higher] distinction: even though there is a distinction between waves and foam, the non-difference of the ocean is maintained; likewise, even though there is a distinction between the enjoyer and the enjoyed, the non-duality of Brahman is not sublated. If it is argued that the non-duality understood through the harmony (*samanvaya*) of the scriptures is sublated by the distinction between the enjoyer and the enjoyed, which is well-established through perception and other means of knowledge, we say: no. For the distinction existing in the form of waves and so forth does not sublate the ocean...

Since non-difference is observed through their identical form, there is no contradiction between difference and non-difference. Furthermore, the conventional discourse regarding the contradiction between difference and non-difference finds its scope even in an absolutely unitary reality that is devoid of any distinction of forms. Therefore, since the systematic arrangement is established by the distinction of forms—non-duality in the form of Brahman and duality in the form of the enjoyer and the enjoyed—there is no inconsistency whatsoever.
[This is] indeed a contradiction. [The author] of the sixth section considers: Do difference and non-difference exist as ultimate realities (*tāttvika*) or as conventional realities (*vyāvahārika*)?

They are ultimate realities because, as in the case of the ocean and so forth, there is no sublation (*bādha*) of those two. They are conventional realities because they are sublated by scripture and reasoning. Since the effect is non-different from the cause, non-dual Brahman is the ultimate reality. [These points are] clear.

The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is as follows: The scriptural text, "There is not even the slightest diversity here," sublates difference. Furthermore, there is a logical reason: because difference and non-difference—which consist of mutual exclusion—cannot coexist in one place, just as duality cannot exist in a single moon. As for what was stated in the previous section—that there is a distinction due to a difference in form—that too is incorrect; for a difference in form is impossible within a reality that is non-dual.

[This is] because it is observed in cases such as the ocean. For according to the maxim, "what is observed cannot be considered untenable," [the distinction is accepted]. If it is argued that here too, the forms of Brahman and the world are observed, we say no; for Brahman is known solely through scripture (*śāstra*). Therefore, since they are sublated by both scripture and reasoning, difference and non-difference are merely conventional (*vyāvahārika*). What then is [the case]?
To this we reply: it is indeed non-duality (*advaita*). Since the effect is not distinct from its cause, only the cause is the reality.
Thus, through examples such as clay, the Śruti establishes that the cause alone is real:
"Just as, my dear, by means of a single clod of clay, all that is made of clay becomes known—the modification is a mere name, a verbal handle... (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.1.4).

"This clay alone is the truth; such, my dear, is that instruction. This is its meaning: A large lump of clay is the cause, and its modifications are the jar, the bowl, and so forth. Regarding this, the logicians (tārkikas) maintain that the substance "clay" is one thing and the objects such as the jar are other things. To refute the notion that jars and the like are separate entities, [the text says... (Note: The provided source text ends abruptly. The translation above reflects the portion available.)

The Śruti refers to them by the word "kāra" (modification). The modifications of the substance clay—specific configurations such as jars and the like—are not separate entities; they are just as [the states of] childhood, youth, and old age are [not separate from] Devadatta. This being the case, even at the time when the form of a jar or the like appears, the independent entity is merely clay alone. Therefore, in clay itself—
Once [the world] has dissolved, that which is the true nature (*tāttvika-svarūpa*) of jars and other things is entirely understood. The specific form (*ākāraviśeṣa*) is not [perceived].

[This is because] if there were no distinction [between the cause and effect], it would lead to the consequence of [the Self] being the enjoyer, as in the case of light (Brahma Sūtra 2.1.13). Furthermore, there is non-difference from That, according to the scriptural passages concerning "origination" (*ārambhaṇa*).

If it is argued that they are known, let them not be known; for since those modifications are non-substantial (*avastubhūta*), they are not fit to be objects of inquiry. Even though these modifications appear to the eye, when they are examined, they possess no essential nature (*svarūpa*) apart from the clay.
They receive nothing more than merely produced names and designations, such as "this is a jar" or "this is a bowl. Therefore...

Because they possess the characteristic of falsity—consisting in being perceived despite being devoid of any real substrate—the modifications (*vikāra*) are unreal. Clay, however, retains its own nature even apart from its modifications; therefore, it is real. In the same way, the instruction regarding Brahman is to be understood. [This applies] the analogy of clay to Brahman and the analogy of the jar and so forth to the world.
Because it is possible [to prove it]. Therefore, since the world is non-different from Brahman, non-dual Brahman is the ultimate reality.

For persons devoid of such inquiry, there exists—through superficial observation—the apprehension of a non-dual Brahman as accepted by the Veda, alongside the apprehension of difference through perception and other means; thus, difference and non-difference appear according to the analogy of the ocean and its waves.

The position that [the Lord] acts as a driver has been established. The seventh section summarizes: "For one who perceives no difference, would there be the performance of beneficial or harmful acts, or not? An act harmful to the soul for its own sake is not logical.
Since the soul and saṃsāra are non-existent, there is no harm to me. For the Lord who perceives thus, there is no distinction between the beneficial and the harmful.

[Objection: The Supreme Lord indeed creates what is beneficial—such as detachment and so forth—for certain living beings who are attached to the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*), and he creates what is harmful—the base [state] which is the cause of hell. And while creating these, he perceives through his omniscience that there is no difference between himself and those living beings. Therefore, it would follow that he himself performs both what is not beneficial and what is harmful.

But this is not tenable. For in the world, no discerning person whatsoever fails to act for their own benefit or acts to their own detriment. Therefore, since [the Lord] would incur the fault of failing to act for his own benefit and so forth, we reply: Because He is omniscient, the Lord perceives the falsity of the transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*) of the individual soul (*jīva*) and His own stainlessness; therefore, there is neither benefit nor harm [to Him].
There is the fault of [the Brahman] being merely figurative. The eighth section formulates the following: "Is creation impossible or possible from that which is one and without a second?

The sequential birth of effects belonging to various classes is not possible. [The reply is: "Brahman is non-dual in reality, yet it possesses ignorance as its auxiliary; it produces various effects through the powers residing in ignorance within that sequence of effects. [The scripture says: "One only, without a second..."

Thus, Brahman is understood to be devoid of internal distinctions—whether of its own kind (*sajātīya*) or of a different kind (*vijātīya*). Furthermore, the effects to be manifested, such as space, air, and so forth, are diverse. Indeed, it is not logical for an effect to possess diversity if its cause lacks diversity;
otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of multiple diverse effects, such as curd and oil, arising from a single cause like milk. Moreover, there is a sequence [of manifestation].
It is understood from scripture that [the powers] of *kāśa* and so forth [are distinct], yet there is nothing to establish a fixed order among them.
Therefore, it follows that the successive production of multiple effects is not possible from the non-dual Brahman; this being the position reached, we reply:
although Brahman is non-dual in its essential nature (*sattva*), it is nevertheless understood through scripture, reasoning, and experience to be accompanied by the aid of *avidyā*.

"The scripture states: 'One should know Māyā as Prakṛti (primordial matter), but the Great Lord as the wielder of Māyā. Māyā is indeed Avidyā (ignorance). Because of the designation of one by the name of the other, there arises the contingency of defects such as the failure to act for the welfare [of beings]. Sūtra 2.1.7: 'If it be argued that [the Lord does not create] because we see [in the world] a withdrawal [of effort], we say no; for [the Lord acts] like one intoxicated. Sūtra 2.1.8."
1. For living beings, illusion is seen through that vision; 2. in some places, *kaci*.
[This is] composed by Vidyāraṇya.

Even in the *Brahmavallī*, because the definition of the indeterminable (*anirvacanīya*) is one and the same; nor does the acceptance of *māyā* entail the consequence of duality (*dvaitāpatti*), since there is no second thing that is real.

Because of its non-existence [as a second entity]. Therefore, even though Brahman is one, it will be capable of producing various effects by virtue of the assistance of *avidyā*. Nor is there a lack of a regulator for the sequence of effects, because the specific powers residing in *avidyā* serve as that regulator. Thus, the sequential creation of various effects from the non-dual Brahman is possible. Ninth [section]...

He brings about the battle of arguments. It is not logical, nor is it even possible, that its transformation (*pariṇāma*) should be logical; for if it were in its entirety, Brahman would become non-eternal, and if it were in part, it would possess parts. Its possession of manifold forms through *māyās* is neither in its entirety nor in part.
Here, the transformation of even the partless [Brahman] is logical only as something illusory (*māyika*). In the *Ārambhaṇa-adhikaraṇa*, regarding the cause and the effect—
The distinction has been established. Therefore, unlike the Vaiśeṣikas and others, the doctrine of "origination" (ārambhavāda) is not accepted by the proponent of Brahman.

Consequently, transformation (pariṇāma) must be admitted according to the analogy of milk and curds. In that regard, does Brahman transform in its entirety or in part? Not the first, because if it were to transform completely, Brahman would face the consequence of impermanence, like milk. As for the second...

There would be the consequence [of Brahman] having parts; therefore, since it follows that there is no transformation (*pariṇāma*), we reply: according to the scriptural text, "By means of his powers of illusion (*māyā*), Indra moves in manifold forms," the world-nature of Brahman through his powers of illusion is a transformation, but this is not real. Consequently, there is no room for the dilemmas regarding whether [the cause] is entirely or partially [transformed]. Therefore, transformation is logical. [End of] the tenth section.
He causes [the world] to appear like a mirage. There is no illusion (*māyā*) for one who is bodiless; if it were to exist, it would not be found.

For all those in the world who are illusionists (*māyāvin*) are indeed embodied. Since the performance of an effect through illusion occurs even without an external cause, let such illusion likewise exist in Brahman according to valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). As for the illusionists in the world, such as magicians (*aindrajālika*), [they are all embodied].

Since it is observed that [magical creations] possess bodies, it follows that Māyā is not possible for the bodiless Brahman; to this we reply: although it is observed that the creators of houses and the like depend upon external means such as clay, wood, and straw distinct from themselves, just as a magician creates houses and so forth without dependence on external means, so too does a worldly illusionist [create] with a body.

Even if it is observed that [the magician] depends on material substances (*rasa*), let there be no such dependence for Brahman in order to establish the existence of *māyā*. Now, if it should be argued that there is direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for a magician’s capacity to create independently of external instruments, then for Brahman as well, regarding the existence of *māyā* without dependence on a body, the scripture— “But the Great Lord is the wielder of *māyā”* (*māyinaṃ tu maheśvaram*)— is the authority.

*Stu*. He sets forth the eleventh section: "Is the Creator satisfied or not? If he is the Creator, he would not be the Creator if he desired a fruit; for if there were no desire, there would be dissatisfaction. [Furthermore,] if he acts without aiming for a fruit, his actions would be like those of a madman—mere play, consolation, or futile effort. Since such things are not undertaken by those who are not mad, therefore, one should know that the Creator is satisfied. Bliss is Brahman. (*Ānando brahma*)

The Supreme Lord is eternally satisfied. If it were admitted that such a being possesses a desire regarding the subject of creation, His eternal satisfaction would be contradicted. If it were not admitted, then He would be creating the world without prior intelligence. [In either case,] there would be the consequence of His being composed of parts (*kṛtsnaprasakti*), or else a contradiction with the scriptural texts declaring His partlessness (*niravayavatva*). (Sūtra 2.1.9) Furthermore, He is endowed with all [powers], because that is seen [in scripture].

Since it would follow that [the Veda] would be equivalent to the speech of a madman, this being the position reached, we reply: [it is established] by intelligent people such as kings and others, even without...

An activity such as hunting is undertaken for sport; moreover, the process of inhalation and exhalation is universal. Furthermore, purposeless movements are frequently observed being performed by children. In the same way, although the Lord is eternally satisfied, He may—being no less than sane—create the entire world even without a specific motive. [The author] summarizes the twelfth section: "As for the inequality..."
If pleasure and pain were not distributed according to the distinctions between human beings, then the Lord, by creating such inequality and withdrawing [the world], would be partial and merciless.

However, the Lord acts by depending upon the previously performed karma and other factors; therefore, there is neither partiality nor cruelty, and the cycle of existence (saṃsāra) is indeed beginningless. The Lord creates gods and others who are extremely happy, animals and others who are extremely miserable, and humans as well.
If the Lord creates pleasure and pain for various classes of persons according to such gradations as "middling" and so forth, how could He not be partial?

And how could He not be merciless when He effects the destruction of the entire world—including gods, animals, humans, and others—which is utterly loathsome even to the lowly? Since it would follow that He is both partial and merciless, we reply: first of all, the Lord [is not partial].

There is no possibility of the charge of partiality against Him, because the cause of the disparity among living beings—characterized as superior, middling, or inferior—is solely their respective past actions (*karma*).
Nor does this entail a loss of the Lord’s sovereignty, since He acts as the inner controller (*antaryāmin*) and presides over those actions.
This being the case, the maxim of "the dawn at the wrong house" (i.e., the fault falling back upon the one who sought it) does not apply; for partiality resides in the [actions], not in the Lord.

Having stated that [the Lord] is the cause of the inequality of actions, if one were again to accept that He is the regulator of those actions in order to establish His independence, it would ultimately lead to the undesirable consequence that the Lord Himself is the cause of inequality.
This fault does not apply; for "regulation" (niyāmakatva) merely means the removal of the lack of restriction regarding the specific potencies of various things.

The powers (*śaktayaḥ*), however, constitute the body of *māyā*; God is not their producer. Therefore, although those various actions become the cause of inequality by virtue of His own powers, there is no consequence of partiality for God, who is the ordainer. Furthermore, because dissolution—like deep sleep—does not produce suffering but rather eliminates all afflictions, He is indeed compassionate.

[Objection: "But surely, while there is no fault of partiality (*vaiṣamya*) for the Lord when He creates in intermediate cycles of creation due to His dependence on the prior karma [of the beings], in the *first* creation, since prior karma is impossible, the fault of partiality remains as it was. [Response: This is not so, because the succession of creations is beginningless (*anādi*).
For the scripture states, 'Neither end nor beginning,' and so forth. Therefore, there is no fault whatsoever. Thus ends the thirteenth section.

[The opponent] objects: "There is no such thing as primordial materiality (*prakṛtitā*), or rather, it does not exist in that which is devoid of qualities (*nirguṇa*). For we observe that only things possessing qualities, such as clay and the like, possess the status of being primordial materiality. We accept that primordial materiality consists in being the locus of transformation (*pariṇāma*); this exists even in that which is devoid of qualities, such as genus (*jāti*) and so forth. Therefore, Brahman is the primordial material cause. Primordial materiality is defined as undergoing modification (*vikriyā*) into the form of an effect."

[The objection is] that [the Lord] possesses qualities (*saguṇa*). And that [possession of qualities] is observed in the world only in things such as clay and the like. Therefore, regarding the qualityless Brahman, [the Sūtra states]: "There is no partiality or cruelty, because [the Lord] is dependent [on other factors]; for thus Scripture shows" (Brahmasūtra 2.1.34). Just as a certain traveler on the road, desiring wealth, in order to deceive the toll-collectors out of fear of them, loses his way while fleeing and returns once again to the very same hovel at dawn.
"Thus, because all dharmas are possible," [Brahma-sūtra 2.1.13]. [Variant readings: *gatveśvaratve* (in the state of being the Lord)]. [Page 245]

To the question, "How is it the material cause (*prakṛti*)?", we reply: although by the etymology "that by which something is produced" (*prakriyate'nayā*), the [Brahman] appears to be subject to modification, nevertheless that state of being modified is possible in two ways—either as a transformative substance (*pariṇāmin*) like milk, or as a substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*) like a rope. In this regard, even though it is impossible for the attributeless [Brahman] to be a transformative substance, [it can still be the material cause as a substratum].

Let it be that Brahman is the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*). For indeed, even in the case of a genus (*jāti*) and so forth, which are devoid of qualities (*nirguṇa*), the status of being a substratum is observed; for we see the occurrence of erroneous usage such as "this is a Śūdra" upon seeing a dirty Brāhmaṇa. Therefore, it is established that Brahman, though devoid of qualities, is the primordial nature (*prakṛti*). In the second quarter (*pāda*), by means of eight topical sections (*adhikaraṇa*), [the author] refutes other doctrines regarding Brahman.

The status of being the cause of the world has been established. Regarding this, he formulates the first section [of the inquiry]: Is the Pradhāna the cause of the world, or not? Since all things, such as jars and the like, are permeated by pleasure, pain, and so forth, it follows that the Pradhāna must be the cause. [Reply: It is not the cause, because the production of appropriate arrangements and activities and so forth are impossible. As for internal pleasure and the like, and external objects such as jars, how could there be such a pervasion (anvaya)?

Pradhāna, consisting of pleasure, pain, and delusion, is the primordial nature (prakṛti) of the world, because pleasure and the other qualities are observed to be inherent in the world. Pots, cloths, and other such objects, when obtained, lead to pleasure because they perform functions such as fetching water or providing clothing. For this very reason, those same pots and so forth become generators of pain for that same person when they are being carried away by others. Furthermore, when [the function of] fetching water— (Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly; the translation reflects the available portion.)
When their purpose has been fulfilled, they no longer produce pleasure or pain; they remain merely as objects of indifference.

This state of being objects of indifference is *moha* (delusion), because the word *moha* is derived from the verbal root *muha*, meaning "to be bewildered," and because no mental modification arises toward objects that are to be disregarded. Therefore, due to the observation of the association with pleasure, pain, and delusion, [the world] must have *Prakṛti* as its primary cause.

The Sāṃkhyas maintain that [the Pradhāna is the cause]; to this we reply: the Pradhāna is not the cause of the world. This is because it is impossible for the non-conscious Pradhāna to possess the capacity for the construction of the world—which consists of bodies, senses, and elements, and which is manifold and characterized by specific, determinate arrangements. For in the world, the construction of a determinate effect requires a manifold...

Since mountains and the like are observed to have an intelligent creator, let this matter of their structural arrangement rest for a moment; even the activity directed toward accomplishing that arrangement is not possible for an insentient entity, because such activity is never seen in things like carts when they are not presided over by a conscious being. Now, if it were admitted that the conscious person (*puruṣa*) is the director of primordial nature (*prakṛti*), then the person’s state of being unattached (*asaṅgatva*) would be lost.
This would result in the fallacy of contradicting one's own tenets. As for the statement that "jars and other objects are endowed with pleasure, pain, and delusion," that is incorrect;

for pleasure and the like are internal, whereas jars and the like are external. Therefore, the Pradhāna is not the cause of the world. [The author] now sets forth the second section: Is there no example from the Kaṇāda school, or is there one regarding the production of something dissimilar? No—

A white cloth is indeed produced from white threads alone; a dyad (dvy-aṇuka) is produced from two atoms (aṇu), which are not themselves minute [in the sense of being non-spherical], from that which is spherical (parimaṇḍala); and a long triad (try-aṇuka) is produced from a non-long dyad—that is the illustration. In the previous section, regarding the claim that the insentient world arises from the sentient Brahman—which is of a different nature—the example of the scorpion from cow-dung and so forth, well-known in the world, was cited against the Sāṃkhyas.

An illustration has been stated. To that extent, the objection raised by the Sāṃkhyas is refuted; furthermore, because their own formulation is untenable, inference is not [valid]. (Sūtra 1.2.18): "Or [the production of the Great and the Long occurs] like [the production of] the Small and the Circular from the Short and the Atomic."

It is accomplished. Having commenced the refutation of the opposing view in this section (*pāda*), the Sāṃkhya doctrine was refuted in the preceding section;
henceforth, the Vaiśeṣika doctrine must be refuted. Furthermore, because that system contains many procedural details—

No person who has not been instructed in that system accepts the theory of instruments (*karaṇavāda*)—which is established through its specific procedure—without an illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*) of a dissimilar production. Therefore, it is investigated whether or not there exists an example established in the Kaṇāda system for the production of something dissimilar. For the time being, the conclusion is that such an example does not exist; because a white cloth [is produced from white threads].

If it is argued that [the cloth] arises from the threads themselves and not from the dyed ones, and therefore it does not exist [as a distinct entity], we reply: there is indeed an illustrative example for the production of a whole (*viśa*). For instance, atoms possess the dimension of sphericity (*pārimāṇḍalya*), but they do not possess the dimension of minuteness (*aṇu*). From two atoms—which are devoid of the dimension of minuteness—the dimension of minuteness [arises].

A dyad (dvyaṇuka) is produced that is not endowed with [the quality of] length. This is one illustration. Likewise, because it is endowed with the dimension of shortness and devoid of the dimension of length, a dyad produces a triad (tryaṇuka) that is endowed with the dimension of length and devoid of the dimension of atomicity (aṇu-parimāṇa). This is another illustration. In this same manner, other instances of its process [should be understood].

Well-known examples should be cited as illustrations. He formulates the third section: "Do atoms produce the world when conjoined? [The answer is: Production occurs through the sequence of dyads and so forth, arising from conjunctions born of the first motion. Since the first motion is impossible under various alternatives such as having a cause or being causeless, there can be no production through conjunction."

"They do not go to the world," [it is said]. When Maheśvara’s desire to create arises while the previously established world has dissolved, then, by the power of the karma of living beings, the first action is produced in the motionless atoms. From that action, one atom unites with another atom. From that conjunction, a dyad (*dvyaṇuka*) is initiated.

Since there is no contradiction in the production of the entire universe through this sequence—starting from three dyads (tryaṇukas) forming one triad (tryaṇuka), and so forth—it follows that conjoined atoms produce the world; to this we reply: Is this initial motion caused by a cause or causeless? If it were causeless, then because there would be no regulating factor, it would follow that it would arise at all times.

There would be the undesirable consequence of the absence of dissolution (*layābhāvaprasaṅga*). It cannot be the perceived, because neither effort (*yatna*) nor impact (*abhighāta*) is possible prior to the production of the body. Furthermore, the eternal effort of God (*īśvara-prayatna*), being constant, cannot be the determining factor for the occasional production of the first action. Nor can the unperceived (*adṛṣṭa*) be the cause of the first action.

Therefore, because of the existence of objects corresponding to words, it is not logical that [the world] consists of mere cognition (*vijñāna-mātra*). He formulates the sixth section (*adhikaraṇa*) as follows:

The establishment of the seven categories (saptapadārtha) occurs either through the method of the sevenfold predication (saptabhaṅgī-naya) or through the existence of the logic that proves them; for their establishment depends upon that [logic].

However, because it propounds contradictory attributes such as existence and non-existence in a single entity, the sevenfold predication is not a valid method (apanyāya), nor does it imply that the object possesses parts. Regarding this, the Ārhats maintain: there are two categories, namely, the living being (jīva) and the non-living being (ajīva).

The *jīva* (soul) is conscious, possesses the dimensions of the body, and is composed of parts. The *ajīva* (non-soul) is of six kinds. Among these, one is the mountain and so forth. The other five are known as influx (*āsrava*), stoppage (*saṃvara*), shedding (*nirjarā*), bondage (*bandha*), and liberation (*mokṣa*). That by which the soul flows toward sense objects is called *āsrava*; it is the collection of the senses. That which covers discrimination is *saṃvara*, such as lack of discernment and the like. [That by which karma is] completely worn away...

By this [verse], it is shown that asceticism (*tapas*) consists of practices such as plucking out the hair or climbing upon heated stones, which serve to exhaust (*nirjarā*) desire, anger, and so forth.

Bondage (*bandha*) is the succession of births and deaths brought about by the eightfold karma. Among these, four are destructive karmas (*ghātikarma*), which are specific forms of demerit (*pāpa*), and four are non-destructive karmas (*aghātikarma*), which are specific forms of merit (*puṇya*). Through the means taught in the scriptures, one should [liberate oneself] from them.

Liberation is the continuous upward movement of the soul that has emerged from the six types of activities (*karma*). These seven categories (*padārtha*) are established by means of the logic of the sevenfold predication (*saptabhaṅgī*): 1) may be existent; 2) may be non-existent;
3) may be both existent and non-existent; 4) may be inexpressible; 5) may be existent and inexpressible; 6) may be non-existent and inexpressible.

And it is also "inexpressible" (avaktavya); thus, there is the sevenfold method (*saptabhaṅgīnaya*) consisting of: "it may be," "it may be existent," "it may be non-existent," and "it may be both existent and non-existent and inexpressible.
This is its meaning: the indeclinable particle *syāt* expresses the sense of "somewhat" (*īṣat*). For opponents are of four kinds:
proponents of existence, proponents of non-existence, proponents of both existence and non-existence, and proponents of the inexpressible (*anirvacanīya*). Furthermore, regarding the inexpressible...

The views of the Jainas (Yamatas), such as those of the Sadasadādis, are considered to be of three kinds. Against these seven types of proponents, seven types of arguments (nyāyas) should be employed. For example: a proponent of existence (sadvādī), having approached a Jaina, asks, "Is there liberation in your doctrine? To this, the Jaina replies, "It exists slightly."

In this manner, other disputants should also be countered by citing such replies as "it does not exist" and so forth. By that much, all the disputants, becoming despondent, will fail to provide an answer. Therefore, since this logic consisting of the sevenfold predication (*saptabhaṅgī*) exists as a means of proof, what wonder is there in the establishment of the seven categories, beginning with the soul (*jīva*)?

This being the position reached, we reply: this doctrine consisting of the sevenfold predication (*saptabhaṅgī*) is illogical. This is because it propounds contradictory attributes for the single category of the soul (*jīva*), such as its being existent in form for one who maintains existence and its being non-existent in form for one who maintains non-existence, and so forth. Furthermore, it is not tenable that the soul possesses parts, as that would entail its impermanence. That [which is] impermanent...

And if [the self] were non-existent, for whom would liberation be a human goal? Therefore, the categories such as the *jīva* are not established by this fallacious reasoning known as the sevenfold predication (*saptabhaṅgī*). Because it possesses the quality of being the substratum of existence for all effects and causes, [the notion of space] has proceeded [from that]; therefore, the ether is neither beginningless nor endless. It is not born.

This is the reason: because the distinction from air and the other elements is well-established in the case of space. The meaning of the word *anna* here is "earth. Why? Because the creation of the five great elements (*pañcamahābhūta*) is the subject under discussion. Furthermore, it is heard in scripture that "the red color is the form of fire, the white is the form of water, and the black is the form of food (*anna*). By the force of the syntactical unity with the word "food" (*anna*), the earth is [meant] here. The seventh section formulates the following: Are space and the rest the agents of their effects, or is Brahman qualified by them?

Since it is stated that "from space comes air, from air comes fire," space and the others possess agency. Furthermore, because it is stated that "the Lord dwells within and controls [them]," Brahman must be the cause of air and so forth, as He is also the seer of fire and the rest. In the previous sections, the preceding...

It has been established on the assumption that the production of each subsequent effect proceeds from Brahman as conditioned by its preceding effect. This is incorrect, because in such cases as "from space comes air, from air comes fire," we hear of the production of subsequent effects from mere space and so forth, independent of Brahman. To this objection, we reply: "He who dwells within space and controls it from within."

In the Antaryāmibrāhmaṇa, beginning with the passage "He who controls the wind from within," the independence of ether and the other elements is refuted. Likewise, in such texts as "That fire thought" and "Those waters thought," the creative agency of fire and the rest is heard to be preceded by reflection (*īkṣaṇa*). Such reflection is not possible for non-conscious entities that are independent of the conscious Brahman. Therefore, [the ether and so forth...]

Brahman alone, as the substrate, is the cause. He formulates the eighth section [of the *Vedāntasūtra*]: "Is the order of dissolution to be known as the same as the order of creation, or rather as the reverse? Since what is established is better than what must be postulated, the order of creation would apply to dissolution. However, in the absence of a cause, the existence of the effect is not logical; therefore, because it has been stated that 'earth [dissolves] into water' and so forth, the reverse order [is correct]."

Regarding the order of dissolution: since the order of ether and the other elements was established for creation, one might argue that the same order applies to dissolution as well. To this we reply: if the cause were dissolved first, it would follow that the effects, being without a material substratum (*nirupādāna*), would have to persist for some time. Furthermore: "O divine sage, the earth, the support of the world, dissolves into water; [water] into fire... [and so on].
Since the *Purāṇa* states that "the waters dissolve into fire, and fire dissolves into air," this sequence is indeed established.
Therefore, dissolution occurs in a sequence beginning with earth and so forth, which is the reverse of the order of creation. The ninth section formulates the inquiry:
Is there a disruption of the stated sequence by the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and the rest, or not? There is, for the vital breath and the senses—

Because they move within the intermediate space (vyoman) of Brahman, the vital breaths (prāṇa) and so forth—being material—are included within the elements; therefore, they do not desire a separate sequence. Consequently, there is no contradiction, nor is a specific order for the vital breaths and so on heard in scripture. It is heard in the *Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad*: "From this [Brahman] is born the vital breath, the mind, and all the senses; as well as space, air, light, water, and earth—the support of the universe."

Regarding the term *dhāriṇī*: since the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and so forth are heard mentioned before ether (*viyat*) and the other elements, it might follow that the previously stated order of creation—beginning with ether—would be subverted. To this we reply: "For, my dear, the mind consists of food (*annamaya*), and the vital breath consists of water (*apomaya*). [Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.5.4]

Since it is heard that speech consists of fire and that the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and so forth are elemental in nature, they are included within the elements themselves; thus, a separate mention of them is not required. Furthermore, the *Muṇḍaka* scripture does not intend to express a sequence, because no sequence is perceived there—unlike in passages such as "from ether comes air, from air comes fire"—and it merely states their origination. Therefore, this [scripture] does not [establish a sequence].

There is a violation of the previously stated sequence by the scripture. By these various topical sections (*adhikaraṇas*), [it is shown that] from Brahman qualified by *māyā* arise ether and so forth—[as established in: "But from the meditation on That alone [arises the world], because of its characteristic marks" (Sūtra 2.3.14); and "But the sequence is the reverse, for that is logical" (Sūtra 2.3.14)].

And it is stated [in the Sūtras]: "If it be argued that consciousness and the mind arise sequentially within [the body] because of their respective marks, we say no, because there is no distinction" (Sūtra 2.3.17).

In the *Brahmavallī*,
the origin of the world ending with the Puruṣa is well-established; and when that is well-established, [the inquiry into] the distinction from the cause—
The infinity of Brahman is well-established because it consists of all space, time, and all things, and thus there is no absence of its effects.

Having supported its infinity as asserted in the statement, "It is truth, knowledge, and infinite," [the text] now seeks to support its being hidden in the cave (guhā), as stated in the verse, "He who knows it as hidden in the cave. This is done by means of the five sheaths, beginning with the one consisting of food (annamaya) and ending with the one consisting of bliss (ānandamaya).
Desiring to distinguish the reality of Brahman from the sheaths (*kośas*), [the text] first shows the food-sheath (*annamaya-kośa*) with the words, "He, verily, this one...

That person who possesses a specific form consisting of a head, hands, and so forth, and who was produced at the beginning of creation through the sequence starting with space—that very one is now experienced as our own body. Although this [body] was not produced at the beginning of creation, nevertheless—

Because it is the effect of food obtained through a succession beginning with the *kāśa* plant, and because it is of the same genus (*sajātīya*), that very [self] is so designated. To clarify this intended meaning, the term "consisting of the essence of food" (*annarasamaya*) is used. The essence of food is sixfold, consisting of sweet, sour, salty, bitter, pungent, and astringent; its modification is that which "consists of the essence of food. The essence of the food consumed by the mother and father resides in their bodies.

Having been transformed sequentially into the form of the seven constituents (dhātus) known as skin, blood, muscle, fat, bone, marrow, and semen, it enters the womb and is further modified into the form of a body. Thus it is declared in the Garbhopaniṣad: "The sixfold rasa [becomes] blood from rasa, muscle from blood, fat from muscle, bones from fat, marrow from bones, and [semen] from marrow."

"That which revolves from the union of semen and blood is the embryo"—by this [statement], the subtle body existing within that gross body composed of the essence of food (*annarasamaya*) is also indicated. This is because it is an effect of the unquintuplicated great elements (*apañcīkṛtabhūta*) and because it is nourished by the food and other substances consumed. Regarding its being an effect of the elements, the Teachers have cited: "The five great elements in their unquintuplicated state..."
And its effect is the seventeenfold subtle body (*liṅga*), which is material (*bhautika*). That it is nourished by food and so forth is recorded by the Chandogas:

"For, my dear, the mind consists of food, the vital breath consists of water, and speech consists of fire. That the restoration of the mind, whose power has been exhausted by fasting, occurs through breaking the fast is established for living beings through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*). Likewise...

In the world, it is observed that the vital breath (*prāṇa*) of one whose strength has been exhausted by the fatigue of a journey is restored by the drinking of water. Similarly, singers are seen to nourish their speech by cleansing their throats through the consumption of luminous substances such as clarified butter and oil.
The gross body, which is the product of food, is joined with such a subtle body (*liṅgadeha*) consisting of mind, vital breath, speech, and so forth.

That which is perceived by us is this very internal [sheath]. By this, the celestial body of Vairāja, consisting of the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*), is to be inferred. That too has been shown by the Teachers in the *Vārttika*: "The God, whose instruments are the directions and so forth, who bears a body composed of the five elements—kindled by the conceit 'I am all'—thus became Virāṭ. This is the sheath consisting of food (*annamaya-kośa*). As for the branches...

The principle of Brahman has been introduced for the purpose of awakening [the seeker] to it by means of the analogy of the moon reflected in water. Now, for the sake of meditating upon this very sheath (*kośa*) in the form of a bird—like the *cityāgni* (altar-fire)—he sets forth its five constituent parts: "Of that, this indeed is... Just as for the fire-altar being built in the form of a bird such as a hawk or a heron, there are five parts: the head, the two wings, the sacrificial body, and the tail.
Or [it may be read as *vāḥ*]. It should be understood in this same way here as well. Above the neck of that *annamaya* (consisting of food) which is to be meditated upon—[the following occurs]:

This very head, being perceived as an established reality, is not here a mere metaphorical designation (*upacāra*). Likewise, these two hands, being perceived as such, are to be meditated upon as wings. This body, which is perceived from below the throat up to above the navel—

The "portion" (bhāga) is the self (ātman), which is the central body (*madhyadeha*) consisting of the space capable of supporting the living entity (*jīva*). This is because of the Vedic scripture stating, "The self is indeed the center of these limbs. That limb which exists below the navel corresponds to the tail of this bird-like form; and that is the "foundation" (*pratiṣṭhā*), meaning the support of the body. The etymology of the word is: "that in which [the body] stands firm" (*pratitiṣṭhati asyām*). This refers to the human body.

It is well known that the lower part of the navel serves as the support for the upper part. In the bodies of cows and other animals, the tail should be seen as providing support by warding off flies and the like. This mention of the tail as a support is for the purpose of meditation (*upāsanā*). Thus, the form of the sheath consisting of food (*annamaya-kośa*) to be meditated upon has been explained. Now, of this sheath, its—
And to provide corroboration for what was stated by the Brāhmaṇa regarding Pāśadyumna, he cites a certain mantra for the sake of establishing the meaning:

"And this too is a verse (tad apy eṣa ślokaḥ). That is to say, with regard to that very matter already mentioned by the Brāhmaṇa concerning the sheath consisting of food (*annamaya-kośa*), this verse about to be cited—beginning with "From food indeed [come] creatures" and ending with "therefore it is called food"—is intended to produce the understanding of corroboration.
There exists a mantra composed of verses (śloka) bound by quarters (pāda). A certain verse was previously cited regarding the meaning stated in the Sūtra.

With the intention of including that [verse] as well, the word "api" (also/even) is employed here. This śloka consists of fourteen quarters; although it lacks the specific characteristics of a meter well-known in the world, it is a certain Vedic *aticchandas* (exceeding meter).

...it will be so. Whatever beings there are—whether born from a womb, from an egg, or having other forms of bodies—that are perceived as depending upon the earth, they all arise from food alone; this has already been explained in detail previously.
Furthermore, by means of this very [food] they live, that is, they sustain their vital breaths (*prāṇa*); this is well known in the world. Now, after living—
At the end of their lifespan, those creatures merge into this food; they enter it; they dissolve into it.

The dissolution of animals and other bodies into fire should be understood by way of their becoming food for tigers and other predators. For indeed, because fire is the "eldest" (the primary cause) of beings—that is, of the bodies of living creatures according to the manner previously stated—for that reason, it is the "all-medicine" (sarva-uṣadha) for all living beings.

It is said that [food] is the remover of hunger and disease for living beings. For when hunger and disease are removed, it becomes the cause of the persistence of existence in the form of life. Therefore, its status as the cause of persistence is established by its being the remover of hunger; thus, it is logical [to call it such]. By this demonstration of its being the cause of origination, persistence, and dissolution, the sheath consisting of food (*annamaya-kośa*) has been elaborated. With the words "Or all," etc., [the author]—
The fruit of the meditation is enjoined: those persons who meditate upon food as Brahman— that is, who form the perception of Brahman upon the symbol (pratīka) of food—
[perceive] food, consecrated by the perception of Brahman and transformed into the shape of a body, [as consisting of] parts beginning with the head and ending with the tail.

They meditate upon [Brahman] as endowed with its constituent parts. Those meditators obtain all food, in the form of what is chewed, eaten, licked, and drunk. Alternatively, they meditate upon Brahman as characterized by that limiting adjunct (upādhi) of food—which has been produced from Brahman through the succession of ether and the other elements—and which exists in the form of the internal human body and in the form of the celestial Virāj.

Those worthy persons, having attained the universal form of Virāj, obtain all that food which is appropriate for every living being from Brahmā down to a blade of grass. In the preceding section, [the text] set forth the sheaths (kośas) as the means of knowledge for one desiring to understand; [this section now describes the result].

It has already been stated that food is indeed for the nourishment of all beings; here, however, it is stated once more for the purpose of praising the object of meditation. Since food is the eldest—that is, preeminent and most developed—among the bodies of living beings, from ourselves up to Virāj...

It is the very essence of battle. Therefore, it is the medicine that cures the entire disease of *saṃsāra* and brings about its cessation. For meditation upon [the Self] as described is the cause of gradual liberation (*kramamukti*) by means of attaining the state of *Virāj*. Furthermore, food is praiseworthy as an object of meditation because it is the cause of the birth and growth of the bodies of all living beings. Even upon a careful consideration of the etymology of the word "food" (*anna*), the praise of food is established through its being the cause of all bodies.

The true nature [of food] is understood as follows: it is called *anna* because it is eaten (*adyate*) by all living beings for the sake of life; or else, it is called *anna* because it eats (*atti*), that is, devours or destroys, all living beings. It is well known in the world that all bodies die due to diseases and other ailments produced by an imbalance in the essence of food (*annarasa*). The word "iti" in the Vedic text marks the conclusion of the cited verse.

The purpose [of this section] is to explain the meaning of the word *ātman* and to conclude the discussion on the sheaths (*kośa*). For that person who desires to know the reality of Brahman hidden within the cave, this sheath consisting of food (*annamaya-kośa*) is taught as a means of awakening. Its status as a "means" is established because it effects the cessation of attachment to external objects—such as son, friend, wife, house, and field—and brings about the realization that the self is limited to the body alone. Indeed, for living beings...

The designation of "self" (ātman) occurs with respect to sons and others by its very nature; and the Śruti reiterates this: "The self, indeed, is the name of the son. It is also recorded in the Aitareyaka: "This self of his is appointed for meritorious deeds, whereas this other self of his, having accomplished its purpose and reached old age, departs. This is the meaning of this passage.

For a householder who has sons, there are two selves: that in the form of a son and that in the form of a father. This self in the form of a son, belonging to this householder, is kept at home for the purpose of performing meritorious acts prescribed by the Śrutis and Smṛtis. But the self in the form of a father, having performed all his own duties and reached old age, dies when his life-span is exhausted.

Thus, the venerable author of the Bhāṣya has cited such an instance of superimposing the nature of the Self upon a son and others: "When a son, a wife, or others are either impaired or complete, one thinks, 'I alone am impaired' or 'I alone am complete,' thereby superimposing external attributes upon the Self.
Because the son's difference from oneself is perceived, the conventional usage of the term "Self" with respect to him is like [the statement] "Devadatta is a lion."

Therefore, in order to make known this very absence of primacy, and to withdraw the notion of "self" from everything external—such as sons, friends, and the rest of the world—and to contract it within the body, the self consisting of food (*annamaya*) is taught. This same intention he will clarify later on: "He who knows thus, having departed from this world, [attains] this self consisting of food..."

[The text] says, "he approaches the Self. However, for one who—due to the intensity of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of attachment to external objects—does not reach a final conclusion regarding the Self consisting of food (*annamaya-ātman*) through mere instruction once, meditation upon that [Self] is taught for the sake of reaching that conclusion. And that meditator, constantly meditating upon the Self consisting of food, being turned away from external objects, [naturally...]

It culminates in the state consisting of food (*annamaya*). If someone, being short-lived, dies while still performing the aforementioned meditation—due to the absence of the subsequent discernment of the *prāṇamaya* and so forth, and thus the lack of completion of the realization of the reality of Brahman (*brahmatattvabodha*)—then, in the manner described, he attains all food. It is with reference to such a case that [the Lord] said: ... [The text continues: ...having intended this very subject, Bha-...
It has been said by the Blessed One: "Having reached the worlds of those who have performed meritorious deeds and having dwelt there for eternal years, one is born among the pure and the illustrious.

"One who is devoted to yoga is born in that [family]"—thus, having taught the sheath consisting of food (*annamaya-kośa*) for the purpose of turning away from the objects of the senses, the meditation upon it and its fruit have been stated as a secondary topic. Now, for one who has turned away from the objects of the senses, he teaches the sheath consisting of vital breath (*prāṇamaya-kośa*) in order to enter even further within than the sheath consisting of food. "From that, indeed... refers to that which is supreme.

It has been established in the Brāhmaṇa that the Self (ātman) itself, through the sequence beginning with space, attained the state of being composed of food (annamaya). That very same point is further clarified by the verse: distinct from this [Self] described in the Brāhmaṇa and presented here by the verse—the one experienced as "I am a human"—there exists within the interior region another Self consisting of vital breath (prāṇamaya).

It is blown upon. By that *prāṇamaya* (consisting of breath), this *annamaya* (consisting of food) is filled. The *prāṇamaya* exists pervading the interior of the body from the feet to the head. Within the *liṅgaśarīra* (subtle body), there exist two things: the power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*) and the power of action (*kriyāśakti*). Between these two, there is a certain entity called *prāṇa*, which is the effect of the power of action. And the modification (*vikāra*) of that *prāṇa* is—

The aggregate of the five functions is the *prāṇamaya*. These functions—known as *prāṇa*, *apāna*, *vyāna*, *udāna*, and *samāna*—are specific activities of that entity called *prāṇa*, and they are produced in locations such as the heart and so forth. Thus it has been said:
"Prāṇa is in the heart, apāna in the anus, samāna is situated in the navel, udāna resides in the region of the throat, and vyāna..."

Regarding the phrase "pervading the entire body": this *prāṇamaya* (consisting of breath), which is of the nature of a collection of functions, must be regarded as the Self (*ātman*) because it is superimposed upon the Self with the sense of "I" and "mine"—that is, "I am the breath"—and because it is apprehended by the notion of "I" (*ahaṃpratyaya*) as the agent of exhalation and other such functions.

What is called "Self-hood" (*ātmatva*) is the state of being the immediate, internal form (*pratyak-svarūpatva*). In that regard, just as with respect to one's son, [the Self] is perceived within the *annamaya* (consisting of food) body...

When that which is of an external nature, such as a son, is taught to be the Self, the primary notion of "Self" regarding him ceases. Likewise, when that which is internal to the body—the *prāṇamaya-ātman*—is taught, the primary status of the body as the Self is refuted. Although there is a similarity between the son and the body in their lack of being the primary Self, due to an internal distinction, the son possesses a secondary (gauṇa) status of Selfhood, whereas the body possesses a false (mithyā) status of Selfhood.

And this has been stated thus by the venerable authors of the Bhāṣya: "Because of the sublation [of the notion] of son, body, and so forth, when there is the existence of the secondary self (gauṇātman) and the false self (mithyātman). The difference between these two should be understood in terms of whether or not their distinction from one's own self is perceived at the time they are conventionally treated as the self. As for the body, which is spoken of as the self by worldly people and the Lokāyatikas who do not know the distinction between the body and the self—

That the identity with one's own self [as previously conceived] is false has been established here by implication through the instruction regarding the self consisting of breath (*prāṇamaya*). This was determined in the third section (pāda) of the third chapter [of the Brahma-sūtras]: "Is the self the body or something other than it? Consciousness is like the power of intoxication;
it arises from the combination of elements in the body, and thus the self is the body, not elsewhere. The perception of the elements is distinct from the elements."

Because it is the subject [of experience]. That very self, distinct from the material body, is the one who partakes in the next world. Since it was previously stated that the mind, consciousness, and so forth do not exist for the sake of the ritual (*kratvartha*), but rather for the sake of the person (*puruṣārtha*), this inquiry is undertaken as a consequence to determine: "Who is this person? This particular section (*adhikaraṇa*) serves as a supplement to both the preceding and the subsequent Mīmāṃsās. [It establishes] the self as distinct from the body...

This is because it establishes the self as one who partakes in heaven and liberation. In this regard, the Lokāyatikas maintain that the body alone is the self, since consciousness is perceived only in the body through the methods of agreement and difference (*anvaya-vyatireka*). And there are [scriptural passages]...

Consciousness is perceived in the body when it exists, but not when it does not exist. Nor should it be suspected that consciousness is a distinct substance from the body because it belongs to a different genus; for just as the power of intoxication arises from the combination of betel nut, betel leaf, and lime, so too [consciousness arises] from the body having assumed a particular form.

How indeed could consciousness, which arises from the elements that are themselves insentient, be of a different nature? Therefore, when it is argued that the conscious body is the Self, we reply: the perception of the elements such as earth must be distinct from those elements, because it is the subject of experience. Whatever is a subject of experience is distinct from its objects; just as [the perceiver] is distinct from form—

[Objection: If that were so, how can you attribute the nature of being composed of material elements (bhautikatva) to one who asserts that such consciousness is the Self? As for the positive and negative concomitances (*anvaya-vyatireka*) stated—that consciousness is perceived only when the body exists and not when it does not—the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is unestablished (*asiddha*). For even when the body is absent, the conscious Self that migrates to the next world is known through scripture (*śāstra*).

[The author] says: Furthermore, the authority of the scripture must be established. In the fourth quarter of the second chapter, the origin of that vital breath (*prāṇa*) which is internal to this body determined to be non-self is considered:

"Should the principal breath be beginningless, or is it born? It is not born; for the activity of the breath is heard [in the scripture] as having existed before creation, in the passage 'Breath existed'."

From whatever [source]... "It breathed" (*ānīt*) refers to the existence of Brahman, because of the negation of wind (*vāyu*). Because it is stated, "From this the *prāṇa* is born," it is said that "this is born. The wind moving within the cavity of the mouth, performing exhalation and inhalation, is the *mukhya-prāṇa*.

It is beginningless. Why? Because in the hymn "Non-being did not exist" (*nāsadāsīt*), by the word "it breathed" (*ānīt*) in the phrase "it breathed without wind" (*ānīdavātam*), [the existence of Brahman] prior to creation is indicated.

Since it is argued that [the word *ānīd*] refers to the activity of speech and breath because of the mention of hearing, we reply: the word *ānīd* does not denote the operation of breath, because of the prohibition "it breathed without wind" (*anītam*). What then? It expresses the existence of Brahman, because it has the same meaning as other scriptural passages establishing the state prior to creation, such as "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone" (*sadeva somyedamagra āsīt*). From this, [breath] is born...

The scriptural statement "He [breathed] breath" (*prāṇam*) clearly establishes the birth of the vital breath (*prāṇa*). Therefore, like the sense organs, the *prāṇa* is born. On that very point, another matter is considered: Is the *prāṇa* air (*vāyu*), or the activity of the sense organs, or something else? From the scriptural mention of "breath," it is air; or rather, it is the common function of the sense organs, because the Sāṃkhyas declare it thus. It appears that the *prāṇa* is not distinct from air, because of the statement regarding their difference: "The *prāṇa* is air. (Note: The provided text contains a fragmentary argument concerning the nature of the *prāṇa*. The final sentence is incomplete, but the core philosophical inquiry concerns whether the *prāṇa* is identical to air, a function of the senses, or a distinct entity.)

This is the scriptural authority (*śruti*). Because it functions as a general property by virtue of being born from air (*vāyu*), there is nothing other than this [air] in the senses. External air itself, having entered and remained within the openings of the mouth like the holes of a flute, is designated by the name "prāṇa. However, there is no such distinct principle (*tattvāntara*) called "prāṇa. Why? Because of the scriptural statement: "That which is prāṇa is air" (*yaḥ prāṇaḥ sa vāyuḥ*). Or alternatively, just as those situated in a cage...

Just as many birds, by moving themselves, cause the cage to move as well, so too the eleven sense organs (akṣas) cause the body to move through their respective functions. Among these, that function common to all the senses known as the movement of the body shall be the vital breath (prāṇa). And thus it has been stated by the Sāṃkhyas: "The function of the instruments is common [to all]."

"The vital breaths (prāṇas) are five, beginning with prāṇa. Since it is thus established that prāṇa is not a distinct principle [from air], we reply: prāṇa alone is the fourth foot of Brahman. This is because, in another scriptural passage concerning the meditation on Brahman as four-footed, it is stated that "it shines by means of the light of air," thereby showing that the internal prāṇa and the external air exist in the relationship of the sustained and the sustainer.

The distinction [between them] has been clearly specified. but the activities of the sense organs—such as seeing, hearing, and smelling—are not of a single kind, nor are they conducive to the movement of the body. Therefore, it remains a conclusion that *prāṇa* is a distinct entity. In that very context...

Another [teacher] has reflected thus: "Is this prāṇa all-pervading or limited? It is all-pervading from the beginning of a tiny insect up to the body of Hiraṇyagarbha, because it is described as being equal in all bodies. Its all-pervasiveness is of a divine nature (ādhidaivika) in the form of both the collective and the individual;
whereas the internal (ādhyātmika) prāṇa is limited and invisible, like a sense organ, even in a creature such as a mosquito."

The individual soul, when in its subtle body known as the *puttikā*, is heard in scripture to attain equality with various bodies up to that of Hiraṇyagarbha; it is said: "Equal to a flea, equal to a mosquito, equal to an elephant, equal to these three worlds, equal to this entire universe. Since this suggests that the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is all-pervading, we reply: [it is] *ādhi-*...

Let there be all-pervasiveness for the divine *prāṇa*, Hiraṇyagarbha, because it exists both as a collective whole (*samaṣṭi*) and as individual manifestations (*vyaṣṭi*), according to the Śruti: "Vāyu alone is the individual manifestation; Vāyu is the collective whole. That very all-pervasiveness is elaborated upon in such Śruti passages as "equal to a gnat" for the purpose of meditation. However, the internal (*ādhyātmika*) *prāṇa* is invisible and limited, like the sense organs.

However, for one who—due to the intensity of the latent impression (*vāsanā*) cultivated over many births that identifies the body as the self—is unable to abandon the notion of the body as the self merely through the instruction regarding the self consisting of vital breath (*prāṇamaya*), the text shows the nature of the object of meditation (*upāsya-svarūpa*) in order to prescribe another form of meditation for him: "That indeed is this person" (*sa vā eṣa puruṣa*). That which was described as being internal to the body is indeed this very *prāṇa*.

Thus being experienced through the closing of the eyes, this person consisting of vital breath (*prāṇamaya*) is indeed of human form. Although it does not possess limbs such as a head by its own nature, nevertheless, having fashioned them [mentally], it should be meditated upon as having the form of a person. Nor should any difficulty in accomplishing this be suspected here; for, following the human form of the previously mentioned person consisting of food (*annamaya*), one should—

Since this *prāṇamaya* (consisting of breath), existing in its fullness within the center, can also be described as having the form of a person (*puruṣaprakāra*), it is like molten copper poured into a mold that takes the shape of an image. In that regard, the specific function called *prāṇa*, which moves upward from the heart through the mouth and nostrils, should be meditated upon as the head. In all [the limbs]...

The specific function known as vyāna, which circulates through the channels (nāḍīs), and the specific function known as apāna, which issues downward from the heart—both of these are to be contemplated as being like two wings. By the word "space" (ākāśa), a particular region situated in the middle of the abdomen near the navel is denoted; by that [term], the samāna wind residing there is indicated.

Form is perceived; and that wind is the self, the middle portion of the sheath consisting of vital breath (*prāṇamaya-kośa*). By the word "earth," the atom (*aṇu*) is also [meant]. [End of] Adhyāya 2, Pāda 4, Adhikaraṇa 6.

In the work composed by Vidyāraṇya, it is stated that the *udāna* breath is indicated [by the term "Brahman"]; for if the primary meaning were accepted, the context of the sheath consisting of vital breath (*prāṇamaya-kośa*) would be contradicted.

Just as the earth is the foundation because it is the cause for the support of living beings, so too the udāna-vāyu is the cause for the support of the vital breaths (prāṇa) and other winds within the body. As long as this udāna-vāyu does not produce the upward departure [of the life-force], the prāṇa, apāna, and the others remain established in the body; therefore, it is the "foundation" (pratiṣṭhā). It belongs to that which possesses the specific function called udāna and performs the fivefold functions.
The followers of the Atharva Veda declare the independence of the principle of *prāṇa* with respect to both its departure (*utkrānti*) and its abiding (*pratiṣṭhā*). [They state]: "He reflected:
'In whom, when I have departed, shall I be departed? Or in whom, when I am established, shall I be established?
He created *prāṇa*. Therefore, for the sake of its abiding, the specific function of the principle of *prāṇa* is *udāna*.

In the form of the syllable *kṣya*, it represents the tail-like portion of the object of meditation, the sheath consisting of vital breath (*prāṇamaya-kośa*). Those specific functions of the vital breaths, such as inhalation (*prāṇa*) and exhalation (*apāna*), which have been conceptualized as the head, wings, and so forth, as well as the principle of the vital breath (*prāṇatattva*) that possesses those functions—all of this is clearly taught in the Maitrāyaṇī Upaniṣad: "In the beginning, Prajāpati existed alone; he did not find delight being alone. He...

Meditating upon himself, he created many offspring. He beheld them as if they were stones—unawakened, breathless, standing like pillars; he did not delight in that. He thought, "I shall enter within them to awaken them. Making himself like the wind, he entered within. Being alone, he was not able; he [became] fivefold.

Having divided itself, it is called that which is prāṇa, apāna, samāna, udāna, and vyāna. Now, that which moves upward is indeed prāṇa; that which moves downward is indeed apāna; that by which these [limbs] are supported is indeed vyāna; and that which is this gross—
He places the subtlest element of manas in the *apāna* and leads it into every limb; this indeed is known as *samāna*.

Beyond that is the form of *vyāna*, and the manifestation between these is *udāna*. Now, that which vomits up and swallows what has been drunk and eaten—this indeed is *udāna*. Formerly, Prajāpati was sporting in his own aloneness.

The meaning of the Śruti is that for the sake of their welfare and for the sake of establishing the worldly transactions of those created bodies, [the Lord], having entered within them in the form of the individual soul (jīvātman) conditioned by the limiting adjunct of the vital air (prāṇavāyu), divides himself fivefold and engages in activity. Just as with the previously mentioned *annamaya* (consisting of food), he cites a verse regarding the *prāṇamaya* (consisting of breath) as well, beginning with "And that too... (*tad apyeṣa*). Those who are characterized by *sattva*—
The gods, such as Indra and others, who are characterized by *rajas*; humans, such as Brahmins and Kṣatriyas and others, who are characterized by *tamas*;

and even animals, such as cows and horses—everyone, following the movement of the vital air (*prāṇavāyu*) residing within their respective bodies, moves themselves as well. For it is the vital air alone that sets the body in motion. Thus the Kauṣītakins record in their tradition.

"Indeed, it is the vital breath (prāṇa) alone, whose self is wisdom, that sustains this body and causes it to rise. Furthermore, the followers of the Atharva Veda record a dialogue concerning the maintenance of the body between the deity presiding over the vital breath and the deities presiding over the elements such as space, as well as the deities presiding over the sense organs such as speech. Among them, the preeminent vital breath said: "Do not fall into delusion."
