"It is I alone who, having divided myself fivefold, support and sustain this arrow. Just as an arrow...

Just as [an arrow] is impelled by an archer, the body is indicated by the word "arrow" because it is impelled by the vital breath (*prāṇa*). That vital breath which produces movement in the bodies of gods, humans, animals, and so forth, is called "the whole life-span" (*sarvāyuṣa*) because it is the cause of the life of all living beings; such is the name of the vital breath. Regarding this aforementioned vital breath—

Those persons who, being unable to abandon the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of the self consisting of food (*annamaya-ātman*) merely by knowing the sheath of bliss (*ānanda-kośa*), worship Brahman as conditioned by the vital breath (*prāṇa*) for the sake of removing that impression— those persons, through the worship of Brahman conditioned by the internal vital breath,
attain a full lifespan in this very birth by avoiding untimely death (*apamṛtyu*). [The text continues with] the divine...

However, through the meditation on the vital breath (prāṇa) known as Hiraṇyagarbha, they themselves become of the nature of Hiraṇyagarbha in a future birth and attain a full lifespan lasting until the great dissolution (mahāpralaya). This repetition of the statement "for the vital breath..."—which was previously mentioned for the purpose of praising the sheaths—is for the purpose of praising the meditation. It demonstrates the intended meaning of the instruction on the sheath consisting of vital breath (prāṇamaya).

"Of that, this is [the self]" refers to that which was just described as consisting of vital breath (prāṇamaya). This very one is the embodied self (śārīra ātmā) existing within the body of the former one, which consists of food (annamaya). When the state of being the self of the one consisting of vital breath becomes firmly established, then the notion of "self" regarding the one consisting of food departs; however, the one consisting of food is the body, whereas the one consisting of vital breath is the...

The certainty arises that "this is my own self," because two selves are impossible; this is the meaning. Now, for the qualified seeker who has turned away from the food-sheath (*annamaya-kośa*), the scripture teaches the mind-sheath (*manomaya-kośa*) in order to lead him further inward from the vital-breath sheath (*prāṇamaya-kośa*), beginning with the words "From that, indeed... Māyā, which rests upon Brahman, is the material cause of the universe and consists of the three qualities (*triguṇā*).
It is essentially composed of *tamas*. Since the portion of the *tamas* quality (*guṇa*) is the cause of the *annamaya-kośa*, in that sheath only dullness (*jāḍya*) is predominantly perceived;

neither the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*) nor the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*) exists therein. Since the portion of the *rajas* quality is the cause of the *prāṇamaya-kośa*, the power of action is perceived in that *prāṇamaya*. [The portion of] the *sattva* quality is the [cause of the] *manomaya*—

Because it is the cause of the three sheaths beginning with *maya*, the power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*) is perceived within those three sheaths. The quality of *sattva* mixed with *tamas* is the cause of the *manomaya-kosa*; therefore, qualities belonging to the portion of *tamas*, such as passion and hatred, are perceived in the *manomaya*. The quality of *sattva* mixed with *rajas* is the cause of the *vijñānamaya-kosa*; therefore, [actions such as] sacrifices and the like are found in the *vijñānamaya*.

The agency of these Vedic rites as well as worldly activities such as agriculture and the like is perceived [in the Self]. The quality of pure *sattva* is the cause of that which consists of bliss (*ānandamaya*); therefore, only specific types of happiness denoted by words such as "dear" (*priya*) are perceived therein. Although the power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*) is one in its essential nature, it is nevertheless threefold due to its internal subdivisions.

There are the power of instrumentality (*karaṇa-śakti*), the power of agency (*kartṛ-śakti*), and the power of experience (*bhoga-śakti*). Among these, that which is produced by the power of instrumentality is the mind (*manas*); its modification, consisting of the collection of functions such as desire and volition, is "consisting of mind" (*manomaya*). And these functions are recorded by the Vājasaneyins: "Desire, volition, doubt, faith, lack of faith, steadfastness, lack of steadfastness, shame, intelligence, fear—all this is mind."
"Not so. Likewise, other scriptural passages such as "thirst," "affection," "passion," and "greed" should be cited.

This [Self] consists of mind (*manomaya*) and has the vital breath (*prāṇa*) as its boundary; it is internal. Precisely because of this proximity, the Self is firmly established in the mind. (Note: *kha* reads *ātmanna*; *gha* reads *rbhoktṛya*; *kha* reads *yādābhya*).

In the *Brahmavallī*, consciousness (*caitanya*) is manifested as the innermost of all; it is solely by virtue of that manifestation that the one consisting of mind (*manomaya*) possesses the nature of the Self (*ātman*). By that internal *manomaya*, the external *prāṇamaya* exists filled, just as [the space within] a vessel is filled by its action—

Just as there is a pervasion of power from the feet to the head, so too the pervasion of the power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*) is perceived. Here, by the internal organ—the mind (*manas*)—all ten external organs, such as speech, sight, and so forth, are indicated. Therefore, it should be understood that all the organs of knowledge (*jñānendriya*) and the organs of action (*karmendriya*) are included within the sheath known as the "consisting of mind" (*manomaya*). These—

The origin of these sense organs was considered in the fourth quarter (pāda) of the second chapter [of the Brahma-sūtras]: "Are the sense organs beginningless or are they created by the Supreme Self? Their beginninglessness is asserted because of the statement that they existed even before creation;

however, they are produced because all intellects are known to arise from a single [source] and because their material nature is heard [in scripture]; thus, their existence prior [to creation] refers only to an intermediate state."

Regarding the argument from creation: [The opponent claims] that in the beginning there was only Being (*sat*), and as for who those *ṛṣis* were, the Śruti states, "The *ṛṣis* are indeed the vital breaths (*prāṇas*).
Since this scripture establishes the existence of the sense organs prior to creation, they must be beginningless. To this we reply:

First of all, the knowledge of all through the knowledge of one would not be possible if the sense organs were unproduced. Likewise, [the text says], "For [the body] consists of food... [and so forth].
"O gentle one, the mind consists of water, the vital breath consists of water, and speech consists of fire"—thus the senses are heard to be effects of the elements.
Furthermore, the clear hearing of the birth of the senses is found in the text: "From this [Self] are born the vital breath, the mind, and all the senses.
As for the statement regarding their existence prior to creation, that must be explained as referring to an intermediate creation. Therefore—
The sense organs arise from the Supreme Self. Regarding this, another point is considered: "Are there seven or eleven organs?

According to the Vedic scripture, "There are seven vital breaths (*prāṇāḥ*). There would be seven [organs] because of the specific mention of the apertures located in the head; however, since the hand and other non-cephalic parts are also mentioned as being moved by the wind (*samīraṇa*) in the Veda, the organs should be known as eleven, in accordance with their respective functions in the body.

[The opponent argues: "There are only seven sense organs (*indriya*). Why? To this we reply: Other [organs] such as the hands and so forth, distinct from those located in the head, are also proclaimed in the Veda. [For example,] the two hands...

And [the organs] must be grasped, and the organ of generation must experience pleasure, and so forth. What is the use of this postulation of sense organs that are all-pervading and devoid of any function? Furthermore, scripture teaches the departure, going, and returning of the individual soul (*jīva*); since these cannot occur in a primary sense for an all-pervading soul, the adjunct (*upādhi*) of the sense organs was accepted in order to establish their primary status. If even this adjunct were all-pervading, [the aforementioned scriptural teachings would remain inexplicable].

Where, then, could [phenomena] such as eclipses (*akrānti*) primarily occur? Therefore, the sense-faculties (*akṣa*) are not all-pervading (*asarvagata*). The author of the Sūtras employed the term "atom" (*aṇu*) with the intention of referring to their being of intermediate dimension while remaining invisible. Furthermore, another point has been considered:
would speech and the other [faculties] be independent or dependent on the gods? If they were not independent, then the experience arising from speech and so forth would belong to the gods.

It might be argued that [the fruit] does not belong to the self. However, while it is heard in scripture that the sacrificial fires and so forth constitute the *tantra* (the common substratum), it is not appropriate for the fires themselves to experience the enjoyment. Since this is already established in the case of the bodies of the gods, the individual soul (*jīva*) experiences [the fruit] through its own karma. Furthermore, the organs such as speech function with independence regarding their respective objects, rather than being dependent upon the presiding deities. Otherwise, the enjoyment produced by speech and the other organs would result in the gods themselves experiencing the fruit.

To the objection that, because [the senses] are triads, there can be no enjoyment for the individual self (jīvātman), we reply: In passages such as "Fire, having become speech, entered the mouth," it is heard that speech and the other organs are presided over by Fire and the other deities. Therefore, the activity of the sense organs is dependent upon the gods.

Yet, this does not imply that the gods are the enjoyers here; for it is impossible for those who have attained the status of a deity—a fruit of great merit—to experience an inferior form of enjoyment.

Because supreme enjoyment is inappropriate for the bodies of deities and because such enjoyment is already established [for them], it is logical that the living beings of humans and others experience the enjoyment brought about by the senses as directed by the deities as the fruit of their own karma. Therefore, the senses are dependent upon the deities. Furthermore, another point is considered: the senses are the functions of the vital breath (prāṇa); they are not a separate principle from the vital breath.

Or rather, [they are] the functions (*vṛtti*) [of the vital breath], because their nature as such is heard in scripture and because they are designated by the name "prāṇa. Since distinctions such as those between the stages of life (*āśrama*) are mentioned, the terms "nature" and "name" are used in a secondary sense (*gauṇa*). The others [the senses] are [so called] because they are observers; [it is said] that "the prāṇa is the leader of the senses and the body. Here, the senses such as speech and so on ought to be the functions of the principal prāṇa. Why? Because their nature as being of the form of prāṇa is heard in scripture.

For there is the scriptural statement: "All these became his very form. Furthermore, in common worldly usage, those [organs] are designated by the word "prāṇa" itself, as in such expressions as, "The prāṇas of one who is dying have not yet departed. And scripture declares the identity of speech and the other organs with the act of breathing (prāṇana), stating: "One does not say 'voices,' nor 'eyes,' nor 'ears,' nor 'minds'."
"They call them simply 'the vital breaths' (prāṇa). Since it might thus be concluded that there are no principles other than the vital breath, we reply:

Death, having become weariness, overtook them; therefore, speech and the others become weary in their respective domains, as stated in the passage beginning with "Speech becomes weary. Then, [Death] could not reach this one—the middle vital breath which is here.

"Whether moving or not moving, he does not suffer"—this states that there is no fatigue for the vital breath (*prāṇa*) in its own function; this is one distinction. Likewise, in the *Prāṇasaṃvāda*, having described the absence of death or rising from death in the body upon the departure or entry of speech and the other [senses], it shows that death and rising occur upon the departure or entry of the vital breath. Therefore, because of such statements regarding distinctions, [the vital breath is distinct].

The status of speech and the other organs as being the nature of breath (*prāṇa*) and as having "breath" as their name is secondary (*gauṇa*). Furthermore, according to the analogy of the master and the servant, there is the presiding over [the senses] by the breaths, because of the scriptural teaching thereof (Sūtra 2.4.7). And those [other seven] are the sense-organs (*indriya*), because they are designated as such, with the exception of the best one (the breath) (Sūtra 2.4.8).

Which are the organs? Prāṇa is the leader of the senses and of the body; therefore, because of its distinction from [mere] exertion and the like, the senses are distinct principles (tattva) from prāṇa. And the preeminence of the mind [is established] over the vocal and other organs by their own—

It is logical that [the mind] is the basis for one's own activities; for speech and the other organs engage in their respective functions only by prioritizing the mental modification (manovṛtti) denoted by the word "prajñā," which consists of the desire to speak, the desire to see, the desire to hear, and so forth. The Kauṣītakins set forth this point in detail through positive and negative concomitance: "Having mounted upon speech by means of prajñā, one utters all names through speech..."

The positive concomitance (*anvaya*) is as follows: "Having mounted upon the eye by means of wisdom (*prajñā*), one perceives all forms through the eye," and so forth. For indeed, speech devoid of wisdom would not cause any name whatsoever to be perceived; rather, one says, "My mind was elsewhere; I did not perceive this name.
Nor would the eye devoid of wisdom cause any form whatsoever to be perceived; rather, one says, "My mind was elsewhere... [I did not perceive this form].

The distinction [is shown] by such statements as, "Alas, I did not know this form. Having taught that one's own Self is within this sheath consisting of mind—which is the collective aggregate of all the senses—the text proceeds to show the nature of the object of meditation, intending to prescribe a method of worship for the purpose of firmly establishing that very Self in the heart. This is done with the words beginning, "He, verily... He who consists of mind, [distinguished] from the sheath consisting of vital breath...

That very Self which was previously taught as the innermost essence is now experienced in the form "I am conceiving," and for the purpose of meditation, it assumes a human form endowed with five limbs. As before, following the analogy of molten copper poured into a mold, it takes on the shape of a person by conforming to the *prāṇamaya* (the vital sheath). The three beginning with the *yajus* are the mantras found within the three Vedas; that which is pointed out or enjoined [is the sacrifice].

The word *neneti* refers to an injunctive Brāhmaṇa passage. The mantras contained in the fourth Veda, which were seen by the great seers named Atharvan and Aṅgiras, are the *Atharvāṅgirasaḥ*. Their status as a foundation (*pratiṣṭhā*) consists in their being the means for attaining desired worldly goals and avoiding undesired ones. Although the Yajus and other Vedas consist of sound and are not in the form of mental recitation (*manas*), [they are nonetheless included].

Nevertheless, the specific mental modifications that contemplate that [Brahman] are indicated by the words "Yajus" and so forth. As before, he cites a verse regarding this mind-made [Brahman] as well: "And that too... Because expressive words, together with the mind which makes them known, turn back without reaching the bliss that constitutes the very nature of Brahman—that bliss of Brahman—[is what they seek].

The wise person, meditating upon [Brahman] as qualified by the mental adjunct (*manomaya-upādhi*), never fears at any time. Because genus, quality, and so forth are absent, no denotative word applies to Brahman. This has been stated in the *Naiṣkarmyasiddhi*: "The grounds for the application of words are the emergence of the genitive relation, quality, action, and genus; none of these exist in the Self, therefore the Self is not denoted."
Thus, even the mind, when conceptualizing objects, conceives of them as being "like this" or "like that.

Neither of these two [attributes] is possible in Brahman. Therefore, the mind turns away from Brahman. This has been stated in the *Pañcakośaviveka*: "If one should ask, 'What is it like?', there is no 'like this' there indeed."

The *Taittirīyopaniṣaddīpikā*, verse 121, states: "The subject is not an object of the senses; because it is one's own self, it is not beyond perception. As was previously explained regarding the *annamaya* [sheath]...

The meditation on Brahman as qualified by the adjunct of the *prāṇamaya* (consisting of vital breath) has been described; likewise, here too, the meditation on [Brahman] as qualified by the adjunct of the *manomaya* (consisting of mind) is intended. Otherwise, the conceptualization of the head, wings, and so forth among the *yajus* and other parts would result in futility. In the word "vidvān" (the knower), the verbal root *vid* signifies meditation (*upāsanā*). [This is because] there is no distinction between the acts of knowing (*vid*) and meditating (*upāsti*).

Because their synonymy is observed in various contexts; this has been illustrated by the authors of the Bhāṣya in the Āvṛttyadhikaraṇa. In some places, having begun with *vid* (to know), they conclude with *upās* (to meditate upon); for example, in the passage "He who knows what he knows," [the text continues] "Teach me, O Venerable One, that deity; I shall meditate upon that deity. Regarding the passage, "One should meditate [upon] the mind as Brahman," it says: "He who knows thus shines and glows with fame, glory, and the splendor of Brahman.
Therefore, in this context, knowing is meditation. And by means of that meditation, there is no fear either here or hereafter.

For one who meditates uninterruptedly, there is an absence of fear in this world because there is no opportunity for passion, hatred, and the like; and there is also [freedom from fear] in the next world due to the existence of gradual liberation (*kramamukti*).

There is an absence of fear regarding the next world. By intending both [this world and the next], the word "kadācana" (at any time) was used. He shows the purport of this [section] to be the instruction on the mind-made self (*manomaya*). Regarding the phrase "of that": the meaning is that a firm conviction arises that the one consisting of breath (*prāṇamaya*) is the body, and its master, the one consisting of mind (*manomaya*), is the Self (*ātman*). In the *Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad*, in the dialogue between Bālāki and Ajātaśatru, [the text addresses] one who maintains that the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is the Self.

In order to teach Bālāki that the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is not the Self, Ajātaśatru went with Bālāki to the side of a certain sleeping man and addressed him by four names of the vital breath well-known from the scriptures; when the man did not rise despite this, he determined that the vital breath was not the Self because of its insentience, and [concluded] regarding the vital breaths—

In order to demonstrate that the self is conscious, he repeatedly pressed that man with his hand and awakened him; thereupon, the conscious self arose. And so it is heard in scripture: "The two [Naciketas and Death] approached a sleeping man and addressed him with these names: 'O Great One! O You clad in white! O King Soma! But he did not arise. [Death] then [pressed him] with his foot..."
...with a sound, he caused him to awaken. He indeed arose.

Now, for the sake of entering even further inward from the sheath consisting of breath (*prāṇamaya*)—which has already been transcended—to teach the sheath consisting of consciousness (*vijñānamaya*), [the text says]: "From that, indeed...

That which consists of mind (*manomaya*), whose nature is a collection of functions such as desire and volition, was taught as the Self because it serves as an adjunct (*upādhi*) to the innermost Self (*pratyagātman*). From that...

From this [self] which is experienced as "I desire" and "I will," there exists another inner self called the *vijñānamaya* (consisting of consciousness). With that *vijñānamaya* situated within, the *manomaya* (consisting of mind) situated outside remains filled. Just as in the power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*), which is the effect of the quality of *sattva*, there is a portion mixed with *tamas* such as attachment, aversion, and so forth—

The mind (*manas*) becomes endowed with the quality of *sattva*. Likewise, a portion mixed with *rajas* becomes consciousness (*vijñāna*), endowed with the attribute of agency (*kartṛtva*). Among the functions of the mind, it is that specific function-knowledge in the form "I am the agent" which perceives that entity endowed with the attribute of agency; that entity is consciousness, and it is its modification.

Consisting of consciousness (*vijñānamaya*). For consciousness is the effect of the quality of *sattva* mixed with *rajas*, appearing in the form of the ego-apprehender (*abhimantṛ*) who is the object of the notion of "I" (*ahaṃ-pratyaya*). Even though it does not itself move, it is perceived as if moving due to the movement of its limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*). Just as when a jar is being carried to another location, the space delimited by that jar is carried to another place, but not in its own right; so it is with this [Self].

The meaning is made clear by the word "as if" (*iva*) in the scripture: when the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) meditates, the conscious self (*cidātman*) itself is perceived as if meditating; likewise, when the adjunct moves about, it is perceived as if moving itself. It is precisely this cycle of transmigratory existence—consisting of departure, going, and returning, brought about by the adjunct—that the Blessed Lord [describes].

[The text] explained: "But because its essence consists of those qualities, it is designated as such. The *liṅga-śarīra* (subtle body) has been examined in the Mīmāṃsā treatise as consisting solely of the eleven sense-faculties (*indriya-tattva*) together with the vital principle (*prāṇa-tattva*) endowed with its five functions (*pañca-vṛtti*). If it is argued that no such entity called "consciousness" (*vijñāna*) exists as a distinct principle, [the answer is:

even though there is no discussion of it in the *Prāṇapāda*, it was nonetheless discussed in the preceding *Jīvapāda* as that which brings about the attributes of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra-dharma*) upon the individual self (*jīvātman*).

This is because it has already been examined in the passage beginning with "Because its essence consists of those qualities" (*tadguṇasāratvāt*). Even if the principle called consciousness (*vijñāna*), which is the intellect (*buddhi*), is accepted, the number seventeen of the subtle body (*liṅgaśarīra*) is completed. And that number has been stated by the Blessed One: "The five gross elements in their subtle state (*apavīkṛta*), along with their effects, constitute the seventeenfold subtle body. Countable principles (*tattva*) have been shown by the teacher Viśvarūpa: "The five organs of cognition, likewise the five organs of action, the five vital airs (*vāyu*), intellect (*buddhi*), and mind (*manas*)—they know these as the seventeen. Now, one might object: there are only four distinct modifications (*vṛtti-bheda*) of the single internal organ principle (*antaḥkaraṇa-tattva*), namely those called mind (*manas*), intellect (*buddhi*), ego (*ahaṃkāra*), and consciousness (*citta*). [Of these,] that which consists of doubt...

The mind (*manas*) is characterized by deliberation; the intellect (*buddhi*) consists of determination; the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*) consists of self-conceit; and the heart-mind (*citta*) consists of consciousness—these are the definitions of the mental modifications (*vṛtti*). These four modifications and their respective objects have been enumerated by the followers of the Atharva Veda:
"the mind and that which is to be thought, the intellect and that which is to be understood, the ego-sense and that which is to be made an 'I', and the heart-mind and that which is to be perceived."

If it is argued that [the two are] joined, we say no; for one must admit a difference in essence between those two as they exist in the form of the instrument (*karaṇa*) and the agent (*kartṛ*).

It is being carried away. Possessed of shadow [consciousness] and being the agent through its nature as consciousness, it is independent like a charioteer; by means of the instrument in the form of the mind (*manas*), which is like a rein, it restrains the senses which are like horses and sets the body—which is like a chariot—into operation.
Therefore, there is a difference in essence between the intellect (*buddhi*) and the mind (*manas*). This is understood from the fact that the intellect is stable and exists at a single time.

The word "consciousness" (*vijñāna*) is also recorded in that very same [text]: "But the person who has consciousness as his charioteer and holds the reins of the mind, he reaches the end of the path—that supreme abode of Viṣṇu. The excellence [of consciousness] is recorded in that same place with the intention of expressing its internal nature: "Higher than the senses are the objects, and higher than the objects is the mind; but higher than the mind..."

Regarding the term "intellect" (*buddhi*): likewise, the Śruti, in teaching Yoga in the form of *nirodha-samādhi* for the purpose of perceiving the inner Self (*pratyagātman*), demonstrates the interiority of consciousness (*vijñāna*). It says: "The wise man should restrain speech in the mind; he should restrain that [mind] in the knowing Self. First, one restrains the external senses, such as speech and the rest, within the internal mind, and then that mind [is restrained] even further than that—into the Self.

One should restrain [the breath] within the self of knowledge (*jñānātman*). Here, by the term "self of knowledge," it is the *vijñānamaya* (consisting of consciousness) that is denoted, and not the conscious self (*cidātman*), because the latter will be mentioned later in the phrase, "one should restrain that in the peaceful self" (*tadyacchecchānta ātmani*). For the sake of transmigratory existence, the individual self (*pratyagātman*), whose true nature is the Supreme Brahman, first assumes consciousness as an adjunct (*upādhi*), then the mind, and after that, the vital breath (*prāṇa*) which is external even to that.

This very sequence is handed down by the Vājasaneyins in the context of the description of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*): "Now this self (*ātman*) consists of consciousness (*vijñānamaya*), consists of mind (*manomaya*), and consists of vital breath (*prāṇamaya*). "And he alone eats the fruit," according to the Vedic revelation: "Of these two, one eats the sweet pippala fruit. This very one is the agent and enjoyer, the individual self (*jīvātman*) as established in the systems of the Naiyāyikas and others. And the Sāṃkhyas speak thus: "The internal organ is threefold. Among those, there is one called *manas*, which completes the number eleven of the sense organs. [Then there is] *ahaṃkāra*—

The second principle is [the *mahat-tattva*]. The third is the *mahat-tattva*. Among these, they define *ahaṃkāra* as follows: "Self-conceit (*abhimāna*) is *ahaṃkāra*. This very *ahaṃkāra*, endowed with the reflection of consciousness (*cit*), is here the "consisting of cognition" (*vijñānamaya*). Because the "consisting of mind" (*manomaya*) is filled by that which consists of cognition, even the "consisting of food" (*annamaya*)—which is filled by the "consisting of vital breath" (*prāṇamaya*) pervaded by such a "consisting of mind"—is [filled] down to the feet.

The conceit "I am the head" and "I am a human being" is perceived. Now, for the purpose of instilling the realization of one's own self as consisting of consciousness (*vijñānamaya*), the scripture prescribes a meditation and defines the nature of that which is to be meditated upon with the words: "He, indeed... That very agent who is well-known in the manner previously described—in the Vedas, in the systems of the Naiyāyikas and others, and in worldly usage—is this [very same person].

The "consisting of consciousness" (*vijñānamaya*), which is experienced as "I am the agent," becomes manifest in the form of a person through the conceptualization of a head, wings, and so forth— just as one worships the "consisting of mind" (*manomaya*) by imagining it with a head, wings, and so on, even though it is itself like a copper statue.
Although faith and the other [qualities] are effects of the "consisting of mind" because they are modifications (*vṛtti*), nevertheless, for the "consisting of consciousness," they are the agent.

Intending to show that because [the Self] possesses the nature of being the agent, the instrument, and the owner, the mental modifications (manovṛttayaḥ) also belong to it, [the author says]: Taittirīyopaniṣaddīpikā, verse 125.

For that which consists of consciousness (*vijñānamaya*), faith (*śraddhā*) is said to be the head. Faith is the supreme conviction regarding the reality taught by the teacher and the scriptures, as well as regarding the means for its realization. Here, by the terms *ṛta* and *satya*, two types of mental modifications (*vṛtti*)—characterized by the egoistic identification with those respective functions—are intended. Yoga is the pair of meditative absorptions (*samādhi*), namely the cognitive (*saṃprajñāta*) and the non-cognitive (*asaṃprajñāta*). He who...

Because it is stated in the Yoga Sūtra that "Yoga is the cessation of the fluctuations of the mind," and because by the word *mahaḥ* (the Great) is intended the principle known as *hiraṇyagarbha*— the first effect of the unmanifest (*avyākṛta*) mentioned in another Śruti as being "higher than the Great"—
which exists as the collective totality (*samaṣṭi*) of all individual agents who are accessible through the notion of "I. And that [Great Principle]...
"Stay! Having this very point in mind, it is recited in the *Uttaratāpanīya*: "Hiraṇyagarbha is the conceited one who identifies with all.
Regarding this [self] consisting of consciousness (*vijñānamaya*), he cites a verse as before: "And that is this...
That very consciousness, endowed with the power of agency, performs sacrifices such as the Jyotiṣṭoma; its [agency]...

That locus is conceptually constructed through exhaustion within the Witness-Consciousness, the Self. Likewise, even worldly activities such as agriculture and trade are performed by consciousness alone. All the gods, beginning with Indra, worship this internal consciousness—which is the agent of all worldly and Vedic actions—in the form of the Supreme Brahman (Jyeṣṭha-Brahman), which is the nature of the Mahat-tattva.

The body known as Hiraṇyagarbha is the first-born, the eldest body; for there is a Vedic scripture stating: "He who is this great, first-born Yakṣa. *Yakṣa* means worshipful. Likewise, another Vedic scripture says: "Hiraṇyagarbha came into being in the beginning," and there is also Smṛti: "He is indeed the first embodied one; he is called Puruṣa; he is Brahmā, the original creator of beings, at the beginning."

Regarding the phrase "samavartata": if a person, like Indra and others, should meditate upon Brahman as qualified by the adjunct of consciousness (*vijñānopādhika*), and if those who meditate upon it do not become negligent toward that Brahman qualified by consciousness for as long as they live— meaning, if they do not abandon the continuous flow of the realization "I am this aforementioned Brahman" and instead persist in the notion "I am a human being, an agent, an enjoyer, happy, or miserable"— [then the result follows].

Negligence consists in conducting oneself like an ordinary person. If one does not do so, then, while still existing in this body, one abandons all sins—which are the causes of suffering in future births—and, having enjoyed all pleasures in the world of Brahmā that are accomplished by mere thought, one is liberated upon the arising of the knowledge of reality. [This applies even to] the women and... of Indra and the other gods.

Even in the absence of the study of the Vedas, there exists eligibility for the Vedic knowledge of Brahman. However, although Śūdras and others lack eligibility through the gateway of the Vedas, they do possess eligibility in the Smṛtis, Purāṇas, and so forth; this was deliberated upon in the third pāda of the first adhyāya: "Are the gods not eligible for knowledge, or are they eligible? Because of their bodilessness... [and so on].

Their eligibility [for knowledge] is established by the removal of their mortality. Because they possess non-contradictory knowledge, mantras, and so forth; because of the existence of their bodies and vital essence;
and because of their desire [for liberation] and the ease with which [knowledge] is attainable, gods and others are eligible. This is heard in the third chapter of the *Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad*:
"Therefore, whichever among the gods awakened to that, he indeed became that; likewise among the seers. Among the gods and others, whosoever...

The meaning is that he, being Brahman, awakened; he himself became Brahman. In this regard, it follows that gods and others have no qualification for knowledge (*vidyā*).
Why? Because it has been stated that one who is desirous, capable, learned, and not excluded by the scriptures is qualified;
however, these grounds for qualification are impossible in the case of bodiless gods. Nor [is there a basis for their qualification] from mantras, explanatory passages (*arthavāda*), and so forth.

[The opponent argues: "There is corporeality for [deities] such as Vāyu; since mantras and the like, which form a single syntactical unit with injunctions (*vidhi*), lack *tātparya* (purport) toward their own literal meaning.
To this, we reply: Arthavādas are indeed of three kinds: *guṇavāda* (figurative statement), *anuvāda* (reiteration), and *bhūtārthavāda* (statement of an existing fact).
As they say: "In case of contradiction, it is *guṇavāda*; when [the fact] is already determined, it is *anuvāda*; and when both are absent, it is *bhūtārthavāda*."

"Discourse (*vāda*) is considered to be threefold. In such cases as "The sacrificial post is the sun" (*ādityo yūpaḥ*) or "The grass-bundle is the sacrificer" (*yajamānaḥ prastaraḥ*), since there is a contradiction with direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), the qualities of being the means for accomplishing the sacrifice—which belong to the sacrificial post and so forth—are indicated by the words "sun" and so on; thus, this is a discourse based on qualities (*guṇavāda*). In instances such as "Fire is the remedy for cold" (*agnir himasya bheṣajam*) or "Vāyu is the swiftest deity" (*vāyur vai kṣepiṣṭhā devatā*), it is a discourse based on what is established by other means of knowledge (*mānāntarasiddhārthavāda*).

Therefore, they are restatements (*anuvāda*). Let there be no intentionality regarding their own literal meaning in both of these cases. For in the case of non-contradictory historical statements (*bhūtārthavāda*) such as "Indra raised his thunderbolt against Vṛtra," it is impossible to preclude intentionality regarding their own meaning within a theory that maintains intrinsic validity (*svataḥprāmāṇya*); thus, having first established a subordinate intentionality regarding their own meaning through syntactic unity (*padaikavākyatā*), [the text] subsequently—

Through syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*), the explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) concerning established facts (*bhūta*) serve to establish the primary purport (*mahātātparya*) in the injunctions (*vidhi*). This same principle should also be applied to the mantras (*mantra*). Thus, when gods and others possess embodied forms (*vigrahavattva*) by the force of the mantras, explanatory passages, and so forth, their capacity for hearing and other such acts becomes easily established. Furthermore, their desire for liberation follows from observing that sovereignty (*aiśvarya*) is subject to decay and is comparative (*sātiśaya*).

The subject matter of the knowledge of Brahman (*brahmavidyā*) is applicable [to them]. Furthermore, "learnedness" (*vidvattā*) is easily attainable even for those devoid of initiation (*upanayana*) and Vedic study, because the Vedas manifest themselves spontaneously to them. Therefore, the eligibility of gods and others for knowledge cannot be precluded.
Even though, in the case of gods such as Āditya, their meditation upon Āditya and others—within the qualified (*saguṇa*) Brahma-knowledges interspersed with meditations on Āditya—is [the object].

Since there is no possibility of others such as the Ādityas [attaining this state], and because the fruit of knowledge—characterized by the attainment of the nature of the Āditya and so forth—is already established for them, they may have no further qualification [for this meditation]. Nevertheless, what fault is there in their qualification for the knowledge of the attributeless (nirguṇa) Brahman? Therefore, there is indeed such a qualification. Furthermore, the question of the Śūdra’s qualification has been considered in that very same context: "Does the Śūdra qualify? etc.

Whether in the *vidyā* or not, a Śūdra possesses the qualification [for knowledge], just as gods and others who are not of the three *varṇas* do. The gods have the Vedas manifest to them of their own accord, whereas the Śūdra is excluded from formal Vedic study (*adhyayana*). Thus, he lacks qualification for the revealed scripture (*śruti*), but his qualification for the traditional law (*smārta*) is not barred.
This is recorded in the *Saṃvarga-vidyā* of the fourth chapter of the *Chāndogya*: "He brought these... (the Śūdra).

"You shall converse with him through this very mouth. This is the meaning: A certain disciple named Jānaśruti, having brought a thousand cows, a daughter, a pearl necklace, a chariot, and some women as a gift, approached his teacher named Raikva.
These are the words of that Raikva: "O Śūdra Jānaśruti, these [gifts], such as the thousand cows..."
"You have brought [it]," meaning you have presented it; by this very means—through the gift of a daughter and so forth—you shall gladden my heart and then instruct me.

In that regard, it follows that even a Śūdra has the right to the study of Vedic knowledge. Why? Because it is indicated here that he was distressed due to his exclusion from the three higher castes, as is heard from his hearing of their disregard for him and his subsequent approach to them (Brahmins). Sūtra 1.3.34.

Having reached the position that [the knowledge of Brahman] is possible even for a Śūdra who is not of the three higher castes, based on the example of Devadatta, we reply: There is [a distinction regarding] the gods—

There is indeed a distinction between the two types of Śūdras. Although they lack initiation (*upanayana*) and formal Vedic study, the gods possess the Vedas manifesting spontaneously within them due to the merit (*sukṛta*) previously accumulated. The Śūdra, however, lacks such merit and therefore does not have the Vedas manifesting spontaneously;
nor does he possess the study of the Vedas because of his absence of initiation. Thus, regarding the qualification known as "learnedness" (*vidvattā*)—

Due to the absence of the requisite cause, a Śūdra has no entitlement to the knowledge derived from the Vedas (śrauta-vidyā). How then is it that the word "Śūdra" applied to Jānaśruti in the cited passage is used? We reply: this is an etymological (yaugika) usage, not a conventional (rūḍha) one. He is called a Śūdra because he "distressed (dudrāva) his teacher with grief (śucā)" born of his lack of knowledge. Nor does conventional usage override etymological derivation here, because conventional usage is impossible in this context. A—
Because in the *Saindhavaputra-upākhyāna*, Jānaśruti’s status as a Kṣatriya is understood through the presentation of his sovereignty and the instigation by the *kṣattṛ* (steward). If it be objected:
"If a Śūdra lacks the qualification for Vedic knowledge, then even if he possesses the desire for liberation (*mumukṣā*), liberation would not be attained," we say: not so.
For when the knowledge of Brahman arises through the medium of the Smṛtis, Purāṇas, and so forth, liberation is established. Therefore, a Śūdra is not [unqualified].

One is qualified for knowledge (*vidyā*). The abandonment of merit and demerit by one who knows Brahman with attributes (*saguṇabrahmavid*) even prior to the fall of the body has been considered in the third quarter of the third chapter. Is the abandonment of karma in the midst of the path, or rather before death? Or is the abandonment after crossing the Virajā river, according to the *Kauṣītaki* Śruti? [The former is correct], because there is an absence of fruits to be obtained through karma [once the path is traversed].

Because of the exclusion [of the two paths] in meditation (*dhyāna*), the sequence of the Kauṣītakins—which prescribes abandonment prior to the *Tāṇḍi* scripture—must be set aside. The abandonment of good and evil deeds mentioned in the preceding section must occur midway on the path to the world of Brahman (*brahmaloka*), because that [abandonment] is heard of immediately after crossing the river situated on the path near that world: "He comes to the river Vairañjanā..."

"He transcends by means of the mind alone; thus his good and evil deeds are shaken off. Since it might be argued that, therefore, the abandonment [of the deeds] occurs in the middle of the path, we reply: because there is no fruit to be attained through good and evil deeds other than the attainment of Brahman along the path to the world of Brahman, carrying those two [deeds] as far as the river would be purposeless. Furthermore, they are not abandoned prior to death...

The abandonment of good and evil deeds in the middle of the path is not possible, because it is impossible for one devoid of a body to perform such a practice. Nor is there a lack of authoritative evidence for their abandonment prior to death; for this is understood from the *Tāṇḍya* Śruti: "As a horse shakes off its hairs... And this being so, having crossed the river according to the Śruti—

This sequence stated by Kauṣītaki—namely, "renunciation"—is to be set aside. Therefore, the abandonment of good and evil deeds occurs for the worshiper even prior to death. Now, having understood that [the self] consists of consciousness (*vijñānamaya*), he shows that the state of being the body of the worshiper’s mind-stuff (*manomaya*) culminates in the intellect (*buddhi*): "Of him, this... This is to be construed as before.

In the world, an instrument such as an axe does not possess the nature of the Self (*ātman*). Likewise, because the mind-made sheath (*manomaya-kośa*), being an instrument, lacks the nature of the Self, its inclusion within the category of the body remains as the only alternative. Now, in order to dispel the notion of the nature of the Self even with respect to the consciousness-made sheath (*vijñānamaya-kośa*), he teaches the bliss-made sheath (*ānandamaya*) with the words beginning "Therefore, verily... This is bliss.

The essential nature of the supreme Brahman is bliss; "He understood that Brahman is bliss. Consciousness and bliss are Brahman—because there is nothing further to be crossed over in the hereafter, for thus it is stated by others (Sūtra 3.3.28). [This is known] from such scriptural passages as "Brahman is knowledge and bliss" (*brahma-vidyā-kṣeti*). That which is a modification (*vikāra*) of that bliss—the aggregate consisting of "dear," "joy," and so forth, which will be described later—is the "consisting of bliss" (*ānandamaya*).
Although bliss is itself devoid of modification, nevertheless, like space conditioned by adjuncts such as jars and the like, it appears as such through its association with *sattva*.

When limitation is imagined through the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) of the modifications of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇavṛtti*), [the Self] undergoes modification in the form of "dear" and so forth.

This very one consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*) is internal to and distinct from this one consisting of consciousness (*vijñānamaya*), which is joined with the conceit of agency. By that one consisting of bliss, this previously mentioned one consisting of consciousness is filled, just as the body pervaded by the one consisting of breath (*prāṇamaya*) is filled.

The activity of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), namely movement, is perceived; and just as when the body is pervaded by that which consists of mind (*manomaya*) and is characterized by the vital breath, the power of knowledge characterized by consciousness—which is the effect of the mind—is perceived throughout the entire body; and just as when the body is pervaded by that which consists of discernment (*vijñānamaya*) and is characterized by both mind and vital breath, the sense of agency, "I am the doer," is perceived throughout the whole body.

It is explained as follows: when the body is pervaded by that which consists of bliss (*ānandamaya*), and is thus distinguished by consciousness (*vijñāna*), mind (*manas*), and vital breath (*prāṇa*), specific instances of pleasure are perceived in the hands, feet, and other parts. This is the state of being filled with bliss. If it is argued that pleasure and pain are also perceived in the hands and so forth, let them indeed be perceived; however, this is due to the body being filled by the mind-made layer (*manomaya*), which is the cause of mental states consisting of suffering.

Because that is logically consistent. That suffering is a property of the *manomaya* (the mind-made self) and bliss is a property of the *ānandamaya* (the bliss-filled self) will be made clear later on.

Here, this must be considered: what is this so-called "bliss"? Is it the cessation of suffering, or is it a positive entity? On this point, the initial view is that it is the absence of suffering. In the world, [bliss is understood as the cessation] of hunger, thirst, disease, and so forth.

Because we observe the cognition of pleasure upon the cessation of pain, one might object: "While the opposing pain is present, pleasure in its positive form (*bhāvarūpa*) is obscured; therefore, at the time of the manifestation of pleasure, the cessation of pain must be required. Thus, because they occur simultaneously, the nature of pleasure consists in the cessation of pain. If this is argued, we say no. Apart from the cessation of pain, at the time of being freed from a fever—
Since there is no experience of anything that has the nature of a positive entity (*bhāva*), it follows that bliss (*ānanda*) is merely the cessation of suffering (*duḥkha-nivṛtti*);

to this we reply: because the sound of a lute arises spontaneously, even without the reflection upon suffering, its status as a positive entity is established through the manifestation of bliss. If, however, it were a non-entity (*abhāva*), it would necessarily be preceded by the recollection of suffering, since it would have to be defined in relation to its counter-positive (*pratiyogin*).

It would be perceived; for in cases such as "the absence of a jar" or "the absence of a cloth," there is a rule that the cognition is preceded by [the cognition of] the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*). And this has been established by the former teachers themselves: bliss is not the absence of suffering, because it is not definable by that [suffering]. Whatever is not defined by suffering is not the absence of suffering, just like a jar. Or alternatively: this bliss...

This [bliss] is of the nature of a positive entity (*bhāvarūpa*), because it is not defined by its counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*), like a jar. Or else: this bliss is of the nature of a positive entity, because it possesses gradation (*sātiśayatva*), like suffering. This possession of gradation will become clear later on with respect to the blisses of the universal sovereign (*sārvabhauma*) and others. Once its status as a positive entity is established, this must further be considered: is this bliss of the nature of an action (*kriyārūpa*), or rather a quality (*guṇa*)?

Is it of the nature of action, or the reflection of something, or an undivided entity, or perhaps an unlimited and independent one? In this regard, it first follows that it is of the nature of action. Why? Because the word "ānanda" (bliss) is derived from the verbal root *ṇad*, meaning "to prosper. Furthermore, the Kauṣītakins [mention it] among the organs of action.

They declare that the object of the organ of generation is endowed with the activity of pleasure. Having mounted upon the organ of generation by means of wisdom, one experiences through the organ of generation. Thence... [page 272] [omitted portions as per instructions] ...is experienced.

"He attains pleasure (*rati*) and procreation (*prajāti*). Here, the contact between the parts of the body, being pervaded by the pleasurable activity produced by the organ of generation, is denoted by the word "pleasure" (*ānanda*). The play occurring at the time of that contact is "pleasure" (*rati*). Procreation (*prajāti*) is the birth of offspring, which is the fruit resulting from that contact. This is just as speaking and other such activities are produced by the organs of speech and the rest.
These are specific actions. Likewise, the pleasure produced by the organ of generation is also a specific action. And so the Sāṃkhyas say:

"Speech, grasping, movement, excretion, and pleasure are the functions of the five [organs]. Furthermore, the followers of the Atharvaveda enumerate the objects of the organs of action as being characterized by the aforementioned actions: speech and that which is to be spoken, the two hands and...

"One must give, and one must enjoy the organ of generation, and one must experience bliss, and one must discharge the vital air, and one must walk with the feet. If it is argued that because this activity of bliss produced by the organ of generation is included within the *manomaya* (the mental sheath), it is therefore incorrect for the *ānandamaya* (the bliss-sheath) to be interior to the *vijñānamaya* (the knowledge-sheath), we say: not so. For the activity you have described—

Because it is the "empty" bliss that is intended here. And as for that bliss, the view of the Vaiśeṣikas is that it is a momentary quality produced by the conjunction of the mind with a self endowed with agency and enjoyership; for they accept these nine—intellect, pleasure, pain, desire, and so forth—as specific qualities of the self. The Sāṃkhyas, however...
They think thus: "Because the Self is unattached (*asaṅga*), desire and the rest are transformations of the three qualities (*guṇa*) residing in *prakṛti*.

Among these, pleasure is a transformation of the quality of goodness (*sattva*); activity is a transformation of the quality of passion (*rajas*); and negligence is a transformation of the quality of darkness (*tamas*). And so it has been said by the Blessed One as well: "Goodness attaches one to pleasure, O Bhārata; passion attaches one to action."
"But darkness (tamas), veiling knowledge, engenders negligence," so it is said. However, the followers of the Nyāyaikadeśins (*Nyāya-ekadeśins*) say this:

whatever sensory pleasure exists, that is indeed suffering because it is accompanied by suffering. The accompaniment of suffering should be understood from the exertion required to procure the means [of pleasure], from the fluctuation in its intensity, and from the destruction of the pleasure itself, which gives rise to suffering. In the state of liberation (*mokṣa*), however, there is eternal happiness.

[The object] is made an object by knowledge, which is an attribute of the Self; therefore, liberation is the goal of human endeavor (*puruṣārtha*). These positions of the Vaiśeṣikas and others have been imagined by the intellects of men. But the Śruti declares that the bliss of sense objects is but a fragment of the eternal bliss that constitutes the very nature of the Self—a substance that is independent. This is His supreme [bliss].

Nanda: "Other beings subsist on only a fraction of this very bliss. A certain yogi, revealing his own discernment, spoke regarding this very point: "Subsisting in the midst of the ocean of milk that is bliss, I have indeed spent so much time in vain, tasting those mere droplets of its objects that arise from fire."

"Of deluded mind"—this bliss (*ānanda*) is of two kinds: that which is delimited by reflection (*pratibimba*) and that which is undivided (*avacchinna*). Regarding the position of reflection, it has been illustrated by the former teachers as follows: "Now, here the bliss of the objects (*viṣayānanda*), which partakes of the nature of a portion of the bliss of Brahman (*brahmānanda*), is described as being the means [to it]; the Śruti declared its status as a portion when it said: 'This is his supreme bliss, which is... (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.32).

[The Self] consists of the essence of a single flavor. Other beings enjoy only a fraction of this [Self]. The fluctuations (vṛtti) of the mind are threefold: peaceful, terrible, and deluded. Dispassion, forbearance, magnanimity, and so forth are the peaceful fluctuations. Craving, affection, passion, greed, and so forth are the terrible fluctuations. Delusion, fear, and so forth are said to be the deluded [fluctuations].

[The various states of being are like reflections in Brahman. In all these states, the conscious nature of Brahman is reflected; in those that are tranquil, bliss is also reflected. "He became the form of every form, the counterpart," so says the Śruti. The comparison is with the sun—

The author of the aphorisms composed this sutra beginning with "kādi": "The self of beings is indeed one, yet it is situated in every being; it is seen as both one and many, like the moon in water. This moon, though not entered into the water, is indistinct in turbid water, whereas it is clear in pure water; likewise, Brahman appears in two ways within mental states—terrible and deluded due to impurity, and happy..."

That [consciousness] is here concealed. Due to a slight degree of purity, the aspect of consciousness (cidaṃśa) is reflected therein, just as a reflection occurs in extremely clear water. However, there is no emergence of pure consciousness (cinmātra) here from its own radiance; rather, it is like how both heat and light emerge together from firewood. In the same way, the emergence occurs within the tranquil consciousness of the face.

"Timāmutaḥ"—thus has the reflection-pakṣa (theory) been explained. Now, the limitation-pakṣa (avacchinna-pakṣa) is stated: the bliss that constitutes the very nature of the individual self (jīvātman), which manifests by itself within the limiting adjuncts (upādhi) such as the body and the senses—that is what is "limited" (avacchinna), because it is the object of supreme delight. As for the self's nature as bliss—

And the Vājasaneyins record that it has two objects: "This Self is dearer than a son, dearer than wealth, dearer than everything else—this which is the innermost Self. That which exists as the Self, experienced through the notion of "I," the witness of the body, senses, and so forth—that very thing is the most internal essential nature; it is indeed dearer than wealth, sons, and all else.
That which is most dear is that which is proximate to the self according to a graduated scale of proximity. The author of the Vārttika demonstrates this gradation:
"A son is dearer than wealth; a body is dearer than a son; likewise, the senses are dearer than a body; life-breath is dearer than the senses;
and the Self is supremely dearer than life-breath. Among things distinct from the Self, such as wealth and so forth, [the degree of dearness] is determined by their being subordinate to the Self.
Love [for others] is conditioned by limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*); however, because it is love for the Self that is unconditional, that love possesses supremacy.

All of this has been elaborated upon in the Maitreyī-brāhmaṇa through numerous examples, beginning with: "Verily, it is not for the sake of the husband that the husband is dear, but for the sake of the Self that the husband is dear," and so forth. These [passages are as follows]:...

Some have summarized the illustrations as follows: "The husband, wife, son, wealth, cattle, Brahmins, the worlds, the gods, the Vedas, and all beings are dear for the sake of the Self. Because it is the primary object of affection, the Self is the essential nature of primary bliss (*ānanda*). It is limited because it exists only within each individual body. And that [Self] is innate—

Because it is blissful, it has the form of a reflection (*vimba*). Its reflection (*pratibimba*) appears within peaceful mental states that have as their objects favorable wealth, children, and so forth. Since that reflection—like a reflection in water or a mirror—is false, and because even if the delimited entity (*avacchinna*) were real, it would still be possessed of the defect of limitation (*avaccheda-doṣa*), neither of these two possesses primary bliss. However, that which is undelimited...

Bliss, which is of the nature of Brahman, is the primary [bliss]. And so the Chandogas record in the dialogue between Nārada and Sanatkumāra: "But bliss indeed is what one must desire to understand. "O Venerable One, I desire to understand bliss. [The text continues: "It reveals itself in water... in water... [End of fragment]. 131. "He" refers to that which is the Infinite (*bhūman*). That which is the Infinite is bliss; there is no bliss in the finite. The Infinite alone is bliss; therefore, the Infinite indeed must be sought after. [Nārada said: "Venerable sir, I wish to seek after the Infinite. [Yājñavalkya replied: "Where one sees nothing else, hears nothing else..."

"When one sees nothing else, hears nothing else, and understands nothing else, that is the Infinite (bhūmā). But where one sees something else, hears something else, and understands something else, that is the finite (alpa). That which is the Infinite is indeed immortal; but that which is finite is mortal. This is the meaning of this passage: having been thus entreated by Nārada, "Carry me across to the further shore of sorrow," Sanatkumāra [taught] the nature of bliss for the sake of crossing over sorrow.

He said, "This must be investigated by you. To Nārada, who had accepted that investigation, he taught the meaning of the term *bhūman* as supreme bliss (*sukha*). The state of being much is *bhūman*. Just as it was stated previously that the word *brahman* denotes unsurpassed greatness because there is an absence of the two causes for limitation—namely, the context and a qualifying word—so too here, [the word *bhūman* denotes] unsurpassed abundance...

The word *bhūman* signifies abundance. For in the world, happiness is not seen in the scarcity of wealth; rather, happiness is seen only in the abundance of wealth. Therefore, having stated that only *bhūman*, which consists of happiness, is to be investigated, [the teacher] taught the definition of *bhūman* to one inclined toward such investigation by means of the passage beginning with "where there is nothing else," and so forth. Indeed, in worldly practice, someone...

The seer perceives a form other than himself with his eye; this is a certain "triplicity" consisting of the seer, the seen, and the act of seeing. That entity in which there exist no such triplicities—such as the hearer, the heard, and hearing; the knower, the known, and knowing—is the *bhūman* (the Infinite). But that illusory form in which these triplicities do exist is merely an illusory form.

The "small" (alpa) is perishable, whereas between those two, the "plenum" (bhūman) is devoid of destruction. However, because the causes of suffering arise within that small, dualistic state, that small is essentially suffering. But in the plenum, which is non-dual, because of the absence of such causes, the plenum is essentially bliss. Thus, this plenum is the essence of bliss in deep sleep and samādhi, where the threefold division (tripuṭī) is absent.

What is experienced? In the states of waking and emergence, which are characterized by the threefold subject-object-consciousness structure, a limited object in the form of worldly activity is experienced as being of the nature of suffering by both the ignorant and the knower of reality. Therefore, because it is mixed with suffering, the bliss that constitutes the very nature of the individual self (*jīvātman*) and the bliss of the mental modification (*vṛttyānanda*), which is its reflection, are not [experienced].

[Objection: But [one might argue] that the ground (bhūman) alone is the primary bliss; this is established. [Reply: To instill the realization of one's own selfhood in the *ānandamaya*, which is a modification (*vikāra*) of this bliss and consists of forms such as "dear" (*priya*), "joy" (*moda*), and so forth, the text shows its true nature (*svarūpa*) for the purpose of meditation, beginning with the words "He indeed," and so on.
That which is the *ānandamaya*, situated within the *vijñānamaya*, is indeed this very "I," the happy one.

That which is experienced as the "enjoyer" follows the human form—consisting of head, wings, and so forth—of the *vijñānamaya* (the self composed of consciousness), and is itself likewise of human form.

*Priya*, *moda*, and *pramoda* are the joys reflected in the states of the *sattva* quality. Among these, *priya* is that which arises from seeing a beloved son or other such objects; *moda* is that which arises from obtaining them; and *pramoda* is that which arises from the assistance rendered by them.

Bliss (*ānanda*) is that which is reflected in ignorance (*ajñāna*), which serves as the substrate for the aforementioned mental modifications (*vṛtti*). Alternatively, that bliss is the delimited (*avacchinna*) prototype (*bimba*) situated in its place, which constitutes the nature of the individual self (*jīvātman*) as the counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*) of the reflections in the mental modifications. Unconditioned (*anavacchinna*) and primary bliss is Brahman; that alone is the foundation (*pratiṣṭhā*) and support (*ādhāra*) of the others. Of the conditioned...

[This is] because the worlds of Brahmā and their forms are dependent upon that [Self]. Although joy (*priya*), delight (*moda*), and extreme delight (*pramoda*)—being specific modifications (*vṛtti*) of the mind which is of the nature of an instrument—are external to the one consisting of consciousness (*vijñānamaya*), which is of the nature of the agent; nevertheless, for the internal, limited individual soul (*jīva*)—

Because it bears the reflection of bliss—that is, the undivided bliss of Brahman—it is intended as being internal; thus, the Self consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*) is said to be more internal than the Self consisting of consciousness (*vijñānamaya*). When one who meditates upon this very Self consisting of bliss realizes it through contemplation, then there arises one-pointed concentration even upon Brahman, which is figuratively designated as its "tail."

The mental state, having been directed [toward the goal], directly realizes the reality of Brahman due to the absence of any reflected image; for the Śruti states, "But it is seen by this very intellect when it has turned toward Itself. Just as one who proceeds toward a gem's luster under the delusion that it is the gem itself eventually realizes the reality of the gem, so too is this direct realization of the reality of Brahman established by implication as the fruit of meditation (*upāsti*).

Intending this, the Śruti, without mentioning any other fruit, concludes its instruction on the reality of Brahman—which serves as the support for the entire universe—merely with the words, "Brahman is the tail, the support. Thereafter, it cites a verse that establishes Brahman as the primary essence within this sheath consisting of bliss, beginning with: "And concerning that, there is this [verse]. For in the world, when performing tasks such as fetching water...
With reference to a jar, which is the object of worldly transactions such as seeing and touching, all living beings say, "This jar exists";
conversely, they say, "The jar does not exist. Therefore, one who is possessed of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of such worldly transactions—

One person considers Brahman, which is beyond human transaction, to be non-existent. However, another discerning person, through scripture, reasoning, and experience, realizes the non-existence of the elements and elemental things that are subject to worldly transaction, because they are determined to be composed of *māyā*.
Yet, because scripture and other means determine that Brahman—which transcends worldly transaction—is real, he perceives it as truly existent. In this regard:

The person who knows the non-existence of Brahman would himself be non-existent; for it has been established that the sheaths beginning with the one composed of food (*annamaya*) are not the Self, and because [the opponent] does not himself admit the existence of a Brahman distinct from them. However, for that person who knows that there exists a Brahman transcending the five sheaths, that very Brahman is his own true nature (*svarūpa*). Therefore, Brahman exists.

Those who have reached the further shore of the scriptures know this person—who is discerning, existing, and endowed with a self—by means of his own cognition. Alternatively, he who knows [the Self] as non-existent becomes himself non-existent and truly wicked; for since the entire path of the righteous, characterized by the system of castes, stages of life, and so forth, exists for the purpose of attaining Brahman, one who denies Brahman is a defiler of the entire path of the righteous.

He becomes one who asserts existence (*astika*). They say that one who speaks of existence is the opposite of what was previously described, being a true person who establishes others on every path of truth.

With this very intention, the Kaṭhas record in their scripture: "It is as 'existent' alone that it is to be perceived. Now, in order to strengthen the disciple's—desirous of knowing the nature of bliss (*ānandamaya*)—understanding of the Self regarding the reality of Brahman, he says: "Of him, this very [Self]..."
That which is the one consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*) is indeed the embodied self (*śārīra*), the master, of that preceding one consisting of consciousness (*vijñānamaya*).

The one consisting of consciousness is the body; the one consisting of bliss is the Self—this is how it should be applied for the sake of the practitioner (*upāsaka*). However, for the sake of the seeker who desires to know, it should be applied thus: "That very entity which was called the 'tail of Brahman' is indeed the [Self] of that preceding one, [consisting of] joy..."

The embodied self (*śārīra ātmā*) consists of the fourfold group beginning with pleasure (*moda*); that body, characterized by the pleasant (*priya*) and so forth, has Brahman alone as its Self when situated within that body.
With this very point in mind, the authors of the *Vārttika* say: "For all those who possess a false self, [Brahman] is the Self of all things, being the essence of the Self.

The definition of qualities such as truthfulness: they describe that Self as one from whom all saṃsāra has been entirely cast away. For a snake does not become possessed of its own nature [as a snake] through a self consisting of the superimposition of a staff and so forth; rather, it is by means of its true self as the essence of the rope [that it exists].

"...is possessed of [bliss]. Now, the Mīmāṃsā [analysis]: therein, the inquiry of the "Ekadeśins" (Partialists) was shown in the first section (*pāda*) of the first chapter: "Is the one consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*) the transmigrating soul (*saṃsārī*) or Brahman? This must be the transmigrating soul, because of the word 'maya' having the sense of a modification (*vikāra*), and because of the mention of limbs such as 'pleasure' (*priya*) and so forth. On account of repetition, the opening statement, and other reasons, the one consisting of bliss must be Brahman; [the suffix] *maya* [denotes] abundance..."

The suffix *mayaṭ* is used in the sense of "consisting of," while terms such as *priya* (dear) and so forth function as limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*). In the Taittirīyaka, five categories—designated as *annamaya*, *prāṇamaya*, *manomaya*, *vijñānamaya*, and *ānandamaya*—which consist respectively of the body, vital breath, mind, intellect, and bliss, are enumerated in sequence, each being more internal than the preceding one. Among these, the *ānandamaya*, which is the innermost of all, is neither a transmigrating soul (*saṃsārī*) nor the Supreme Self (*paramātman*).

Thus, there is doubt. First, it is concluded that this refers to the transmigrating soul (saṃsārī). Why? Because the etymology "consisting of bliss" (*ānandamaya*) signifies a modification of bliss, and such a state is possible for the transmigrating soul; it is not possible for the changeless Supreme Self. Furthermore: "Joy is indeed its head; delight is its right wing; extreme delight is its left wing; bliss... [is its trunk].

The Self (*ātman*)—of which "Brahman is the tail, the support" is said to be the fifth limb of the one consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*)—is as follows: pleasure (*priya*) is that which arises from the sight of an object desired; joy (*moda*) is that which arises from the attainment of it; delight (*pramoda*) is that which arises from the enjoyment of it; bliss (*ānanda*) is the general state of happiness appearing during deep sleep and so forth, characterized by ignorance (*ajñāna*); and Brahman is happiness devoid of all limiting adjuncts (*nirupādhika*). Mi-...

The five constituent parts, beginning with the head, are conceived as having the form of the head and so forth for the sake of facilitating the practice of meditation (*upāsanā*). Of this imagined *ānandamaya*, there are three parts: the head and the two wings. By the word "self" (*ātman*), the central body is designated as the fourth part. The tail is the posterior portion. The support (*pratiṣṭhā*) is the foundation, the fifth part. Not...

Furthermore, parts are not logically possible for the partless Supreme Self. Therefore, when it has been argued that the one consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*) must be the transmigrating soul alone, we reply: the one consisting of bliss is the Supreme Self. Why? Because of repetition. [The text] repeats the term "consisting of bliss" through such passages as, "This is the investigation of bliss," and "He reaches this Self consisting of bliss. Thus, the one consisting of bliss is the Supreme Self.
[The suffix -maya] is applied. Furthermore, repetition is an indicator of the primary purport (*tātparya*). And we have already stated that the primary purport of the Vedāntas lies in Brahman alone.

Moreover, because of the introductory statement "Brahman is truth, knowledge, and infinite," and because of [attributes such as] being the creator of the entire universe in the passage "It created all this," the one consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*) is Brahman. Nor is there any inconsistency regarding the word *mayaṭ* when applied to Brahman, for it signifies abundance (*prācurya*).

Because of its possibility; even the limbs such as "the beloved" and so forth will be produced by limiting conditions (*upādhi*) such as the perception of objects. Therefore, the view of the *ekadeśins* (partial authorities) is that the Supreme Self consists of bliss (*ānandamaya*). Now, according to our own system, the subject matter (*adhikaraṇa*) is stated:
Is the Brahman heard of as the "tail" a limb of another, or is it the primary subject itself? It may be a limb of the one consisting of bliss.

Because the status of being a "limb" (aṅga) is well-established for the tail; since a plowshare is impossible here, there is an indication by means of the tail (puccha) to signify the substratum (ādhāra). Therefore, bliss is the support upon which this [Self] rests, and thus it abides as the primary entity. As for that which is heard in the text, "Brahman is the tail, the support," it is Brahman.

Thus, the doubt arises: is this [the "tail"] indicated as a limb of that which consists of bliss (*ānandamaya*), or is it presented as itself being primary? On the prima facie view, it is obtained that it is a limb of the *ānandamaya*, because in common worldly usage the word "tail" (*puccha*) is well known to denote a limb. To this, it is replied: the word "tail" does not denote a limb; rather—

The word *puccha* (tail) denotes a tail. A tail is not possible for that which consists of bliss (*ānandamaya*), because a tail is a limb belonging to the "consisting of food" (*annamaya*) category, such as cows and other animals. Therefore, since the primary meaning of the word "tail" is impossible here, by virtue of contextual fitness, it indicates its secondary meaning (lakṣaṇā) as a support. Brahman is the support of the individual soul (*jīva*) who consists of bliss, being the substratum for that conceptualization.

Because it is not so [if it were the Supreme Self]. Nor is the *ānandamaya* (consisting of bliss) the Supreme Self; for even if one accepts the sense of "abundance" (*prācurya*), there is still the perception of the existence of some slight suffering. Therefore, it is taught primarily as the substratum of the individual soul (*jīva*). Likewise, the repetition of "Brahman" in such passages as "He becomes that very thing he meditates upon; if he knows Brahman as 'I am Brahman'" (*asaṃ eva sa bhavati... asaṃ brahmeti veda cet*), and the introduction of Brahman in "The knower of Brahman attains [Brahman]" (*brahmavid āpnoti*), are consistent with this.

It becomes the limit. Therefore, according to the principle of the person mentioned in the Kaṭha [Upaniṣad], Brahman alone is that which is to be known, and not the creation of ether and so forth, nor the sheaths consisting of food and the rest. That principle was stated in the third pāda of the third chapter:

"Is everything, beginning with the series starting from Akṣara, to be known, or is it the Person alone? Everything is to be known because it is heard [in scripture]; thus the sentences would be many."

Indeed, the goal of man is knowledge of the Person; therefore, the effort of the Śruti toward that end is great. For the sake of realizing Him, the senses and so forth are taught as the means of cognition, and thus the one Person is the sole object to be known. This is recited in the Kaṭha Upaniṣad: "Higher than the senses are the objects; higher than the objects is the mind; higher than the mind is the intellect; higher than the intellect is the Great Self; higher than the Great is the Unmanifest; [higher than the Unmanifest is...]"

"The Person (Puruṣa) is beyond that. There is nothing higher than the Puruṣa; that is the ultimate limit, that is the supreme goal. This is its meaning: having first mentally contemplated objects, one subsequently perceives external objects through the senses.
In this regard, the superiority of the senses over external objects is well known because they are internal to them. And [superiority] over the senses... having contemplated—
Objects that have reached the state of being objects of pride (*māna*) are internal; more internal than those is the mental modification (*manovṛtti*) consisting of desire (*abhilāṣa*).

More internal even than the modification is the intellect (*buddhi*), which possesses that modification as its attribute. More internal even than the intellect is the Self in the form of Hiraṇyagarbha, denoted by the term "the Great" (*mahat*), which serves as the material cause of the intellect. More internal even than the Great is the Unmanifest (*avyakta*), known as the root [cause], which serves as its material cause.

The Unmanifest (avyakta) is internal; even more internal than that is the Person (puruṣa), whose nature is consciousness (cidrūpa) and who serves as its substratum. There is nothing more internal than the Person. The Person alone is the ground where the gradation of internality comes to rest;
he is the supreme destination for those desiring the goals of human life (puruṣārtha). In this regard, the Person is [established] by the Śruti through its primary purport.
[The self] is that which is to be established. In this way, the series beginning with the sense organs is also indeed to be established; otherwise, the introduction of them would be purposeless.

If it is argued that there would be a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) in establishing many things, [we reply]: "Certainly. Such sentences do indeed exist, because a single unified sentence (*ekavākyatva*) is impossible [in that case]. To this prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*), we say: [the knowledge of the person regarding the entirety of transmigratory existence...]

Since it removes ignorance which is the cause of bondage, the Person alone is to be presented as the object of knowledge. For this very reason, in the supplementary passage [of the scripture], it says:
"For the purpose of meditation, because there is no other purpose" (Brahma-sūtra 3.3.14). [Note: Variants in manuscripts:
1. gha. *svaprā*; 2. gha. *śādādhā*; 3. kha tha cāsa; 4. ka. kha. ḍa. *lakṣya pa*].
