135 Yoga has been taught with great effort precisely for the sake of knowing the Puruṣa. "This Self, hidden in all beings, does not shine forth; but it is seen by subtle seers through a subtle intellect. This is the meaning: that—
The Self, being hidden within the interior, does not manifest to those whose faces are turned outward; however, it manifests to those whose faces are turned inward.

Those who are inward-turned and whose nature is to perceive subtle reality are able to see it through a mind that has attained one-pointedness by means of yogic practice and which has the subtle entity as its object. Furthermore, even if the Puruṣa alone is the subject to be established, there is no contradiction with the traditional lineage.
The teaching is not purposeless, because for one whose mind is directed outward, there is a gradual entry into the Person through a succession of means.

Therefore, by this reasoning, it is the Person alone who is to be known. The creation of ether and the other elements was described in order to establish the infinity of Brahman; the five sheaths beginning with the "food-sheath" (annamaya) were introduced in order to establish its being hidden in the cave of the heart. That which is to be known—

But that is indeed Brahman. And it is established that this [Brahman], characterized by existence, knowledge, and so forth, is the nature of the inner self (pratyagātman) as residing within the cave of the heart.

Having thus concluded the section on hearing (*śravaṇa*), which consists of the instruction on Brahman, he now introduces the questions of the disciple at the commencement of the section on reflection (*manana*), which consists of providing arguments for those whose minds are turned outward, beginning with the words "Now, therefore" (*athātaḥ*). [This is] because of the instruction...

Since many doubts arise in the disciple due to defects in his intellect regarding the subject matter taught immediately thereafter, questions corresponding to what has been taught are therefore put forward. Here, the Śruti itself clearly states elsewhere the sequential relationship between hearing (śravaṇa) and reflection (manana), which is intended by the word "atha" (now/thereafter): "It is to be heard and it is to be reflected upon."

The essential nature of these two is thus recorded in tradition: "It is to be heard from the statements of the Śruti, and it is to be reflected upon by means of reasoning. Their respective purposes are declared in the scripture as follows: "The knot of the heart is severed; all doubts are cut away.

This means that when the reality of Brahman is known through instruction, the identification of the inner self with the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*)—which is the cause of transmigration—is destroyed.

The knot of form (*rūpa-granthi*) is dissolved. By means of reflection (*manana*) in the form of an investigation into the logical proof (*upapatti-paryālocana*), doubts are severed. Therefore, the meaning is that questions are here formulated in the form of presenting the doubts that are to be severed. He sets forth the questions that were promised: "Or does the ignorant one [attain]? By that which was stated—"The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme"—that [Brahman], being present in the intellect, [is the subject].
Two questions are raised regarding the ignorant one who possesses the three paths (*tri-yogin*). The word *uta* indicates a question; it functions in the sense of "what" (*kim*).
The word *cana* expresses the meaning of the particle *api*. The phrase "this world" (*amuṃ lokam*) refers to the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) present before one.
Is it that some ignorant person, having departed from the body, goes to the Supreme Self? This is the first [question] based on the Śruti. Or rather, does he not go?

The second question is established by the sense [of the text]. Likewise, there are two questions concerning the man of knowledge; thus, there are four questions in total. Since Brahman—the cause of the entire universe—has entered into bodies in the form of the individual soul (jīva) and is common to both the man of knowledge and the ignorant, it follows that if the man of knowledge attains Him, the ignorant man would also attain Him; and if the ignorant man does not attain Him, the man of knowledge would likewise not attain Him.

This is the intended meaning of Diti’s four questions. Alternatively, there are only two questions concerning the learned and the ignorant that are actually heard; the use of the plural number is due to their being combined with the question implied by the preceding statement. In the preceding statement, the subject of the existence of Brahman was indicated by the presentation of two alternatives: "If one knows 'Brahman exists' and if one knows 'Brahman does not exist.'"
1 ka. ṅa. upādiṣṭaḥ | 2 va. vidyate | 3 ka. gha. ṅa. 'yepi | kha. ye dvau | [page 279] 136
In this first question of the Brahmavallī composed by Vidyāraṇya, as an answer to this inquiry, the Guru proceeds to establish the existence of Brahman by means of the account of creation.

He assigns [the mantras]. Regarding the passage "He desired": that very entity designated as the "Brahman, the tail, the support"—which was described as the embodied self (*śārīra ātmā*) of the five sheaths (*kośa*) beginning with the one consisting of food (*annamaya*) and ending with the one consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya*)—this very self, being prior to creation, alone and without a second, having conjoined with its own power, desired. Within itself—

The meaning is that the power of *māyā*, having resorted [to Him], undergoes transformation in the form of desire (*kāmanā*). For indeed, desire is not possible for one who is immutable and whose sole essence is consciousness, except through *māyā*. Even if the Lord possesses a desire fashioned by *māyā*, one might object: "In that case, like the individual soul (*jīva*), He would not be eternally satisfied because of His state of desiring. This is not so; for here, [His desires arise] from play (*līlā*) and the like.
This has been resolved in the Mīmāṃsā by means of an illustration. Furthermore, there is no disparity with the individual soul (jīva) because there is never any obstruction to his desired object.

For this very reason, it is recorded elsewhere that he is "one whose desires are true" and "one whose resolve is true. Only the manner of his desire is specified: "May I become many; may I be abundant. Now, as for the ether (ākāśa) [being compared] to a jar and so forth—

It is observed that becoming many is brought about by limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) consisting of other things; but how can there be multiplicity for that which is non-dual? To this objection, it is said: "May I become many"—that is, may I arise with an excellence (*prakarṣeṇa*) over my previously established essential nature (*svarūpa*). Now, one might object: a father who already exists produces a son, but he does not produce himself. If that were so, then here too, for Brahman, the producer of the world— [The text continues: ...there would be no production of itself. [Response: This is not a fault, because the meaning is that He becomes the cause of the world through the manifestation of His own power. Or rather, the sense is that He becomes many by means of the manifestation of His own powers, just as a single light appears manifold through its reflections in various vessels. Furthermore, since the Lord is omnipresent, He is indeed present within the bodies of all beings; thus, He is the producer of the world even while being Himself the produced. Moreover, the statement "He became many" is intended to show that He is the material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*) of the world, just as clay is the material cause of jars and other objects. Therefore, the Supreme Lord, who is non-dual, is the cause of the world through the manifestation of His own powers. Thus, the non-duality of Brahman remains uncontradicted. Furthermore, the scripture states: "From Him, when He is born, the breath, mind, and all senses are born; from Him, space is born; from Him, the wind is born; from Him, the fire is born; from Him, the waters are born; from Him, the earth and the supporting mountains are born. Since these effects are seen to possess the qualities of their cause, and since the qualities of pleasure, pain, and delusion are perceived in the world, it follows that the cause must also possess those qualities. And since Brahman is the cause, He is established as possessing those qualities. However, the statement that Brahman is devoid of qualities (*nirguṇa*) refers to the fact that He is free from the qualities of *prakṛti* (primordial matter). Therefore, the Supreme Lord, who is non-dual, is the cause of the world. Thus, the non-duality of Brahman is established. Q.E.D.

If it is argued that the statement "may I be born" (prajāyeya) is untenable because [Brahman] lacks its own production, we say no; for there is no absolute difference between Brahman and the name-and-form (nāmarūpa) that are being produced. Just as waves and the like emerging from the ocean are not absolutely distinct from it, so too, while the power of Brahman—namely Māyā—remains, name-and-form, which were previously unmanifest, become manifest later.

Being itself does not appear as a real entity while abandoning its own nature as Being; it is precisely with this intention that the Vājasaneyins declare: "In the beginning, this was indeed undifferentiated; it was differentiated by name and form alone. Therefore, since the world appears in the form of the universe through the *māyā* of Brahman alone, the statement "Let me be born" is appropriate.

He proceeds. That Supreme Self, desiring in the manner described, performed austerity (*atapyata*). By the word "austerity" (*tapaḥ*), knowledge is meant, according to another Vedic text which states, "His austerity consists of knowledge. The meaning is that he engaged in the contemplation of the arrangement of the world about to be created. Indeed, there is no purpose for the Supreme Lord to be served by austerity in the form of *kṛcchra*, *cāndrāyaṇa*, or similar penances.

Thus it is said: That Supreme Lord, having reflected upon the objects to be created, fashioned this entire universe—conforming to the causes of the karma of living beings—according to place, time, name, and form, as it is experienced by all living beings in all their various states.
Herein, the existence of the Supreme Self is established by the reasons of His being a desirer, a reflector, and the creator of the world.
It is explained as follows: First, the proponent of non-existence (asadvādī) thinks thus: "Whatever exists, all that consists of name and form.

This pervasion is observed in the elements such as space, as well as in the elemental bodies of gods, animals, and so forth. However, the Supreme Self is other than name and form. [As it is said: "Space, indeed, is the bearer of name and form; that which is between them..."
This is because of another scriptural passage (*śrutyantara*). As for the conventional usage such as "the Supreme Self" (*paramātman*) or "Brahman," that too serves to establish its existence;
this is the meaning. [The phrase] "if that were so" (*tadīti*) means [the same].
1. *atyantabhinna* (absolutely distinct). 2. *gha nṛtyādi* (dancing, etc.).

It is not capable of being established, because it is a mere conceptual construction (*vikalpamātra*), like a human horn and so forth. For the *Pātañjala-sūtra* states: "Conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is that which follows verbal cognition and is devoid of a real object. Therefore, name and form (*nāmarūpa*) are excluded from Brahman.

If [the opponent] argues that by negating its own pervader (māna), one must also negate its own existence (sadbhāva), then such scriptural passages as "In the beginning this was either non-existent or existent," "From which words turn back," "Now follows the instruction: 'Not this, not this'," and "Neither gross nor subtle, neither short nor long," would be contradicted. Therefore, he concludes, "Brahman does not exist. Against this proponent of non-existence (asadvādin):
The existence [of Brahman] is established: the Supreme Self is of the nature of Being (*sad-rūpa*), because He is a desirer, like one who desires heaven and so forth;

because He is a deliberator, like a king or a sage; and because He is a creator, like a potter and others. As for that "existence" of name and form which you have cited, that very thing is the Brahman intended by us. Within Brahman, which is of the nature of Being and serves as the substratum, name and form [arise] through *māyā*.

Because the two [entities] are imagined; however, the meaning of the passage beginning with "or non-existent" will be explained later. Furthermore, intending that Brahman is of the nature of existence (*sat*) because it is the enterer—just as a person is the enterer into a house or similar place—the text demonstrates its entry with the words "That which this...
Having created the entire collection of bodies, from Hiraṇyagarbha down to the stationary objects, whatever exists, it [Brahman] entered that very thing which was created.

The meaning is that the Supreme Self entered [the body] which had been produced. Here, this must be considered: is that Supreme Self who is the creator who entered in that very same form, or rather in another form?

If it is argued that He entered in the form of the creator itself—because the suffix *-ktvā* in the word *sṛṣṭvā* indicates that the acts of creating and entering have the same agent—this is not so. For [in the case of clay],...

Because it is logically impossible for the material cause (*upādāna*) to enter [the effect] as a solid mass (*piṇḍavat*). Indeed, that very lump of clay which has transformed into the form of a jar does not itself enter into that jar. Likewise, how could the Creator, who has transformed into the form of the body, enter into those very bodies? Well then, let there be entry by means of another form, just as in the case of a modification of a lump of clay.

Furthermore, in the case of a jar, other clay in the form of powder enters it. Likewise, if there were no entry in the form of the Lord (Īśvara), there would have to be entry in the form of the individual soul (jīva). This is not so; for that which is non-dual lacks two distinct forms. Even if that were admitted, there would be no space to enter. As the material cause (upādāna), He already exists pervading all effects from the very beginning. Such being the case, [there is] no voidness of the Supreme Self (paramātman).

In the absence of any spatial location (*pradeśa*), where could this [Self] enter? If it is argued that it enters into the Supreme Self itself while it remains there, we say no; for the scripture states, "It entered into that very thing," indicating entry into the created effect. If it is argued that the created effect in the form of a body undergoes a further transformation into the form of another effect characterized as the individual soul (*jīva*), and that this transformation is what constitutes "entry"—we say no; for [this would be like] the transformation into the shape of a jar...

Furthermore, since no transformation into the form of a body is observed for the [Supreme Self], if it be argued that its entry occurs like the reflection of the sun in water and so forth, we say: not so. This is because [the Self] is all-pervading (*aparicchinna*), formless (*amūrta*), and because there is no substratum for a reflection situated at a remote location. The solar orb, being limited (*paricchinna*) and material (*mūrta*), [can appear] in water or similar media located at a distance.

[The reflection] becomes manifest; however, Brahman is neither limited nor material, nor does it possess any limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) situated at a remote location. Therefore, entry cannot be established by any means whatsoever. To this it is replied: this entry must be established as being identical with the creation of the world, which consists of an inconceivable arrangement.

Just as the Supreme Lord created the universe by the power of *māyā*, so too let him enter it by the power of *māyā* alone. Now, it might be argued: 1. He is all-pervading; 2. [He enters] by way of entry... [text fragment].

This creation, consisting of ether and the rest, which is composed of *māyā*, is not presented by the Śruti as having the nature of reality; what then? within the intellect (*buddhi*) situated in the lotus of the heart— as possessing specific attributes such as being the seer, the hearer, and the cognizer.

Thus, this is figuratively designated as its "entry. That which is referred to by the word "that" (tat) is the Witness, the illuminator of the unmanifest; that which is indicated by the word "this" (etad) is the manifest, perceived as residing within the effects.

The non-dual substratum and the dualistic entity residing in the effects—between these two, the statement of non-difference as "This is That" (sa eṣaḥ) may not be challenged as difficult to accomplish. For one who does not know the true nature of reality, nothing is difficult; even [the world] turned blue [by indigo]...
Salutations! Look with your eye like one wearing blue garments. This consideration of what is fit and what is unfit applies to human transactions;

That which is endowed with the nature of manifestation is described as the perception of consciousness as the living self (jīvatva). The entry of the reflection of consciousness (cidābhāsa) occurs spontaneously within the individual delusion (pratyamoha). Persisting through its effects, this adjunct (upādhi) serves as the means for the entry of consciousness, just as the redness of a hibiscus flower is superimposed upon a crystal. This entry of the reflection of consciousness is likewise superimposed upon the pure consciousness.

Having created the universe, from the subtle thread (sūtra) up to the gross post (sthāṇu), by means of His own māyā, that Supreme One entered it with His nature as the sole reflection of Himself. The limit for this entry is said to be "up to the tips of the fingernails. Consciousness is perceived through the sensation of heat extending to the tips of the nails. Having pervaded the body of consciousness both generally and specifically, He abides therein. Ha...

By means of these two examples, the twofold mode of existence is here described through two types [of illustrations]: "Just as fire resides within wood, pervading the entire piece of wood, so too the Self is situated, pervading the whole body. It remains [there]. Just as razors are distinguished within a razor-case due to the difference in their positions, so too are the consciousnesses distinguished according to the differentiation of the channels (nāḍīs). The remaining functions within the body, which are intent upon the perception of sound and the other sense objects, have been clarified through the introductory statement and by means of the purport (*tātparya*) word by word. Now, the logical reasoning (*nyāya*) that supports that [conclusion] is being investigated: Is the entry like that into the house of Devadatta, or rather—
Is it like a shadow? Or like the reflection of the sun in water? Or like substance, quality, and so forth? Or perhaps like a fruit and its seed?

Not the first [option], because of its all-pervasiveness. Devadatta is limited and possesses parts, but the Self is not so; for the reality of the Self, being neither excluded from nor included within [anything else], limitation and the like are impossible—thus it is "not this, not this" (neti neti).
Because of this exclusion: for that undivided, partless reality whose essence is the Self, there can certainly be no arrival at another location through separation from its previous location.

Nor is it the second [alternative], because of the absence of transformation; for a snake does not take the form of an ant-hill until the end. The elements undergo transformation, but the Self is not subject to transformation. Nor is it the third, like the sun and water, between the body and the conscious Self. Not...

The entrance into that [body] occurs through conjunction and disjunction; it is not the fourth [category], because qualities and so forth are dependent on substance and thus lack independence. Nor is it the self, for this body is not the self, according to the Śruti which declares him to be the Lord of all. It is not the fifth [category], because the seed is subject to modification, whereas the self is devoid of modification; the self is determined in the scriptures to be free from the six kinds of change. The substratum—

O son of Rādhā, there is indeed a disparity between the serpent and the stone, or between the fruit and the seed, due to their relationship as part and whole; thus, there is no tautology there. If it is argued that there is no fault because the limited individual soul (jīva) alone enters into bodies, it is not so, because it is the Creator himself who enters.
For the Śruti says: "Having created that, He then entered into that very thing. There would be identity between the Creator and the Enterer, just as one who has eaten [is the same as the eater].

It is like [the expression] "he goes. Therefore, entry by any means whatsoever is not possible. This being the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*), the entry is now established: "This [Self], whose nature is non-entered, because it is not limited by directions, space, and so forth—its entry must be merely conceptual (*kalpita*), like the reflection of the sun in vessels of water. Even though there is inequality in parts such as division and so on, a similarity is intended to be expressed."

By whom can the similarity in perception and other factors regarding the presence of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) be denied? Being perceived within a limiting adjunct, appearing as something else, and the appearance of multiplicity—these are the same in both the example and the illustrated case. The solar disc, being abundant in light, cannot be seen directly; nevertheless, its reflection is clearly observed within water. Such is the self (*ātman*), which is self-luminous.

It is not perceived when free from limiting adjuncts (*anupādhika*); however, it is clearly perceived when there is the limiting adjunct of the insentient body and so forth. Just as the eye, struck by a mirror, turns back and pervades its own face, thereby showing the face in a reversed orientation; even so, this intellect (*dhī*), pervading the Self which is devoid of the body and other adjuncts, shows that immutable Self as if endowed with modifications (*vikriyā*). Thus it is said: "The immutable [Self] appears joined with modifications."

It should illuminate: even though one, the sun appears as many due to the diversity of its vessels; likewise, although I am one, I appear as many due to the diversity of various bodies. That cause, which has shaken off all multiplicity and is undivided, is such that it is the witness of nothing other than itself; yet, through this delusion of "entering," it becomes this [world]. Previously, the inner Self was devoid of the forms of the seer and so forth, [and free from] name and form.

When there is the act of perceiving, one becomes endowed with the state of being a seer and so forth. That which has the form of a seer, a hearer, and so on, and that which is devoid of being a seer and so on—the intellect and its causal adjuncts are designated as the *kṣetrajña* (the knower of the field) and the *Īśvara* (the Lord). He who, remaining changeless, knows "I am smelling this fragrance"—he is the witness of all and deserves to be characterized by the two preceding [states]. Just as the sun in the sky, though not produced from a vessel of water, [is reflected therein]...

It is perceived by the Fourth (turya); likewise, the witness of all, whose nature is light, is perceived within the intellect (dhī) which is characterized as the agent, the enjoyer, and so forth—just as the sun is seen inside a jar through its rays.

The moon is perceived from the tip of a branch that is not of its own nature; likewise, the conscious Self (cidātman) is perceived through the cause-condition (upādhi) which is insentient. This very delusion of being a living individual (jīvatva-bhrānti) serves the purpose of the realization of the inner Self (pratyagbodha). Through the analogy of the sun reflected in vessels of water, "entry" is thus conceptualized. For that which is devoid of direction, space, and time, entry is like that of a snake into a hole; it is not, however, the direct [entry] of the Supreme.

Thus, it is imagined by ignorance (*avidyā*). Yet, through ignorance and due to a lack of discrimination, the Witness alone—even though He is solitary—is perceived as possessing the attributes of effects such as the intellect (*buddhi*), like a reflection. Fire, the sun, and the wind are the examples proclaimed by the Śruti. Therefore, the Self, whose nature is unentered [by objects], entered the world of effects. Just as a single fire [pervades] the world...

Like a single piece of wood or a vessel, it has entered into various forms; though not having entered by its own nature, it appears as if it has entered. Just as the one wind, though not having entered by its own nature, becomes manifold in form as it enters the world through various fans; and just as the sun, though remaining outside, appears to have entered into water-vessels, so too the Self, though not having entered, is perceived as if it had entered.

Just as creation and the rest have been established [as being unreal], let entrance also be viewed in the same way. Therefore, creation and the rest do not stand to reason when conceived [as real]. There is no connection of the non-existent with birth, nor is it accepted for the existent because of its already existing nature. There is no modification in that which is situated in the cave (the Self); therefore, birth arises from ignorance. This verse, "form after form," is indeed clear.

For the sake of perceiving the true nature of the self—which is by its very essence renunciation—the Lord spoke of creation and other topics. Through the illustration of the razor-blade and the bowl, the specific entry [of the self] into the senses is clearly established; likewise, through the illustration of the fire-drill and the wood, the general entry is shown. By means of this substratum, it is stated that the self pervades all effects as their presiding presence. This substratum—
Nowhere is the pervasion of the pervaded and the pervader accepted as being complete in its essential nature without the presence of superimposition.

For pervasion is never observed between two things that are absolutely distinct, such as a cow and a horse; nor is it observed between what is absolutely non-distinct, because in that case the relationship of the pervaded and the pervader is excluded. Since both absolute difference and absolute identity are thus untenable, they remain as mere appearances; therefore, only the substrate and the superimposed [remain].

Thus, this pervasion occurs by the power of those two alone; just as a snake enters a garland through darkness and not of its own accord, so too the effects of the ignorance of the inner self (pratyagajñāna) enter the Self itself by force of Māyā. This entry is twofold: as pervasiveness and as perceptibility.

We shall now refute those objections which are established [only] on the basis of such entry, should it be argued that the Supreme [Self] has entered [the world]. If the Supreme [Self] were indeed the one who entered...

[Objection: From the perspective of its manifoldness, multiplicity would also accrue to Maheśvara due to his non-difference from that [world]. [Reply: This fault does not apply to this objection, because the opposite is possible. Why is it not urged that unity results from the identity of many with one? Furthermore, scripture (*āgama*) serves as the regulator here, and it would preclude difference. Nor is the rope divided by the imagined differences such as the snake and so forth.
It is said: "One God is seated here as many," according to the Vedic revelation. Therefore, this Lord should be accepted as being one alone, like space (*viyat*).

If it is argued that because the Supreme is non-different from those who have entered into transmigratory existence (*saṃsāritva*), the state of being a transmigrator would necessarily follow for Him—that is not so, because of the scriptural teaching that He transcends hunger and other such afflictions. If it is further argued that this is not the case because [the Lord] is seen to experience pleasure, pain, delusion, and so forth—that is not correct.

"He is not touched by the sufferings of the world, for he is outside the world"—so says the Śruti. This reflection of consciousness (*cidābhāsa*) produced by limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) is what appears; therein, the experience of suffering and the like will find its scope. If the Self were to become a sufferer... [text fragment].

The Taittirīyopaniṣaddīpikā, 141:
Who could be a witness while suffering? There can be no witnesshood for one who suffers, nor likewise suffering for a witness.

If there were no modification, one would not be a sufferer; how could there be witnesshood for that which is subject to change? Because I am the witness of thousands of mental modifications, I am changeless. Pleasures and the like qualify the intellect—which is associated with the reflection of consciousness and which identifies itself as the self within the aggregate of the body and senses. Just as an indifferent bystander might observe a man with a staff who is intent on a quarrel, [so does the Self observe the mind].
The Witness is likewise uncomposite regarding the cognition of pleasure, pain, and so forth. This being so, let it be observed that suffering is perceived only as something external;
this Veda negates the senses and other means of knowledge with respect to the inward Self. For the Śruti says: "By what, my dear, should one know the Knower?
And the Śruti also says: "It is indeed other than the known and the unknown. [I am not the sufferer. "I am suffering..."
The threefold consciousness, which has the reflection of the self as its sole object, is superimposed upon the self by the weary; it is merely a figurative designation used by the learned.
Great suffering is observed at the tip of the nose, and even in the big toe; how then can that suffering, residing in the limbs of the body, belong to the self?

If suffering were located in the innermost self (*pratīci*), it would pervade the entire body just like consciousness. Furthermore, because it would be of the nature of a knower like consciousness, it would not be disagreeable to us.

[It] would be so; for according to the Vedic revelation (*śruti*), "everything is dear for the sake of one's own enjoyment. If it is argued that happiness has the Self alone as its object, that is not tenable. Where there is the conception of another, there one perceives another; thus, duality consisting of pleasure and so forth is taught as having the limited self (*śāntātmā*) as its object. But where the Self alone is everything, who then perceives what? Thus [it is said].

Duality, such as pleasure and pain, is excluded from the nature of the Buddha; it does not please you, O sinful one, and thus it is experienced by me. Through a vision directed inward, no worldly existence whatsoever exists in the Self. That the Self possesses desire, aversion, and so forth—such is the bondage of conventional agreement. Let that be established by logicians, yet it is not at all tenable through reasoning. It is eternal...

If the self were an object of cognition, it would suffer through the mind; if the self were not visible, the consequence would be the non-existence of a seer. Since it is partless, its being both an object of sight and a seer is not tenable. If it possessed parts, it would be impermanent;
therefore, the self cannot be a sufferer. Since the state of being free from suffering is desired for the supreme [Self], and because there is no other besides it, for whom [could suffering exist]?

You have undertaken the study of the Upaniṣads for the sake of the cessation of suffering; yet, whatever effort you have exerted here regarding the cause of suffering—namely, the ignorance concerning the inner Self (pratyagajñāna)—I have undertaken the study of the Upaniṣads solely for the purpose of accomplishing the destruction of that very [ignorance]. Just as a person who perceives only nine [counting] might, due to delusion, not realize "I am the tenth," even while looking at those nine, so too one who perceives only the non-Self (anātman) in its entirety—[does not realize the Self].

One who has not yet fully realized the truth of the Self does not perceive the oneness of the Self, even while observing non-self objects. Yet, by the flaming rays of the perfect knowledge arising from the statement "You are the tenth," one whose ignorance regarding the tenth person—the Self—has been consumed, perceives: "I am the tenth. Likewise, by the fire of knowledge arising from statements such as "That Thou Art" (*tattvamasi*), having burned away the darkness of non-self and that which is born therefrom—

[The Self] attains its own unity. Through means such as the scriptures and the teacher, which arise from the cause of ignorance regarding the inner Self (pratyagajñāna), it attained through *māyā* that unity with itself which is opposed [to its previous state]. Even though the [Self] has entered [the body], no fault whatsoever can be established against it by opponents;
therefore, the entry is well-established. Other passages concerning the entry [of the Self] are also...
These [passages] are to be explained as follows: "A person entered into the body" is a statement from the Madhu Brāhmaṇa. [The word] *virājam* [refers to] the Self of the seer of the gods...

"Having created those sheaths (kośas) called the Vākya-brahman, He enters them and, though undeluded, remains as if deluded, acting through Māyā alone"—so says the *Uttaratāpanīya*.
For the omnipresent One to enter the body, the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) consisting of the vital air (*prāṇavāyu*) is the means. And so it is stated in the *Maitri*:
That which they declare in the Upaniṣads: "Having made himself like the wind, he entered within.

The entry and exit of that wind are superimposed upon the Self and thus used in common parlance. This very point is recited by the followers of the Atharva Veda: "He reflected: 'In whom departing shall I depart? Or in whom established [shall I be established]? "

"He created the vital breath (prāṇa), thinking, 'I shall stand firm. Although the entire subtle body (liṅgadeha) serves as the medium for the Self's entry into the gross body, it should be understood that the vital breath holds primacy therein. That subtle-body adjunct, having entered through the tips of the feet and ascended upwards, becomes established in the thighs, the belly, the chest, and the head.
Thus, the Aitareyins record this very point in the passage beginning with, "He entered this Puruṣa by means of his two feet; Brahman [entered]...
Now, an objection may be raised: having first recorded the Supreme Self's deliberation regarding the door of entry in the sentence, "He considered: 'By which way shall I enter?
and then, in the sentence, "Having split open this very suture, He entered by that door," it is stated that He entered through the opening situated in the crown of the head (the *mūrdhan*).
The followers of the Aitareya recension record that [the soul] pierces that door in the form of the *suṣumṇā* and enters within through that door.
If it is argued that there is thus a contradiction between the two statements, it is not so; for they are established as distinct in their respective domains.

Entry via the tips of the feet pertains to the subtle body (*liṅgadeha*), which is the cause for worldly activity. [Entry via the crown pertains to] the state of meditative absorption (*samādhi*) which manifests reality.

Furthermore, that which is recited by the Chandogas [is as follows]:

"Having entered by means of this living self (*jīva-ātman*), let me manifest names and forms. In the passage regarding the "threefold entry," it is the individual soul (*jīva*) that follows [the breath], because of its proximity. This is so despite the statement, "By means of the soul, let me differentiate [names and forms]," where [the soul] appears to be separated [from the immediate context].

The logical connection would be as follows: for the individual soul (*jīva*) does not possess the power to create mountains, rivers, and so forth; however, the Lord (*īśvara*) is endowed with all powers, as it is heard in scripture that "His supreme power is manifold. Furthermore, the use of the first person in the phrase "let me evolve" (*vyākaravāṇi*) is also consistent only with the position of the Lord. Therefore, the Lord alone is the creator of names and forms. How then [is this] in the case of jars, cloths, and the like?
We say that the potter and others possess the status of creator only through the impulsion of God. Therefore, it is established that God alone is the agent of all things.

In that very [chapter], beginning from the tenth topic up to the seventeenth topic within the third quarter (pāda), eight topics concerning the individual soul (jīva) are undertaken. Among those, he formulates the tenth topic: "Of the soul..."

For these two—death and birth—belong either to the body or to the self (ātman). This is because of the statement, "A son has been born to me," and likewise because of the performance of the *jātakarman* (birth rites) and so forth. Indeed, these two refer primarily to the body, while they are applied figuratively to the living being (*jīva*). The *jātakarman* exists because of worldly usage, such as the expression "a son has been born to me," and because of the scriptural injunction regarding the *saṃskāra* rites like the *jātakarman* for one who is "deprived of life" (*jīvāpeta*). Thus, from the perspective of worldly convention, there is the practice of saying "my son is born," and according to scripture, there are the purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) such as the *jātakarman*.

When it is argued that birth and death belong to the individual soul (*jīva*), we reply: if one were to accept birth and death for the *jīva*, the unavoidable consequence would follow that what was done by one would perish (*kṛtanāśa*) and what was not done by one would be encountered (*akṛtābhyāgama*). Therefore, birth and death belong only to the body and are metaphorically attributed (*upacaryete*) to the *jīva*. It is with reference to these metaphorical [events] alone that worldly convention and the ritual scriptures (*karmaśāstra*) proceed. However, the Upaniṣadic scripture...

"It is indeed this [body] bereft of the living soul that dies; the living soul does not die. Having stated that the primary death belongs only to the body separated from the living soul, he negates it for the living soul. Therefore, birth and death belong to the physical form. He introduces the eleventh section: At the beginning of the kalpa, is the living soul of Brahmā born like the ether, or not?

Because it is stated that [Brahman] was non-dual prior to creation, it is born like sparks from a fire; yet, when the intellect is produced, the non-dual Brahman itself appears as the individual soul (*jīva*) due to limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*).

The birth of the soul is thus conditional, whereas its eternity is heard of in reality. The scriptural statement of non-duality prior to creation—namely, "One only, without a second"—would not be tenable if the soul were something distinct from Brahman that had not arisen [from it].

Furthermore, Scripture establishes the origination of the individual soul (jīva) by means of the illustration of sparks: "Just as small sparks fly forth from a fire, even so from this Self all vital breaths, all worlds, all deities, all beings, and all these selves issue forth. Therefore, at the beginning of a kalpa, like the ether and the other elements—

When it is argued that the individual soul (jīva) is born from Brahman, we reply: That very non-dual Brahman enters into the form of the individual soul once the intellect (buddhi) has arisen. This is because of the scriptural text: "Having created that, He Himself entered into it. Therefore, since the individual soul is not produced [as a new entity], there is no contradiction with the scriptures concerning non-duality. As for the scriptural reference to sparks, it proceeds with the intention of referring to birth conditioned by limiting adjuncts (upādhi); otherwise, [it would contradict the doctrine of non-duality].

Otherwise, there would be defects such as the destruction of what has been done (*kṛtanāśa*) and the acquisition of what has not been done (*kṛtābhyāgama*). However, with reference to the true nature of reality (*vastutattva*), the Śruti declares its eternity:
"He is eternal among the eternal, the conscious among the conscious. Therefore, at the beginning of a kalpa, the individual soul (*jīva*) is not produced.
But the designation [of the soul] as being dependent on the moving and the non-moving is figurative (*bhākta*), because it exists only when that [body] exists.

He sets forth twelve arguments [against the opponent]: "The individual soul (jīva) is held to be non-conscious by nature;

yet it is conscious by nature because consciousness is absent during deep sleep and so forth, whereas in the waking state, consciousness is produced by the mind. Precisely because it is Brahman, it is of the nature of consciousness, and that consciousness is not lost even in deep sleep. For the Śruti declares: 'For there is no destruction of the seer,' since the perception of duality ceases when duality itself is destroyed. The logicians (Tārkikas), however, maintain [the following regarding] deep sleep:

[The opponent claims: "In states such as fainting and deep meditative absorption (samādhi), because of the absence of consciousness, the individual soul (jīva) is of the nature of non-consciousness; however, in the waking state, a quality called consciousness arises from the conjunction of the self and the mind. This is incorrect, because scripture declares that it is Brahman itself, whose nature is consciousness, that enters [the body] in the form of the individual soul. Furthermore, consciousness is not lost during deep sleep and similar states, since [the Self] persists as the witness of those very states.
Otherwise, it would be impossible to account for the recollection of deep sleep and so forth. If it is asked, "How then is there no perception of duality during deep sleep and the like?
we reply: "Because of the cessation of duality. And thus says the Śruti: "That which one does not see while dreaming—that indeed one sees, yet one does not see;
for there is no loss of the seer, because of its imperishability. But there is no second thing existing there, other than that, distinct from it, which one might see."

"Should see" (śyet)—this is its meaning. Regarding this, what is said by worldly people—that in deep sleep (*suṣupti*) the individual soul (*jīva*) sees nothing—is incorrect. It is merely designated through delusion that the soul, though seeing at that time, does not see.
As for the reason why it sees in that manner, it is stated: there is no loss of the vision (*dṛṣṭi*) which constitutes the very nature of the Self, the seer.

For [it] exists, because its nature is devoid of destruction; otherwise, even for one who maintains the doctrine of annihilation (*lopavādin*), it would be impossible to speak of an annihilation that lacks a witness. If so, what is the reason for the worldly people's delusion that "he does not see"? To this, the cause is stated: that which is other than the Brahman-consciousness, known as the world, divided into the forms of action, agent, and fruit—this duality...

That third state does not exist for it, because it has merged into its own cause. Therefore, just as in the waking state, there is an absence of the worldly transactions involving the seer, the seen, and the act of seeing; thus, the notion that "he does not see" is merely an illusion of common people. Consequently, the individual soul (*jīva*) is of the nature of consciousness (*cid-rūpa*). He formulates the thirteenth section [of the commentary]: "Is the soul minute (*aṇu*) or all-pervading (*sarvaga*)? 'This is minute,' so [it is said]."

Why is this so? Because of the scriptural statements regarding its departure, movement, and return, that [jīva] is indeed minute (aṇu). Its minuteness is due to its having the intellect (buddhi), along with its reflection, as its limiting adjunct (upādhi). However, the all-pervasiveness of the jīva is heard from scripture because of its essential nature as Brahman. Its minuteness is also heard in scripture: "This atomic self (ātman) is to be known by the mind. "It departs from this body" refers to its departure (utkrānti). And—

"Going" (*gati*) means that they all go to the moon itself; "returning" (*āgamana*) means that they come back again from that world. For departure and the other stages are not possible for one who is omnipresent. Even if those stages were possible for one of intermediate size, it would contradict the scriptural teaching of atomicity (*aṇutva*), and its impermanence would also be unavoidable. Therefore, when it is argued that the individual soul (*jīva*) is atomic, we reply: [it is] consciousness...

The intellect (buddhi), together with its reflection (tibimba), is non-omnipresent; because the individual soul (jīva) has that as its limiting adjunct (upādhi), its atomicity, its departure [from the body], and so forth are logically established. However, the soul is omnipresent by its own nature, since it is of the very form of Brahman. Its omnipresence is heard in such scriptural passages as: "Verily, this great unborn Self is all-pervading, the inner Self of all beings. Therefore, the soul is omnipresent.

The Taittirīyopaniṣaddīpikā, [page] 145, formulates the fourteenth topical section (adhikaraṇa): Is the individual soul (jīva) a non-agent or rather an agent? [It is an agent], because agency is possible for the intellect (dhi).

Those who consider themselves followers of Sāṃkhya ask: "What would be gained by [attributing] the status of agent to the individual soul (jīva)? They argue that because it is an instrument (*karaṇa*), the intellect (*buddhi*) is not the agent; for sacrificial rites, Vedic studies, and worldly activities do not occur without an agent. Therefore, the soul possesses agency. Since the intellect is subject to transformation (*pariṇāmin*), agency—which consists in being permeated by action—is possible for it, but not for the unattached Self (*ātman*). Thus they say.

What has been stated by the Sāṃkhyas is inconsistent. It is impossible to postulate agency for the intellect (*buddhi*), whose capacity is established as being that of an instrument (*karaṇa*); for such agency is not observed in tools like axes, and because if the intellect were the agent, another instrument would have to be postulated. Nor can it be said that "let there be no agency," for [this would contradict] the activities such as sacrifice mentioned in the earlier section (*pūrvakāṇḍa*).

Because the activities such as hearing (*śravaṇa*) mentioned in the *Uttara-kāṇḍa*, as well as worldly activities such as agriculture, depend upon an agent, the individual soul (*jīva*) is therefore the agent. The fifteenth section formulates [the inquiry]: Is agency real, or is it imagined? It must be real, because that which is established by scriptural injunctions such as "one should sacrifice" (*yajeta*) is not sublated.

"Because it is indeed unattached"—this means that agency, which was previously established [in the preceding section], is sublated by the scriptural statement "for this Person is indeed unattached," just as the redness [superimposed] upon a crystal is sublated. This is because agency is superimposed due to the proximity of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) such as the intellect (*buddhi*), the eyes, and other instruments. When the objection is raised that agency must be real because there is no sublation of it, we reply: the lack of attachment to agency is sublated by the scripture, "for this Person is indeed unattached. Just as [the redness of a *japā* flower...]* *Note: The provided source text ends abruptly; the translation reflects the available portion.*

Just as redness is superimposed upon a crystal due to the proximity of a flower, so too is agency superimposed upon the Self due to the proximity of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*). This is illustrated by the sixteenth section: "Is its motivator passion and the like, or is it God? [The answer is:
From passion, as in agriculture, activity is observed; [if it were from] God, there would be inequality in His impelling. [It is] like rain toward crops, [so is] God toward living beings."

Because of its inequality, attachment is dependent upon an internal controller; therefore, God is its instigator. In the world, it is observed that for farmers and others, attachment and aversion alone are the instigators. Following that analogy, one must also accept that for the individual soul (*jīva*), who is the agent of merit and demerit, those two alone are the instigators.
If God were the instigator, why would He impel some souls toward merit and others toward demerit?

Inequality is unavoidable; therefore, since it follows that the Lord is not the instigator [of actions], we reply: first of all, the charge of the fault of inequality does not apply to the Lord, because He is a common cause, like rain. Just as, although rain is the cause for the growth of crops, the diversity among rice, barley, and other grains is due solely to the seeds themselves; so too, the Lord causes the individual souls (*jīvas*) to act according to their respective [karmic conditions].

Even if [the Lord] acts as a common instigator by granting permission through the command "Do this," there is no partiality, because the cause of inequality lies in the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of previously performed actions. If it is argued that actions serve solely as causes for their own fruits and not as causes for other actions, that is true; however, an action, while impelling the individual soul (*jīva*) toward the attainment of a fruit consisting of pleasure or pain, necessarily [gives rise to] another action.
Thus, its status as a cause is unavoidable, as it also brings about [the body] itself. However, the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) are the direct causes of action.
And so, how could there be the consequence of partiality for the Lord? As for the observation that passion is seen to be the motivator, which was cited, that is indeed so;
yet [the Lord remains the agent] because the scriptures would otherwise be purposeless (Sūtra 2.3.33). Furthermore, "and as the carpenter [acts] in both ways" (Sūtra 2.3.40).

The seventeenth section summarizes the point: "Is there a confusion between the individual soul and the Lord, or is there a fixed distinction, based on the two scriptural statements? Since they concern non-difference and difference, confusion is not avoided.

Through conceptualizations based on limiting adjuncts—such as being a part, being delimited, or being a reflection—the distinction between the individual soul and the Lord is established for all souls."

And [there is] mutual [contradiction]. The scriptural texts such as "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*) establish the non-difference (*abheda*) between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*). On the other hand, through passages such as "The Self is to be seen," a difference is perceived in the form of the seer and the object of sight. This being the case, by the force of the scriptures concerning difference, it is impossible to deny the existence of the individual soul for the time being. Furthermore, by the scripture concerning non-difference, it cannot be established as being distinct from the Lord.

It cannot be avoided. Therefore, the confusion (*sāṃkarya*) of the existing individual soul (*jīva*) with the Lord (*īśvara*) is unavoidable; furthermore, the confusion of the souls among themselves follows as a consequence through their non-difference from the Lord. Thus, when it is argued that for the proponent of Brahman (*brahmavādin*) there is no distinction between the soul and the Lord, we reply: although there is indeed an absolute, real difference between the soul and the Lord, like that between a cow and a buffalo—

Nevertheless, even though this is not the case [in ultimate reality], the scriptures describe the individual soul (*jīva*) as threefold by relying on a distinction constructed through limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) during the state of empirical transaction (*vyavahāra*). From the statement, "A portion of My very self, having become a living being in the world of living beings, is eternal," its nature as a part (*aṃśatva*) is understood.
Furthermore, from the Śruti passage, "Being the same, he wanders between both worlds," the consciousness-nature of the *jīva* consisting of consciousness (*vijñānamaya*) is [established].
Because it is designated as having a dimension equal to that expressed by the word "self" (*ātman*), its state of being limited is perceived, like the space within a jar.

However, from such statements as, "The one Self of all beings is situated in every single being; it is seen as one and also as many, like the moon in water," its nature as a reflection is understood. Therefore, for the proponent of Brahman (*brahmavādin*), the distinction between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*) is easily established. [This applies] to the individual souls...
And thus, the establishment of conventional usage—like the many reflected images of the sun in numerous vessels of water—is all the more easily explained.

Therefore, it is established that there is no fault whatsoever. As for the manner of transmigratory existence (saṃsāra), consisting of the soul’s journey to other worlds, it has been investigated in six sections (adhikaraṇas) in the first quarter (pāda) of the third chapter. Among those, the first section is formulated as follows:

The soul departs either enveloped or unenveloped by the subtle elements (*bhūtasūkṣma*). Because these subtle elements are easily available, it departs indeed enveloped by them. However, because the seeds [of the gross elements] are difficult to obtain, and because the senses cannot function without a substratum, the living being (*jīva*) departs enveloped by those [seeds] due to the emergence from the fifth state. Thus, the living being—previously described as having the vital breath (*prāṇa*) as its limiting adjunct—[leaves] the body...
At the time of attaining a new body, departing from here, one goes enveloped by the subtle elements (*sūkṣmabhūta*), which are the seeds of the future body.
Since the five gross elements (*pañcabhūta*) are easily available everywhere, it might be argued that there is no purpose in leading them from here. To this we reply:
although the mere elements are easily available, the seeds of the body are not available everywhere; therefore, they must be led from here.

Furthermore, it is not possible for the sense organs, which serve as the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) of the individual soul (*jīva*), to travel to the next world without being supported by the elements, since this is not observed during the state of life. And the Śruti declares thus: "In the fifth oblation, the waters come to be called 'man'. [Brahma Sūtra 3.1.1] And:
"The part [of the Lord] is designated as manifold; otherwise, some record that He possesses the nature of the Dāśas, Kitavas, and so forth" [Brahma Sūtra 2.3.42].
Immediately after that, he proceeds enveloped [by subtle elements], as established by the questions and the explanations.

Brahman itself became transformed into the form of the world's differentiation, such as "the existent" (*sat*) and "the non-existent" (*tyat*). Brahman must indeed be of the nature of existence (*sad-rūpa*).

The intention of the Śruti is that [the world] is like milk and other substances because it has been transformed into the form of a bowstring (jyākāra). Having established the existence of Brahman through logical arguments, He establishes it further by the experience of the wise, beginning with the words "whatever this" (yad idaṃ kiṃca). Whatever is seen as this world, consisting of the enjoyer and the enjoyed, is not in reality the world; rather, it is the true, uncontradicted Brahman.
The discerning ones declare this. Therefore, it is illogical that Brahman—which is established through the experience of the wise—should be non-existent.

He cites a mantra that reveals the existence of this aforementioned Brahman, beginning with "And that [is] this," and so forth. Prior to its manifestation, this world—which is manifested through name and form—was indeed non-existent, meaning it was unmanifest. Then, from that very source...

It may be asked: however, Brahman alone occupies both positions. Because it is so, that Brahman is expressed by the word *sukṛtam* (the well-done). From such Śruti and Smṛti passages as, "Whatever I am directed to do by the Lord residing in the heart, that I perform," and so forth. Furthermore, the well-known notion of being an independent agent belongs to Brahman.
This establishes its existence. Therefore, in order to establish it by another means, he speaks of its nature as bliss (*ānanda-rūpatā*) with the words "That which...
and so forth. That which was previously mentioned and denoted by the word "well-done" (*sukṛta*), namely Brahman—that referent of the term "Brahman"—is indeed *rasa* (essence/flavor).
Even in the world, that substance such as honey and the like, which is the cause of bliss characterized by satisfaction, is called *rasa*.
Brahman also becomes "rasa" (flavor) because it is the cause of the bliss characteristic of those who know reality, which is the state of having accomplished all that was to be done.

Brahman’s nature as *rasa* consists in its being tasted through the knowledge of mental modifications (*manovṛtti*) produced by the Vedāntic texts, which are to be relished. Tasting is the apprehension of flavor preceded by affection (*prīti*). And Brahman is indeed apprehended with affection by those desiring to know It. Affection—

Furthermore, pleasure (*ānanda*) is not possible without *rasa*. Therefore, by the word *rasa*, the nature of Brahman as bliss is expressed. Now, one might object: even in the absence of the nature of bliss, dharma is grasped by those seeking knowledge (*jijñāsu*) precisely with affection. This is not so; for there is no intrinsic affection toward dharma. Affection toward dharma exists only through the limiting condition (*upādhi*) of its being a means to the happiness characterized by heaven. Brahman, however, is itself—

Therefore, it cannot be the means for the attainment of any other supreme state. Consequently, because it is the primary object of experience, Brahman is of the nature of bliss (*ānanda*). This very quality of being bliss is established by the passage beginning with "For [Brahman] is indeed the essence" (*rasaṃ hyevāyaṃ*);

this person who knows reality, having obtained—that is, having directly realized—the essence, becomes possessed of bliss, thinking, "I am blessed. This is the worldly distinction of one who knows reality.

The cause of satisfaction is not the acquisition of garlands, sandalwood, women, and so forth; rather, it is the acquisition of the Self alone. This is because for one who is dispassionate, there is no mental conception of acquiring garlands and the like. As stated in such scriptural passages as, "There is nothing higher than the acquisition of the Self.

Therefore, the existence of Brahman must be accepted, both because it is the cause of the satisfaction of the wise and because its nature is bliss. By the word "hi" (for/indeed), [the reason is affirmed].

The well-known consensus among the learned has indeed been demonstrated. Furthermore, intending to show that Brahman exists because it is the cause of both the bodily activities and the bliss derived from sense objects, he demonstrates its causality for both through the passage beginning with "Who, indeed, could breathe... (*ko hyevānyāt*). The word *ākāśe* may end either in the locative case or the nominative. The same meaning should be understood here as well. However, in the case where [the word] ends in the nominative case (*prathamāntatva*), the sense is: "it shines forth on all sides by virtue of its self-luminosity" (*svaprakāśatvena*);
that is to say, in a manner other than this [other-dependent nature].

The space shines as the "Brahman-year. If this bliss, which is of the nature of the Self and described as "rasa" (essence/flavor) in the preceding passage, did not exist, then who indeed—who could possibly—act within the body by means of the organs such as speech and the rest? Or rather, who would move them?

The verbal root [in *prāṇa*] signifies "motionless activity. Who indeed would breathe—that is, who would perform the act of breathing, which is respiration? The followers of the Atharva Veda declare that the Self is the agent of actions accomplished by means of the sense organs, such as sight, and so forth: "For this is the seer, the toucher, the hearer, the smeller, the taster, the thinker, the knower, the doer, the conscious self, the Person. In the world, regarding the vital breath—

Because one observes birth and death in the body and the vital breath (*prāṇa*), the fool establishes the false doctrine that the *prāṇa* alone is the Self. Relying on that very [view], Bālāki, who asserted that the *prāṇa* is the Self, engaged in a dialogue with Ajātaśatru, the proponent of the True Self, in the *Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad*. Therefore, in order to dispel the misconception that the *prāṇa* is the agent of actions such as seeing, [the text asks]: "Who is it that breathes?"...
This is stated separately [from the previous verse]. If the Self were non-existent as bliss, who would perform the act of breathing by means of the instrument, the vital breath (*prāṇa*)?

That the vital breath possesses only the status of an instrument (*karaṇatva*) with respect to the act of breathing, whereas agency (*kartṛtva*) belongs to the Self—this meaning is also clearly recorded in the *Upastibrāhmaṇa*: "He who breathes by means of the breath, he is your Self, the innermost of all."

Although it is not possible for the unattached Self of Bliss (*ānandātman*) to be the agent of the activities of the senses and so forth by its own nature, nevertheless, such agency is possible for that which is conditioned by the sheath consisting of consciousness (*vijñānamaya-kośa*). Therefore, Brahman exists because it is the cause of activity. This very Bliss, which is the cause of activity, gladdens—that is, satisfies—all living beings with desired objects.

When an object is obtained, the mind, having abandoned its orientation toward objects, experiences the inward-turned bliss of the inner Self (pratyagātman) before the desire for another object arises. This is what is called "the bliss of objects" in the world; the word "hi" is used here to indicate that this is well-known among discerning people. Therefore, because it is the cause of that [bliss], Brahman exists—this must be accepted.

It should be understood as follows. Thus, by establishing the existence of Brahman through reasons such as its being the desirer [of desires], the doubt as to whether "it exists" or "it does not exist" has been refuted. Now, since there is much to be said regarding the doubt concerning the subject of the ignorant (*avidvat*), which follows in sequence, that [doubt] shall be set aside for the moment; instead, he dispels the doubt regarding the attainment of Brahman for the subject of the knower (*vidvat*) by means of the passage beginning with "For when... (*yadā hyeva*).

When this seeker of knowledge attains firm establishment—that is, the strengthening of the realization of his own Self—within this very Brahman, which is accessible through one's own experience by means of the practice of true being (*sadbhāva*), then at that moment, that wise one reaches the state of fearlessness, which is free from the fear of birth, death, and so forth. By the word "then" (*eva*), any delay of time is excluded; for as soon as he knows, at that very instant [he attains it].

[One] attains [it]. In this sense, the word "hi" (for/indeed) indicates the well-known status among the wise. Brahman is qualified by the four attributes beginning with "invisible" (*adṛśya*). It is "invisible" because it cannot be grasped by the senses such as the eyes; for this very reason, it is declared in the Kaṭha Upaniṣad:
"It cannot be attained by speech, nor by the mind, nor by the eye. Its own characteristic mark (*liṅga*) is...

The meaning is that the beneficial and the selfless (anātman) are not accessible even through inference. This too has been declared elsewhere: "It is free from conceptual construction, infinite, and devoid of logical reasons and illustrative examples. Although the three bodies are indicative marks (liṅga) related to the individual soul (jīvātman), and the status of being the creator of the world is an indicative mark of the Lord (Īśvara), nevertheless, nothing [of these] serves to establish the reality of Brahman as the Self, which is beyond phenomenal manifestation (niṣprapañca).

There is an indicative mark (*liṅga*). That which can be explained exhaustively is "defined" (*nirukta*); the opposite of that is "undefined" (*anirukta*). There is not even a small fraction of the reality of Brahman [that is defined]. One does not attain [the goal] through [such definitions].

There is no word whatsoever that can denote it, according to the Vedic scripture: "From which words turn back. By the three qualifiers beginning with "unseen" (*adṛśyatva*), its being accessible through perception, inference, and scripture is negated. By that much, its distinction from the entire phenomenal complex of effects (*kāryaprapañca*) is established. It is "without abode" (*anilayana*), meaning without a support. [As asked: "In what, O Venerable One, is He established?"

Thus, from another Vedic scripture (*itara-śruti*), [it is understood that the Self] is in its own majesty. Although the root ignorance (*mūlājñāna*) lacks being cognizable by the three means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa-traya*), it possesses the status of a substratum because it is dependent upon Brahman; therefore, the term "without abode" (*anilayana*) is used to indicate its distinction from that [ignorance]. By the word "fearless support" (*abhayaṃ pratiṣṭhām*), the absence of duality (*dvaita-rāhitya*) is expressed. For, based on the etymology "that from which one fears," *bhaya* [is fear].

An entity distinct from Brahman is being described, based on another Vedic scripture which states, "From duality, indeed, fear arises. One should construe the passage as follows: "I am one thing and Brahman is another"—such duality is *bhaya* (fear); that which is devoid of it is *abhaya* (fearlessness). Thus, one attains a firm foundation (*pratiṣṭhām labhate*) in such a way that fear ceases to exist. Through the certainty of the knower's attainment of Brahman, doubt is thereby dispelled.

Thus, by the certainty that there is no attainment of Brahman for one who lacks knowledge, [the text] removes doubt. Regarding the passage beginning with "For when this one," etc.—the word *uc* functions in the sense of the word *api* (even). The word *ara* signifies "small" (*alpa*). The word *antara* signifies "difference" (*bheda*). When this worldly person creates even a slight difference or separateness from himself in this Brahman—[then he does not see].

One perceives Brahman as distinct from oneself; at that very moment, the fear of saṃsāra, such as birth and death, arises for him. With the intention of showing that the distinction between the individual soul (jīva) and Brahman lacks reality, it is said "even the slightest. By the word "hi" (for), he demonstrates the scriptural authority for the attainment of saṃsāra by one who perceives duality: "He goes from death to death who sees here any diversity."

"He sees [it as separate]; Brahman would cast him away who knows Brahman as other than the Self"—such scriptural passages (śruti) are to be considered. Now, one might raise the objection: "If a person knows the qualified Brahman (saguṇa-brahma) which is to be meditated upon according to the meaning of the Karma-kāṇḍa, then by virtue of possessing knowledge (vidyāvatva), he too should attain liberation just like one who knows the unqualified Brahman (nirguṇa-brahma). Anticipating this, the author refutes it: "ta-" [the remainder of the sentence follows].

"Even in you alone. The word "even" (*tu*) removes any doubt regarding liberation. For even a learned person who does not reflect—that is, one who does not know the reality of Brahman—possesses the vision of duality; therefore, that very same fear exists for him, just as it does for the utterly deluded, namely the fear of the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*).
To show that fear exists even for one who possesses other forms of knowledge but is devoid of the knowledge of the reality of Brahman, he cites this verse:

"He takes away"—this is explained by the passage beginning with "And that [is] this," and so forth. He who, having performed excellent knowledge and action in a previous birth, has been born in this birth as the deity Vāyu—even he, though possessed of such greatness and being a god himself, blows (pavate) continuously and tirelessly out of fear (*bhīṣā*) of this Brahman in the form of the Inner Ruler (*antaryāmin*). He moves about constantly, never resting.

The same should be applied to the sun and the others; the ellipsis is that "Agni and Indra perform their respective functions. In relation to the four aforementioned deities, Death is the fifth, and it is always running here and there to kill living beings whose lifespan has been exhausted. Although the Brahman—which is unattached and devoid of qualities—cannot be a cause of fear, [the text continues:]
Nevertheless, this is possible for Him who possesses the limiting adjunct of *māyā* by virtue of being the Inner Ruler (*antaryāmin*). As stated by the authors of the *Vārttika*:

"In relation to the effects that are to be regulated, He is the Regulator, the destroyer of darkness. And another Śruti says: "He who controls Vāyu from within—He is your Self, the Inner Ruler, the Immortal. Under the governance of this Imperishable, O Gārgī..."

One may cite such passages as, "The sun and the moon stand held apart," and so forth. Because of its being the cause, it might be the *pradhāna* or the *jīva* [due to its] karma..."

Not from the mouth. The Inner Controller (Antaryāmī) is the Supreme Lord because of [the attributes of] being one with the individual soul (jīva), immortality, and so forth; it is neither the Pradhāna nor the individual soul, because [the soul] is that which is governed. In the fifth chapter of the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad, Yājñavalkya says to Uddālaka:
"He who dwells in the earth, yet is within the earth, whom the earth does not know, whose body is the earth, who..."

"He who dwells within the earth, yet controls it from within—He is your Self, the Inner Controller, the Immortal. Regarding this, when a doubt arises as to whether the Inner Controller mentioned in relation to the world beginning with the earth is the Pradhāna, that is the initial position (pūrvapakṣa);
for since the Pradhāna is the material cause of the entire world, it is possible for it to be the regulator of its own effects. Alternatively, [it might be] the individual soul (jīva).

[Objection: The individual soul (*jīva*) is the inner controller (*antaryāmī*), for it has performed actions consisting of merit and demerit (*dharma-adharma*). And that action, in order to bestow its own fruit, brings forth the world as the means for experiencing that fruit. Therefore, since the soul is the producer of the world by way of action, it follows that the soul is the inner controller. To this we reply: "This is your Self, the inner controller, the immortal. Thus, there is an identity between the inner controller and the soul.

Furthermore, death is mentioned [in scripture]. Likewise, through the teaching that He is the inner ruler (*antaryāmin*) within all things, such as the earth, the intermediate space, and so forth, His omnipresence is understood. For these reasons, the Inner Ruler is the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*). Nor is it possible for the Primal Matter (*pradhāna*) to be the Inner Ruler; for [the scripture] declares, "The unseen Seer, the unheard Hearer," thereby establishing His nature as a Seer, a Hearer, and so on.

No, because that [fear] is impossible for the insentient *pradhāna*. Nor is the individual soul (*jīva*) the inner ruler (*antaryāmī*), because it is heard in scripture that the soul is itself subject to control: "He who rules the self from within. Therefore, the inner ruler is the Supreme Lord. Fear of Him exists only for the ignorant, not for the knower of reality. Thus, the answer to all the questions has been provided.

[The word] *panam*. In order to determine both that which was stated previously—"he enjoys all desires together with [Brahman]"—and that which was indicated as its nature being bliss in the aphorism "He is indeed rasa," the author introduces the inquiry with the words "That very one" (*saiṣā*). By the word "that" (*tat*), the well-known status of this inquiry from another Vedic text is demonstrated; for in the *Bṛhadāraṇyaka*, it is said: "He who among men is successful..."

"He becomes prosperous, a lord over others, most fully endowed with all human enjoyments; that is the supreme bliss of men"—by such passages, the determination of bliss (*ānanda*) is elaborated. "Accomplished" (*rāddha*) means endowed with success characterized by the vigor of the body, senses, and so forth.
"Prosperous" (*samṛddha*) means perfected with qualities such as knowledge (*vidyā*). By the word "this" (*etad*), that which is to be described in the immediately following text is referred to.

He demonstrates this: Does this bliss of Brahman arise, like worldly bliss, through the relationship between an object and a subject, or is it innate? This inquiry proceeds. In that regard, other forms of objective bliss are introduced in succession as means for discerning the innate bliss of Brahman. Of these [blisses], the bliss of Brahman—
Thus, its status as a means for determining the nature of a "fragment" (leśatva) is established. That state of being a fragment is to be understood as follows:

when discrimination (*viveka*) is obscured by ignorance (*avidyā*) and while ignorance is increasing, [the Lord] is designated as possessing those attributes in all beings from Hiraṇyagarbha down to humans, among the inner rulers (*antaryāmin*) of the divine and other realms (Sūtra 1.2.5).
