Among living beings, the bliss of Brahman— due to the influence of their respective karmas and the connection with means such as sense objects— becomes worldly, established as something flickering and subject to diminution, being manifested according to one's specific cognition. That very same [bliss], however—

Through the excellence of knowledge, desire, and action, [bliss] is perceived— increasing a hundredfold at each successive stage from human Gandharvas up to Hiraṇyagarbha— as being directly experienced by a learned Śrotriya whose desires have not been destroyed. However, when the distinction between object and subject created by ignorance ceases through true knowledge, the one, naturally inherent, and perfectly full Self alone remains.

It remains [there]. First, it shows that bliss which is well-known to us among the pleasures of the sense-objects, which serve as its gateways, by means of the passage beginning with "He who is young" (*yuvā syāt*). Because a human being in childhood is ignorant of the qualities of sense-objects, there is no pleasure from objects such as garlands, sandalwood paste, or women. In old age, although one is knowledgeable of them, because of the inability to enjoy them, this [pleasure] does not exist.

It does not exist. Therefore, intending that youth alone remains, it is said, "he should be young. Even in youth, because one who is seized by ugliness, anger, and so forth experiences an abundance of suffering, the term "virtuous youth" (*sādhuyuvā*) is used to signify the absence of those defects.
Furthermore, even for such a person, if there is an absence of even a single one among the sixty-four arts (*kalās*) or the fourteen branches of knowledge (*vidyās*), suffering would still arise.

To exclude that [possibility], the word "meditator" (*adhyāyaka*) is used. Even for one who possesses knowledge, happiness does not arise if there is sluggishness in performing duties due to lack of vigor and so forth, or if one lacks appetite for eating and the like; therefore, to exclude that, the word "most zealous" (*āśiṣṭha*) is used. This means being most swift, acting quickly in all tasks. Or else, in all matters of eating—

Among the qualities of a hero, one who possesses an abundance of appetite for food is called *āśitṛtama*. Even for such a person, if there is an absence of mental fortitude (*manodāya*), there would be no steadfastness (*dhṛti*) in battle and similar situations; therefore, to exclude that possibility, the term *dṛḍhiṣṭha* (most firm) is used.

Furthermore, even one endowed with patience might be incapable of mounting a horse or performing other tasks if he lacks physical strength; thus, to prevent this, the term *baliṣṭha* (most powerful) is employed.

This much has been said regarding the perfection of the state of being an enjoyer. Now, the perfection of the objects of enjoyment is stated by the words "his is this": that entire earth, surrounded on all four sides by the ocean, is full of wealth—that is, filled with all kinds of objects of enjoyment. And this is an illustration of what is stated in another Vedic text, beginning with "the lord of others" and so forth. If...

All this may belong to some universal monarch; at that time, this is human bliss. But those [blisses] inferior to this do not truly qualify as bliss at all, because they are mixed with suffering. Indeed, no man other than the aforementioned universal monarch is ever found to be completely satisfied. For bliss, by its very nature, is satisfaction.

For her, there exists some desire for objects that acts as an obstacle. And such a desire necessarily arises in someone toward some object that has not yet been obtained. However, because a universal monarch has obtained all objects existing within the human world, the absence of any opposing obstacle allows his satisfaction to manifest without hindrance. This being the case, to the extent that desires are ceased—

To whatever extent it becomes superior, to that same extent bliss (*ānanda*) is also elevated. Intending this very point, he cites an example greater than the previously mentioned bliss: "Those who... Those aforementioned human joys belonging to those established as universal emperors (*sārvabhauma*), numbering one hundred—that entire collection of bliss constitutes a single joy of the *manuṣya-gandharvas*.
The degree of satisfaction found in a hundred universal monarchs is equal to that found in a single human gandharva.

In this kalpa, those who were humans but attained the state of Gandharvas through the performance of specific knowledge and rituals are the human-Gandharvas (*manuṣya-gandharva*). By virtue of their possession of powers such as invisibility (*antardhāna*), they are superior to ordinary humans; and that superiority—

It is shown in the *Ṛtīka*: "The Gandharvas are fragrant, able to assume any form at will, and possess powers such as invisibility; they are skilled in dance, song, and so forth, and are non-worldly (*alaukika*). Therefore, for them, there is generally no obstruction to bliss, just as there is for humans. Even when attachment occasionally occurs, there is the perfection of means for its abandonment. This being so..."

The manifestation of a particular degree of happiness is logically established from a particular degree of serenity of mind. Since the bliss of a sovereign ruler can be inferred by us through his human nature, a learned Vedic scholar (*śrotriya*) was not cited in that context.
Human *gandharvas*, however, dwell in the intermediate region (*antarikṣa*); for it is said that the intermediate region is frequented by hosts of *yakṣas*, *gandharvas*, and *apsarases*.

This is because of another Vedic text (*śruti*). Therefore, since that bliss is not established [for everyone], a learned scholar (*śrotriya*) is cited to demonstrate its establishment in the world of men; for according to Pāṇini’s sūtra, "one who has studied the *chandas* is a *śrotriya*. Indeed, he [the *śrotriya*] experiences the objects that are the causes of bliss existing in all worlds, which otherwise would require great effort to attain.

Having ascertained through both scripture and experience that there are the defects of superiority and impermanence, one becomes free from desire for those [objects]. When this is so, whatever bliss belongs to one who enjoys the objects found in the world of human Gandharvas—even for a learned Śrotriya—such bliss exists only to that extent. However, freedom from being overcome by desire belongs even to a fool who is ignorant of the world of the Gandharvas.

Even though [the objects] exist now, for one who learns of them from the scriptures at a later time, the desire for enjoyment of those worldly objects arises and subsequently ceases. However, for the learned *śrotriya* who perceives the defects therein, since no desire ever arises at any time, his state of being free from desire (*akāmahatatva*) is firmly established. Now, it may be argued that at that time, due to the Gandharvas' dancing, singing, and so forth, there might occasionally be an arousal of such activity...

If it is argued that joy (*ānanda*) is appropriately designated by the term "delight" (*harṣa*), and that this does not exist for a learned *śrotriya* who is free from desire (*akāmahata*), then let this delight not be [the primary meaning]. Because that [delight] is momentary and a modification of the mind, it lacks the nature of primary bliss (*mukhyānanda*).
Rather, when the desire for objects has ceased upon their attainment and modifications such as delight have subsided, that which...

Satisfaction (*tṛpti*) follows destruction (*bhaṅga*), and that is the primary bliss. And so it is remembered in the Smṛti: "Whatever sensual pleasure there is in the world, and whatever great divine pleasure there is—these do not equal even a sixteenth part of the bliss of the destruction of craving. Furthermore, for one who has heard the Vedas and is untouched by desire, there exists a bliss following satisfaction that is equal to that of the Gandharvas. As it is said:

In the subsequent sections as well, following the increasing excellence of the mind’s clarity, the progressive manifestation of bliss characterized by satisfaction should be explained. Among these, he states the third section:
"Those who are a hundred of the human... The celestial Gandharvas are singers born in the world of the gods at the very time of creation. The fourth...

The *Taittirīyopaniṣaddīpikā* (159) says: "Those who [are] a hundredfold of those born of noble birth (*ājānajānaḥ*). This refers to those who, even beyond the enjoyment of the gods born of noble birth (*ājāneja*), have attained a superior enjoyment.

Having performed specific Vedic rites, those who attain divinity through such action are the gods known as *karmadevas*. He states the seventh stage: "those who are the hundred *karmadevas*. Here, the thirty-three *havirbhuj* (oblation-eating) deities are intended by the word "gods. He states the eighth stage: "those who are the hundred [of] gods. Indra is the lord of the *havirbhuj* deities. He states the ninth stage: "those..."

"Those who are the hundred of Indra"—Bṛhaspati is the preceptor of Indra. He recites the tenth cycle: "Those who are the hundred of Bṛhaspati"—Prajāpati is the Virāṭ Puruṣa. He recites the eleventh cycle: "Those who are the hundred of Prajāpati"—Brahmā is Hiraṇyagarbha, pervading the entire sphere of transmigratory existence, the Sūtrātman who is both the collective whole and its individual manifestations.

He is the foremost among embodied beings, according to the Śruti: "Hiraṇyagarbha came into being in the beginning. And according to the Smṛti: "He is indeed the first embodied one; he is called Puruṣa; he is the original creator of all beings, and Brahmā came into being in the beginning.
Therefore, the excellence of worldly bliss finds its ultimate rest in him. In the manner described, [the bliss] of all [others] rests in the learned Śrotriya.

By the existence of these gifts, he attains all desires; thus this meaning is established. In this way, the excellence of worldly bliss, which serves as a door to supreme bliss, has been illustrated by scripture and by the direct perception of those learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*).
Now, he shows the bliss of Brahman, which is to be realized, with the words: "He who is this... By the word *puruṣa* (person)...

The person who desires to know is intended here. In him, there exists a certain bliss. The existence of that [bliss] is indicated in sequence by these two words—"that" (*tat*) and "this" (*idam*)—through both logical proof and the proof of direct experience. Among these, the logical proof is elaborated in another Vedic scripture: "But it is for the sake of the Self that everything becomes dear."

Having thus made this proposition, it is established that because all categories of objects of enjoyment—such as sons, wealth, and so forth—are dear only insofar as they subsist in the Self, the Self must be of the nature of bliss (*ānanda*) by virtue of being the object of supreme love for others. Likewise, because everyone always desires, "May I exist forever; may there never be non-existence for me," the Self's nature as bliss is established by all.
It is experienced by the three [states]. The word "ca" (and) is for the purpose of including the bliss belonging to those living beings who are of the same class as one desiring to know.

By this, every bliss—whether pertaining to the self (*ādhyātmika*) or to external beings (*ādhibhautika*)—is fully encompassed. In the Veda, in passages such as "from this world to that world," the words *idam* (this) and *adas* (that) generally denote the perceptible and the imperceptible respectively. Therefore, here too—
That bliss which resides in the body beyond our perception is intended by this word "this" (asau).

The particle "ca" (and) is for the purpose of including the bliss residing in other deities of the same class as the sun; by this, all bliss pertaining to the divine realm (*ādhidevika*) is comprehended. And this being so, [it includes] all [bliss] within the internal self (*adhyātma*), the elemental world (*adhibhūta*), and the divine realm (*adhidaiva*).

Whatever bliss exists within limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), all of that is in its essential nature (*svarūpa*) one and the same, and does not differ. Indeed, distinctions such as "human bliss" or "divine bliss" are perceived only by means of a prior reference to their respective adjuncts. Just as the distinction characterized by degrees of intensity—such as "the space within a jar" or "the space within a hut"—is due solely to the reference to their adjuncts, so it is in this case.

The Brahman-bliss, which is undivided and of a single essence, and its differentiation produced by limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) ranging from Hiraṇyagarbha down to the level of stationary objects, is clearly declared in another Śruti passage: "This is his supreme bliss; of this very bliss... "In the Brahman-city, all other beings subsist upon a mere fraction [of it]. Of this bliss—which is of one undivided essence and stands in the place of the ocean—the blisses of Hiraṇyagarbha and others are like mere drops. This very bliss is one; it is that which is to be enjoyed."

The conclusion has been established through such inquiry that [Brahman] is to be understood as blissful. By the passage beginning with "He who," he demonstrates the fruit of experiencing the bliss as described:

that person who knows his own bliss in the manner stated attains that bliss through this very sequence. Brahman, characterized by existence, consciousness, and so forth, by the power of its own *māyā*-energy...

Having created the universe beginning with the ether and ending within our own bodies, [the Self] dwells within, as if having entered the cave consisting of the five sheaths such as the body, in its unconditioned form, ready for direct realization. And that is of the nature of indivisible, singular essence and supreme bliss; this is the manner described. The sequence for the attainment of bliss by one who has known it in that manner is now set forth.

The world created by Brahman is twofold: the enjoyer (*bhoktṛ*) and the object of enjoyment (*bhogya*). Among these, the portion of the world that begins with the Self (*ātman*), whose nature is inward consciousness (*pratyak-caitanya*), and extends up to the body—comprehended through the notion of "I" (*ahaṃ-pratyaya*)—is the enjoyer. The portion of the world external to the body, perceived through the notion of "this" (*idaṃ-pratyaya*) in the form of son, wife, and so forth, is the object of enjoyment. Although the empirical usage of the term "Self" (*ātman*) applies there [to the enjoyer], even though...

Because everyone recognizes that one is "happy" or "unhappy" based on the pleasure and pain of others, [one might think they are the self]. Nevertheless, since the distinctness of sons and others from oneself is clearly manifest, their status as the self is merely figurative and not primary; with this intention, the Śruti taught the "annamaya" (consisting of food) as the self in order to dispel the notion of selfhood regarding them. The seeker of knowledge also [realizes] that this—
Having departed from this world—which is accessible through effort—and having looked back upon sons and other relatives, one becomes indifferent toward them after passing away;

one approaches and attains this *annamaya* (consisting of food), which is taught by the Śruti. The meaning is that, having abandoned the conceit of ownership regarding the pleasure and pain of sons and others, one comes to rest in the *annamaya* alone. In this manner, [one proceeds] successively from the *prāṇamaya* and so forth.

The transition (*pasaṃkramaṇa*) is to be understood as follows: having approached that which consists of bliss (*ānandamaya*), and there too having gradually abandoned the fourfold set beginning with "the beloved" (*priya*), one arrives at the conclusion that Brahman is the "tail" (*puccha*); the meaning is that one culminates in the indivisible, single-flavored bliss. Now, by the word "one who knows thus" (*evaṃvid*), is the Supreme Self intended, or is it something other than that? Not the first, because of its being the knower...

Because it is impossible for [the Self] to be a knower by virtue of being distinct [from the body]. Nor is the second [alternative] tenable, because it contradicts such scriptural texts as "That thou art. This is not a fault; for both are possible:

the Supreme Self itself possesses the state of being a knower through its form qualified by adjuncts (upādhi) such as the body and senses, while it possesses the state of being the object of knowledge in its nature as undivided, single-flavored bliss.
But is it not heard in scripture that "he who knows thus approaches"? Approaching— (End of provided text)
The term "attainment" (*prāpti*) here refers to the acquisition of a firm connection, as is observed in such cases as "a leech moves from one blade of grass to another.

If it is argued that such a transition, as described, is impossible for the knower who is qualified by limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) such as the body and senses within the states consisting of food (*annamaya*) and so forth—this is not so; for by the word "transition" (*saṃkrama*), what is intended here is the fruit of knowledge (*vidyā-phala*), characterized by the destruction of delusion.

And so it has been stated by the authors of the Bhāṣya: "In this case, regarding the destruction of the delusion of ignorance, the word 'transition' (*saṃkrama*) is used figuratively. For mere knowledge is not the means for a literal transition; for we do not observe such a transition occurring merely through the knowledge that [something] consists of collyrium, and so forth. By the very phrase "having departed from this world," the first part—

If it is argued that the destruction of the delusion regarding external objects such as sons and so forth has been stated in the context of the journey (*yāya*), then [we reply]: this is clearly so because of the acceptance of both [the self and the elements] through the teaching on the transition into the "consisting of food" (*annamaya*).

The commentary on the Taittirīya Upaniṣad (Taittirīyopaniṣaddīpikā), [page] 161:
Let it be intended that the delusion regarding sons and so forth shall not arise again; for this very reason, we maintain that [the realization] culminates in the body alone.

The intention regarding transition (*saṃkramaṇa*) has been stated. By this very logic, when there is knowledge of the self consisting of breath (*prāṇamaya*), the state of being the self consisting of food (*annamaya*)—which has perished—is not produced again; this is the transition into the self consisting of breath. The same should be understood for the subsequent stages as well.

Even though the selves beginning with that of food lack the status of being the primary Self, they possess the characteristic of being accessible through the notion of "I" (*ahaṃ-pratyaya*). This is the exhaustion [of the inquiry].
The word "Self" (ātman) is employed in the phrase "the Self consisting of food" (annamaya ātmā) by accepting the well-known sense of "Self.

With the intention that the fourfold limbs—beginning with "pleasure"—belonging to the sheath consisting of bliss (ānandamaya-kośa) are, in their primary sense, beyond the reach of speech and mind within the Bliss that is Brahman, the scripture does not mention the transition [into that state], even though it exists. Now, as for what was intended...

In order to clarify that Brahman is within the range of the mind (*manasagocaratva*), he cites a verse: "And that [is expressed] by this... This should be understood as it was explained in the commentary on the verse introducing the *manomaya* (the one consisting of mind). Furthermore, words are denoters of objects, and they are conventionally established (*vyutpanna*) with respect to objects possessing conceptual distinctions (*savikalpa*). However, because speakers perceive a commonality of "object-ness" (*vastutvasāmānya*), they apply them even to Brahman, which is devoid of conceptual distinctions (*nirvikalpa*).
Even when applied for the purpose of expression, words cease without having fully denoted [their object]; they desist due to their own inherent capacity for denotation.

Furthermore, the mind always operates with respect to supersensuous objects in accordance with words, and not independently. This being so, when words have ceased their operation here, the mind itself also ceases along with them. Therefore, [this is] the bliss of Brahman—its [true nature].

Because it exceeds the bliss of the *nyagarbha* (the bliss within the heart), it cannot be described or even comprehended as being "this much. When words, through the function of indication (*lakṣaṇā*), convey that very bliss which constitutes the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of Brahman, the person who realizes it through the mind in that same way does not fear anything whatsoever. In the preceding passage, in accordance with the context, [it was described] as qualified by the adjunct (*upādhi*) of the mind-made (*manomaya*).

For one who meditates upon Brahman here in this life or in another birth, there is never any fear at any time; this was said with the intention that there exists a remedy for fear arising from a cause. However, in this case, it is said "from anything whatsoever" (*kutaścana*) with the intention that for one who knows the non-dual bliss of Brahman through valid means of knowledge, there is simply no cause for fear at all. For [the scripture says], "Verily, from duality... (*dvitīyād vai bhayaṃ...*).

The intention is that whatever exists as something other than oneself is a cause of fear, and that such a thing does not exist in the non-dual Brahman. As stated by the authors of the *Vākyavṛtti*: "Having thus determined the meaning of 'Thou' (*tvamartha*), one should then contemplate the meaning of 'That' (*tadartha*) both by way of the exclusion of what it is not (*atadvyāvṛtti*) and directly through affirmation (*vidhimukha*). In this regard, [the text continues]: "Brahman is Truth, Knowledge, and Infinite..."

"Hm" is this [meditation] characterized by affirmation (*vidhimukha*). In this cognition consisting of affirmation, the synthesis (*upasaṃhāra*) of qualities such as bliss and self-luminosity has been previously illustrated. "From which words turn back"—this is characterized by negation (*vyāvṛttirūpa*). In that [cognition], the synthesis of attributes such as "neither gross nor subtle nor short" was considered in the third quarter of the third chapter.

There is no non-collection or collection of the negations; nor is there a synthesis (*saṃhṛti*) [of them] as such, because their status as the Self cannot be conceived in the same way as bliss (*ānanda*) and other qualities. Since the negations—whether those heard in the various texts or those brought together—are equal in their capacity to characterize the Self, therefore, for the sake of firmness, there is a synthesis [of them]. [This is seen] in the passage beginning with "neither gross, nor subtle, nor short," etc., which serves to reveal Brahman through Gārgī’s question.

"But there is an inclusion of the meditations on the syllables [of the word *om*] because of the commonality and the presence of that [quality], as in the case of the *aupasada* [sacrifices]; this has been stated [in the Sūtra]. In the *Brahmavallī*, certain prohibitions are heard in the Śruti; likewise, in the *Kaṭhavallīs*: "Soundless, touchless, formless, undecaying. E-

This may be cited as an example elsewhere as well. In that regard, it might be argued that there is no mutual subsumption (*upasaṃhāra*) among the negations, because—unlike attributes such as bliss (*ānanda*), existence (*sat*), and reality (*satya*)—they lack the nature of being the very essence of the Self (*ātmasvarūpatva*), and thus there is no purpose in their subsumption. To this we reply:
just as the negations heard within one's own Vedic branch (*svaśākhā*), although they do not constitute the essential nature of the Self, nevertheless serve to characterize the Self.

The same applies to the prohibitions that have been collected from other recensions (*śākhā*). Nor can it be argued that the inclusion of others is redundant because the indicative function is already established by the prohibitions stated in one's own recension; for its purpose is to provide greater strength and firmness.
Otherwise, if that were established merely by two or three prohibitions within one's own recension, it would follow that the others would be redundant.

Therefore, the negations must be applied [universally]. Once the negation "not this, not this" has been so applied, a certain distinction regarding it was considered in the second quarter (pāda) of that very section: "Is Brahman also negated by 'not this, not this,' or is it not?
Both Brahman and the world are negated by the double repetition; this repetition expressed by the word 'not' refers to all that is perceivable."

In order to negate [the world], it is stated at the conclusion of this extensive section in the Brāhmaṇa—beginning with "There are indeed two forms of Brahman, the formed and the formless," and after elaborating upon the formed nature characterized by earth, water, and fire, and the formless nature characterized by air, ether, and so forth—in order to teach Brahman: "Now therefore... [athāta ā-]. This is the limit; that which is not this [world] remains as the one Brahman, which is neither real nor unreal.

"The teaching is 'not this, not this' (neti neti). This is its meaning: the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣin*) considers that after the two forms have been described, since the possessor of those forms—Brahman—must be stated, this "not this, not this" is the instruction regarding Brahman. [He argues that] if the entire world were negated by a single word "not," the second word "not" would be redundant; therefore, by means of the negative particle (*na*),...

When it is argued that by the second [negation] even Brahman is excluded, we reply: first of all, the second negation is not purposeless, because it serves a specific purpose. And when there is a repetition (*vīpsā*), the verbal indication "whatever is seen" will result in the negation: "all that is not Brahman. Without the repetition, however, by means of a single negative particle alone—

Since the manifest and unmanifest have been introduced as the subjects under discussion, when they are negated by the use of the word "iti," it would follow that the absence of death (the state of liberation) and root ignorance—which have not been negated—possess the nature of Brahman. Now, one might object: even if there is repetition (*vīpsā*), the same fault remains; for since repetition is unrestricted, Brahman too would be negated. This is not so, because Brahman is not an object of perception (*dṛśya*).

Furthermore, because [the word "iti"] lacks the nature of a pronoun (*tvābhāva*), it is unfit to serve as the indicator of that which is to be negated. Moreover, having solemnly undertaken with great zeal to instruct [the disciple] regarding Brahman by saying, "Now, therefore, is the instruction," how could the Śruti not contradict itself by negating that very Brahman?
Furthermore, the remainder of the passage would not be consistent with a negation of Brahman; for in the remainder of the passage, it says, "The Truth of truth... (satyasya satyam).

By such statements, a name has been assigned to indicate the absolute reality of the intended Brahman, which exceeds the worldly reality of mountains, rivers, oceans, and so forth. Under the view that everything is negated, all of this would be rendered meaningless.
Therefore, Brahman is not negated. Now, as for what was said—that "one does not fear from anything"—that is incorrect; for [if it were so], dharmas—

*Taittirīyopaniṣaddīpikā*, 16.3:
Anticipating the objection that the torment produced by [the pursuit of] dharma exists because it is a cause of fear, he says: "This, indeed, is both..."

When the time of death is near, such a thought produces distress in the minds of all living beings. If one asks what that thought is like, it is described as follows: "Formerly, when I was in my youth and possessed the vigor of body and senses, and while I had the abundance of means such as wealth, why did I not perform virtuous deeds such as sacrifices and charity—which are the proper means for attaining the heavenly world and other goals?"

"I have not done this," he thinks; "Why have I committed such sinful acts as the theft of another's property, which are the means to hell? This very anxiety, which is the cause of distress for everyone, does not afflict this one person alone who knows Brahman. He states the reason for the absence of distress: "He who, in this manner... That person who understands these two—meritorious and sinful actions—in this way, as being the causes of distress...
Through both scripture and reasoning, he knows this: that person, in order to ward off the torment induced by karma, protects himself—he pleases and strengthens himself.

The verbal root *spṛ* signifies "pleasure" and "strength. By the firm conviction that "this self is the witness, not the doer of merit or demerit," he becomes free from torment and filled with joy. Through the conviction "I am Brahman," [he attains] merit...

Because even ignorance—which is the cause of the entire cycle of existence, including merit (*dharma*), its fruits, and so forth—has ceased, he becomes powerful. The meaning is that for him, there is never any defeat caused by merit, demerit, and the like. Now, [an objection may be raised]: if the Self is a non-agent and is Brahman, then merit and demerit must necessarily be produced by the body and senses engaged in activity, even those performed in the past.

Anticipating the doubt that [merit and demerit] indeed exist, he says: "For both indeed... That person who thus knows that merit and demerit are the causes of suffering and that self-knowledge is the remover of suffering—these two, merit and demerit, he perceives as touching the Self alone.
For it is a rule of grammar that verbal roots have multiple meanings. From the perspective of the scripture (śāstra-dṛṣṭyā)...

He who contemplates merit and demerit as being nothing other than the very nature of the Supreme Self, and not as having the form of merit and demerit imagined through *māyā*— in this regard, the word "hi" (for/indeed) is employed to show the well-known consensus among those who know reality (*tattvavid*). When the knower of Brahman [perceives] merit and demerit, whether previously performed or to be performed hereafter, as non-different from his own self...
The intention is this: if they do not exist at all, then what need is there to say that the suffering caused by concern for them does not exist?

Furthermore, the absence of sin has been considered in the first quarter (pāda) of the fourth chapter [of the Brahma-sūtras]: "Does the knower have the taint of sin or not? Because it is not experienced, and because the scriptures proclaim 'it is destroyed,' he has no taint; for he is a non-agent."

By the power of meditation, one is not tainted even by the magnitude of the object; both non-clinging (*aśleṣa*) and destruction (*nāśa*) have been taught for the ignorant (*ajña*), while the traditional saying (*ghoṣa*) "even in hundreds of millions of aeons, karma that has not been experienced does not perish" is meaningful as it refers to the non-destruction of sin without experience, being well-known in all scriptures.

Thus, when it is argued that there is indeed a taint of sin even for the knower of Brahman, we reply: first, regarding the Nirguṇa [Brahman]— *Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. In the *Brahmavallī*, it is heard that there is a non-clinging (*aśleṣa*) of sin that might be suspected to arise due to the functioning of the body and senses after the direct realization [of Brahman]. For instance:

"Just as water does not cling to a lotus leaf, even so evil action does not cling to one who knows this. Prior to direct realization, however, the destruction of the accumulated mass of sins from this life and previous births is heard [in scripture]: "Just as a tuft of reed-wool thrown into a fire is utterly consumed, even so all his evils are utterly consumed. "Not until it has been experienced," and so forth.

The scripture, however, concerns those who lack knowledge of Brahman with and without attributes; therefore, there is no taint of sin for the knower. The absence of merit is also considered in that very context: "Is he tainted by merit or not? He is not tainted, because of what is heard in the scriptures. For scriptural knowledge is not contradicted by scriptural merit. His non-tainting is equal [to his non-tainting by sin] due to the inherent power of reality."

[The opponent argues: "Regarding the two [types of] evil: it has been heard that merit (*puṇya*) is likewise crossed over as if it were evil; thus, while there may be no stain of evil, there exists a stain of merit. Since merit, being scriptural (*śruta*), does not contradict the knowledge of Brahman derived from scripture (*śrauta*)," so it is reached. To this we reply: the Self is a non-agent; by the very nature of reality, it is not stained by merit any more than by evil. This applies even to those possessing knowledge of the qualified [Brahman].
There is no meritorious action (puṇya) that is desirable and distinct from mere worship; because it is a cause for inferior births and bodies just like sin, it is indeed equal to sin.
Therefore, the Śruti refers to it as "sin" itself in the supplementary passage of the Dahara-vidyā: "All evils (pāpmānaḥ) turn back from here.
This is its meaning: whatever was enumerated in the preceding passage—namely, good deeds (sukṛta), evil deeds (duṣkṛta), and their fruits—is what is intended.

All those evils turn away from this worshiper. Furthermore, the Śruti states, "For he indeed crosses over both," declaring that for the knower, the crossing over of both merit and demerit is exactly equal. Therefore, one is not tainted by merit any more than by demerit. The non-destruction of those [karmas] already set in motion (prārabdha) has been considered in that very context: "In the case of the commenced, do they perish or not?"—saṃ-

They perish as if being carried away. In both cases, the absence of agency and the sublation thereof are indeed similar. From the scriptural teaching of *saṃsāra* persisting until the fall of the body, and also from experience, as well as from the analogies of the arrow, the wheel, and so forth, it follows that [the self] does not perish even regarding the *ārabdha* (commenced) karma. Regarding the two types of accumulated merit and demerit prior to knowledge—namely, the *ārabdha* and the *anārabdha*—the self’s lack of agency is equal in both.

And the sublation of that [karma] is equal [in both cases]. Therefore, since it follows that even for those karmas already begun—as well as those not yet begun—destruction occurs at the very moment the rise of knowledge takes place, we reply: from scripture, experience, and reasoning, the non-destruction of those karmas already begun is understood. This is based on the scriptural text: "For him there is delay only so long as he is not released; then he shall be merged [into the Absolute]. The meaning of this is as follows: for that knower of reality, liberation...

Even though it is "hanging down," it does not hang down excessively; rather, it hangs on only so long as the body is not released from the vital breaths (prāṇas), due to the non-exhaustion of the lifespan ordained at the time of conception. Then, when the separation of the body and the vital breaths occurs, one attains Brahman. Thus, by this scripture, even for the knower of reality, transmigratory existence persists until the end of the body.

Thus, the experience of the learned is also clearly accepted in this matter. Furthermore, the reasoning is stated: just as in the world, although an archer possesses independence regarding the acceptance or rejection of arrows fixed upon the bowstring, no such independence is seen once the arrow has been released; that arrow, when its momentum is exhausted, falls of its own accord. In the same way, the potter—

The same non-attachment applies to the other [karma] as well, but upon the fall [of the body]. (A. 4, Pāda 1, Adhikaraṇa 10) But only those [two types of karma] whose effects have not yet begun [are destroyed], because that is observed.

The analogy of the potter’s wheel must be cited here. Likewise, in the case of the subject under discussion, let the knowledge of Brahman possess independence in destroying even *anārabdha* (uncommenced) karma, but not with respect to *ārabdha* (commenced) karma;
for commenced karma has already begun to bear its fruit. If by these [scriptural] statements—

If the persistence of those [karmas] already commenced were not admitted, then, due to the absence of an instructor, the tradition of knowledge (*vidyā-sampradāya*) would be severed. It cannot be said that one who is ignorant is the instructor; for an enlightened person (*vidvān*) is liberated at the very moment of realization—so who indeed could possibly be the instructor? Therefore, there is no destruction of those [karmas] already set in motion. There is likewise an absence of destruction for obligatory rites (*nityakarman*).
It was considered right there: "The obligatory rite, such as the Agnihotra and so forth, does not perish [merely because it is performed].
For this greatness of the reality (vastu-mahimā) is never obstructed anywhere. Even when a portion of the attached fruit is destroyed, the other [portion] does not perish.

Because it has been employed for the sake of knowledge (vidyā), however, there is no connection with future existence, as in the case of optional rites (kāmya). Prior to knowledge, in this very life—"

Or, regarding that obligatory daily rite such as the *agnihotra* performed during other lifetimes, it follows that its destruction—just like that of optional rites (*kāmyakarman*)—must be admitted through the power of the realization of the Self as the non-agent; this being the position reached, we reply: there are two aspects to obligatory duty (*nityakarman*).
One aspect primarily bestows purity of mind (*cittaśuddhi*); the other aspect, by way of association (*anuṣaṅgeṇa*), bestows fruits such as heaven. Therefore—

Let its destruction indeed occur; however, because that which possesses purity of mind is utilized for the sake of knowledge (*vidyā*), its destruction cannot be described. For in the world, rice and other grains that have been exhausted through enjoyment are not considered "destroyed. As for the obligatory (*nitya*) rite subsequent to knowledge, like the optional (*kāmya*) rite, there is no connection (*aśleṣa*) [with the agent]. Even for one who is devoid of the meditations connected to the auxiliary parts (*aṅgāvabaddhopāsti*), [the same applies].

The applicability of ritual action (*tyāgakarman*) to knowledge (*vidyā*) is considered in that very same [section]. Is it only when conjoined with the meditation on the limbs (*aṅgopāsti*) that it is useful for knowledge, or is it used even alone because of its excellence? Since the scripture states, "That which is powerful by itself becomes more powerful when conjoined with knowledge," both are means to knowledge due to this gradation. Thus, the means to knowledge is established.

Action is considered to be of two kinds: that which is accompanied by meditations connected with its constituent parts (*aṅgāvabaddhopāsti*), and that which is devoid of such meditations. Since action accompanied by meditation is more excellent, it follows that only such action is a means to knowledge (*vidyā*), and not action devoid of meditation. To this we reply: the scriptural text, "Whatever one performs with knowledge, that alone becomes more powerful," [refers to] action accompanied by meditation.

By stating that there is "excessive vigor" (*atiśayena vīryam*), [the author] permits even for one who lacks formal meditation (*nirupāsana*) the mere presence of vigor; otherwise, the suffix *tara* would be untenable. Therefore, both those with meditation (*sopāsana*) and those without meditation (*nirupāsana*) possess the status of being means to knowledge (*vidyā-sādhana*) according to their relative degree. The certainty of liberation for the knower (*jñānin*) was considered in the third section (*pāda*) of the third chapter. Bra—

Is liberation for the knower of reality occasional or certain? It is occasional, because of the description of rebirth for those such as Apāntaratamas. O wise ones, the fruit of the worship of the Lord is to be experienced through various bodies; having experienced it, the *adhikāra-puruṣas* (those with specific offices) are then certainly liberated. In the Purāṇas, the teacher Apāntaratamas, the promoter of the Vedas, [arose] by the command of Viṣṇu.
It is recorded in tradition that at the end of the Dvāpara age, he assumed another body in the form of Kṛṣṇa-Dvaipāyana. Likewise, Sanatkumāra [states]:
"But the Agnihotra and so forth are for the sake of that very work, because it is seen thus" (Sūtra 4.1.12); "For by means of knowledge alone" (Sūtra 4.1.13);
and "The persistence of those who hold office lasts as long as their office" (Sūtra 3.3.19).

When it is argued that for those who know the reality (tattvavid), liberation occurs only occasionally because they forget the ritual procedure (*riti*), we reply as follows: These persons whom you have cited are all sustainers of the world. In a previous *kalpa*, having worshipped the Supreme Lord through great austerity, they obtained their respective offices to be enjoyed in various bodies in this *kalpa*. And when their *prārabdha* karma is exhausted...

They shall be liberated from their karma. Thus, since it is impossible to prevent the burning away of even uncommenced (*anārabdha*) karma by the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*), liberation for the knower of reality is indeed certain. A reflection on this matter, in the form of an objection and its resolution, has been conducted in the first quarter (*pāda*) of the fourth chapter [of the *Brahma-sūtra*]. Is there or is there not liberation for those possessed of commenced karma that yields many births?

When knowledge (*vidyā*) is lost, action (*karman*) yields its fruit; therefore, there is no liberation (*mukti*). One should indeed enjoy what has been commenced (*prārabdha*), but one must not let knowledge lapse. Since there is no connection [to the previous state] due to the persistence of that same condition—as in the case of one who has awakened from sleep—how could there be no liberation? There is no liberation for those persons who possess [unexhausted] *adhikāra* (eligibility/office). When many births have been accepted for the sake of experiencing *prārabdha*, therein [occurs] the loss of the knowledge previously acquired.

When it is argued that because the fruit of whatever action is performed during one's life must necessarily occur within a succession of successive births as long as that fruit has not yet been experienced, we reply: An action already commenced (*ārabdha-karma*) must cause its own fruits—pleasure and pain—to be experienced, for it was undertaken solely for that purpose. Indeed, no action was previously performed for the sake of obstructing knowledge (*vidyā*); therefore, by the power of such [obstructive] action, [the knowledge would be hindered].

One might suspect that knowledge (vidyā) is lost; yet knowledge is not destroyed merely by the interruption of death, because we observe its non-destruction even when interrupted by deep sleep (suṣupti). Therefore, while knowledge remains established, there is liberation for those qualified [for it], since no connection (aśleṣa) occurs with the karmas performed even over many births. Although this has been determined in the section on the "Combination of Attributes" (Guṇopasaṃhāra), nevertheless...
Thus, the objection and its resolution are faultless. He concludes the meaning of the section with the word "iti" (thus).

By the word "iti," that which has been expounded by the textual passage beginning with "brahmavidāpnoti param" and ending with "ya evaṃ veda" is referred to. And that is the secret knowledge (*upaniṣad*); for the supreme good is seated (*upaniṣanna*) within this.

This is because of such etymological derivation; the ellipsis is "such knowledge has been declared. Thus ends the second section, called the *Brahmavaca*, in the *Vāruṇī Upaniṣad* of the Yajurveda Āraṇyaka, within the *Vedārthaprakāśa* composed by the venerable Sāyaṇācārya, under the patronage of the supreme lord Mādhava Vidyāraṇya, the upholder of the empire of the illustrious Bukkaṇa.
This Brahmavallī is completed.

In the second section (anuvāka), the knowledge of Brahman (brahmavidyā) was defined. Now, in the third section, its means (sādhanas) are defined.
Although the external means—ritual acts (karmas) and meditative practices (upāsanās)—were already mentioned in the Sāṃhitya Upaniṣad, [they are treated here again].
Nevertheless, since the internal means consisting of reflection (*vicāra*) has not yet been stated, even though [external] benefits have been mentioned, that is now being set forth here.

When that is explained, its constituent parts, such as reflection (*manana*) and so on, will also be explained. In this regard, he first relates a narrative for the purpose of praising knowledge (*vidyā*), beginning with the words "Bhṛgu... and so on. There was a certain great seer (*maharṣi*) named Bhṛgu... a cowherd... [and so forth].
He is the one who sets [the ritual] in motion. By the word "vai" (indeed), that well-known tradition found in the Mantras and Brāhmaṇas is recalled;
for it is recited in the Mantra and Brāhmaṇa: "O Lord of Vows, I establish you with the vow of the Bhṛgus and the Aṅgirases"—thus one should establish [the fire] for the Bhṛgus and Aṅgirases.
And that Bhṛgu was the son of Varuṇa, who approached his father Varuṇa for instruction as a guru.

Furthermore, approaching a teacher (*gurūpasatti*) is prescribed in another Vedic scripture: "To gain knowledge of that, one should approach a teacher alone" (*tadvijñānārthaṃ sa gurumevābhigacchet*).
The mantra for approaching the teacher begins with "Teach me! (*adhīhi*) and so forth: "O Blessed One (*bhagavaḥ*), O venerable teacher (*guro*)," and so on.

"Study this further; remember it with your mind, and having remembered it, teach it"—this is the meaning. Whether such narratives are for the purpose of praising knowledge (*vidyā-stuti*) was considered in the fourth quarter of the third chapter [of the *Mīmāṃsā-sūtra*]: "Is the narrative for the sake of the *pāriplava* [ritual recitation], or is it a praise of knowledge? Since praise is more significant as a subordinate element of performance, it serves the purpose of the *pāriplava*. [The answer is: No.

Because of the specific qualification "Vaivasvata is the king" found therein, and because there is no unity of context with the knowledge (*vidyā*), this must be a glorification of that knowledge. Furthermore, the narrative heard in the Upaniṣad—beginning with "Yājñavalkya had two wives" and "Janaka of Videha sat down"—must be for the purpose of the *pāriplava* (the recitation at the horse sacrifice). At the Aśvamedha sacrifice, the king...

Having seated the king together with his family in three [sessions], the Adhvaryu priest must recite Vedic narratives and other meritorious stories before him; this ritual act is called *pāriplava*, as it is enjoined by the scriptural statement, "He should recount the *pāriplava*. If that were its purpose, then the narratives known as the Upaniṣads would be utilized for the sake of performance. Performance is superior.

Since it might be argued that the Upanishadic narratives are for the purpose of the *pāriplava* (the sacrificial recitation), we reply: because specific narratives such as "On the first day, King Manu Vaivasvata;

on the second day, King Yama Vaivasvata," and so forth, are designated for the *pāriplava*, it is impossible for the Upanishadic narratives to be subordinate to that [ritual]. They are, rather, intended to praise the proximate meditations (*vidyā*).

However, it is obtained as a single syntactical unit with the sentences concerning knowledge (*vidyā*). Therefore, the narrative is a glorification (*stāvaka*) of that knowledge. It shows the instruction on the means for awakening to Brahman. Regarding the phrase "to him": to that Bhṛgu who had approached him accompanied by mantras, he spoke this—beginning with food—as the means for awakening. [He spoke of] food and so forth, which are the material causes (*upādāna-kāraṇa*) of the sheaths (*kośa*) consisting of food (*anna-maya*), vital breath (*prāṇa-maya*), and mind (*manas-maya*).

"The mind, speech, sight, and hearing are also doors, just like the mind. The word "also" (api) is intended to indicate those [organs] not explicitly mentioned, namely the organs of perception such as the skin and so forth, and the organs of action such as the hands, feet, and so forth. If it is argued that these are merely secondary (gauṇa) meanings—just as in the expression "the moon is at the tip of the branch"—it is not so, because they have been specifically distinguished [as primary]. (Sūtra 3.4.4).

Just as a branch of a tree serves as the door for perceiving the moon, so too do food, vital breath (*prāṇa*), and the rest serve as the doors for perceiving the Brahman situated within the cave. And that status of being a door is clearly stated in the *Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad*:
"Those who [know] the breath of breath, the eye of the eye, the ear of the ear, and the food of food, and the mind of mind..."

The wise know the mind; they have discerned that Brahman is the ancient, immortal one. Because it is the substratum for the conceptualization of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and so forth, Brahman—which takes the form of the vital breaths and the like—is easily known through the medium of the vital breaths and so on. The intention is that Brahman is to be sought among food, the vital breaths, and the rest, which are accessible to the notion of "I. Now, regarding the investigation of the cause of water, which is the defining characteristic of Brahman:

He shows the instruction with the words beginning with "Then" (*tataḥ*). Having heard the door [to knowledge], Varuṇa, observing that Bhṛgu was exceedingly eager for its comprehension, spoke again of his own accord—even without Bhṛgu’s question—due to the excellence of his compassion.
The particle *ha* is used to indicate eagerness and renown. These five great elements, beginning with space (*ākāśa*), are... [the earth].
From which reality all living beings—endowed with the three bodies and extending from Hiraṇyagarbha down to a blade of grass—are born;
the word "vai" (indeed) is used to indicate the well-known fact from other scriptural passages such as "He created these worlds";
and by which reality the elements, once produced, live and maintain their existence, and toward which they go when undergoing destruction.

The elements (*bhūtāni*) completely enter into that reality (*vastu*), meaning they dissolve into it entirely. Just as the arising, subsistence, and dissolution of foam, waves, bubbles, and so forth occur within the ocean, so it is with this. Investigate that reality which is the cause of the world’s origin, subsistence, and dissolution. That very reality is the Brahman you have asked about. The word "iti" marks the conclusion of the answer. [Thus speaks] the investigator.

And this was considered in the first pāda of the first chapter: "Whether [Brahman] is to be investigated or not, since superimposition (adhyāsa) has not been defined, it does not deserve investigation because there is no doubt and no fruit. Superimposition is established by the notion of 'I', while Brahman is declared in the Śruti to be unattached; therefore, because of the doubt and because of the existence of liberation, Brahman is to be investigated through the Veda."

"Indeed, the Self, my dear, is to be seen, it is to be heard"—here, aiming at the vision of the Self as the fruit, hearing (*śravaṇa*) is enjoined as the means to that end. "Hearing" consists of a logical inquiry (*nyāyavicāra*) conducive to determining the purport (*tātparya*) of the Vedānta texts with respect to Brahman. This very sentence enjoining such inquiry is the subject matter (*viṣaya*). Nor is this subject matter...

It is summarized by a single verse; for, by the summary of the doubt itself, the summary of its subject matter is understood by implication. The doubt is whether the treatise—which determines the principles (*nyāya*) consisting of the inquiry into Brahman—is not to be commenced or is indeed to be commenced. In every case, the two sets of arguments for the prima facie (*pūrva-pakṣa*) and the final conclusion (*uttara-pakṣa*) are to be inferred as the seeds of the doubt. Among these, it is first established that it is "not to be commenced," because of the absence of both a subject matter (*viṣaya*) and a purpose (*prayojana*).
For that which is doubtful becomes the object of inquiry. Brahman, however, is not doubtful. To explain:

is it doubtful in its aspect as Brahman or in its aspect as the Self? Not the first, because the aspect of Brahman is ascertained by such scriptural passages as "Brahman is Truth, Knowledge, Infinite. Nor the second, because [the aspect of the Self] is [ascertained] by the notion of "I" (*ahaṃpratyaya*).

This is because [the self] is also determined [as distinct]. If it is argued that the notion of "I" is merely fatigued due to the habitual identification with the self, we say no; for superimposition cannot be established. This is because the body and the self—being inert and conscious respectively, and thus opposed in nature like darkness and light—cannot be related as a substrate and its attribute, as in the case of mother-of-pearl and silver.
Now, therefore, the desire to know Brahman. (1.1.1) [Variant readings: 1. vāḍava; 2. dīyana]

The superimposition of mutual identity, as in the case of a shell-silver illusion, cannot be established here. Therefore, since that which is determined by the two non-erroneous means of knowledge—scripture and direct experience—is free from doubt, it does not constitute an object for inquiry. Nor do we perceive any purpose [for such inquiry], because liberation is not observed even when Brahman and the Self have been determined in the manner described above. Therefore—

The prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that since Brahman does not admit of inquiry, the scripture (*śāstra*) need not be commenced. To this it is replied: the scripture must be commenced because of the existence of both a subject matter (*viṣaya*) and a purpose (*prayojana*). The reality of the self as Brahman is doubtful due to the contradiction between scriptural testimony and the notion of "I" (*ahaṃ-pratyaya*). The scripture, in the passage "This Self is Brahman," teaches that Brahman, which is without attachment, is the very Self. [And yet] "I am... [the ego-sense persists].

One grasps the Self through the superimposition (*adhyāsa*) of identity with the body and so forth, by means of the notion of "I" (*aham-buddhi*). Furthermore, the fact that this superimposition is difficult to define is an ornament to our position. Therefore, the object of inquiry is a doubtful reality. And it is well known from both scripture (*śruti*) and the experience of the wise (*vidvat-anubhava*) that the purpose (*prayojana*), characterized as liberation, results from the ascertainment of that [reality]. Consequently, [the inquiry proceeds] by way of an investigation into the Vedānta texts.

The established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that the scripture must be commenced because Brahman is a fit object for inquiry. For inquiry culminates in the determination of the true nature of a thing through its definition (*lakṣaṇa*) and means of knowledge (*māna*). And the definition was considered in that very context:
"Does a definition of Brahman exist or not? It does not exist; for birth and so forth belong to other things, and [qualities] such as truthfulness are unestablished [in Him]."

[This is] for the benefit [of the seeker]. The state of being the cause, which culminates in Brahman, would be like a mark [on a person], such as a garland or a serpent. For it is indeed worldly attributes such as "truth" and so forth that indicate the indivisible [Brahman]. [As stated in the scripture: "From which these beings are born;
by which, once born, they live; into which they enter when they depart—desire to know that; that is Brahman. [And: "Truth, knowledge..."

The subject matter consists of the two statements, "the infinite Brahman" and "they go. The meaning is that they "go" while dying. Here, a doubt arises as to whether the definition of Brahman heard in this context is applicable or not; it is not applicable. To explain: is the definition of Brahman its being the origin and so forth of the world, or is it its being Truth and so forth? It cannot be the former, because since that [origin and so forth] resides in the world, it lacks a direct connection with Brahman.

In the second case as well, if one accepts truth, knowledge, and so forth as they are commonly understood in the world, Brahman would not be established as partless because these terms would have distinct meanings.

However, it is improper for truth and the rest to serve as a definition if they are not [universally] accepted. Therefore, neither an extrinsic definition (*taṭasthalakṣaṇa*) nor an intrinsic definition (*svarūpalakṣaṇa*) exists. To this, it is replied: although origination and the rest reside in something else, their causality resides in Brahman.
It will be an extrinsic definition (*taṭasthalakṣaṇa*) connected through conceptual construction (*kalpanā*), just as in the case of "that which is a serpent is a garland.

Since it is possible to define a thing even by means of a conceptualized [attribute], such as "that which is the cause of the world is Brahman," there is no contradiction—just as there is no contradiction when words with distinct referents, such as "father," "son," "protector," and "son-in-law," all ultimately converge upon the single person Devadatta. Thus...

If words such as "truth" (*satya*), which in common worldly usage denote distinct objects, are shown to culminate in the indivisible Brahman, then both [the definitions] are established: that it is the *svarūpalakṣaṇa* (essential definition). To demonstrate that definition, the authorship of the Veda with respect to that very [Brahman] is considered: "Is Brahman not the author of the Veda, or is it both author and non-author? By means of the eternal, formless speech"—thus is its eternity [established].

Because of the description [of the Veda], because of the statements regarding its being the breath of the Creator and so forth, and because of its similarity to the past, the Veda is eternal. [The Lord is the author] because He illumines everything;
"From whom the birth etc. of this [world proceed]" (Sūtra 1.1.2); and "Because He is the source of the scripture" (Sūtra 1.1.3). [The order of the letters...]

By the grace of Bhṛgu, one becomes all-knowing. This which is the Ṛgveda, the Yajurveda, and the Sāmaveda is the very breath of this Great Being. [From] Vidya-araṇya-viracitā [Bhṛguvallī].

The word "da" refers to the subject matter of the sentence. The meaning is that whatever exists, such as the Ṛgveda and so forth, is established for that eternally perfected Brahman without effort, like a breath. There is a doubt as to whether Brahman creates the Veda or not.
He does not create it, because the Veda is eternal; for in this mantra, "O Virūpa, [the Veda] is eternal by speech," the term "Virūpa" refers to...

Having awakened her, he prays: "Impel me toward praise with eternal speech. Eternal speech is indeed the Veda itself, according to the traditional teaching (smṛti): "Eternal speech, without beginning or end, was emitted by the Self-born in the beginning as the divine Veda, from which all activities proceed. Thus, when it is argued that Brahman is not the author of the Veda, we reply: Brahman is the author of the Veda.

It must be so. Why? Because, according to the analogy of breathing, it is understood that [the Vedas] arise without effort. Furthermore, from the scriptural statement, "From that sacrifice in which everything is offered, the Ṛg-verses and Sāman-chants were born," the origin of the Veda is clearly heard to proceed from Brahman—who is denoted by the word 'sacrifice'—as he is being offered as the oblation in all sacrifices. Precisely because they arise without effort, they differ from the works composed by Kālidāsa and others based on intentional design.

Its authorlessness (*apauruṣeyatva*) is due to its distinctness from [human] agency; its eternity consists in its arising at every new creation (*pratisarga*) with the same form as before, in the manner of a continuous stream (*pravāha*).
By establishing Brahman’s authorship of the Veda—which manifests the established order of the entire universe—Brahman’s omniscience is thereby established.

Having thus justified the definition, the establishment of the scripture (*āgama*) was considered in that very context. There is also the status of being cognizable by other means of knowledge (*anyameyatā*).

Or rather, what is its status as being cognizable by the Veda alone? Since it is an established entity like a jar, it could be measured even by something other than the Veda. However, due to its lack of form, marks, and so forth, it lacks the fitness to be an object of other means of knowledge. Its status as being cognizable by the Veda alone is declared in such passages as "Him who is known through the Upaniṣads" (*taṃ tv aupaniṣadam*).
This refers to the statement made by Yājñavalkya to Śākalya: "I ask you about that Person known through the Upaniṣads" (*taṃ tv aupaniṣadaṃ puruṣaṃ pṛcchāmi*), concerning the Supreme Brahman.

It is understood that the person consisting of form (*rūpa-puruṣa*) is to be known through the *Upaniṣads*. That scriptural passage is the subject matter. In this regard, the doubt is whether Brahman is accessible through perception and other means of knowledge or not. The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is clear: because it lacks form, taste, and so forth, it is not amenable to the senses; and because it is devoid of logical marks (*liṅga*), similarity (*sādṛśya*), and the like, it is not amenable to inference, comparison, and other such means. U-

If it is argued that [Brahman] is known through the Vedas alone—based on the etymology "it is understood only in the Upaniṣads" (paṇiṣatsu eva adhigamyate)—and by the scriptural negation of other means, such as "he who does not know the Veda does not perceive that Great One"—then its status as being cognizable solely through the Vedas is established. If it is further argued that the Commentator, in the *Janmādi-sūtra*, has accepted that it is cognizable through other means as well—since he states that here the means of knowledge consist of scripture (*śruti*) and so forth, as well as experience (*anubhava*) and so forth, according to their respective applicability—then we reply: certainly. However, initially, scripture...

Because it is accepted that after Brahman has been known through that [Veda] alone, inference and experience subsequently function as restatements (anuvāda); therefore, Brahman is knowable solely through the Veda. Furthermore, the fact that the Veda is the means of valid knowledge regarding Brahman has already been considered in that very context. [Now, the question arises: Do the Vedāntas concern the agent, the deity, and so forth, or do they concern Brahman? [Objection: They must teach the agent and so forth, because they are useful for ritual performance (*anuṣṭhāna*). [Reply: No, because they belong to different contexts (*prakaraṇa*).

The Taittirīyopaniṣaddīpikā, 171:
[It might be argued that] the sentences revealing creation are intended for the sake of practice; if that were so, [it would follow that] the Vedāntas are [merely] for the sake of performance.

[If they were otherwise], there would be no utility. However, if they have Brahman as their ultimate purport, they would be purposeless because [if that were the case], performance [of rituals] would be impossible.

Therefore, the Vedāntas teach the agent, the deity, and the means [of ritual action]. To this it is replied: The Vedāntas have Brahman as their ultimate purport. Why? Because it is impossible for those [Vedāntic texts] read in separate contexts to be subordinate to ritual action by way of teaching the agent and so forth.

Furthermore, it is possible for [the Upanishads] to have Brahman as their primary purport by means of the six marks that determine the intended meaning (*tātparya-niścaya-hetu-liṅga-ṣaṭka*). These six marks have been defined by the former teachers as follows: "The opening and the conclusion, repetition, novelty, fruit, corroboration, and justification are the marks for determining the intended meaning. "The opening" is: "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone" (*sadeva somyedamagra āsīt*). "The conclusion" is: "All this has that as its self" (*aitadātmyam idaṃ sarvam*).

The conclusion is "That is your Self; you are That" (*tat tvam asi*). The single mark [of identity] is the uniformity of those two [the individual soul and Brahman] in their nature as Brahman and the object of knowledge. The repetition is the frequent statement, "You are That. Novelty (*apūrvatva*) is the state of not being known through any other means of valid cognition. The fruit is the knowledge of everything through the knowledge of one. The five types of explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) are creation, sustenance, dissolution, entry, and governance. [The illustrative examples are] clay, etc.—

The illustrations are the logical arguments (*upapatti*). By these marks, the fact that [the texts] have Brahman as their ultimate purport is to be determined. Nor is there a lack of purpose in the absence of ritual performance; for, as in the case of "This is not a snake," the cessation of harm is possible through mere understanding. The absence of the Vedāntas' being subordinate to injunctions has been considered in that very context: "They desire to effect a realization [of Brahman], having come to rest in Brahman."

Furthermore, because they are scriptures (*śāstra*), they are the enjoiners (*vidhātṛ*) due to the mention of reflection (*manana*) and so forth; for there is no injunction in that which is not dependent on an agent. Scripture-hood also exists because of the praising [of Brahman]. Therefore, prior to realization, reflection and so forth culminate in Brahman—thus the *ekadeśin* (partialist) maintains. Even though the Vedāntas have Brahman as their ultimate goal, they do not terminate in Brahman alone; rather, they do so through indirectness (*pārokṣyeṇa*).

Having established the reality of Brahman, [the scriptures] subsequently effect its direct realization. This being the case, the status of the Vedāntas as a "śāstra" (treatise/instruction) is justified by their teaching. Furthermore, having enjoined hearing—which consists of verbal knowledge—through the injunction "it is to be heard," the subsequent stages such as reflection (*manana*) and meditation (*nididhyāsana*), which consist of experiential knowledge, are clearly enjoined through the statements "it is to be reflected upon" and "it is to be meditated upon."

Therefore, when it is argued that the Vedāntas are injunctions for realization (*pratipatti*), we reply: an injunction for realization is not possible. This is because it is not dependent on a person (*apuruṣatantra*), as it is impossible to do, not do, or do otherwise [realization]. Furthermore, being a scripture (*śāstratva*) is not necessarily restricted to the teaching of what is to be performed; it is established even by the glorification of an already existing reality (*siddhavastu*). Nor, once the knowledge produced by the words has arisen, is there...

It is not logical to say that reflection (*manana*) and so forth—which consist of experiential realization—are being enjoined [as a means to knowledge]. For, just as in the case of "You are the tenth," the word itself generates immediate perception; therefore, prior to verbal comprehension, reflection and other such activities in the form of mental operations are enjoined in order to remove improbability and contrary impressions. Thus, in statements such as "That thou art" (*tat tvam asi*), [it is the word that effects realization].

Regarding the statement, "The Vedāntas are settled upon Brahman": this inquiry, which results in the determination of the true nature of Brahman by means of the Vedānta, is enjoined by the scriptural passage, "Seek to know That. This injunction is also heard in another recension:
"It is to be heard, it is to be reflected upon, it is to be meditated upon. To that same effect, it is recorded in the Smṛti:

[From the *Bhṛguvallī*] "He is to be heard from the words of the Vedas, and He is to be reflected upon through reasonings; having reflected, He should be constantly meditated upon—these are the [means of knowledge]."

"Not the causes. 'Reflection' (*manana*) would be the practice of reasoning that supports those statements. 'Meditation' (*nididhyāsana*) is one-pointedness of mind..."
And also in the forest, in reflection (*manana*). For the wise hold that hearing (*śravaṇa*) is the internal factor for the arising of knowledge;

reflection (*manana*), which is thinking by way of the exclusion of other [views], is external; and likewise, tranquility (*śānti*), self-control (*dānti*), and so forth, stand within the category of what must be done (*itikartavyatā*).
These very things—hearing, reflection, and meditative absorption (*nididhyāsana*)—are described in the Kahola Brāhmaṇa as "scholarship" (*pāṇḍitya*) and "childlike innocence" (*bālya*).

The word *mauna* (sagehood) includes those [stages] prescribed [in the passage]: "A Brahmin, having become disillusioned with scholarship (*pāṇḍitya*), should remain in a state of childlike simplicity (*bālya*); having become disillusioned with both childlike simplicity and scholarship, he then becomes a sage (*muni*); and having become disillusioned with both non-sagehood and sagehood, he then becomes a true Brahmin. Having "become disillusioned" (*nirvidya*)—meaning having fully accomplished the practice of this triad—one [realizes] the nature of Brahman.

The meaning is that one becomes a *mukhapātra-brāhmaṇa* by virtue of such a state. Here, *manana* (reflection) is indicated by the word *bālya* (childhood), which is intended for the purification of the intellect (*dhī*). That the term is intended for the purification of the intellect was considered in the fourth quarter of the third chapter [of the Brahma-sūtras]:

"Is *bālya* [childhood] a stage of life, acting according to one's will, or the purification of the intellect? [It must be the latter] because of its well-known usage; since that [stage of life] is not something to be enjoined, acting according to one's will..."

Let it be so, and not otherwise. Since reflection (*manana*) has already been employed [as a means], what is intended here is the purity of being (*bhāva-śuddhi*). Neither of the other two [options] is intended, because they are utterly useless and even contradictory. In the phrase "one should remain in childhood" (*bālyena tiṣṭhāset*), by the well-known derivation that "childhood" (*bālya*) is the state (*bhāva*) of a child, it would refer to age (*vayas*). If, however, that [age] were to be enjoined as a duty, then [the compound] would have to be analyzed as "the action of childhood" (*bālyasya karma*).

"Let there be acting according to one's will, speaking as one pleases, and so forth; even if all these goals are attained, there is no purity of intellect—this is what constitutes 'childishness'. To this we reply:

between the two stages called "scholarship" (*pāṇḍitya*) and "sagehood" (*mauna*), which correspond respectively to hearing (*śravaṇa*) and meditative absorption (*nididhyāsana*), it is reflection (*manana*) that is intended by the Śruti as the duty to be performed. And for that [reflection], purity of being (*bhāva-śuddhi*) is necessary, because [otherwise] one would be seized by defects such as passion, hatred, pride, and humiliation.

Because it is impossible to conceive [of anything] apart from that which possesses external objects; furthermore, the etymological derivation "the action (*karman*) of a child (*bāla*)" applies equally to the conduct of a child's desires and to the purity of one's inner disposition (*bhāva*). However, mere age and unrestrained desire are utterly useless for contemplation (*manana*), and are indeed its opposites, because they destroy contemplation in the mind of one who is either deluded or whose mind is directed toward external objects. Therefore, [it is] the state—

Purity alone is childhood, and nothing else; both [childhood and purity] are intended for the injunction regarding the state of a sage (*munitva*). Whether silence (*mauna*) is something not to be enjoined or something to be enjoined—why is it not enjoined? Since silence, which denotes knowledge, is already attained through scholarship (*pāṇḍitya*), and since both [childhood and silence] signify knowledge, silence as the continuous steadfastness in knowledge is not distinct from scholarship. Therefore, it is to be enjoined in order to bring about its distinction [from scholarship] during the period of childhood.

In the Kahola Brāhmaṇa it is heard: "Therefore, a Brāhmaṇa, having desisted from scholarship, should seek to abide in childlike simplicity; and having desisted from both childlike simplicity and scholarship, he then becomes a sage. This is its meaning: because the state of Brahman is [attained] by not manifesting [external signs], according to the connection [of the text]; [this constitutes] an injunction for another auxiliary means, as a third [factor] for one who possesses that [scholarship]. Because the origin of the Bhṛgu-valaya is established by scripture, and because the elements appear as being permeated by "Being" (sat)—as in "Earth exists," "Water exists"—the real entity Being is the material cause (upādāna) of the elements. And that entity is Brahman. Regarding the production of the elemental derivatives (bhautika):

The elements (*bhūtāni*) are intermediate states of Being (*sat*), just as a lump of clay is an intermediate state of [clay]; however, the material cause (*upādāna*) is Being itself, just as clay is the cause of a pot.
This is because material objects appear as permeated by Being, such that one perceives "the pot exists" or "the body exists.
It is just as for common, unrefined people, the threads are the material cause of a cloth that is permeated by those burnt threads.

"Space, time, and so forth arise because they are divisible, like a jar or a bowl"—this is how one should argue against those who maintain their eternity. Because the entire world to be created is diverse, the omniscience and omnipotence of the Creator, Brahman, are established through the impossibility of that diversity otherwise. For indeed, [the construction of] a diverse palace—

The capacity to create that [universe] is never observed in anyone without the two powers of will (*icchā*) and knowledge (*jñāna*). Although the Brahman, being devoid of sense organs, lacks the means of perception (*pratyakṣa-pramāṇa*) which are the causes for knowing all things, nevertheless, its omniscience must be accepted on the basis of scripture (*śruti*) and reasoning (*yukti*). The scripture states: "He who is all-knowing, all-perceiving. And the reasoning should be viewed as follows: [He is] all-perceiving—

Consciousness reflected in the transformations of *māyā*—which take the form of the mental modifications (*vṛtti*)—is called "universal experience" (*sarvānubhava*). Because of its superimposed relationship with objects, its omniscience regarding present objects is established. Furthermore, upon the cessation of past objects and the corresponding *māyā*-modifications delimited by them, their latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) constitute its knowledge of past objects, just as in the case of ordinary people like ourselves.

Illusions take the form of memory as transformations of one's own *māyā*. Through the experience of that which is reflected therein, even past omniscience is established. Likewise, since the determination of objects yet to be created is observed in potters and others even before the act of creation, future omniscience is also established by virtue of the transformation of one's own *māyā*. Therefore, omniscience is logical.
Furthermore, all powers are established by the Śruti and Smṛti. The Śruti states: "His supreme power is manifold.

The Smṛti states: "The powers of all entities are beyond the scope of inconceivable knowledge; for those powers of existence, such as creation and so forth, belong to Brahman. For such an omnipotent Brahman, the causality of the origin and so forth of the universe is the defining characteristic (lakṣaṇa).

Although origination and so forth reside in the world, causality— which has that [world] as its counter-correlate— can function as a definition because it exists in Brahman, the object to be defined. Nor does the inclusion of the nature of the object to be defined within the definition— as in "the moon is that which possesses preeminent light"— result in a loss of Brahman’s immutability (*kūṭasthatva*), provided that causality is understood not as consisting in the penetration of activity (*kriyāveśa*), but rather as the state of being the cause of that [world].

It should be said: [this objection] is set aside because, like the [presence of] a crow, it is merely adventitious (*aupādhika*) and thus extrinsic (*taṭastha*). In the expression "Devadatta’s house has a crow," the state of being the locus of the crow is not included within the house itself; for even when the crow is gone, there is no perception of the destruction of any part of the house. Therefore, since the house possesses this property only through the adventitious condition (*upādhi*) of the crow's dwelling there, it is the locus of the crow—[but the house does not become non-existent when the crow leaves].

One's own [nature]. Just as there is an incidental definition (*taṭasthalakṣaṇa*), so too the causality of birth, destruction, and other such attributes is an incidental definition. And because that definition is illusory, there is no loss of non-duality (*advaita*). Just as in the cases "that which is the snake is the rope" and "that which is the silver is the mother-of-pearl," even though the snake and the silver are illusory, they serve as definitions of the rope by virtue of their superimposed relationship; so it is here.

Being the cause shall also be a defining characteristic [of Brahman], because even in its state as the cause, Brahman is merely the substratum (adhiṣṭhāna), according to the scriptural teaching regarding modification.
