Since Māyā alone is the efficient cause (prayojaka) in the portion [of the world] consisting of names and forms, there is no loss of Brahman’s quality of being unattached (asaṅgatva). Because Brahman pervades the entire universe in the form of existence (sattā) and manifestation (sphūrti), and because Māyā also pervades it in the form of undergoing modification (vikriyamāṇatva), both combined constitute the material cause (upādāna). In that regard, regarding the distinction between the subordinate and the primary, either the principle of the two threads (dvisūtranyāya) may apply according to the speaker's intention, or—

Either the analogy of power and the possessor of power (*śakti-śaktimad*) or the analogy of the substratum and the superimposed (*adhiṣṭhāna-āropya*) should be applied. Just as two threads joined together to form a rope constitute the material cause (*upādāna*) with equal primacy, so too some say that both Brahman and Māyā have equal primacy in the world. Others, however, think thus: just as it is said, "The fire possessing power burns," [so too is the relationship between Brahman and Māyā].

Even though power (*śakti*) acts as the means for burning, fire remains primary because power is dependent upon it; likewise, since Māyā is subordinate as a power, Brahman, who possesses that power, alone is primary. Others, however, say this: just as at the time of delusion, even though the body of the snake does not exist apart from the rope, the rope is—

Just as the snake is primary because it is what is being designated by the word "rope," so too is Māyā primary. In every respect, the status of being the cause of the world heard in the scriptures is logically established for Brahman as qualified by Māyā.

Thus, inquiry is the means for the realization of Brahman, which is indicated by the defining characteristic (lakṣaṇa) of being the cause of the world, considered as an extrinsic definition (taṭasthalakṣaṇa).

In the first section, he demonstrates the conclusion reached by the learned Bhṛgu through the words beginning with "He [performed] austerity" (*sa tapaḥ*). As for the Smṛti text stating that there are four stages of life (āśramas), it will apply to those who are incapable due to blindness or other such conditions, and not to those whose domestic duties remain unimpaired. For indeed...

Nor is there eligibility for a person who is lame for a rite involving the Viṣṇu-strides and so forth. Therefore, since there is no stage of life (āśrama) characterized by celibacy (*ūrdhvaretas*) suitable for the knowledge of the Self for one endowed with the proficiency of sight and other senses, this being the position reached, we reply: there is indeed a stage of life characterized by celibacy; for even in the absence of an explicit scriptural injunction, it is established as something new (*apūrva*).

Because it is possible to conceive of it as being for that purpose; nor is there the fault of killing a hero (*vīra*), since the killing of a hero refers to the context of householders who have extinguished their sacred fires. As for what was stated in the Smṛti regarding its applicability to those who are blind and so forth—that is incorrect. Furthermore, whether one is uninitiated or initiated, a graduate (*snātaka*) or not a graduate, one who has extinguished his fires or is without fires, on whichever day he becomes free from passion (*virajet*)—

"One should renounce on that very day"—because of this injunction for renunciation as a separate rule for those who are dispassionate and have not yet entered the householder stage, one should not assume an injunction for other stages of life (āśrama) for those possessing keen faculties such as sight. This is because a direct injunction is found in the Jābāla Śruti: "Having completed the stage of studenthood, one should become a householder; having been a householder, one should become a forest-dweller..."

"One should go [to another stage]"—therefore, there exists another stage of life (*āśrama*). Regarding this very point, it has been considered that there is no descending from the stages of life. Is there a descent from the stages of life or not? It occurs through passion; or rather, like the ascent, it is optional based on faith in the previous dharma. Because passion is strictly prohibited, only that which is prescribed possesses the nature of dharma. As for the ascent...

There is no descent from the higher stages according to scripture, as seen in statements such as "Having completed the student life (*brahmacarya*), one should become a householder; having been a householder, one should become a forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*); and having been a forest-dweller, one should renounce.

While the ascent through the stages of life (*āśrama*) occurs according to one's own will, it might be argued that a descent—such as from the state of a wandering mendicant (*pārivrājya*) back to that of a forest-dweller—is also logical in certain cases, whether due to the influence of passion or out of devotion to a previous stage of life. [This concludes the prima facie argument.]
"Jaimini [holds that there is] a re-examination [of the soul], for he rejects the absence of scriptural injunction"; Jaimini Sūtra 3.4.2, Section 1.

"But for one who has become that [state], there is no non-becoming of that state, according to Jaimini as well, because of the restrictive rules and the absence of [prior] form"; Jaimini Sūtra 3.4.10, Section 1.
Gha. Thus.

We reply: First of all, passion is prohibited because it is rooted in false knowledge (*mithyājñāna*). Furthermore, faith in the duties (*dharma*) of the previous stage of life (*āśrama*) is not appropriate;
for those duties lack the status of *dharma* with respect to one belonging to a subsequent stage of life, as they have not been prescribed for him. Indeed, that which can be performed by someone...

That which is performed and is believed in becomes one's duty (*dharma*). Rather, that which is prescribed for someone is his duty. Furthermore, from this it follows that there is no returning; by the prohibition of descending (*avaroha*), ascending (*āroha*) is restricted. No traditional practice (*śiṣṭācāra*) regarding descending is observed, as there is for ascending. Therefore, there is no descending. [End of] Āśrama-śeṣa.
The expiation for that very case has been considered: "Is there no expiation for one who is *ūrdhvaretas* (one who has restrained his vital energy), or is there?

Because of the statement regarding 'not being seen' [in the scriptures], there is none; however, for a killer, the sacrificial animal is a donkey. For a killer, this is indeed a minor offense (*upapātaka*), like the consumption of honey or meat.
Purity comes from both expiation and consecration (*saṃskāra*); such is the authoritative teaching. Having attained the state of *ūrdhvaretas* through lifelong celibacy (*naiṣṭhika-brahmacarya*)."

Furthermore, there is no expiation for one who has fallen away due to attachment to women. This is because of the statement regarding the non-perception of an expiation: "For him who, having ascended to the lifelong religious duty (*naiṣṭhika-dharma*), falls away again—I see no expiation by which that self-slayer might be purified. However, there is an expiation: "Now, if a student (*brahmacārī*) should approach a woman, he shall sacrifice a donkey as an animal victim."

It might be argued thus: "That is not so, because that [penance] pertains to the student (*vratī*). This statement regarding penance refers to one known as the *upakurvāṇaka*, who performs the vow of celibacy (*brahmacarya*) as an auxiliary to the study of the Vedas. Therefore, for one who has become a perpetual celibate (*ūrdhvaretas*), there is no penance. To this we reply: Just as for the *upakurvāṇaka* there is [the prohibition of] honey and meat...

Regarding the consumption [of forbidden food], there exist both an expiation (*prāyaścitta*) and a re-initiation (*punaḥ-saṃskāra*), as it is a minor offense (*upapātaka*). Similarly, for one who has sublimated his vital energy (*ūrdhvaretas*), engaging in sexual activity with anyone other than the wife of a guru and so forth is indeed a minor offense, but not a major offense (*mahāpātaka*). Consequently, purification occurs through expiation and re-initiation. This is because, if it were not enumerated among the major offenses, it would be a minor offense.

If it is asked, "If penance is prescribed by relying on the state of being a *kaṭa* (one who has committed a minor offense), then what is the status of the statement regarding 'non-perception' [of the sin]? we reply that that statement is intended to emphasize effort. For this very reason, he says, "I see no penance," meaning "there is none.

However, there is indeed penance in the form of a donkey-sacrifice (*gardabha-paśu*), because of the equality of the status of a religious student (*brahmacārin*). Likewise for forest-dwellers (*vanastha*) and wandering mendicants (*parivrājaka*).

In both cases, an expiation is prescribed in the Smṛtis: "A forest-dweller (vānaprastha), upon a breach of initiation, should perform the Kṛcchra penance for twelve nights and then increase the great thicket (mahākakṣa).
A mendicant (bhikṣu) should act like a forest-dweller, with the exception of the increase of Soma. The "increase of the thicket" refers to the planting of trees in the forest;
the "increase of Soma" is likewise that same [planting]. It is shown in that very [text] that purification regarding the next world (*āmuṣmika*) alone occurs through expiation. Śu...

Whether one who has fallen [from virtue] is to be accepted or rejected by the learned depends on the removal of his fault. If it is removed, he is to be accepted; otherwise, purification achieved through penance would be in vain. Purification would then belong only to the next world, and for that reason, the learned reject such a person. However, from the scriptural statements regarding the unseen result (*adṛṣṭa*) of penance, purification in this world is also intended. This is because the purification produced by the aforementioned penances would otherwise be inexplicable.

When it is argued that there is social interaction with the learned for one who has performed penance, we reply: [there is none], because even regarding the qualification for the next world (*āmuṣmikādhikāra*), such [interaction] is improper due to the inference of his fall (*patana*). (Sūtra 3.4.11) "But he is outside [the community] in both cases... (Sūtra 3.4.42).

Also because of Smṛti and practice. In these stages of life (*āśrama*), since austerity characterized by outward activity—which aims at attaining specific worldly states—lacks the quality of being a means to knowledge, it was considered therein that only austerity characterized by cessation (*nivṛtti*) in the form of one-pointed concentration and so forth is a cause of knowledge. [The question arises: Does a person in a stage of life who desires worldly results deserve to be established in Brahman or not? [The answer is: According to the opportunity, he certainly deserves to know Brahman; there is no obstruction.

"Because of this, one-pointedness of mind is the culmination in Brahman (*brahmaniṣṭhā*). How could that belong to a ritualist? Therefore, only the renouncer of action (*karmatyāgī*) is entitled to the culmination in Brahman, and no other. Having introduced the stages of life with the words, 'There are three branches of dharma,' and having declared that all these who follow the stages of life attain worlds of merit, [the scripture] concludes: 'He who is established in Brahman attains immortality.'"

The steadfastness in Brahman (*brahmaniṣṭhā*) is taught as a means for attaining liberation. This steadfastness in Brahman is possible even for those belonging to the [other] stages of life (*āśrama*) who desire the worlds of merit, because it is easy for them to practice steadfastness in Brahman according to their leisure after having performed the duties of their respective stages of life.
Indeed, there is no prohibition stating that one who desires the worlds cannot know Brahman. Therefore, all—

It may be argued that for the ascetic (*śrāmaṇa*), there exists the state of being established in Brahman (*brahmaniṣṭhā*). To this we reply: what is called "being established in Brahman" is meditative absorption (*samādhi*) in Brahman with a mind focused on nothing else, achieved by abandoning all worldly activities. This is not possible for one who is a hero in ritual action (*karmaśūra*), because the performance of rituals and their abandonment are mutually contradictory. Therefore, the state of being established in Brahman belongs only to those who have abandoned ritual action. Now, [if it be argued that] bhū...
In the second section, he demonstrates the perfected certainty [of his understanding] by means of the passage beginning with "Having understood that" (*tadvijñāya*).

Having understood—that is, having specifically ascertained through the presence of the defining characteristics—that the aforementioned food is Brahman, yet being dissatisfied with that [understanding] due to the influence of doubt, he desires to know further. Once again, preceded by a mantra, he approached his teacher; indeed, he did not succumb to indolence. Apa-...

This is the intention of Bhṛgu, who was satisfied with the seasons. The Vājasaneyins indeed teach this very point: "They say that food is Brahman. But that is not so; for "food indeed putrefies without life-breath. The foul odor of food is clearly perceived in the body, which is its product. This is also shown in the Viṣṇu Purāṇa: "One should not become dispassionate merely because of the foul odor of one's own body."

"What else could be taught to that man who has already attained the cause of detachment? Therefore, it is incorrect to claim that food—which is the cause of the body's origin, maintenance, and dissolution—is Brahman. To that Bhṛgu who had approached him, Varuṇa taught as the means precisely that previously mentioned austerity (*tapas*) characterized by one-pointedness (*aikāgrya*). And of that austerity, [he taught] the direct realization of Brahman...

With the intention of emphasizing its internal proximity [to Brahman], the identity of austerity (*tapas*) and Brahman is figuratively expressed. Once Brahman has been taught through the defining statement regarding its nature as truth, knowledge, and so forth, Brahman might be understood as something merely indirect—like merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*)—by virtue of being an object of knowledge derived from scripture (*āgama*). Thinking that it can be seen through one-pointed concentration, Varuṇa, without stating the essential nature of Brahman [directly], [taught] austerity...

Thus he spoke. And Bhṛgu, with a one-pointed mind, having applied the previously mentioned definition of being the cause of the world, determined that the vital breath (prāṇa) is Brahman. The followers of the Aitareya recension record, by way of negative concomitance, that the vital breath is the cause of the body's origin: "Verily, without the vital breath, semen is not emitted; or rather, [without the vital breath] semen..."

"It might be poured out, it might rot, or it might not come into being. A certain soul, joined with the subtle body (*liṅgadeha*), having arrived from heaven or hell by way of rain, enters this [food] and then enters a man.

When it subsequently enters the womb of a woman along with the semen, then that semen, having been dried up by the vital air (*prāṇavāyu*) that has entered within it, produces the body through the sequence of the embryo and so forth.

The meaning is that in the absence of *prāṇa*, it does not produce a body. Just as it is the cause of origination, so too is it the cause of life, as is recorded by the Kauṣītakins: "As long as *prāṇa* dwells in this body, so long is there life. It is well known that upon the departure of *prāṇa*, the death of the deity [the body] occurs. Therefore, even in the absence of being the material cause (*upādānatva*), with respect to the triad beginning with birth—

"Because it is a friend, the vital breath (prāṇa) is Brahman"—this was Bhṛgu’s conclusion. Now, [the text] shows the conclusion reached in the third section with the words "Having understood that," etc. Since the vital breath is insentient, its being Brahman is improper; for in such passages as "Brahman is consciousness" and "Brahman is bliss," Brahman is perceived to be sentient. Furthermore, the mind is sentient because it possesses the power of cognition. And [Brahman is the source of] birth...

The characteristic of being the instrumental cause exists in the mind (*manas*). Just as it was stated previously that the entry of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) into the embryo is the cause for the production of the body, so too is the entry of the vital breath dependent upon the mind; this is recorded by the followers of the *Atharvaveda* in the dialogue between the question and the answer. Gārgya’s question is: "How does [the vital breath] come into this body? [The answer is: "By means of the mind..."
Therefore, Pippalāda’s answer is: "By that [volition], he enters this body. "Mano-kṛtaḥ" means "made by the mind.
It refers to the kind of intention (*saṃkalpa*) arising at the time of death in the mind impelled by karma—such as, "I shall obtain such a state.
By that intention, produced at the conclusion of the previous body, the vital breath (*prāṇa*) enters into this body.

This very meaning is clearly declared in that same scripture: "When the senses have merged into the mind, by means of that consciousness he enters the vital breath; the vital breath, joined with heat (tejas), together with the self, leads him to the world as it has been conceived. At the time of death, accompanied by the sense organs such as speech and the rest, which have attained the dissolution of their functions into the mind, the individual soul—

In that [state], he becomes endowed with the functions appropriate for his future body. Together with that knowledge of the future body as its object, this individual soul (jīva) enters into the vital breath (prāṇa) and becomes dominated by the vital breath. And that vital breath, joined with "heat" (tejas)—characterized by meditation on the future body—causes the entire subtle body (liṅgadeha), along with the individual soul, to reach the world that follows one's volition.

In this regard, an illustration is recorded in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad: "Just as a caterpillar, having reached the end of a blade of grass, takes hold of another support and draws itself together [toward it], even so this Self, having struck down this body and made it unconscious, takes hold of another support and draws itself together [toward it]. Thus, the leech moves among blades of grass.
Having reached the tip of one blade of grass, [a snake] first grasps another blade of grass with its mouth, and then leads its posterior part to that other blade of grass.

In the same way, at the time of death, the individual soul (jīvātman), by relinquishing the sense of "mine" regarding this present body, causes it to go into ignorance (avidyā) and reach a state devoid of consciousness; then, conceiving of another body with the mind, it withdraws the entire body—
It leads its own self, as distinguished by the body, to another body. Therefore, living beings, characterized by their bodies, are born from the mind.

Since the means of livelihood, such as agriculture and trade, must be deliberated upon and accomplished by the mind, the mind is the cause of life. Furthermore, according to the method described, through the abandonment of ego-identification by means of the mind, it is also the cause of dissolution at death.

However, in the two non-dual states of deep sleep (*suṣupti*) and meditative absorption (*samādhi*), happiness alone remains, self-luminous. And of that...

It might be suspected that [the state of deep sleep] is merely the absence of suffering; however, it is impossible for an absence to be self-luminous (*svaprakāśa*). Self-luminosity consists in appearing without the aid of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Indeed, non-duality (*advaita*) is not cognized by a means of valid cognition at that time; for if it were so cognized, duality would result, which would entail the destruction of the state of deep sleep. Its "appearing" should be understood as the absence of any contradiction. When...

When people accept the states of waking and dreaming without contradiction, they likewise accept deep sleep and meditative absorption (samādhi) without contradiction. Therefore, because it manifests without any means of proof, it is self-luminous (svaprakāśa). [Notes on variants:

Non-duality (*advaita*) is not the mere absence of suffering; for non-duality is the object of joy in both deep sleep and meditative absorption (*samādhi*), when all sense objects have been withdrawn.
It is of the nature of bliss. All people, when there is no other duty to perform, lie down desiring the happiness of deep sleep (*sauṣupta-sukha*).

And those who possess knowledge of reality (*tattvajñānin*) enter into non-conceptual meditative absorption (*nirvikalpa-samādhi*) solely out of a longing for happiness. Both of them, at a later time, recollect that happiness, thinking, "I slept happily" and "I remained absorbed in meditation happily. From these two...

Through the two examples of deep sleep (*suṣupti*) and meditative absorption (*samādhi*), it should be understood that non-duality (*advaita*) is bliss even prior to the creation of duality. Therefore, from this very bliss whose nature is non-duality, these dualistic beings—beginning with ether (*ākāśa*) and including Hiraṇyagarbha and the rest—are produced. Now, one might object: do not creation and dissolution, consisting of duality and non-duality respectively, recur again and again in succession like day and night?

Since this is so, because it is impossible for two mutually contradictory forms to belong to a single entity, one must be declared to be innate (*svābhāvika*) and the other adventitious (*āgantuka*). In that case, which is logically the innate and which the adventitious? It is said: the independence from means of proof (*sādhananairapekṣya*) of non-duality is well-established in deep sleep.

The waking state, however, is dualistic in nature, characterized by its dependence on numerous external means such as sense objects and the like. Therefore, bliss, which is inherently non-dual, is the material cause (*upādāna*) of this adventitious world that is dualistic in form. Just as the single ocean is the cause for the arising, subsistence, and dissolution of the many phenomena such as foam, waves, and bubbles, so it is with this world. This very world—

Bhṛgu directly realized Brahman—which is characterized by non-duality and bliss, and defined as the cause—through austerity characterized by one-pointed concentration (*ekāgrya*). Therefore, that alone is the primary means. And for the accomplishment of that supreme austerity, which consists of one-pointedness, various methods have been elaborated in the Yoga treatises of Patañjali and others. As it has been said:
In the *Kathopaniṣad*, it has been stated that for the direct realization of Brahman— which is of the nature of bliss and investigated as the cause of the universe—

meditation (*tapas*) in the form of one-pointedness of mind is the internal means. Just as there is no other reality superior to the four principles beginning with food (*anna*) and ending with consciousness (*vijñāna*), likewise, there is no other reality superior even to bliss (*ānanda*).

To ward off the doubt that [this] might be something else, he concludes the knowledge (*vidyā*) with the words "That very [knowledge]" (*saiṣā*). By the word "that" (*tat*), the well-known status from another Vedic text is expressed.

One Vedic text says: "Brahmā was the first among the gods to come into being; the creator of the universe, the protector of the world. He taught the knowledge of Brahman—the foundation of all knowledge—to Atharvan, his eldest son. Then, to Āśvalāyana...
He approached the Blessed One, the Supreme Lord (Parameṣṭhin), and said: "Teach me, O Blessed One, the most excellent knowledge of Brahman" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 3.1).

Furthermore, another Śruti text states this. The word *etad* expresses the well-known experience born of one-pointed concentration of mind. That which was obtained by Bhṛgu is the *Bhārgavī*; that which was proclaimed by Varuṇa is the *Vāruṇī*. Such a knowledge [is established] in the supreme ether, the reality of Brahman.

[The preceding section] is concluded. Therefore, that which was stated—"from this very Self, space (ākāśa) was produced"—refers to this lower space. Indeed, O Gārgī, that which is heard as the undifferentiated (avyākṛta), wherein "space is woven like warp and woof," is this intermediate space. That which is heard in the scripture as "the Ṛg-verses in the imperishable, supreme space" refers to the indestructible conceptualization of the Ṛg and other Vedas.
That reality of Brahman which is established by and expounded in the Ṛgveda and other scriptures is this supreme ether (*vyoman*). For there is nothing higher than this—what else could there be?

There is nothing further to be known beyond this; thus the Śvetāśvataras declare: "This is to be known as eternally abiding within the Self;
indeed, there is nothing else whatsoever to be known beyond this. Therefore, knowledge is complete in this Brahman.

This knowledge is easily accessible for one who is single-minded and possesses the highest qualification. However, for one whose mind is restless due to the desire for worldly fruits, [the text] prescribes meditation as a means to achieve one-pointedness of mind under the guise of describing the methods for attaining those fruits.
"He who thus..."—the word "thus" (evam) refers back to what has been previously mentioned, beginning from "Food is Brahman" up to "Bliss is Brahman."

The section ending with "Hm" is the subject under discussion. In that context, because food is the first gateway to the knowledge of Brahman, the text enjoins the contemplation of Brahman upon that symbol (pratīka). That person who meditates on food as Brahman becomes established through the absence of mental instability; furthermore, he becomes endowed with abundant food, capable of eating it, and free from disease and other ailments. Pu...

One becomes prosperous through offspring such as sons and grandsons, through livestock such as cattle and horses, and through spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) consisting of the study of the Vedas and Shastras, as well as through the fame produced by those respective subjects. Since one attains the knowledge of Brahman by means of this [study] which serves as a gateway when it is practiced, therefore this practitioner should not revile food, just as one would not revile a teacher. Thus, this non-reviling—

The vow of this Upāsaka must be fulfilled according to the prescribed rule; if it is transgressed, the worship would become deficient in its constituent parts. Now, in order to enjoin another form of worship, he shows the object of that worship with the words, "Prāṇa indeed... Just as food eaten becomes situated within the body, so too, because of its abiding in the middle of the body, Prāṇa itself is the food. It is that which resides in the center...

Because it sustains that food which is of the nature of breath (*prāṇa*), the body is the "eater of food" (*annāda*), having the form of the enjoyer. Like a pillar situated in the middle of a house, the body is supported by the breath situated within it; thus, the body is established in the breath. That the breath sustains the body is heard in the *Prāṇasaṃvāda*: "I alone, dividing myself fivefold, support this body (*bāṇa*)."

"I sustain [it]. Furthermore, it is directly perceived that the body is that which sustains the vital breath (*prāṇa*). This mutual dependence between the vital breath and the body should be reflected upon. Moreover, it was previously stated that the vital breath possesses the nature of food (*anna*) by virtue of its internal abiding; the body, too, has the nature of food because it is an effect of food. This being so, since both possess the nature of food, they stand in a relationship of mutual support according to the manner previously described.
One should also reflect that "the wind alone is established in the breaths. Having stated the object of worship, the text enjoins its meditation with the words, "He who [knows] this...

Then it shows another object of worship: "The waters, indeed... Because the water that has been drunk is digested by the fire of the stomach, the waters possess the nature of food (*anna*). And light (*jyotis*) possesses the nature of non-food (*ananna*). In the rainwater, lightning—

From the observation of bodily heat and the observation of perspiration, it follows that water and light are mutually established in one another; for this very reason, they are not distinct from each other. He enjoins their meditation with the words, "He who... In the preceding section, it was stated that food obtained at the time of eating should not be rejected on account of an incorrect perception regarding its nature. Here, however, [it is taught] that one should have plenty [of food] to give to guests.
The accomplishment [of the meditation] is thus described. Furthermore, he shows another object of worship: "The earth indeed...
Because it exists in the middle of the space that extends both below and above, the earth has the nature of food (*anna*), and space has the nature of being the eater (*anāda*).
Since space is perceived above the bewildered person, there is a relationship of container and contained between the two. Vi-...

However, from the perspective of the *cāradṛṣṭi* (the view of movement), space (*ākāśa*) is the support; one should contemplate the mutual non-separateness of these two. He prescribes the meditation: "He who [knows] this food... One should not turn away anyone who has come to one's own house for the purpose of lodging. In this context, he incidentally prescribes the means for fulfilling the aforementioned vow: "Therefore... because [one should give] to the guest...

When lodging has been provided, food must also be given; otherwise, there is the hearing of scriptural warnings regarding transgression (*pratyavāya*). Thus, for that person of small intellect in whose house a Brahmin dwells without eating, the traditional texts (*āmnāya*) declare the loss of all fruits—both of this world and the next—for the non-giver. Therefore, among the four means of livelihood—sacrificing for others, teaching, and receiving gifts—one should give food by whichever means possible.

One should procure an abundance of food by means of this [rite]. Here, he shows the practice of the learned (*śiṣṭācāra*): "We have prepared food for him. When someone comes to one's house, those who possess knowledge say of that person who has arrived, "We have prepared food for him," meaning they are well-provided with food; they do not, however, refuse it. He shows a specific reward for the excellence of the gift in order to achieve a superior result from the preparation of abundant food: "e-"
"Or that [is it]" means: this very food which has been prepared becomes "cooked from the mouth. That is to say, by means of a primary location—a specific sacred site or *tīrtha*;

at a primary time—such as a solar transit (*saṃkrānti*) or the new moon; for a primary guest—one devoted to the Vedas, the scriptures, their study, and their practice; by a primary mode of conduct—consisting of faith, prostration, hospitality, and so forth; and with a primary gift...
The meaning is that it is given with a pure (sāttvika) disposition. This is the gift of the sattvic nature described by the Blessed One:
"That gift which is given with the thought 'it ought to be given,' to one who does not return the favor, at the proper place and time, and to a worthy recipient—that gift is remembered as sāttvika.
The man who thus knows this mode of sāttvika giving and, having known it, practices it—for him, in another birth...

This [gift] is accomplished precisely according to the primary order. The two statements, "from the middle" and "from the end," are to be explained as referring to gifts of the *rājasa* and *tāmasa* types respectively; and this has been shown by the Blessed One: "That which is given for the sake of a return favor, or again with a view toward a fruit, and which is given with distress—that is declared to be *rājasa*. That gift which is given at an improper place and time, and to unworthy recipients..."

"That which is offered without respect and with contempt is declared to be tāmasa. The statement regarding the fruit should also be explained in accordance with that. In the context of the vows (*vrata*) that constitute the limbs of meditation (*upāsanā*), a specific fruit corresponding to the act of giving has been stated. Now, he prescribes certain meditations themselves, beginning with "In security," and so forth. As for the symbol (*pratīka*) consisting of the organ of speech—

Thus it is said: one should meditate upon that Brahman as abiding in the form of *kṣema* (security). *Kṣema* means protection. Brahman abides in the form of *yoga* and *kṣema* respectively within the two symbols of the out-breath (*prāṇa*) and the in-breath (*apāna*), which are the exhalation and inhalation.
*Yoga* is the acquisition of wealth and such things not yet obtained; its preservation is *kṣema*. By the word "action" (*karman*), [the text refers to] sacrifice, battle, and so forth.

Divine activities are intended here. For a Brāhmaṇa, there is the activity of performing fire-sacrifices (*homa*) and so forth in the hands; for a Kṣatriya, there is the activity of fighting and so forth in the hands. This should be understood accordingly in other cases as well. In this form of action, Brahman resides in the two hands as its instruments; it resides in the two feet in the form of movement; and [it resides] in the form of the evacuation of waste.

"Situated at the anus. Thus have been described the human *samājñās*—meditations (*upāsanā*) performed upon the limbs of the human body, beginning with "peace" (*kṣema*) as speech and ending with "liberation" (*vimukti*) as the anus. The term *samājñā* refers to actions that are properly (*samyak*) accomplished all around (*samantāt*). Because of the use of the plural number, each one is to be meditated upon separately.

The *Vidyāraṇya-viracita* states that which is understood from the *Bhṛguvallī*. It prescribes other forms of meditation (*upāsanā*) beginning with "Now, the goddesses... and so forth, and then "Now, humans... and so forth.

After the exposition of the five meditations (*pañcopāsti*) has been understood, the meditations pertaining to the bodies of the Goddess and the God are now described. Brahman exists in the form of satisfaction within the deity presiding over rain; it exists in the form of strength within the deity presiding over lightning; it exists in the form of glory within the deities of cattle; and [it exists] in the form of light within the deities of the constellations.
It exists in the form of the three: procreation (*prajāti*) is the begetting of a son; immortality (*amṛta*) is sport with a woman;

and bliss (*ānanda*) is the activity consisting of the union with the limbs of another, produced by the secret organ. By these three, it resides in the deity presiding over the generative organ (*upastha*). The status of this triad as the object of the secret organ is [established] in the Kau...

The followers of the Pītakas (Yajurvedins) maintain that by mounting the organ of generation (*upastha*) with wisdom (*prajñā*), one attains bliss (*ānanda*), delight (*rati*), and procreation (*prajāti*).

Brahman is established within the deity who presides over space (*ākāśa*) in the form of all that exists—the world consisting of the primary elements (*bhūta*) and their derivatives (*bhautika*). In these meditations, such as "He is secure in speech," and so forth, [the result] is according to the specific meditation.

The fruit [of meditation] is to be observed; for there is a scriptural text stating, "In whatever way one meditates upon it, that very thing one becomes. With this very meaning of the scripture in mind, he cites certain meditations together with their fruits, beginning with the words "That as its support," and so forth. When one meditates upon that Brahman as the *pratiṣṭhā*—the cause of stability—one becomes possessed of the causes for the maintenance of life, such as food, clothing, and the like. Great...

Endowed with the quality of greatness (*mahattva*); "great" (*mahān*) means prosperous through wealth and other such means. *Manas* is endowed with the power of reflection (*manana*); *mānavaḥ* is one who possesses the power of reflection. *Namaḥ* is bowing; it is endowed with the act of bowing, which is subjugation. For this worshipper (*asmā upāsakāya*), desires (*kāmāḥ*) bow down—that is, they become subject to his own control. *Brahma* is the Veda; *brahmavān* is one who has the Veda under his own control. Of Brahman...

The *parimara* of a Brahmin is the death of those who surround him and harbor hatred toward him. For the practitioner who surrounds this [fire], the enemies who surround him and harbor hatred die. Even those adversaries (*bhrātṛvya*) who do not harbor hatred, yet are of such a nature as enemies, likewise die all around. By means of the aforementioned meditations—

This demonstrates both that which is to be experienced and that which is the fruit of experience for one who has attained one-pointedness of mind either in this birth or in another birth. This is shown by the passage beginning with "He who... and so forth. Although the meaning of the section starting from "He who is this person" up to "having approached this self consisting of bliss" was already stated in the preceding section, here it is presented as various forms of meditation—

In order to demonstrate that this austerity, consisting of one-pointedness of mind (*cittaikāgrya*), culminates in the supreme goal of human life (*paramapuruṣārtha*), it is stated once again: because bliss (*ānanda*)— which is described as the "tail" (*puccha*) in the sheath consisting of bliss (*ānandamaya-kośa*) and which is an undivided single essence— is realized as the Self (*ātman*), [there is no longer any desire] for the four sheaths beginning with "dear" (*priya*) and "joy" (*moda*), nor for the sheaths preceding them.

Since he has completely abandoned the delusion of identifying with all the causes of bondage as being his own self, he is indeed liberated. Nevertheless, he is designated by people as "living" because the body, senses, and so forth are seen by them. Therefore, because of living from the perspective of the world and being liberated from his own perspective, he is a *jīvanmukta*. And he, as previously described—
Having entered the self in this manner, he remains like any other man until the fall of the body. What does he do?
Having become one who takes his desires as food and one whose form is at will, he moves through these worlds in succession, eating food according to his desire—that is, by his own will.

Transcending the scriptural injunctions and prohibitions that establish the distinction between what may and may not be eaten, he eats in the house of anyone whatsoever. Thus it is heard in scripture: "Subsisting on alms from all castes, with his stomach as his bowl. [In this state] there is no deficiency.

And because it has been stated, "What rule or what prohibition can there be for one who wanders thus? [he is called] *kāmarūpī*, meaning one whose form or attire (*veṣadhāraṇa*) is according to his will (*kāmataḥ*); for the scripture says, "His emblems are unmanifest and his conduct is unmanifest.
These worlds are specific regions of the earth such as Kāśī, Dvāravatī, and so forth; he wanders through them in succession, but does not have a fixed home anywhere.

Having made [it so], he dwells there; for the scripture says, "He is one who dwells without a home and is without effort. Or else, according to the manner stated in the teaching known as the *Upadeśasāhasrī*: "All living beings from Brahmā down to the stationary objects are remembered as my city"—in this way, when the certainty of being the Self of all has been established, whatever worlds those persons traverse, all that is their own.

The meaning is that he remains content with this alone. Furthermore, what is he doing? "Singing this *sāman*," that is, the mantra consisting of song which will be described immediately hereafter; or rather, the mantra that establishes equality, because of the Vedic text: "It is *sāman* because it is equal (*sama*) to everything. It is also heard in scripture that it is *sāman* because it is always equal to all.

Singing—that is, performing the chant according to the sequence prescribed in the Sāmaveda—has as its fruit the manifestation of one's own nature as the Self of all to the disciples. Now, he shows the essential form of the *sāman* with the words "hā 3 vu hā 3," and so forth. Here, when the syllables of the word *aho*, which denotes wonder, undergo a modification for the sake of chanting, the word *hāvu* is produced.

The repetition three times is for the purpose of highlighting the excellence [of this realization]. The meaning is that it is a matter of great wonder that I, who previously existed only within my own body, have attained the nature of Brahman, which is the Self of all, through mere knowledge obtained by the grace of the Guru and the scriptures.
By the words "I am food," etc., the experience of being the Self of all is made manifest. Whatever food there is—three...

All that which is produced from barley, wheat, and so forth, I alone am in that food; for while the portion consisting of name and form is unreal, the portion that is the substratum—whose nature is Being-Consciousness-Bliss—is my own essential self. This should likewise be understood regarding the verses concerning food and fame. The conscious eater of food consists of Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, cows, horses, and so on. Fame—

*Saṃgha* means either a multitude or a verse (*padya*). One who forms—that is, brings about—a *saṃgha* in the form of an army and so forth is a "verse-maker" (*ślokakṛt*), such as a king or similar figure. Alternatively, one who composes verses in works such as poetry is a "verse-maker," namely a learned man (*vidvān*). Here, the distributive repetition (*vīpsā*) within the sentence is for the purpose of including all those who eat food and all those who possess knowledge. Even therein, this consists of the nature of all things—

It is not necessary [to state it once]; the threefold repetition is for the purpose of generating confidence, as in the case of truth (*satya*). And its status as a cause for confidence is well-known in both the world and the Veda. "I swear to you three times," etc., is the worldly renown; "for the gods are three-truth" (*triṣatyā hi devāḥ*) is the Vedic renown. "The first-born of *ṛta*, of the *ṛta* Brahman"—the first-born...

There exists the Being, Hiraṇyagarbha, because He is the substratum for the conceptualization of Hiraṇyagarbha. "I existed even before the gods," such as Indra and the others, because Indra and the rest were created by His Self. And that creation is recited in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad: "He created the Kṣatra, which is the form of excellence, those who are these Kṣatriyas among the gods, such as Indra..."

"Rudra is Soma," and so forth. I am the support of immortality—that is, of liberation—like the nave of a wheel. Just as the nave of a chariot wheel is the support for the spokes and the rim, so too am I the support of liberation, because of the scriptural teaching that "the knower of the Self transcends sorrow" through the knowledge of the Self. The teacher who [knows] me in this way...

He who gives himself—that is, imparts himself—to his disciples as instruction, he alone is the teacher; having thus awakened them to the state of the Supreme Self (paramātmatā) in the manner described, he protects the disciples. Alternatively, that noble person who gives me—who am of the nature of food—to the Brāhmaṇas and others, that very man who is the giver of food becomes [the recipient] in the form of a Brāhmaṇa or similar caste.
It protects in the manner that will be explained. Through such passages as "From food, life-breaths arise," the succession of effects produced by food is taught;
and in the *Yājñika Upaniṣad*, it will be stated: "Therefore, one who gives food gives all these.
The meaning is that I alone am the one to be known in the form of the Supreme Self, and I am the very food to be given. I am the deity in the form of food.
I devour that man who, devoid of restraint, eats food by himself alone, being possessed by greed and excessively miserly;

the meaning is that I destroy him by casting him into the Mahāraurava and other hells. This is according to the Vedic revelation: "He becomes one whose nature is solely sin, eating solely [for himself]," and the Smṛti: "But those sinful ones eat their own filth who cook for their own sake. I am the universe, the all.

I have overcome the world—that is, the entire collection of worlds; being myself in the form of the Lord, I have withdrawn [all things] at the time of dissolution. The word *suvaḥ* indicates the Sun situated in heaven. The particle *na* has the sense of comparison:
just as the Sun is itself of the nature of light, independent of any other light, even so am I [the nature of the eye and other senses].

"I am indeed the light of consciousness, free from all dependence. Anticipating the question—"Of whom is this experience of being the Self of all, as propounded by this Sāman, the fruit?"—he says: "He who thus... This is the fruit for that person who, through the stages beginning with the *annamaya*, directly realizes the Self that is the undivided single essence, described by the statement "Brahman is the tail [the support]. Even though...

"He who knows thus"—the knower who shares in the fruit has already been indicated; nevertheless, this teaching is for the sake of a twofold restriction: that the fruit belongs only to the knower and not to the non-knower, and that for the knower, the fruit necessarily comes to pass. Thus, "he who knows thus" is mentioned again. He concludes the meaning of the section with the word "iti. Beginning from "Bhṛgu Vāruṇi... and so forth, [it continues] until "ya... (he who...).

That very knowledge which has been set forth by the textual portion ending with the words "one should know thus" (evaṃ veda) is referred to by the word "this" (iyam). And that [knowledge] is denoted by the term "Upaniṣad. The etymological derivation of that term has already been explained in detail previously. The completion of this Upaniṣad is the intended sense of the remaining part of the sentence.
May Vidyātīrtha Maheśvara, dispelling the darkness of the heart by illuminating the meaning of the Vedas, bestow the four goals of human life.

Thus ends the third Anuvāka, titled "The Bhṛgu Valī," in the Vāruṇī Upaniṣad of the Yajur Āraṇyaka, within the *Vedārthaprakāśa* composed by the venerable Sāyaṇācārya, under the supreme lordship of Mādhava Vidyāraṇya, who bears the yoke of the empire of the glorious Śrīkaṇṭha. || 3 ||
